\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Preface}}\label{Preface}
\logpage{[ 1, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X874E1D45845007FE}{}
{
  \index{About GAP manual@About \textsf{GAP} manual} Welcome to \textsf{GAP}. This is one of the manuals documenting the core part of \textsf{GAP}, the others being the \emph{\textsf{GAP} Tutorial}  and \emph{HPC\texttt{\symbol{45}}GAP Reference Manual}.  

 There is also a document \texttt{CHANGES.md} on the changes from earlier versions in the root directory. This preface
serves not only to introduce ``The \textsf{GAP} Reference Manual'', but also as an introduction to the whole system. 

 \textsf{GAP} stands for \emph{Groups, Algorithms and Programming}. The name was chosen to reflect the original aim of the system, which is
introduced in this reference manual. Since that choice, the system has become
somewhat broader, and you will also find information about algorithms and
programming for other algebraic structures, such as semigroups and algebras. 

 This manual, the \emph{\textsf{GAP} Reference Manual} contains the official definitions of \textsf{GAP} functions. It should contain all the information needed to use \textsf{GAP}, and is not intended to be read
cover\texttt{\symbol{45}}to\texttt{\symbol{45}}cover. 

 To get started a new user may first look at parts of the \emph{\textsf{GAP} Tutorial}. 

 A lot of the functionality of the system and a number of contributed
extensions are provided as ``\textsf{GAP} packages'' which are developed independently of the core part of \textsf{GAP} and can be loaded into a \textsf{GAP} session. Each package comes with a its own manual which is also available
through the \textsf{GAP} help system. 

 This manual is divided into chapters, sections and subsections.
Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{The Help System} describes the \emph{help system}, which provides access to all the manuals from a running \textsf{GAP} session. Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Running GAP} gives technical advice for \emph{running} \textsf{GAP}. Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{The Programming Language} introduces the \textsf{GAP} language, and the next chapters deal with the \emph{environment} provided by \textsf{GAP} for the user. These are followed by the main bulk of chapters which are
devoted to the various mathematical structures that \textsf{GAP} can handle. 

 Subsequent sections of this preface explain the structure of the system and
provide copyright and licensing information. 

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{The \textsf{GAP} System}}\label{The GAP System}
\logpage{[ 1, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X863F306C7D32F4B0}{}
{
            \textsf{GAP} is a \emph{free}, \emph{open} and \emph{extensible} software package for computation in discrete abstract algebra. The terms ``free'' and ``open'' describe the conditions under which the system is distributed
\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}} in brief, it is \emph{free of charge} (except possibly for the immediate costs of delivering it to you), you are \emph{free to pass it on} within certain limits, and all of the workings of the system are \emph{open for you to examine and change}. Details of these conditions can be found in Section  (\textbf{Reference: Copyright and License}). 

 The system is ``extensible'' in that you can write your own programs in the \textsf{GAP} language, and use them in just the same way as the programs which form part of
the system (the ``library''). Indeed, we actively support the contribution, refereeing and distribution
of extensions to the system, in the form of ``\textsf{GAP} packages''. Further details of this can be found in Chapter  (\textbf{Reference: Using and Developing GAP Packages}), and on our website. 

 Development of \textsf{GAP} began at Lehrstuhl D f{\"u}r Mathematik, RWTH\texttt{\symbol{45}}Aachen, under
the leadership of Joachim Neub{\"u}ser in 1985. Version 2.4 was released in
1988 and version 3.1 in 1992. In 1997 coordination of \textsf{GAP} development, now very much an international effort, was transferred to St
Andrews. A complete internal redesign and almost complete rewrite of the
system was completed over the following years and version 4.1 was released in
July 1999. A sign of the further internationalization of the project was the \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4.4 release in 2004, which has been coordinated from Colorado
State University, Fort Collins. 

 More information on the motivation and development of \textsf{GAP} to date, can be found on our website in a section entitled ``Some History of \textsf{GAP}'': \href{https://www.gap-system.org/about/history/} {\texttt{https://www.gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system.org/about/history/}}. 

 For those readers who have used an earlier version of \textsf{GAP}, an overview of the changes from \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4.4 and a brief summary of changes from earlier versions is
given in \texttt{CHANGES.md} file in the main directory. 

 The system that you are getting now consists of a ``core system'' and a number of packages. The core system consists of four main parts. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item  A \emph{kernel}, written in C, which provides the user with 
\begin{itemize}
\item  automatic dynamic storage management, which the user needn't bother about when
programming; 
\item  a set of time\texttt{\symbol{45}}critical basic functions, e.g. ``arithmetic'', operations for integers, finite fields, permutations and words, as well as
natural operations for lists and records; 
\item  an interpreter for the \textsf{GAP} language, an untyped imperative programming language with functions as first
class objects and some extra built\texttt{\symbol{45}}in data types such as
permutations and finite field elements. The language supports a form of
object\texttt{\symbol{45}}oriented programming, similar to that supported by
languages like C++ and Java but with some important differences. 
\item  a small set of system functions allowing the \textsf{GAP} programmer to handle files and execute external programs in a uniform way,
regardless of the particular operating system in use. 
\item  a set of programming tools for testing, debugging, and timing algorithms. 
\item  a ``read\texttt{\symbol{45}}eval\texttt{\symbol{45}}print loop'' (REPL) user interface. 
\end{itemize}
 
\item  A much larger \emph{library of \textsf{GAP} functions} that implement algebraic and other algorithms. Since this is written entirely
in the \textsf{GAP} language, the \textsf{GAP} language is both the main implementation language and the user language of the
system. Therefore a user can, as easily as the original programmers,
investigate and vary algorithms of the library and add new ones to it, first
for their own use and eventually for the benefit of all \textsf{GAP} users. 
\item  A \emph{library of group theoretical data} which contains various libraries of groups, including the library of small
groups (containing all groups of order at most 2000, except those of order
1024) and others. Large libraries of ordinary and Brauer character tables and
Tables of Marks are included as packages. 
\item  The \emph{documentation}. This is available as on\texttt{\symbol{45}}line help, as printable files in
PDF format and as HTML for viewing with a web browser. 
\end{enumerate}
 

 Also included with the core system are some test files and a few small
utilities which we hope you will find useful. 

 \textsf{GAP} \emph{packages} are self\texttt{\symbol{45}}contained extensions to the core system. A package
contains \textsf{GAP} code and its own documentation and may also contain data files or external
programs to which the \textsf{GAP} code provides an interface. These packages may be loaded into \textsf{GAP} using the \texttt{LoadPackage} (\textbf{Reference: LoadPackage}) command, and both the package and its documentation are then available just as
if they were parts of the core system. Some packages may be loaded
automatically, when \textsf{GAP} is started, if they are present. Some packages, because they depend on
external programs, may only be available on the operating systems where those
programs are available (usually UNIX). You should note that, while the
packages included with this release are the most recent versions ready for
release at this time, new packages and new versions may be released at any
time and can be easily installed in your copy of \textsf{GAP}. 

  With \textsf{GAP} there are two packages (the library of ordinary and Brauer character tables,
and the library of tables of marks) which contain functionality developed from
parts of the \textsf{GAP} core system. These have been moved into packages for ease of maintenance and
to allow new versions to be released independently of new releases of the core
system. The library of small groups should also be regarded as a package,
although it does not currently use the standard package mechanism. Other
packages contain functionality which has never been part of the core system,
and may extend it substantially, implementing specific algorithms to enhance
its capabilities, providing data libraries, interfaces to other computer
algebra systems and data sources such as the electronic version of the Atlas
of Finite Group Representations; therefore, installation and usage of packages
is recommended. 

 Further details about \textsf{GAP} packages can be found in chapter  (\textbf{Reference: Using and Developing GAP Packages}), and on the \textsf{GAP} website at \href{https://www.gap-system.org/packages/authors/} {\texttt{https://www.gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system.org/packages/authors/}}.    }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Authors and Maintainers}}\label{Authors and Maintainers}
\logpage{[ 1, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X877A62A1781C2147}{}
{
  \textsf{GAP} is the work of very many people, some of whom still maintain parts of the
system. A complete list of authors can be found at \href{https://github.com/gap-system/gap/blob/master/COPYRIGHT} {\texttt{https://github.com/gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system/gap/blob/master/COPYRIGHT}}. All \textsf{GAP} packages have their own authors and maintainers. It should however be noted
that some packages provide interfaces between \textsf{GAP} and an external program, a copy of which is included for convenience, and
that, in these cases, we do not claim that the package authors or maintainers
wrote, or maintain, this external program. Similarly, the system and some
packages include large data libraries that may have been computed by many
people. We try to make clear in each case what credit is attributable to whom. 

 We have, for some time, operated a refereeing system for contributed packages,
both to ensure the quality of the software we distribute, and to provide
recognition for the authors. We now consider this to be a refereeing system
for modules, and we would note, in particular that, although it does not use
the standard package interface, the library of small groups has been refereed
and accepted on exactly the same basis as the accepted packages.  

 We also include with this distribution a number of packages which have not
(yet) gone through our refereeing process. Some may be accepted in the future,
in other cases the authors have chosen not to submit them. More information
can be found on our website \href{https://www.gap-system.org} {\texttt{https://www.gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system.org}}. 

 }

\logpage{[ 1, 3, 0 ]}

\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{The Help System}}\label{The Help System}
\logpage{[ 2, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8755A2C67B197C63}{}
{
  This chapter describes the \textsf{GAP} help system. The help system lets you read the documentation interactively.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Invoking the Help}}\label{Invoking the Help}
\logpage{[ 2, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7E2C53D2844DD8C3}{}
{
  The basic command to read \textsf{GAP}'s documentation from within a \textsf{GAP} session is as follows. 

 \index{getting help} \texttt{?[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape book}}:][?]\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape topic}}} 

 For an explanation and some examples see{\nobreakspace} (\textbf{Tutorial: Help}). 

 Note that the first question mark must appear in the \emph{first position} after the \texttt{gap{\textgreater} } prompt. The search strings \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape book}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape topic}} are normalized in a certain way (see the end of this section for details)
before the search starts. This makes the search case insensitive and there can
be arbitrary white space after the first question mark. 

 When there are several manual sections that match the query a numbered list of
topics is displayed. These matches can be accessed with \texttt{?\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape number}}}. 

 There are some further specially handled commands which start with a question
mark. They are explained in Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Browsing through the Sections}. 

 By default \textsf{GAP} shows the help sections as text in the terminal (window), page by page if the
shown text does not fit on the screen. But there are several other choices to
read (other formats of) the documents: via a viewer for \texttt{pdf} files or via a web browser. This is explained below in Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Changing the Help Viewer}. 

 \emph{Details of the string normalization process} 

 Here is a precise description how the search strings \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape book}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape topic}} are normalized before a search starts: backslashes and double or single quotes
are removed, parentheses and braces are substituted by blanks,
non\texttt{\symbol{45}}ASCII characters are considered as
ISO\texttt{\symbol{45}}latin1 characters and the accented letters are
substituted by their non\texttt{\symbol{45}}accented counterpart. Finally
white space is normalized. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Browsing through the Sections}}\label{Browsing through the Sections}
\logpage{[ 2, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7BE8068878B7D7D1}{}
{
  Help books for \textsf{GAP} are organized in chapters, sections, and subsections. There are a few special
commands starting with a question mark (in the first position after the \texttt{gap{\textgreater} } prompt) which allow browsing a book section or chapter wise. 

 \index{browsing forward} \texttt{?{\textgreater}} 

 \index{browsing backwards} \texttt{?{\textless}} 

 The two help commands \texttt{?{\textless}} and \texttt{?{\textgreater}} allow one to browse through a whole help book. \texttt{?{\textless}} displays the section or subsection preceding the previously shown
(sub)section, and \texttt{?{\textgreater}} takes you to the section or subsection following the previously shown one. 

 \index{browsing forward one chapter} \texttt{?{\textgreater}{\textgreater}} 

 \index{browsing backwards one chapter} \texttt{?{\textless}{\textless}} 

 \texttt{?{\textless}{\textless}} takes you back to the beginning of the current chapter. If you are already at
the start of a chapter \texttt{?{\textless}{\textless}} takes you to the beginning of the previous chapter. \texttt{?{\textgreater}{\textgreater}} takes you to the beginning of the next chapter. 

 \index{browsing the previous section browsed} \texttt{?\texttt{\symbol{45}}} 

 \index{browsing the next section browsed} \texttt{?+} 

 \textsf{GAP} remembers the last few sections that you have read. \texttt{?\texttt{\symbol{45}}} takes you to the one that you have read before the current one, and displays
it again. Further applications of \texttt{?\texttt{\symbol{45}}} take you further back in this history. \texttt{?+} reverses this process, i.e., it takes you back to the section that you have
read after the current one. It is important to note that \texttt{?\texttt{\symbol{45}}} and \texttt{?+} do not alter the history like the other help commands. 

 \index{list of available books} \texttt{?books} 

 This command shows a list of the books which are currently known to the help
system. For each book there is a short name which is used with the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape book}} part of the basic help query and there is a long name which hopefully tells
you what this book is about. 

 A short name which ends in \texttt{(not loaded)} refers to a \textsf{GAP} package whose documentation is loaded but which needs a call of \texttt{LoadPackage} (\ref{LoadPackage}) before you can use the described functions. 

 \index{table of sections for help books} \texttt{?[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape book}}:]sections} 

 \index{table of chapters for help books} \texttt{?[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape book}}:][chapters]} 

 These commands show tables of contents for all available, respectively the
matching books. For some books these commands show the same, namely the whole
table of contents. 

 \index{redisplay a help section} \texttt{?} 

 \index{redisplay with next help viewer} \texttt{?\&} 

 These commands redisplay the last shown help section. In the form \texttt{?\&} the next preferred help viewer is used for the display (provided one has
chosen several viewers), see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{SetHelpViewer} (\ref{SetHelpViewer}) below. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Changing the Help Viewer}}\label{Changing the Help Viewer}
\logpage{[ 2, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X863FF9087EDA8DF9}{}
{
  \index{document formats (text, dvi, ps, pdf, HTML)} Books of the \textsf{GAP} help system or package manuals can be available in several formats. Currently
the following formats occur (not all of them may be available for all books): 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{text}]  This is used for display in the terminal window in which \textsf{GAP} is running. Complicated mathematical expressions may not be easy to read in
this format. 
\item[{pdf}]  Adobe's \texttt{pdf} format. Can be used for printing and onscreen reading on most current systems
(with freely available software). Some manual books contain hyperlinks in this
format. 
\item[{HTML}]  The format of web pages. Can be used with any web browser. There may be
hyperlink information available which allows a convenient browsing through the
book via cross\texttt{\symbol{45}}references. This format has the problem that
complicated formulae may be not be easy to read since there is no syntax for
formulae in HTML. (Some older manual books use special symbol fonts for
formulae and need a particular configuration of the web browser for correct
display. Some manuals may use technology for quite sophisticated formula
display.) 
\end{description}
 

 Depending on your operating system and available additional software you can
use several of these formats with \textsf{GAP}'s help system. This is configured with the following command. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetHelpViewer}}
\logpage{[ 2, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87C1BFB2826488B0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetHelpViewer({\mdseries\slshape viewer1, viewer2, ...})\index{SetHelpViewer@\texttt{SetHelpViewer}}
\label{SetHelpViewer}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This command takes an arbitrary number of arguments which must be strings
describing a viewer. The recognized viewers are explained below. A call with
no arguments shows the current setting. 

 The first given arguments are those with higher priority. So, if a help
section is available in the format needed by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape viewer1}}, this viewer is used. If not, availability of the format for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape viewer2}} is checked and so on. Recall that the command \texttt{?\&} displays the last seen section again but with the next possible viewer in your
list, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Browsing through the Sections}. 

 The viewer \texttt{"screen"} (see below) is always silently appended since we assume that each help book is
available in text format. 

 If you want to change the default setting you can use a call of \texttt{SetUserPreference( "HelpViewers", [ ... ] );} (the list in the second argument containing the viewers you want) in your \texttt{gap.ini} file (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{sect:gap.ini}). 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{"screen"}}]  This is the default setting. The help is shown in text format using the \texttt{Pager} (\ref{Pager}) command. Hint: Text versions of manuals are formatted assuming that your
terminal displays at least 80 characters per line, if this is not the case
some sections may look very bad. We suggest to use a terminal in \texttt{UTF\texttt{\symbol{45}}8} encoding with a fixed width font (this is the default on most modern
Linux/Windows/Mac systems anyway). Terminals in \texttt{ISO\texttt{\symbol{45}}8859\texttt{\symbol{45}}X} encoding will also work reasonably well (so far, since we do not yet use many
special characters which such terminals could not display). 
\item[{\texttt{"firefox"}, \texttt{"chrome"}, \texttt{"mozilla"}, \texttt{"netscape"}, \texttt{"konqueror"}}]  If a book is available in HTML format this is shown using the corresponding
web browser. How well this works, for example by using a running instance of
this browser, depends on your particular start script of this browser. (Note,
that for some old books the browser must be configured to use symbol fonts.) 
\item[{\texttt{"browser"}}]  (for MS Windows) If a book is available in HTML format, it will be opened
using the Windows default application (typically, a web browser). 
\item[{\texttt{"links2"}, \texttt{"w3m"}, \texttt{"lynx"}}]  If a book is available in HTML format this is shown using the text based \texttt{"links2"} (in graphics mode), \texttt{w3m} or \texttt{lynx} web browser, respectively, inside the terminal running \textsf{GAP}. (Formulae in some older books which use symbol fonts may be unreadable.) 
\item[{\texttt{"mac default browser"}, \texttt{"browser"}, \texttt{"safari"}, \texttt{"firefox"}}]  (for macOS) If a book is available in HTML format this is shown in a web
browser. The options \texttt{"safari"} and \texttt{"firefox"} use the corresponding browsers. The other two options use the program default
browser (which can be set in Safari's preferences, in the "General" tab). 
\item[{\texttt{"xpdf"}}]  (on X window systems) If a book is available in pdf format it is shown with
the onscreen viewer program \texttt{xpdf} (which must be installed on your system). This is a nice program, once it is
running it is reused by \textsf{GAP} for the next displays of help sections. 
\item[{\texttt{"acroread"}}]  If a book is available in pdf format it is shown with the onscreen viewer
program \texttt{acroread} (which must be available on your system). This program does not allow remote
commands or startup with a given page. Therefore the page numbers you have to
visit are just printed on the screen. When you are looking at several sections
of the same book, this viewer assumes that the \texttt{acroread} window still exists. When you go to another book a new acroread window is
launched. 
\item[{\texttt{"pdf viewer"}, \texttt{"skim"}, \texttt{"preview"}, \texttt{"adobe reader"}}]  (for macOS) If a book is available in pdf format this is shown in a pdf
viewer. The options \texttt{"skim"}, \texttt{"preview"} and \texttt{"adobe reader"} use the corresponding viewers. The other two options use the pdf viewer which
you have chosen to open pdf files from the Finder. Note that only \texttt{"Skim"} seems to be capable to open a pdf file on a given page. For the other help
viewers, the page numbers where the information can be found will just be
printed on the screen. None of the help viewers seems to be capable of opening
a pdf at a given named destination (i. e., jump to precisely the place where
the information can be found). The pdf viewer \texttt{"Skim"} is open source software, it can be downloaded from \texttt{https://skim\texttt{\symbol{45}}app.sourceforge.io/}. 
\item[{\texttt{"less"} or \texttt{"more"}}]  This is the same as \texttt{"screen"} but additionally the user preferences \texttt{"Pager"} and \texttt{"PagerOptions"} are set, see the section{\nobreakspace}\ref{The Pager Command} for more details. 
\end{description}
 

 Please, send ideas for further viewer commands to \href{mailto://support@gap-system.org} {\texttt{support@gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system.org}}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{The Pager Command}}\label{The Pager Command}
\logpage{[ 2, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X84AFFC817B282359}{}
{
  \textsf{GAP} contains a builtin pager which shows a text string which does not fit on the
screen page by page. Its functionality is very rudimentary and
self\texttt{\symbol{45}}explaining. This is because (at least under UNIX)
there are powerful external standard programs which do this job. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Pager}}
\logpage{[ 2, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7ED03E41792C3840}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Pager({\mdseries\slshape lines})\index{Pager@\texttt{Pager}}
\label{Pager}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function can be used to display a text on screen using a pager, i.e., the
text is shown page by page. 

 There is a default builtin pager in \textsf{GAP} which has very limited capabilities but should work on any system. 

 At least on a UNIX system one should use an external pager program like \texttt{less} or \texttt{more}. \textsf{GAP} assumes that this program has command line options \texttt{+nr} and \texttt{+/str} which start the display of the text with line number \texttt{nr} or at the line with the first occurrence of the string \texttt{str}. 

 Which pager is used can be controlled by setting the user preference \texttt{"Pager"}. The default value is \texttt{"builtin"} which means that the internal pager is used. 

 On UNIX systems you probably want to set the user preference \texttt{"Pager"} to the value \texttt{"less"} or \texttt{"more"}, you can do this for example in your \texttt{gap.ini} file (see \ref{sect:gap.ini}). In that case you can also tell \textsf{GAP} a list of standard options for the external pager, via the user preference \texttt{"PagerOptions"}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
    SetUserPreference( "Pager", "less" );
    SetUserPreference( "PagerOptions", ["-f","-r","-a","-i","-M","-j2"] );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape lines}} can have one of the following forms: 

 
\begin{enumerate}
\item  a string (i.e., lines are separated by newline characters) 
\item  a list of strings (without newline characters) which are interpreted as lines
of the text to be shown 
\item  a record with component \texttt{lines} as in 1. or 2. and optional further components 
\end{enumerate}
 

 In case{\nobreakspace}3. currently the following additional components are
used: 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{formatted}}]  can be \texttt{false} or \texttt{true}. If set to \texttt{true} the builtin pager tries to show the text exactly as it is given (avoiding \textsf{GAP}'s automatic line breaking), 
\item[{\texttt{start}}]  must be a positive integer or a string. An integer is interpreted as the
number of the first line shown by the pager, a string is interpreted as a
search string such that the first line containing this string is the first
line shown by the pager (in both cases, one may see the beginning of the text
via back scrolling), 
\item[{\texttt{exitAtEnd}}]  can be \texttt{false} or \texttt{true}. If set to \texttt{true} (the default), the builtin pager is terminated as soon as the end of the list
is shown; otherwise entering the \textsc{q} key is necessary in order to return from the pager. 
\end{description}
 

 The \texttt{Pager} command is used by \textsf{GAP}'s help system for displaying help sections in text format. But, of course, it
may be used for other purposes as well. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@s6 := SymmetricGroup(6);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@words := ["This", "is", "a", "very", "stupid", "example"];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l := List(s6, p-> Permuted(words, p));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Pager(List(l, a-> JoinStringsWithSeparator(a," ")));;|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

 }

                  
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Running GAP}}\label{Running GAP}
\logpage{[ 3, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79CCD3A6821E5A37}{}
{
  \index{options} This chapter contains information about the command line options for \textsf{GAP} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Command Line Options}), about some files in user specific \textsf{GAP} root directory (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{sect:gap.ini}) and about saving and loading a \textsf{GAP} workspace (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Saving and Loading a Workspace}).  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Command Line Options}}\label{Command Line Options}
\logpage{[ 3, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X782751D5858A6EAF}{}
{
  \index{features!under UNIX} \index{UNIX!features} \index{options!under UNIX} \index{UNIX!options} \index{GAPInfo.CommandLineOptions@\texttt{GAPInfo.CommandLineOptions}} When you start \textsf{GAP} from a command line or from a script you may specify a number of options on
the command\texttt{\symbol{45}}line to change the default behaviour of \textsf{GAP}. All these options start with a hyphen \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}}, followed by a single letter. Options must not be grouped, e.g., \texttt{gap \texttt{\symbol{45}}gq} is invalid, use \texttt{gap \texttt{\symbol{45}}g \texttt{\symbol{45}}q} instead. Some options require an argument, this must follow the option and
must be separated by whitespace, e.g., \texttt{gap \texttt{\symbol{45}}m 256m}, it is not correct to say \texttt{gap \texttt{\symbol{45}}m256m} instead. Certain boolean options (\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}b}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}q}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}e}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}A}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}D}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}M}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}T}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}X}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}Y}) toggle the current value so that \texttt{gap \texttt{\symbol{45}}b \texttt{\symbol{45}}b} is equivalent to \texttt{gap} and to \texttt{gap \texttt{\symbol{45}}b \texttt{\symbol{45}}q \texttt{\symbol{45}}b
\texttt{\symbol{45}}q} etc. 

 \textsf{GAP} for UNIX will distinguish between upper and lower case options. 

 As described in the \textsf{GAP} installation instructions (see the \texttt{INSTALL.md} file in the \textsf{GAP} root directory), usually you will not execute \textsf{GAP} directly. Instead you will call a (shell) script, with the name \texttt{gap}, which in turn executes \textsf{GAP}. This script sets some options which are necessary to make \textsf{GAP} work on your system. This means that the default settings mentioned below may
not be what you experience when you execute \textsf{GAP} on your system. 

 During a \textsf{GAP} session, one can find the current values of command line options in the record \texttt{GAPInfo.CommandLineOptions} (see \texttt{GAPInfo} (\ref{GAPInfo})), whose component names are the command line options (without the leading \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}}). 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\index{-A@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}A}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}A}}]  By default, some needed and suggested \textsf{GAP} packages (see \ref{Using and Developing GAP Packages}) are loaded, if present, into the \textsf{GAP} session when it starts. This option disables (actually toggles) the loading of
suggested packages, which can be useful for debugging or testing. The needed
packages (and their needed packages, and so on) are loaded in any case. 
\item[{\index{-b@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}b}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}b}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} to suppress the banner. That means that \textsf{GAP} immediately prints the prompt. This is useful when, after a while, you get
tired of the banner. This option can be repeated to enable the banner; each \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}b} toggles the state of banner display. 
\item[{\index{-c@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}c}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}c }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gapcode}}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} to execute the given \textsf{GAP} code as if it was entered into a temporary file which then is processed
together with the other files given to GAP (see the explanation at the end of
this list for further details on how filenames are processed). 
\item[{\index{-D@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}D}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}D}}]  The \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}D} option tells \textsf{GAP} to print short messages when it is reading files or loading modules. This
option may be repeated to toggle this behavior on and off. The message, 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  #I  READ_GAP_ROOT: loading 'lib/kernel.g' as GAP file
\end{Verbatim}
 

 tells you that \textsf{GAP} has started to read the library file \texttt{lib/kernel.g}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  #I  READ_GAP_ROOT: loading 'lib/kernel.g' statically
\end{Verbatim}
 

 tells you that \textsf{GAP} has used the compiled version of the library file \texttt{lib/kernel.g}. This compiled module was statically linked to the \textsf{GAP} kernel at the time the kernel was created. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  #I  READ_GAP_ROOT: loading 'lib/kernel.g' dynamically
\end{Verbatim}
 

 tells you that \textsf{GAP} has loaded the compiled version of the library file \texttt{lib/kernel.g}. This compiled module was dynamically loaded to the \textsf{GAP} kernel at runtime from a corresponding \texttt{.so} file. 

 Obviously, this is a debugging option and most users will not need it. 
\item[{\index{-E@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}E}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}E}}]  If your \textsf{GAP} installation uses the \texttt{readline} library for command line editing (see \ref{sec:readline}), this may be disabled by using \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}E} option. This option may be repeated to toggle this behavior on and off. If
your \textsf{GAP} installation does not use the \texttt{readline} library (you can check by \texttt{IsBound(GAPInfo.UseReadline);} if this is the case), this option will have no effect at all. 
\item[{\index{-e@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}e}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}e}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} not to quit when receiving a \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}D} on an empty input line (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{quit}). This option should not be used when the input is a file or pipe. This
option may be repeated to toggle this behavior on and off. 
\item[{\index{-f@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}f}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}f}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} to enable the line editing and history (see \ref{Line Editing}). 

 In general line editing will be enabled if the input is connected to a
terminal. There are rare circumstances, for example when using a remote
session with a corrupted telnet implementation, when this detection fails. Try
using \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}f} in this case to enable line editing. This option does not toggle; you must use \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}n} to disable line editing. 
\item[{\index{-g@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}g}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}g}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} to print a message every time a full garbage collection is performed. (This is
available only if the \texttt{GASMAN} garbage collector is used, see \ref{Garbage Collection}.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  #G  FULL 44580/2479kb live   57304/4392kb dead   734/4096kb free
\end{Verbatim}
 

 For example, this tells you that there are 44580 live objects that survived a
full garbage collection, that 57304 unused objects were reclaimed by it, and
that 734 kilobytes from a total allocated memory of 4096 kilobytes are
available afterwards. 
\item[{\index{-g -g@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}g \texttt{\symbol{45}}g}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}g \texttt{\symbol{45}}g}}]  If you give the option \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}g} twice, \textsf{GAP} prints a information message every time a partial or full garbage collection
is performed. (This is available only if the \texttt{GASMAN} garbage collector is used, see \ref{Garbage Collection}.) The message, 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  #G  PART 9405/961kb+live   7525/1324kb+dead   2541/4096kb free
\end{Verbatim}
 

 for example, tells you that 9405 objects survived the partial garbage
collection and 7525 objects were reclaimed, and that 2541 kilobytes from a
total allocated memory of 4096 kilobytes are available afterwards. 
\item[{\index{-h@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}h}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}h}}] 
\item[{\index{--help@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}help}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}help}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} to print a summary of all available options. \textsf{GAP} exits after printing the summary, all options coming after are ignored. 
\item[{\index{-K@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}K}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}K }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}}}] 
\item[{\index{--limitworkspace@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}limitworkspace}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}limitworkspace }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}}}]  is like the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}o} option. But while the latter actually allocates more memory if the system
allows it and then prints a warning inside a break loop the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}K} options tells \textsf{GAP} not even to try to allocate more memory. Instead \textsf{GAP} just exits with an appropriate message. The default is that this feature is
switched off. You have to set it explicitly when you want to enable it. 
\item[{\index{-L@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}L}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}L }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filename}}}]  The option \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}L} tells \textsf{GAP} to load a saved workspace. See section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Saving and Loading a Workspace}. (This is available only if the \texttt{GASMAN} garbage collector is used, see \ref{Garbage Collection}.) 
\item[{\index{-l@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}l}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}l }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}}}] 
\item[{\index{--roots@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}roots}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}roots }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}}}]  can be used to set or modify \textsf{GAP}'s list of root directories (see \ref{GAP Root Directories}). The default if no \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}l } option is given is the current directory \texttt{./}. This option can be used several times. Depending on the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r} option a further user specific path is prepended to the list of root
directories (the path in \texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot}). 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}} should be a list of directories separated by semicolons. No whitespace is
permitted before or after a semicolon. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}} does not start or end with a semicolon, then \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}} replaces the existing list of root directories. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}} starts with a semicolon, then \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}} is appended to the existing list of root directories. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}} ends with a semicolon and does not start with one, then the new list of root
directories is the concatenation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}} and the existing list of root directories. After \textsf{GAP} has completed its startup procedure and displays the prompt, the list of root
directories can be seen in the variable \texttt{GAPInfo.RootPaths}, see \texttt{GAPInfo} (\ref{GAPInfo}). 

 Usually this option is used inside a startup script to specify where \textsf{GAP} is installed on the system. The \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}l} option can also be used by individual users to tell \textsf{GAP} about privately installed modifications of the library, additional \textsf{GAP} packages and so on. Section \ref{GAP Root Directories} explains how several root paths can be used to do this. 

 \textsf{GAP} will attempt to read the file \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape root{\textunderscore}dir}}\texttt{/lib/init.g} during startup where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape root{\textunderscore}dir}} is one of the directories in its list of root directories. If \textsf{GAP} cannot find its \texttt{init.g} file it will print the following warning. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  gap: hmm, I cannot find 'lib/init.g' maybe use option '-l <gaproot>'?
\end{Verbatim}
 

 It is not possible to use \textsf{GAP} without the library files, so you must not ignore this warning. You should
leave \textsf{GAP} and start it again, specifying the correct root path using the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}l} option. 
\item[{\index{--packagedirs@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}packagedirs}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}packagedirs }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}}}]  can be used to add paths to \textsf{GAP}'s list of package directories (see \ref{GAP Package Directories}). The list always contains all subdirectories \texttt{pkg} in a \textsf{GAP} root directory. 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}} should be a list of directories separated by semicolons. No whitespace is
permitted before or after a semicolon, and the first and last character of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path{\textunderscore}list}} may not be a semicolon. After \textsf{GAP} has completed its startup procedure and displays the prompt, the list of
package directories can be seen in the variable \texttt{GAPInfo.PackageDirectories}, see \texttt{GAPInfo} (\ref{GAPInfo}). 

 Usually this option is used inside a startup script to specify where
additional \textsf{GAP} packages are located on the system. The \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}packagedirs} option can also be used by individual users to tell \textsf{GAP} about additional \textsf{GAP} packages, without the need to set up a complete root directory structure. 
\item[{\index{-M@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}M}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}M}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} not to check for, nor to use, compiled versions of library files. This option
may be repeated to toggle this behavior on and off. 
\item[{\index{-m@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}m}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}m }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}}}] 
\item[{\index{--minworkspace@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}minworkspace}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}minworkspace }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} to allocate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}} bytes at startup time. If the last character of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}} is \texttt{k} or \texttt{K} it is taken as kilobytes, if the last character is \texttt{m} or \texttt{M} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}} is taken as megabytes and if it is \texttt{g} or \texttt{G} it is taken as gigabytes. 

 This amount of memory should be large enough so that computations do not
require too many garbage collections. On the other hand, if \textsf{GAP} allocates more memory than is physically available, it will spend most of the
time paging. 
\item[{\index{-n@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}n}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}n}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} to disable the line editing and history (see \ref{Line Editing}). 

 You may want to do this if the command line editing is incompatible with
another program that is used to run \textsf{GAP}. For example if \textsf{GAP} is run from inside a GNU Emacs shell window, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}n} should be used since otherwise every input line will be echoed twice, once by
Emacs and once by \textsf{GAP}. This option does not toggle; you must use \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}f} to enable line editing. 
\item[{\index{-O@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}O}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}O}}]  disables loading obsolete variables (see Chapter \ref{Replaced and Removed Command Names}). This option is used mainly for testing purposes, for example in order to
make sure that a \textsf{GAP} package or one's own \textsf{GAP} code does not rely on the obsolete variables. 
\item[{\index{-o@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}o}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}o }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}}}] 
\item[{\index{--maxworkspace@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}maxworkspace}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}maxworkspace }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} to allocate at most \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}} bytes without asking. The option argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}} is specified as with the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}m} option. 

 If more than this amount is required during the \textsf{GAP} session, \textsf{GAP} prints an error message and enters a break loop. In that case you can enter \texttt{return;} which implicitly doubles the amount given with this option. 
\item[{\index{-q@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}q}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}q}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} to be quiet. This means that \textsf{GAP} displays neither the banner nor the prompt \texttt{gap{\textgreater}}. This is useful if you want to run \textsf{GAP} as a filter with input and output redirection and want to avoid the banner and
the prompts appearing in the output file. This option may be repeated to
disable quiet mode; each \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}q} toggles quiet mode. 
\item[{\index{-R@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}R}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}R}}]  The option \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}R} tells \textsf{GAP} not to load a saved workspace previously specified via the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}L} option. This option does not toggle. 
\item[{\index{-r@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r}}]  The option \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r} tells \textsf{GAP} to ignore any user specific configuration files. In particular, the user
specific root directory \texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot} is not added to the \textsf{GAP} root directories and so \texttt{gap.ini} and \texttt{gaprc} files that may be contained in that directory are not read, see \ref{sect:gap.ini}. Multiple \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r} options toggle this behaviour. 
\item[{\index{-s@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}s}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}s }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}}}]  With this option \textsf{GAP} does not use \texttt{sbrk} to get memory from the operating system. Instead it uses \texttt{mmap}, \texttt{malloc} or some other command for the amount given with this option to allocate space
for the \texttt{GASMAN} memory manager. Usually \textsf{GAP} does not really use all of this memory, the options \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}m}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}o}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}K} still work as documented. This feature assumes that the operating system only
assigns physical memory to the \textsf{GAP} process when it is accessed, so that specifying a large amount of memory with \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}s} should not cause any performance problem. The advantage of using this option
is that \textsf{GAP} can work together with kernel modules which allocate a lot of memory with \texttt{malloc}. 

 The option argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape memory}} is specified as with the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}m} option. 
\item[{\index{-T@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}T}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}T}}]  suppresses the usual break loop behaviour of \textsf{GAP}. With this option \textsf{GAP} behaves as if the user \texttt{quit} immediately from every break loop, and also suppresses displaying any error
backtrace. This is intended for automated testing of \textsf{GAP}. This option may be repeated to toggle this behavior on and off. 
\item[{\index{--version@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}version}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}version}}]  tells \textsf{GAP} to print its version and then exit immediately, all options coming after are
ignored. 
\item[{\index{-x@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}x}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}x }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape length}}}] 
\item[{\index{--width@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}width}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}width }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape length}}}]  With this option you can tell \textsf{GAP} how long lines are. \textsf{GAP} uses this value to decide when to split long lines. After starting \textsf{GAP} you may use \texttt{SizeScreen} (\ref{SizeScreen}) to alter the line length. 

 The default value is 80, unless another value can be obtained from the
Operating System, which is the right value if you have a standard terminal
application. If you have a larger monitor, or use a smaller font, or redirect
the output to a printer, you may want to increase this value. 
\item[{\index{-y@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}y}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}y }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape length}}}] 
\item[{\index{--line@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}line}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}line }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape length}}}]  With this option you can tell \textsf{GAP} how many lines your screen has. \textsf{GAP} uses this value to decide after how many lines of on\texttt{\symbol{45}}line
help it should wait. After starting \textsf{GAP} you may use \texttt{SizeScreen} (\ref{SizeScreen}) to alter the number of lines. 

 The default value is 24, unless another value can be obtained from the
Operating System, which is the right value if you have a standard terminal
application. If you have a larger monitor, or use a smaller font, or redirect
the output to a printer, you may want to increase this value. 
\item[{\index{options!command line, filenames} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filename}} ...}]  Further arguments are taken as filenames of files that are read by \textsf{GAP} during startup, after the system and private init files are read, but before
the first prompt is printed. Filenames ending with \texttt{.tst} are processed by \texttt{Test} (\ref{Test}), all other files by \texttt{Read} (\ref{Read}). These files and also commands specified via the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}c} option are processed in the order in which they appear on the command line. If
a file cannot be opened or if executing the code in it raises an error, then
the usual error handling for \texttt{Read} (\ref{Read}) respectively \texttt{Test} (\ref{Test}) kicks in. If this enters a break loop, then exiting that break loop also exits \textsf{GAP}. 
\end{description}
 

 \index{options!command line, internal} \index{-C@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}C}} \index{-P@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}P}}\index{-p@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}p}} Additional options, such as \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}C}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}P} and\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}p} are used internally by the \textsf{gac} script (see \ref{Kernel modules}) and/or on specific operating systems. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{The gap.ini and gaprc files}}\label{sect:gap.ini}
\logpage{[ 3, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7FD66F977A3B02DF}{}
{
  When you start \textsf{GAP}, it looks for files with the names \texttt{gap.ini} and \texttt{gaprc} in its root directories (see \ref{GAP Root Directories}), and reads the first \texttt{gap.ini} and the first \texttt{gaprc} file it finds. These files are used for certain initializations, as follows. 

 The file \texttt{gap.ini} is read early in the startup process. Therefore, the parameters set in this
file can influence the startup process, such as which packages are
automatically loaded (see \texttt{LoadPackage} (\ref{LoadPackage})) and whether library files containing obsolete variables are read (see
Chapter \ref{Replaced and Removed Command Names}). On the other hand, only calls to a restricted set of \textsf{GAP} functions are allowed in a \texttt{gap.ini} file. Usually, it should only contain calls of \texttt{SetUserPreference} (\ref{SetUserPreference}). This file can be generated (or updated when new releases introduce further
user preferences) with the command \texttt{WriteGapIniFile} (\ref{WriteGapIniFile}). This file is read whenever \textsf{GAP} is started, with or without a workspace. 

 The file \texttt{gaprc} is read after the startup process, before the first input file given on the
command line (see \ref{Command Line Options}). So the contents of this file cannot influence the startup process, but all \textsf{GAP} library functions can be called in this file. When \textsf{GAP} is started with a workspace then the file is read only if no \texttt{gaprc} file had been read before the workspace was created. (With this setup, it is
on the one hand possible that administrators provide a \textsf{GAP} workspace for several users such that the user's \texttt{gaprc} file is read when \textsf{GAP} is started with the workspace, and on the other hand one can start \textsf{GAP}, read one's \texttt{gaprc} file, save a workspace, and then start from this workspace \emph{without} reading one's \texttt{gaprc} file again.) 

 Note that by default, the user specific \textsf{GAP} root directory \texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot} is the first \textsf{GAP} root directory. So you can put your \texttt{gap.ini} and \texttt{gaprc} files into this directory. 

 This mechanism substitutes the much less flexible reading of a users \texttt{.gaprc} file in versions of \textsf{GAP} up to 4.4. For compatibility this \texttt{.gaprc} file is still read if the directory \texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot} does not exist, see \ref{obsolete-gaprc} how to migrate your old setup.  
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{The gap.ini file}}\label{subsect:gap.ini file}
\logpage{[ 3, 2, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X87DF11C885E73583}{}
{
  \index{gap.ini@\texttt{gap.ini}} The file \texttt{gap.ini} is read after the declaration part of the \textsf{GAP} library is read, before the declaration parts of the packages needed and
suggested by \textsf{GAP} are read, and before the implementation parts of \textsf{GAP} and of the packages are read. 

 The file \texttt{gap.ini} is expected to consist of calls to the function \texttt{SetUserPreference} (\ref{SetUserPreference}), see Section{\nobreakspace}\texttt{SetUserPreference} (\ref{SetUserPreference}). 

 Since the file \texttt{gap.ini} is read before the implementation part of \textsf{GAP} is read, not all \textsf{GAP} functions may be called in the file. Assignments of numbers, lists, and
records are admissible as well as calls to basic functions such as \texttt{Concatenation} (\ref{Concatenation:for several lists}) and \texttt{JoinStringsWithSeparator} (\ref{JoinStringsWithSeparator}). 

 Note that the file \texttt{gap.ini} is read also when \textsf{GAP} is started with a workspace. }

  
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{The gaprc file}}\label{subsect:gaprc file}
\logpage{[ 3, 2, 2 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X84D4CF587D437C00}{}
{
  If a file \texttt{gaprc} is found it is read after \textsf{GAP}'s \texttt{init.g}, but before any of the files mentioned on the command line are read. You can
use this file for your private customizations. (Many users may be happy with
using just user preferences in the \texttt{gap.ini} file (see above) for private customization.) For example, if you have a file
containing functions or data that you always need, you could read this from \texttt{gaprc}. Or if you find some of the names in the library too long, you could define
abbreviations for those names in \texttt{gaprc}. The following sample \texttt{gaprc} file does both. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  Read( "/usr/you/dat/mygroups.grp" );
  Ac := Action;
  AcHom := ActionHomomorphism;
  RepAc := RepresentativeAction;
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that only one \texttt{gaprc} file is read when \textsf{GAP} is started. When a workspace is created in a \textsf{GAP} session after a \texttt{gaprc} file has been read then no more \texttt{gaprc} file will be read when \textsf{GAP} is started with this workspace. 

 Also note that the file must be called \texttt{gaprc}. If you use a Windows text editor, in particular if your default is not to
show file suffixes, you might accidentally create a file \texttt{gaprc.txt} or \texttt{gaprc.doc} which GAP will not recognize. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Configuring User preferences}}\logpage{[ 3, 2, 3 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7B0AD104839B6C3C}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetUserPreference({\mdseries\slshape [package, ]name, value})\index{SetUserPreference@\texttt{SetUserPreference}}
\label{SetUserPreference}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UserPreference({\mdseries\slshape [package, ]name})\index{UserPreference@\texttt{UserPreference}}
\label{UserPreference}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ShowUserPreferences({\mdseries\slshape package1, package2, ...})\index{ShowUserPreferences@\texttt{ShowUserPreferences}}
\label{ShowUserPreferences}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{WriteGapIniFile({\mdseries\slshape [dir][,] [ignorecurrent]})\index{WriteGapIniFile@\texttt{WriteGapIniFile}}
\label{WriteGapIniFile}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Some aspects of the behaviour of \textsf{GAP} can be customized by the user via \emph{user preferences}. Examples include the way help sections are displayed or the use of colors in
the terminal. 

 User preferences are specified via a pair of strings, the first is the (case
insensitive) name of a package (or \texttt{"GAP"} for the core \textsf{GAP} library) and the second is some arbitrary case sensitive string. 

 User preferences can be set to some \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape value}} with \texttt{SetUserPreference}. The current value of a user preference can be found with \texttt{UserPreference}. In both cases, if no package name is given the default \texttt{"GAP"} is used. If a user preference is not known or not set then \texttt{UserPreference} returns \texttt{fail}. 

 The stored values of user preferences are always immutable, see Section \ref{Mutability and Copyability}. 

 The function \texttt{ShowUserPreferences} with no argument shows in a pager an overview of all known user preferences
together with some explanation and the current value. If one or more strings \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape package1}}, ... are given then only the user preferences for these packages are shown.
The \textsf{Browse} package provides the function \texttt{BrowseUserPreferences} (\textbf{Browse: BrowseUserPreferences}) which gives an overview of the known user preferenes and also admits editing
the values of the preferences. 

 The easiest way to make use of user preferences is probably to use the
function \texttt{WriteGapIniFile}, usually without argument. This function creates a file \texttt{gap.ini} in your user specific \textsf{GAP} root directory (\texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot}). If such a file already exists the function will make a backup of it first.
This newly created file contains descriptions of all known user preferences
and also calls of \texttt{SetUserPreference} for those user preferences which currently do not have their default value.
You can then edit that file to customize (further) the user preferences for
future \textsf{GAP} sessions. 

 Should a later version of \textsf{GAP} or some packages introduce new user preferences then you can call \texttt{WriteGapIniFile} again since it will set the previously known user preferences to their current
values. 

 Optionally, a different directory for the resulting \texttt{gap.ini} file can be specified as argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dir}} to \texttt{WriteGapIniFile}. Another optional argument is the boolean value \texttt{true}, if this is given, the settings of all user preferences in the current
session are ignored. 

 Note that your \texttt{gap.ini} file is read by \textsf{GAP} very early during its startup process. A consequence is that the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape value}} argument in a call of \texttt{SetUserPreference} must be some very basic \textsf{GAP} object, usually a boolean, a number, a string or a list of those. A few user
preferences support more complicated settings. For example, the user
preference \texttt{"UseColorPrompt"} admits a record as its value whose components are available only after the \textsf{GAPDoc} package has been loaded, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{ColorPrompt} (\ref{ColorPrompt}). If you want to specify such a complicated value, then move the corresponding
call of \texttt{SetUserPreference} from your \texttt{gap.ini} file into your \texttt{gaprc} file (also in the directory \texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot}). This file is read much later. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetUserPreference( "Pager", "less" );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetUserPreference("PagerOptions",|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@                     [ "-f", "-r", "-a", "-i", "-M", "-j2" ] );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UserPreference("Pager");|
  "less"
\end{Verbatim}
 The first two lines of this example will cause \textsf{GAP} to use the programm \texttt{less} as a pager. This is highly recommended if \texttt{less} is available on your system. The last line displays the current setting. 

 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareUserPreference}}
\logpage{[ 3, 2, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F1DF6757B248014}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareUserPreference({\mdseries\slshape record})\index{DeclareUserPreference@\texttt{DeclareUserPreference}}
\label{DeclareUserPreference}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function can be used (also in packages) to introduce new user
preferences. It declares a user preference, determines a default value and
contains documentation of the user preference. After declaration a user
preference will be shown with \texttt{ShowUserPreferences} (\ref{ShowUserPreferences}) and \texttt{WriteGapIniFile} (\ref{WriteGapIniFile}). 

 When this declaration is evaluated it is checked, if this user preference is
already set in the current session. If not the value of the user preference is
set to its default. (Do not use \texttt{fail} as default value since this indicated that a user preference is not set.)

 The argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape record}} of \texttt{DeclareUserPreference} must be a record with the following components. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{name}}]  a string or a list of strings, the latter meaning several preferences which
belong together, 
\item[{\texttt{description}}]  a list of strings describing the preference(s), one string for each paragraph;
if several preferences are declared together then the description refers to
all of them, 
\item[{\texttt{default}}]  the default value that is used, or a function without arguments that computes
this default value; if several preferences are declared together then the
value of this component must be the list of default values for the individual
preferences. 
\end{description}
 

 The following components of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape record}} are optional. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{check}}]  a function that takes a value as its argument and returns either \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}, depending on whether the given value is admissible for this preference; if
several preferences are declared together then the number of arguments of the
function must equal the length of the \texttt{name} list, 
\item[{\texttt{values}}]  the list of admissible values, or a function without arguments that returns
this list, 
\item[{\texttt{multi}}]  \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}, depending on whether one may choose several values from the given list or
just one; needed (and useful only) if the \texttt{values} component is present, 
\item[{\texttt{package}}]  the name of the \textsf{GAP} package to which the preference is assigned; if the declaration happens inside
a file that belongs to this package then the value of this component is
computed, using \texttt{GAPInfo.PackageCurrent}; otherwise, the default value for \texttt{package} is \texttt{"GAP"}, 
\item[{\texttt{omitFromGapIniFile}}]  if the value is \texttt{true} then this user preference is ignored by \texttt{WriteGapIniFile} (\ref{WriteGapIniFile}). 
\end{description}
 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UserPreference( "MyFavouritePrime" );|
  fail
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DeclareUserPreference( rec(|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@       name:= "MyFavouritePrime",|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@       description:= [ "is not used, serves as an example" ],|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@       default:= 2,|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@       omitFromGapIniFile:= true ) );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UserPreference( "MyFavouritePrime" );|
  2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetUserPreference( "MyFavouritePrime", 17 );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UserPreference( "MyFavouritePrime" );|
  17
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{User Preferences Defined by \textsf{GAP}}}\label{subsect:User Preferences Defined by GAP}
\logpage{[ 3, 2, 5 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X870A11E7864F9CA7}{}
{
  Here is the list of those user preferences that are currently declared via \texttt{DeclareUserPreference} (\ref{DeclareUserPreference}) for \textsf{GAP} itself. The preferences that are declared for \textsf{GAP} packages belong to the documentation of these packages. 
\begin{description}
\item[{ \index{Autocompleter@\texttt{Autocompleter}} \texttt{Autocompleter} }]  Set how names are filtered during tab\texttt{\symbol{45}}autocomplete, this
can be: \texttt{"default"}: case\texttt{\symbol{45}}sensitive matching. \texttt{"case\texttt{\symbol{45}}insensitive"}: case\texttt{\symbol{45}}insensitive matching, or a record with two
components named \texttt{filter} and \texttt{completer}, which are both functions which take two arguments. \texttt{filter} takes a list of names and a partial identifier and returns all the members of \texttt{names} which are a valid extension of the partial identifier. \texttt{completer} takes a list of names and a partial identifier and returns the partial
identifier as extended as possible (it may also change the identifier, for
example to correct the case, or spelling mistakes), or returns \texttt{fail} to leave the existing partial identifier. 

 This preference is ignored if \textsf{GAP} was not compiled with readline support. 

 Default: \texttt{"default"}. 
\item[{ \index{Editor@\texttt{Editor}} \index{EditorOptions@\texttt{EditorOptions}} \texttt{Editor}, \texttt{EditorOptions} }]  Determines the editor and options (used by \textsf{GAP}'s \texttt{Edit} (\ref{Edit}) command). Under macOS, the value \texttt{"open"} for \texttt{Editor} will work. For further options, see the \textsf{GAP} help for \texttt{Edit} (\ref{Edit}). If you want to use the editor defined in your (shell) environment then leave
the \texttt{Editor} and \texttt{EditorOptions} preferences empty. 

 The defaults are computed at runtime. 
\item[{ \index{ExcludeFromAutoload@\texttt{ExcludeFromAutoload}} \texttt{ExcludeFromAutoload} }]  These packages are not loaded at \textsf{GAP} startup. This doesn't work for packages which are needed by the \textsf{GAP} library, or which are already loaded in a workspace. 

 Default: \texttt{""}. 
\item[{ \index{HelpViewers@\texttt{HelpViewers}} \index{XpdfOptions@\texttt{XpdfOptions}} \index{XdviOptions@\texttt{XdviOptions}} \texttt{HelpViewers}, \texttt{XpdfOptions}, \texttt{XdviOptions} }]  Here you can choose your preferred help viewers. See the help for \texttt{SetHelpViewer} (\ref{SetHelpViewer}) for further options. 

 Try \texttt{HelpViewers:= [ "screen", "firefox", "xpdf" ];}. 

 (For \texttt{"screen"} we also suggest to set the \texttt{Pager} entry to \texttt{"less"}.) 

 Defaults: \texttt{[ [ "screen" ], "", "" ]}. 
\item[{ \index{HistoryBackwardSearchSkipIdenticalEntries@\texttt{HistoryBackwardSearchSkipIdenticalEntries}} \texttt{HistoryBackwardSearchSkipIdenticalEntries} }]  When a command is executed multiple times, it is also stored in history
multiple times. Setting this option to \texttt{true} skips identical entries when searching backwards in history. 

 Admissible values: \texttt{true}, \texttt{false}. 

 Default: \texttt{false}. 
\item[{ \index{HistoryMaxLines@\texttt{HistoryMaxLines}} \index{SaveAndRestoreHistory@\texttt{SaveAndRestoreHistory}} \texttt{HistoryMaxLines}, \texttt{SaveAndRestoreHistory} }]  \texttt{HistoryMaxLines} is the maximal amount of input lines held in \textsf{GAP}'s command line history. 

 If \texttt{SaveAndRestoreHistory} is \texttt{true} then \textsf{GAP} saves its command line history before terminating a \textsf{GAP} session, and prepends the stored history when \textsf{GAP} is started. If this is enabled it is suggested to set \texttt{HistoryMaxLines} to some finite value. It is also possible to set \texttt{HistoryMaxLines} to \texttt{infinity} (\ref{infinity}) to keep arbitrarily many lines. 

 These preferences are ignored if \textsf{GAP} was not compiled with readline support. 

 Defaults: \texttt{[ 10000, true ]}. 
\item[{ \index{InfoPackageLoadingLevel@\texttt{InfoPackageLoadingLevel}} \texttt{InfoPackageLoadingLevel} }]  Info messages concerning package loading up to this level are printed. The
level can be changed in a running session using \texttt{SetInfoLevel} (\ref{SetInfoLevel}). 

 Admissible values: \texttt{1}, \texttt{2}, \texttt{3}, \texttt{4}. 

 Default: \texttt{1}. 
\item[{ \index{MaxBitsIntView@\texttt{MaxBitsIntView}} \texttt{MaxBitsIntView} }]  Maximal bit length of integers to \texttt{View} unabbreviated. Default is about $30$ lines of a $80$ character wide terminal. Set this to \texttt{0} to avoid abbreviated ints. 

 Default: \texttt{8000}. 
\item[{ \index{PartialPermDisplayLimit@\texttt{PartialPermDisplayLimit}} \index{NotationForPartialPerms@\texttt{NotationForPartialPerms}} \texttt{PartialPermDisplayLimit}, \texttt{NotationForPartialPerms} }]  options for the display of partial perms 

 Defaults: \texttt{[ 100, "component" ]}. 
\item[{ \index{TransformationDisplayLimit@\texttt{TransformationDisplayLimit}} \index{NotationForTransformations@\texttt{NotationForTransformations}} \texttt{TransformationDisplayLimit}, \texttt{NotationForTransformations} }]  options for the display of transformations 

 Defaults: \texttt{[ 100, "input" ]}. 
\item[{ \index{PackagesToIgnore@\texttt{PackagesToIgnore}} \texttt{PackagesToIgnore} }]  These packages are not regarded as available. This doesn't work for packages
which are needed by the \textsf{GAP} library, or which are already loaded in a workspace. 

 Default: \texttt{""}. 
\item[{ \index{PackagesToLoad@\texttt{PackagesToLoad}} \texttt{PackagesToLoad} }]  A list of names of packages which should be loaded during startup. For
backwards compatibility, the default lists most of packages that were
autoloaded in \textsf{GAP} 4.4 (add or remove packages as you like). 

 Default: \texttt{[ "autpgrp", "alnuth", "crisp", "ctbllib", "factint", "fga", "irredsol",
"laguna", "PackageManager", "polenta", "polycyclic", "resclasses", "sophus",
"tomlib" ]}. 
\item[{ \index{Pager@\texttt{Pager}} \index{PagerOptions@\texttt{PagerOptions}} \texttt{Pager}, \texttt{PagerOptions} }]  For displaying help pages on screen and other things \textsf{GAP} has a rudimentary builtin pager. We recommend using a more sophisticated
external program. For example, when you have the program \texttt{less} on your computer we recommend: 

 \texttt{Pager := "less";} 

 \texttt{PagerOptions := ["\texttt{\symbol{45}}f", "\texttt{\symbol{45}}r",
"\texttt{\symbol{45}}a", "\texttt{\symbol{45}}i", "\texttt{\symbol{45}}M",
"\texttt{\symbol{45}}j2"];} 

 If you want to use \texttt{more}, we suggest to use the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}f} option. If you want to use the pager defined in your environment then leave
the \texttt{Pager} and \texttt{PagerOptions} preferences empty. 

 The defaults are computed at runtime. 
\item[{ \index{ReadObsolete@\texttt{ReadObsolete}} \texttt{ReadObsolete} }]  May be useful to say \texttt{false} here to check if you are using commands which may vanish in a future version
of \textsf{GAP} 

 Admissible values: \texttt{true}, \texttt{false}. 

 Default: \texttt{true}. 
\item[{ \index{ReproducibleBehaviour@\texttt{ReproducibleBehaviour}} \texttt{ReproducibleBehaviour} }]  This preference disables code in \textsf{GAP} which changes behaviour based on time spent, and therefore can produce
different results depending on how much time is taken by other programs
running on the same computer. This option may lead to slower or
lower\texttt{\symbol{45}}quality results. Note that many algorithms in \textsf{GAP} use the global random number generator, which is NOT affected by this option.
This only tries to ensure the same version of \textsf{GAP}, with the same package versions loaded, on the same machine, running the same
code, in a fresh \textsf{GAP} session, will produce the same results. 

 Admissible values: \texttt{true}, \texttt{false}. 

 Default: \texttt{false}. 
\item[{ \index{ShortBanners@\texttt{ShortBanners}} \texttt{ShortBanners} }]  If this option is set to \texttt{true}, package banners printed during loading will only show the name, version and
description of a package. 

 Admissible values: \texttt{true}, \texttt{false}. 

 Default: \texttt{false}. 
\item[{ \index{UseColorPrompt@\texttt{UseColorPrompt}} \texttt{UseColorPrompt} }]  In a color capable terminal (almost any terminal application) you can run \textsf{GAP} such that the prompts, the input and output are distinguished by colors.
Options are \texttt{true}, \texttt{false} or some record as explained in the help section for \texttt{ColorPrompt} (\ref{ColorPrompt}). 

 Default: \texttt{true}. 
\item[{ \index{UseColorsInTerminal@\texttt{UseColorsInTerminal}} \texttt{UseColorsInTerminal} }]  Almost all current terminal emulations support color display, setting this to \texttt{true} implies a default display of most manuals with color markup. It may influence
the display of other things in the future. 

 Admissible values: \texttt{true}, \texttt{false}. 

 Default: \texttt{true}. 
\item[{ \index{ViewLength@\texttt{ViewLength}} \texttt{ViewLength} }]  A bound for the number of lines printed when \texttt{View}ing some large objects. 

 Default: \texttt{3}. 
\item[{ \index{WhereDepth@\texttt{WhereDepth}} \texttt{WhereDepth} }]  The number of stack frames shown by \texttt{Where} and \texttt{WhereWithVars} when called without an explicit depth argument, e.g. in the default \texttt{OnBreak} handler. 

 Default: \texttt{5}. 
\end{description}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Saving and Loading a Workspace}}\label{Saving and Loading a Workspace}
\logpage{[ 3, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7CB282757ACB1C09}{}
{
  \textsf{GAP} workspace files are binary files that contain the data of a \textsf{GAP} session. Currently saving and loading workspace files are supported only when
the \texttt{GASMAN} garbage collector is used, see Section \ref{Garbage Collection}. 

 One can produce a workspace file with \texttt{SaveWorkspace} (\ref{SaveWorkspace}), and load it into a new \textsf{GAP} session using the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}L} command line option, see Section \ref{Command Line Options}. 

 One purpose of workspace files is of course the possibility to save a ``snapshot'' image of the current \textsf{GAP} workspace in a file. 

 The recommended way to start \textsf{GAP} is to load an existing workspace file, because this reduces the startup time
of \textsf{GAP} drastically. So if you have installed \textsf{GAP} yourself then you should think about creating a workspace file immediately
after you have started \textsf{GAP}, and then using this workspace file later on, whenever you start \textsf{GAP}. If your \textsf{GAP} installation is shared between several users, the system administrator should
think about providing such a workspace file. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SaveWorkspace}}
\logpage{[ 3, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X876544A57C73C488}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SaveWorkspace({\mdseries\slshape filename})\index{SaveWorkspace@\texttt{SaveWorkspace}}
\label{SaveWorkspace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{save} will save a ``snapshot'' image of the current \textsf{GAP} workspace in the file \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filename}}. This image then can be loaded by another copy of \textsf{GAP} which then will behave as at the point when \texttt{SaveWorkspace} was called. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:=1;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SaveWorkspace("savefile");|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@quit;|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \texttt{SaveWorkspace} can only be used at the main \texttt{gap{\textgreater}} prompt. It cannot be included in the body of a loop or function, or called
from a break loop. }

 }

\logpage{[ 3, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C825AF087A27884}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ARCH{\textunderscore}IS{\textunderscore}UNIX({\mdseries\slshape })\index{ARCH{\textunderscore}IS{\textunderscore}UNIX@\texttt{ARC}\-\texttt{H{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{I}\-\texttt{S{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{UNIX}}
\label{ARCHuScoreISuScoreUNIX}

{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ARCH{\textunderscore}IS{\textunderscore}MAC{\textunderscore}OS{\textunderscore}X({\mdseries\slshape })\index{ARCH{\textunderscore}IS{\textunderscore}MAC{\textunderscore}OS{\textunderscore}X@\texttt{ARC}\-\texttt{H{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{I}\-\texttt{S{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{M}\-\texttt{A}\-\texttt{C{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{O}\-\texttt{S{\textunderscore}X}}
\label{ARCHuScoreISuScoreMACuScoreOSuScoreX}
