  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@       od;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@       OnBreak := SavedOnBreak;      # restore OnBreak afterwards|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@     end;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@     OnBreak := ENTBOnBreak;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@     Error();|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   end;|
  function( arg... ) ... end
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Here is a somewhat trivial demonstration of the use of \texttt{ErrorNoTraceBack}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|ErrorNoTraceBack("Gidday!", " How's", " it", " going?\n");A
  Error,
  Gidday! How's it going?
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  @gapbrkprompt|brk>A @gapinput|quit;A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Now we call \texttt{Error} (\ref{Error}) with the same arguments to show the difference. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|Error("Gidday!", " How's", " it", " going?\n");A
  Error, Gidday! How's it going?
  Hello
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  @gapbrkprompt|brk>A @gapinput|quit;A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Observe that the value of \texttt{OnBreak} before the \texttt{ErrorNoTraceBack} call was restored. However, we had changed \texttt{OnBreak} from its default value; to restore \texttt{OnBreak} to its default value, we should do the following. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@OnBreak := Where;;|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{OnBreakMessage}}
\logpage{[ 6, 4, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80711C807C99C220}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{OnBreakMessage({\mdseries\slshape })\index{OnBreakMessage@\texttt{OnBreakMessage}}
\label{OnBreakMessage}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{Break loop message} When a break loop is entered by a call to \texttt{Error} (\ref{Error}) the message at the end starting with ``\texttt{you can enter 'quit;' to ...}'' is produced by the function \texttt{OnBreakMessage}, which just like \texttt{OnBreak} (\ref{OnBreak}) is a user\texttt{\symbol{45}}configurable global variable that is a \emph{function} with \emph{no arguments}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@OnBreakMessage(); # By default, OnBreakMessage prints the following|
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Perhaps you are familiar with what's possible in a break loop, and so don't
need to be reminded. In this case, you might wish to do the following (the
first line just makes it easy to restore the default value later). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NormalOnBreakMessage := OnBreakMessage;; # save the default value|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@OnBreakMessage := function() end;        # do-nothing function|
  function(  ) ... end
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@OnBreakMessage();|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@OnBreakMessage := NormalOnBreakMessage;; # reset|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 With \texttt{OnBreak} (\ref{OnBreak}) still set away from its default value, calling \texttt{Error} (\ref{Error}) as we did above, now produces: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|Error("!\n");A
  Error, !
  Hello
  @gapbrkprompt|brk>A @gapinput|quit; # to get back to outer loopA
\end{Verbatim}
 

 However, suppose you are writing a function which detects an error condition
and \texttt{OnBreakMessage} needs to be changed only \emph{locally}, i.e., the instructions on how to recover from the break loop need to be
specific to that function. The same idea used to define \texttt{ErrorNoTraceBack} (see \texttt{OnBreak} (\ref{OnBreak})) can be adapted to achieve this. The function \texttt{CosetTableFromGensAndRels} (\ref{CosetTableFromGensAndRels}) is an example in the \textsf{GAP} code where the idea is actually used. }

 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Where}}
\logpage{[ 6, 4, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A7FFA2B7C1EF5A3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Where({\mdseries\slshape nr})\index{Where@\texttt{Where}}
\label{Where}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{WhereWithVars({\mdseries\slshape nr})\index{WhereWithVars@\texttt{WhereWithVars}}
\label{WhereWithVars}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{Backtrace!GAP3 name for Where} \index{Stack trace} shows the last \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} commands on the execution stack during whose execution the error occurred. If
not given, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} defaults to the value of the \texttt{WhereDepth} user preference (initially 5). If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} or the \texttt{WhereDepth} preference is not a non\texttt{\symbol{45}}negative integer, it is treated as
5. (Assume, for the following example, that after the last example \texttt{OnBreak} (\ref{OnBreak}) has been set back to its default value.). \texttt{WhereWithVars} acts the same as \texttt{Where} while also showing the arguments and local variables of each function. 

 \texttt{WhereWithVars} acts the same as \texttt{Where} while also showing the arguments and local variables of each function. 

 The following example assumes that \texttt{OnBreak} (\ref{OnBreak}) is set to its default value. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!|D,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt|gap>D !gapinput|StabChain(SymmetricGroup(1000)); # After this we typed ^CD
  Error, user interrupt
  *[1] genlabels := Filtered( genlabels, function ( x )
          return pnt ^ sgs[x] = pnt;
      end );
     @ GAPROOT/lib/stbc.gi:426
   [2] StabChainBaseStrongGenerators( dom{[ 1 .. Length( dom ) - 1 ]}, sgs, () )
     @ GAPROOT/lib/gpprmsya.gi:2006
   [3] StabChainOp( G, rec(
       ) )
     @ GAPROOT/lib/stbc.gi:28
   [4] StabChainImmutable( arg[1] )
     @ GAPROOT/lib/stbc.gi:18
  <function "StabChain">( <arguments> )
   called from read-eval loop at *stdin*:2
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  !gapbrkprompt|brk>D !gapinput|Where(2);D
  *[1] genlabels := Filtered( genlabels, function ( x )
          return pnt ^ sgs[x] = pnt;
      end );
     @ GAPROOT/lib/stbc.gi:426
   [2] StabChainBaseStrongGenerators( dom{[ 1 .. Length( dom ) - 1 ]}, sgs, () )
     @ GAPROOT/lib/gpprmsya.gi:2006
  ...  at *errin*:1
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that the variables displayed even in the first line of the \texttt{Where} list (after the \texttt{called from} line) may be already one environment level higher and \texttt{DownEnv} (\ref{DownEnv}) may be necessary to access them. 

 At the moment this backtrace does not work from within compiled code (this
includes the method selection which by default is compiled into the kernel).
If this creates problems for debugging, call \textsf{GAP} with the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}M} option (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Command Line Options}) to avoid loading compiled code. 

 (Function calls to \texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) and methods installed for binary operations are handled in a special way. In
rare circumstances it is possible therefore that they do not show up in a \texttt{Where} log but the log refers to the \emph{last} proper function call that happened before.) 

 The command line option \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}T} to \textsf{GAP} disables the break loop. This is mainly intended for testing purposes and for
special applications. If this option is given then errors simply cause \textsf{GAP} to return to the main loop. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Variable Access in a Break Loop}}\label{Variable Access in a Break Loop}
\logpage{[ 6, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7EE5CF2C8419F061}{}
{
  In a break loop access to variables of the current break level and higher
levels is possible, but if the same variable name is used for different
objects or if a function calls itself recursively, of course only the variable
at the lowest level can be accessed. 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DownEnv and UpEnv}}\logpage{[ 6, 5, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79E66DA2875303B0}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DownEnv({\mdseries\slshape nr})\index{DownEnv@\texttt{DownEnv}}
\label{DownEnv}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UpEnv({\mdseries\slshape nr})\index{UpEnv@\texttt{UpEnv}}
\label{UpEnv}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CurrentEnv({\mdseries\slshape })\index{CurrentEnv@\texttt{CurrentEnv}}
\label{CurrentEnv}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{DownEnv} moves down \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} steps in the environment and allows one to inspect variables on this level; if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} is negative it steps up in the environment again; \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} defaults to 1 if not given. \texttt{UpEnv} acts similarly to \texttt{DownEnv} but in the reverse direction (the mnemonic rule to remember the difference
between \texttt{DownEnv} and \texttt{UpEnv} is the order in which commands on the execution stack are displayed by \texttt{Where} (\ref{Where})). \texttt{CurrentEnv} returns the currently selected environment. At present this is the local
variables bag used by the break loop for local variable lookup; outside such a
context it returns \texttt{fail}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=|AC,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  |gappromptAgap>C |gapinputAOnBreak := function() end;; # eliminate back-tracing on entry to break loopC
  |gappromptAgap>C |gapinputAtest:= function( n )C
  |gappromptA>C |gapinputA   if n > 3 then Error( "!\n" ); fi; test( n+1 ); end;;C
  |gappromptAgap>C |gapinputAtest( 1 );C
  Error, !
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>C |gapinputAWhere();C
  Stack trace:
  *[1] Error( "!\n" );
     @ *stdin*:3
   [2] test( n + 1 );
     @ *stdin*:3
   [3] test( n + 1 );
     @ *stdin*:3
   [4] test( n + 1 );
     @ *stdin*:3
  <function "test">( <arguments> )
   called from read-eval loop at *errin*:1
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>C |gapinputAn;C
  4
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>C |gapinputADownEnv();C
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>C |gapinputAn;C
  3
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>C |gapinputAWhere();C
  Stack trace:
   [1] Error( "!\n" );
     @ *stdin*:3
  *[2] test( n + 1 );
     @ *stdin*:3
   [3] test( n + 1 );
     @ *stdin*:3
   [4] test( n + 1 );
     @ *stdin*:3
  <function "test">( <arguments> )
   called from read-eval loop at *errin*:5
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>C |gapinputADownEnv( 2 );C
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>C |gapinputAn;C
  1
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>C |gapinputAWhere();C
  Stack trace:
   [1] Error( "!\n" );
     @ *stdin*:3
   [2] test( n + 1 );
     @ *stdin*:3
   [3] test( n + 1 );
     @ *stdin*:3
  *[4] test( n + 1 );
     @ *stdin*:3
  <function "test">( <arguments> )
   called from read-eval loop at *errin*:8
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>C |gapinputADownEnv( -2 );C
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>C |gapinputAn;C
  3
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>C |gapinputAquit;C
  |gappromptAgap>C |gapinputAOnBreak := Where;; # restore OnBreak to its default valueC
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that the change of the environment caused by \texttt{DownEnv} only affects variable access in the break loop. If you use \texttt{return} to continue a calculation \textsf{GAP} automatically jumps to the right environment level again. 

 Note also that search for variables looks first in the chain of outer
functions which enclosed the definition of a currently executing function,
before it looks at the chain of calling functions which led to the current
invocation of the function. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=|AB,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  |gappromptAgap>B |gapinputAfoo := function()B
  |gappromptA>B |gapinputAlocal x; x := 1;B
  |gappromptA>B |gapinputAreturn function() local y; y := x*x; Error("!!\n"); end;B
  |gappromptA>B |gapinputAend;B
  function(  ) ... end
  |gappromptAgap>B |gapinputAbar := foo();B
  function(  ) ... end
  |gappromptAgap>B |gapinputAfun := function() local x; x := 3; bar(); end;B
  function(  ) ... end
  |gappromptAgap>B |gapinputAfun();B
  Error, !!
  Stack trace:
  *[1] Error( "!!\n" );
     @ *stdin*:4
   [2] bar(  );
     @ *stdin*:7
  <function "fun">( <arguments> )
   called from read-eval loop at *stdin*:8
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>B |gapinputAx;B
  1
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>B |gapinputADownEnv(1);B
  |gapbrkpromptAbrk>B |gapinputAx;B
  3
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Here the \texttt{x} of \texttt{foo} which contained the definition of \texttt{bar} is found before that of \texttt{fun} which caused its execution. Using \texttt{DownEnv} we can access the \texttt{x} from \texttt{fun}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Error and ErrorCount}}\label{sect:Error}
\logpage{[ 6, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7BC8D2E37ADE9062}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Error}}
\logpage{[ 6, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E7AD8D87EBA1A08}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Error({\mdseries\slshape messages, ...})\index{Error@\texttt{Error}}
\label{Error}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{Error} signals an error from within a function. First the messages \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape messages}} are printed, this is done exactly as if \texttt{Print} (\ref{Print}) (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{View and Print}) were called with these arguments. Then a break loop (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Break Loops}) is entered, unless the standard error output is not connected to a terminal.
You can leave this break loop with \texttt{return;} to continue execution with the statement following the call to \texttt{Error}. \texttt{ErrorNoReturn} (\ref{ErrorNoReturn}) operates identically to \texttt{Error}, except it does not allow using \texttt{return;} to continue execution. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ErrorNoReturn}}
\logpage{[ 6, 6, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A5C000D7E4984DD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ErrorNoReturn({\mdseries\slshape messages, ...})\index{ErrorNoReturn@\texttt{ErrorNoReturn}}
\label{ErrorNoReturn}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{ErrorNoReturn} signals an error from within a function. First the messages \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape messages}} are printed, this is done exactly as if \texttt{Print} (\ref{Print}) (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{View and Print}) were called with these arguments. Then a break loop (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Break Loops}) is entered, unless the standard error output is not connected to a terminal.
This break loop can only be exited with \texttt{quit;}. The function differs from \texttt{Error} (\ref{Error}) by not allowing execution to continue. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ErrorCount}}
\logpage{[ 6, 6, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86A11BCC7FECEEA4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ErrorCount({\mdseries\slshape })\index{ErrorCount@\texttt{ErrorCount}}
\label{ErrorCount}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{ErrorCount} returns a count of the number of errors (including user interruptions) which
have occurred in the \textsf{GAP} session so far. The count is incremented by each error, even if \textsf{GAP} was started with the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}T} option to disable the break loop. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Leaving GAP}}\label{Leaving GAP}
\logpage{[ 6, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83704B1080FD9B40}{}
{
  \index{quit!in emergency} \index{exit} \index{at exit functions} \index{saving on exit} The normal way to terminate a \textsf{GAP} session is to enter either \texttt{quit;} (note the semicolon) or an end\texttt{\symbol{45}}of\texttt{\symbol{45}}file
character (usually \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}D}) at the \texttt{gap{\textgreater} } prompt in the main read eval print loop. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{QUIT}}
\logpage{[ 6, 7, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7ECC75048583853B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{QUIT\index{QUIT@\texttt{QUIT}}
\label{QUIT}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 An emergency way to leave \textsf{GAP} is to enter \index{QUIT@\texttt{QUIT}!emergency quit} \texttt{QUIT} at any \texttt{gap{\textgreater}} or \texttt{brk{\textgreater}} or \texttt{brk{\textunderscore}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nn}}{\textgreater}} prompt. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GapExitCode}}
\logpage{[ 6, 7, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X838B50A9790DE55B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GapExitCode({\mdseries\slshape [ret]})\index{GapExitCode@\texttt{GapExitCode}}
\label{GapExitCode}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{GapExitCode} sets the exit value which is returned to the operating system (or parent
process) when \textsf{GAP} exits. This may be an integer in the range [\texttt{\symbol{45}}128..127]
(other values are reduced modulo 256), or a boolean. \texttt{true} corresponds to the return value 0, which by convention is treated as
"success". \texttt{false} corresponds to the return value 1, which by convention is treated as
"failure". The exit value is not changed if no argument is given. 

 The \emph{previous} exit code is returned. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{QuitGap}}
\logpage{[ 6, 7, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7AB1567987922580}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{QuitGap({\mdseries\slshape [ret]})\index{QuitGap@\texttt{QuitGap}}
\label{QuitGap}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{QuitGap} acts similarly to the keyword \texttt{QUIT}, except \texttt{QUIT} cannot be called from a function. It exits \textsf{GAP} cleanly, calling any function installed using \texttt{InstallAtExit} (\ref{InstallAtExit}). The optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ret}} will be passed to \texttt{GapExitCode} (\ref{GapExitCode}). 

 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ForceQuitGap}}
\logpage{[ 6, 7, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85A8DD6B7A20DD89}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ForceQuitGap({\mdseries\slshape [ret]})\index{ForceQuitGap@\texttt{ForceQuitGap}}
\label{ForceQuitGap}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{ForceQuitGap} is similar to \texttt{QuitGap} (\ref{QuitGap}), except it ignores any functions installed with \texttt{InstallAtExit} (\ref{InstallAtExit}), or any other functions normally run at GAP exit, such as flushing any
partially outputted lines to both the screen and files, and exits GAP
immediately. The optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ret}} will be passed to \texttt{GapExitCode} (\ref{GapExitCode}). 

 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InstallAtExit}}
\logpage{[ 6, 7, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A2C380986F46FEE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallAtExit({\mdseries\slshape func})\index{InstallAtExit@\texttt{InstallAtExit}}
\label{InstallAtExit}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{QUITTING\index{QUITTING@\texttt{QUITTING}}
\label{QUITTING}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 Before actually terminating, \textsf{GAP} will call (with no arguments) all of the functions that have been installed
using \texttt{InstallAtExit}. These typically perform tasks such as cleaning up temporary files created
during the session, and closing open files. If an error occurs during the
execution of one of these functions, that function is simply abandoned, no
break loop is entered. 

  
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InstallAtExit(function() Print("bye\n"); end);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@quit;|
  bye
\end{Verbatim}
 

 During execution of these functions, the global variable \texttt{QUITTING} will be set to \texttt{true} if \textsf{GAP} is exiting because the user typed \texttt{QUIT} and \texttt{false} otherwise. Since \texttt{QUIT} is considered as an emergency measure, different action may be appropriate. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SaveOnExitFile}}
\logpage{[ 6, 7, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X843C07A4869EAA1D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SaveOnExitFile\index{SaveOnExitFile@\texttt{SaveOnExitFile}}
\label{SaveOnExitFile}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 If, when \textsf{GAP} is exiting due to a \texttt{quit} or end\texttt{\symbol{45}}of\texttt{\symbol{45}}file (i.e. not due to a \texttt{QUIT}) the variable \texttt{SaveOnExitFile} is bound to a string value, then the system will try to save the \textsf{GAP} workspace to that file, see \texttt{SaveWorkspace} (\ref{SaveWorkspace}). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Line Editing}}\label{Line Editing}
\logpage{[ 6, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X82234FD181899530}{}
{
  In most installations \textsf{GAP} will be compiled to use the Gnu readline library (see the line \texttt{Libs used:} on \textsf{GAP} startup). In that case skip to the next section \ref{sec:readline}. (The line editing commands described in the rest of this section were
available in previous versions of \textsf{GAP}, they will work almost the same in the standard configuration of the Gnu
readline library.) 

 \textsf{GAP} allows one you to edit the current input line with a number of editing
commands. Those commands are accessible either as \emph{control keys} or as \emph{escape keys}. You enter a control key by pressing the \textsc{Ctrl} key, and, while still holding the \textsc{Ctrl} key down, hitting another key \texttt{key}. You enter an escape key by hitting \textsc{Esc} and then hitting another key \texttt{key}. Below we denote control keys by \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}}\texttt{key} and escape keys by \textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}}\texttt{key}. The case of \texttt{key} does not matter, i.e., \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}A} and \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}a} are equivalent. 

 Normally, line editing will be enabled if the input is connected to a
terminal. Line editing can be enabled or disabled using the command line
options \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}f} and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}n} respectively (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Command Line Options}), however this is a machine dependent feature of \textsf{GAP}. 

 Typing \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}key} or \textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}key} for characters not mentioned below always inserts \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}}\texttt{key} resp.{\nobreakspace}\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}}\texttt{key} at the current cursor position. 

 The first few commands allow you to move the cursor on the current line. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}A}}]  move the cursor to the beginning of the line. 
\item[{\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}B}}]  move the cursor to the beginning of the previous word. 
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}B}}]  move the cursor backward one character. 
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}F}}]  move the cursor forward one character. 
\item[{\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}F}}]  move the cursor to the end of the next word. 
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}E}}]  move the cursor to the end of the line. 
\end{description}
 

 The next commands delete or kill text. The last killed text can be reinserted,
possibly at a different position, with the ``yank'' command \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}Y}. 
\begin{description}
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}H} or \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape del}}}]  delete the character left of the cursor. 
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}D}}]  delete the character under the cursor. 
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}K}}]  kill up to the end of the line. 
\item[{\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}D}}]  kill forward to the end of the next word. 
\item[{\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}del}}]  kill backward to the beginning of the last word. 
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}X}}]  kill entire input line, and discard all pending input. 
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}Y}}]  insert (yank) a just killed text. 
\end{description}
 

 The next commands allow you to change the input. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}T}}]  exchange (twiddle) current and previous character. 
\item[{\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}U}}]  uppercase next word. 
\item[{\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}L}}]  lowercase next word. 
\item[{\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}C}}]  capitalize next word. 
\end{description}
 

 The \textsc{Tab} character, which is in fact the control key \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}I}, looks at the characters before the cursor, interprets them as the beginning
of an identifier and tries to complete this identifier. If there is more than
one possible completion, it completes to the longest common prefix of all
those completions. If the characters to the left of the cursor are already the
longest common prefix of all completions hitting \textsc{Tab} a second time will display all possible completions. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\textsc{tab}}]  complete the identifier before the cursor. 
\end{description}
 

 The next commands allow you to fetch previous lines, e.g., to correct typos,
etc. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}L}}]  insert last input line before current character. 
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}P}}]  redisplay the last input line, another \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}P} will redisplay the line before that, etc. If the cursor is not in the first
column only the lines starting with the string to the left of the cursor are
taken. 
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}N}}]  Like \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}P} but goes the other way round through the history. 
\item[{\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}{\textless}}}]  goes to the beginning of the history. 
\item[{\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}{\textgreater}}}]  goes to the end of the history. 
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}O}}]  accepts this line and perform a \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}N}. 
\end{description}
 

 Finally there are a few miscellaneous commands. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}V}}]  enter next character literally, i.e., enter it even if it is one of the
control keys. 
\item[{\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}U}}]  execute the next line editing command 4 times. 
\item[{\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}}\texttt{num}}]  execute the next line editing command \texttt{num} times. 
\item[{\textsc{Esc\texttt{\symbol{45}}Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}L}}]  redisplay input line. 
\end{description}
 

 The four arrow keys (cursor keys) can be used instead of \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}B}, \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}F}, \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}P}, and \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}N}, respectively. }

 
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Editing using the \texttt{readline} library}}\label{sec:readline}
\logpage{[ 6, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7AD8D65F7BA1C3E0}{}
{
  The descriptions in this section are valid only if your \textsf{GAP} installation uses the \texttt{readline} library for command line editing. You can check by \texttt{IsBound(GAPInfo.UseReadline);} if this is the case. 

 You can use all the features of \texttt{readline}, as for example explained in \href{https://tiswww.case.edu/php/chet/readline/rluserman.html} {\texttt{https://tiswww.case.edu/php/chet/readline/rluserman.html}}. Therefore the command line editing in \textsf{GAP} is similar to the \texttt{bash} shell and many other programs. On a Unix/Linux system you may also have a
manpage, try \texttt{man readline}. 

 Compared to the command line editing which was used in \textsf{GAP} up to version{\nobreakspace}4.4 (or compared to not using the \texttt{readline} library) using \texttt{readline} has several advantages: 
\begin{itemize}
\item Most keys still do the same as explained in \ref{Line Editing} (in the default configuration). 
\item There are many additional commands, e.g. undoing (\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}{\textunderscore}}, keyboard macros (\textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}x(}, \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}x)} and \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}xe}), file name completion (hit \textsc{Esc} two or four times), showing matching parentheses, \texttt{vi}\texttt{\symbol{45}}style key bindings, deleting and yanking text, ...
\item Lines which are longer than a physical terminal row can be edited more
conveniently.
\item Arbitrary unicode characters can be typed into string literals. 
\item The key bindings can be configured, either via your \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{126}}/.inputrc} file or by \textsf{GAP} commands, see \ref{ssec:readlineCustom}.
\item The command line history can be saved to and read from a file, see \ref{ssec:cmdlinehistory}.
\item Adventurous users can even implement completely new command line editing
functions on \textsf{GAP} level, see \ref{ssec:readlineUserFuncs}.
\end{itemize}
 

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Readline customization}}\label{ssec:readlineCustom}
\logpage{[ 6, 9, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7C38F9E0783D9442}{}
{
 \index{ReadlineInitLine@\texttt{ReadlineInitLine}}  You can use your readline init file (by default \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{126}}/.inputrc} on Unix/Linux) to customize key bindings. If you want settings be used only
within \textsf{GAP} you can write them between lines containing \texttt{\$if GAP} and \texttt{\$endif}. For a detailed documentation of the available settings and functions see \href{ https://tiswww.case.edu/php/chet/readline/rluserman.html} {here}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=From readline init file]
  $if GAP
    set blink-matching-paren on
    "\C-x\C-o": dump-functions
    "\ep": kill-region
  $endif
\end{Verbatim}
 Alternatively, from within \textsf{GAP} the command \texttt{ReadlineInitLine(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape line}});} can be used, where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape line}} is a string containing a line as in the init file. 

 Caveat: \textsf{GAP} overwrites the following keys (after reading the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{126}}/.inputrc} file): \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}C\texttt{\symbol{45}}g}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}C\texttt{\symbol{45}}i}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}C\texttt{\symbol{45}}n}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}C\texttt{\symbol{45}}o}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}C\texttt{\symbol{45}}p}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}C\texttt{\symbol{45}}r}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}C\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{92}}}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}e{\textless}}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}e{\textgreater}}, \texttt{Up}, \texttt{Down}, \texttt{TAB}, \texttt{Space}, \texttt{PageUp}, \texttt{PageDown}. So, do not redefine these in your \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{126}}/.inputrc}. 

 Note that after pressing \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}v} the next special character is input verbatim. This is very useful to bind keys
or key sequences. For example, binding the function key \textsc{F3} to the command \texttt{kill\texttt{\symbol{45}}whole\texttt{\symbol{45}}line} by using the sequence \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}v} \textsc{F3} looks on many terminals like this: \texttt{ReadlineInitLine("\texttt{\symbol{92}}"\texttt{\symbol{94}}[OR\texttt{\symbol{92}}":kill\texttt{\symbol{45}}whole\texttt{\symbol{45}}line");}. (You can get the line back later with \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}y}.) 

 The \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}g} key can be used to type any unicode character by its code point. The number of
the character can either be given as a count, or if the count is one the input
characters before the cursor are taken (as decimal number or as hex number
which starts with \texttt{0x}. For example, the double stroke character {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} can be
input by any of the three key sequences \textsc{Esc 8484 Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}g}, \textsc{8484 Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}g} or \textsc{0x2124 Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}g}. 

 Some terminals bind the \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}s} and \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}q} keys to stop and restart terminal output. Furthermore, sometimes \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{92}}} quits a program. To disable this behaviour (and maybe use these keys for
command line editing) you can use \texttt{Exec("stty stop undef; stty start undef; stty quit undef");} in your \textsf{GAP} session or your \texttt{gaprc} file (see \ref{sect:gap.ini}). 

 }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{The command line history}}\label{ssec:cmdlinehistory}
\logpage{[ 6, 9, 2 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X846C3DED84AD7593}{}
{
  \textsf{GAP} can save your input lines for later reuse. The keys \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}p} (or \textsc{Up}), \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}n} (or \textsc{Down}), \textsc{ESC{\textless}} and \textsc{ESC{\textgreater}} work as documented in \ref{Line Editing}, that is they scroll backward and forward in the history or go to its
beginning or end. Also, \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}o} works as documented, it is useful for repeating a sequence of previous lines.
(But \textsc{Ctrl\texttt{\symbol{45}}l} clears the screen as in other programs.) 

 The command line history can be used across several instances of \textsf{GAP} via the following two commands. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SaveCommandLineHistory}}
\logpage{[ 6, 9, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C1F4D04861C1197}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SaveCommandLineHistory({\mdseries\slshape [fname][,] [app]})\index{SaveCommandLineHistory@\texttt{SaveCommandLineHistory}}
\label{SaveCommandLineHistory}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\textbf{\indent Returns:\ }
\texttt{fail} or number of saved lines

\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ReadCommandLineHistory({\mdseries\slshape [fname][,] [app]})\index{ReadCommandLineHistory@\texttt{ReadCommandLineHistory}}
\label{ReadCommandLineHistory}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\textbf{\indent Returns:\ }
\texttt{fail} or number of added lines



 The first command saves the lines in the command line history to the file
given by the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}}. The default for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}} is \texttt{history} in the user's \textsf{GAP} root path \texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot} or \texttt{"\texttt{\symbol{126}}/.gap{\textunderscore}hist"} if this directory does not exist. If the optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape app}} is \texttt{true} then the lines are appended to that file otherwise the file is overwritten. 

 The second command is the converse, it reads the lines from file \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}}. If the optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape app}} is true the lines are appended to the history, else it \emph{prepends} them. 

 By default, the command line history stores up to 1000 input lines. command
line history. This number may be restricted or enlarged via via \texttt{SetUserPreference("HistoryMaxLines", num);} which may be set to a non negative number \texttt{num} to store up to \texttt{num} input lines or to \texttt{infinity} to store arbitrarily many lines. An automatic storing and restoring of the
command line history can be configured via \texttt{SetUserPreference("SaveAndRestoreHistory", true);}. 

 Note that these functions are only available if your \textsf{GAP} is configured to use the \texttt{readline} library. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Writing your own command line editing functions}}\label{ssec:readlineUserFuncs}
\logpage{[ 6, 9, 4 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X87D4EA197A263FB7}{}
{
 \index{InstallReadlineMacro@\texttt{InstallReadlineMacro}} \index{InvocationReadlineMacro@\texttt{InvocationReadlineMacro}}  It is possible to write new command line editing functions in \textsf{GAP} as follows. 

 The functions have one argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape l}} which is a list with five entries of the form \texttt{[count, key, line, cursorpos, markpos]} where \texttt{count} and \texttt{key} are the last pressed key and its count (these are not so useful here because
users probably do not want to overwrite the binding of a single key), then \texttt{line} is a string containing the line typed so far, \texttt{cursorpos} is the current position of the cursor (point), and \texttt{markpos} the current position of the mark. 

 The result of such a function must be a list which can have various forms: 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{[str]}}] with a string \texttt{str}. In this case the text \texttt{str} is inserted at the cursor position.
\item[{\texttt{[kill, begin, end]}}]  where \texttt{kill} is \texttt{true} or \texttt{false} and \texttt{begin} and \texttt{end} are positions on the input line. This removes the text from the lower position
to before the higher position. If \texttt{kill} is \texttt{true} the text is killed, i.e. put in the kill ring for later yanking. 
\item[{\texttt{[begin, end, str]}}] where \texttt{begin} and \texttt{end} are positions on the input line and \texttt{str} is a string. Then the text from position \texttt{begin} to before \texttt{end} is substituted by \texttt{str}. 
\item[{\texttt{[1, lstr]}}]  where \texttt{lstr} is a list of strings. Then these strings are displayed like a list of possible
completions. The input line is not changed. 
\item[{\texttt{[2, chars]}}] where \texttt{chars} is a string. The characters from \texttt{chars} are used as the next characters from the input. (At most 512 characters are
possible.)
\item[{\texttt{[100]}}] This rings the bell as configured in the terminal.
\end{description}
 In the first three cases the result list can contain a position as a further
entry, this becomes the new cursor position. Or it can contain two positions
as further entries, these become the new cursor position and the new position
of the mark. 

 Such a function can be installed as a macro for \texttt{readline} via \texttt{InstallReadlineMacro(name, fun);} where \texttt{name} is a string used as name of the macro and \texttt{fun} is a function as above. This macro can be called by a key sequence which is
returned by \texttt{InvocationReadlineMacro(name);}. 

 As an example we define a function which puts double quotes around the word
under or before the cursor position. The space character, the characters in \texttt{"(,)"}, and the beginning and end of the line are considered as word boundaries. The
function is then installed as a macro and bound to the key sequence \textsc{Esc} \textsc{Q}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@EditAddQuotes := function(l)|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  local str, pos, i, j, new;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  str := l[3];|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  pos := l[4];|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  i := pos;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  while i > 1 and (not str[i-1] in ",( ") do|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@    i := i-1;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  od;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  j := pos;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  while IsBound(str[j]) and not str[j] in ",) " do|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@    j := j+1;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  od;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  new := "\"";|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  Append(new, str{[i..j-1]});|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  Append(new, "\"");|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  return [i, j, new];|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@end;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InstallReadlineMacro("addquotes", EditAddQuotes);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@invl := InvocationReadlineMacro("addquotes");;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ReadlineInitLine(Concatenation("\"\\eQ\":\"",invl,"\""));;|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Editing Files}}\label{Editing Files}
\logpage{[ 6, 10, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D8E1CF47E97A764}{}
{
  In most cases, it is preferable to create longer input (in particular \textsf{GAP} programs) separately in an editor, and to read in the result via \texttt{Read} (\ref{Read}). Note that \texttt{Read} (\ref{Read}) by default reads from the directory in which \textsf{GAP} was started (respectively under Windows the directory containing the \textsf{GAP} binary), so you might have to give an absolute path to the file. 

 If you cannot create several windows, the \texttt{Edit} (\ref{Edit}) command may be used to leave \textsf{GAP}, start an editor, and read in the edited file automatically. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Edit}}
\logpage{[ 6, 10, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82E5859C8113BA4D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Edit({\mdseries\slshape filename})\index{Edit@\texttt{Edit}}
\label{Edit}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{Edit} starts an editor with the file whose filename is given by the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filename}}, and reads the file back into \textsf{GAP} when you exit the editor again. 

 \textsf{GAP} will call your preferred editor if you call \texttt{SetUserPreference("Editor", \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path}});} where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape path}} is the path to your editor, e.g., \texttt{/usr/bin/vim}. On Windows you can use \texttt{edit.com}. 

 Under macOS, you should use \texttt{SetUserPreference("Editor", "open");}, this will open the file in the default editor. If you call \texttt{SetUserPreference("EditorOptions", ["\texttt{\symbol{45}}t"]);}, the file will open in \texttt{TextEdit}, and \texttt{SetUserPreference("EditorOptions", ["\texttt{\symbol{45}}a",
"{\textless}appl{\textgreater}"]);} will open the file using the application \texttt{{\textless}appl{\textgreater}}. 

 This can for example be done in your \texttt{gap.ini} file, see Section \ref{subsect:gap.ini file}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Editor Support}}\label{Editor Support}
\logpage{[ 6, 11, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7B67FF1E87FE67D1}{}
{
  \index{utilities for editing GAP files} \index{vi@\texttt{vi}} \index{vim@\texttt{vim}} \index{emacs@\texttt{emacs}} In the \texttt{etc} subdirectory of the \textsf{GAP} installation we provide some setup files for the editor \texttt{vim}. 

 \texttt{vim} is a powerful editor that understands the basic \texttt{vi} commands but provides much more functionality. You can find more information
about it (and download it) from \href{https://www.vim.org} {\texttt{https://www.vim.org}}. 

 To get support for \textsf{GAP} syntax in vim, create in your home directory a directory \texttt{.vim} with subdirectories \texttt{.vim/syntax} and \texttt{.vim/indent} (If you are not using Unix, refer to the \texttt{vim} documentation on where to place syntax files). Then copy the file \texttt{etc/vim/gap.vim} to \texttt{.vim/syntax/gap.vim} and the file \texttt{etc/vim/gap{\textunderscore}indent.vim} to \texttt{.vim/indent/gap.vim}. 

 Then edit the \texttt{.vimrc} file in your home directory. Add lines as in the following example: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|C,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  if has("syntax")
    syntax on             " Default to no syntax highlighting
  endif
  
  " For GAP files
  augroup gap
    " Remove all gap autocommands
    au!
  autocmd BufRead,BufNewFile *.g,*.gi,*.gd set filetype=gap comments=s:##\ \ ,m:##\ \ ,e:##\ \ b:#
  
  " I'm using the external program `par' for formatting comment lines starting
  " with `##  '. Include these lines only when you have par installed.
    autocmd BufRead,BufNewFile *.g,*.gi,*.gd set formatprg="par w76p4s0j"
    autocmd BufWritePost,FileWritePost *.g,*.gi,*.gd set formatprg="par w76p0s0j"
  augroup END
\end{Verbatim}
 

 See the headers of the two mentioned files for additional comments and adjust
details according to your personal taste. Send comments and suggestions to \href{mailto://support@gap-system.org} {\texttt{support@gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system.org}}. 

 Users of \texttt{emacs}/\texttt{xemacs} may wish to take a look at the \href{https://melpa.org/#/gap-mode} {major-mode for editing GAP files} by Ivan Andrus. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Changing the Screen Size}}\label{sect:SizeScreen}
\logpage{[ 6, 12, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83279E897ACCFFFA}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SizeScreen}}
\logpage{[ 6, 12, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8723E0A1837894F3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SizeScreen({\mdseries\slshape [sz]})\index{SizeScreen@\texttt{SizeScreen}}
\label{SizeScreen}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Called with no arguments, \texttt{SizeScreen} returns the size of the screen as a list with two entries. The first is the
length of each line, the second is the number of lines. 

 Called with one argument that is a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sz}}, \texttt{SizeScreen} sets the size of the screen; The first entry of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sz}}, if bound, is the length of each line, and the second entry of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sz}}, if bound, is the number of lines. The values for unbound entries of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sz}} are left unaffected. The function returns the new values. 

 Note that those parameters can also be set with the command line options \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}x} for the line length and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}y} for the number of lines (see Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Command Line Options}). 

 To check/change whether line breaking occurs for files and streams
see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{PrintFormattingStatus} (\ref{PrintFormattingStatus}) and{\nobreakspace}\texttt{SetPrintFormattingStatus} (\ref{SetPrintFormattingStatus}). 

 The line length must be between $20$ and $4096$ characters (inclusive) and the number of lines must be at least $10$. Values outside this range will be adjusted to the nearest endpoint of the
range. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Teaching Mode}}\label{Teaching Mode}
\logpage{[ 6, 13, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X87847E5087D6F47D}{}
{
  When using \textsf{GAP} in the context of (undergraduate) teaching it is often desirable to simplify
some of the system output and functionality defaults (potentially at the cost
of making the printing of objects more expensive). This can be achieved by
turning on a teaching mode: 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TeachingMode}}
\logpage{[ 6, 13, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BE2515F82425404}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TeachingMode({\mdseries\slshape [switch]})\index{TeachingMode@\texttt{TeachingMode}}
\label{TeachingMode}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 When called with a boolean argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape switch}}, this function will turn teaching mode respectively on or off. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:=Z(11)^3;|
  Z(11)^3
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@TeachingMode(true);|
  #I  Teaching mode is turned ON
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a;|
  ZmodnZObj(8,11)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@TeachingMode(false);|
  #I  Teaching mode is turned OFF
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a;|
  Z(11)^3
\end{Verbatim}
 At the moment, teaching mode changes the following things 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{Prime Field Elements}]  Elements of fields of prime order are printed as \texttt{ZmodnZObj} (\ref{ZmodnZObj:for two integers}) instead as power of a primitive root. 
\item[{Quadratic Irrationalities}]  Elements of a quadratic extension of the rationals are printed using the
square root \texttt{ER} (\ref{ER}) instead of using roots of unity. 
\item[{Creation of some small groups}]  The group creator functions \texttt{CyclicGroup} (\ref{CyclicGroup}), \texttt{AbelianGroup} (\ref{AbelianGroup}), \texttt{ElementaryAbelianGroup} (\ref{ElementaryAbelianGroup}), and \texttt{DihedralGroup} (\ref{DihedralGroup}) create by default (if no other representation is specified) not a pc group,
but a finitely presented group, which makes the generators easier to
interpret. 
\end{description}
 }

 }

 }

            
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Debugging and Profiling Facilities}}\label{Debugging and Profiling Facilities}
\logpage{[ 7, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8345F6817DFD6394}{}
{
  This chapter describes some functions that are useful mainly for debugging and
profiling purposes. 

 Probably the most important debugging tool in \textsf{GAP} is the break loop (see Section \ref{Break Loops}) which can be entered by putting an \texttt{Error} (\ref{Error}) statement into your code or by hitting Control\texttt{\symbol{45}}C. In the
break loop one can inspect variables, stack traces and issue commands as usual
in an interactive \textsf{GAP} session. See also the \texttt{DownEnv} (\ref{DownEnv}), \texttt{UpEnv} (\ref{UpEnv}), \texttt{Where} (\ref{Where}) and \texttt{WhereWithVars} (\ref{WhereWithVars}) functions. 

 Sections{\nobreakspace}\ref{sect:ApplicableMethod} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Tracing Methods} show how to get information about the methods chosen by the method selection
mechanism (see chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Method Selection}). 

 The final sections describe functions for collecting statistics about
computations (see \texttt{Runtime} (\ref{Runtime}), \ref{Profiling}).  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Recovery from NoMethodFound\texttt{\symbol{45}}Errors}}\label{Recovery from NoMethodFound-Errors}
\logpage{[ 7, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83C45B0A797AAF96}{}
{
  When the method selection fails because there is no applicable method, an
error as in the following example occurs and a break loop is entered: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|IsNormal(2,2);A
  Error, no method found! For debugging hints type ?Recovery from NoMethodFound
  Error, no 1st choice method found for `IsNormal' on 2 arguments
  called from read-eval loop at *stdin*:1
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop
  @gapbrkprompt|brk>A @gapinput|A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 This only says, that the method selection tried to find a method for \texttt{IsNormal} on two arguments and failed. In this situation it is crucial to find out, why
this happened. Therefore there are a few functions which can display further
information. Note that you can leave the break loop by the \texttt{quit} command (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{quit}) and that the information about the incident is no longer accessible
afterwards. 

   

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ShowArguments}}
\logpage{[ 7, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86B5FEC67A9394DC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ShowArguments({\mdseries\slshape })\index{ShowArguments@\texttt{ShowArguments}}
\label{ShowArguments}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function is only available within a break loop caused by a ``No Method Found''\texttt{\symbol{45}}error. It prints as a list the arguments of the operation
call for which no method was found.   }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ShowArgument}}
\logpage{[ 7, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X834BD9928773DCC1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ShowArgument({\mdseries\slshape nr})\index{ShowArgument@\texttt{ShowArgument}}
\label{ShowArgument}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function is only available within a break loop caused by a ``No Method Found''\texttt{\symbol{45}}error. It prints the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th arguments of the operation call for which no method was
found. \texttt{ShowArgument} needs exactly one argument which is an integer between 0 and the number of
arguments the operation was called with. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ShowDetails}}
\logpage{[ 7, 1, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D25D904800D5CBA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ShowDetails({\mdseries\slshape })\index{ShowDetails@\texttt{ShowDetails}}
\label{ShowDetails}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function is only available within a break loop caused by a ``No Method Found''\texttt{\symbol{45}}error. It prints the details of this error: The operation,
the number of arguments, a flag which indicates whether the operation is being
traced, a flag which indicates whether the operation is a constructor method,
and the number of methods that refused to apply by calling \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}). The last number is called \texttt{Choice} and is printed as an ordinal. So if exactly $k$ methods were found but called \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}) and there were no more methods it says \texttt{Choice: }$k$\texttt{th}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ShowMethods}}
\logpage{[ 7, 1, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F6996CA872478B8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ShowMethods({\mdseries\slshape [verbosity]})\index{ShowMethods@\texttt{ShowMethods}}
\label{ShowMethods}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function is only available within a break loop caused by a ``No Method Found''\texttt{\symbol{45}}error. It prints an overview about the installed methods
for those arguments the operation was called with (using \ref{sect:ApplicableMethod}. The verbosity can be controlled by the optional integer parameter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape verbosity}}. The default is 2, which lists all applicable methods. With verbosity 1 \texttt{ShowMethods} only shows the number of installed methods and the methods matching, which can
only be those that were already called but refused to work by calling \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}). With verbosity 3 not only all installed methods but also the reasons why
they do not match are displayed. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ShowOtherMethods}}
\logpage{[ 7, 1, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E5E2E7B85029E34}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ShowOtherMethods({\mdseries\slshape [verbosity]})\index{ShowOtherMethods@\texttt{ShowOtherMethods}}
\label{ShowOtherMethods}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function is only available within a break loop caused by a ``No Method Found''\texttt{\symbol{45}}error. It prints an overview about the installed methods
for a different number of arguments than the number of arguments the operation
was called with (using \ref{sect:ApplicableMethod}. The verbosity can be controlled by the optional integer parameter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape verbosity}}. The default is 1 which lists only the number of applicable methods. With
verbosity 2 \texttt{ShowOtherMethods} lists all installed methods and with verbosity 3 also the reasons, why they
are not applicable. Calling \texttt{ShowOtherMethods} with verbosity 3 in this function will normally not make any sense, because
the different numbers of arguments are simulated by supplying the
corresponding number of ones, for which normally no reasonable methods will be
installed. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Inspecting Applicable Methods}}\label{sect:ApplicableMethod}
\logpage{[ 7, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7FDA1D4B87BD25A8}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ApplicableMethod}}
\logpage{[ 7, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80848FF486BD6F9F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ApplicableMethod({\mdseries\slshape opr, args[, printlevel[, nr]]})\index{ApplicableMethod@\texttt{ApplicableMethod}}
\label{ApplicableMethod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ApplicableMethodTypes({\mdseries\slshape opr, args[, printlevel[, nr]]})\index{ApplicableMethodTypes@\texttt{ApplicableMethodTypes}}
\label{ApplicableMethodTypes}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Called with two arguments, \texttt{ApplicableMethod} returns the method of highest rank that is applicable for the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} with the arguments in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args}}. The default \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape printlevel}} is \texttt{0}. If no method is applicable then \texttt{fail} is returned. 

 If a positive integer is given as the fourth argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} then \texttt{ApplicableMethod} returns the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th applicable method for the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} with the arguments in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args}}, where the methods are ordered according to descending rank. If less than \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} methods are applicable then \texttt{fail} is returned. 

 If the fourth argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} is the string \texttt{"all"} then \texttt{ApplicableMethod} returns a list of all applicable methods for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} with arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args}}, ordered according to descending rank. 

 Depending on the integer value \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape printlevel}}, additional information is printed. Admissible values and their meaning are
as follows. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{0}]  no information, 
\item[{1}]  information about the applicable method, 
\item[{2}]  also information about the not applicable methods of higher rank, 
\item[{3}]  also for each not applicable method the first reason why it is not applicable, 
\item[{4}]  also for each not applicable method all reasons why it is not applicable. 
\item[{6}]  also the function body of the selected method(s) 
\end{description}
 

 When a method returned by \texttt{ApplicableMethod} is called then it returns either the desired result or the string \texttt{"TRY{\textunderscore}NEXT{\textunderscore}METHOD"}, which corresponds to a call to \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}) in the method and means that the method selection would call the next
applicable method. 

 \emph{Note:} The \textsf{GAP} kernel provides special treatment for the infix operations \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}+}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod} and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}in}. For some kernel objects (notably cyclotomic numbers, finite field elements
and row vectors thereof) it calls kernel methods circumventing the method
selection mechanism. Therefore for these operations \texttt{ApplicableMethod} may return a method which is not the kernel method actually used. 

 The function \texttt{ApplicableMethodTypes} takes the \emph{types} or \emph{filters} of the arguments as argument (if only filters are given of course family
predicates cannot be tested). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MethodsOperation}}
\logpage{[ 7, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D88B5FE839FFD02}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MethodsOperation({\mdseries\slshape oper, n})\index{MethodsOperation@\texttt{MethodsOperation}}
\label{MethodsOperation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Return a list of records that describe the installed methods for the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oper}}, with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} arguments. 

 Each record has at least the following components. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{func}] the method itself, a \textsf{GAP} function,
\item[{rank}] the rank of the method, an integer or infinity,
\item[{info}] a string that describes when the method is applicable,
\item[{location}] filename and start line where the method gets installed.
\end{description}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Tracing Methods}}\label{Tracing Methods}
\logpage{[ 7, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D43A2D885B37739}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TraceMethods (for operations)}}
\logpage{[ 7, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80B044017C9E4137}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TraceMethods({\mdseries\slshape opr1, opr2, ...})\index{TraceMethods@\texttt{TraceMethods}!for operations}
\label{TraceMethods:for operations}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TraceMethods({\mdseries\slshape oprs})\index{TraceMethods@\texttt{TraceMethods}!for a list of operations}
\label{TraceMethods:for a list of operations}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 After the call of \texttt{TraceMethods}, whenever a method of one of the operations \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr1}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr2}}, ... is called, the information string used in the installation of the method
is printed. The second form has the same effect for each operation from the
list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oprs}} of operations. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TraceAllMethods}}
\logpage{[ 7, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D34CADB813A4AF1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TraceAllMethods({\mdseries\slshape })\index{TraceAllMethods@\texttt{TraceAllMethods}}
\label{TraceAllMethods}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Invokes \texttt{TraceMethods} for all operations. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UntraceMethods (for operations)}}
\logpage{[ 7, 3, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EB04D387C53E4C1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UntraceMethods({\mdseries\slshape opr1, opr2, ...})\index{UntraceMethods@\texttt{UntraceMethods}!for operations}
\label{UntraceMethods:for operations}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UntraceMethods({\mdseries\slshape oprs})\index{UntraceMethods@\texttt{UntraceMethods}!for a list of operations}
\label{UntraceMethods:for a list of operations}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 turns the tracing off for all operations \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr1}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr2}}, ... or in the second form, for all operations in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oprs}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@TraceMethods( [ Size ] );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Group( (1,2,3), (1,2) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( g );|
  #I  Size: for a permutation group at /gap5/lib/grpperm.gi:487
  #I  Setter(Size): system setter
  #I  Size: system getter
  #I  Size: system getter
  6
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UntraceMethods( [ Size ] );|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UntraceAllMethods}}
\logpage{[ 7, 3, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B3018AA82D55949}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UntraceAllMethods({\mdseries\slshape })\index{UntraceAllMethods@\texttt{UntraceAllMethods}}
\label{UntraceAllMethods}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Equivalent to calling \texttt{UntraceMethods} for all operations. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TraceImmediateMethods}}
\logpage{[ 7, 3, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81078D3387A38E31}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TraceImmediateMethods({\mdseries\slshape [flag]})\index{TraceImmediateMethods@\texttt{TraceImmediateMethods}}
\label{TraceImmediateMethods}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UntraceImmediateMethods({\mdseries\slshape })\index{UntraceImmediateMethods@\texttt{UntraceImmediateMethods}}
\label{UntraceImmediateMethods}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{TraceImmediateMethods} enables tracing for all immediate methods if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape flag}} is either \texttt{true}, or not present. \texttt{UntraceImmediateMethods}, or \texttt{TraceImmediateMethods} with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape flag}} equal \texttt{false} turns tracing off. (There is no facility to trace \emph{specific} immediate methods.) 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@TraceImmediateMethods( );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Group( (1,2,3), (1,2) );;|
  #I RunImmediateMethods
  #I  immediate: Size
  #I  immediate: IsCyclic
  #I  immediate: IsCommutative
  #I  immediate: IsTrivial
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( g );|
  #I  immediate: IsPerfectGroup
  #I  immediate: IsNonTrivial
  #I  immediate: Size
  #I  immediate: IsFreeAbelian
  #I  immediate: IsTorsionFree
  #I  immediate: IsNonTrivial
  #I  immediate: IsPerfectGroup
  #I  immediate: GeneralizedPcgs
  #I  immediate: IsEmpty
  6
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UntraceImmediateMethods( );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UntraceMethods( [ Size ] );|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 This example gives an explanation for the two calls of the ``system getter'' for \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}). Namely, there are immediate methods that access the known size of the group.
Note that the group \texttt{g} was known to be finitely generated already before the size was computed, the
calls of the immediate method for \texttt{IsFinitelyGeneratedGroup} (\ref{IsFinitelyGeneratedGroup}) after the call of \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}) have other arguments than \texttt{g}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TraceInternalMethods}}
\logpage{[ 7, 3, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81B000CF86BA1534}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TraceInternalMethods({\mdseries\slshape })\index{TraceInternalMethods@\texttt{TraceInternalMethods}}
\label{TraceInternalMethods}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UntraceInternalMethods({\mdseries\slshape })\index{UntraceInternalMethods@\texttt{UntraceInternalMethods}}
\label{UntraceInternalMethods}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GetTraceInternalMethodsCounts({\mdseries\slshape })\index{GetTraceInternalMethodsCounts@\texttt{GetTraceInternalMethodsCounts}}
\label{GetTraceInternalMethodsCounts}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ClearTraceInternalMethodsCounts({\mdseries\slshape })\index{ClearTraceInternalMethodsCounts@\texttt{ClearTraceInternalMethodsCounts}}
\label{ClearTraceInternalMethodsCounts}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{TraceInternalMethods} enables tracing for all internal methods. Internal methods are methods which
implement many fundamental operations in GAP. In this version of GAP, the
internal methods which can be traced are: 
\begin{description}
\item[{Zero, ZeroMut}] Mutable and Immutable \texttt{Zero} (\ref{Zero})
\item[{AInv, AInvMut}] Mutable and Immutable \texttt{AdditiveInverse} (\ref{AdditiveInverse})
\item[{One, OneMut}] Mutable and Immutable \texttt{One} (\ref{One})
\item[{Inv, InvMut}] Mutable and Immutable \texttt{Inverse} (\ref{Inverse})
\item[{Sum}] The operator \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}+} (\ref{bSlash+})
\item[{Diff}] The operator \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}} operator
\item[{Prod}] The operator \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*} (\ref{bSlash*})
\item[{Quo}] The operator \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/} (\ref{bSlash/})
\item[{LQuo}] The left\texttt{\symbol{45}}quotient operator
\item[{Pow}] The operator \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}} (\ref{bSlash^})
\item[{Comm}] The operator \texttt{Comm} (\ref{Comm})
\item[{Mod}] The operator \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod} (\ref{bSlashmod})
\end{description}
 

 \texttt{UntraceInternalMethods} turns tracing off. As these methods can be called hundreds of thousands of
times in simple GAP code, there isn't a statement printed each time one is
called. Instead, the method \texttt{GetTraceInternalMethodsCounts} returns how many times each operation has been applied to each type of
variable (the type of a variable can be found with the \texttt{TNAM{\textunderscore}OBJ} method). The return value for two argument operators is a record of records \texttt{r}, where \texttt{r.op} stores information about operator \texttt{op}. For one argument operators \texttt{r.op.i} stores how many times \texttt{op} was called with an argument of type \texttt{i}, while for two argument operators \texttt{r.op.i.j} stores how many times \texttt{op} was called with arguments of type \texttt{i} and \texttt{j}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@TraceInternalMethods();|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@2+3+4+5+6;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@2.0+2.0;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@3^(1,2,3);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GetTraceInternalMethodsCounts();|
  rec( Pow := rec( integer := rec( ("permutation (small)") := 1 ) ),
  Sum := rec( integer := rec( integer := 4 ),
      macfloat := rec( macfloat := 1 ) ) )
  # 'macfloat' is a floating point number
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UntraceInternalMethods();|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Info Functions}}\label{Info Functions}
\logpage{[ 7, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7A9C902479CB6F7C}{}
{
  The \index{verbosity of GAP output}\texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) mechanism permits operations to display intermediate results or information
about the progress of the algorithms. Information is always given according to
one or more \emph{info classes}. Each of the info classes defined in the \textsf{GAP} library usually covers a certain range of algorithms, so for example \texttt{InfoLattice} covers all the cyclic extension algorithms for the computation of a subgroup
lattice. 

 Note that not all info classes defined in the \textsf{GAP} library are currently documented. Many \textsf{GAP} packages define additional info classes, which are typically documented in the
corresponding package documentation. The function \texttt{ShowUsedInfoClasses} (\ref{ShowUsedInfoClasses}) will show all info classes which \textsf{GAP} considers while executing code. 

 The amount of information to be displayed by each info class can be separately
specified by the user. This is done by selecting a
non\texttt{\symbol{45}}negative integer \emph{level} for the info class: no information will be displayed at level 0, and the
higher the level, the more information that will be displayed. At creation, an
info class has level 0. By default, all built\texttt{\symbol{45}}in GAP info
classes have level 0, except for the following info classes, which have level
1: 
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{InfoWarning} (\ref{InfoWarning}),
\item \texttt{InfoPackageLoading} (\ref{InfoPackageLoading}),
\item \texttt{InfoDebug},
\item \texttt{InfoPerformance},
\item \texttt{InfoTempDirectories},
\item \texttt{InfoPrimeInt}, and
\item \texttt{InfoSLP}.
\end{itemize}
 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NewInfoClass}}
\logpage{[ 7, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7AA1A1CF79F20790}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewInfoClass({\mdseries\slshape name})\index{NewInfoClass@\texttt{NewInfoClass}}
\label{NewInfoClass}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 creates a new info class with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. }

 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareInfoClass}}
\logpage{[ 7, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B3709C584B3DA1E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareInfoClass({\mdseries\slshape name})\index{DeclareInfoClass@\texttt{DeclareInfoClass}}
\label{DeclareInfoClass}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 creates a new info class with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} and binds it to the global variable \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The variable must previously be writable, and is made
read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only by this function. }

 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetInfoLevel}}
\logpage{[ 7, 4, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A43B9E68765EE9E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetInfoLevel({\mdseries\slshape infoclass, level})\index{SetInfoLevel@\texttt{SetInfoLevel}}
\label{SetInfoLevel}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Sets the info level for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape infoclass}} to the non\texttt{\symbol{45}}negative integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape level}}. }

 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoLevel}}
\logpage{[ 7, 4, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B2ADC37783104B9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoLevel({\mdseries\slshape infoclass})\index{InfoLevel@\texttt{InfoLevel}}
\label{InfoLevel}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the info level of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape infoclass}}. }

 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ShowUsedInfoClasses}}
\logpage{[ 7, 4, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BA636EF80A1435A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ShowUsedInfoClasses({\mdseries\slshape infoclass})\index{ShowUsedInfoClasses@\texttt{ShowUsedInfoClasses}}
\label{ShowUsedInfoClasses}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Called with argument \texttt{true}, this makes \textsf{GAP} print the info class and level of any executed \texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) statement. Calling with the argument \texttt{false} stops this printing. Each level of each info class is only printed once. The
history of printed info classes and levels is reset whenever \texttt{true} is passed. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ShowUsedInfoClasses(true);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Intersection(Group((1,3,2,4,5,6)), Group((1,2,3,4,5,6)));|
  #I Would print info with SetInfoLevel(InfoBckt,1)
  #I Would print info with SetInfoLevel(InfoBckt,3)
  #I Would print info with SetInfoLevel(InfoBckt,5)
  Group(())
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Intersection(Group((1,3,2,4,5,6)), Group((1,2,3,4,5,6)));|
  Group(())
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ShowUsedInfoClasses(false);|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Info}}
\logpage{[ 7, 4, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X864E4B6886E2697D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Info({\mdseries\slshape infoclass, level, info[, moreinfo, ...]})\index{Info@\texttt{Info}}
\label{Info}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 If the info level of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape infoclass}} is at least \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape level}}, then the remaining arguments, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, and possibly \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape moreinfo}} and so on, are evaluated. (Technically, \texttt{Info} is a keyword and not a function.) 

 By default, the results of these evaluations are viewed, preceded by the
string \texttt{"\#I "} and followed by a newline. 

 If the info level of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape infoclass}} is strictly less than \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape level}}, then the third and subsequent arguments are not evaluated. (The latter can
save substantial time when displaying difficult results.) 

 The behaviour can be customized with \texttt{SetInfoHandler} (\ref{SetInfoHandler}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InfoExample:=NewInfoClass("InfoExample");;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Info(InfoExample,1,"one");Info(InfoExample,2,"two");|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetInfoLevel(InfoExample,1);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Info(InfoExample,1,"one");Info(InfoExample,2,"two");|
  #I  one
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetInfoLevel(InfoExample,2);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Info(InfoExample,1,"one");Info(InfoExample,2,"two");|
  #I  one
  #I  two
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InfoLevel(InfoExample);|
  2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Info(InfoExample,3,Length(Combinations([1..9999])));|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that the last \texttt{Info} call is executed without problems, since the actual level \texttt{2} of \texttt{InfoExample} causes \texttt{Info} to ignore the last argument, which prevents \texttt{Length(Combinations([1..9999]))} from being evaluated; note that an evaluation would be impossible due to
memory restrictions. 

 A set of info classes (called an \emph{info selector}) may be passed to a single \texttt{Info} statement. As a shorthand, info classes and selectors may be combined with \texttt{+} rather than \texttt{Union} (\ref{Union:for a list}). In this case, the message is triggered if the level of \emph{any} of the classes is high enough. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InfoExample:=NewInfoClass("InfoExample");;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetInfoLevel(InfoExample,0);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Info(InfoExample + InfoWarning, 1, "hello");|
  #I  hello
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Info(InfoExample + InfoWarning, 2, "hello");|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetInfoLevel(InfoExample,2);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Info(InfoExample + InfoWarning, 2, "hello");|
  #I  hello
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InfoLevel(InfoWarning);|
  1
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Customizing \texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) statements}}\logpage{[ 7, 4, 7 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X800234B5815CAC97}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetInfoHandler({\mdseries\slshape infoclass, handler})\index{SetInfoHandler@\texttt{SetInfoHandler}}
\label{SetInfoHandler}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetInfoOutput({\mdseries\slshape infoclass, out})\index{SetInfoOutput@\texttt{SetInfoOutput}}
\label{SetInfoOutput}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UnbindInfoOutput({\mdseries\slshape infoclass})\index{UnbindInfoOutput@\texttt{UnbindInfoOutput}}
\label{UnbindInfoOutput}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoOutput({\mdseries\slshape infoclass})\index{InfoOutput@\texttt{InfoOutput}}
\label{InfoOutput}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetDefaultInfoOutput({\mdseries\slshape out})\index{SetDefaultInfoOutput@\texttt{SetDefaultInfoOutput}}
\label{SetDefaultInfoOutput}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\textbf{\indent Returns:\ }
nothing



 This allows one to customize what happens in an \texttt{Info(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape infoclass}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape level}}, ...)} statement.

 In the first function, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape handler}} must be a function with three arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape infoclass}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape level}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}. Here \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} is the list containing the third argument and any subsequent optional
arguments of the \texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) call. 

 The default handler is the function \texttt{DefaultInfoHandler}. \index{DefaultInfoHandler@\texttt{DefaultInfoHandler}} It prints \texttt{"\#I "}, then the third and further arguments of the info statement, and finally a \texttt{"\texttt{\symbol{92}}n"}. 

 If the first argument of an \texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) statement is a sum of Info classes, the handler of the first summand is used. 

 The file or stream to which \texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) statements for individual \texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) classes print can be overridden with \texttt{SetInfoOutput}, retrieved with \texttt{InfoOutput} and reset to the default with \texttt{UnbindInfoOutput}. The initial default for all \texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) classes is the string \texttt{"*Print*"} which means the current output file. The default can be changed with \texttt{SetDefaultInfoOutput}. The argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape out}} can be a filename or an open stream, the special names \texttt{"*Print*"}, \texttt{"*errout*} and \texttt{"*stdout*} are also recognized.
