 For example, \texttt{SetDefaultInfoOutput("*errout*");} would send \texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) output to standard error, which can be interesting if \textsf{GAP}s output is redirected. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoWarning}}
\logpage{[ 7, 4, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A28F77C82D6A3E0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoWarning\index{InfoWarning@\texttt{InfoWarning}}
\label{InfoWarning}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (info class)}}\\


 is an info class to which general warnings are sent at level 1, which is its
default level. More specialised warnings are shown via calls of \texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) at \texttt{InfoWarning} level 2, e.g.{\nobreakspace}information about the autoloading of \textsf{GAP} packages and the initial line matched when displaying an
on\texttt{\symbol{45}}line help topic. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Assertions}}\label{Assertions}
\logpage{[ 7, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86425F067FC63A4C}{}
{
  Assertions are used to find errors in algorithms. They test whether
intermediate results conform to required conditions and issue an error if not. 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetAssertionLevel}}
\logpage{[ 7, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C7596418423660B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetAssertionLevel({\mdseries\slshape lev})\index{SetAssertionLevel@\texttt{SetAssertionLevel}}
\label{SetAssertionLevel}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 assigns the global assertion level to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape lev}}. By default it is zero. }

 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AssertionLevel}}
\logpage{[ 7, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X876C83707F13A0FD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AssertionLevel({\mdseries\slshape })\index{AssertionLevel@\texttt{AssertionLevel}}
\label{AssertionLevel}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the current assertion level. }

 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Assert}}
\logpage{[ 7, 5, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X830E443284780FB9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Assert({\mdseries\slshape lev, cond[, message]})\index{Assert@\texttt{Assert}}
\label{Assert}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 With two arguments, if the global assertion level is at least \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape lev}}, condition \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cond}} is tested and if it does not return \texttt{true} an error is raised. Thus \texttt{Assert(lev, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cond}})} is equivalent to the code 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  if AssertionLevel() >= lev and not <cond> then
    Error("Assertion failure");
  fi;
\end{Verbatim}
 

 If the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape message}} argument form of the \texttt{Assert} statement is provided, and if an error is raised, then this message is printed
as part of the error. 

 Assertions are used at various places in the library. Thus turning assertions
on can slow code execution significantly. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Timing}}\label{Timing}
\logpage{[ 7, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X792BA9A67E64CDED}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Runtimes}}
\logpage{[ 7, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80355C9282B35673}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Runtimes({\mdseries\slshape })\index{Runtimes@\texttt{Runtimes}}
\label{Runtimes}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{Runtimes} returns a record with components bound to integers or \texttt{fail}. Each integer is the cpu time (processor time) in milliseconds spent by \textsf{GAP} in a certain status: 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{user{\textunderscore}time}}]  cpu time spent with \textsf{GAP} functions (without child processes). 
\item[{\texttt{system{\textunderscore}time}}]  cpu time spent in system calls, e.g., file access (\texttt{fail} if not available). 
\item[{\texttt{user{\textunderscore}time{\textunderscore}children}}]  cpu time spent in child processes (\texttt{fail} if not available). 
\item[{\texttt{system{\textunderscore}time{\textunderscore}children}}]  cpu time spent in system calls by child processes (\texttt{fail} if not available). 
\end{description}
 

 Note that this function is not fully supported on all systems. Only the \texttt{user{\textunderscore}time} component is (and may on some systems include the system time). 

 The following example demonstrates tasks which contribute to the different
time components: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@B,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>B !gapinput@Runtimes(); # after startupB
  rec( user_time := 3980, system_time := 60, user_time_children := 0,
    system_time_children := 0 )
  !gapprompt@gap>B !gapinput@Exec("cat /usr/bin/*||wc"); # child process with a lot of file accessB
   893799 7551659 200928302
  !gapprompt@gap>B !gapinput@Runtimes();B
  rec( user_time := 3990, system_time := 60, user_time_children := 1590,
    system_time_children := 600 )
  !gapprompt@gap>B !gapinput@a:=0;;for i in [1..100000000] do a:=a+1; od; # GAP user timeB
  !gapprompt@gap>B !gapinput@Runtimes();B
  rec( user_time := 12980, system_time := 70, user_time_children := 1590,
    system_time_children := 600 )
  !gapprompt@gap>B !gapinput@?blabla  # first call of help, a lot of file accessB
  Help: no matching entry found
  !gapprompt@gap>B !gapinput@Runtimes();B
  rec( user_time := 13500, system_time := 440, user_time_children := 1590,
    system_time_children := 600 )
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Runtime}}
\logpage{[ 7, 6, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E32B27F81870D24}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Runtime({\mdseries\slshape })\index{Runtime@\texttt{Runtime}}
\label{Runtime}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{Runtime} returns the time spent by \textsf{GAP} in milliseconds as an integer. It is the same as the value of the \texttt{user{\textunderscore}time} component given by \texttt{Runtimes} (\ref{Runtimes}), as explained above. 

 See \texttt{StringTime} (\ref{StringTime}) for a translation from milliseconds into hour/minute format. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NanosecondsSinceEpoch}}
\logpage{[ 7, 6, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X844E1CFE80F41760}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NanosecondsSinceEpoch({\mdseries\slshape })\index{NanosecondsSinceEpoch@\texttt{NanosecondsSinceEpoch}}
\label{NanosecondsSinceEpoch}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NanosecondsSinceEpochInfo({\mdseries\slshape })\index{NanosecondsSinceEpochInfo@\texttt{NanosecondsSinceEpochInfo}}
\label{NanosecondsSinceEpochInfo}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NanosecondsSinceEpoch} returns the time in nanoseconds that has passed since some fixed, but
unspecified time in the past. This function is appropriate for doing wallclock
time measurements. The actual resolution depends on the system that \textsf{GAP} is run on. Information about the used timers can be obtained by calling \texttt{NanosecondsSinceEpochInfo}, which returns a record containing members \texttt{Method}, \texttt{Monotonic}, \texttt{Reliable} and \texttt{Resolution}. 

 \texttt{Method} is a string describing the method used to obtain timer values. This will
usually contain the name of the syscall used. 

 \texttt{Monotonic} is a boolean. If it is \texttt{true}, then the values returned by \texttt{NanosecondsSinceEpoch} are guaranteed to be strictly monotonically increasing between two calls, if
it is \texttt{false} then there is no such guarantee. 

 \texttt{Resolution} is an integer reflecting the resolution of the timer used in nanoseconds. 

 \texttt{Reliable} is a boolean. If it is \texttt{true} then the value \texttt{Resolution} is deemed reliable in the sense that it was obtained by querying the operating
system, otherwise \texttt{Resolution} should be treated as an estimate. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{time}}
\logpage{[ 7, 6, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C0F91F982189624}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{time\index{time@\texttt{time}}
\label{time}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 In the read\texttt{\symbol{45}}eval\texttt{\symbol{45}}print loop, \texttt{time} stores the number of milliseconds the last command took (see also \texttt{memory{\textunderscore}allocated} (\ref{memoryuScoreallocated}) for the number of bytes of memory it allocated). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Sleep}}
\logpage{[ 7, 6, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B543F357C7202CF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Sleep({\mdseries\slshape time})\index{Sleep@\texttt{Sleep}}
\label{Sleep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MicroSleep({\mdseries\slshape time})\index{MicroSleep@\texttt{MicroSleep}}
\label{MicroSleep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 These functions make GAP stop execution for a given period of time. The time
to stop is given to \texttt{Sleep} in seconds and \texttt{MicroSleep} in microseconds. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Tracking Memory Usage}}\label{Tracking Memory Usage}
\logpage{[ 7, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X844CB04081A771FB}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TotalMemoryAllocated}}
\logpage{[ 7, 7, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8077B50B844C4EFC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TotalMemoryAllocated({\mdseries\slshape })\index{TotalMemoryAllocated@\texttt{TotalMemoryAllocated}}
\label{TotalMemoryAllocated}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{TotalMemoryAllocated} returns the total amount of memory in bytes allocated by the \textsf{GAP} memory manager since \textsf{GAP} started. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{memory{\textunderscore}allocated}}
\logpage{[ 7, 7, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8156D7208591460F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{memory{\textunderscore}allocated\index{memory{\textunderscore}allocated@\texttt{memory{\textunderscore}allocated}}
\label{memoryuScoreallocated}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 In the read\texttt{\symbol{45}}eval\texttt{\symbol{45}}print loop, \texttt{memory{\textunderscore}allocated} stores the number of bytes of memory allocated by the last completed statement
(see also \texttt{time} (\ref{time}) for the number of milliseconds it took). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Profiling}}\label{Profiling}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7FDF923D7D2937A1}{}
{
  Profiling of code can be used to determine in which parts of a program how
much time has been spent and how much memory has been allocated during
runtime. GAP has two different methods of profiling. GAP can either profile by
function, or line\texttt{\symbol{45}}by\texttt{\symbol{45}}line. Line by line
profiling is currently only used for code coverage, while function profiling
tracks memory and time usage. 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Function Profiling}}\label{FunctionProfiling}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7939F6F182FDA5F1}{}
{
  This section describes how to profiling at the function level. The idea is
that 
\begin{itemize}
\item  first one switches on profiling for those \textsf{GAP} functions the performance of which one wants to check, 
\item  then one runs some \textsf{GAP} computations, 
\item  then one looks at the profile information collected during these computations, 
\item  then one runs more computations (perhaps clearing all profile information
before, see \texttt{ClearProfile} (\ref{ClearProfile})), 
\item  and finally one switches off profiling. 
\end{itemize}
 

 For switching on and off profiling, \textsf{GAP} supports entering a list of functions (see \texttt{ProfileFunctions} (\ref{ProfileFunctions}), \texttt{UnprofileFunctions} (\ref{UnprofileFunctions})) or a list of operations whose methods shall be (un)profiled (\texttt{ProfileMethods} (\ref{ProfileMethods}), \texttt{UnprofileMethods} (\ref{UnprofileMethods})), and \texttt{DisplayProfile} (\ref{DisplayProfile}) can be used to show profile information about functions in a given list. 

 Besides these functions, \texttt{ProfileGlobalFunctions} (\ref{ProfileGlobalFunctions}), \texttt{ProfileOperations} (\ref{ProfileOperations}), and \texttt{ProfileOperationsAndMethods} (\ref{ProfileOperationsAndMethods}) can be used for switching on or off profiling for \emph{all} global functions, operations, and operations together with all their methods,
respectively, and for showing profile information about these functions. 

 Note that \textsf{GAP} will perform more slowly when profiling than when not. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ProfileGlobalFunctions}}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79D6CB927BBEB940}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ProfileGlobalFunctions({\mdseries\slshape [bool]})\index{ProfileGlobalFunctions@\texttt{ProfileGlobalFunctions}}
\label{ProfileGlobalFunctions}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Called with argument \texttt{true}, \texttt{ProfileGlobalFunctions} starts profiling of all functions that have been declared via \texttt{DeclareGlobalFunction} (\ref{DeclareGlobalFunction}). Old profile information for all these functions is cleared. A function call
with the argument \texttt{false} stops profiling of all these functions. Recorded information is still kept, so
you can display it even after turning the profiling off. 

 When \texttt{ProfileGlobalFunctions} is called without argument, profile information for all global functions is
displayed, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{DisplayProfile} (\ref{DisplayProfile}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ProfileOperations}}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C893F68841B990B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ProfileOperations({\mdseries\slshape [bool]})\index{ProfileOperations@\texttt{ProfileOperations}}
\label{ProfileOperations}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Called with argument \texttt{true}, \texttt{ProfileOperations} starts profiling of all operations. Old profile information for all operations
is cleared. A function call with the argument \texttt{false} stops profiling of all operations. Recorded information is still kept, so you
can display it even after turning the profiling off. 

 When \texttt{ProfileOperations} is called without argument, profile information for all operations is
displayed (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{DisplayProfile} (\ref{DisplayProfile})). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ProfileOperationsAndMethods}}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79D41E977DCA2BEE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ProfileOperationsAndMethods({\mdseries\slshape [bool]})\index{ProfileOperationsAndMethods@\texttt{ProfileOperationsAndMethods}}
\label{ProfileOperationsAndMethods}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Called with argument \texttt{true}, \texttt{ProfileOperationsAndMethods} starts profiling of all operations and their methods. Old profile information
for these functions is cleared. A function call with the argument \texttt{false} stops profiling of all operations and their methods. Recorded information is
still kept, so you can display it even after turning the profiling off. 

 When \texttt{ProfileOperationsAndMethods} is called without argument, profile information for all operations and their
methods is displayed, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{DisplayProfile} (\ref{DisplayProfile}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ProfileFunctions}}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81E8A8627C34FD3B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ProfileFunctions({\mdseries\slshape funcs})\index{ProfileFunctions@\texttt{ProfileFunctions}}
\label{ProfileFunctions}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 starts profiling for all function in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape funcs}}. You can use \texttt{ProfileGlobalFunctions} (\ref{ProfileGlobalFunctions}) to turn profiling on for all globally declared functions simultaneously. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UnprofileFunctions}}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79D394EC7BE8D008}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UnprofileFunctions({\mdseries\slshape funcs})\index{UnprofileFunctions@\texttt{UnprofileFunctions}}
\label{UnprofileFunctions}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 stops profiling for all function in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape funcs}}. Recorded information is still kept, so you can display it even after turning
the profiling off. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ProfileMethods}}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X787AC3BE7F991344}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ProfileMethods({\mdseries\slshape ops})\index{ProfileMethods@\texttt{ProfileMethods}}
\label{ProfileMethods}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 starts profiling of the methods for all operations in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ops}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UnprofileMethods}}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87A05F977F033693}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UnprofileMethods({\mdseries\slshape ops})\index{UnprofileMethods@\texttt{UnprofileMethods}}
\label{UnprofileMethods}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 stops profiling of the methods for all operations in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ops}}. Recorded information is still kept, so you can display it even after turning
the profiling off. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DisplayProfile}}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80FEA6A08775A48E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DisplayProfile({\mdseries\slshape [functions][,] [mincount, mintime]})\index{DisplayProfile@\texttt{DisplayProfile}}
\label{DisplayProfile}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GAPInfo.ProfileThreshold\index{GAPInfo.ProfileThreshold@\texttt{GAPInfo.ProfileThreshold}}
\label{GAPInfo.ProfileThreshold}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 Called without arguments, \texttt{DisplayProfile} displays the profile information for profiled operations, methods and
functions. If an argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape functions}} is given, only profile information for the functions in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape functions}} is shown. If two integer values \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mincount}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mintime}} are given as arguments then the output is restricted to those functions that
were called at least \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mincount}} times or for which the total time spent (see below) was at least \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mintime}} milliseconds. The defaults for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mincount}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mintime}} are the entries of the list stored in the global variable \texttt{GAPInfo.ProfileThreshold}. 

 The default value of \texttt{GAPInfo.ProfileThreshold} is \texttt{[ 10000, 30 ]}. 

 Profile information is displayed in a list of lines for all functions
(including operations and methods) which are profiled. For each function, ``count'' gives the number of times the function has been called. ``self/ms'' gives the time (in milliseconds) spent in the function itself, ``chld/ms'' the time (in milliseconds) spent in profiled functions called from within this
function, ``stor/kb'' the amount of storage (in kilobytes) allocated by the function itself, ``chld/kb'' the amount of storage (in kilobytes) allocated by profiled functions called
from within this function, and ``package'' the name of the \textsf{GAP} package to which the function belongs; the entry ``GAP'' in this column means that the function belongs to the \textsf{GAP} library, the entry ``(oprt.)'' means that the function is an operation (which may belong to several
packages), and an empty entry means that \texttt{FilenameFunc} (\ref{FilenameFunc}) cannot determine in which file the function is defined. 

 The list is sorted according to the total time spent in the functions, that is
the sum of the values in the columns ``self/ms'' and ``chld/ms''. 

 At the end of the list, two lines are printed that show the total time used
and the total memory allocated by the profiled functions not shown in the list
(label \texttt{OTHER}) and by all profiled functions (label \texttt{TOTAL}), respectively. 

 An interactive variant of \texttt{DisplayProfile} is the function \texttt{BrowseProfile} (\textbf{Browse: BrowseProfile}) that is provided by the \textsf{GAP} package \textsf{Browse}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ClearProfile}}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7DAF9AB9793AE203}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ClearProfile({\mdseries\slshape })\index{ClearProfile@\texttt{ClearProfile}}
\label{ClearProfile}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 clears all stored profile information. }

  
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{An Example of Function Profiling}}\label{subsect:profiling_example}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 11 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7C5CE32579891120}{}
{
  Let us suppose we want to get information about the computation of the
conjugacy classes of a certain permutation group. For that, first we create
the group, then we start profiling for all global functions and for all
operations and their methods, then we compute the conjugacy classes, and then
we stop profiling. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= PrimitiveGroup( 24, 1 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ProfileGlobalFunctions( true );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ProfileOperationsAndMethods( true );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ConjugacyClasses( g );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ProfileGlobalFunctions( false );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ProfileOperationsAndMethods( false );|
\end{Verbatim}

profiled functions with \texttt{DisplayProfile} (\ref{DisplayProfile}).

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Line By Line Profiling}}\label{linebylineprofiling}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 12 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X812F9CE0817110EA}{}
{
  Line By Line profiling tracks which lines have been executed in a piece of GAP
code. Built into GAP are the methods necessary to generate profiles, the
resulting profiles can be displayed with the 'profiling' package. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Line by Line profiling example}}\label{subsect:linebylineprofexample}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 13 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7E9C65B17B8EF993}{}
{
  There are two kinds of profiles GAP can build: 
\begin{itemize}
\item  Coverage : This records which lines of code are executed
\item  Timing : This records how much time is spend executing each line of code 
\end{itemize}
 A timing profile provides more information, but will take longer to generate
and parse. A timing profile is generated using the functions \texttt{ProfileLineByLine} (\ref{ProfileLineByLine}) and \texttt{UnprofileLineByLine} (\ref{UnprofileLineByLine}), as follows: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ProfileLineByLine("output.gz");|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(AlternatingGroup(10)); ; # Execute some GAP code you want to profile|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UnprofileLineByLine();|
\end{Verbatim}
 For code coverage, use instead the functions \texttt{CoverageLineByLine} (\ref{CoverageLineByLine}) and \texttt{UncoverageLineByLine} (\ref{UncoverageLineByLine}). The profiler will only record lines which are read and executed while the
profiler is running. If you want to perform code coverage or profile GAP's
library, then you can use the GAP command line option
'\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}cover filename.gz', which executes \texttt{CoverageLineByLine} (\ref{CoverageLineByLine}) before GAP starts. Similarly the option
'\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}prof filename.gz' executes \texttt{ProfileLineByLine} (\ref{ProfileLineByLine}) before GAP starts. The profiler is designed for high performance, because of
this, there are some limitations which users should be aware of: 
\begin{itemize}
\item  By default the profiler records the wall\texttt{\symbol{45}}clock time which
has passed, rather than the CPU time taken (because it is lower overhead), so
any time taken writing commands will be charged to the last GAP statement
which was executed. Therefore it is better to write a function which starts
profiling, executes your code, and then stops profiling. 
\item  If you end the filename with ".gz", the resulting file will automatically be
compressed. This is highly recommended! 
\item  The profiler can only track GAP code which occurs in a function
\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}} this is most obvious when looking at
code coverage examples, which will appear to miss lines of code in files not
in a function. 
\item  If the current GAP is forked, using the \texttt{IO{\textunderscore}fork} function in the \textsf{IO} package, a new profile output file will be created for the new child process,
with the process ID of the child attached to the end of the filename. 
\end{itemize}
 Profiles are transformed into a human\texttt{\symbol{45}}readable form with
'profiling' package, for example with the 'OutputAnnotatedCodeCoverageFiles'
function. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ProfileLineByLine}}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 14 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86557887796F66FA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ProfileLineByLine({\mdseries\slshape filename[, options]})\index{ProfileLineByLine@\texttt{ProfileLineByLine}}
\label{ProfileLineByLine}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{ProfileLineByLine} begins GAP recording profiling data to the file \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filename}}. This file will get *very* large very quickly. This file is compressed using
gzip to reduce its size. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape options}} is an optional dictionary, which sets various configuration options. These are 
\begin{description}
\item[{coverage}]  Boolean (defaults to false). If this is enabled, only information about which
lines are read and executed is stored. Enabling this is the same as calling \texttt{CoverageLineByLine} (\ref{CoverageLineByLine}). Using this ignores all other options.
\item[{wallTime}]  Boolean (defaults to true). Sets if time should be measured using
wall\texttt{\symbol{45}}clock time (true) or CPU time (false). (measuring
CPU\texttt{\symbol{45}}time has a higher overhead). 
\item[{recordMem}]  Boolean (defaults to false). Instead of recording the CPU time taken by
statements, record the total size of all new objects created by each line. 
\item[{resolution}]  Integer (defaults to 0). By default profiling will record a trace of all
executed code. When \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape resolution}} non\texttt{\symbol{45}}zero, GAP instead samples which piece of code is being
executed every \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape resolution}} nanoseconds. Increasing this improves performance and produces smaller traces,
at the cost of accuracy. GAP will still accurately record which statements are
executed at least once.
\end{description}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CoverageLineByLine}}
\logpage{[ 7, 8, 15 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87CC48807DB4C008}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CoverageLineByLine({\mdseries\slshape filename})\index{CoverageLineByLine@\texttt{CoverageLineByLine}}
\label{CoverageLineByLine}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{CoverageLineByLine} begins GAP recording code coverage to the file \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filename}}. This is equivalent to calling \texttt{ProfileLineByLine} (\ref{ProfileLineByLine}) with coverage=true. }

}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Stops profiling which was previously started with \texttt{ProfileLineByLine} (\ref{ProfileLineByLine}) or \texttt{CoverageLineByLine} (\ref{CoverageLineByLine}). }

\label{UncoverageLineByLine}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Stops profiling which was previously started with \texttt{ProfileLineByLine} (\ref{ProfileLineByLine}) or \texttt{CoverageLineByLine} (\ref{CoverageLineByLine}). }

\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Information about the version used}}\label{Information about the version used}
\logpage{[ 7, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7EE874867C0BEEDD}{}
{
  \index{GAPInfo.Version@\texttt{GAPInfo.Version}} The global variable \texttt{GAPInfo.Version} (see \texttt{GAPInfo} (\ref{GAPInfo})) contains the version number of the version of \textsf{GAP}. Its value can be checked other version number using \texttt{CompareVersionNumbers} (\ref{CompareVersionNumbers}). 

 To produce sample citations for the used version of \textsf{GAP} or for a package available in this \textsf{GAP} installation, use \texttt{Cite} (\ref{Cite}). 

 If you wish to report a problem to \textsf{GAP} Support or \textsf{GAP} Forum, it may be useful to not only report the version used, but also to
include the \textsf{GAP} banner displays the information about the architecture for which the \textsf{GAP} binary is built, used libraries and loaded packages. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Test Files}}\label{Test Files}
\logpage{[ 7, 10, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X801051CC86594630}{}
{
  Test files are used to check that \textsf{GAP} produces correct results in certain computations. A selection of test files
for the library can be found in the \texttt{tst} directory of the \textsf{GAP} distribution. 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Starting and stopping test}}\logpage{[ 7, 10, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8213757B7ACC76E6}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{START{\textunderscore}TEST({\mdseries\slshape name})\index{START{\textunderscore}TEST@\texttt{START{\textunderscore}TEST}}
\label{STARTuScoreTEST}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{STOP{\textunderscore}TEST({\mdseries\slshape name})\index{STOP{\textunderscore}TEST@\texttt{STOP{\textunderscore}TEST}}
\label{STOPuScoreTEST}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{START{\textunderscore}TEST} and \texttt{STOP{\textunderscore}TEST} may be optionally used in files that are read via \texttt{Test} (\ref{Test}). If used, \texttt{START{\textunderscore}TEST} reinitializes 
\begin{itemize}
\item  the caches (see \texttt{FlushCaches} (\ref{FlushCaches})), 
\item  the global random number generators (see \texttt{GlobalMersenneTwister} (\ref{GlobalMersenneTwister})), and 
\item  the global options stack (see Chapter \ref{Options Stack}), 
\end{itemize}
 in order to be independent of the reading order of several test files. 

 Furthermore, the assertion level (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Assert} (\ref{Assert})) is set to $2$ (if it was lower before) by \texttt{START{\textunderscore}TEST} and set back to the previous value in the subsequent \texttt{STOP{\textunderscore}TEST} call. 

 Also \texttt{STOP{\textunderscore}TEST} reinitializes the global options stack, otherwise it could happen that options
which got set during the tests are not reset after the tests. 

 To use this feature, a test file should be started with a line 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@START_TEST( "arbitrary identifier string" );|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 (Note that the \texttt{gap{\textgreater} } prompt is part of the line!) 

 and should be finished with a line 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@STOP_TEST( "same identifier string as for START_TEST" );|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 If you want to run a quick test of your \textsf{GAP} installation (though this is not required), you can read in a test script that
exercises some \textsf{GAP}'s capabilities. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Read( Filename( DirectoriesLibrary( "tst" ), "testinstall.g" ) );|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  test file         time(msec)
  -------------------------------------------
  testing: ................/gap4r5/tst/zlattice.tst
  zlattice.tst               0
  testing: ................/gap4r5/tst/gaussian.tst
  gaussian.tst              10
  [ further lines deleted ]
\end{Verbatim}
 If you want to run a more advanced check (this is not required and make take
up to an hour), you can read \texttt{teststandard.g} which is an extended test script performing all tests from the \texttt{tst} directory. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Read( Filename( DirectoriesLibrary( "tst" ), "teststandard.g" ) );|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Test}}
\logpage{[ 7, 10, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87712F9D8732193C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Test({\mdseries\slshape fname[, optrec]})\index{Test@\texttt{Test}}
\label{Test}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\textbf{\indent Returns:\ }
\texttt{true} or \texttt{false}.



 The argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}} must be the name of a file or an open input stream. The content of this file
or stream should contain \textsf{GAP} input and output. The function \texttt{Test} runs the input lines, compares the actual output with the output stored in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}} and reports differences. With an optional record as argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape optrec}} details of this process can be adjusted. Note that the \texttt{rewriteToFile} option is especially useful for generating test files. 

 More precisely, the content of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}} must have the following format. \\
 Lines starting with \texttt{"gap{\textgreater}{\nobreakspace}"} are considered as \textsf{GAP} input, they can be followed by lines starting with \texttt{"{\textgreater}{\nobreakspace}"} if the input is continued over several lines. \\
 To allow for comments in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}} the following lines are ignored by default: lines at the beginning of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}} that start with \texttt{"\#"} or are empty, and one empty line together with one or more lines starting with \texttt{"\#"}.\\
 All other lines are considered as \textsf{GAP} output from the preceding \textsf{GAP} input. 

 Lines which begin "\#@" define special configuration options for tests. The \texttt{\#@local} and \texttt{\#@exec} options can only be used before any \textsf{GAP} input, and the other commands can only be used between individual tests (just
before a line starting \texttt{gap{\textgreater}}, or at end of the file). Currently defined options are: 
\begin{description}
\item[{\#@local identifierlist}] Run all the tests in the input as if it is in a function with local variable
list \texttt{identifierlist}, which is a comma\texttt{\symbol{45}}separated list of identifiers. Multiple
\#@local lines may be used. These lines should \emph{not} end with a comma or semicolon. If this option is used then an error will occur
unless \emph{all} the variables used are included in the local list. 

 As an example, the \textsf{Utils} package has a test file \texttt{tst/iterator.tst} which starts with the lines: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  #@local  c3c3, cart, G, h, it1, it2, iter, iter0, iter4, iterL
  #@local  L, n, pairs0, pairs4, pairsL, s3, s4
\end{Verbatim}
 
\item[{\#@exec gapcode}] Execute the code \texttt{gapcode} before any test in the input is run. This allows defining global variables
when using \texttt{\#@local}. 
\item[{\#@if EXPR ... \texttt{\symbol{123}}\#@elif EXPR ...\texttt{\symbol{125}}
[\#@else ...] \#@fi}] A \texttt{\#@if} allows to conditionally skip parts of the test input depending on the value of
a boolean expression. The exact behavior is done as follows: 

 If the first \textsf{GAP} expression \texttt{EXPR} evaluates to \texttt{true}, then the lines after the \texttt{\#@if} are used until either a \texttt{\#@elif}, \texttt{\#@else} or \texttt{\#@fi} is reached. If an \texttt{\#@elif} is present, then the lines after \texttt{\#@elif} are used if and only if its \texttt{EXPR} evaluates to \texttt{true} and all previous \texttt{\#@if} and \texttt{\#@elif} clauses had expressions evaluating to \texttt{false}. In this case the lines after \texttt{\#@elif} are used until either a \texttt{\#@elif}, \texttt{\#@else} or \texttt{\#@fi} is reached. If an \texttt{\#@else} is present then the lines after the \texttt{\#@else} are used if and only if \texttt{EXPR} evaluated to \texttt{false} in all \texttt{\#@if} and \texttt{\#@elif} clauses. Finally, once \texttt{\#fi} is reached, evaluation continues normally. 

 Note that each \texttt{EXPR} is evaluated after all \texttt{\#@exec} lines have been executed but before any tests are run. Thus, it cannot depend
on test results or packages loaded in tests, but it can depend on packages
loaded via \texttt{\#@exec}. 

 In addition \texttt{\#@if} clauses cannot be nested within each other. 

 As an example, the \textsf{GAP} test suite contains the test file \texttt{tst/testinstall/pperm.tst} which contains the lines: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!|D,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  #@if GAPInfo.BytesPerVariable = 8
  !gapprompt|gap>D !gapinput|HASH_FUNC_FOR_PPERM(f, 10 ^ 6) in [260581, 402746];D
  true
  #@else
  !gapprompt|gap>D !gapinput|HASH_FUNC_FOR_PPERM(f, 10 ^ 6);D
  953600
  #@fi
\end{Verbatim}
 
\end{description}
 By default the actual \textsf{GAP} output is compared exactly with the stored output, and if these are different
some information about the differences is printed. 

 If any differences are found then \texttt{Test} returns \texttt{false}, otherwise \texttt{true}. 

 If the optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape optrec}} is given it must be a record. The following components of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape optrec}} are recognized and can change the default behaviour of \texttt{Test}: 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{ignoreComments}}] If set to \texttt{false} then no lines in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}} are ignored as explained above (default is \texttt{true}).
\item[{\texttt{width}}] The screen width used for the new output (default is \texttt{80}). 
\item[{\texttt{compareFunction}}] This must be a function that gets two strings as input, the newly generated
and the stored output of some \textsf{GAP} input. The function must return \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}, indicating if the strings should be considered equivalent or not. By default \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=} (\ref{bSlash=}) is used. \\
 Two strings are recognized as abbreviations in this component: \texttt{"uptowhitespace"} checks if the two strings become equal after removing all white space. And \texttt{"uptonl"} compares the string up to trailing newline characters. 
\item[{\texttt{transformFunction}}] This must be a function that gets one string as input, either the newly
generated or the stored output of some \textsf{GAP} input. The function must return a new string which will be used to compare the
actual and the expected output. By default \texttt{IdFunc} (\ref{IdFunc}) is used. \\
 Two strings are recognized as abbreviations in this component: \texttt{"removewhitespace"} removes all white space. And \texttt{"removenl"} removes all trailing newline characters. 
\item[{\texttt{reportDiff}}] A function that gets six arguments and reports a difference in the output: the \textsf{GAP} input, the expected \textsf{GAP} output, the newly generated output, the name of tested file, the line number
of the input, the time to run the input. (The default is demonstrated in the
example below.)
\item[{\texttt{rewriteToFile}}] If this is bound to a string it is considered as a file name and that file is
written with the same input and comment lines as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}} but the output substituted by the newly generated version; if it is bound to \texttt{true}, then this is treated as if it was bound to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}} (default is \texttt{false}). This is especially useful for generating test files because it ensures that
the test files are formatted exactly as \texttt{Test} expects them to be. 
\item[{\texttt{writeTimings}}] If this is bound to a string it is considered as a file name, that file is
written and contains timing information for each input in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fname}}. 
\item[{\texttt{compareTimings}}] If this is bound to a string it is considered as name of a file to which
timing information was stored via \texttt{writeTimings} in a previous call. The new timings are compared to the stored ones. By
default only commands which take more than a threshold of 100 milliseconds are
considered, and only differences of more than 20\% are considered significant.
These defaults can be overwritten by assigning a list \texttt{[timingfile, threshold, percentage]} to this component. (The default of \texttt{compareTimings} is \texttt{false}.)
\item[{\texttt{reportTimeDiff}}] This component can be used to overwrite the default function to display timing
differences. It must be a function with 5 arguments: \textsf{GAP} input, name of test file, line number, stored time, new time. 
\item[{\texttt{ignoreSTOP{\textunderscore}TEST}}] By default set to \texttt{true}, in that case the output of \textsf{GAP} input starting with \texttt{"STOP{\textunderscore}TEST"} is not checked.
\item[{\texttt{showProgress}}] If this is \texttt{true} then \textsf{GAP} prints position information and the input line before it is processed; if set
to \texttt{"some"}, then GAP shows the current line number of the test being processed; if set
to \texttt{false}, no progress updates are displayed (default is \texttt{"some"} if GAP's output goes to a terminal, otherwise \texttt{false}). 
\item[{\texttt{subsWindowsLineBreaks}}] If this is \texttt{true} then \textsf{GAP} substitutes DOS/Windows style line breaks
"\texttt{\symbol{92}}r\texttt{\symbol{92}}n" by UNIX style line breaks
"\texttt{\symbol{92}}n" after reading the test file. (default is \texttt{true}).
\item[{\texttt{returnNumFailures}}] If this is \texttt{true} then \textsf{GAP} returns the number of input lines of the test file which had differences in
their output, instead of returning \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}.
\end{description}
 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>A !gapinput@tnam := Filename(DirectoriesLibrary(), "../doc/ref/demo.tst");;A
  !gapprompt@gap>A !gapinput@mask := function(str) return Concatenation("| ",A
  !gapprompt@>A !gapinput@         JoinStringsWithSeparator(SplitString(str, "\n", ""), "\n| "),A
  !gapprompt@>A !gapinput@         "\n"); end;;A
  !gapprompt@gap>A !gapinput@Print(mask(StringFile(tnam)));A
  | # this is a demo file for the 'Test' function
  | #
  | gap> g := Group((1,2), (1,2,3));
  | Group([ (1,2), (1,2,3) ])
  |
  | # another comment following an empty line
  | # the following fails:
  | gap> a := 13+29;
  | 41
  !gapprompt@gap>A !gapinput@ss := InputTextString(StringFile(tnam));;A
  !gapprompt@gap>A !gapinput@Test(ss);A
  ########> Diff in test stream, line 8:
  # Input is:
  a := 13+29;
  # Expected output:
  41
  # But found:
  42
  ########
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>A !gapinput@RewindStream(ss);A
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>A !gapinput@dtmp := DirectoryTemporary();;A
  !gapprompt@gap>A !gapinput@ftmp := Filename(dtmp,"demo.tst");;A
  !gapprompt@gap>A !gapinput@Test(ss, rec(reportDiff := Ignore, rewriteToFile := ftmp));A
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>A !gapinput@Test(ftmp);A
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>A !gapinput@Print(mask(StringFile(ftmp)));A
  | # this is a demo file for the 'Test' function
  | #
  | gap> g := Group((1,2), (1,2,3));
  | Group([ (1,2), (1,2,3) ])
  |
  | # another comment following an empty line
  | # the following fails:
  | gap> a := 13+29;
  | 42
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TestDirectory}}
\logpage{[ 7, 10, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87AF67528799481F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TestDirectory({\mdseries\slshape inlist[, optrec]})\index{TestDirectory@\texttt{TestDirectory}}
\label{TestDirectory}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\textbf{\indent Returns:\ }
\texttt{true} or \texttt{false}.



 The argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape inlist}} must be either a single filename or directory name, or a list of filenames and
directories. The function \texttt{TestDirectory} will create a list of files to be tested by taking any files in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape inlist}}, and recursively searching any directories in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape inlist}} for files ending in \texttt{.tst}. Each of these files is then run through \texttt{Test} (\ref{Test}), and the results printed, and \texttt{true} returned if all tests passed. 

 If the optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape optrec}} is given it must be a record. Note that the \texttt{rewriteToFile} option is especially useful for generating test files. The following
components of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape optrec}} are recognized and can change the default behaviour of \texttt{TestDirectory}: 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{testOptions}}] A record which will be passed on as the second argument of \texttt{Test} (\ref{Test}) if present.
\item[{\texttt{earlyStop}}] If \texttt{true}, stop as soon as any \texttt{Test} (\ref{Test}) fails (defaults to \texttt{false}). 
\item[{\texttt{showProgress}}] Print information about how tests are progressing (defaults to \texttt{"some"} if GAP's output goes to a terminal, otherwise \texttt{false}). 
\item[{\texttt{suppressStatusMessage}}] suppress displaying status messages \texttt{\#I Errors detected while testing} and \texttt{\#I No errors detected while testing} after the test (defaults to \texttt{false}). 
\item[{\texttt{rewriteToFile}}] If \texttt{true}, then rewrite each test file to disc, with the output substituted by the
results of running the test (defaults to \texttt{false}). This is especially useful for generating test files because it ensures that
the test files are formatted exactly as \texttt{Test} (\ref{Test}) expects them to be. 
\item[{\texttt{exclude}}] A list of file and directory names which will be excluded from testing
(defaults to \texttt{[]}). 
\item[{\texttt{exitGAP}}] Rather than returning \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}, exit GAP with the return value of GAP set to success or fail, depending on
if all tests passed (defaults to \texttt{false}). 
\end{description}
 }

 See also \texttt{TestPackage} (\ref{TestPackage}) for the information on running standard tests for \textsf{GAP} packages. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Debugging Recursion}}\label{Debugging Recursion}
\logpage{[ 7, 11, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X85FF55448787CCA0}{}
{
  The \textsf{GAP} interpreter monitors the level of nesting of \textsf{GAP} functions during execution. By default, whenever this nesting reaches a
multiple of $5000$, \textsf{GAP} enters a break loop (\ref{Break Loops}) allowing you to terminate the calculation, or enter \textsc{Return}\texttt{;} to continue it. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|dive:= function(depth) if depth>1 then dive(depth-1); fi; return; end;A
  function( depth ) ... end
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|dive(100);A
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|OnBreak:= function() Where(2); end;; # shorter tracebackA
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|dive(6000);A
  Error, recursion depth trap (5000)
  Stack trace:
  *[1] dive( depth - 1 );
     @ *stdin*:1
   [2] dive( depth - 1 );
     @ *stdin*:1
  ...  at *stdin*:4
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  !gapbrkprompt|brk>A !gapinput|return;A
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|dive(11000);A
  Error, recursion depth trap (5000)
  Stack trace:
  *[1] dive( depth - 1 );
     @ *stdin*:1
   [2] dive( depth - 1 );
     @ *stdin*:1
  ...  at *stdin*:5
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  !gapbrkprompt|brk>A !gapinput|return;A
  Error, recursion depth trap (10000)
  Stack trace:
  *[1] dive( depth - 1 );
     @ *stdin*:1
   [2] dive( depth - 1 );
     @ *stdin*:1
  ...  at *stdin*:5
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  !gapbrkprompt|brk>A !gapinput|return;A
  gap>
\end{Verbatim}
 

 This behaviour can be controlled using the following procedures. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetRecursionTrapInterval}}
\logpage{[ 7, 11, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D8968FC7E24A4E5}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetRecursionTrapInterval({\mdseries\slshape interval})\index{SetRecursionTrapInterval@\texttt{SetRecursionTrapInterval}}
\label{SetRecursionTrapInterval}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GetRecursionDepth({\mdseries\slshape })\index{GetRecursionDepth@\texttt{GetRecursionDepth}}
\label{GetRecursionDepth}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{GetRecursionDepth} returns the nesting level of the GAP interpreter. This is reset to 0 every
time the break loop is entered. \texttt{SetRecursionTrapInterval} sets the depth of the stack at which GAP will enter the Break loop. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape interval}} must be a non\texttt{\symbol{45}}negative small integer (between 0 and $2^{28}$). An \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape interval}} of 0 suppresses the monitoring of recursion altogether. In this case excessive
recursion may cause \textsf{GAP} to crash. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|GetRecursionDepth();A
  0
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|dive := function(depth)A
  !gapprompt|>A !gapinput| if depth>1 thenA
  !gapprompt|>A !gapinput|   dive(depth-1);A
  !gapprompt|>A !gapinput| elseA
  !gapprompt|>A !gapinput|   Print("Depth ", GetRecursionDepth());A
  !gapprompt|>A !gapinput| fi;A
  !gapprompt|>A !gapinput|end;;A
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|SetRecursionTrapInterval(1000);A
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|OnBreak:= function() Where(2); end;; # shorter tracebackA
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|dive(100);A
  Depth 100
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|dive(2500);A
  Error, recursion depth trap (1000)
  Stack trace:
  *[1] dive( depth - 1 );
     @ *stdin*:4
   [2] dive( depth - 1 );
     @ *stdin*:4
  ...  at *stdin*:12
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  !gapbrkprompt|brk>A !gapinput|return;A
  Error, recursion depth trap (2000)
  Stack trace:
  *[1] dive( depth - 1 );
     @ *stdin*:4
   [2] dive( depth - 1 );
     @ *stdin*:4
  ...  at *stdin*:12
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  !gapbrkprompt|brk>A !gapinput|GetRecursionDepth();A
  0
  !gapbrkprompt|brk>A !gapinput|return;A
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|SetRecursionTrapInterval(2^50);A
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|dive(20000);A
  Depth 20000
  !gapprompt|gap>A !gapinput|dive(2000000);A
  Segmentation fault
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Global Memory Information}}\label{Global Memory Information}
\logpage{[ 7, 12, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X85679F17791D9B63}{}
{
  
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Garbage Collection}}\label{Garbage Collection}
\logpage{[ 7, 12, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7F1F741D7F0899D1}{}
{
  \index{GASMAN@\texttt{GASMAN}} The \textsf{GAP} environment provides automatic memory management, so that the programmer does
not need to concern themselves with allocating space for objects, or
recovering space when objects are no longer needed. The memory manager that
shall be used by \textsf{GAP} is specified at compile time. One of the choices is called \texttt{GASMAN} (\textsf{GAP} Storage MANager). (The name of the currently used garbage collector is stored
in the variable \texttt{GAPInfo.KernelInfo.GC}.) 

 If \textsf{GAP} uses \texttt{GASMAN} then messages reporting garbage collections performed by \texttt{GASMAN} can be switched on by the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}g} command line option (see section \ref{Command Line Options}). There are also some facilities to access information from \texttt{GASMAN} from \textsf{GAP} programs, see below. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CollectGarbage}}
\logpage{[ 7, 12, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7848AB367F3A1221}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CollectGarbage({\mdseries\slshape full})\index{CollectGarbage@\texttt{CollectGarbage}}
\label{CollectGarbage}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\textbf{\indent Returns:\ }
 nothing. 



 This function forces a garbage collection. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape full}} is \texttt{true} then it triggers a full garbage collection, otherwise a partial one. 

 \textsf{GAP} invokes its garbage collector automatically, thus there is normally no need to
call \texttt{CollectGarbage}. 

 The function \texttt{CollectGarbage} was introduced in \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4.12. In older \textsf{GAP} versions, one can use \texttt{GASMAN( "collect" )} (if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape full}} is \texttt{true}) or \texttt{GASMAN( "partial" )} (if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape full}} is not \texttt{true}) instead. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CollectGarbage( false );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CollectGarbage( true );|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GasmanStatistics}}
\logpage{[ 7, 12, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X836977DE80416F3D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GasmanStatistics({\mdseries\slshape })\index{GasmanStatistics@\texttt{GasmanStatistics}}
\label{GasmanStatistics}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function is meaningful only if \texttt{GASMAN} is the garbage collector used by \textsf{GAP}, see Section \ref{Garbage Collection}. 

 \texttt{GasmanStatistics} returns a record containing some information from the garbage collection
mechanism. The record may contain up to four components: \texttt{full}, \texttt{partial}, \texttt{npartial}, and \texttt{nfull}. 

 The \texttt{full} component will be present if a full garbage collection has taken place since \textsf{GAP} started. It contains information about the most recent full garbage
collection. It is a record, with eight components: \texttt{livebags} contains the number of bags which survived the garbage collection; \texttt{livekb} contains the total number of kilobytes occupied by those bags; \texttt{deadbags} contains the total number of bags which were reclaimed by that garbage
collection and all the partial garbage collections preceding it, since the
previous full garbage collection; \texttt{deadkb} contains the total number of kilobytes occupied by those bags; \texttt{freekb} reports the total number of kilobytes available in the \textsf{GAP} workspace for new objects; \texttt{totalkb} reports the actual size of the workspace; \texttt{time} reports the CPU time in milliseconds spent on the last garbage collection and \texttt{cumulative} the total CPU time in milliseconds spent on that type of garbage collection
since \textsf{GAP} started. 

 These figures should be viewed with some caution. They are stored internally
in fixed length integer formats, and \texttt{deadkb} and \texttt{deadbags} are liable to overflow if there are many partial collections before a full
collection. Also, note that \texttt{livekb} and \texttt{freekb} will not usually add up to \texttt{totalkb}. The difference is essentially the space overhead of the memory management
system. 

 The \texttt{partial} component will be present if there has been a partial garbage collection since
the last full one. It is also a record with the same six components as \texttt{full}. In this case \texttt{deadbags} and \texttt{deadkb} refer only to the number and total size of the garbage bags reclaimed in this
partial garbage collection and \texttt{livebags}and \texttt{livekb} only to the numbers and total size of the young bags that were considered for
garbage collection, and survived. 

 The \texttt{npartial} and \texttt{nfull} components will contain the number of full and partial garbage collections
performed since \textsf{GAP} started. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GasmanMessageStatus}}
\logpage{[ 7, 12, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85327FA5872E0356}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GasmanMessageStatus({\mdseries\slshape })\index{GasmanMessageStatus@\texttt{GasmanMessageStatus}}
\label{GasmanMessageStatus}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetGasmanMessageStatus({\mdseries\slshape stat})\index{SetGasmanMessageStatus@\texttt{SetGasmanMessageStatus}}
\label{SetGasmanMessageStatus}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function is meaningful only if \texttt{GASMAN} is the garbage collector used by \textsf{GAP}, see Section \ref{Garbage Collection}. 

 \texttt{GasmanMessageStatus} returns one of the strings \texttt{"none"}, \texttt{"full"}, or \texttt{"all"}, depending on whether the garbage collector is currently set to print
messages on no collections, full collections only, or all collections,
respectively. 

 Calling \texttt{SetGasmanMessageStatus} with the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stat}}, which should be one of the three strings mentioned above, sets the garbage
collector messaging level. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GasmanLimits}}
\logpage{[ 7, 12, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80C683247E94769F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GasmanLimits({\mdseries\slshape })\index{GasmanLimits@\texttt{GasmanLimits}}
\label{GasmanLimits}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function is meaningful only if \texttt{GASMAN} is the garbage collector used by \textsf{GAP}, see Section \ref{Garbage Collection}. 

 \texttt{GasmanLimits} returns a record with three components: \texttt{min} is the minimum workspace size as set by the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}m} command line option in kilobytes. The workspace size will never be reduced
below this by the garbage collector. \texttt{max} is the maximum workspace size, as set by the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}o} command line option, also in kilobytes. If the workspace would need to grow
past this point, \textsf{GAP} will enter a break loop to warn the user. A value of 0 indicates no limit. \texttt{kill} is the absolute maximum, set by the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}K} command line option. The workspace will never be allowed to grow past this
limit. }

 }

 }

            
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Options Stack}}\label{Options Stack}
\logpage{[ 8, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7FD84061873F72A2}{}
{
  \textsf{GAP} supports a \emph{global options system}. This is intended as a way for the user to provide guidance to various
algorithms that might be used in a computation. Such guidance should not
change mathematically the specification of the computation to be performed,
although it may change the algorithm used. A typical example is the selection
of a strategy for the Todd\texttt{\symbol{45}}Coxeter coset enumeration
procedure. An example of something not suited to the options mechanism is the
imposition of exponent laws in the $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}Quotient algorithm. 

 The basis of this system is a global stack of records. All the entries of each
record are thought of as options settings, and the effective setting of an
option is given by the topmost record in which the relevant field is bound. 

 The reason for the choice of a stack is the intended pattern of use: 

 \texttt{PushOptions( rec( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stuff}} ) );} 

 \texttt{DoSomething( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args}} );} 

 \texttt{PopOptions();} 

 This can be abbreviated, to \texttt{DoSomething( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args}} : \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stuff}} );} with a small additional abbreviation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stuff}} permitted. See \ref{Function Call With Options} for details. The full form can be used where the same options are to run
across several calls, or where the \texttt{DoSomething} procedure is actually an infix operator, or other function with special
syntax. 

 An alternative to this system is the use of additional optional arguments in
procedure calls. This is not felt to be sufficient because many procedure
calls might cause, for example, a coset enumeration and each would need to
make provision for the possibility of extra arguments. In this system the
options are pushed when the user\texttt{\symbol{45}}level procedure is called,
and remain in effect (unless altered) for all procedures called by it. 

 Note that in some places in the system optional records containing options
which are valid only for the immediate function or method call are in fact
used.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Functions Dealing with the Options Stack}}\label{sect:Options Stack}
\logpage{[ 8, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X794C5B5A80203CF9}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PushOptions}}
\logpage{[ 8, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D4939FF7FB37FBE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PushOptions({\mdseries\slshape options{\textunderscore}record})\index{PushOptions@\texttt{PushOptions}}
\label{PushOptions}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function pushes a record of options onto the global option stack. Note
that \texttt{PushOptions( rec( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opt}}:= fail ) )} has the effect of resetting the option \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opt}}, since an option that has never been set has the value \texttt{fail} returned by \texttt{ValueOption} (\ref{ValueOption}). 

 Note that there is no check for misspelt or undefined options. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PopOptions}}
\logpage{[ 8, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7818A5278679FD43}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PopOptions({\mdseries\slshape })\index{PopOptions@\texttt{PopOptions}}
\label{PopOptions}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function removes the top\texttt{\symbol{45}}most options record from the
options stack if there is one. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ResetOptionsStack}}
\logpage{[ 8, 1, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83D1190984DA3B85}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ResetOptionsStack({\mdseries\slshape })\index{ResetOptionsStack@\texttt{ResetOptionsStack}}
\label{ResetOptionsStack}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 unbinds (i.e. removes) all the options records from the options stack. 

 \emph{Note:} \texttt{ResetOptionsStack} should \emph{not} be used within a function. Its intended use is to clean up the options stack
in the event that the user has \texttt{quit} from a \texttt{break} loop, so leaving a stack of
no\texttt{\symbol{45}}longer\texttt{\symbol{45}}needed options
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{quit}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{OnQuit}}
\logpage{[ 8, 1, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78D87D1081BF99FE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{OnQuit({\mdseries\slshape })\index{OnQuit@\texttt{OnQuit}}
\label{OnQuit}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 called when a user selects to \texttt{quit;} a break loop entered via execution of \texttt{Error} (\ref{Error}). As \textsf{GAP} starts up, \texttt{OnQuit} is defined to do nothing, in case an error is encountered during \textsf{GAP} start\texttt{\symbol{45}}up. Later in the loading process we redefine \texttt{OnQuit} to do a variant of \texttt{ResetOptionsStack} (\ref{ResetOptionsStack}) to ensure the options stack is empty after a user quits an \texttt{Error} (\ref{Error})\texttt{\symbol{45}}induced break loop. (\texttt{OnQuit} differs from \texttt{ResetOptionsStack} (\ref{ResetOptionsStack}) in that it warns when it does something rather than the other way round.)
Currently, \texttt{OnQuit} is not advertised, since exception handling may make it obsolete. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ValueOption}}
\logpage{[ 8, 1, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F9373AD7DB88D1F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ValueOption({\mdseries\slshape opt})\index{ValueOption@\texttt{ValueOption}}
\label{ValueOption}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function is a method for accessing the options stack without changing it; \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opt}} should be the name of an option, i.e.{\nobreakspace}a string. A function which
makes decisions that might be affected by options should examine the result of \texttt{ValueOption}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opt}} is currently not set then \texttt{fail} is returned. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DisplayOptionsStack}}
\logpage{[ 8, 1, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EDA4EB67D43FE33}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DisplayOptionsStack({\mdseries\slshape })\index{DisplayOptionsStack@\texttt{DisplayOptionsStack}}
\label{DisplayOptionsStack}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function prints a human\texttt{\symbol{45}}readable display of the
complete options stack. 

 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoOptions}}
\logpage{[ 8, 1, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X832F41187B150C19}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoOptions\index{InfoOptions@\texttt{InfoOptions}}
\label{InfoOptions}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (info class)}}\\


 This info class can be used to enable messages about options being changed
(level 1) or accessed (level 2). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Options Stack {\textendash} an Example}}\label{sect:Options Stack Example}
\logpage{[ 8, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7BB781647CAAE9B4}{}
{
  The example below shows simple manipulation of the Options Stack, first using \texttt{PushOptions} (\ref{PushOptions}) and \texttt{PopOptions} (\ref{PopOptions}) and then using the special function calling syntax. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@foo := function()|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@Print("myopt1 = ", ValueOption("myopt1"),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@      " myopt2 = ",ValueOption("myopt2"),"\n");|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@end;|
  function(  ) ... end
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@foo();|
  myopt1 = fail myopt2 = fail
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PushOptions(rec(myopt1 := 17));|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@foo();|
  myopt1 = 17 myopt2 = fail
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DisplayOptionsStack();|
  [ rec(
        myopt1 := 17 ) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PopOptions();|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@foo();|
  myopt1 = fail myopt2 = fail
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@foo( : myopt1, myopt2 := [Z(3),"aardvark"]);|
  myopt1 = true myopt2 = [ Z(3), "aardvark" ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DisplayOptionsStack();|
  [  ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

                
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Files and Filenames}}\label{Files and Filenames}
\logpage{[ 9, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X82BCD4297920C903}{}
{
  Files are identified by filenames, which are represented in \textsf{GAP} as strings. Filenames can be created directly by the user or a program, but of
course this is operating system dependent. 

 Filenames for some files can be constructed in a system independent way using
the following functions. This is done by first getting a directory object for
the directory the file shall reside in, and then constructing the filename.
However, it is sometimes necessary to construct filenames of files in
subdirectories relative to a given directory object. In this case the
directory separator is \emph{always} \texttt{/} even under DOS or MacOS. 

 Section \ref{Directories} describes how to construct directory objects for the common \textsf{GAP} and system directories. Using the command \texttt{Filename} (\ref{Filename:for a directory and a string}) it is possible to construct a filename pointing to a file in these
directories. There are also functions to test for accessibility of files,
see{\nobreakspace}\ref{File Access}.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Portability}}\label{Portability}
\logpage{[ 9, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83D8AAA484EE95D9}{}
{
  For portability filenames and directory names should be restricted to at most
8 alphanumerical characters optionally followed by a dot \texttt{.} and between 1 and 3 alphanumerical characters. Upper case letters should be
avoided because some operating systems do not make any distinction between
case, so that \texttt{NaMe}, \texttt{Name} and \texttt{name} all refer to the same file whereas some operating systems are case sensitive.
To avoid problems only lower case characters should be used. 

 Another function which is system\texttt{\symbol{45}}dependent is \texttt{LastSystemError} (\ref{LastSystemError}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LastSystemError}}
\logpage{[ 9, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87D278437A916905}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LastSystemError({\mdseries\slshape })\index{LastSystemError@\texttt{LastSystemError}}
\label{LastSystemError}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{LastSystemError} returns a record describing the last system error that has occurred. This
record contains at least the component \texttt{message} which is a string. This message is, however, highly operating system dependent
and should only be used as an informational message for the user. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{GAP Root Directories}}\label{GAP Root Directories}
\logpage{[ 9, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7A4973627A5DB27D}{}
{
  \index{GAPInfo.RootPaths@\texttt{GAPInfo.RootPaths}} \index{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot@\texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot}} When \textsf{GAP} is started it determines a list of directories which we call the \emph{\textsf{GAP} root directories}. In a running \textsf{GAP} session this list can be found in \texttt{GAPInfo.RootPaths}. 

 The core part of \textsf{GAP} knows which files to read relative to its root directories. For example when \textsf{GAP} wants to read its library file \texttt{lib/group.gd}, it appends this path to each path in \texttt{GAPInfo.RootPaths} until it finds the path of an existing file. The first file found this way is
read. 

 Any subdirectories named \texttt{pkg/} in one of the directories in \texttt{GAPInfo.RootPaths} are added to \texttt{GAPInfo.PackageDirectories} (see \ref{GAP Package Directories}), which controls where \textsf{GAP} looks for available packages. 

 The root directories are specified via one or several of the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}l paths} command line options, see \ref{Command Line Options}. Furthermore, by default \textsf{GAP} automatically prepends a user specific \textsf{GAP} root directory to the list; this can be avoided by calling \textsf{GAP} with the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r} option. The name of this user specific directory depends on your operating
system, it can be found in \texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot}. This directory can be used to tell \textsf{GAP} about personal preferences, to always load some additional code, to install
additional packages, or to overwrite some \textsf{GAP} files. See \ref{sect:gap.ini} for more information how to do this. After \textsf{GAP} has been started, one can add additional root directories via the function \texttt{ExtendRootDirectories} (\ref{ExtendRootDirectories}). 

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{GAP Package Directories}}\label{GAP Package Directories}
\logpage{[ 9, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8223D52E78AF4420}{}
{
  \index{GAPInfo.PackageDirectories@\texttt{GAPInfo.PackageDirectories}} When \textsf{GAP} is started it determines a list of directories potentially containing
packages. We refer to these as the \emph{\textsf{GAP} package directories}. In a running \textsf{GAP} session this list can be found in \texttt{GAPInfo.PackageDirectories}. 

 Every subdirectory \texttt{pkg} in a \textsf{GAP} root directory is automatically added to this list. Further package
directories can be specified via one or several \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}packagedirs paths} command line options, see \ref{Command Line Options}, or after \textsf{GAP} has been started via the function \texttt{ExtendPackageDirectories} (\ref{ExtendPackageDirectories}). The order of the directories in \texttt{GAPInfo.PackageDirectories} is as follows: first the package directories specified via the command line
option \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}packagedirs}, then the subdirectories \texttt{pkg} of the \textsf{GAP} root directories that were known at startup in the same order, and finally the
directories added after \textsf{GAP} has been started. 

 \textsf{GAP} looks for available packages by examining each of the directories in \texttt{GAPInfo.PackageDirectories}. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Directories}}\label{Directories}
\logpage{[ 9, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X85030B35865A1080}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsDirectory}}
\logpage{[ 9, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82B3E24683942597}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsDirectory({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsDirectory@\texttt{IsDirectory}}
\label{IsDirectory}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 \texttt{IsDirectory} is a category of directories. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Directory}}
\logpage{[ 9, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86A71E927EEC7EAD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Directory({\mdseries\slshape string})\index{Directory@\texttt{Directory}}
\label{Directory}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a directory object for the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape string}}. \texttt{Directory} understands \texttt{"."} for ``current directory'', that is, the directory in which \textsf{GAP} was started. It also understands absolute paths. 

 If the variable \texttt{GAPInfo.UserHome} is defined (this may depend on the operating system) then \texttt{Directory} understands a string with a leading \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{126}}} (tilde) character for a path relative to the user's home directory (but a
string beginning with \texttt{"\texttt{\symbol{126}}other{\textunderscore}user"} is \emph{not} interpreted as a path relative to \texttt{other{\textunderscore}user}'s home directory, as in a UNIX shell). 

 Paths are otherwise taken relative to the current directory. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DirectoryTemporary}}
\logpage{[ 9, 4, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8222B1A886E6195E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DirectoryTemporary({\mdseries\slshape })\index{DirectoryTemporary@\texttt{DirectoryTemporary}}
\label{DirectoryTemporary}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a directory object in the category \texttt{IsDirectory} (\ref{IsDirectory}) for a \emph{new} temporary directory. This is guaranteed to be newly created and empty
immediately after the call to \texttt{DirectoryTemporary}. \textsf{GAP} will make a reasonable effort to remove this directory upon termination of the \textsf{GAP} job that created the directory. 

 If \texttt{DirectoryTemporary} is unable to create a new directory, \texttt{fail} is returned. In this case \texttt{LastSystemError} (\ref{LastSystemError}) can be used to get information about the error. 

 A warning message is given if more than 1000 temporary directories are created
in any \textsf{GAP} session. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DirectoryCurrent}}
\logpage{[ 9, 4, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BAD8036849E8430}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DirectoryCurrent({\mdseries\slshape })\index{DirectoryCurrent@\texttt{DirectoryCurrent}}
\label{DirectoryCurrent}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the directory object for the current directory. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ChangeDirectoryCurrent}}
\logpage{[ 9, 4, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81DDD2E87F68E086}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ChangeDirectoryCurrent({\mdseries\slshape path})\index{ChangeDirectoryCurrent@\texttt{ChangeDirectoryCurrent}}
\label{ChangeDirectoryCurrent}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Changes the current directory. Returns \texttt{true} on success and \texttt{fail} on failure. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DirectoriesLibrary}}
\logpage{[ 9, 4, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87ED469A85343A3C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DirectoriesLibrary({\mdseries\slshape [name]})\index{DirectoriesLibrary@\texttt{DirectoriesLibrary}}
\label{DirectoriesLibrary}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{DirectoriesLibrary} returns the directory objects for the \textsf{GAP} library \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} as a list. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} must be one of \texttt{"lib"} (the default), \texttt{"doc"}, \texttt{"tst"}, and so on. 

 The string \texttt{""} is also legal and with this argument \texttt{DirectoriesLibrary} returns the list of \textsf{GAP} root directories. The return value of this call differs from \texttt{GAPInfo.RootPaths} in that the former is a list of directory objects and the latter a list of
strings. 

 The directory \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} must exist in at least one of the root directories, otherwise \texttt{fail} is returned.   

 As the files in the \textsf{GAP} root directories (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{GAP Root Directories}) can be distributed into different directories in the filespace a list of
directories is returned. In order to find an existing file in a \textsf{GAP} root directory you should pass that list to \texttt{Filename} (\ref{Filename:for a directory and a string}) as the first argument. In order to create a filename for a new file inside a \textsf{GAP} root directory you should pass the first entry of that list. However, creating
files inside the \textsf{GAP} root directory is not recommended, you should use \texttt{DirectoryTemporary} (\ref{DirectoryTemporary}) instead. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DirectoriesSystemPrograms}}
\logpage{[ 9, 4, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X808E2C187DD984B4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DirectoriesSystemPrograms({\mdseries\slshape })\index{DirectoriesSystemPrograms@\texttt{DirectoriesSystemPrograms}}
\label{DirectoriesSystemPrograms}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{DirectoriesSystemPrograms} returns the directory objects for the list of directories where the system
programs reside, as a list. Under UNIX this would usually represent \texttt{\$PATH}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DirectoryContents}}
\logpage{[ 9, 4, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B225E5282534EDA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DirectoryContents({\mdseries\slshape dir})\index{DirectoryContents@\texttt{DirectoryContents}}
\label{DirectoryContents}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function returns a list of filenames/directory names that reside in the
directory \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dir}}. The argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dir}} can either be given as a string indicating the name of the directory or as a
directory object (see \texttt{IsDirectory} (\ref{IsDirectory})). If an error occurs (the specified directory does not exist or has no read
