  awk    ls     mkdir
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# current directory, here the root directory|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Process( DirectoryCurrent(), ls, stdin, stdout, ["-c"] );;|
  bin    lib    trans  tst    CVS    grp    prim   thr    two
  src    dev    etc    tbl    doc    pkg    small  tom
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# create a temporary directory|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@tmpdir := DirectoryTemporary();;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Process( tmpdir, ls, stdin, stdout, ["-c"] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrintTo( Filename( tmpdir, "emil" ) );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Process( tmpdir, ls, stdin, stdout, ["-c"] );;|
  emil
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prg}} is the filename of the program to launch, for portability it should be the
result of \texttt{Filename} (\ref{Filename:for a directory and a string}) and should pass \texttt{IsExecutableFile} (\ref{IsExecutableFile}). Note that \texttt{Process} does \emph{no} searching through a list of directories, this is done by \texttt{Filename} (\ref{Filename:for a directory and a string}). 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stream\texttt{\symbol{45}}in}} is the input stream that delivers the characters to the process. For
portability it should either be \texttt{InputTextNone} (\ref{InputTextNone}) (if the process reads no characters), \texttt{InputTextUser} (\ref{InputTextUser}), the result of a call to \texttt{InputTextFile} (\ref{InputTextFile}) from which no characters have been read, or the result of a call to \texttt{InputTextString} (\ref{InputTextString}). 

 \texttt{Process} is free to consume \emph{all} the input even if the program itself does not require any input at all. 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stream\texttt{\symbol{45}}out}} is the output stream which receives the characters from the process. For
portability it should either be \texttt{OutputTextNone} (\ref{OutputTextNone}) (if the process writes no characters), \texttt{OutputTextUser} (\ref{OutputTextUser}), the result of a call to \texttt{OutputTextFile} (\ref{OutputTextFile}) to which no characters have been written, or the result of a call to \texttt{OutputTextString} (\ref{OutputTextString}). 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape options}} is a list of strings which are passed to the process as command line argument.
Note that no substitutions are performed on the strings, i.e., they are passed
immediately to the process and are not processed by a command interpreter
(shell). Further note that each string is passed as one argument, even if it
contains \emph{space} characters. Note that input/output redirection commands are \emph{not} allowed as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape options}}. 

 In order to find a system program use \texttt{PathSystemProgram} (\ref{PathSystemProgram}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@date := PathSystemProgram( "date" );|
  "/bin/date"
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The next example shows how to execute \texttt{date} with no argument and no input, and collect the output into a string stream. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@str := "";; a := OutputTextString(str,true);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Process( DirectoryCurrent(), date, InputTextNone(), a, [] );|
  0
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CloseStream(a);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Print(str);|
  Fri Jul 11 09:04:23 MET DST 1997
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Exec}}
\logpage{[ 11, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81402C91833986FC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Exec({\mdseries\slshape cmd, option1, ..., optionN})\index{Exec@\texttt{Exec}}
\label{Exec}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{Exec} runs a shell in the current directory to execute the command given by the
string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cmd}} with options \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape option1}}, ..., \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape optionN}}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Exec( "date" );|
  Thu Jul 24 10:04:13 BST 1997
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cmd}} is interpreted by the shell and therefore we can make use of the various
features that a shell offers as in following example. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|B,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>B @gapinput|Exec( "echo \"GAP is great!\" > foo" );B
  @gapprompt|gap>B @gapinput|Exec( "cat foo" );B
  GAP is great!
  @gapprompt|gap>B @gapinput|Exec( "rm foo" );B
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \texttt{Exec} calls the more general operation \texttt{Process} (\ref{Process}). The function \texttt{Edit} (\ref{Edit}) should be used to call an editor from within \textsf{GAP}. }

 }

 }

              
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Objects and Elements}}\label{Objects and Elements}
\logpage{[ 12, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86710F997832ABA4}{}
{
  An \emph{object} is anything in \textsf{GAP} that can be assigned to a variable, so nearly everything in \textsf{GAP} is an object. 

 Different objects can be regarded as equal with respect to the equivalence
relation ``\texttt{=}'', in this case we say that the objects describe the same \emph{element}.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Objects}}\label{Objects}
\logpage{[ 12, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X78497E777FB3E402}{}
{
  Nearly all things one deals with in \textsf{GAP} are \emph{objects}. For example, an integer is an object, as is a list of integers, a matrix, a
permutation, a function, a list of functions, a record, a group, a coset or a
conjugacy class in a group. 

 Examples of things that are not objects are comments which are only lexical
constructs, \texttt{while} loops which are only syntactical constructs, and expressions, such as \texttt{1 + 1}; but note that the value of an expression, in this case the integer \texttt{2}, is an object. 

 Objects can be assigned to variables, and everything that can be assigned to a
variable is an object. Analogously, objects can be used as arguments of
functions, and can be returned by functions. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsObject}}
\logpage{[ 12, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B130AC98415CAFB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsObject({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsObject@\texttt{IsObject}}
\label{IsObject}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 \texttt{IsObject} returns \texttt{true} if the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is an object. Obviously it can never return \texttt{false}. 

 It can be used as a filter in \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) when one of the arguments can be anything. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Elements as equivalence classes}}\label{Elements as equivalence classes}
\logpage{[ 12, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X780C66027A49D110}{}
{
  \index{elements!definition} The equality operation ``\texttt{=}'' defines an equivalence relation on all \textsf{GAP} objects. The equivalence classes are called \emph{elements}. 

 There are basically three reasons to regard different objects as equal.
Firstly the same information may be stored in different places. Secondly the
same information may be stored in different ways; for example, a polynomial
can be stored sparsely or densely. Thirdly different information may be equal
modulo a mathematical equivalence relation. For example, in a finitely
presented group with the relation $a^2 = 1$ the different objects $a$ and $a^3$ describe the same element. 

 As an example of all three reasons, consider the possibility of storing an
integer in several places of the memory, of representing it as a fraction with
denominator 1, or of representing it as a fraction with any denominator, and
numerator a suitable multiple of the denominator. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Sets}}\label{Sets}
\logpage{[ 12, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83BE0C20875DD285}{}
{
  In \textsf{GAP} there is no category whose definition corresponds to the mathematical property
of being a set, however in the manual we will often refer to an object as a \emph{set} in order to convey the fact that mathematically, we are thinking of it as a
set. In particular, two sets $A$ and $B$ are equal if and only if, $x \in A \iff x \in B$. 

 There are two types of object in \textsf{GAP} which exhibit this kind of behaviour with respect to equality, namely domains
(see Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Domains}) and lists whose elements are strictly sorted see \texttt{IsSSortedList} (\ref{IsSSortedList}). In general, \emph{set} in this manual will mean an object of one of these types. 

 More precisely: two domains can be compared with ``\texttt{\symbol{123}}\texttt{=}\texttt{\symbol{125}}'', the answer being \texttt{true} if and only if the sets of elements are equal (regardless of any additional
structure) and; a domain and a list can be compared with ``\texttt{=}'', the answer being \texttt{true} if and only if the list is equal to the strictly sorted list of elements of
the domain. 

 A discussion about sorted lists and sets can be found in Section \ref{Sorted Lists and Sets}. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Domains}}\label{Domains}
\logpage{[ 12, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7BAF69417BB925F6}{}
{
  An especially important class of objects in \textsf{GAP} are those whose underlying mathematical abstraction is that of a structured
set, for example a group, a conjugacy class, or a vector space. Such objects
are called \emph{domains}. The equality relation between domains is always equality \emph{as sets}, so that two domains are equal if and only if they contain the same elements. 

 Domains play a central role in \textsf{GAP}. In a sense, the only reason that \textsf{GAP} supports objects such as integers and permutations is the wish to form domains
of them and compute the properties of those domains. 

 Domains are described in Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Domains and their Elements}. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Identical Objects}}\label{Identical Objects}
\logpage{[ 12, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X84545F3985C60F5B}{}
{
  Two objects that are equal \emph{as objects} (that is they actually refer to the same area of computer memory) and not only
w.r.t. the equality relation ``\texttt{=}'' are called \emph{identical}. Identical objects do of course describe the same element. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsIdenticalObj}}
\logpage{[ 12, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7961183378DFB902}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsIdenticalObj({\mdseries\slshape obj1, obj2})\index{IsIdenticalObj@\texttt{IsIdenticalObj}}
\label{IsIdenticalObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{IsIdenticalObj} tests whether the objects \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj1}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj2}} are identical (that is they are either equal immediate objects or are both
stored at the same location in memory. 

 If two copies of a simple constant object (see section \ref{Mutability and Copyability}) are created, it is not defined whether \textsf{GAP} will actually store two equal but non\texttt{\symbol{45}}identical objects, or
just a single object. For mutable objects, however, it is important to know
whether two values refer to identical or non\texttt{\symbol{45}}identical
objects, and the documentation of operations that return mutable values should
make clear whether the values returned are new, or may be identical to values
stored elsewhere. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsIdenticalObj( 10^6, 10^6);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsIdenticalObj( 10^30, 10^30);|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsIdenticalObj( true, true);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Generally, one may compute with objects but think of the results in terms of
the underlying elements because one is not interested in locations in memory,
data formats or information beyond underlying equivalence relations. But there
are cases where it is important to distinguish the relations identity and
equality. This is best illustrated with an example. (The reader who is not
familiar with lists in \textsf{GAP}, in particular element access and assignment, is referred to
Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Lists}.) 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l1:= [ 1, 2, 3 ];; l2:= [ 1, 2, 3 ];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l1 = l2;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsIdenticalObj( l1, l2 );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l1[3]:= 4;; l1; l2;|
  [ 1, 2, 4 ]
  [ 1, 2, 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l1 = l2;|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 The two lists \texttt{l1} and \texttt{l2} are equal but not identical. Thus a change in \texttt{l1} does not affect \texttt{l2}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l1:= [ 1, 2, 3 ];; l2:= l1;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l1 = l2;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsIdenticalObj( l1, l2 );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l1[3]:= 4;; l1; l2;|
  [ 1, 2, 4 ]
  [ 1, 2, 4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l1 = l2;|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 Here, \texttt{l1} and \texttt{l2} are identical objects, so changing \texttt{l1} means a change to \texttt{l2} as well. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsNotIdenticalObj}}
\logpage{[ 12, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X811976EC78EC5E29}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsNotIdenticalObj({\mdseries\slshape obj1, obj2})\index{IsNotIdenticalObj@\texttt{IsNotIdenticalObj}}
\label{IsNotIdenticalObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 tests whether the objects \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj1}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj2}} are not identical. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Mutability and Copyability}}\label{Mutability and Copyability}
\logpage{[ 12, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7F0C119682196D65}{}
{
  An object in \textsf{GAP} is said to be \emph{immutable} if its mathematical value (as defined by $=$) does not change under any operation. More explicitly, suppose $a$ is immutable and $O$ is some operation on $a$, then if $a = b$ evaluates to \texttt{true} before executing $O(a)$, $a = b$ also evaluates to \texttt{true} afterwards. (Examples for operations $O$ that change mutable objects are \texttt{Add} (\ref{Add}) and \texttt{Unbind} (\ref{Unbind:unbind a list entry}) which are used to change list objects, see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Lists}.) An immutable object \emph{may} change, for example to store new information, or to adopt a more efficient
representation, but this does not affect its behaviour under $=$. 

 There are two points here to note. Firstly, ``operation'' above refers to the functions and methods which can legitimately be applied to
the object, and not the \texttt{!.} operation whereby virtually any aspect of any \textsf{GAP} level object may be changed. The second point which follows from this, is that
when implementing new types of objects, it is the programmer's responsibility
to ensure that the functions and methods they write never change immutable
objects mathematically. 

 In fact, most objects with which one deals in \textsf{GAP} are immutable. For instance, the permutation \texttt{(1,2)} will never become a different permutation or a
non\texttt{\symbol{45}}permutation (although a variable which previously had \texttt{(1,2)} stored in it may subsequently have some other value). 

 For many purposes, however, \emph{mutable} objects are useful. These objects may be changed to represent different
mathematical objects during their life. For example, mutable lists can be
changed by assigning values to positions or by unbinding values at certain
positions. Similarly, one can assign values to components of a mutable record,
or unbind them. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsCopyable}}
\logpage{[ 12, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X811EFD727EBD1ADC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsCopyable({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsCopyable@\texttt{IsCopyable}}
\label{IsCopyable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 If a mutable form of an object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} can be made in \textsf{GAP}, the object is called \emph{copyable}. Examples of copyable objects are of course lists and records. A new mutable
version of the object can always be obtained by the operation \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}). 

 Objects for which only an immutable form exists in \textsf{GAP} are called \emph{constants}. Examples of constants are integers, permutations, and domains. Called with a
constant as argument, \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}) and \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}) return this argument. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsMutable}}
\logpage{[ 12, 6, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7999AD1D7A4F1F46}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsMutable({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsMutable@\texttt{IsMutable}}
\label{IsMutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 tests whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is mutable. 

 If an object is mutable then it is also copyable (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsCopyable} (\ref{IsCopyable})), and a \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}) method should be supplied for it. Note that \texttt{IsMutable} must not be implied by another filter, since otherwise \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}) would be able to create paradoxical objects in the sense that \texttt{IsMutable} for such an object is \texttt{false} but the filter that implies \texttt{IsMutable} is \texttt{true}. 

 In many situations, however, one wants to ensure that objects are \emph{immutable}. For example, take the identity of a matrix group. Since this matrix may be
referred to as the identity of the group in several places, it would be fatal
to modify its entries, or add or unbind rows. We can obtain an immutable copy
of an object with \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Immutable}}
\logpage{[ 12, 6, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F0ABF2C870B0CBB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Immutable({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{Immutable@\texttt{Immutable}}
\label{Immutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns an immutable structural copy (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{StructuralCopy} (\ref{StructuralCopy})) of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} in which the subobjects are immutable \emph{copies} of the subobjects of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is immutable then \texttt{Immutable} returns \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} itself. 

 \textsf{GAP} will complain with an error if one tries to change an immutable object. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MakeImmutable}}
\logpage{[ 12, 6, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80CE136D804097C7}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MakeImmutable({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{MakeImmutable@\texttt{MakeImmutable}}
\label{MakeImmutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 One can turn the (mutable or immutable) object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} into an immutable one with \texttt{MakeImmutable}; note that this also makes all subobjects of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} immutable, so one should call \texttt{MakeImmutable} only if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} and its mutable subobjects are newly created. If one is not sure about this, \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}) should be used. 

 Note that it is \emph{not} possible to turn an immutable object into a mutable one; only mutable copies
can be made (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Duplication of Objects}). 

 Using \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}), it is possible to store an immutable identity matrix or an immutable list of
generators, and to pass around references to this immutable object safely.
Only when a mutable copy is really needed does the actual object have to be
duplicated. Compared to the situation without immutable objects, much
unnecessary copying is avoided this way. Another advantage of immutability is
that lists of immutable objects may remember whether they are sorted
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Sorted Lists and Sets}), which is not possible for lists of mutable objects. 

 Since the operation \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}) must work for any object in \textsf{GAP}, it follows that an immutable form of every object must be possible, even if
it is not sensible, and user\texttt{\symbol{45}}defined objects must allow for
the possibility of becoming immutable without notice. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Mutability of Iterators}}\label{subsect:mutability iterators}
\logpage{[ 12, 6, 5 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7FBA5F4D7C6872BD}{}
{
  An interesting example of mutable (and thus copyable) objects is provided by \emph{iterators}, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Iterators}. (Of course an immutable form of an iterator is not very useful, but clearly \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}) will yield such an object.) Every call of \texttt{NextIterator} (\ref{NextIterator}) changes a mutable iterator until it is exhausted, and this is the only way to
change an iterator. \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}) for an iterator \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape iter}} is defined so as to return a mutable iterator that has no mutable data in
common with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape iter}}, and that behaves equally to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape iter}} w.r.t.{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsDoneIterator} (\ref{IsDoneIterator}) and (if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape iter}} is mutable) \texttt{NextIterator} (\ref{NextIterator}). Note that this meaning of the ``shallow copy'' of an iterator that is returned by \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}) is not as obvious as for lists and records, and must be explicitly defined. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Mutability of Results of Arithmetic Operations}}\label{subsect:mutability arithmetic operations}
\logpage{[ 12, 6, 6 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7ADB82997A16E853}{}
{
  Many operations return immutable results, among those in particular attributes
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Attributes}). Examples of attributes are \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}), \texttt{Zero} (\ref{Zero}), \texttt{AdditiveInverse} (\ref{AdditiveInverse}), \texttt{One} (\ref{One}), and \texttt{Inverse} (\ref{Inverse}). Arithmetic operations, such as the binary infix operations \texttt{+}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}}, \texttt{*}, \texttt{/}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}, \texttt{mod}, the unary \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}}, and operations such as \texttt{Comm} (\ref{Comm}) and \texttt{LeftQuotient} (\ref{LeftQuotient}), return \emph{mutable} results, \emph{except} if all arguments are immutable. So the product of two matrices or of a vector
and a matrix is immutable if and only if the two matrices or both the vector
and the matrix are immutable (see also{\nobreakspace}\ref{Arithmetic for Lists}). There is one exception to this rule, which arises where the result is less
deeply nested than at least one of the argument, where mutable arguments may
sometimes lead to an immutable result. For instance, a mutable matrix with
immutable rows, multiplied by an immutable vector gives an immutable vector
result. The exact rules are given in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Arithmetic for Lists}. 

 It should be noted that \texttt{0 * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}} is equivalent to \texttt{ZeroSameMutability( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} )}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}} is equivalent to \texttt{AdditiveInverseSameMutability( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} )}, \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}0} is equivalent to \texttt{OneSameMutability( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}})}, and \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}1} is equivalent to \texttt{InverseSameMutability( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} )}. The suffix ``SameMutability'' indicates that the result is mutable if and only if the argument is mutable. 

 The operations \texttt{ZeroOp} (\ref{ZeroOp}), \texttt{AdditiveInverseOp} (\ref{AdditiveInverseOp}), \texttt{OneOp} (\ref{OneOp}), and \texttt{InverseOp} (\ref{InverseOp}) return \emph{mutable} results whenever a mutable version of the result exists, contrary to the
attributes \texttt{Zero} (\ref{Zero}), \texttt{AdditiveInverse} (\ref{AdditiveInverse}), \texttt{One} (\ref{One}), and \texttt{Inverse} (\ref{Inverse}). 

 If one introduces new arithmetic objects then one need not install methods for
the attributes \texttt{One} (\ref{One}), \texttt{Zero} (\ref{Zero}), etc. The methods for the associated operations \texttt{OneOp} (\ref{OneOp}) and \texttt{ZeroOp} (\ref{ZeroOp}) will be called, and then the results made immutable. 

 All methods installed for the arithmetic operations must obey the rule about
the mutability of the result. This means that one may try to avoid the perhaps
expensive creation of a new object if both operands are immutable, and of
course no problems of this kind arise at all in the (usual) case that the
objects in question do not admit a mutable form, i.e., that these objects are
not copyable. 

 In a few, relatively low\texttt{\symbol{45}}level algorithms, one wishes to
treat a matrix partly as a data structure, and manipulate and change its
entries. For this, the matrix needs to be mutable, and the rule that attribute
values are immutable is an obstacle. For these situations, a number of
additional operations are provided, for example \texttt{TransposedMatMutable} (\ref{TransposedMatMutable}) constructs a mutable matrix (contrary to the attribute \texttt{TransposedMat} (\ref{TransposedMat})), while \texttt{TriangulizeMat} (\ref{TriangulizeMat}) modifies a mutable matrix (in place) into upper triangular form. 

 Note that being immutable does not forbid an object to store knowledge. For
example, if it is found out that an immutable list is strictly sorted then the
list may store this information. More precisely, an immutable object may
change in any way, provided that it continues to represent the same
mathematical object. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Duplication of Objects}}\label{Duplication of Objects}
\logpage{[ 12, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X786B942B82D684BD}{}
{
  \index{Copy} \index{copy!an object} \index{clone!an object} 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ShallowCopy}}
\logpage{[ 12, 7, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X846BC7107C352031}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ShallowCopy({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{ShallowCopy@\texttt{ShallowCopy}}
\label{ShallowCopy}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{ShallowCopy} returns a \emph{new mutable} object \emph{equal} to its argument, if this is possible. The subobjects of \texttt{ShallowCopy( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} )} are \emph{identical} to the subobjects of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. 

 If \textsf{GAP} does not support a mutable form of the immutable object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Mutability and Copyability}) then \texttt{ShallowCopy} returns \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} itself. 

 Since \texttt{ShallowCopy} is an operation, the concrete meaning of ``subobject'' depends on the type of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. But for any copyable object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, the definition should reflect the idea of ``first level copying''. 

 The definition of \texttt{ShallowCopy} for lists (in particular for matrices) can be found in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Duplication of Lists}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StructuralCopy}}
\logpage{[ 12, 7, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C1E70587EBDD2CB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StructuralCopy({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{StructuralCopy@\texttt{StructuralCopy}}
\label{StructuralCopy}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 In a few situations, one wants to make a \emph{structural copy} \texttt{scp} of an object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. This is defined as follows. \texttt{scp} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} are identical if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is immutable. Otherwise, \texttt{scp} is a mutable copy of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} such that each subobject of \texttt{scp} is a structural copy of the corresponding subobject of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. Furthermore, if two subobjects of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} are identical then also the corresponding subobjects of \texttt{scp} are identical. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@obj:= [ [ 0, 1 ] ];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@obj[2]:= obj[1];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@obj[3]:= Immutable( obj[1] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@scp:= StructuralCopy( obj );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@scp = obj; IsIdenticalObj( scp, obj );|
  true
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsIdenticalObj( scp[1], obj[1] );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsIdenticalObj( scp[3], obj[3] );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsIdenticalObj( scp[1], scp[2] );|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 

 That both \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}) and \texttt{StructuralCopy} return the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} itself if it is not copyable is consistent with this definition, since there
is no way to change \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} by modifying the result of any of the two functions, because in fact there is
no way to change this result at all. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Other Operations Applicable to any Object}}\label{Other Operations Applicable to any Object}
\logpage{[ 12, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86E7193D848C53FC}{}
{
  There are a number of general operations which can be applied, in principle,
to any object in \textsf{GAP}. Some of these are documented elsewhere {\textendash}see \texttt{String} (\ref{String}), \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}) and \texttt{Display} (\ref{Display}). Others are mainly somewhat technical. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetName}}
\logpage{[ 12, 8, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85D6D47B83BD02A1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetName({\mdseries\slshape obj, name})\index{SetName@\texttt{SetName}}
\label{SetName}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 for a suitable object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} sets that object to have name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} (a string). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Name}}
\logpage{[ 12, 8, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F14EF9D81432113}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Name({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{Name@\texttt{Name}}
\label{Name}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the name, a string, previously assigned to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} via a call to \texttt{SetName} (\ref{SetName}). The name of an object is used \emph{only} for viewing the object via this name. 

 There are no methods installed for computing names of objects, but the name
may be set for suitable objects, using \texttt{SetName} (\ref{SetName}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@R := PolynomialRing(Integers,2);|
  Integers[x_1,x_2]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetName(R,"Z[x,y]");|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@R;|
  Z[x,y]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Name(R);|
  "Z[x,y]"
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoText}}
\logpage{[ 12, 8, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X871562FD7F982C12}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoText({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{InfoText@\texttt{InfoText}}
\label{InfoText}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 is a mutable string with information about the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. There is no default method to create an info text. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsInternallyConsistent}}
\logpage{[ 12, 8, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F6C5C3287E8B816}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsInternallyConsistent({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsInternallyConsistent@\texttt{IsInternallyConsistent}}
\label{IsInternallyConsistent}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 For debugging purposes, it may be useful to check the consistency of an object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} that is composed from other (composed) objects. 

 There is a default method of \texttt{IsInternallyConsistent}, with rank zero, that returns \texttt{true}. So it is possible (and recommended) to check the consistency of subobjects
of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} recursively by \texttt{IsInternallyConsistent}. 

 (Note that \texttt{IsInternallyConsistent} is not an attribute.) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MemoryUsage}}
\logpage{[ 12, 8, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F4D216B7DF7BE9D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MemoryUsage({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{MemoryUsage@\texttt{MemoryUsage}}
\label{MemoryUsage}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Returns the amount of memory in bytes used by the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} and its subobjects. Note that in general, objects can reference each other in
very difficult ways such that determining the memory usage is a recursive
procedure. In particular, computing the memory usage of a complicated
structure itself uses some additional memory, which is however no longer used
after completion of this operation. This procedure descends into lists and
records, positional and component objects; however it deliberately does not
take into account the type and family objects. For functions, it only takes
the memory usage of the function body, not of the local context the function
was created in, although the function keeps a reference to that as well. }

 }

 }

           
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Types of Objects}}\label{Types of Objects}
\logpage{[ 13, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7E8202627B421DB1}{}
{
  Every \textsf{GAP} object has a \emph{type}. The type of an object is the information which is used to decide whether an
operation is admissible or possible with that object as an argument, and if
so, how it is to be performed (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Method Selection}). 

 For example, the types determine whether two objects can be multiplied and
what function is called to compute the product. Analogously, the type of an
object determines whether and how the size of the object can be computed. It
is sometimes useful in discussing the type system, to identify types with the
set of objects that have this type. Partial types can then also be regarded as
sets, such that any type is the intersection of its parts. 

 The type of an object consists of two main parts, which describe different
aspects of the object. 

 The \emph{family} determines the relation of the object to other objects. For example, all
permutations form a family. Another family consists of all collections of
permutations, this family contains the set of permutation groups as a subset.
A third family consists of all rational functions with coefficients in a
certain family. 

 The other part of a type is a collection of \emph{filters} (actually stored as a bit\texttt{\symbol{45}}list indicating, from the
complete set of possible filters, which are included in this particular type).
These filters are all treated equally by the method selection, but, from the
viewpoint of their creation and use, they can be divided (with a small number
of unimportant exceptions) into categories, representations, attribute testers
and properties. Each of these is described in more detail below. 

 This chapter does not describe how types and their constituent parts can be
created. Information about this topic can be found in Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Creating New Objects}. 

 \emph{Note:} Detailed understanding of the type system is not required to use \textsf{GAP}. It can be helpful, however, to understand how things work and why \textsf{GAP} behaves the way it does. 

   A discussion of the type system can be found in \cite{BreuerLinton98}.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Families}}\label{Families}
\logpage{[ 13, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X846063757EC05986}{}
{
  The family of an object determines its relationship to other objects. 

 More precisely, the families form a partition of all \textsf{GAP} objects such that the following two conditions hold: objects that are equal
w.r.t. \texttt{=} lie in the same family; and the family of the result of an operation depends
only on the families of its operands. 

 The first condition means that a family can be regarded as a set of elements
instead of a set of objects. Note that this does not hold for categories and
representations (see below), two objects that are equal w.r.t. \texttt{=} need not lie in the same categories and representations. For example, a
sparsely represented matrix can be equal to a densely represented matrix.
Similarly, each domain is equal w.r.t. \texttt{=} to the sorted list of its elements, but a domain is not a list, and a list is
not a domain. 

 Families are probably the least obvious part of the \textsf{GAP} type system, so some remarks about the role of families are necessary. When
one uses \textsf{GAP} as it is, one will (better: should) not meet families at all. The two
situations where families come into play are the following. 

 First, since families are used to describe relations between arguments of
operations in the method selection mechanism (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Method Selection}, and also Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Types of Objects}), one has to prescribe such a relation in each method installation
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Method Installation}); usual relations are \texttt{ReturnTrue} (\ref{ReturnTrue}) (which means that any relation of the actual arguments is admissible), \texttt{IsIdenticalObj} (\ref{IsIdenticalObj}) (which means that there are two arguments that lie in the same family), and \texttt{IsCollsElms} (which means that there are two arguments, the first being a collection of
elements that lie in the same family as the second argument). 

 Second {\textendash}and this is the more complicated situation{\textendash}
whenever one creates a new kind of objects, one has to decide what its family
shall be. If the new object shall be equal to existing objects, for example if
it is just represented in a different way, there is no choice: The new object
must lie in the same family as all objects that shall be equal to it. So only
if the new object is different (w.r.t.{\nobreakspace}the equality ``\texttt{=}'') from all other \textsf{GAP} objects, we are likely to create a new family for it. Note that enlarging an
existing family by such new objects may be problematic because of implications
that have been installed for all objects of the family in question. The choice
of families depends on the applications one has in mind. For example, if the
new objects in question are not likely to be arguments of operations for which
family relations are relevant (for example binary arithmetic operations), one
could create one family for all such objects, and regard it as ``the family of all those \textsf{GAP} objects that would in fact not need a family''. On the other extreme, if one wants to create domains of the new objects then
one has to choose the family in such a way that all intended elements of a
domain do in fact lie in the same family. (Remember that a domain is a
collection, see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Domains}, and that a collection consists of elements in the same family, see
Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Collections} and Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Families}.) 

 Let us look at an example. Suppose that no permutations are available in \textsf{GAP}, and that we want to implement permutations. Clearly we want to support
permutation groups, but it is not a priori clear how to distribute the new
permutations into families. We can put all permutations into one family; this
is how in fact permutations are implemented in \textsf{GAP}. But it would also be possible to put all permutations of a given degree into
a family of their own; this would for example mean that for each degree, there
would be distinguished trivial permutations, and that the stabilizer of the
point \texttt{5} in the symmetric group on the points \texttt{1}, \texttt{2}, $\ldots$, \texttt{5} is not regarded as equal to the symmetric group on \texttt{1}, \texttt{2}, \texttt{3}, \texttt{4}. Note that the latter approach would have the advantage that it is no problem
to construct permutations and permutation groups acting on arbitrary (finite)
sets, for example by constructing first the symmetric group on the set and
then generating any desired permutation group as a subgroup of this symmetric
group. 

 So one aspect concerning a reasonable choice of families is to make the
families large enough for being able to form interesting domains of elements
in the family. But on the other hand, it is useful to choose the families
small enough for admitting meaningful relations between objects. For example,
the elements of different free groups in \textsf{GAP} lie in different families; the multiplication of free group elements is
installed only for the case that the two operands lie in the same family, with
the effect that one cannot erroneously form the product of elements from
different free groups. In this case, families appear as a tool for providing
useful restrictions. 

 As another example, note that an element and a collection containing this
element never lie in the same family, by the general implementation of
collections; namely, the family of a collection of elements in the family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} is the collections family of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{CollectionsFamily} (\ref{CollectionsFamily})). This means that for a collection, we need not (because we cannot) decide
about its family. 

 A few functions in \textsf{GAP} return families, see \texttt{CollectionsFamily} (\ref{CollectionsFamily}) and \texttt{ElementsFamily} (\ref{ElementsFamily}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FamilyObj}}
\logpage{[ 13, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CF70EAC84284919}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FamilyObj({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{FamilyObj@\texttt{FamilyObj}}
\label{FamilyObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the family of the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. 

 The family of the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is itself an object, its family is \texttt{FamilyOfFamilies}. 

 It should be emphasized that families may be created when they are needed. For
example, the family of elements of a finitely presented group is created only
after the presentation has been constructed. Thus families are the dynamic
part of the type system, that is, the part that is not fixed after the
initialisation of \textsf{GAP}. 

 Families can be parametrized. For example, the elements of each finitely
presented group form a family of their own. Here the family of elements and
the finitely presented group coincide when viewed as sets. Note that elements
in different finitely presented groups lie in different families. This
distinction allows \textsf{GAP} to forbid multiplications of elements in different finitely presented groups. 

 As a special case, families can be parametrized by other families. An
important example is the family of \emph{collections} that can be formed for each family. A collection consists of objects that lie
in the same family, it is either a nonempty dense list of objects from the
same family or a domain. 

 Note that every domain is a collection, that is, it is not possible to
construct domains whose elements lie in different families. For example, a
polynomial ring over the rationals cannot contain the integer \texttt{0} because the family that contains the integers does not contain polynomials. So
one has to distinguish the integer zero from each zero polynomial. 

 Let us look at this example from a different viewpoint. A polynomial ring and
its coefficients ring lie in different families, hence the coefficients ring
cannot be embedded ``naturally'' into the polynomial ring in the sense that it is a subset. But it is possible
to allow, e.g., the multiplication of an integer and a polynomial over the
integers. The relation between the arguments, namely that one is a coefficient
and the other a polynomial, can be detected from the relation of their
families. Moreover, this analysis is easier than in a situation where the
rationals would lie in one family together with all polynomials over the
rationals, because then the relation of families would not distinguish the
multiplication of two polynomials, the multiplication of two coefficients, and
the multiplication of a coefficient with a polynomial. So the wish to describe
relations between elements can be taken as a motivation for the introduction
of families. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NewFamily}}
\logpage{[ 13, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7FB4123E7E22137D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewFamily({\mdseries\slshape name[, req[, imp[, famfilter]]]})\index{NewFamily@\texttt{NewFamily}}
\label{NewFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NewFamily} returns a new family \texttt{fam} with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape req}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape imp}}, if present, are filters of which \texttt{fam} shall be a subset. Any type that is created for \texttt{fam} (see \texttt{NewType} (\ref{NewType})) will describe objects in these filters, and thus any object that is created
in \texttt{fam} (see \texttt{Objectify} (\ref{Objectify})) will lie automatically in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape req}}\texttt{ and }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape imp}}. (Thus it does not matter whether one uses \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape req}} or \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape imp}} or both in the call, the distinction has only historical reasons.) 

 The filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famfilter}}, if given, specifies a filter that will hold for the object \texttt{fam} itself (not for objects in \texttt{fam}). 

 Families are always represented as component objects (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects}). This means that individual components can be set in \texttt{fam} in order to store and access useful information about it. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Filters}}\label{Filters}
\logpage{[ 13, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X84EFA4C07D4277BB}{}
{
  A \emph{filter} is a special unary \textsf{GAP} function that returns either \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}, depending on whether or not the argument lies in the set defined by the
filter. Filters are used to express different aspects of information about a \textsf{GAP} object, which are described below (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Categories}, \ref{Representation}, \ref{Attributes}, \ref{Setter and Tester for Attributes}, \ref{Properties}, \ref{Other Filters}). 

 Presently any filter in \textsf{GAP} is implemented as a function which corresponds to a set of positions in the
bitlist which forms part of the type of each \textsf{GAP} object, and returns \texttt{true} if and only if the bitlist of the type of the argument has the value \texttt{true} at all of these positions. 

 The intersection (or meet) of two filters \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt1}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt2}} is again a filter, it can be formed as 

 \index{and@\texttt{and}!for filters} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt1}} \texttt{and} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt2}} 

 See \ref{Operations for Booleans} for more details. 

 For example, \texttt{IsList and IsEmpty} is a filter that returns \texttt{true} if its argument is an empty list, and \texttt{false} otherwise. The filter \texttt{IsGroup} (\ref{IsGroup}) is defined as the intersection of the category \texttt{IsMagmaWithInverses} (\ref{IsMagmaWithInverses}) and the property \texttt{IsAssociative} (\ref{IsAssociative}). 

 A filter that is not the meet of other filters is called a \emph{simple filter}. For example, each attribute tester (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Setter and Tester for Attributes}) is a simple filter. Each simple filter corresponds to a position in the
bitlist currently used as part of the data structure representing a type. 

 Every filter has a \emph{rank}, which is used to define a ranking of the methods installed for an operation,
see Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Method Installation}. The rank of a filter can be accessed with \texttt{RankFilter} (\ref{RankFilter}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RankFilter}}
\logpage{[ 13, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82E62B997C05E05E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RankFilter({\mdseries\slshape filt})\index{RankFilter@\texttt{RankFilter}}
\label{RankFilter}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For simple filters, an \emph{incremental rank} is defined when the filter is created, see the sections about the creation of
filters: \texttt{NewCategory} (\ref{NewCategory}), \texttt{NewRepresentation} (\ref{NewRepresentation}), \texttt{NewAttribute} (\ref{NewAttribute}), \texttt{NewProperty} (\ref{NewProperty}), \texttt{NewFilter} (\ref{NewFilter}). For an arbitrary filter, its rank is given by the sum of the incremental
ranks of the \emph{involved} simple filters; in addition to the implied filters, these are also the
required filters of attributes (again see the sections about the creation of
filters). In other words, for the purpose of computing the rank and \emph{only} for this purpose, attribute testers are treated as if they would imply the
requirements of their attributes.  }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NamesFilter}}
\logpage{[ 13, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A78ECC67E2C9D78}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NamesFilter({\mdseries\slshape filt})\index{NamesFilter@\texttt{NamesFilter}}
\label{NamesFilter}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NamesFilter} returns a list of names of the \emph{implied} simple filters of the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}}, these are all those simple filters \texttt{imp} such that every object in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} also lies in \texttt{imp}. For implications between filters, see \texttt{ShowImpliedFilters} (\ref{ShowImpliedFilters}) as well as sections{\nobreakspace}\ref{Logical Implications}, \texttt{NewCategory} (\ref{NewCategory}), \texttt{NewRepresentation} (\ref{NewRepresentation}), \texttt{NewAttribute} (\ref{NewAttribute}), \texttt{NewProperty} (\ref{NewProperty}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FilterByName}}
\logpage{[ 13, 2, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F6645D87DD26CF0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FilterByName({\mdseries\slshape name})\index{FilterByName@\texttt{FilterByName}}
\label{FilterByName}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 finds the filter with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} in the global FILTERS list. This is useful to find filters that were created
but not bound to a global variable. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ShowImpliedFilters}}
\logpage{[ 13, 2, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F9568A67F3840DE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ShowImpliedFilters({\mdseries\slshape filter})\index{ShowImpliedFilters@\texttt{ShowImpliedFilters}}
\label{ShowImpliedFilters}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Displays information about the filters that may be implied by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}}. They are given by their names. \texttt{ShowImpliedFilters} first displays the names of all filters that are unconditionally implied by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}}. It then displays implications that require further filters to be present
(indicating by \texttt{+} the required further filters). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]

     CategoryCollections(IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse)
     IsGeneralizedDomain
     IsMagma
     IsMagmaWithOne
     IsMagmaWithInversesIfNonzero
     IsMagmaWithInverses
     IsAssociative
     HasMultiplicativeNeutralElement
     IsGeneratorsOfSemigroup
     IsSimpleSemigroup
     IsRegularSemigroup
     IsInverseSemigroup
     IsCompletelyRegularSemigroup
     IsGroupAsSemigroup
     IsMonoidAsSemigroup
     IsOrthodoxSemigroup
     IsSupersolvableGroup
     IsSolvableGroup
     IsNilpotentByFinite
  
  
  May imply with:
  +IsFinitelyGeneratedGroup
     IsPolycyclicGroup
  
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FiltersType}}
\logpage{[ 13, 2, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X836FAA18861BE387}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FiltersType({\mdseries\slshape type})\index{FiltersType@\texttt{FiltersType}}

}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\

}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a list of the filters in the type \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape type}}, or in the type of the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape object}} respectively.
