 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Categories}}\label{Categories}
\logpage{[ 13, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7CC6903E78F24167}{}
{
  The \emph{categories} of an object are filters (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}) that determine what operations an object admits. For example, all integers
form a category, all rationals form a category, and all rational functions
form a category. An object which claims to lie in a certain category is
accepting the requirement that it should have methods for certain operations
(and perhaps that their behaviour should satisfy certain axioms). For example,
an object lying in the category \texttt{IsList} (\ref{IsList}) must have methods for \texttt{Length} (\ref{Length}), \texttt{IsBound\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{IsBoundbSlash[bSlash]}) and the list element access operation \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{bSlash[bSlash]}). 

 An object can lie in several categories. For example, a row vector lies in the
categories \texttt{IsList} (\ref{IsList}) and \texttt{IsVector} (\ref{IsVector}); each list lies in the category \texttt{IsCopyable} (\ref{IsCopyable}), and depending on whether or not it is mutable, it may lie in the category \texttt{IsMutable} (\ref{IsMutable}). Every domain lies in the category \texttt{IsDomain} (\ref{IsDomain}). 

 Of course some categories of a mutable object may change when the object is
changed. For example, after assigning values to positions of a mutable
non\texttt{\symbol{45}}dense list, this list may become part of the category \texttt{IsDenseList} (\ref{IsDenseList}). 

 However, if an object is immutable then the set of categories it lies in is
fixed. 

 All categories in the library are created during initialization, in particular
they are not created dynamically at runtime. 

 The following list gives an overview of important categories of arithmetic
objects. Indented categories are to be understood as subcategories of the non
indented category listed above it. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
      IsObject
          IsExtLElement
          IsExtRElement
              IsMultiplicativeElement
                  IsMultiplicativeElementWithOne
                      IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse
          IsExtAElement
              IsAdditiveElement
                  IsAdditiveElementWithZero
                      IsAdditiveElementWithInverse
\end{Verbatim}
 Every object lies in the category \texttt{IsObject} (\ref{IsObject}). 

 The categories \texttt{IsExtLElement} (\ref{IsExtLElement}) and \texttt{IsExtRElement} (\ref{IsExtRElement}) contain objects that can be multiplied with other objects via \texttt{*} from the left and from the right, respectively. These categories are required
for the operands of the operation \texttt{*}. 

 The category \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElement} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElement}) contains objects that can be multiplied from the left and from the right with
objects from the same family. \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElementWithOne} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElementWithOne}) contains objects \texttt{obj} for which a multiplicatively neutral element can be obtained by taking the $0$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power \texttt{obj\texttt{\symbol{94}}0}. \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse}) contains objects \texttt{obj} for which a multiplicative inverse can be obtained by forming \texttt{obj\texttt{\symbol{94}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}1}. 

 Likewise, the categories \texttt{IsExtAElement} (\ref{IsExtAElement}), \texttt{IsAdditiveElement} (\ref{IsAdditiveElement}), \texttt{IsAdditiveElementWithZero} (\ref{IsAdditiveElementWithZero}) and \texttt{IsAdditiveElementWithInverse} (\ref{IsAdditiveElementWithInverse}) contain objects that can be added via \texttt{+} to other objects, objects that can be added to objects of the same family,
objects for which an additively neutral element can be obtained by
multiplication with zero, and objects for which an additive inverse can be
obtained by multiplication with \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}1}. 

 So a vector lies in \texttt{IsExtLElement} (\ref{IsExtLElement}), \texttt{IsExtRElement} (\ref{IsExtRElement}) and \texttt{IsAdditiveElementWithInverse} (\ref{IsAdditiveElementWithInverse}). A ring element must additionally lie in \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElement} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElement}). 

 As stated above it is not guaranteed by the categories of objects whether the
result of an operation with these objects as arguments is defined. For
example, the category \texttt{IsMatrix} (\ref{IsMatrix}) is a subcategory of \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse}). Clearly not every matrix has a multiplicative inverse. But the category \texttt{IsMatrix} (\ref{IsMatrix}) makes each matrix an admissible argument of the operation \texttt{Inverse} (\ref{Inverse}), which may sometimes return \texttt{fail}. Likewise, two matrices can be multiplied only if they are of appropriate
shapes. 

 Analogous to the categories of arithmetic elements, there are categories of
domains of these elements. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
      IsObject
          IsDomain
              IsMagma
                  IsMagmaWithOne
                      IsMagmaWithInversesIfNonzero
                          IsMagmaWithInverses
              IsAdditiveMagma
                  IsAdditiveMagmaWithZero
                      IsAdditiveMagmaWithInverses
              IsExtLSet
              IsExtRSet
\end{Verbatim}
 Of course \texttt{IsDomain} (\ref{IsDomain}) is a subcategory of \texttt{IsObject} (\ref{IsObject}). A domain that is closed under multiplication \texttt{*} is called a magma and it lies in the category \texttt{IsMagma} (\ref{IsMagma}). If a magma is closed under taking the identity, it lies in \texttt{IsMagmaWithOne} (\ref{IsMagmaWithOne}), and if it is also closed under taking inverses, it lies in \texttt{IsMagmaWithInverses} (\ref{IsMagmaWithInverses}). The category \texttt{IsMagmaWithInversesIfNonzero} (\ref{IsMagmaWithInversesIfNonzero}) denotes closure under taking inverses only for nonzero elements, every
division ring lies in this category. 

 Note that every set of categories constitutes its own notion of generation,
for example a group may be generated as a magma with inverses by some
elements, but to generate it as a magma with one it may be necessary to take
the union of these generators and their inverses. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsCategory}}
\logpage{[ 13, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X792A23BF82BDF66B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsCategory({\mdseries\slshape object})\index{IsCategory@\texttt{IsCategory}}
\label{IsCategory}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns \texttt{true} if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape object}} is a category (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Categories}), and \texttt{false} otherwise. 

 Note that \textsf{GAP} categories are \emph{not} categories in the usual mathematical sense. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CategoriesOfObject}}
\logpage{[ 13, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85C6EB707A406A5A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CategoriesOfObject({\mdseries\slshape object})\index{CategoriesOfObject@\texttt{CategoriesOfObject}}
\label{CategoriesOfObject}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a list of the names of the categories in which \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape object}} lies. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2),(1,2,3));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CategoriesOfObject(g);|
  [ "IsListOrCollection", "IsCollection", "IsExtLElement",
    "CategoryCollections(IsExtLElement)", "IsExtRElement",
    "CategoryCollections(IsExtRElement)",
    "CategoryCollections(IsMultiplicativeElement)",
    "CategoryCollections(IsMultiplicativeElementWithOne)",
    "CategoryCollections(IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse)",
    "CategoryCollections(IsAssociativeElement)",
    "CategoryCollections(IsFiniteOrderElement)", "IsGeneralizedDomain",
    "CategoryCollections(IsPerm)", "IsMagma", "IsMagmaWithOne",
    "IsMagmaWithInversesIfNonzero", "IsMagmaWithInverses" ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CategoryByName}}
\logpage{[ 13, 3, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85D07C3E7F4D4043}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CategoryByName({\mdseries\slshape name})\index{CategoryByName@\texttt{CategoryByName}}
\label{CategoryByName}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the category with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} if it is found, or fail otherwise. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NewCategory}}
\logpage{[ 13, 3, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87F68F887B44DBBD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewCategory({\mdseries\slshape name, super[, rank]})\index{NewCategory@\texttt{NewCategory}}
\label{NewCategory}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NewCategory} returns a new category \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cat}} that has the name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} and is contained in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}}, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}. This means that every object in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cat}} lies automatically also in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}}. We say also that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}} is an implied filter of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cat}}. 

 For example, if one wants to create a category of group elements then \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}} should be \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse}) or a subcategory of it. If no specific supercategory of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cat}} is known, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}} may be \texttt{IsObject} (\ref{IsObject}). 

 The optional third argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rank}} denotes the incremental rank (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}) of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cat}}, the default value is 1. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareCategory}}
\logpage{[ 13, 3, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X879DE2A17A6C6E92}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareCategory({\mdseries\slshape name, super[, rank]})\index{DeclareCategory@\texttt{DeclareCategory}}
\label{DeclareCategory}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 does the same as \texttt{NewCategory} (\ref{NewCategory}) and then binds the result to the global variable \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The variable must previously be writable, and is made
read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only by this function. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CategoryFamily}}
\logpage{[ 13, 3, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X787BACEE7937EF01}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CategoryFamily({\mdseries\slshape cat})\index{CategoryFamily@\texttt{CategoryFamily}}
\label{CategoryFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For a category \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cat}}, \texttt{CategoryFamily} returns the \emph{family category} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cat}}. This is a category in which all families lie that know from their creation
that all their elements are in the category \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cat}}, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Families}. 

 For example, a family of associative words is in the category \texttt{CategoryFamily( IsAssocWord )}, and one can distinguish such a family from others by this category. So it is
possible to install methods for operations that require one argument to be a
family of associative words. 

 \texttt{CategoryFamily} is quite technical, and in fact of minor importance. }

 

 See also \texttt{CategoryCollections} (\ref{CategoryCollections}). }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Representation}}\label{Representation}
\logpage{[ 13, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8698205F8648EB33}{}
{
  The \emph{representation} of an object is a set of filters (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}) that determines how an object is actually represented. For example, a matrix
or a polynomial can be stored sparsely or densely; all dense polynomials form
a representation. An object which claims to lie in a certain representation is
accepting the requirement that certain fields in the data structure be present
and have specified meanings. 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Basic Representations of Objects}}\logpage{[ 13, 4, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X805F1C3B7C730062}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsInternalRep({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsInternalRep@\texttt{IsInternalRep}}
\label{IsInternalRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Representation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsDataObjectRep({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsDataObjectRep@\texttt{IsDataObjectRep}}
\label{IsDataObjectRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Representation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPositionalObjectRep({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsPositionalObjectRep@\texttt{IsPositionalObjectRep}}
\label{IsPositionalObjectRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Representation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsComponentObjectRep({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsComponentObjectRep@\texttt{IsComponentObjectRep}}
\label{IsComponentObjectRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Representation)}}\\


 \textsf{GAP} distinguishes four essentially different ways to represent objects. First
there are the representations \texttt{IsInternalRep} for internal objects such as integers and permutations, and \texttt{IsDataObjectRep} for other objects that are created and whose data are accessible only by
kernel functions. The data structures underlying such objects cannot be
manipulated at the \textsf{GAP} level. 

 All other objects are either in the representation \texttt{IsComponentObjectRep} or in the representation \texttt{IsPositionalObjectRep}, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Positional Objects}. 

 An object can belong to several representations in the sense that it lies in
several subrepresentations of \texttt{IsComponentObjectRep} or of \texttt{IsPositionalObjectRep}. The representations to which an object belongs should form a chain and
either two representations are disjoint or one is contained in the other. So
the subrepresentations of \texttt{IsComponentObjectRep} and \texttt{IsPositionalObjectRep} each form trees. In the language of Object Oriented Programming, we support
only single inheritance for representations. 

 These trees are typically rather shallow, since for one representation to be
contained in another implies that all the components of the data structure
implied by the containing representation, are present in, and have the same
meaning in, the smaller representation (whose data structure presumably
contains some additional components). 

 Objects may change their representation, for example a mutable list of
characters can be converted into a string. 

 All representations in the library are created during initialization, in
particular they are not created dynamically at runtime. 

 Examples of subrepresentations of \texttt{IsPositionalObjectRep} are \texttt{IsModulusRep}, which is used for residue classes in the ring of integers, and \texttt{IsDenseCoeffVectorRep}, which is used for elements of algebras that are defined by structure
constants. 

 An important subrepresentation of \texttt{IsComponentObjectRep} is \texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep} (\ref{IsAttributeStoringRep}), which is used for many domains and some other objects. It provides automatic
storing of all attribute values (see Section \ref{Attributes}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsRepresentation}}
\logpage{[ 13, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86D42C7783ACA5F4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsRepresentation({\mdseries\slshape object})\index{IsRepresentation@\texttt{IsRepresentation}}
\label{IsRepresentation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns \texttt{true} if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape object}} is a representation (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Representation}), and \texttt{false} otherwise. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RepresentationsOfObject}}
\logpage{[ 13, 4, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BBE93BE7977750F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RepresentationsOfObject({\mdseries\slshape object})\index{RepresentationsOfObject@\texttt{RepresentationsOfObject}}
\label{RepresentationsOfObject}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a list of the names of the representations \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape object}} has. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2),(1,2,3));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RepresentationsOfObject(g);|
  [ "IsComponentObjectRep", "IsAttributeStoringRep" ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NewRepresentation}}
\logpage{[ 13, 4, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CC8106F809E15CF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewRepresentation({\mdseries\slshape name, super[, slots[, req]]})\index{NewRepresentation@\texttt{NewRepresentation}}
\label{NewRepresentation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NewRepresentation} returns a new representation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rep}} that has the name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} and is a subrepresentation of the representation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}}. This means that every object in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rep}} lies automatically also in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}}. We say also that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}} is an implied filter of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rep}}. 

 Each representation in \textsf{GAP} is a subrepresentation of exactly one of the four representations \texttt{IsInternalRep} (\ref{IsInternalRep}), \texttt{IsDataObjectRep} (\ref{IsDataObjectRep}), \texttt{IsComponentObjectRep} (\ref{IsComponentObjectRep}), \texttt{IsPositionalObjectRep} (\ref{IsPositionalObjectRep}). The data describing objects in the former two can be accessed only via \textsf{GAP} kernel functions, the data describing objects in the latter two is accessible
also in library functions, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Positional Objects} for the details. 

 The optional third and fourth arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape slots}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape req}} are (and always were) unused and are only provided for backwards
compatibility. Note that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape slots}} was required (but still unused) before GAP 4.12. 

 The incremental rank (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}) of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rep}} is 1. 

 Examples for the use of \texttt{NewRepresentation} can be found in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects}, \ref{Positional Objects}, and also in \ref{A Second Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareRepresentation}}
\logpage{[ 13, 4, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C81FB2682AE54CD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareRepresentation({\mdseries\slshape name, super[, slots[, req]]})\index{DeclareRepresentation@\texttt{DeclareRepresentation}}
\label{DeclareRepresentation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 does the same as \texttt{NewRepresentation} (\ref{NewRepresentation}) and then binds the result to the global variable \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The variable must previously be writable, and is made
read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only by this function. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Attributes}}\label{Attributes}
\logpage{[ 13, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7C701DBF7BAE649A}{}
{
  The attributes of an object describe knowledge about it. 

 An attribute is a unary operation without side\texttt{\symbol{45}}effects. 

 An object may store values of its attributes once they have been computed, and
claim that it knows these values. Note that ``store'' and ``know'' have to be understood in the sense that it is very cheap to get such a value
when the attribute is called again. 

 The value returned by an attribute is in general immutable (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Mutability and Copyability}), except if the attribute had been specially constructed as ``mutable attribute'', see \texttt{NewAttribute} (\ref{NewAttribute}). 

 Note that functions installed as methods for attributes may return mutable
objects, the attribute returns the value of \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}) for the result. Thus it is recommended that these methods ensure their return
values are immutable, e.g., by calling \texttt{MakeImmutable} (\ref{MakeImmutable}) if this is possible, in order to avoid that \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}) creates an unnecessary copy of the object. 

 It depends on the representation of an object (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Representation}) which attribute values it stores. An immutable object in the representation \texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep} (\ref{IsAttributeStoringRep}) stores \emph{all} attribute values once they are computed. 

 Note that it is impossible to get rid of a stored attribute value because the
system may have drawn conclusions from the old attribute value, and just
removing the value might leave the data structures in an inconsistent state.
If necessary, a new object can be constructed. 

 Each method that is installed for an attribute via \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) must require exactly one argument, and this must lie in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}} that was entered as second argument of \texttt{NewAttribute} (\ref{NewAttribute}) resp. \texttt{NewProperty} (\ref{NewProperty}). 

 As for any operation, for attributes one can install a method taking an
argument that does not lie in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} via \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod}), or a method for more than one argument. For example, \texttt{IsTransitive} (\ref{IsTransitive:for a group, an action domain, etc.}) is an attribute for a $G$\texttt{\symbol{45}}set that can also be called for the two arguments, being a
group $G$ and its action domain. If attributes are called with more than one argument
then the return value is not stored in any of the arguments. 

 Properties are a special form of attributes that have the value \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}, see section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Properties}. 

 Examples of attributes for multiplicative elements are \texttt{Inverse} (\ref{Inverse}), \texttt{One} (\ref{One}), and \texttt{Order} (\ref{Order}). \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}) is an attribute for domains, \texttt{Centre} (\ref{Centre}) is an attribute for magmas, and \texttt{DerivedSubgroup} (\ref{DerivedSubgroup}) is an attribute for groups. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsAttribute}}
\logpage{[ 13, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7973C8F4782D15A1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsAttribute({\mdseries\slshape object})\index{IsAttribute@\texttt{IsAttribute}}
\label{IsAttribute}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns \texttt{true} if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape object}} is an attribute (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Attributes}), and \texttt{false} otherwise. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{KnownAttributesOfObject}}
\logpage{[ 13, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F7960338163AA88}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{KnownAttributesOfObject({\mdseries\slshape object})\index{KnownAttributesOfObject@\texttt{KnownAttributesOfObject}}
\label{KnownAttributesOfObject}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a list of the names of the attributes whose values are known for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape object}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2),(1,2,3));;Size(g);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@KnownAttributesOfObject(g);|
  [ "Size", "OneImmutable", "NrMovedPoints", "MovedPoints",
    "GeneratorsOfMagmaWithInverses", "MultiplicativeNeutralElement",
    "HomePcgs", "Pcgs", "StabChainMutable", "StabChainOptions" ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NewAttribute}}
\logpage{[ 13, 5, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B9654807858A3B0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewAttribute({\mdseries\slshape name, filter[, "mutable"][, rank]})\index{NewAttribute@\texttt{NewAttribute}}
\label{NewAttribute}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NewAttribute} returns a new attribute getter with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} that is applicable to objects with the property \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}}. 

 Contrary to the situation with categories and representations, the tester of
the new attribute does \emph{not} imply \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}}. This is exactly because of the possibility to install methods that do not
require \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}}. 

 For example, the attribute \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}) was created with second argument a list or a collection, but there is also a
method for \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}) that is applicable to a character table, which is neither a list nor a
collection. 

 For the optional third and fourth arguments, there are the following
possibilities. 
\begin{itemize}
\item  The integer argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rank}} causes the attribute tester to have this incremental rank (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}), 
\item  If the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mutable}} is the string \texttt{"mutable"} or the boolean \texttt{true}, then the values of the attribute are mutable. 
\item  If the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mutable}} is the boolean \texttt{false}, then the values of the attribute are immutable. 
\end{itemize}
 

 When a value of such mutable attribute is set then this value itself is
stored, not an immutable copy of it, and it is the user's responsibility to
set an object that is mutable. This is useful for an attribute whose value is
some partial information that may be completed later. For example, there is an
attribute \texttt{ComputedSylowSubgroups} for the list holding those Sylow subgroups of a group that have been computed
already by the function \texttt{SylowSubgroup} (\ref{SylowSubgroup}), and this list is mutable because one may want to enter groups into it as
they are computed. 

 Mutable and immutable attributes behave differently w. r. t. repeated calls of
the function that sets the attribute value, see \texttt{Setter} (\ref{Setter}). 

 If no argument for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rank}} is given, then the rank of the tester is 1. 

 Each method for the new attribute that does \emph{not} require its argument to lie in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}} must be installed using \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareAttribute}}
\logpage{[ 13, 5, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A00FC8A7A677A56}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareAttribute({\mdseries\slshape name, filter[, "mutable"][, rank]})\index{DeclareAttribute@\texttt{DeclareAttribute}}
\label{DeclareAttribute}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 does the same as \texttt{NewAttribute} (\ref{NewAttribute}) and then binds the result to the global variable \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The variable must previously be writable, and is made
read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only by this function. It also binds
read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only global variables with names \texttt{Has\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}} and \texttt{Set\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}} for the tester and setter of the attribute (see Section \ref{Setter and Tester for Attributes}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsAttributeStoringRep}}
\logpage{[ 13, 5, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A951C33839AF2C1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsAttributeStoringRep@\texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep}}
\label{IsAttributeStoringRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Representation)}}\\


 Objects in this representation have default methods to get stored values of
attributes and {\textendash}if they are immutable{\textendash} to store
attribute values automatically once they have been computed. \index{system getter} \index{system setter} (These methods are called the ``system getter'' and the ``system setter'' of the attribute, respectively.) 

 As a consequence, for immutable objects in \texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep}, subsequent calls to an attribute will return the \emph{same} object. 

 \emph{Mutable} objects in \texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep} are allowed, but attribute values are not stored automatically in them. Such
objects are useful because they may later be made immutable using \texttt{MakeImmutable} (\ref{MakeImmutable}), at which point they will start storing all attribute values. 

 Note that one can force an attribute value to be stored in a mutable object in \texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep}, by explicitly calling the attribute setter. This feature should be used with
care. For example, think of a mutable matrix whose rank or trace gets stored,
and the values later become wrong when somebody changes the matrix entries. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Group( (1,2)(3,4), (1,3)(2,4) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsAttributeStoringRep( g );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HasSize( g );  Size( g );  HasSize( g );|
  false
  4
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r:= 7/4;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsAttributeStoringRep( r );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Int( r );  HasInt( r );|
  1
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Setter and Tester for Attributes}}\label{Setter and Tester for Attributes}
\logpage{[ 13, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79DE5208877AE42A}{}
{
  \index{setter} \index{tester} For every attribute, the \emph{attribute setter} and the \emph{attribute tester} are defined. 

 To check whether an object belongs to an attribute \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}}, the tester of the attribute is used, see \texttt{Tester} (\ref{Tester}). To store a value for the attribute \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} in an object, the setter of the attribute is used, see \texttt{Setter} (\ref{Setter}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Tester}}
\logpage{[ 13, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87D5B5AC7DAF932D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Tester({\mdseries\slshape attr})\index{Tester@\texttt{Tester}}
\label{Tester}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For an attribute \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}}, \texttt{Tester(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}})} is a filter (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}) that returns \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}, depending on whether or not the value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} for the object is known. For example, \texttt{Tester( Size )( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} )} is \texttt{true} if the size of the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is known. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Setter}}
\logpage{[ 13, 6, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7FD8952C841D2B1F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Setter({\mdseries\slshape attr})\index{Setter@\texttt{Setter}}
\label{Setter}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For an attribute \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}}, \texttt{Setter(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}})} is called automatically when the attribute value has been computed for an
immutable object which does not already have a value stored for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}}. One can also call the setter explicitly, for example, \texttt{Setter( Size )( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} )} sets \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} as size of the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} if the size was not yet known. 

 Calling the setter an of attribute for an object which stores already a value
for this attribute \emph{has no effect}, except if the attribute has been created as a \emph{mutable} attribute (see \texttt{NewAttribute} (\ref{NewAttribute})). For mutable attributes, each call of the setter \emph{replaces the stored value}. (Usually mutable attributes are used to store a mutable list or record once,
and later add data to this value, and then one should take care not to call
the setter of the attribute again.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@imm_attr:= NewAttribute( "imm_attr", IsGroup );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mut_attr:= NewAttribute( "mut_attr", IsGroup, "mutable" );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G:= SymmetricGroup( 4 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Setter( imm_attr )( G, 0 );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@imm_attr( G );|
  0
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Setter( imm_attr )( G, 1 );  # This call has no effect.|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@imm_attr( G );|
  0
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Setter( mut_attr )( G, 0 );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mut_attr( G );|
  0
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Setter( mut_attr )( G, 1 );  # This call replaces the stored value.|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mut_attr( G );|
  1
\end{Verbatim}
 

 For each attribute \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} that is declared with \texttt{DeclareAttribute} (\ref{DeclareAttribute}) resp.{\nobreakspace}\texttt{DeclareProperty} (\ref{DeclareProperty}), tester and setter are automatically made accessible by the names \texttt{Has\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}}} and \texttt{Set\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}}}, respectively. For example, the tester for \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}) is called \texttt{HasSize}, and the setter is called \texttt{SetSize}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2,3,4),(1,2));;Size(g);|
  24
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HasSize(g);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetSize(g,99);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(g);|
  24
\end{Verbatim}
 

 For two properties \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop1}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop2}}, the intersection \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop1}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop2}}} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}) is again a property for which a setter and a tester exist. Setting the value
of this intersection to \texttt{true} for a \textsf{GAP} object means to set the values of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop1}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop2}} to \texttt{true} for this object. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@prop:= IsFinite and IsCommutative;|
  <Property "(IsFinite and IsCommutative)">
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Group( (1,2,3), (4,5) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Tester( prop )( g );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Setter( prop )( g, true );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Tester( prop )( g );  prop( g );|
  true
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 

 It is \emph{not allowed} to set the value of such an intersection to \texttt{false} for an object. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Setter( prop )( Rationals, false );|
  Error, You cannot set an "and-filter" except to true
  not in any function at *stdin*:8
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop
  !gapbrkprompt@brk>| !gapinput@|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AttributeValueNotSet}}
\logpage{[ 13, 6, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8529F8A17884A32C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AttributeValueNotSet({\mdseries\slshape attr, obj})\index{AttributeValueNotSet@\texttt{AttributeValueNotSet}}
\label{AttributeValueNotSet}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 If the value of the attribute \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} is already stored for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, \texttt{AttributeValueNotSet} simply returns this value. Otherwise the value of \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}}( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} )} is computed and returned \emph{without storing it} in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. This can be useful when ``large'' attribute values (such as element lists) are needed only once and shall not be
stored in the object. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HasAsSSortedList(g);|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AttributeValueNotSet(AsSSortedList,g);|
  [ (), (4,5), (1,2,3), (1,2,3)(4,5), (1,3,2), (1,3,2)(4,5) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HasAsSSortedList(g);|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The normal behaviour of attributes (when called with just one argument) is
that once a method has been selected and executed, and has returned a value
the setter of the attribute is called, to (possibly) store the computed value.
In special circumstances, this behaviour can be altered dynamically on an
attribute\texttt{\symbol{45}}by\texttt{\symbol{45}}attribute basis, using the
functions \texttt{DisableAttributeValueStoring} (\ref{DisableAttributeValueStoring}) and \texttt{EnableAttributeValueStoring} (\ref{EnableAttributeValueStoring}). 

 In general, the code in the library assumes, for efficiency, but not for
correctness, that attribute values \emph{will} be stored (in suitable objects), so disabling storing may cause substantial
computations to be repeated. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoAttributes}}
\logpage{[ 13, 6, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79120CE37BB69D11}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoAttributes\index{InfoAttributes@\texttt{InfoAttributes}}
\label{InfoAttributes}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (info class)}}\\


 This info class (together with \texttt{InfoWarning} (\ref{InfoWarning})) is used for messages about attributes. Messages are shown under the
following circumstances: 
\begin{itemize}
\item  \texttt{EnableAttributeValueStoring} (\ref{EnableAttributeValueStoring}) is used (level 2).
\item  \texttt{DisableAttributeValueStoring} (\ref{DisableAttributeValueStoring}) is used (level 3).
\item  When trying to assign to non\texttt{\symbol{45}}mutable attribute which
already is set to a different value (level 3).
\item  When the test filter for an attribute (i.e., \texttt{HasFOO}) is set, but no value is assigned (level 3).
\end{itemize}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DisableAttributeValueStoring}}
\logpage{[ 13, 6, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7851E2DB79656DB0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DisableAttributeValueStoring({\mdseries\slshape attr})\index{DisableAttributeValueStoring@\texttt{DisableAttributeValueStoring}}
\label{DisableAttributeValueStoring}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 disables the usual call of \texttt{Setter( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} )} when a method for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} returns a value. In consequence the values will never be stored. Note that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} must be an attribute and \emph{not} a property. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{EnableAttributeValueStoring}}
\logpage{[ 13, 6, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E5DACBE7A9A9AD1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{EnableAttributeValueStoring({\mdseries\slshape attr})\index{EnableAttributeValueStoring@\texttt{EnableAttributeValueStoring}}
\label{EnableAttributeValueStoring}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 enables the usual call of \texttt{Setter( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} )} when a method for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} returns a value. In consequence the values may be stored. This will usually
have no effect unless \texttt{DisableAttributeValueStoring} (\ref{DisableAttributeValueStoring}) has previously been used for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}}. Note that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} must be an attribute and \emph{not} a property. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g := Group((1,2,3,4,5),(1,2,3));|
  Group([ (1,2,3,4,5), (1,2,3) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@KnownAttributesOfObject(g);|
  [ "LargestMovedPoint", "GeneratorsOfMagmaWithInverses",
    "MultiplicativeNeutralElement" ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetInfoLevel(InfoAttributes,3);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DisableAttributeValueStoring(Size);|
  #I  Disabling value storing for Size
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(g);|
  60
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@KnownAttributesOfObject(g);|
  [ "OneImmutable", "LargestMovedPoint", "NrMovedPoints",
    "MovedPoints", "GeneratorsOfMagmaWithInverses",
    "MultiplicativeNeutralElement", "StabChainMutable",
    "StabChainOptions" ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(g);|
  60
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@EnableAttributeValueStoring(Size);|
  #I  Enabling value storing for Size
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(g);|
  60
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@KnownAttributesOfObject(g);|
  [ "Size", "OneImmutable", "LargestMovedPoint", "NrMovedPoints",
    "MovedPoints", "GeneratorsOfMagmaWithInverses",
    "MultiplicativeNeutralElement", "StabChainMutable",
    "StabChainOptions" ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Properties}}\label{Properties}
\logpage{[ 13, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X871597447BB998A1}{}
{
  The properties of an object are those of its attributes (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Attributes}) whose values can only be \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}. 

 The main difference between attributes and properties is that a property
defines two sets of objects, namely the usual set of all objects for which the
value is known, and the set of all objects for which the value is known to be \texttt{true}. 

 (Note that it makes no sense to consider a third set, namely the set of
objects for which the value of a property is \texttt{true} whether or not it is known, since there may be objects for which the
containment in this set cannot be decided.) 

 For a property \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}}, the containment of an object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} in the first set is checked again by applying \texttt{Tester( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}} )} to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} lies in the second set if and only if \texttt{Tester( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}} )( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} ) and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}}( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} )} is \texttt{true}. 

 If a property value is known for an immutable object then this value is also
stored, as part of the type of the object. To some extent, property values of
mutable objects also can be stored, for example a mutable list all of whose
entries are immutable can store whether it is strictly sorted. When the object
is mutated (for example by list assignment) the type may need to be adjusted. 

 Important properties for domains are \texttt{IsAssociative} (\ref{IsAssociative}), \texttt{IsCommutative} (\ref{IsCommutative}), \texttt{IsAnticommutative} (\ref{IsAnticommutative}), \texttt{IsLDistributive} (\ref{IsLDistributive}) and \texttt{IsRDistributive} (\ref{IsRDistributive}), which mean that the multiplication of elements in the domain satisfies $( a * b ) * c = a * ( b * c )$, $a * b = b * a$, $a * b = - ( b * a )$, $a * ( b + c ) = a * b + a * c$, and $( a + b ) * c = a * c + b * c$, respectively, for all $a$, $b$, $c$ in the domain.

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NewProperty}}
\logpage{[ 13, 7, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F2D6FD979FE23DD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewProperty({\mdseries\slshape name, filter[, rank]})\index{NewProperty@\texttt{NewProperty}}
\label{NewProperty}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NewProperty} returns a new property \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}} with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} (see also{\nobreakspace}\ref{Properties}). The filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}} describes the involved filters of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}}. As in the case of attributes, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}} is not implied by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}}. 

 The optional third argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rank}} denotes the incremental rank (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}) of the property \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}} itself, i.e. \emph{not} of its tester; the default value is 1. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareProperty}}
\logpage{[ 13, 7, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F4602F082682A04}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareProperty({\mdseries\slshape name, filter[, rank]})\index{DeclareProperty@\texttt{DeclareProperty}}
\label{DeclareProperty}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 does the same as \texttt{NewProperty} (\ref{NewProperty}) and then binds the result to the global variable \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The variable must previously be writable, and is made
read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only by this function. It also binds
read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only global variables with names \texttt{Has\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}} and \texttt{Set\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}} for the tester and setter of the property (see Section \ref{Setter and Tester for Attributes}). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Other Filters}}\label{Other Filters}
\logpage{[ 13, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7997705185C7E720}{}
{
  There are situations where one wants to express a kind of knowledge that is
based on some heuristic. 

 For example, the filters (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}) \texttt{CanEasilyTestMembership} (\ref{CanEasilyTestMembership}) and \texttt{CanEasilyComputePcgs} (\ref{CanEasilyComputePcgs}) are defined in the \textsf{GAP} library. Note that such filters do not correspond to a mathematical concept,
contrary to properties (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Properties}). Also it need not be defined what ``easily'' means for an arbitrary \textsf{GAP} object, and in this case one cannot compute the value for an arbitrary \textsf{GAP} object. In order to access this kind of knowledge as a part of the type of an
object, \textsf{GAP} provides filters for which the value is \texttt{false} by default, and it is changed to \texttt{true} in certain situations, either explicitly (for the given object) or via a
logical implication (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Logical Implications}) from other filters. 

 For example, a \texttt{true} value of \texttt{CanEasilyComputePcgs} (\ref{CanEasilyComputePcgs}) for a group means that certain methods are applicable that use a pcgs
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Polycyclic Generating Systems}) for the group. There are logical implications to set the filter value to \texttt{true} for permutation groups that are known to be solvable, and for groups that have
already a (sufficiently nice) pcgs stored. In the case one has a solvable
matrix group and wants to enable methods that use a pcgs, one can set the \texttt{CanEasilyComputePcgs} (\ref{CanEasilyComputePcgs}) value to \texttt{true} for this particular group. 

 A filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} of the kind described here is different from the other filters introduced in
the previous sections. In particular, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} is not a category (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Categories}) or a property (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Properties}) because its value may change for a given object, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} is not a representation (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Representation}) because it has nothing to do with the way an object is made up from some
data. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} is similar to an attribute tester (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Setter and Tester for Attributes}), the only difference is that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} does not refer to an attribute value; note that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} is also used in the same way as an attribute tester; namely, the \texttt{true} value may be required for certain methods to be applicable. 

 In order to change the value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} for an object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, one can use logical implications (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Logical Implications}) or \texttt{SetFilterObj} (\ref{SetFilterObj}), \texttt{ResetFilterObj} (\ref{ResetFilterObj}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NewFilter}}
\logpage{[ 13, 8, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X821635DA7821ED74}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewFilter({\mdseries\slshape name[, implied][, rank]})\index{NewFilter@\texttt{NewFilter}}
\label{NewFilter}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NewFilter} returns a simple filter with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Other Filters}). 

 The optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape implied}}, if given, must be a filter, meaning that for each object in the new filter,
also \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape implied}} will be set. Note that resetting the new filter with \texttt{ResetFilterObj} (\ref{ResetFilterObj}) does \emph{not} reset \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape implied}}. If the new filter is intended to be set or reset manually for existing
objects then the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape implied}} will cause trouble; if the filter is not intended to be set or reset manually
then perhaps calling \texttt{NewCategory} (\ref{NewCategory}) is more appropriate than calling \texttt{NewFilter}. 

 The optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rank}} denotes the incremental rank (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}) of the filter, the default value is 1. 

 The default value of the new simple filter for each object is \texttt{false}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareFilter}}
\logpage{[ 13, 8, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X846EA18A7D36626C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareFilter({\mdseries\slshape name[, implied][, rank]})\index{DeclareFilter@\texttt{DeclareFilter}}
\label{DeclareFilter}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 does the same as \texttt{NewFilter} (\ref{NewFilter}) and then binds the result to the global variable \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The variable must previously be writable, and is made
read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only by this function. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetFilterObj}}
\logpage{[ 13, 8, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C92D53E7920CE02}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetFilterObj({\mdseries\slshape obj, filter})\index{SetFilterObj@\texttt{SetFilterObj}}
\label{SetFilterObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{SetFilterObj} sets the value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}} (and of all filters implied by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}}) for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} to \texttt{true}. 

 This may trigger immediate methods. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ResetFilterObj}}
\logpage{[ 13, 8, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8117FD03870FB02E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ResetFilterObj({\mdseries\slshape obj, filter})\index{ResetFilterObj@\texttt{ResetFilterObj}}
\label{ResetFilterObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{ResetFilterObj} sets the value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}} for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} to \texttt{false}. (Implied filters of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} are not touched. This might create inconsistent situations if applied
carelessly). }

   }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Types}}\label{Types}
\logpage{[ 13, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7E340B8C833BC440}{}
{
  We stated above (see \ref{Types of Objects}) that, for an object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, its \emph{type} is formed from its family and its filters. There is also a third component,
used in a few situations, namely defining data of the type. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TypeObj}}
\logpage{[ 13, 9, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D3E6B6482BE5B16}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TypeObj({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{TypeObj@\texttt{TypeObj}}
\label{TypeObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the type of the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. 

 The type of an object is itself an object. 

 Two types are equal if and only if the two families are identical, the filters
are equal, and, if present, also the defining data of the types are equal. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DataType}}
\logpage{[ 13, 9, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85A60A7F8083C1C4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DataType({\mdseries\slshape type})\index{DataType@\texttt{DataType}}
\label{DataType}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 The last part of the type, defining data, has not been mentioned before and
seems to be of minor importance. It can be used, e.g., for cosets $U g$ of a group $U$, where the type of each coset may contain the group $U$ as defining data. As a consequence, two such cosets mod $U$ and $V$ can have the same type only if $U = V$. The defining data of the type \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape type}} can be accessed via \texttt{DataType}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NewType}}
\logpage{[ 13, 9, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CE39E9478AEC826}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewType({\mdseries\slshape family, filter[, data]})\index{NewType@\texttt{NewType}}
\label{NewType}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NewType} returns the type given by the family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape family}} and the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}}. The optional third argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}} is any object that denotes defining data of the desired type. 

 For examples where \texttt{NewType} is used, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects}, \ref{Positional Objects}, and the example in Chapter \ref{An Example -- Residue Class Rings}. }

 }

 }

             
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Integers}}\label{Integers}
\logpage{[ 14, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X853DF11B80068ED5}{}
{
  One of the most fundamental datatypes in every programming language is the
integer type. \textsf{GAP} is no exception. 

 \textsf{GAP} integers are entered as a sequence of decimal digits optionally preceded by a ``\texttt{+}'' sign for positive integers or a ``\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}}'' sign for negative integers. The size of integers in \textsf{GAP} is only limited by the amount of available memory, so you can compute with
integers having thousands of digits. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@-1234;|
  -1234
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890;|
  123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890
\end{Verbatim}
 Note that in a few places, only certain small integer values can be used. A \emph{small integer} (also referred to as \emph{immediate integer}) is an integer $n$ satisfying \texttt{INTOBJ{\textunderscore}MIN} $ \leq n \leq $ \texttt{INTOBJ{\textunderscore}MAX}, where \texttt{INTOBJ{\textunderscore}MIN} and \texttt{INTOBJ{\textunderscore}MAX} equal either $-2^{28}$ and $2^{28}-1$ (on 32\texttt{\symbol{45}}bit systems) or $-2^{60}$ and $2^{60}-1$ (on 64\texttt{\symbol{45}}bit systems). \index{small integer} \index{immediate integer} \index{INTOBJ{\textunderscore}MIN} \index{INTOBJ{\textunderscore}MAX} For example, the elements of a range are restricted to small integers
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Ranges}). 

 Many more functions that are mainly related to the prime residue group of
integers modulo an integer are described in chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Number Theory}, and functions dealing with combinatorics can be found in
chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Combinatorics}.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Integers: Global Variables}}\label{sect:Integers: Global Variables}
\logpage{[ 14, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X838230CE810107A3}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Integers (global variable)}}
\logpage{[ 14, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E20D82B79DE5129}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Integers\index{Integers@\texttt{Integers}!global variable}
\label{Integers:global variable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PositiveIntegers\index{PositiveIntegers@\texttt{PositiveIntegers}}
\label{PositiveIntegers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NonnegativeIntegers\index{NonnegativeIntegers@\texttt{NonnegativeIntegers}}
\label{NonnegativeIntegers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 These global variables represent the ring of integers and the semirings of
positive and nonnegative integers, respectively. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( Integers ); 2 in Integers;|
  infinity
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \texttt{Integers} is a subset of \texttt{Rationals} (\ref{Rationals}), which is a subset of \texttt{Cyclotomics} (\ref{Cyclotomics}). See Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Cyclotomic Numbers} for arithmetic operations and comparison of integers. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsIntegers}}
\logpage{[ 14, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X818683B17F8C97F3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsIntegers({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsIntegers@\texttt{IsIntegers}}
\label{IsIntegers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPositiveIntegers({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsPositiveIntegers@\texttt{IsPositiveIntegers}}
\label{IsPositiveIntegers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsNonnegativeIntegers({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsNonnegativeIntegers@\texttt{IsNonnegativeIntegers}}
\label{IsNonnegativeIntegers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 are the defining categories for the domains \texttt{Integers} (\ref{Integers:global variable}), \texttt{PositiveIntegers} (\ref{PositiveIntegers}), and \texttt{NonnegativeIntegers} (\ref{NonnegativeIntegers}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsIntegers( Integers );  IsIntegers( Rationals );  IsIntegers( 7 );|
  true
  false
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Elementary Operations for Integers}}\label{Elementary Operations for Integers}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X80CF510B8080C7CA}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87AEADF07DC8303B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsInt({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsInt@\texttt{IsInt}}
\label{IsInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 Every rational integer lies in the category \texttt{IsInt}, which is a subcategory of \texttt{IsRat} (\ref{IsRat}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPosInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82A854757DFA9C76}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPosInt({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsPosInt@\texttt{IsPosInt}}
\label{IsPosInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 Every positive integer lies in the category \texttt{IsPosInt}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Int}}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87CA734380B5F68C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Int({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{Int@\texttt{Int}}
\label{Int}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 \texttt{Int} returns an integer \texttt{int} whose meaning depends on the type of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}. For example: 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} is a rational number (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Rational Numbers}) then \texttt{int} is the integer part of the quotient of numerator and denominator of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{QuoInt} (\ref{QuoInt})). 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} is an element of a finite prime field (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Finite Fields}) then \texttt{int} is the smallest nonnegative integer such that \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} = int * One( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} )}. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} is a string (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Strings and Characters}) consisting entirely of decimal digits \texttt{'0'}, \texttt{'1'}, $\ldots$, \texttt{'9'}, and optionally a sign \texttt{'\texttt{\symbol{45}}'} (at the first position), then \texttt{int} is the integer described by this string. For all other strings, \texttt{fail} is returned. See \texttt{Int} (\ref{Int:for strings}). 

 The operation \texttt{String} (\ref{String}) can be used to compute a string for rational integers, in fact for all
cyclotomics. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Int( 4/3 );  Int( -2/3 );|
  1
  0
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@int:= Int( Z(5) );  int * One( Z(5) );|
  2
  Z(5)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Int( "12345" );  Int( "-27" );  Int( "-27/3" );|
  12345
  -27
  fail
\end{Verbatim}
 }

\logpage{[ 14, 2, 4 ]}\nobreak

{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsEvenInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{IsEvenInt@\texttt{IsEvenInt}}
\label{IsEvenInt}

 tests if the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is not divisible by 2. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AbsInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X782095927FB9F1DB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AbsInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{AbsInt@\texttt{AbsInt}}
\label{AbsInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{absolute value of an integer} \texttt{AbsInt} returns the absolute value of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, i.e., \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is positive, \texttt{\symbol{45}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is negative and 0 if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is 0. 

 \texttt{AbsInt} is a special case of the general operation \texttt{EuclideanDegree} (\ref{EuclideanDegree}). 

 See also \texttt{AbsoluteValue} (\ref{AbsoluteValue}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AbsInt( 33 );|
  33
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AbsInt( -214378 );|
  214378
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AbsInt( 0 );|
  0
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SignInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X842614817FE48D62}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SignInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{SignInt@\texttt{SignInt}}
\label{SignInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{sign!of an integer} \texttt{SignInt} returns the sign of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, i.e., 1 if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is positive, \texttt{\symbol{45}}1 if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is negative and 0 if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is 0. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SignInt( 33 );|
  1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SignInt( -214378 );|
  -1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SignInt( 0 );|
  0
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LogInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8197C4E882BAF14E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LogInt({\mdseries\slshape n, base})\index{LogInt@\texttt{LogInt}}
\label{LogInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{LogInt} returns the integer part of the logarithm of the positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} with respect to the positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}}, i.e., the largest positive integer $e$ such that $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}}^e \leq \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}$. The function \texttt{LogInt} will signal an error if either \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} or \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}} is not positive. 

 For \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}} $= 2$ this is very efficient because the internal binary representation of the
integer is used. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LogInt( 1030, 2 );|
  10
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@2^10;|
  1024
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LogInt( 1, 10 );|
  0
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RootInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83D9B5C87EEA2A77}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RootInt({\mdseries\slshape n[, k]})\index{RootInt@\texttt{RootInt}}
\label{RootInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{root!of an integer} \index{square root!of an integer} \texttt{RootInt} returns the integer part of the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}th root of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. If the optional integer argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}} is not given it defaults to 2, i.e., \texttt{RootInt} returns the integer part of the square root in this case. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is positive, \texttt{RootInt} returns the largest positive integer $r$ such that $r^{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}} \leq \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}$. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is negative and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}} is odd \texttt{RootInt} returns \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}RootInt( \texttt{\symbol{45}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}} )}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is negative and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}} is even \texttt{RootInt} will cause an error. \texttt{RootInt} will also cause an error if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}} is 0 or negative. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootInt( 361 );|
  19
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootInt( 2 * 10^12 );|
  1414213
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootInt( 17000, 5 );|
  7
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@7^5;|
  16807
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SmallestRootInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F98A0CE7B9FD366}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SmallestRootInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{SmallestRootInt@\texttt{SmallestRootInt}}
\label{SmallestRootInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{root!of an integer, smallest} \texttt{SmallestRootInt} returns the smallest root of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. 

 The smallest root of an integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is the integer $r$ of smallest absolute value for which a positive integer $k$ exists such that $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} = r^k$. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SmallestRootInt( 2^30 );|
  2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SmallestRootInt( -(2^30) );|
  -4
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that $(-2)^{30} = +(2^{30})$. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SmallestRootInt( 279936 );|
  6
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LogInt( 279936, 6 );|
  7
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SmallestRootInt( 1001 );|
  1001
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsSquareInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 11 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83B998E486893FED}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsSquareInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{IsSquareInt@\texttt{IsSquareInt}}
\label{IsSquareInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{IsSquareInt} tests whether the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is the square of an integer or not. This test is much faster than the simpler \texttt{RootInt}$(n)^2=n$ because it first tests whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is a square residue modulo some small integers. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ListOfDigits}}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 12 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X862D1BD786EFFDA9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ListOfDigits({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{ListOfDigits@\texttt{ListOfDigits}}
\label{ListOfDigits}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For a positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} this function returns a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape l}}, consisting of the digits of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} in decimal representation. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ListOfDigits(3142);|
  [ 3, 1, 4, 2 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Random (for integers)}}
\logpage{[ 14, 2, 13 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8185784B7E228DEA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Random({\mdseries\slshape Integers})\index{Random@\texttt{Random}!for integers}
\label{Random:for integers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\


 \texttt{Random} for integers returns pseudo random integers between $-10$ and $10$ distributed according to a binomial distribution. To generate uniformly
distributed integers from a range, use the construction \texttt{Random( [ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape low}} .. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape high}} ] )} {\nobreakspace}(see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Random} (\ref{Random:for lower and upper bound})). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Quotients and Remainders}}\label{Quotients and Remainders}
\logpage{[ 14, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7A9FD25D81D88D1B}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{QuoInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X849D0F807F697D35}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{QuoInt({\mdseries\slshape n, m})\index{QuoInt@\texttt{QuoInt}}
\label{QuoInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{integer part of a quotient} \texttt{QuoInt} returns the integer part of the quotient of its integer operands. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} are positive, \texttt{QuoInt} returns the largest positive integer $q$ such that $q * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} \leq \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}$. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} or \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} or both are negative the absolute value of the integer part of the quotient is
the quotient of the absolute values of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}, and the sign of it is the product of the signs of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. 

 \texttt{QuoInt} is used in a method for the general operation \texttt{EuclideanQuotient} (\ref{EuclideanQuotient}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@QuoInt(5,3);  QuoInt(-5,3);  QuoInt(5,-3);  QuoInt(-5,-3);|
  1
  -1
  -1
  1
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{BestQuoInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X795170A385AC8FEE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{BestQuoInt({\mdseries\slshape n, m})\index{BestQuoInt@\texttt{BestQuoInt}}
\label{BestQuoInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{BestQuoInt} returns the best quotient $q$ of the integers \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. This is the quotient such that $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}-q*\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}$ has minimal absolute value. If there are two quotients whose remainders have
the same absolute value, then the quotient with the smaller absolute value is
chosen. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@BestQuoInt( 5, 3 );  BestQuoInt( -5, 3 );|
  2
  -2
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RemInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 3, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X805ADD5A826D844D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RemInt({\mdseries\slshape n, m})\index{RemInt@\texttt{RemInt}}
\label{RemInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{remainder of a quotient} \texttt{RemInt} returns the remainder of its two integer operands. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} is not equal to zero, \texttt{RemInt} returns \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} \texttt{\symbol{45}} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} * QuoInt( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} )}. Note that the rules given for \texttt{QuoInt} (\ref{QuoInt}) imply that the return value of \texttt{RemInt} has the same sign as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and its absolute value is strictly less than the absolute value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. Note also that the return value equals \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} mod \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}} when both \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} are nonnegative. Dividing by \texttt{0} signals an error. 

 \texttt{RemInt} is used in a method for the general operation \texttt{EuclideanRemainder} (\ref{EuclideanRemainder}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RemInt(5,3);  RemInt(-5,3);  RemInt(5,-3);  RemInt(-5,-3);|
  2
  -2
  2
  -2
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GcdInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 3, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A4FEFCA8128E3C3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GcdInt({\mdseries\slshape m, n})\index{GcdInt@\texttt{GcdInt}}
\label{GcdInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{GcdInt} returns the greatest common divisor of its two integer operands \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, i.e., the greatest integer that divides both \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. The greatest common divisor is never negative, even if the arguments are. We
define \texttt{GcdInt( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}, 0 ) = GcdInt( 0, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} ) = AbsInt( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} )} and \texttt{GcdInt( 0, 0 ) = 0}. 

 \texttt{GcdInt} is a method used by the general function \texttt{Gcd} (\ref{Gcd:for (a ring and) several elements}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GcdInt( 123, 66 );|
  3
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Gcdex}}
\logpage{[ 14, 3, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8775930486BD0C5B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Gcdex({\mdseries\slshape m, n})\index{Gcdex@\texttt{Gcdex}}
\label{Gcdex}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a record \texttt{g} describing the extended greatest common divisor of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. The component \texttt{gcd} is this gcd, the components \texttt{coeff1} and \texttt{coeff2} are integer cofactors such that \texttt{g.gcd = g.coeff1 * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} + g.coeff2 * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}}, and the components \texttt{coeff3} and \texttt{coeff4} are integer cofactors such that \texttt{0 = g.coeff3 * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} + g.coeff4 * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}}. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} both are nonzero, \texttt{AbsInt( g.coeff1 )} is less than or equal to \texttt{AbsInt(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}) / (2 * g.gcd)}, and \texttt{AbsInt( g.coeff2 )} is less than or equal to \texttt{AbsInt(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}) / (2 * g.gcd)}. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} or \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} or both are zero \texttt{coeff3} is \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} / g.gcd} and \texttt{coeff4} is \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} / g.gcd}. 

 The coefficients always form a unimodular matrix, i.e., the determinant \texttt{g.coeff1 * g.coeff4 \texttt{\symbol{45}} g.coeff3 * g.coeff2} is $1$ or $-1$. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Gcdex( 123, 66 );|
  rec( coeff1 := 7, coeff2 := -13, coeff3 := -22, coeff4 := 41,
    gcd := 3 )
\end{Verbatim}
 This means $3 = 7 * 123 - 13 * 66$, $0 = -22 * 123 + 41 * 66$. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Gcdex( 0, -3 );|
  rec( coeff1 := 0, coeff2 := -1, coeff3 := 1, coeff4 := 0, gcd := 3 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Gcdex( 0, 0 );|
  rec( coeff1 := 1, coeff2 := 0, coeff3 := 0, coeff4 := 1, gcd := 0 )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \texttt{GcdRepresentation} (\ref{GcdRepresentation:for (a ring and) several elements}) provides similar functionality over arbitrary Euclidean rings. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LcmInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 3, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B33143E78A8DDE3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LcmInt({\mdseries\slshape m, n})\index{LcmInt@\texttt{LcmInt}}
\label{LcmInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the least common multiple of the integers \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. 

 \texttt{LcmInt} is a method used by the general operation \texttt{Lcm} (\ref{Lcm:for (a ring and) several elements}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LcmInt( 123, 66 );|
  2706
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CoefficientsQadic}}
\logpage{[ 14, 3, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79B466E984CD52D4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CoefficientsQadic({\mdseries\slshape i, q})\index{CoefficientsQadic@\texttt{CoefficientsQadic}}
\label{CoefficientsQadic}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape q}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}adic representation of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} as a list $l$ of coefficients satisfying the equality $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} = \sum_{{j = 0}} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape q}}^j \cdot l[j+1]$ for an integer $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape q}} > 1$. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l:=CoefficientsQadic(462,3);|
  [ 0, 1, 0, 2, 2, 1 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CoefficientsMultiadic}}
\logpage{[ 14, 3, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83124F86839DC7E6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CoefficientsMultiadic({\mdseries\slshape ints, int})\index{CoefficientsMultiadic@\texttt{CoefficientsMultiadic}}
\label{CoefficientsMultiadic}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
