 returns the multiadic expansion of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape int}} modulo the integers given in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ints}} (in ascending order). It returns a list of coefficients in the \emph{reverse} order to that in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ints}}.  }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ChineseRem}}
\logpage{[ 14, 3, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84A1900E82902B5F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ChineseRem({\mdseries\slshape moduli, residues})\index{ChineseRem@\texttt{ChineseRem}}
\label{ChineseRem}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{Chinese remainder} \texttt{ChineseRem} returns the combination of the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape residues}} modulo the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape moduli}}, i.e., the unique integer \texttt{c} from \texttt{[0..Lcm(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape moduli}})\texttt{\symbol{45}}1]} such that \texttt{c = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape residues}}[i]} modulo \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape moduli}}[i]} for all \texttt{i}, if it exists. If no such combination exists \texttt{ChineseRem} signals an error. 

 Such a combination does exist if and only if \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape residues}}[i] = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape residues}}[k] mod Gcd( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape moduli}}[i], \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape moduli}}[k] )} for every pair \texttt{i}, \texttt{k}. Note that this implies that such a combination exists if the moduli are
pairwise relatively prime. This is called the Chinese remainder theorem. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ChineseRem( [ 2, 3, 5, 7 ], [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ] );|
  53
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ChineseRem( [ 6, 10, 14 ], [ 1, 3, 5 ] );|
  103
\end{Verbatim}
 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!|B,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt|gap>B !gapinput|ChineseRem( [ 6, 10, 14 ], [ 1, 2, 3 ] );B
  Error, the residues must be equal modulo 2
  Stack trace:
  *[1] Error( "the residues must be equal modulo ", g.gcd );
     @ GAPROOT/lib/integer.gi:391
  <function "ChineseRem">( <arguments> )
   called from read-eval loop at *stdin*:2
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  !gapbrkprompt|brk>B !gapinput|B
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PowerModInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 3, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E404B1183DBC82A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PowerModInt({\mdseries\slshape r, e, m})\index{PowerModInt@\texttt{PowerModInt}}
\label{PowerModInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}^{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape e}}} \pmod{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}}$ for integers \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape e}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. 

 Note that \texttt{PowerModInt} can reduce intermediate results and thus will generally be faster than using \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape e}}\texttt{ mod }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}, which would compute $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}^{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape e}}}$ first and reduces the result afterwards. 

 \texttt{PowerModInt} is a method for the general operation \texttt{PowerMod} (\ref{PowerMod}). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Prime Integers and Factorization}}\label{Prime Integers and Factorization}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X82005E587F0CB02A}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Primes}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86F5E4CD82FEB9F4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Primes\index{Primes@\texttt{Primes}}
\label{Primes}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 \texttt{Primes} is a strictly sorted list of the 168 primes less than 1000. 

 This is used in \texttt{IsPrimeInt} (\ref{IsPrimeInt}) and \texttt{FactorsInt} (\ref{FactorsInt}) to cast out small primes quickly. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Primes[1];|
  2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Primes[100];|
  541
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPrimeInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78FDA4437EDCA70C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPrimeInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{IsPrimeInt@\texttt{IsPrimeInt}}
\label{IsPrimeInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsProbablyPrimeInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{IsProbablyPrimeInt@\texttt{IsProbablyPrimeInt}}
\label{IsProbablyPrimeInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{IsPrimeInt} returns \texttt{false} if it can prove that the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is composite and \texttt{true} otherwise. By convention \texttt{IsPrimeInt(0) = IsPrimeInt(1) = false} and we define \texttt{IsPrimeInt(\texttt{\symbol{45}}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}\texttt{) = IsPrimeInt(}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}\texttt{)}. 

 \texttt{IsPrimeInt} will return \texttt{true} for every prime \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. \texttt{IsPrimeInt} will return \texttt{false} for all composite \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} $< 10^{18}$ and for all composite \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} that have a factor $p < 1000$. So for integers \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} $< 10^{18}$, \texttt{IsPrimeInt} is a proper primality test. It is conceivable that \texttt{IsPrimeInt} may return \texttt{true} for some composite \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} $> 10^{18}$, but no such \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is currently known. So for integers \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} $> 10^{18}$, \texttt{IsPrimeInt} is a probable\texttt{\symbol{45}}primality test. \texttt{IsPrimeInt} will issue a warning when its argument is probably prime but not a proven
prime. (The function \texttt{IsProbablyPrimeInt} will do a similar calculation but not issue a warning.) The warning can be
switched off by \texttt{SetInfoLevel( InfoPrimeInt, 0 );}, the default level is $1$ (also see \texttt{SetInfoLevel} (\ref{SetInfoLevel}) ). 

 If composites that fool \texttt{IsPrimeInt} do exist, they would be extremely rare, and finding one by pure chance might
be less likely than finding a bug in \textsf{GAP}. We would appreciate being informed about any example of a composite number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} for which \texttt{IsPrimeInt} returns \texttt{true}. 

 \texttt{IsPrimeInt} is a deterministic algorithm, i.e., the computations involve no random
numbers, and repeated calls will always return the same result. \texttt{IsPrimeInt} first does trial divisions by the primes less than 1000. Then it tests that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is a strong pseudoprime w.r.t. the base 2. Finally it tests whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is a Lucas pseudoprime w.r.t. the smallest quadratic nonresidue of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. A better description can be found in the comment in the library file \texttt{primality.gi}. 

 The time taken by \texttt{IsPrimeInt} is approximately proportional to the third power of the number of digits of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. Testing numbers with several hundreds digits is quite feasible. 

 \texttt{IsPrimeInt} is a method for the general operation \texttt{IsPrime} (\ref{IsPrime}). 

 Remark: In future versions of \textsf{GAP} we hope to change the definition of \texttt{IsPrimeInt} to return \texttt{true} only for proven primes (currently, we lack a sufficiently good primality
proving function). In applications, use explicitly \texttt{IsPrimeInt} or \texttt{IsProbablyPrimeInt} with this change in mind. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPrimeInt( 2^31 - 1 );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPrimeInt( 10^42 + 1 );|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PrimalityProof}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CD977B17B4A7A4B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrimalityProof({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{PrimalityProof@\texttt{PrimalityProof}}
\label{PrimalityProof}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Construct a machine verifiable proof of the primality of (the probable prime) \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, following the ideas of \cite{BLS1975}. The proof consists of various Fermat and Lucas pseudoprimality tests, which
taken as a whole prove the primality. The proof is represented as a list of
witnesses of two kinds. The first kind, \texttt{[ "F", divisor, base ]}, indicates a successful Fermat pseudoprimality test, where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is a strong pseudoprime at \texttt{base} with order not divisible by $(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}-1)/divisor$. The second kind, \texttt{[ "L", divisor, discriminant, P ]} indicates a successful Lucas pseudoprimality test, for a quadratic form of
given \texttt{discriminant} and middle term \texttt{P} with an extra check at $(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}+1)/divisor$. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPrimePowerInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8443125D7FD6F2A6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPrimePowerInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{IsPrimePowerInt@\texttt{IsPrimePowerInt}}
\label{IsPrimePowerInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{IsPrimePowerInt} returns \texttt{true} if the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is a prime power and \texttt{false} otherwise. 

 An integer $n$ is a \emph{prime power} if there exists a prime $p$ and a positive integer $i$ such that $p^i = n$. If $n$ is negative the condition is that there must exist a negative prime $p$ and an odd positive integer $i$ such that $p^i = n$. The integers 1 and \texttt{\symbol{45}}1 are not prime powers. 

 Note that \texttt{IsPrimePowerInt} uses \texttt{SmallestRootInt} (\ref{SmallestRootInt}) and a probable\texttt{\symbol{45}}primality test (see \texttt{IsPrimeInt} (\ref{IsPrimeInt})). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPrimePowerInt( 31^5 );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPrimePowerInt( 2^31-1 );  # 2^31-1 is actually a prime|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPrimePowerInt( 2^63-1 );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Filtered( [-10..10], IsPrimePowerInt );|
  [ -8, -7, -5, -3, -2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NextPrimeInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78744C367A94C69F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NextPrimeInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{NextPrimeInt@\texttt{NextPrimeInt}}
\label{NextPrimeInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NextPrimeInt} returns the smallest prime which is strictly larger than the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. 

 Note that \texttt{NextPrimeInt} uses a probable\texttt{\symbol{45}}primality test (see \texttt{IsPrimeInt} (\ref{IsPrimeInt})). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NextPrimeInt( 541 ); NextPrimeInt( -1 );|
  547
  2
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PrevPrimeInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X819060E17E83728A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrevPrimeInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{PrevPrimeInt@\texttt{PrevPrimeInt}}
\label{PrevPrimeInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{PrevPrimeInt} returns the largest prime which is strictly smaller than the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. 

 Note that \texttt{PrevPrimeInt} uses a probable\texttt{\symbol{45}}primality test (see \texttt{IsPrimeInt} (\ref{IsPrimeInt})). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrevPrimeInt( 541 ); PrevPrimeInt( 1 );|
  523
  -2
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FactorsInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82C989DB84744B36}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FactorsInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{FactorsInt@\texttt{FactorsInt}}
\label{FactorsInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FactorsInt({\mdseries\slshape n: RhoTrials := trials})\index{FactorsInt@\texttt{FactorsInt}!using Pollard's Rho}
\label{FactorsInt:using Pollard's Rho}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{FactorsInt} returns a list of factors of a given integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} such that \texttt{Product( FactorsInt( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} ) ) = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}}. If $|n| \leq 1$ the list \texttt{[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}]} is returned. Otherwise the result contains probable primes, sorted by absolute
value. The entries will all be positive except for the first one in case of a
negative \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. 

 See \texttt{PrimeDivisors} (\ref{PrimeDivisors}) for a function that returns a set of (probable) primes dividing \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. 

 Note that \texttt{FactorsInt} uses a probable\texttt{\symbol{45}}primality test (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsPrimeInt} (\ref{IsPrimeInt})). Thus \texttt{FactorsInt} might return a list which contains composite integers. In such a case you will
get a warning about the use of a probable prime. You can switch off these
warnings by \texttt{SetInfoLevel( InfoPrimeInt, 0 );} (also see \texttt{SetInfoLevel} (\ref{SetInfoLevel})). 

 The time taken by \texttt{FactorsInt} is approximately proportional to the square root of the second largest prime
factor of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, which is the last one that \texttt{FactorsInt} has to find, since the largest factor is simply what remains when all others
have been removed. Thus the time is roughly bounded by the fourth root of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. \texttt{FactorsInt} is guaranteed to find all factors less than $10^6$ and will find most factors less than $10^{10}$. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} contains multiple factors larger than that \texttt{FactorsInt} may not be able to factor \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and will then signal an error. 

 \texttt{FactorsInt} is used in a method for the general operation \texttt{Factors} (\ref{Factors}). 

 In the second form, \texttt{FactorsInt} calls \texttt{FactorsRho} with a limit of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape trials}} on the number of trials it performs. The default is 8192. Note that Pollard's
Rho is the fastest method for finding prime factors with roughly
5\texttt{\symbol{45}}10 decimal digits, but becomes more and more inferior to
other factorization techniques like e.g. the Elliptic Curves Method (ECM) the
bigger the prime factors are. Therefore instead of performing a huge number of
Rho \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape trials}}, it is usually more advisable to install the \textsf{FactInt} package and then simply to use the operation \texttt{Factors} (\ref{Factors}). The factorization of the 8\texttt{\symbol{45}}th Fermat number by Pollard's
Rho below takes already a while. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@FactorsInt( -Factorial(6) );|
  [ -2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Set( FactorsInt( Factorial(13)/11 ) );|
  [ 2, 3, 5, 7, 13 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@FactorsInt( 2^63 - 1 );|
  [ 7, 7, 73, 127, 337, 92737, 649657 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@FactorsInt( 10^42 + 1 );|
  [ 29, 101, 281, 9901, 226549, 121499449, 4458192223320340849 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@FactorsInt(2^256+1:RhoTrials:=100000000);|
  [ 1238926361552897,
    93461639715357977769163558199606896584051237541638188580280321 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PrimeDivisors}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80E7A5D381C64CC9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrimeDivisors({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{PrimeDivisors@\texttt{PrimeDivisors}}
\label{PrimeDivisors}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 \texttt{PrimeDivisors} returns for a non\texttt{\symbol{45}}zero integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} a set of its positive (probable) primes divisors. In rare cases the result
could contain a composite number which passed certain primality tests, see \texttt{IsProbablyPrimeInt} (\ref{IsProbablyPrimeInt}) and \texttt{FactorsInt} (\ref{FactorsInt}) for more details. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrimeDivisors(-12);|
  [ 2, 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrimeDivisors(1);|
  [  ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PartialFactorization}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X786FF92C7C54BF97}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PartialFactorization({\mdseries\slshape n[, effort]})\index{PartialFactorization@\texttt{PartialFactorization}}
\label{PartialFactorization}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{PartialFactorization} returns a partial factorization of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. No assertions are made about the primality of the factors, except of those
mentioned below. 

 The argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape effort}}, if given, specifies how intensively the function should try to determine
factors of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. The default is \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape effort}}{\nobreakspace}={\nobreakspace}5. 

 
\begin{itemize}
\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape effort}}{\nobreakspace}={\nobreakspace}0, trial division by the primes below 100 is
done. Returned factors below $10^4$ are guaranteed to be prime. 
\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape effort}}{\nobreakspace}={\nobreakspace}1, trial division by the primes below 1000 is
done. Returned factors below $10^6$ are guaranteed to be prime. 
\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape effort}}{\nobreakspace}={\nobreakspace}2, additionally trial division by the numbers
in the lists \texttt{Primes2} and \texttt{ProbablePrimes2} is done, and perfect powers are detected. Returned factors below $10^6$ are guaranteed to be prime. 
\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape effort}}{\nobreakspace}={\nobreakspace}3, additionally \texttt{FactorsRho} (Pollard's Rho) with \texttt{RhoTrials} = 256 is used. 
\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape effort}}{\nobreakspace}={\nobreakspace}4, as above, but \texttt{RhoTrials} = 2048. 
\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape effort}}{\nobreakspace}={\nobreakspace}5, as above, but \texttt{RhoTrials} = 8192. Returned factors below $10^{12}$ are guaranteed to be prime, and all prime factors below $10^6$ are guaranteed to be found. 
\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape effort}}{\nobreakspace}={\nobreakspace}6 and the package \textsf{FactInt} is loaded, in addition to the above quite a number of special cases are
handled. 
\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape effort}}{\nobreakspace}={\nobreakspace}7 and the package \textsf{FactInt} is loaded, the only thing which is not attempted to obtain a full
factorization into
Baillie\texttt{\symbol{45}}Pomerance\texttt{\symbol{45}}Selfridge\texttt{\symbol{45}}Wagstaff
pseudoprimes is the application of the MPQS to a remaining composite with more
than 50 decimal digits. 
\end{itemize}
 

 Increasing the value of the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape effort}} by one usually results in an increase of the runtime requirements by a factor
of (very roughly!) 3 to{\nobreakspace}10. (Also see \texttt{CheapFactorsInt} (\textbf{EDIM: CheapFactorsInt})). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List([0..5],i->PartialFactorization(97^35-1,i));|
  [ [ 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 11, 31, 43,
        2446338959059521520901826365168917110105972824229555319002965029 ],
    [ 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 11, 31, 43, 967,
        2529823122088440042297648774735177983563570655873376751812787 ],
    [ 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 11, 31, 43, 967,
        2529823122088440042297648774735177983563570655873376751812787 ],
    [ 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 11, 31, 43, 967, 39761, 262321,
        242549173950325921859769421435653153445616962914227 ],
    [ 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 11, 31, 43, 967, 39761, 262321, 687121,
        352993394104278463123335513593170858474150787 ],
    [ 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 11, 31, 43, 967, 39761, 262321, 687121,
        20241187, 504769301, 34549173843451574629911361501 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PrintFactorsInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X803D431087B6FF28}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrintFactorsInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{PrintFactorsInt@\texttt{PrintFactorsInt}}
\label{PrintFactorsInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 prints the prime factorization of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} in human\texttt{\symbol{45}}readable form. See also \texttt{StringPP} (\ref{StringPP}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrintFactorsInt( Factorial( 7 ) ); Print( "\n" );|
  2^4*3^2*5*7
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PrimePowersInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 11 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82148B347E294C87}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrimePowersInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{PrimePowersInt@\texttt{PrimePowersInt}}
\label{PrimePowersInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the prime factorization of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} as a list $[ p_1, e_1, \ldots, p_k, e_k ]$ with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} = $p_1^{{e_1}} \cdot p_2^{{e_2}} \cdot ... \cdot p_k^{{e_k}}$. 

 For negative integers, the absolute value is taken. Zero is not allowed as
input. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrimePowersInt( Factorial( 7 ) );|
  [ 2, 4, 3, 2, 5, 1, 7, 1 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrimePowersInt( 1 );|
  [  ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DivisorsInt}}
\logpage{[ 14, 4, 12 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X809E0E1B83AF7695}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DivisorsInt({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{DivisorsInt@\texttt{DivisorsInt}}
\label{DivisorsInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{divisors!of an integer} \texttt{DivisorsInt} returns a list of all divisors of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. The list is sorted, so that it starts with 1 and ends with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. We define that \texttt{DivisorsInt( \texttt{\symbol{45}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} ) = DivisorsInt( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} )}. 

 Since the set of divisors of 0 is infinite calling \texttt{DivisorsInt( 0 )} causes an error. 

 \texttt{DivisorsInt} may call \texttt{FactorsInt} (\ref{FactorsInt}) to obtain the prime factors. \texttt{Sigma} (\ref{Sigma}) and \texttt{Tau} (\ref{Tau}) compute the sum and the number of positive divisors, respectively. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DivisorsInt( 1 ); DivisorsInt( 20 ); DivisorsInt( 541 );|
  [ 1 ]
  [ 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20 ]
  [ 1, 541 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Residue Class Rings}}\label{Residue Class Rings}
\logpage{[ 14, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X864BF040862409FC}{}
{
  \index{mod@\texttt{mod}!residue class rings} \index{modulo!residue class rings} \texttt{ZmodnZ} (\ref{ZmodnZ}) returns a residue class ring of \texttt{Integers} (\ref{Integers}) modulo an ideal. These residue class rings are rings, thus all operations for
rings (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Rings}) apply. See also Chapters{\nobreakspace}\ref{Finite Fields} and \ref{Number Theory}. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod (for residue class rings)}}
\logpage{[ 14, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87B1210B8581D5B2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod({\mdseries\slshape r/s, n})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod}!for residue class rings}
\label{bSlashmod:for residue class rings}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape s}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} are integers, \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} / \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape s}}} as a reduced fraction is \texttt{p/q}, where \texttt{q} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} are coprime, then \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} / \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape s}} mod \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}} is defined to be the product of \texttt{p} and the inverse of \texttt{q} modulo \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. See Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Arithmetic Operators} for more details and definitions. 

 With the above definition, \texttt{4 / 6 mod 32} equals \texttt{2 / 3 mod 32} and hence exists (and is equal to 22), despite the fact that 6 has no inverse
modulo 32. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ZmodnZ}}
\logpage{[ 14, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79CE76AD82B3E2B2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZmodnZ({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{ZmodnZ@\texttt{ZmodnZ}}
\label{ZmodnZ}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZmodpZ({\mdseries\slshape p})\index{ZmodpZ@\texttt{ZmodpZ}}
\label{ZmodpZ}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZmodpZNC({\mdseries\slshape p})\index{ZmodpZNC@\texttt{ZmodpZNC}}
\label{ZmodpZNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{ZmodnZ} returns a ring $R$ isomorphic to the residue class ring of the integers modulo the ideal
generated by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. The element corresponding to the residue class of the integer $i$ in this ring can be obtained by \texttt{i * One( R )}, and a representative of the residue class corresponding to the element $x \in R$ can be computed by \texttt{Int}$( x )$. 

 \index{mod!Integers} \texttt{ZmodnZ( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} )} is equal to \texttt{Integers mod \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}}. 

 \texttt{ZmodpZ} does the same if the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} is a prime integer, additionally the result is a field. \texttt{ZmodpZNC} omits the check whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} is a prime. 

 Each ring returned by these functions contains the whole family of its
elements if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is not a prime, and is embedded into the family of finite field elements of
characteristic \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is a prime. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ZmodnZObj (for a residue class family and integer)}}
\logpage{[ 14, 5, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X838F36507D985EDA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZmodnZObj({\mdseries\slshape Fam, r})\index{ZmodnZObj@\texttt{ZmodnZObj}!for a residue class family and integer}
\label{ZmodnZObj:for a residue class family and integer}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZmodnZObj({\mdseries\slshape r, n})\index{ZmodnZObj@\texttt{ZmodnZObj}!for two integers}
\label{ZmodnZObj:for two integers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 If the first argument is a residue class family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} then \texttt{ZmodnZObj} returns the element in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} whose coset is represented by the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}. 

 If the two arguments are an integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} and a positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} then \texttt{ZmodnZObj} returns the element in \texttt{ZmodnZ( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} )} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{ZmodnZ} (\ref{ZmodnZ})) whose coset is represented by the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r:= ZmodnZ(15);|
  (Integers mod 15)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@fam:=ElementsFamily(FamilyObj(r));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:= ZmodnZObj(fam,9);|
  ZmodnZObj( 9, 15 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a+a;|
  ZmodnZObj( 3, 15 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Int(a+a);|
  3
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsZmodnZObj}}
\logpage{[ 14, 5, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D0107DD79753901}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsZmodnZObj({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsZmodnZObj@\texttt{IsZmodnZObj}}
\label{IsZmodnZObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsZmodnZObjNonprime({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsZmodnZObjNonprime@\texttt{IsZmodnZObjNonprime}}
\label{IsZmodnZObjNonprime}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsZmodpZObj({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsZmodpZObj@\texttt{IsZmodpZObj}}
\label{IsZmodpZObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsZmodpZObjSmall({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsZmodpZObjSmall@\texttt{IsZmodpZObjSmall}}
\label{IsZmodpZObjSmall}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsZmodpZObjLarge({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsZmodpZObjLarge@\texttt{IsZmodpZObjLarge}}
\label{IsZmodpZObjLarge}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 The elements in the rings $Z / n Z$ are in the category \texttt{IsZmodnZObj}. If $n$ is a prime then the elements are of course also in the category \texttt{IsFFE} (\ref{IsFFE}), otherwise they are in \texttt{IsZmodnZObjNonprime}. \texttt{IsZmodpZObj} is an abbreviation of \texttt{IsZmodnZObj and IsFFE}. This category is the disjoint union of \texttt{IsZmodpZObjSmall} and \texttt{IsZmodpZObjLarge}, the former containing all elements with $n$ at most \texttt{MAXSIZE{\textunderscore}GF{\textunderscore}INTERNAL}. 

 The reasons to distinguish the prime case from the nonprime case are 
\begin{itemize}
\item  that objects in \texttt{IsZmodnZObjNonprime} have an external representation (namely the residue in the range $[ 0, 1, \ldots, n-1 ]$), 
\item  that the comparison of elements can be defined as comparison of the residues,
and 
\item  that the elements lie in a family of type \texttt{IsZmodnZObjNonprimeFamily} (note that for prime $n$, the family must be an \texttt{IsFFEFamily}). 
\end{itemize}
 

 The reasons to distinguish the small and the large case are that for small $n$ the elements must be compatible with the internal representation of finite
field elements, whereas we are free to define comparison as comparison of
residues for large $n$. 

 Note that we \emph{cannot} claim that every finite field element of degree 1 is in \texttt{IsZmodnZObj}, since finite field elements in internal representation may not know that
they lie in the prime field. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Check Digits}}\label{Check Digits}
\logpage{[ 14, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7904B6D681EBF091}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CheckDigitISBN}}
\logpage{[ 14, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82BABA8F868BD425}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CheckDigitISBN({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{CheckDigitISBN@\texttt{CheckDigitISBN}}
\label{CheckDigitISBN}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CheckDigitISBN13({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{CheckDigitISBN13@\texttt{CheckDigitISBN13}}
\label{CheckDigitISBN13}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CheckDigitPostalMoneyOrder({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{CheckDigitPostalMoneyOrder@\texttt{CheckDigitPostalMoneyOrder}}
\label{CheckDigitPostalMoneyOrder}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CheckDigitUPC({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{CheckDigitUPC@\texttt{CheckDigitUPC}}
\label{CheckDigitUPC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 These functions can be used to compute, or check, check digits for some
everyday items. In each case what is submitted as input is either the number
with check digit (in which case the function returns \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}), or the number without check digit (in which case the function returns the
missing check digit). The number can be specified as integer, as string (for
example in case of leading zeros) or as a sequence of arguments, each
representing a single digit. The check digits tested are the
10\texttt{\symbol{45}}digit ISBN (International Standard Book Number) using \texttt{CheckDigitISBN} (since arithmetic is module 11, a digit 11 is represented by an X); the newer
13\texttt{\symbol{45}}digit ISBN\texttt{\symbol{45}}13 using \texttt{CheckDigitISBN13}; the numbers of 11\texttt{\symbol{45}}digit US postal money orders using \texttt{CheckDigitPostalMoneyOrder}; and the 12\texttt{\symbol{45}}digit UPC bar code found on groceries using \texttt{CheckDigitUPC}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|CheckDigitISBN("052166103");A
  Check Digit is 'X'
  'X'
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|CheckDigitISBN("052166103X");A
  Checksum test satisfied
  true
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|CheckDigitISBN(0,5,2,1,6,6,1,0,3,1);A
  Checksum test failed
  false
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|CheckDigitISBN(0,5,2,1,6,6,1,0,3,'X'); # note single quotes!A
  Checksum test satisfied
  true
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|CheckDigitISBN13("9781420094527");A
  Checksum test satisfied
  true
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|CheckDigitUPC("07164183001");A
  Check Digit is 1
  1
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|CheckDigitPostalMoneyOrder(16786457155);A
  Checksum test satisfied
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CheckDigitTestFunction}}
\logpage{[ 14, 6, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85F1A6A5870485B9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CheckDigitTestFunction({\mdseries\slshape l, m, f})\index{CheckDigitTestFunction@\texttt{CheckDigitTestFunction}}
\label{CheckDigitTestFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function creates check digit test functions such as \texttt{CheckDigitISBN} (\ref{CheckDigitISBN}) for check digit schemes that use the inner products with a fixed vector modulo
a number. The scheme creates will use strings of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape l}} digits (including the check digits), the check consists of taking the standard
product of the vector of digits with the fixed vector \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} modulo \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}; the result needs to be 0. The function returns a function that then can be
used for testing or determining check digits. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@isbntest:=CheckDigitTestFunction(10,11,[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,-1]);|
  function( arg... ) ... end
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@isbntest("038794680");|
  Check Digit is 2
  2
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Random Sources}}\label{Random Sources}
\logpage{[ 14, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X85361FAE8088C006}{}
{
  \textsf{GAP} provides \texttt{Random} (\ref{Random:for a list or collection}) methods for many collections of objects. On a lower level these methods use \emph{random sources} which provide random integers and random choices from lists. 

 See \texttt{IsRandomSource} (\ref{IsRandomSource}) for the user interface for random sources, and Section \ref{Implementing new kinds of random sources} for information about developing new kinds of random sources. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsRandomSource}}
\logpage{[ 14, 7, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82E31A697E389F1D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsRandomSource({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsRandomSource@\texttt{IsRandomSource}}
\label{IsRandomSource}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 This is the category of random source objects. The \emph{user interface} for these objects consists of the following functions. 

 \texttt{RandomSource} (\ref{RandomSource}) creates a new random source \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}}, say. 

 \texttt{Random( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} )} yields a random element of the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}, and \texttt{Random( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape low}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape high}} )} yields a random integer between \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape low}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape high}} (inclusive), see \texttt{Random} (\ref{Random:for random source and list}). 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}} supports resetting (see \texttt{State} (\ref{State})) then \texttt{State( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}} )} yields a copy \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape state}}, say, of the current state of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}} such that \texttt{Reset( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape state}} )} resets \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}} to the given state. 

 One idea behind providing several independent (pseudo) random sources is to
make algorithms which use some sort of random choices deterministic. They can
use their own new random source created with a fixed seed and so do exactly
the same in different calls. 

 Random source objects lie in the family \texttt{RandomSourcesFamily}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Random (for random source and list)}}
\logpage{[ 14, 7, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X821004F286282D49}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Random({\mdseries\slshape rs, list})\index{Random@\texttt{Random}!for random source and list}
\label{Random:for random source and list}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Random({\mdseries\slshape rs, coll})\index{Random@\texttt{Random}!for random source and collection}
\label{Random:for random source and collection}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Random({\mdseries\slshape rs, low, high})\index{Random@\texttt{Random}!for random source and two integers}
\label{Random:for random source and two integers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 This operation returns a random element from the dense, nonempty list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} or the nonempty collection \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coll}}, or an integer in the range from the given (possibly large) integers \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape low}} to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape high}}, respectively. 

 The choice should only depend on the random source \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}} and have no effect on other random sources. 

 It is not defined what happens if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} or \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coll}} is empty, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} is not dense, or \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape low}} is larger than \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape high}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mysource := RandomSource(IsMersenneTwister, 42);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Random(mysource, 1, 10^60);|
  999331861769949319194941485000557997842686717712198687315183
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{State and Reset for Random Sources}}\label{State and Reset for Random Sources}
\logpage{[ 14, 7, 3 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86FFFBC9790F9742}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{State({\mdseries\slshape rs})\index{State@\texttt{State}}
\label{State}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Reset({\mdseries\slshape rs[, seed]})\index{Reset@\texttt{Reset}}
\label{Reset}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 These are the basic operations for random sources (see \texttt{IsRandomSource} (\ref{IsRandomSource})). 

 \texttt{State} returns a data structure which admits recovering the state of the random
source such that a sequence of random calls using this random source can be
reproduced. If a random source cannot be reset (say, it uses truly random
physical data) then \texttt{State} returns \texttt{fail}. 

 \texttt{Reset( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}} )} resets the random source \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}} to a state described by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}}, if the random source can be reset; otherwise it does nothing. Here \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}} can be an output of \texttt{State} and then \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}} gets reset to that state. For historical reasons, random sources accept
integer values as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}}. We recommend that new code should not rely on this; always use the output of
a prior call to \texttt{State} as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}}, or omit it. Without the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}} argument a fixed default seed is used. \texttt{Reset} returns the state of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rs}} before the call. 

 Most methods for \texttt{Random} (\ref{Random:for a list or collection}) in the \textsf{GAP} library that do not take a random source as argument use the \texttt{GlobalMersenneTwister} (\ref{GlobalMersenneTwister}) as random source. It can be reset into a known state as in the following
example. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@seed := Reset(GlobalMersenneTwister);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@seed = State(GlobalMersenneTwister);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List([1..10],i->Random(Integers));|
  [ -3, 2, -1, -2, -1, -1, 1, -4, 1, 0 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List([1..10],i->Random(Integers));|
  [ -1, -1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -2, -1, -2, 0 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Reset(GlobalMersenneTwister, seed);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List([1..10],i->Random(Integers));|
  [ -3, 2, -1, -2, -1, -1, 1, -4, 1, 0 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Kinds of Random Sources}}\label{Kinds of Random Sources}
\logpage{[ 14, 7, 4 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7AC96008820FAF1F}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsMersenneTwister({\mdseries\slshape rs})\index{IsMersenneTwister@\texttt{IsMersenneTwister}}
\label{IsMersenneTwister}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsGAPRandomSource({\mdseries\slshape rs})\index{IsGAPRandomSource@\texttt{IsGAPRandomSource}}
\label{IsGAPRandomSource}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsGlobalRandomSource({\mdseries\slshape rs})\index{IsGlobalRandomSource@\texttt{IsGlobalRandomSource}}
\label{IsGlobalRandomSource}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GlobalMersenneTwister\index{GlobalMersenneTwister@\texttt{GlobalMersenneTwister}}
\label{GlobalMersenneTwister}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GlobalRandomSource\index{GlobalRandomSource@\texttt{GlobalRandomSource}}
\label{GlobalRandomSource}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 Currently, the \textsf{GAP} library provides three types of random sources, distinguished by the three
listed categories. 

 \texttt{IsMersenneTwister} are random sources which use a fast random generator of 32 bit numbers, called
the Mersenne twister. The pseudo random sequence has a period of $2^{19937}-1$ and the numbers have a $623$\texttt{\symbol{45}}dimensional equidistribution. For more details and the
origin of the code used in the \textsf{GAP} kernel, see: \href{http://www.math.sci.hiroshima-u.ac.jp/~m-mat/MT/emt.html} {\texttt{http://www.math.sci.hiroshima\texttt{\symbol{45}}u.ac.jp/\texttt{\symbol{126}}m\texttt{\symbol{45}}mat/MT/emt.html}}. 

 Use the Mersenne twister if possible, in particular for generating many large
random integers. 

 There is also a predefined global random source \texttt{GlobalMersenneTwister} which is used as the default random source by those library methods for \texttt{Random} (\ref{Random:for a list or collection}) that do not take a random source as an argument. 

 \texttt{IsGAPRandomSource} uses the same number generator as \texttt{IsGlobalRandomSource}, but you can create several of these random sources which generate their
random numbers independently of all other random sources. 

 \texttt{IsGlobalRandomSource} gives access to the \emph{classical} global random generator which was used by \textsf{GAP} in former releases. You do not need to construct new random sources of this
kind which would all use the same global data structure. Just use the existing
random source \texttt{GlobalRandomSource}. This uses the additive random number generator described in \cite{TACP2} (Algorithm A in{\nobreakspace}3.2.2 with lag $30$). 

 Other kinds of random sources are implemented by \textsf{GAP} packages. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RandomSource}}
\logpage{[ 14, 7, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CB0B5BC82F8FD8F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RandomSource({\mdseries\slshape cat[, seed]})\index{RandomSource@\texttt{RandomSource}}
\label{RandomSource}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 This operation is used to create new random sources. The first argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cat}} is the category describing the type of the random generator, for example one
of the categories listed in Section \ref{Kinds of Random Sources}. 

 An optional \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}} can be given to specify the initial state. For details, see Section \ref{State and Reset for Random Sources}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rs1 := RandomSource(IsMersenneTwister);|
  <RandomSource in IsMersenneTwister>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l1 := List([1..10000], i-> Random(rs1, [1..6]));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@state1 := State(rs1);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rs2 := RandomSource(IsMersenneTwister);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l2 := List([1..10000], i-> Random(rs2, [1..6]));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l1 = l2;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l3 := List([1..10000], i-> Random(rs1, [1..6]));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l1 = l3;|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rs3 := RandomSource(IsMersenneTwister, state1);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l4 := List([1..10000], i-> Random(rs3, [1..6]));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l3 = l4;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@n := Random(rs1, 1, 2^220);|
  1077726777923092117987668044202944212469136000816111066409337432400
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Implementing new kinds of random sources}}\label{Implementing new kinds of random sources}
\logpage{[ 14, 7, 6 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8653AE447D94C1DC}{}
{
  If one wants to implement a new kind of random sources then the first step is
the declaration of a new category \texttt{C}, say, that implies \texttt{IsRandomSource} (\ref{IsRandomSource}), analogous to the categories listed in Section \ref{Kinds of Random Sources}, as follows. 

 \texttt{DeclareCategory( "C", IsRandomSource );}. 

 Then the following method installations are needed. 

 \index{Init@\texttt{Init} (initialize a random source object)} \texttt{InstallMethod( Init, [ C, IsObject ], function( prers, seed ) ... end );} 

 Here \texttt{prers} is an empty component object (which has already the filter \texttt{C}), and \texttt{seed} is an integer or a state value as returned by \texttt{State} (\ref{State}) that describes the initial state of the random source. The function should
fill in the actual data and then return the (now initialized) object \texttt{prers}. The default used for \texttt{seed} is the integer \texttt{1}. A given state value need not be copied by the function. 

 \texttt{InstallMethod( Random, [ C, IsInt, IsInt ], function( rs, low, high ) ... end
);} 

 Here \texttt{rs} is an already initialized random source object in the category \texttt{C}, and the function returns an integer between \texttt{low} and \texttt{high} (inclusive). It is not defined what happens when \texttt{low} is larger than \texttt{high}. 

 \texttt{InstallMethod( State, [ C ], function( rs ) ... end );} 

 If \texttt{rs} supports resetting then the function must return an object that describes the
current state of \texttt{rs}. This object must be an independent copy, that is, calling \texttt{Random} (\ref{Random:for random source and list}) for \texttt{rs} must not change the object that was returned by \texttt{State} (\ref{State}); otherwise \texttt{ReturnFail} (\ref{ReturnFail}) should be installed. 

 \texttt{InstallMethod( Reset, [ C, IsObject ], function( rs, seed ) ... end );} 

 If \texttt{rs} supports resetting then the function must reinitialize \texttt{rs} to the integer or \texttt{State} (\ref{State}) value \texttt{seed} and must return the \texttt{State} (\ref{State}) value of \texttt{rs} before these changes; if resetting is not supported then \texttt{ReturnNothing} (\ref{ReturnNothing}) should be installed. Reset need not copy a given state. Note that the generic
unary \texttt{Reset} (\ref{Reset}) method uses the default seed \texttt{1}. 

 Examples of implementations as described here are given by the random sources
with defining filter \texttt{IsMersenneTwister} (\ref{IsMersenneTwister}) or \texttt{IsRealRandomSource}. (For the latter, see \texttt{RandomSource} (\textbf{IO: RandomSource}) in the \textsf{GAP} package \textsf{IO}.) }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Bitfields}}\label{Bitfields}
\logpage{[ 14, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7A0311DF78DB4FD8}{}
{
  Bitfields are a low\texttt{\symbol{45}}level feature intended to support
efficient subdivision of immediate integers into bitfields of various widths.
This is typically useful in implementing space\texttt{\symbol{45}}efficient
and/or cache\texttt{\symbol{45}}efficient data structures. This feature should
be used with care because (\emph{inter alia}) it has different limitations on 32\texttt{\symbol{45}}bit and
64\texttt{\symbol{45}}bit architectures. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MakeBitfields}}
\logpage{[ 14, 8, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85C7BD9E7FCC6C10}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MakeBitfields({\mdseries\slshape width....})\index{MakeBitfields@\texttt{MakeBitfields}}
\label{MakeBitfields}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function sets up the machinery for a set of bitfields of the given
widths. All bitfield values are treated as unsigned. The total of the widths
must not exceed 60 bits on 64\texttt{\symbol{45}}bit architecture or 28 bits
on a 32\texttt{\symbol{45}}bit architecture. For performance reasons some
checks that one might wish to do are omitted. In particular, the builder and
setter functions do not check if the value[s] passed to them are negative or
too large (unless \textsf{GAP} is specially compiled for debugging). Behaviour when such arguments are passed
is undefined. You can tell which type of architecture you are running on by
accessing \texttt{GAPInfo.BytesPerVariable} which is 8 on 64\texttt{\symbol{45}}bits and 4 on 32. The return value when $n$ widths are given is a record whose fields are 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{widths}}] a copy of the arguments, for convenience,
\item[{\texttt{getters}}]  a list of $n$ functions of one argument each of which extracts one of the fields from an
immediate integer
\item[{\texttt{setters}}]  a list of $n$ functions each taking two arguments: a packed value and a new value for one of
its fields and returning a new packed value. The $i$th function returned the new packed value in which the $i$th field has been replaced by the new value. Note that this does NOT modify
the original packed value.
\end{description}
 Two additional fields may be present if any of the field widths is one. Each
is a list and only has entried bound in the positions corresponding to the
width 1 fields. 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{booleanGetters}}] if the $i$th position of this list is set, it contains a function which extracts the $i$th field (which will have width one) and returns \texttt{true} if it contains 1 and \texttt{false} if it contains 0
\item[{\texttt{booleanSetters}}] if the $i$th position of this list is set, it contains a function of two arguments. The
first argument is a packed value, the second is \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}. It returns a new packed value in which the $i$th field is set to 1 if the second argument was \texttt{true} and 0 if it was \texttt{false}. Behaviour for any other value is undefined.
\end{description}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{BuildBitfields}}
\logpage{[ 14, 8, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8068CE3781F4003C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{BuildBitfields({\mdseries\slshape widths, vals...})\index{BuildBitfields@\texttt{BuildBitfields}}
\label{BuildBitfields}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function takes one or more argument. Its first argument is a list of
field widths, as found in the \texttt{widths} entry of a record returned by \texttt{MakeBitfields}. The remaining arguments are unsigned integer values, equal in number to the
entries of the list of field widths. It returns a small integer in which those
entries are packed into bitfields of the given widths. The first entry
occupies the least significant bits. DeclareGlobalFunction("BuildBitfields"); 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@bf := MakeBitfields(1,2,3);|
  rec( booleanGetters := [ function( data ) ... end ],
    booleanSetters := [ function( data, val ) ... end ],
    getters := [ function( data ) ... end, function( data ) ... end,
        function( data ) ... end ],
    setters := [ function( data, val ) ... end, function( data, val ) ... end,
        function( data, val ) ... end ], widths := [ 1, 2, 3 ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x := BuildBitfields(bf.widths,0,3,5);|
  46
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@bf.getters[3](x);|
  5
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@y := bf.setters[1](x,1);|
  47
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x;|
  46
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@bf.booleanGetters[1](x);|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@bf.booleanGetters[1](y);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

 }

          
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Number Theory}}\label{Number Theory}
\logpage{[ 15, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7FB995737B7ED8A2}{}
{
  \index{prime residue group} \textsf{GAP} provides a couple of elementary number theoretic functions. Most of these deal
with the group of integers coprime to $m$, called the \emph{prime residue group}. The order of this group is $\phi(m)$ (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Phi} (\ref{Phi})), and $\lambda(m)$ (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Lambda} (\ref{Lambda})) is its exponent. This group is cyclic if and only if $m$ is 2, 4, an odd prime power $p^n$, or twice an odd prime power $2 p^n$. In this case the generators of the group, i.e., elements of order $\phi(m)$, are called \emph{primitive roots} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{PrimitiveRootMod} (\ref{PrimitiveRootMod})). 

 Note that neither the arguments nor the return values of the functions listed
below are groups or group elements in the sense of \textsf{GAP}. The arguments are simply integers.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoNumtheor (Info Class)}}\label{sect:InfoNumtheor}
\logpage{[ 15, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7845C1F97A1742C7}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoNumtheor}}
\logpage{[ 15, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X796F0DFE7D5D211C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoNumtheor\index{InfoNumtheor@\texttt{InfoNumtheor}}
\label{InfoNumtheor}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (info class)}}\\


 \texttt{InfoNumtheor} is the info class (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Info Functions}) for the functions in the number theory chapter. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Prime Residues}}\label{Prime Residues}
\logpage{[ 15, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X823386567DAC22E6}{}
{
  \index{prime residue group} 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PrimeResidues}}
\logpage{[ 15, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7FA3F5347B7004BA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrimeResidues({\mdseries\slshape m})\index{PrimeResidues@\texttt{PrimeResidues}}
\label{PrimeResidues}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{PrimeResidues} returns the set of integers from the range \texttt{[ 0 .. Abs( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} )\texttt{\symbol{45}}1 ]} that are coprime to the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. 

 \texttt{Abs(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}})} must be less than $2^{28}$, otherwise the set would probably be too large anyhow. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrimeResidues( 0 );  PrimeResidues( 1 );  PrimeResidues( 20 );|
  [  ]
  [ 0 ]
  [ 1, 3, 7, 9, 11, 13, 17, 19 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Phi}}
\logpage{[ 15, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85A0C67982D9057A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Phi({\mdseries\slshape m})\index{Phi@\texttt{Phi}}
\label{Phi}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \index{order!of the prime residue group} \index{prime residue group!order} \index{Euler's totient function} \texttt{Phi} returns the number $\phi(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}})$ of positive integers less than the positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} that are coprime to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. 

 Suppose that $m = p_1^{{e_1}} p_2^{{e_2}} \cdots p_k^{{e_k}}$. Then $\phi(m)$ is $p_1^{{e_1-1}} (p_1-1) p_2^{{e_2-1}} (p_2-1) \cdots p_k^{{e_k-1}} (p_k-1)$. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Phi( 12 );|
  4
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Phi( 2^13-1 );  # this proves that 2^(13)-1 is a prime|
  8190
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Phi( 2^15-1 );|
  27000
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Lambda}}
\logpage{[ 15, 2, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85296F3087611B03}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Lambda({\mdseries\slshape m})\index{Lambda@\texttt{Lambda}}
\label{Lambda}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \index{Carmichael's lambda function} \index{prime residue group!exponent} \index{exponent!of the prime residue group} \texttt{Lambda} returns the exponent $\lambda(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}})$ of the group of prime residues modulo the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. 

 $\lambda(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}})$ is the smallest positive integer $l$ such that for every $a$ relatively prime to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} we have $a^l \equiv 1 \pmod{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}}$. Fermat's theorem asserts $a^{{\phi(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}})}} \equiv 1 \pmod{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}}$; thus $\lambda(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}})$ divides $\phi(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}})$ (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Phi} (\ref{Phi})). 

 Carmichael's theorem states that $\lambda$ can be computed as follows: $\lambda(2) = 1$, $\lambda(4) = 2$ and $\lambda(2^e) = 2^{{e-2}}$ if $3 \leq e$, $\lambda(p^e) = (p-1) p^{{e-1}}$ (i.e. $\phi(m)$) if $p$ is an odd prime and $\lambda(m*n) = $\texttt{Lcm}$( \lambda(m), \lambda(n) )$ if $m, n$ are coprime. 

 Composites for which $\lambda(m)$ divides $m - 1$ are called Carmichaels. If $6k+1$, $12k+1$ and $18k+1$ are primes their product is such a number. There are only 1547 Carmichaels
below $10^{10}$ but 455052511 primes. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Lambda( 10 );|
  4
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Lambda( 30 );|
  4
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Lambda( 561 );  # 561 is the smallest Carmichael number|
  80
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GeneratorsPrimeResidues}}
\logpage{[ 15, 2, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D191CF67E5018BE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GeneratorsPrimeResidues({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{GeneratorsPrimeResidues@\texttt{GeneratorsPrimeResidues}}
\label{GeneratorsPrimeResidues}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} be a positive integer. \texttt{GeneratorsPrimeResidues} returns a description of generators of the group of prime residues modulo \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. The return value is a record with components 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{primes}: }]  a list of the prime factors of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, 
\item[{\texttt{exponents}: }]  a list of the exponents of these primes in the factorization of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, and 
\item[{\texttt{generators}: }]  a list describing generators of the group of prime residues; for the prime
factor $2$, either a primitive root or a list of two generators is stored, for each
other prime factor of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, a primitive root is stored. 
\end{description}
 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsPrimeResidues( 1 );|
  rec( exponents := [  ], generators := [  ], primes := [  ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsPrimeResidues( 4*3 );|
  rec( exponents := [ 2, 1 ], generators := [ 7, 5 ],
    primes := [ 2, 3 ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsPrimeResidues( 8*9*5 );|
  rec( exponents := [ 3, 2, 1 ],
    generators := [ [ 271, 181 ], 281, 217 ], primes := [ 2, 3, 5 ] )
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Primitive Roots and Discrete Logarithms}}\label{Primitive Roots and Discrete Logarithms}
\logpage{[ 15, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83103A5385821BAE}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{OrderMod}}
\logpage{[ 15, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82373F3D8277EE9E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{OrderMod({\mdseries\slshape n, m[, bound]})\index{OrderMod@\texttt{OrderMod}}
\label{OrderMod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{multiplicative order of an integer} \texttt{OrderMod} returns the multiplicative order of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} modulo the positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} are not coprime the order of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is not defined and \texttt{OrderMod} will return \texttt{0}. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} are relatively prime the multiplicative order of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} modulo \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} is the smallest positive integer $i$ such that $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}^i \equiv 1 \pmod{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}}$. If the group of prime residues modulo \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} is cyclic then each element of maximal order is called a primitive root modulo \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsPrimitiveRootMod} (\ref{IsPrimitiveRootMod})). 

 If no a priori known multiple \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape bound}} of the desired order is given, \texttt{OrderMod} usually spends most of its time factoring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} for computing $\lambda(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}})$ (see \texttt{Lambda} (\ref{Lambda})) as the default for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape bound}}, and then factoring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape bound}} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{FactorsInt} (\ref{FactorsInt})). 

 If an incorrect \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape bound}} is given then the result will be wrong. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@OrderMod( 2, 7 );|
  3
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@OrderMod( 3, 7 );  # 3 is a primitive root modulo 7|
  6
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@m:= (5^166-1) / 167;;   # about 10^113|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@OrderMod( 5, m, 166 );  # needs minutes without third argument|
  166
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LogMod}}
\logpage{[ 15, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81AD9C7779A7BA89}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LogMod({\mdseries\slshape n, r, m})\index{LogMod@\texttt{LogMod}}
\label{LogMod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LogModShanks({\mdseries\slshape n, r, m})\index{LogModShanks@\texttt{LogModShanks}}
\label{LogModShanks}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{logarithm!discrete} computes the discrete \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}logarithm of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} modulo the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. It returns a number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape l}} such that $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}^{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape l}}} \equiv \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} \pmod{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}}$ if such a number exists. Otherwise \texttt{fail} is returned. 

 \texttt{LogModShanks} uses the Baby Step \texttt{\symbol{45}} Giant Step Method of Shanks (see for
example \cite[section 5.4.1]{Coh93}) and in general requires more memory than a call to \texttt{LogMod}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l:= LogMod( 2, 5, 7 );  5^l mod 7 = 2;|
  4
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LogMod( 1, 3, 3 );  LogMod( 2, 3, 3 );|
  0
  fail
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DLog}}
\logpage{[ 15, 3, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84A138947E8C49A8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DLog({\mdseries\slshape base, x[, m]})\index{DLog@\texttt{DLog}}
\label{DLog}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\textbf{\indent Returns:\ }
an integer



 \index{logarithm!discrete} The argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}} must be a multiplicative element and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape x}} must lie in the cyclic group generated by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}}. The third argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} must be the order of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}} or its factorization. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} is not given, it is computed first. This function returns the discrete
logarithm, that is an integer $e$ such that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}}$^e = $ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape x}}. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} is prime then Shanks' algorithm is used (which needs $O(\sqrt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}})$ space and time). Otherwise let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} $ = r l$ and $e = a + b r$ with $0 \leq a < r$. Then $a =$ \texttt{DLog}$(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}}^l, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape x}}^l, r)$ and $b = $ \texttt{DLog}$(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}}^r, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape x}}/\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}}^a, l)$. 

 This function is used for a method of \texttt{LogFFE} (\ref{LogFFE}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@q:= 67^12;|
  8182718904632857144561
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@z:= Z(q);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DLog(z, z+1);|
  2874413785388345993274
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DLog(z, z^2+1);|
  1667375214152688471247
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DLog(z, Z(67));|
  123980589464134199160
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PrimitiveRootMod}}
\logpage{[ 15, 3, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82440BB9812FF148}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrimitiveRootMod({\mdseries\slshape m[, start]})\index{PrimitiveRootMod@\texttt{PrimitiveRootMod}}
\label{PrimitiveRootMod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{primitive root modulo an integer} \index{prime residue group!generator} \index{generator!of the prime residue group} \texttt{PrimitiveRootMod} returns the smallest primitive root modulo the positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} and \texttt{fail} if no such primitive root exists. If the optional second integer argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape start}} is given \texttt{PrimitiveRootMod} returns the smallest primitive root that is strictly larger than \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape start}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# largest primitive root for a prime less than 2000:|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrimitiveRootMod( 409 );|
  21
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrimitiveRootMod( 541, 2 );|
  10
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# 327 is the largest primitive root mod 337:|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrimitiveRootMod( 337, 327 );|
  fail
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# there exists no primitive root modulo 30:|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrimitiveRootMod( 30 );|
  fail
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPrimitiveRootMod}}
\logpage{[ 15, 3, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X790466C07BD90E20}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPrimitiveRootMod({\mdseries\slshape r, m})\index{IsPrimitiveRootMod@\texttt{IsPrimitiveRootMod}}
\label{IsPrimitiveRootMod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{test!for a primitive root} \index{prime residue group!generator} \index{generator!of the prime residue group} \texttt{IsPrimitiveRootMod} returns \texttt{true} if the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} is a primitive root modulo the positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}, and \texttt{false} otherwise. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} is less than 0 or larger than \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} it is replaced by its remainder. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPrimitiveRootMod( 2, 541 );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPrimitiveRootMod( -539, 541 );  # same computation as above;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPrimitiveRootMod( 4, 541 );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ForAny( [1..29], r -> IsPrimitiveRootMod( r, 30 ) );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# there is no a primitive root modulo 30|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Roots Modulo Integers}}\label{Roots Modulo Integers}
\logpage{[ 15, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7F9069D77AC48054}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Jacobi}}
\logpage{[ 15, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83449DBC80495971}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Jacobi({\mdseries\slshape n, m})\index{Jacobi@\texttt{Jacobi}}
\label{Jacobi}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{quadratic residue} \index{residue!quadratic} \texttt{Jacobi} returns the value of the \emph{Kronecker\texttt{\symbol{45}}Jacobi symbol} $J(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}})$ of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} modulo the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. It is defined as follows: 

 If $n$ and $m$ are not coprime then $J(n,m) = 0$. Furthermore, $J(n,1) = 1$ and $J(n,-1) = -1$ if $m < 0$ and $+1$ otherwise. And for odd $n$ it is $J(n,2) = (-1)^k$ with $k = (n^2-1)/8$. For odd primes $m$ which are coprime to $n$ the Kronecker\texttt{\symbol{45}}Jacobi symbol has the same value as the
Legendre symbol (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Legendre} (\ref{Legendre})). 

 For the general case suppose that $m = p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdots p_k$ is a product of $-1$ and of primes, not necessarily distinct, and that $n$ is coprime to $m$. Then $J(n,m) = J(n,p_1) \cdot J(n,p_2) \cdots J(n,p_k)$. 

 Note that the Kronecker\texttt{\symbol{45}}Jacobi symbol coincides with the
Jacobi symbol that is defined for odd $m$ in many number theory books. For odd primes $m$ and $n$ coprime to $m$ it coincides with the Legendre symbol. 

 \texttt{Jacobi} is very efficient, even for large values of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}, it is about as fast as the Euclidean algorithm (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Gcd} (\ref{Gcd:for (a ring and) several elements})). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Jacobi( 11, 35 );  # 9^2 = 11 mod 35|
  1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# this is -1, thus there is no r such that r^2 = 6 mod 35|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Jacobi( 6, 35 );|
  -1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# this is 1 even though there is no r with r^2 = 3 mod 35|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Jacobi( 3, 35 );|
  1
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Legendre}}
\logpage{[ 15, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81464ABF7F10E544}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Legendre({\mdseries\slshape n, m})\index{Legendre@\texttt{Legendre}}
\label{Legendre}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{quadratic residue} \index{residue!quadratic} \texttt{Legendre} returns the value of the \emph{Legendre symbol} of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} modulo the positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. 

 The value of the Legendre symbol $L(n/m)$ is 1 if $n$ is a \emph{quadratic residue} modulo $m$, i.e., if there exists an integer $r$ such that $r^2 \equiv n \pmod{m}$ and $-1$ otherwise. 

 If a root of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} exists it can be found by \texttt{RootMod} (\ref{RootMod}). 

 While the value of the Legendre symbol usually is only defined for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} a prime, we have extended the definition to include composite moduli too. The
Jacobi symbol (see \texttt{Jacobi} (\ref{Jacobi})) is another generalization of the Legendre symbol for composite moduli that
is much cheaper to compute, because it does not need the factorization of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} (see \texttt{FactorsInt} (\ref{FactorsInt})). 

 A description of the Jacobi symbol, the Legendre symbol, and related topics
can be found in \cite{Baker84}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Legendre( 5, 11 );  # 4^2 = 5 mod 11|
  1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# this is -1, thus there is no r such that r^2 = 6 mod 11|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Legendre( 6, 11 );|
  -1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# this is -1, thus there is no r such that r^2 = 3 mod 35|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Legendre( 3, 35 );|
  -1
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RootMod}}
\logpage{[ 15, 4, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83E3ED577B7A04ED}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RootMod({\mdseries\slshape n[, k], m})\index{RootMod@\texttt{RootMod}}
\label{RootMod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{quadratic residue} \index{residue!quadratic} \index{root!of an integer modulo another} \texttt{RootMod} computes a \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}th root of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} modulo the positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}, i.e., a $r$ such that $r^{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}} \equiv \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} \pmod{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}}$. If no such root exists \texttt{RootMod} returns \texttt{fail}. If only the arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} are given, the default value for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}} is $2$. 

 A square root of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} exists only if \texttt{Legendre(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}) = 1} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Legendre} (\ref{Legendre})). If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} has $r$ different prime factors then there are $2^r$ different roots of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} mod \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}. It is unspecified which one \texttt{RootMod} returns. You can, however, use \texttt{RootsMod} (\ref{RootsMod}) to compute the full set of roots. 

 \texttt{RootMod} is efficient even for large values of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}, in fact the most time is usually spent factoring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} (see \texttt{FactorsInt} (\ref{FactorsInt})). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# note 'RootMod' does not return 8 in this case but -8:|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootMod( 64, 1009 );|
  1001
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootMod( 64, 3, 1009 );|
  518
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootMod( 64, 5, 1009 );|
  656
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List( RootMod( 64, 1009 ) * RootsUnityMod( 1009 ),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@      x -> x mod 1009 );  # set of all square roots of 64 mod 1009|
  [ 1001, 8 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RootsMod}}
\logpage{[ 15, 4, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84D3F03B862841F8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RootsMod({\mdseries\slshape n[, k], m})\index{RootsMod@\texttt{RootsMod}}
\label{RootsMod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{RootsMod} computes the set of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}th roots of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} modulo the positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}, i.e., the list of all $r$ such that $r^{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}} \equiv \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} \pmod{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}}$. If only the arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} are given, the default value for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}} is $2$. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootsMod( 1, 7*31 );  # the same as `RootsUnityMod( 7*31 )'|
  [ 1, 92, 125, 216 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootsMod( 7, 7*31 );|
  [ 21, 196 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootsMod( 5, 7*31 );|
  [  ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootsMod( 1, 5, 7*31 );|
  [ 1, 8, 64, 78, 190 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RootsUnityMod}}
\logpage{[ 15, 4, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81F856E682A8ECBA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RootsUnityMod({\mdseries\slshape [k, ]m})\index{RootsUnityMod@\texttt{RootsUnityMod}}
\label{RootsUnityMod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{modular roots} \index{root!of 1 modulo an integer} \texttt{RootsUnityMod} returns the set of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th roots of unity modulo the positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}, i.e., the list of all solutions $r$ of $r^{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}} \equiv \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} \pmod{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}}$. If only the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} is given, the default value for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}} is $2$.
