\logpage{[ 27, 7, 22 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X855820848179CC28}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StartsWith({\mdseries\slshape string, prefix})\index{StartsWith@\texttt{StartsWith}}
\label{StartsWith}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{EndsWith({\mdseries\slshape string, suffix})\index{EndsWith@\texttt{EndsWith}}
\label{EndsWith}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{Prefix} \index{Suffix} Determines whether a string starts or ends with another string. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StringFormatted}}
\logpage{[ 27, 7, 23 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8235AD797868E872}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StringFormatted({\mdseries\slshape string, data...})\index{StringFormatted@\texttt{StringFormatted}}
\label{StringFormatted}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrintFormatted({\mdseries\slshape string, data...})\index{PrintFormatted@\texttt{PrintFormatted}}
\label{PrintFormatted}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrintToFormatted({\mdseries\slshape stream, string, data...})\index{PrintToFormatted@\texttt{PrintToFormatted}}
\label{PrintToFormatted}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 These functions perform a string formatting operation. They accept a format
string, which can contain replacement fields which are delimited by braces
\texttt{\symbol{123}}\texttt{\symbol{125}}. Each replacement field contains a
numeric or positional argument, describing the element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}} to replace the braces with. 

 There are three formatting functions, which differ only in how they output the
formatted string. \texttt{StringFormatted} returns the formatted string, \texttt{PrintFormatted} prints the formatted string and \texttt{PrintToFormatted} appends the formatted string to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stream}}, which can be either an output stream or a filename. 

 The arguments after \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape string}} form a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}} of values used to substitute the replacement fields in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape string}}, using the following formatting rules: 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape string}} is treated as a normal string, except for occurrences of \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{123}}} and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{125}}}, which follow special rules, as follows: 

 The contents of \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{123}} \texttt{\symbol{125}}} is split by a \texttt{!} into \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{123}}id!format\texttt{\symbol{125}}}, where both \texttt{id} and \texttt{format} are optional. If the \texttt{!} is omitted, the bracket is treated as \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{123}}id\texttt{\symbol{125}}} with no \texttt{format}. 

 \texttt{id} is interpreted as follows: 
\begin{description}
\item[{An integer \texttt{i}}]  Take the \texttt{i}th element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}}. 
\item[{A string \texttt{str}}]  If this is used, the first element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}} must be a record \texttt{r}. In this case, the value \texttt{r.(str)} is taken. 
\item[{No id given}]  Take the \texttt{j}th element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}}, where \texttt{j} is the number of replacement fields with no id in the format string so far. If
any replacement field has no id, then all replacement fields must have no id. 
\end{description}
 A single brace can be outputted by doubling, so \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{123}}\texttt{\symbol{123}}} in the format string produces \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{123}}} and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{125}}\texttt{\symbol{125}}} produces \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{125}}}. 

 The \texttt{format} decides how the variable is printed. \texttt{format} must be one of \texttt{s} (which uses \texttt{String} (\ref{String})), \texttt{v} (which uses \texttt{ViewString} (\ref{ViewString})) or \texttt{d} (which calls \texttt{DisplayString} (\ref{DisplayString})). The default value for \texttt{format} is \texttt{s}. }

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|StringFormatted("I have {} cats and {} dogs", 4, 5);A
  "I have 4 cats and 5 dogs"
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|StringFormatted("I have {2} cats and {1} dogs", 4, 5);A
  "I have 5 cats and 4 dogs"
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|StringFormatted("I have {cats} cats and {dogs} dogs", rec(cats:=3, dogs:=2));A
  "I have 3 cats and 2 dogs"
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|StringFormatted("We use {{ and }} to mark {dogs} dogs", rec(cats:=3, dogs:=2));A
  "We use { and } to mark 2 dogs"
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|sym3 := SymmetricGroup(3);;A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|StringFormatted("String: {1!s}, ViewString: {1!v}", sym3);A
  "String: SymmetricGroup( [ 1 .. 3 ] ), ViewString: Sym( [ 1 .. 3 ] )"
\end{Verbatim}
 The following two functions convert basic strings to lists of numbers and vice
versa. They are useful for examples of text encryption. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NumbersString}}
\logpage{[ 27, 7, 24 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7848A9D878FD59BB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NumbersString({\mdseries\slshape s, m[, table]})\index{NumbersString@\texttt{NumbersString}}
\label{NumbersString}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NumbersString} takes a string message \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape s}} and returns a list of integers, each not exceeding the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} that encode the message using the scheme $A=11$, $B=12$ and so on (and converting lower case to upper case). If a list of characters
is given in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape table}}, it is used instead for encoding). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l:=NumbersString("Twas brillig and the slithy toves",1000000);|
  [ 303311, 291012, 281922, 221917, 101124, 141030, 181510, 292219,
    301835, 103025, 321529 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StringNumbers}}
\logpage{[ 27, 7, 25 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X787EAB117816578E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StringNumbers({\mdseries\slshape l, m[, table]})\index{StringNumbers@\texttt{StringNumbers}}
\label{StringNumbers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{StringNumbers} takes a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape l}} of integers that was encoded using \texttt{NumbersString} (\ref{NumbersString}) and the size integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}, and returns a message string, using the scheme $A=11$, $B=12$ and so on. If a list of characters is given in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape table}}, it is used instead for decoding). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StringNumbers(l,1000000);|
  "TWAS BRILLIG AND THE SLITHY TOVES"
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StringOfMemoryAmount}}
\logpage{[ 27, 7, 26 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82975B6480932683}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StringOfMemoryAmount({\mdseries\slshape numbytes})\index{StringOfMemoryAmount@\texttt{StringOfMemoryAmount}}
\label{StringOfMemoryAmount}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function returns a human\texttt{\symbol{45}}readable string representing \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape numbytes}} of memory. It is used in printing amounts of memory allocated by tests and
benchmarks. Binary prefixes (representing powers of 1024) are used. }

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StringOfMemoryAmount(123456789);|
  "117MB"
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Character Conversion}}\label{Character Conversion}
\logpage{[ 27, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X844BDC8578A3B508}{}
{
  The following functions convert characters in their internal integer values
and vice versa. Note that the number corresponding to a particular character
might depend on the system used. While most systems use an extension of ASCII,
in particular character values outside the range \texttt{[ 32 .. 126 ]} might differ between architectures. 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IntChar}}
\logpage{[ 27, 8, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X826D95D680F87D23}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IntChar({\mdseries\slshape char})\index{IntChar@\texttt{IntChar}}
\label{IntChar}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns an integer value in the range \texttt{[ 0 .. 255 ]} that corresponds to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape char}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CharInt}}
\logpage{[ 27, 8, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87B6C1AF7E4A6639}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CharInt({\mdseries\slshape int})\index{CharInt@\texttt{CharInt}}
\label{CharInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a character that corresponds to the integer value \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape int}}, which must be in the range \texttt{[ 0 .. 255 ]}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@c:=CharInt(65);|
  'A'
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IntChar(c);|
  65
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SIntChar}}
\logpage{[ 27, 8, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8159CE81798DDA76}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SIntChar({\mdseries\slshape char})\index{SIntChar@\texttt{SIntChar}}
\label{SIntChar}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a signed integer value in the range \texttt{[ \texttt{\symbol{45}}128 .. 127 ]} that corresponds to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape char}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CharSInt}}
\logpage{[ 27, 8, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78E6611A829DDA3E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CharSInt({\mdseries\slshape int})\index{CharSInt@\texttt{CharSInt}}
\label{CharSInt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a character which corresponds to the signed integer value \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape int}}, which must be in the range \texttt{[ \texttt{\symbol{45}}128 .. 127 ]}. 

 The signed and unsigned integer functions behave the same for values in the
range \texttt{[ 0 .. 127 ]}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SIntChar(c);|
  65
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@c:=CharSInt(-20);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SIntChar(c);|
  -20
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IntChar(c);|
  236
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SIntChar(CharInt(255));|
  -1
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Operations to Evaluate Strings}}\label{Operations to Evaluate Strings}
\logpage{[ 27, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X78D9BD857F890C0A}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Int (for strings)}}
\logpage{[ 27, 9, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B6D118184F692A0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Int({\mdseries\slshape str})\index{Int@\texttt{Int}!for strings}
\label{Int:for strings}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 \index{evaluation!strings} returns an integer as represented by the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape str}}. The argument string may optionally start with the sign character \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}}, followed by a sequence of decimal digits. For any other input \texttt{fail} is returned. 

 For backwards compatibility, the empty string is accepted, in which case $0$ is returned as result. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Int("12345");|
  12345
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Int("123/45");|
  fail
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Int("1+2");|
  fail
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Int("-12");|
  -12
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Int("");|
  0
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Rat (for strings)}}
\logpage{[ 27, 9, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87AD395584294FF2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Rat({\mdseries\slshape str})\index{Rat@\texttt{Rat}!for strings}
\label{Rat:for strings}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 \index{evaluation!strings} returns a rational as represented by the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape str}}. The argument string may optionally start with the sign character \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}}, followed by either a sequence of decimal digits or by two sequences of
decimal digits that are separated by one of the characters \texttt{/} or \texttt{.}, where the latter stands for a decimal dot. For any other input \texttt{fail} is returned. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Rat("123/45");|
  41/15
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Rat("-123.45");|
  -2469/20
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IntHexString}}
\logpage{[ 27, 9, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X796D366B7DDEFF67}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IntHexString({\mdseries\slshape str})\index{IntHexString@\texttt{IntHexString}}
\label{IntHexString}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{evaluation!strings} returns an integer as represented by the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape str}}. The argument string may optionally start with the sign character \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}}, followed by a sequence of hexadecimal digits. Here the letters \texttt{a}\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{f} or \texttt{A}\texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{F} are used as \emph{digits} $10$ to $15$. Any other input results in an error. 

 This function can be used (together with \texttt{HexStringInt} (\ref{HexStringInt})) for efficiently storing and reading large integers from respectively into \textsf{GAP}. Note that the translation between integers and their hexadecimal
representation costs linear computation time in terms of the number of digits,
while translation from and into decimal representation needs substantial
computations. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IntHexString("-abcdef0123456789");|
  -12379813738877118345
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HexStringInt(last);|
  "-ABCDEF0123456789"
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Ordinal}}
\logpage{[ 27, 9, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C0C29C87CBA97B7}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Ordinal({\mdseries\slshape n})\index{Ordinal@\texttt{Ordinal}}
\label{Ordinal}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the ordinal of the integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} as a string. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Ordinal(2);  Ordinal(21);  Ordinal(33);  Ordinal(-33);|
  "2nd"
  "21st"
  "33rd"
  "-33rd"
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{EvalString}}
\logpage{[ 27, 9, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7DE4CCD285440659}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{EvalString({\mdseries\slshape expr})\index{EvalString@\texttt{EvalString}}
\label{EvalString}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 passes the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape expr}} through an input text stream so that \textsf{GAP} interprets it, and returns the result. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:=10;|
  10
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@EvalString("a^2");|
  100
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \texttt{EvalString} is intended for \emph{single} expressions. A sequence of commands may be interpreted by using the functions \texttt{InputTextString} (\ref{InputTextString}) and \texttt{ReadAsFunction} (\ref{ReadAsFunction:for streams}) together; see \ref{Operations for Input Streams} for an example. 

 If \texttt{EvalString} is used inside a function, then it doesn't know about the local variables and
the arguments of the function. A possible workaround is to define global
variables in advance, and then to assign the values of the local variables to
the global ones, like in the example below. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@global_a := 0;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@global_b := 0;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@example := function ( local_a )|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@    local  local_b;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@    local_b := 5;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@    global_a := local_a;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@    global_b := local_b;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@    return EvalString( "global_a * global_b" );|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@end;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@example( 2 );|
  10
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CrcString}}
\logpage{[ 27, 9, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D4B9D7A7995C55D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CrcString({\mdseries\slshape str})\index{CrcString@\texttt{CrcString}}
\label{CrcString}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\textbf{\indent Returns:\ }
an integer



 \index{hash function} \index{checksum} This function computes a CRC (cyclic redundancy check) number from a string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape str}}. See also \texttt{CrcFile} (\ref{CrcFile}) and \texttt{HexSHA256} (\ref{HexSHA256}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CrcString("GAP example string");|
  -50451670
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{HexSHA256}}
\logpage{[ 27, 9, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7873D1F28779B490}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{HexSHA256({\mdseries\slshape string})\index{HexSHA256@\texttt{HexSHA256}}
\label{HexSHA256}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{HexSHA256({\mdseries\slshape stream})\index{HexSHA256@\texttt{HexSHA256}!for a stream}
\label{HexSHA256:for a stream}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \index{hash function} \index{checksum} Return the SHA\texttt{\symbol{45}}256 cryptographic checksum of the bytes in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape string}}, resp. of the data in the input stream object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stream}} (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Streams} to learn about streams) when read from the current position until EOF
(end\texttt{\symbol{45}}of\texttt{\symbol{45}}file). 

 The checksum is returned as string with 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HexSHA256("abcd");|
  "88d4266fd4e6338d13b845fcf289579d209c897823b9217da3e161936f031589"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HexSHA256(InputTextString("abcd"));|
  "88d4266fd4e6338d13b845fcf289579d209c897823b9217da3e161936f031589"
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Pluralize}}
\logpage{[ 27, 9, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83FF17E782E6FFF3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Pluralize({\mdseries\slshape [count, ]string[, plural]})\index{Pluralize@\texttt{Pluralize}}
\label{Pluralize}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\textbf{\indent Returns:\ }
A string



 This function returns an attempt at the appropriate pluralization of a string
(considered as a singular English noun), using several rules and heuristics of
English grammar. 

 The arguments to this function are an optional non\texttt{\symbol{45}}negative
integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape count}} (the number of objects in question), a non\texttt{\symbol{45}}empty string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape string}} (the singular form of the object in question), and an optional additional
string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape plural}} (the plural form of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape string}}). 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape plural}} is given, then \texttt{Pluralize} uses it as the plural form of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape string}}, otherwise \texttt{Pluralize} makes an informed guess at the plural. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape count}} is not given, then \texttt{Pluralize} returns this plural form of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape string}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape count}} is given and has value $n \neq 1$, then this string is prepended by
"\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textgreater}n\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless} "; else if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape count}} has value $1$, then \texttt{Pluralize} returns \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape string}}, prepended by
"\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textgreater}1\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless} ". 

 Note that \texttt{StripLineBreakCharacters} (\ref{StripLineBreakCharacters}) can be used to remove the control characters \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}} and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textgreater}} from the return value. }

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Pluralize( "generator" );|
  "generators"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Pluralize( 1, "generator" );|
  "\>1\< generator"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Pluralize( 0, "generator" );|
  "\>0\< generators"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Pluralize( "man", "men" );|
  "men"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Pluralize( 1, "man", "men" );|
  "\>1\< man"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Print( Pluralize( 2, "man", "men" ) );|
  2 men
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Print( Pluralize( 2, "vertex" ) );|
  2 vertices
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Print( Pluralize( 3, "matrix" ) );|
  3 matrices
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Print( Pluralize( 4, "battery" ) );|
  4 batteries
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Calendar Arithmetic}}\label{Calendar Arithmetic}
\logpage{[ 27, 10, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X78F20AA1804D524F}{}
{
  All calendar functions use the Gregorian calendar. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DaysInYear}}
\logpage{[ 27, 10, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87BA46787FF000E8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DaysInYear({\mdseries\slshape year})\index{DaysInYear@\texttt{DaysInYear}}
\label{DaysInYear}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the number of days in the year \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape year}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DaysInMonth}}
\logpage{[ 27, 10, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8791B0B386D59ADB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DaysInMonth({\mdseries\slshape month, year})\index{DaysInMonth@\texttt{DaysInMonth}}
\label{DaysInMonth}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the number of days in month number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape month}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape year}}, and \texttt{fail} if \texttt{month} is not in the valid range. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DaysInYear(1998);|
  365
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DaysInMonth(3,1998);|
  31
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DMYDay}}
\logpage{[ 27, 10, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CED84C07CD5E2CF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DMYDay({\mdseries\slshape day})\index{DMYDay@\texttt{DMYDay}}
\label{DMYDay}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 converts a number of days, starting
1\texttt{\symbol{45}}Jan\texttt{\symbol{45}}1970, to a list \texttt{[ day, month, year ]} in Gregorian calendar counting. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DayDMY}}
\logpage{[ 27, 10, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A79DEE07A41B8EF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DayDMY({\mdseries\slshape dmy})\index{DayDMY@\texttt{DayDMY}}
\label{DayDMY}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the number of days from
01\texttt{\symbol{45}}Jan\texttt{\symbol{45}}1970 to the day given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dmy}}, which must be a list of the form \texttt{[ day, month, year ]} in Gregorian calendar counting. The result is \texttt{fail} on input outside valid ranges. 

 Note that this makes not much sense for early dates like: before 1582 (no
Gregorian calendar at all), or before 1753 in many English speaking countries
or before 1917 in Russia. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{WeekDay}}
\logpage{[ 27, 10, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87D03FC0809DB6EC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{WeekDay({\mdseries\slshape date})\index{WeekDay@\texttt{WeekDay}}
\label{WeekDay}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the weekday of a day given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape date}}, which can be a number of days since
1\texttt{\symbol{45}}Jan\texttt{\symbol{45}}1970 or a list \texttt{[ day, month, year ]}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StringDate}}
\logpage{[ 27, 10, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C74C33784CDED6C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StringDate({\mdseries\slshape date})\index{StringDate@\texttt{StringDate}}
\label{StringDate}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 converts \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape date}} to a readable string. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape date}} can be a number of days since 1\texttt{\symbol{45}}Jan\texttt{\symbol{45}}1970
or a list \texttt{[ day, month, year ]}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DayDMY([1,1,1970]);DayDMY([2,1,1970]);|

  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DMYDay(12345);|
  [ 20, 10, 2003 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@WeekDay([11,3,1998]);|

  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StringDate([11,3,1998]);|

 }

\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Obtaining LaTeX Representations of Objects}}\label{Obtaining LaTeX Representations of Objects}
\logpage{[ 27, 11, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X78024C8087F3E07F}{}
{
  \index{LaTeX!for GAP objects} For the purpose of generating {\LaTeX} source code with \textsf{GAP} it is recommended to add new functions which will print the {\LaTeX} source or return {\LaTeX} strings for further processing. 

 An alternative approach could be based on methods for the default {\LaTeX} representation for each appropriate type of objects. However, there is no
clear notion of a default {\LaTeX} code for any non\texttt{\symbol{45}}trivial mathematical object; moreover,
different output may be required in different contexts. 

 While customisation of such an operation may require changes in a variety of
methods that may be distributed all over the library, the user will have a
clean overview of the whole process of {\LaTeX} code generation if it is contained in a single function. Furthermore, there
may be kinds of objects which are not detected by the method selection, or
there may be a need in additional parameters specifying requirements for the
output. 

 This is why having a special purpose function for each particular case is more
suitable. \textsf{GAP} provides several functions that produce {\LaTeX} strings for those situations where this is nontrivial and reasonable. A useful
example is \texttt{LaTeXStringDecompositionMatrix} (\ref{LaTeXStringDecompositionMatrix}) from the \textsf{GAP} library, others can be found entering \texttt{?LaTeX} at the \textsf{GAP} prompt. Package authors are encouraged to add an index entry \texttt{LaTeX} to the documentation of all {\LaTeX} string producing functions. This way, entering \texttt{?LaTeX} will give an overview of all documented functionality in this direction. }

 }

              
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Dictionaries and General Hash Tables}}\label{Dictionaries and General Hash Tables}
\logpage{[ 28, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X867203C5877489A2}{}
{
  People and computers spend a large amount of time with searching. Dictionaries
are an abstract data structure which facilitates searching for objects.
Depending on the kind of objects the implementation will use a variety of
possible internal storage methods that will aim to provide the fastest
possible access to objects. These internal methods include 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{Hash Tables}]  for objects for which a hash function has been defined. 
\item[{Direct Indexing}]  if the domain is small and cheaply enumerable 
\item[{Sorted Lists}]  if a total order can be computed easily 
\item[{Plain lists}]  for objects for which nothing but an equality test is available. 
\end{description}
  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Using Dictionaries}}\label{Using Dictionaries}
\logpage{[ 28, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81560C4083E27955}{}
{
  The standard way to use dictionaries is to first create a dictionary (using \texttt{NewDictionary} (\ref{NewDictionary}), and then to store objects (and associated information) in it and look them
up. 

 For the creation of objects the user has to make a few choices: Is the
dictionary only to be used to check whether objects are known already, or
whether associated information is to be stored with the objects. This second
case is called a \emph{lookup dictionary} and is selected by the second parameter of \texttt{NewDictionary} (\ref{NewDictionary}). 

 The second choice is to indicate which kind of objects are to be stored. This
choice will decide the internal storage used. This kind of objects is
specified by the first parameter to \texttt{NewDictionary} (\ref{NewDictionary}), which is a ``sample'' object. 

 In some cases however such a sample object is not specific enough. For example
when storing vectors over a finite field, it would not be clear whether all
vectors will be over a prime field or over a field extension. Such an issue
can be resolved by indicating in an (optional) third parameter to \texttt{NewDictionary} (\ref{NewDictionary}) a \emph{domain} which has to be a collection that will contain all objects to be used with
this dictionary. (Such a domain may also be used internally to decide that
direct indexing can be used). 

 The reason for this choice of giving two parameters is that in some cases no
suitable collection of objects has been defined in \textsf{GAP} \texttt{\symbol{45}} for example for permutations there is no object
representing the symmetric group on infinitely many points. 

 Once a dictionary has been created, it is possible to use \texttt{RepresentationsOfObject} (\ref{RepresentationsOfObject}) to check which representation is used by \textsf{GAP}. 

 In the following example, we create a dictionary to store permutations with
associated information. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@d:=NewDictionary((1,2,3),true);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AddDictionary(d,(1,2),1);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AddDictionary(d,(5,6),9);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AddDictionary(d,(4,7),2);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LookupDictionary(d,(5,6));|
  9
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LookupDictionary(d,(5,7));|
  fail
\end{Verbatim}
 A typical example of this use would be in an orbit algorithm. The dictionary
would be used to store the elements known in the orbit together with their
respective orbit positions. 

 We observe that this dictionary is stored internally by a sorted list. On the
other hand, if we have an explicit, sorted element list, direct indexing is to
be used. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RepresentationsOfObject(d);|
  [ "IsComponentObjectRep", "IsNonAtomicComponentObjectRep",
    "IsDictionaryDefaultRep", "IsListDictionary",
    "IsListLookupDictionary", "IsSortDictionary",
    "IsSortLookupDictionary" ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@d:=NewDictionary((1,2,3),true,Elements(SymmetricGroup(5)));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RepresentationsOfObject(d);|
  [ "IsComponentObjectRep", "IsNonAtomicComponentObjectRep",
    "IsDictionaryDefaultRep", "IsPositionDictionary",
    "IsPositionLookupDictionary" ]
\end{Verbatim}
 (Just indicating \texttt{SymmetricGroup(5)} as a third parameter would still keep the first storage method, as indexing
would be too expensive if no explicit element list is known.) 

 The same effect happens in the following example, in which we work with
vectors: Indicating only a vector only enables sorted index, as it cannot be
known whether all vectors will be defined over the prime field. On the other
hand, providing the vector space (and thus limiting the domain) enables the
use of hashing (which will be faster). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@v:=GF(2)^7;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@d:=NewDictionary(Zero(v),true);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RepresentationsOfObject(d);|
  [ "IsComponentObjectRep", "IsNonAtomicComponentObjectRep",
    "IsDictionaryDefaultRep", "IsListDictionary",
    "IsListLookupDictionary", "IsSortDictionary",
    "IsSortLookupDictionary" ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@d:=NewDictionary(Zero(v),true,v);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RepresentationsOfObject(d);|
  [ "IsComponentObjectRep", "IsNonAtomicComponentObjectRep",
    "IsDictionaryDefaultRep", "IsPositionDictionary",
    "IsPositionLookupDictionary" ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Dictionaries}}\label{Dictionaries}
\logpage{[ 28, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7B571EA282AF70D7}{}
{
  This section contains the formal declarations for dictionaries. For
information on how to use them, please refer to the previous
section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Using Dictionaries}. There are several ways how dictionaries are implemented: As lists, as sorted
lists, as hash tables or via binary lists. A user however will just have to
call \texttt{NewDictionary} (\ref{NewDictionary}) and obtain a ``suitable'' dictionary for the kind of objects she wants to create. It is possible however
to create hash tables (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{General Hash Tables}) and dictionaries using binary lists (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{DictionaryByPosition} (\ref{DictionaryByPosition})). 

 The use of two objects, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape objcoll}} to parametrize the objects a dictionary is able to store might look confusing.
However there are situations where either of them might be needed: 

 The first situation is that of objects, for which no formal ``collection object'' has been defined. A typical example here might be subspaces of a vector space. \textsf{GAP} does not formally define a ``Grassmannian'' or anything else to represent the multitude of all subspaces. So it is only
possible to give the dictionary a ``sample object''. 

 The other situation is that of an object which might represent quite varied
domains. The permutation $(1,10^6)$ might be the nontrivial element of a cyclic group of order 2, it might be a
representative of $S_{{10^6}}$. In the first situation the best approach might be just to have two entries
for the two possible objects, in the second situation a much more elaborate
approach might be needed. 

 An algorithm that creates a dictionary will usually know a priori, from what
domain all the objects will be, giving this domain permits to use a more
efficient dictionary. 

 This is particularly true for vectors. From a single vector one cannot decide
whether a calculation will take place over the smallest field containing all
its entries or over a larger field. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NewDictionary}}
\logpage{[ 28, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E78E3E983A5C895}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewDictionary({\mdseries\slshape obj, look[, objcoll]})\index{NewDictionary@\texttt{NewDictionary}}
\label{NewDictionary}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 creates a new dictionary for objects such as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape objcoll}} is given the dictionary will be for objects only from this collection, knowing
this can improve the performance. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape objcoll}} is given, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} may be replaced by \texttt{false}, i.e. no sample object is needed. 

 The function tries to find the right kind of dictionary for the basic
dictionary functions to be quick. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape look}} is \texttt{true}, the dictionary will be a lookup dictionary, otherwise it is an ordinary
dictionary. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Dictionaries via Binary Lists}}\label{Dictionaries via Binary Lists}
\logpage{[ 28, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86BD015B7B889329}{}
{
  As there are situations where the approach via binary lists is explicitly
desired, such dictionaries can be created deliberately. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DictionaryByPosition}}
\logpage{[ 28, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X865D5BE1830A448D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DictionaryByPosition({\mdseries\slshape list, lookup})\index{DictionaryByPosition@\texttt{DictionaryByPosition}}
\label{DictionaryByPosition}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 creates a new (lookup) dictionary which uses \texttt{PositionCanonical} (\ref{PositionCanonical}) in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} for indexing. The dictionary will have an entry \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dict}}\texttt{!.blist} which is a bit list corresponding to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} indicating the known values. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape look}} is \texttt{true}, the dictionary will be a lookup dictionary, otherwise it is an ordinary
dictionary. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsDictionary}}
\logpage{[ 28, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87F7247E784021C2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsDictionary({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsDictionary@\texttt{IsDictionary}}
\label{IsDictionary}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 A dictionary is a growable collection of objects that permits to add objects
(with associated values) and to check whether an object is already known. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsLookupDictionary}}
\logpage{[ 28, 3, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D776BC67ABDDCCE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsLookupDictionary({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsLookupDictionary@\texttt{IsLookupDictionary}}
\label{IsLookupDictionary}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 A \emph{lookup dictionary} is a dictionary, which permits not only to check whether an object is
contained, but also to retrieve associated values, using the operation \texttt{LookupDictionary} (\ref{LookupDictionary}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AddDictionary}}
\logpage{[ 28, 3, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86C4F0507AD98B8A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AddDictionary({\mdseries\slshape dict, key[, val]})\index{AddDictionary@\texttt{AddDictionary}}
\label{AddDictionary}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 adds \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape key}} to the dictionary \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dict}}, storing the associated value \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} in case \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dict}} is a lookup dictionary. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape key}} is not an object of the kind for which the dictionary was specified, or if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape key}} is known already to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dict}}, the results are unpredictable. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{KnowsDictionary}}
\logpage{[ 28, 3, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X808C885D7E267285}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{KnowsDictionary({\mdseries\slshape dict, key})\index{KnowsDictionary@\texttt{KnowsDictionary}}
\label{KnowsDictionary}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 checks, whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape key}} is known to the dictionary \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dict}}, and returns \texttt{true} or \texttt{false} accordingly. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape key}} \emph{must} be an object of the kind for which the dictionary was specified, otherwise the
results are unpredictable. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LookupDictionary}}
\logpage{[ 28, 3, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X863706BF847A47EB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LookupDictionary({\mdseries\slshape dict, key})\index{LookupDictionary@\texttt{LookupDictionary}}
\label{LookupDictionary}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 looks up \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape key}} in the lookup dictionary \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dict}} and returns the associated value. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape key}} is not known to the dictionary, \texttt{fail} is returned. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{General Hash Tables}}\label{General Hash Tables}
\logpage{[ 28, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8444087381BBA88A}{}
{
  These sections describe some particularities for hash tables. These are
intended mainly for extending the implementation \texttt{\symbol{45}} programs
requiring hash functionality ought to use the dictionary interface described
above. 

 We hash by keys and also store a value. Keys cannot be removed from the table,
but the corresponding value can be changed. Fast access to last hash index
allows you to efficiently store more than one array of values
{\textendash}this facility should be used with care. 

 This code works for any kind of object, provided you have a \texttt{DenseIntKey} (\ref{DenseIntKey}) method to convert the key into a positive integer. This method should ideally
be implemented efficiently in the core. 

Note that, for efficiency, it is currently impossible to create a hash table
with non\texttt{\symbol{45}}positive integers. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Hash keys}}\label{Hash keys}
\logpage{[ 28, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X85CD6C9B85DE7C54}{}
{
  The crucial step of hashing is to transform key objects into integers such
that equal objects produce the same integer. 

 The actual function used will vary very much on the type of objects. However \textsf{GAP} provides already key functions for some commonly encountered objects. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DenseIntKey}}
\logpage{[ 28, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79DEEB5783513838}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DenseIntKey({\mdseries\slshape objcoll, obj})\index{DenseIntKey@\texttt{DenseIntKey}}
\label{DenseIntKey}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a function that can be used as hash key function for objects such as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} in the collection \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape objcoll}}. Typically, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape objcoll}} will be a large domain. If the domain is not available, it can be given as \texttt{false} in which case the hash key function will be determined only based on \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. (For a further discussion of these two arguments see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{NewDictionary} (\ref{NewDictionary})). 

 The function returned by \texttt{DenseIntKey} is guaranteed to give different values for different objects. If no suitable
hash key function has been predefined, \texttt{fail} is returned. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SparseIntKey}}
\logpage{[ 28, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87FC10AC81E5F6BA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SparseIntKey({\mdseries\slshape objcoll, obj})\index{SparseIntKey@\texttt{SparseIntKey}}
\label{SparseIntKey}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a function that can be used as hash key function for objects such as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} in the collection \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape objcoll}}. In contrast to \texttt{DenseIntKey} (\ref{DenseIntKey}), the function returned may return the same key value for different objects.
If no suitable hash key function has been predefined, \texttt{fail} is returned. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Dense hash tables}}\label{Dense hash tables}
\logpage{[ 28, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X84D1A83C8247E7FB}{}
{
  Dense hash tables are used for hashing dense sets without collisions, in
particular integers. Keys are stored as an unordered list and values as an
array with holes. The position of a value is given by the function returned by \texttt{DenseIntKey} (\ref{DenseIntKey}), and so \texttt{KeyIntDense} must be one\texttt{\symbol{45}}to\texttt{\symbol{45}}one. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DenseHashTable}}
\logpage{[ 28, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X874FAA447930C7DA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DenseHashTable({\mdseries\slshape })\index{DenseHashTable@\texttt{DenseHashTable}}
\label{DenseHashTable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Construct an empty dense hash table. This is the only correct way to construct
such a table. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Sparse hash tables}}\label{Sparse hash tables}
\logpage{[ 28, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7FDB74417A19E674}{}
{
  Sparse hash tables are used for hashing sparse sets. Stores keys as an array
with fail denoting an empty position, stores values as an array with holes.
Uses the result of calling \texttt{SparseIntKey} (\ref{SparseIntKey})) of the key. \texttt{DefaultHashLength} is the default starting hash table length; the table is doubled when it
becomes half full. 

 In sparse hash tables, the integer obtained from the hash key is then
transformed to an index position by taking it modulo the length of the hash
array. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SparseHashTable}}
\logpage{[ 28, 7, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8757D3A785290640}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SparseHashTable({\mdseries\slshape [intkeyfun[, startlength]]})\index{SparseHashTable@\texttt{SparseHashTable}}
\label{SparseHashTable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Construct an empty sparse hash table. This is the only correct way to
construct such a table. If the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape intkeyfun}} is given, this function will be used to obtain numbers for the keys passed to
it. If also \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape startlength}} is given, the hash table will be initialized at that size. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DoubleHashArraySize}}
\logpage{[ 28, 7, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80FDDF957887B4FC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DoubleHashArraySize({\mdseries\slshape hash})\index{DoubleHashArraySize@\texttt{DoubleHashArraySize}}
\label{DoubleHashArraySize}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Double the size of the hash array and rehash all the entries. This will also
happen automatically when the hash array is half full. }

 }

 }

             
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Records}}\label{Records}
\logpage{[ 29, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7AA1073C7E943DD7}{}
{
  \index{type!records} \emph{Records} are next to lists the most important way to collect objects together. A record
is a collection of \emph{components}. Each component has a unique \emph{name}, which is an identifier that distinguishes this component, and a \emph{value}, which is an object of arbitrary type. We often abbreviate \emph{value of a component} to \emph{element}. We also say that a record \emph{contains} its elements. You can access and change the elements of a record using its
name. 

 Record literals are written by writing down the components in order between ``\texttt{rec(}'' and ``\texttt{)}'', and separating them by commas ``\texttt{,}''. Each component consists of the name, the assignment operator ``\texttt{:=}'', and the value. The \emph{empty record}, i.e., the record with no components, is written as \texttt{rec()}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rec( a := 1, b := "2" ); # a record with two components|
  rec( a := 1, b := "2" )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rec( a := 1, b := rec( c := 2 ) ); # record may contain records|
  rec( a := 1, b := rec( c := 2 ) )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 We may use the \texttt{Display} (\ref{Display}) function to illustrate the hierarchy of the record components. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Display( last );|
  rec(
    a := 1,
    b := rec(
        c := 2 ) )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Records usually contain elements of various types, i.e., they are usually not
homogeneous like lists.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsRecord and RecNames}}\label{sect:IsRecord}
\logpage{[ 29, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X864F92347B5A3FF0}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsRecord}}
\logpage{[ 29, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X782A998E7D9EC406}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsRecord({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsRecord@\texttt{IsRecord}}
\label{IsRecord}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsRecordCollection({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsRecordCollection@\texttt{IsRecordCollection}}
\label{IsRecordCollection}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsRecordCollColl({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsRecordCollColl@\texttt{IsRecordCollColl}}
\label{IsRecordCollColl}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 \index{test!for records} 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsRecord( rec( a := 1, b := 2 ) );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsRecord( IsRecord );|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RecNames}}
\logpage{[ 29, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X837F1E1F866FB1A0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RecNames({\mdseries\slshape record})\index{RecNames@\texttt{RecNames}}
\label{RecNames}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns a duplicate\texttt{\symbol{45}}free list of strings corresponding to
the names of the record components of the record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape record}}. 

 The list is sorted by \texttt{RNamObj} (\ref{RNamObj:for a string}) for reasons of efficiency; see \texttt{SortBy} (\ref{SortBy}). Therefore the ordering is consistent within one \textsf{GAP} session, but it is not necessarily consistent across different sessions. To
obtain a result that is consistent across \textsf{GAP} sessions, apply \texttt{Set} (\ref{Set}) to the returned list. 

 Note that given a string \texttt{name} containing the name of a record component, you can access the record component
via \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape record}}.(name)}, see Sections{\nobreakspace}\ref{Accessing Record Elements} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Record Assignment}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r := rec( a := 1, b := 2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Set(RecNames( r )); # 'Set' because ordering depends on GAP session|
  [ "a", "b" ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Set(RecNames( r ), x -> r.(x));|
  [ 1, 2 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that it is most efficient to assign components to a (new or old) record
in the order given by \texttt{RecNames}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Accessing Record Elements}}\label{Accessing Record Elements}
\logpage{[ 29, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7EAAE25D7A17F778}{}
{
  \index{accessing!record elements} \index{record!component access} \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}} 

 The above construct evaluates to the value of the record component with the
name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} in the record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}. Note that the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} is not evaluated, i.e. it is taken literal. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r := rec( a := 1, b := 2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r.a;|
  1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r.b;|
  2
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \index{record!component variable} \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}.(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}})} 

 This construct is similar to the above construct. The difference is that the
second operand \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} is evaluated. It must evaluate to a string or an integer otherwise an error is
signalled. The construct then evaluates to the element of the record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} whose name is, as a string, equal to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@old := rec( a := 1, b := 2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@new := rec();|
  rec(  )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@for i in RecNames( old ) do|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@ new.(i) := old.(i);|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@od;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Display( new );|
  rec(
    a := 1,
    b := 2 )
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Record Assignment}}\label{Record Assignment}
\logpage{[ 29, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X806DE3BD78742CA4}{}
{
  \index{assignment!to a record} \index{record!component assignment} \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} := \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}} 

 The record assignment assigns the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, which may be an object of arbitrary type, to the record component with the
name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}, which must be an identifier, of the record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}. That means that accessing the element with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} of the record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} will return \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} after this assignment. If the record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} has no component with the name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}, the record is automatically extended to make room for the new component. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r := rec( a := 1, b := 2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r.a := 10;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Display( r );|
  rec(
    a := 10,
    b := 2 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r.c := 3;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Display( r );|
  rec(
    a := 10,
    b := 2,
    c := 3 )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that assigning to a record changes the record. 

 The function \texttt{IsBound} (\ref{IsBound:for a record component}) can be used to test if a record has a component with a certain name, the
function \texttt{Unbind} (\ref{Unbind:unbind a record component}) can be used to remove a component with a certain name again. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBound(r.a);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBound(r.d);|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Unbind(r.b);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Display( r );|
  rec(
    a := 10,
    c := 3 )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \index{record!component variable assignment} \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}.(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}) := \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}} 

 This construct is similar to the above construct. The difference is that the
second operand \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} is evaluated. It must evaluate to a string or an integer otherwise an error is
signalled. The construct then assigns \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} to the record component of the record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} whose name is, as a string, equal to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Identical Records}}\label{Identical Records}
\logpage{[ 29, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86BC2672803863FB}{}
{
  With the record assignment (see \ref{Record Assignment}) it is possible to change a record. This section describes the semantic
consequences of this fact which are essentially the same as for lists
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Identical Lists}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  r := rec( a := 1 );
  r := rec( a := 1, b := 2 );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The second assignment does not change the first record, instead it assigns a
new record to the variable \texttt{r}. On the other hand, in the following example the record is changed by the
second assignment. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  r := rec( a := 1 );
  r.b := 2;
\end{Verbatim}
 

 To understand the difference first think of a variable as a name for an
object. The important point is that a record can have several names at the
same time. An assignment \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape var}} := \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}} means in this interpretation that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape var}} is a name for the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}. At the end of the following example \texttt{r2} still has the value \texttt{rec( a := 1 )} as this record has not been changed and nothing else has been assigned to \texttt{r2}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  r1 := rec( a := 1 );
  r2 := r1;
  r1 := rec( a := 1, b := 2 );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 But after the following example the record for which \texttt{r2} is a name has been changed and thus the value of \texttt{r2} is now \texttt{rec( a := 1, b := 2 )}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  r1 := rec( a := 1 );
  r2 := r1;
  r1.b := 2;
\end{Verbatim}
 

 We shall say that two records are \emph{identical} if changing one of them by a record assignment also changes the other one.
This is slightly incorrect, because if \emph{two} records are identical, there are actually only two names for \emph{one} record. However, the correct usage would be very awkward and would only add to
the confusion. Note that two identical records must be equal, because there is
only one records with two different names. Thus identity is an equivalence
relation that is a refinement of equality. 

 Let us now consider under which circumstances two records are identical. 

 If you enter a record literal then the record denoted by this literal is a new
record that is not identical to any other record. Thus in the following
example \texttt{r1} and \texttt{r2} are not identical, though they are equal of course. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  r1 := rec( a := 1 );
  r2 := rec( a := 1 );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Also in the following example, no records in the list \texttt{l} are identical. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  l := [];
  for i in [1..10] do
    l[i] := rec( a := 1 );
  od;
\end{Verbatim}
 

 If you assign a record to a variable no new record is created. Thus the record
value of the variable on the left hand side and the record on the right hand
side of the assignment are identical. So in the following example \texttt{r1} and \texttt{r2} are identical records. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  r1 := rec( a := 1 );
  r2 := r1;
\end{Verbatim}
 

 If you pass a record as argument, the old record and the argument of the
function are identical. Also if you return a record from a function, the old
record and the value of the function call are identical. So in the following
example \texttt{r1} and \texttt{r2} are identical records. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  r1 := rec( a := 1 );
  f := function ( r ) return r; end;
  r2 := f( r1 );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The functions \texttt{StructuralCopy} (\ref{StructuralCopy}) and \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}) accept a record and return a new record that is equal to the old record but
that is \emph{not} identical to the old record. The difference between \texttt{StructuralCopy} (\ref{StructuralCopy}) and \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}) is that in the case of \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}) the corresponding components of the new and the old records will be identical,
whereas in the case of \texttt{StructuralCopy} (\ref{StructuralCopy}) they will only be equal. So in the following example \texttt{r1} and \texttt{r2} are not identical records. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  r1 := rec( a := 1 );
  r2 := ShallowCopy( r1 );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 If you change a record it keeps its identity. Thus if two records are
identical and you change one of them, you also change the other, and they are
still identical afterwards. On the other hand, two records that are not
identical will never become identical if you change one of them. So in the
following example both \texttt{r1} and \texttt{r2} are changed, and are still identical. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  r1 := rec( a := 1 );
  r2 := r1;
  r1.b := 2;
\end{Verbatim}
 

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Comparisons of Records}}\label{Comparisons of Records}
\logpage{[ 29, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83A7E6607B1D63BC}{}
{
  \index{equality!of records} \index{inequality!of records} \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec1}} = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec2}}} 

 \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec1}} {\textless}{\textgreater} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec2}}} 

 Two records are considered equal, if for each component of one record the
other record has a component of the same name with an equal value and vice
versa. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rec( a := 1, b := 2 ) = rec( b := 2, a := 1 );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rec( a := 1, b := 2 ) = rec( a := 2, b := 1 );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rec( a := 1 ) = rec( a := 1, b := 2 );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rec( a := 1 ) = 1;|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \index{ordering!of records} \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec1}} {\textless} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec2}}} 

 \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec1}} {\textless}= \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec2}}} 

 To compare records we imagine that the components of both records are sorted
according to their names (the sorting depends on the \textsf{GAP} session, more precisely the order in which component names were first used).
Then the records are compared lexicographically with unbound elements
considered smaller than anything else. Precisely one record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec1}} is considered less than another record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec2}} if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec2}} has a component with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name2}} and either \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec1}} has no component with this name or \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec1}}.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name2}} {\textless} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec2}}.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name2}}} and for each component of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec1}} with name \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name1}} {\textless} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name2}}} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec2}} has a component with this name and \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec1}}.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name1}} = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rec2}}.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name1}}}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rec( axy := 1, bxy := 2 ) < rec( bxy := 2, axy := 1 ); # are equal|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rec( axy := 1 ) < rec( axy := 1, bxy := 2 ); # unbound is < 2|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# in new session the .axy components are compared first|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rec( axy := 1, bxy := 2 ) < rec( axy := 2, bxy := 0 ); # 1 < 2|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rec( axy := 1 ) < rec( axy := 0, bxy := 2 ); # 0 < 1|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rec( bxy := 1 ) < rec( bxy := 0, axy := 2 ); # unbound is < 2|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsBound and Unbind for Records}}\label{IsBound and Unbind for Records}
\logpage{[ 29, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79BE8D0E829E7ACE}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsBound (for a record component)}}
\logpage{[ 29, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A13E8F87CAAA0AF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsBound({\mdseries\slshape r.name})\index{IsBound@\texttt{IsBound}!for a record component}
\label{IsBound:for a record component}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{IsBound} returns \texttt{true} if the record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} has a component with the name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} (which must be an identifier) and \texttt{false} otherwise. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} must evaluate to a record, otherwise an error is signalled. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r := rec( a := 1, b := 2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBound( r.a );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBound( r.c );|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Unbind (unbind a record component)}}
\logpage{[ 29, 6, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CA9AEFE7DB71604}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Unbind({\mdseries\slshape r.name})\index{Unbind@\texttt{Unbind}!unbind a record component}
\label{Unbind:unbind a record component}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{Unbind} deletes the component with the name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} in the record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}. That is, after execution of \texttt{Unbind}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} no longer has a record component with this name. Note that it is not an error
to unbind a nonexisting record component. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} must evaluate to a record, otherwise an error is signalled. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r := rec( a := 1, b := 2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Unbind( r.a ); r;|
  rec( b := 2 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Unbind( r.c ); r;|
  rec( b := 2 )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that \texttt{IsBound} (\ref{IsBound:for a record component}) and \texttt{Unbind} are special in that they do not evaluate their argument, otherwise \texttt{IsBound} (\ref{IsBound:for a record component}) would always signal an error when it is supposed to return \texttt{false} and there would be no way to tell \texttt{Unbind} which component to remove. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Record Access Operations}}\label{Record Access Operations}
\logpage{[ 29, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X784897E180815EDA}{}
{
  Internally, record accesses are done using the operations listed in this
section. For the records implemented in the kernel, kernel methods are
provided for all these operations but otherwise it is possible to install
methods for these operations for any object. This permits objects to simulate
record behavior. 

 To save memory, records do not store a list of all component names, but only
numbers identifying the components. There numbers are called \emph{RNams}. \textsf{GAP} keeps a global list of all RNams that are used and provides the functions \texttt{NameRNam} (\ref{NameRNam}) and \texttt{RNamObj} (\ref{RNamObj:for a string}) to translate RNams to strings that give the component names and vice versa. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NameRNam}}
\logpage{[ 29, 7, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87BF90FA7F7A3B1B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NameRNam({\mdseries\slshape nr})\index{NameRNam@\texttt{NameRNam}}
\label{NameRNam}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a string representing the component name corresponding to the RNam \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RNamObj (for a string)}}
\logpage{[ 29, 7, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78199B6B84A017B9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RNamObj({\mdseries\slshape str})\index{RNamObj@\texttt{RNamObj}!for a string}
\label{RNamObj:for a string}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RNamObj({\mdseries\slshape int})\index{RNamObj@\texttt{RNamObj}!for a positive integer}
\label{RNamObj:for a positive integer}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a number (the RNam) corresponding to the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape str}}. It is also possible to pass a positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape int}} in which case the decimal expansion of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape int}} is used as a string. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NameRNam(798);|
  "BravaisSupergroups"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RNamObj("blubberflutsch");|
  2075
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NameRNam(last);|
  "blubberflutsch"
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The correspondence between strings and RNams is not predetermined ab initio,
but RNams are assigned to component names dynamically on a ``first come, first serve'' basis. Therefore, depending on the version of the library you are using and on
the assignments done so far, the \emph{same} component name may be represented by \emph{different} RNams in different \textsf{GAP} sessions. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{\texttt{\symbol{92}}.}}
\logpage{[ 29, 7, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7821AC097821AC09}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}.({\mdseries\slshape obj, rnam})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}.@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}.}}
\label{bSlash.}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsBound\texttt{\symbol{92}}.({\mdseries\slshape obj, rnam})\index{IsBound\texttt{\symbol{92}}.@\texttt{IsBound\texttt{\symbol{92}}.}}
\label{IsBoundbSlash.}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}.\texttt{\symbol{92}}:\texttt{\symbol{92}}=({\mdseries\slshape obj, rnam, val})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}.\texttt{\symbol{92}}:\texttt{\symbol{92}}=@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}.\texttt{\symbol{92}}:\texttt{\symbol{92}}=}}
\label{bSlash.bSlash:bSlash=}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Unbind\texttt{\symbol{92}}.({\mdseries\slshape obj, rnam})\index{Unbind\texttt{\symbol{92}}.@\texttt{Unbind\texttt{\symbol{92}}.}}
\label{UnbindbSlash.}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \index{record component!operation} \index{record boundness test!operation} \index{record assignment!operation} \index{record unbind!operation} These operations are called for record accesses to arbitrary objects. If
applicable methods are installed, they are called when the object is accessed
as a record. 

 For records, the operations implement component access, test for element
boundness, component assignment and removal of the component represented by
the RNam \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rnam}}. 

 The component identifier \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rnam}} is always required to be in \texttt{IsPosInt} (\ref{IsPosInt}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r:= rec( a:= 1 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBound\.( r, RNamObj( "a" ) );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@\.( r, RNamObj( "a" ) );|
  1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBound\.( r, RNamObj( "b" ) );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@\.\:\=( r, RNamObj( "b" ), 2 );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r;|
  rec( a := 1, b := 2 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Unbind\.( r, RNamObj( "b" ) );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r;|
  rec( a := 1 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G:= SymmetricGroup( 4 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G.1;|
  (1,2,3,4)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@\.( G, RNamObj( 1 ) );|
  (1,2,3,4)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@meth:= ApplicableMethod( \., [ G, 4711 ] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@meth( G, RNamObj( 1 ) );|
  (1,2,3,4)
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

 }

         
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Collections}}\label{Collections}
\logpage{[ 30, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8050A8037984E5B6}{}
{
  A \emph{collection} in \textsf{GAP} consists of elements in the same family (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Families}). The most important kinds of collections are \emph{homogeneous lists} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Lists}) and \emph{domains} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Domains}). Note that a list is never a domain, and a domain is never a list. A list is
a collection if and only if it is nonempty and homogeneous. 

 Basic operations for collections are \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}) and \texttt{Enumerator} (\ref{Enumerator}); for \emph{finite} collections, \texttt{Enumerator} (\ref{Enumerator}) admits to delegate the other operations for collections (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Attributes and Properties for Collections} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Operations for Collections}) to functions for lists (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Lists}). Obviously, special methods depending on the arguments are needed for the
computation of e.g.{\nobreakspace}the intersection of two \emph{infinite} domains.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsCollection (Filter)}}\label{sect:IsCollection}
\logpage{[ 30, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8084F03A78ABD4F8}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsCollection}}
\logpage{[ 30, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79C9FC7F86E2738C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsCollection({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsCollection@\texttt{IsCollection}}
\label{IsCollection}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 tests whether an object is a collection. 

 Some of the functions for lists and collections are described in the chapter
about lists, mainly in Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Operations for Lists}. In the current chapter, we describe those functions for which the ``collection aspect'' seems to be more important than the ``list aspect''. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Collection Families}}\label{Collection Families}
\logpage{[ 30, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X85D8D8F684B02DDF}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CollectionsFamily}}
\logpage{[ 30, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84E5A67E87D8DD66}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CollectionsFamily({\mdseries\slshape Fam})\index{CollectionsFamily@\texttt{CollectionsFamily}}
\label{CollectionsFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For a family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}}, \texttt{CollectionsFamily} returns the family of all collections over \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}}, that is, of all dense lists and domains that consist of objects in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}}. 

 The \texttt{NewFamily} (\ref{NewFamily}) call in the standard method of \texttt{CollectionsFamily} is executed with second argument \texttt{IsCollection} (\ref{IsCollection}), since every object in the collections family must be a collection, and with
third argument the collections categories of the involved categories in the
implied filter of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}}. 

 Note that families (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Families}) are used to describe relations between objects. Important such relations are
that between an element $e$ and each collection of elements that lie in the same family as $e$, and that between two collections whose elements lie in the same family.
Therefore, all collections of elements in the family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} form the new family \texttt{CollectionsFamily( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} )}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsCollectionFamily}}
\logpage{[ 30, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X856AC2DF7F7CBAAF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsCollectionFamily({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsCollectionFamily@\texttt{IsCollectionFamily}}
\label{IsCollectionFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 is \texttt{true} if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} is a family of collections, and \texttt{false} otherwise. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ElementsFamily}}
\logpage{[ 30, 2, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X864BB3748546F63F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ElementsFamily({\mdseries\slshape Fam})\index{ElementsFamily@\texttt{ElementsFamily}}
\label{ElementsFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} is a collections family (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsCollectionFamily} (\ref{IsCollectionFamily})) then \texttt{ElementsFamily} returns the family from which \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} was created by \texttt{CollectionsFamily} (\ref{CollectionsFamily}). The way a collections family is created, it always has its elements family
stored. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} is not a collections family then an error is signalled. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@fam:= FamilyObj( (1,2) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@collfam:= CollectionsFamily( fam );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@fam = collfam;  fam = ElementsFamily( collfam );|
  false
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@collfam = FamilyObj( [ (1,2,3) ] );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@collfam = FamilyObj( Group( () ) );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@collfam = CollectionsFamily( collfam );|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CategoryCollections}}
\logpage{[ 30, 2, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78C38017804B2EA7}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CategoryCollections({\mdseries\slshape filter})\index{CategoryCollections@\texttt{CategoryCollections}}
\label{CategoryCollections}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}} be a filter that is \texttt{true} for all elements of a family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}}, by the construction of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}}. Then \texttt{CategoryCollections} returns the \emph{collections category} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}}. This is a category that is \texttt{true} for all elements in \texttt{CollectionsFamily( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} )}. 

 For example, the construction of \texttt{PermutationsFamily} (\ref{PermutationsFamily}) guarantees that each of its elements lies in the filter \texttt{IsPerm} (\ref{IsPerm}), and each collection of permutations (permutation group or dense list of
permutations) lies in the category \texttt{CategoryCollections( IsPerm )}. \texttt{CategoryCollections( IsPerm )}. Note that this works only if the collections category is created \emph{before} the collections family. So it is necessary to construct interesting
collections categories immediately after the underlying category has been
created. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareCategoryCollections}}
\logpage{[ 30, 2, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85ABC1B4829778C7}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareCategoryCollections({\mdseries\slshape name})\index{DeclareCategoryCollections@\texttt{DeclareCategoryCollections}}
\label{DeclareCategoryCollections}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Calls \texttt{CategoryCollections} (\ref{CategoryCollections}) on the category that is bound to the global variable with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} to obtain its collections category, and binds the latter to the global
variable with name \texttt{nname}.
