 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} is a domain that is closed under the operational structure given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}} then \texttt{As\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} returns a domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape E}} that consists of the same elements (that is, \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape E}}}) and that has this operational structure (that is, \texttt{Is\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape E}} )} is \texttt{true}); if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} is not closed under the structure given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}} then \texttt{As\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} returns \texttt{fail}. 

 If additional information besides generators are necessary to define \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} then the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} describes the value of this information for the desired domain. For example,
if we want to view \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} as a vector space over the field with two elements then we may call \texttt{AsVectorSpace( GF(2), \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} )}; this allows us to change the underlying field of scalars, for example if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} is a vector space over the field with four elements. Again, if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} is not equal to a domain with the desired structure and additional information
then \texttt{fail} is returned. 

 In the case that no additional information \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} is related to the structure given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}, the operation \texttt{As\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} is in fact an attribute (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Attributes}). 

 See the index of the \textsf{GAP} Reference Manual for an overview of the available \texttt{As\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} functions. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Changing the Representation}}\label{Changing the Representation}
\logpage{[ 31, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X860FCCBE7A41412F}{}
{
  Often it is useful to answer questions about a domain via computations in a
different but isomorphic domain. In the sense that this approach keeps the
structure and changes the underlying set of elements, it can be viewed as a
counterpart of keeping the set of elements and changing its structure
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Changing the Structure}). 

 One reason for doing so can be that computations with the elements in the
given domain are not very efficient. For example, if one is given a solvable
matrix group (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Matrix Groups}) then one can compute an isomorphism to a polycyclicly presented group $G$, say (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Polycyclic Groups}); the multiplication of two matrices {\textendash}which is essentially
determined by the dimension of the matrices{\textendash} is much more
expensive than the multiplication of two elements in $G$ {\textendash}which is essentially determined by the composition length of $G$. 

 \index{IsomorphismRepStruct@\texttt{Isomorphism\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Rep}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}}} \texttt{Isomorphism\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Rep}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} )} 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} is a domain that is closed under the operational structure given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}} then \texttt{Isomorphism\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Rep}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} returns a mapping \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape hom}} from \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} to a domain $E$ having structure given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}, such that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape hom}} respects the structure \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Rep}} describes the representation of the elements in $E$. If no domain $E$ with the required properties exists then \texttt{fail} is returned. 

 For example, \texttt{IsomorphismPermGroup} (\ref{IsomorphismPermGroup}) takes a group as its argument and returns a group homomorphism
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Group Homomorphisms}) onto an isomorphic permutation group (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Permutation Groups}) provided the original group is finite; for infinite groups, \texttt{IsomorphismPermGroup} (\ref{IsomorphismPermGroup}) returns \texttt{fail}. Similarly, \texttt{IsomorphismPcGroup} (\ref{IsomorphismPcGroup}) returns a group homomorphism from its argument to a polycyclicly presented
group (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Pc Groups}) if the argument is polycyclic, and \texttt{fail} otherwise. 

 See the index of the \textsf{GAP} Reference Manual for an overview of the available \texttt{Isomorphism\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Rep}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} functions. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Domain Categories}}\label{Domain Categories}
\logpage{[ 31, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D72F11B82F4A036}{}
{
  As mentioned in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Operational Structure of Domains}, the operational structure of a domain is fixed when the domain is
constructed. For example, if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} was constructed by \texttt{Monoid} (\ref{Monoid:for various generators}) then \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} is in general not regarded as a group in \textsf{GAP}, even if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} is in fact closed under taking inverses. In this case, \texttt{IsGroup} (\ref{IsGroup}) returns \texttt{false} for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}. The operational structure determines which operations are applicable for a
domain, so for example \texttt{SylowSubgroup} (\ref{SylowSubgroup}) is not defined for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} and therefore will signal an error. 

 \index{IsStruct@\texttt{Is\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}}} \texttt{Is\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} )} 

 The functions \texttt{Is\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} implement the tests whether a domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} has the respective operational structure (upon construction). \texttt{Is\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} is a filter (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Types of Objects}) that involves certain categories (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Categories}) and usually also certain properties (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Properties}). For example, \texttt{IsGroup} (\ref{IsGroup}) is equivalent to \texttt{IsMagmaWithInverses and IsAssociative}, the first being a category and the second being a property. 

 Implications between domain categories describe the hierarchy of operational
structures available in \textsf{GAP}. Here are some typical examples. 

 
\begin{itemize}
\item  \texttt{IsDomain} (\ref{IsDomain}) is implied by each domain category, 
\item  \texttt{IsMagma} (\ref{IsMagma}) is implied by each category that describes the closure under multiplication \texttt{*}, 
\item  \texttt{IsAdditiveMagma} (\ref{IsAdditiveMagma}) is implied by each category that describes the closure under addition \texttt{+}, 
\item  \texttt{IsMagmaWithOne} (\ref{IsMagmaWithOne}) implies \texttt{IsMagma} (\ref{IsMagma}); a \emph{magma\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}one} is a magma such that each element (and thus also the magma itself) can be
asked for its zeroth power, 
\item  \texttt{IsMagmaWithInverses} (\ref{IsMagmaWithInverses}) implies \texttt{IsMagmaWithOne} (\ref{IsMagmaWithOne}); a \emph{magma\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}inverses} is a magma such that each element can be asked for its inverse; important
special cases are \emph{groups}, which in addition are associative, 
\item  a \emph{ring} is a magma that is also an additive group, 
\item  a \emph{ring\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}one} is a ring that is also a magma\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}one, 
\item  a \emph{division ring} is a ring\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}one that is also closed
under taking inverses of nonzero elements, 
\item  a \emph{field} is a commutative division ring. 
\end{itemize}
 

 Each operational structure \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}} has associated with it a domain category \texttt{Is\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}}, and operations \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}ByGenerators} for constructing a domain from generators, \texttt{GeneratorsOf\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} for storing and accessing generators w.r.t.{\nobreakspace}this structure, \texttt{Closure\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} for forming the closure, and \texttt{As\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} for getting a domain with the desired structure from one with weaker
operational structure and for testing whether a given domain can be regarded
as a domain with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}. 

 The functions applicable to domains with the various structures are described
in the corresponding chapters of the Reference Manual. For example, functions
for rings, fields, groups, and vector spaces are described in
Chapters{\nobreakspace}\ref{Rings}, \ref{Fields and Division Rings}, \ref{Groups}, and \ref{Vector Spaces}, respectively. More general functions for arbitrary collections can be found
in Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Collections}. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Parents}}\label{Parents}
\logpage{[ 31, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7CBDD36E7B7BE286}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Parent}}
\logpage{[ 31, 7, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BC856CC7F116BB0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Parent({\mdseries\slshape D})\index{Parent@\texttt{Parent}}
\label{Parent}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetParent({\mdseries\slshape D, P})\index{SetParent@\texttt{SetParent}}
\label{SetParent}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{HasParent({\mdseries\slshape D})\index{HasParent@\texttt{HasParent}}
\label{HasParent}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (filter)}}\\


 It is possible to assign to a domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} one other domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} containing \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} as a subset, in order to exploit this subset relation between \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}. Note that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} need not have the same operational structure as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, for example \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} may be a magma and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} a field. 

 The assignment is done by calling \texttt{SetParent}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} is called the \emph{parent} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} has already a parent, calls to \texttt{SetParent} will be ignored. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} has a parent \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} {\textendash}this can be checked with \texttt{HasParent}{\textendash} then \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} can be used to gain information about \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}. First, the call of \texttt{SetParent} causes \texttt{UseSubsetRelation} (\ref{UseSubsetRelation}) to be called. Second, for a domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} with parent, information relative to the parent can be stored in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}; for example, there is an attribute \texttt{NormalizerInParent} for storing \texttt{Normalizer( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} )} in the case that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} is a group. (More about such parent dependent attributes can be found in \ref{In Parent Attributes}.)  Note that because of this relative information, one cannot change the parent;
that is, one can set the parent only once, subsequent calls to \texttt{SetParent} for the same domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} are ignored.  Further note that contrary to \texttt{UseSubsetRelation} (\ref{UseSubsetRelation}), also knowledge about the parent \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} might be used that is discovered after the \texttt{SetParent} call. 

 A stored parent can be accessed using \texttt{Parent}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} has no parent then \texttt{Parent} returns \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} itself, and \texttt{HasParent} will return \texttt{false} also after a call to \texttt{Parent}. So \texttt{Parent} is \emph{not} an attribute, the underlying attribute to store the parent is \texttt{ParentAttr}.  

 Certain functions that return domains with parent already set, for example \texttt{Subgroup} (\ref{Subgroup}), are described in Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Constructing Subdomains}. Whenever a function has this property, the \textsf{GAP} Reference Manual states this explicitly. Note that these functions \emph{do not guarantee} a certain parent, for example \texttt{DerivedSubgroup} (\ref{DerivedSubgroup}) for a perfect group $G$ may return $G$ itself, and if $G$ had already a parent then this is not replaced by $G$. As a rule of thumb, \textsf{GAP} avoids to set a domain as its own parent, which is consistent with the
behaviour of \texttt{Parent}, at least until a parent is set explicitly with \texttt{SetParent}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Group( (1,2,3), (1,2) );; h:= Group( (1,2) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HasParent( g );  HasParent( h );|
  false
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetParent( h, g );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Parent( g );  Parent( h );|
  Group([ (1,2,3), (1,2) ])
  Group([ (1,2,3), (1,2) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HasParent( g );  HasParent( h );|
  false
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Constructing Subdomains}}\label{Constructing Subdomains}
\logpage{[ 31, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7B58FDEF80338DD6}{}
{
  \index{Subdomains} For many domains \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, there are functions that construct certain subsets \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} as domains with parent (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Parents}) already set to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}. For example, if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is a group that contains the elements in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} then \texttt{Subgroup( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} )} returns a group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} that is generated by the elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} and with \texttt{Parent( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} ) = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}}. 

 \index{Substruct@\texttt{Sub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}}} \texttt{Sub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} )} 

 More general, if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} is a domain whose algebraic structure is given by the function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}} (for example \texttt{Group}, \texttt{Algebra}, \texttt{Field}) then the function \texttt{Sub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}} (for example \texttt{Subgroup}, \texttt{Subalgebra}, \texttt{Subfield}) returns domains with structure \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}} and parent set to the first argument. 

 \index{SubstructNC@\texttt{Sub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}NC}} \texttt{Sub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}NC( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} )} 

 Each function \texttt{Sub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}} checks that the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}} generated by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} is in fact a subset of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}. If one wants to omit this check then one can call \texttt{Sub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}NC} instead; the suffix \texttt{NC} stands for ``no check''. 

 \index{AsSubstruct@\texttt{AsSub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}}} \texttt{AsSub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} )} 

 first constructs \texttt{As\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}( [\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, ]\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} )}, where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} depends on \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}, and then sets the parent (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Parents}) of this new domain to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}. 

 \index{IsSubstruct@\texttt{IsSub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}}} \texttt{IsSub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} )} 

 There is no real need for functions that check whether a domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is a \texttt{Sub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}} of a domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, since this is equivalent to the checks whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is a \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is a subset of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}. Note that in many cases, only the subset relation is what one really wants
to check, and that appropriate methods for the operation \texttt{IsSubset} (\ref{IsSubset}) are available for many special situations, such as the test whether a group is
contained in another group, where only generators need to be checked. 

 If a function \texttt{IsSub\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape struct}}} is available in \textsf{GAP} then it is implemented as first a call to \texttt{Is\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} for the second argument and then a call to \texttt{IsSubset} (\ref{IsSubset}) for the two arguments. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Operations for Domains}}\label{Operations for Domains}
\logpage{[ 31, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86D579707B112970}{}
{
  For the meaning of the attributes \texttt{Characteristic} (\ref{Characteristic}), \texttt{One} (\ref{One}), \texttt{Zero} (\ref{Zero}) in the case of a domain argument, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Attributes and Properties of Elements}. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsGeneralizedDomain}}
\logpage{[ 31, 9, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86B4AC017FAF4D12}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsGeneralizedDomain({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsGeneralizedDomain@\texttt{IsGeneralizedDomain}}
\label{IsGeneralizedDomain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsDomain({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsDomain@\texttt{IsDomain}}
\label{IsDomain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 For some purposes, it is useful to deal with objects that are similar to
domains but that are not collections in the sense of \textsf{GAP} because their elements may lie in different families; such objects are called \emph{generalized domains}. An instance of generalized domains are ``operation domains'', for example any $G$\texttt{\symbol{45}}set for a permutation group $G$ consisting of some union of points, sets of points, sets of sets of points
etc., under a suitable action. 

 \texttt{IsDomain} is a synonym for \texttt{IsGeneralizedDomain and IsCollection}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GeneratorsOfDomain}}
\logpage{[ 31, 9, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E353DD1838AB223}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GeneratorsOfDomain({\mdseries\slshape D})\index{GeneratorsOfDomain@\texttt{GeneratorsOfDomain}}
\label{GeneratorsOfDomain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For a domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \texttt{GeneratorsOfDomain} returns a list containing generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} with respect to the trivial operational structure, that is interpreting \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} as a set. The returned list may contain repetitions. 

 See{\nobreakspace}\ref{Constructing Domains} and for \texttt{GeneratorsOf\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Struct}}} methods with respect to other available operational structures. 

 For many domains that have \emph{natural generators by construction} (for example, the natural generators of a free group of rank two are the two
generators stored as value of the attribute \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup} (\ref{GeneratorsOfGroup}), and the natural generators of a free associative algebra are those
generators stored as value of the attribute \texttt{GeneratorsOfAlgebra} (\ref{GeneratorsOfAlgebra})), each \emph{natural} generator can be accessed using the \texttt{.} operator. For a domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}.i} returns the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th generator if $i$ is a positive integer, and if \texttt{name} is the name of a generator of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} then \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}.name} returns this generator. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := DihedralGroup(IsPermGroup, 4);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsOfGroup(G);|
  [ (1,2), (3,4) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsOfDomain(G);|
  [ (), (3,4), (1,2), (1,2)(3,4) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@F := FreeGroup("x");|
  <free group on the generators [ x ]>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsOfGroup(F);|
  [ x ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsOfDomain(F);|
  Error, resulting list would be too large (length infinity)
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Domain}}
\logpage{[ 31, 9, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X826A21287FD3ACC0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Domain({\mdseries\slshape [Fam, ]generators})\index{Domain@\texttt{Domain}}
\label{Domain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DomainByGenerators({\mdseries\slshape Fam, generators})\index{DomainByGenerators@\texttt{DomainByGenerators}}
\label{DomainByGenerators}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{Domain} returns the domain consisting of the elements in the homogeneous list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape generators}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape generators}} is empty then a family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}} must be entered as the first argument, and the returned (empty) domain lies in
the collections family of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}}. 

 \texttt{DomainByGenerators} is the operation called by \texttt{Domain}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Attributes and Properties of Elements}}\label{Attributes and Properties of Elements}
\logpage{[ 31, 10, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7C2B0C1280237CB0}{}
{
  The following attributes and properties for elements and domains correspond to
the operational structure. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Characteristic}}
\logpage{[ 31, 10, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81278E53800BF64D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Characteristic({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{Characteristic@\texttt{Characteristic}}
\label{Characteristic}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 \texttt{Characteristic} returns the \emph{characteristic} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is a family, all of whose elements lie in \texttt{IsAdditiveElementWithZero} (\ref{IsAdditiveElementWithZero}) then its characteristic is the least positive integer $n$, if any, such that \texttt{IsZero(n*x)} is \texttt{true} for all \texttt{x} in the family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, otherwise it is $0$. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is a collections family of a family $g$ which has a characteristic, then the characteristic of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is the same as the characteristic of $g$. 

 For other families \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} the characteristic is not defined and \texttt{fail} will be returned. 

 For any object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} which is in the filter \texttt{IsAdditiveElementWithZero} (\ref{IsAdditiveElementWithZero}) or in the filter \texttt{IsAdditiveMagmaWithZero} (\ref{IsAdditiveMagmaWithZero}) the characteristic of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is the same as the characteristic of its family if that is defined and
undefined otherwise. 

 For all other objects \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} the characteristic is undefined and may return \texttt{fail} or a ``no method found'' error. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{OneImmutable}}
\logpage{[ 31, 10, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8046262384895B2A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{OneImmutable({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{OneImmutable@\texttt{OneImmutable}}
\label{OneImmutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{One({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{One@\texttt{One}}
\label{One}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Identity({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{Identity@\texttt{Identity}}
\label{Identity}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{OneMutable({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{OneMutable@\texttt{OneMutable}}
\label{OneMutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{OneOp({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{OneOp@\texttt{OneOp}}
\label{OneOp}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{OneSameMutability({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{OneSameMutability@\texttt{OneSameMutability}}
\label{OneSameMutability}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{OneImmutable}, \texttt{OneMutable}, and \texttt{OneSameMutability} return the multiplicative neutral element of the multiplicative element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. 

 They differ only w.r.t. the mutability of the result. \texttt{OneImmutable} is an attribute and hence returns an immutable result. \texttt{OneMutable} is guaranteed to return a new \emph{mutable} object whenever a mutable version of the required element exists in \textsf{GAP} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsCopyable} (\ref{IsCopyable})). \texttt{OneSameMutability} returns a result that is mutable if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is mutable and if a mutable version of the required element exists in \textsf{GAP}; for lists, it returns a result of the same immutability level as the
argument. For instance, if the argument is a mutable matrix with immutable
rows, it returns a similar object. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is a multiplicative element then \texttt{OneSameMutability( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} )} is equivalent to \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}0}. 

 \texttt{One} and \texttt{Identity} are synonyms of \texttt{OneImmutable}. \texttt{OneOp} is a synonym of \texttt{OneMutable}. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is a domain or a family then \texttt{One} is defined as the identity element of all elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, provided that all these elements have the same identity. For example, the
family of all cyclotomics has the identity element \texttt{1}, but a collections family (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{CollectionsFamily} (\ref{CollectionsFamily})) may contain matrices of all dimensions and then it cannot have a unique
identity element. Note that \texttt{One} is applicable to a domain only if it is a
magma\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}one (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsMagmaWithOne} (\ref{IsMagmaWithOne})); use \texttt{MultiplicativeNeutralElement} (\ref{MultiplicativeNeutralElement}) otherwise. 

 The identity of an object need not be distinct from its zero, so for example a
ring consisting of a single element can be regarded as a
ring\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}one (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Rings}). This is particularly useful in the case of finitely presented algebras,
where any factor of a free
algebra\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}one is again an
algebra\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}one, no matter whether or
not it is a zero algebra. 

 The default method of \texttt{One} for multiplicative elements calls \texttt{OneMutable} (note that methods for \texttt{OneMutable} must \emph{not} delegate to \texttt{One}); so other methods to compute identity elements need to be installed only for \texttt{OneOp} and (in the case of copyable objects) \texttt{OneSameMutability}. 

 For domains, \texttt{One} may call \texttt{Representative} (\ref{Representative}), but \texttt{Representative} (\ref{Representative}) is allowed to fetch the identity of a domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} only if \texttt{HasOne( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} )} is \texttt{true}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ZeroImmutable}}
\logpage{[ 31, 10, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8040AC7A79FFC442}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZeroImmutable({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{ZeroImmutable@\texttt{ZeroImmutable}}
\label{ZeroImmutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Zero({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{Zero@\texttt{Zero}}
\label{Zero}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZeroMutable({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{ZeroMutable@\texttt{ZeroMutable}}
\label{ZeroMutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZeroOp({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{ZeroOp@\texttt{ZeroOp}}
\label{ZeroOp}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZeroSameMutability({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{ZeroSameMutability@\texttt{ZeroSameMutability}}
\label{ZeroSameMutability}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{ZeroImmutable}, \texttt{ZeroMutable}, and \texttt{ZeroSameMutability} all return the additive neutral element of the additive element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. 

 They differ only w.r.t. the mutability of the result. \texttt{ZeroImmutable} is an attribute and hence returns an immutable result. \texttt{ZeroMutable} is guaranteed to return a new \emph{mutable} object whenever a mutable version of the required element exists in \textsf{GAP} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsCopyable} (\ref{IsCopyable})). \texttt{ZeroSameMutability} returns a result that is mutable if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is mutable and if a mutable version of the required element exists in \textsf{GAP}; for lists, it returns a result of the same immutability level as the
argument. For instance, if the argument is a mutable matrix with immutable
rows, it returns a similar object. 

 \texttt{ZeroSameMutability( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} )} is equivalent to \texttt{0 * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}}. 

 \texttt{Zero} is a synonym of \texttt{ZeroImmutable}. \texttt{ZeroOp} is a synonym of \texttt{ZeroMutable}. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is a domain or a family then \texttt{Zero} is defined as the zero element of all elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, provided that all these elements have the same zero. For example, the family
of all cyclotomics has the zero element \texttt{0}, but a collections family (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{CollectionsFamily} (\ref{CollectionsFamily})) may contain matrices of all dimensions and then it cannot have a unique zero
element. Note that \texttt{Zero} is applicable to a domain only if it is an additive
magma\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}zero (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsAdditiveMagmaWithZero} (\ref{IsAdditiveMagmaWithZero})); use \texttt{AdditiveNeutralElement} (\ref{AdditiveNeutralElement}) otherwise. 

 The default method of \texttt{Zero} for additive elements calls \texttt{ZeroMutable} (note that methods for \texttt{ZeroMutable} must \emph{not} delegate to \texttt{Zero}); so other methods to compute zero elements need to be installed only for \texttt{ZeroMutable} and (in the case of copyable objects) \texttt{ZeroSameMutability}. 

 For domains, \texttt{Zero} may call \texttt{Representative} (\ref{Representative}), but \texttt{Representative} (\ref{Representative}) is allowed to fetch the zero of a domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} only if \texttt{HasZero( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} )} is \texttt{true}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MultiplicativeZeroOp}}
\logpage{[ 31, 10, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86DEB543824C40EB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MultiplicativeZeroOp({\mdseries\slshape elt})\index{MultiplicativeZeroOp@\texttt{MultiplicativeZeroOp}}
\label{MultiplicativeZeroOp}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\textbf{\indent Returns:\ }
A multiplicative zero element.



 for an element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elt}} in the category \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElementWithZero} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElementWithZero}), \texttt{MultiplicativeZeroOp} returns the element $z$ in the family $F$ of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elt}} with the property that $z * m = z = m * z$ holds for all $m \in F$, if such an element can be determined. 

 Families of elements in the category \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElementWithZero} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElementWithZero}) often arise from adjoining a new zero to an existing magma. See{\nobreakspace}\texttt{InjectionZeroMagma} (\ref{InjectionZeroMagma}) or \texttt{MagmaWithZeroAdjoined} (\ref{MagmaWithZeroAdjoined}) for details. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G:=AlternatingGroup(5);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:=Representative(MagmaWithZeroAdjoined(G));|
  <group with 0 adjoined elt: ()>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MultiplicativeZeroOp(x);|
  <group with 0 adjoined elt: 0>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsOne}}
\logpage{[ 31, 10, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X814D78347858EC13}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsOne({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{IsOne@\texttt{IsOne}}
\label{IsOne}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 is \texttt{true} if \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} = One( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} )}, and \texttt{false} otherwise. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsZero}}
\logpage{[ 31, 10, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82BDA47282F9BBA7}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsZero({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{IsZero@\texttt{IsZero}}
\label{IsZero}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 is \texttt{true} if \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} = Zero( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} )}, and \texttt{false} otherwise. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsIdempotent}}
\logpage{[ 31, 10, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CB5896082D29173}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsIdempotent({\mdseries\slshape elt})\index{IsIdempotent@\texttt{IsIdempotent}}
\label{IsIdempotent}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 returns \texttt{true} iff \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elt}} is its own square. (Even if \texttt{IsZero} (\ref{IsZero}) returns \texttt{true} for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elt}}.) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InverseImmutable}}
\logpage{[ 31, 10, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78EE524E83624057}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InverseImmutable({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{InverseImmutable@\texttt{InverseImmutable}}
\label{InverseImmutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Inverse({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{Inverse@\texttt{Inverse}}
\label{Inverse}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InverseMutable({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{InverseMutable@\texttt{InverseMutable}}
\label{InverseMutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InverseOp({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{InverseOp@\texttt{InverseOp}}
\label{InverseOp}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InverseSameMutability({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{InverseSameMutability@\texttt{InverseSameMutability}}
\label{InverseSameMutability}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{InverseImmutable}, \texttt{InverseMutable}, and \texttt{InverseSameMutability} all return the multiplicative inverse of an element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}, that is, an element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape inv}} such that \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape inv}} = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape inv}} * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} = One( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} )} holds; if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} is not invertible then \texttt{fail} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Fail}) is returned. 

 Note that the above definition implies that a (general) mapping is invertible
in the sense of \texttt{Inverse} only if its source equals its range (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Technical Matters Concerning General Mappings}). For a bijective mapping $f$ whose source and range differ, \texttt{InverseGeneralMapping} (\ref{InverseGeneralMapping}) can be used to construct a mapping $g$ with the property that $f$ \texttt{*} $g$ is the identity mapping on the source of $f$ and $g$ \texttt{*} $f$ is the identity mapping on the range of $f$. 

 The operations differ only w.r.t. the mutability of the result. \texttt{InverseImmutable} is an attribute and hence returns an immutable result. \texttt{InverseMutable} is guaranteed to return a new \emph{mutable} object whenever a mutable version of the required element exists in \textsf{GAP}. \texttt{InverseSameMutability} returns a result that is mutable if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} is mutable and if a mutable version of the required element exists in \textsf{GAP}; for lists, it returns a result of the same immutability level as the
argument. For instance, if the argument is a mutable matrix with immutable
rows, it returns a similar object. 

 \texttt{InverseSameMutability( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} )} is equivalent to \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}1}. 

 \texttt{Inverse} is a synonym of \texttt{InverseImmutable}. \texttt{InverseOp} is a synonym of \texttt{InverseMutable}. 

 The default method of \texttt{InverseImmutable} calls \texttt{InverseMutable} (note that methods for \texttt{InverseMutable} must \emph{not} delegate to \texttt{InverseImmutable}); other methods to compute inverses need to be installed only for \texttt{InverseMutable} and (in the case of copyable objects) \texttt{InverseSameMutability}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AdditiveInverseImmutable}}
\logpage{[ 31, 10, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84BB723C81D55D63}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AdditiveInverseImmutable({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{AdditiveInverseImmutable@\texttt{AdditiveInverseImmutable}}
\label{AdditiveInverseImmutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AdditiveInverse({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{AdditiveInverse@\texttt{AdditiveInverse}}
\label{AdditiveInverse}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AdditiveInverseMutable({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{AdditiveInverseMutable@\texttt{AdditiveInverseMutable}}
\label{AdditiveInverseMutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AdditiveInverseOp({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{AdditiveInverseOp@\texttt{AdditiveInverseOp}}
\label{AdditiveInverseOp}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AdditiveInverseSameMutability({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{AdditiveInverseSameMutability@\texttt{AdditiveInverseSameMutability}}
\label{AdditiveInverseSameMutability}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{AdditiveInverseImmutable}, \texttt{AdditiveInverseMutable}, and \texttt{AdditiveInverseSameMutability} all return the additive inverse of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}. 

 They differ only w.r.t. the mutability of the result. \texttt{AdditiveInverseImmutable} is an attribute and hence returns an immutable result. \texttt{AdditiveInverseMutable} is guaranteed to return a new \emph{mutable} object whenever a mutable version of the required element exists in \textsf{GAP} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsCopyable} (\ref{IsCopyable})). \texttt{AdditiveInverseSameMutability} returns a result that is mutable if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} is mutable and if a mutable version of the required element exists in \textsf{GAP}; for lists, it returns a result of the same immutability level as the
argument. For instance, if the argument is a mutable matrix with immutable
rows, it returns a similar object. 

 \texttt{AdditiveInverseSameMutability( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} )} is equivalent to \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}}. 

 \texttt{AdditiveInverse} is a synonym of \texttt{AdditiveInverseImmutable}. \texttt{AdditiveInverseOp} is a synonym of \texttt{AdditiveInverseMutable}. 

 The default method of \texttt{AdditiveInverse} calls \texttt{AdditiveInverseMutable} (note that methods for \texttt{AdditiveInverseMutable} must \emph{not} delegate to \texttt{AdditiveInverse}); so other methods to compute additive inverses need to be installed only for \texttt{AdditiveInverseMutable} and (in the case of copyable objects) \texttt{AdditiveInverseSameMutability}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Order}}
\logpage{[ 31, 10, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84F59A2687C62763}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Order({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{Order@\texttt{Order}}
\label{Order}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 is the multiplicative order of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}. This is the smallest positive integer $n$ such that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}} $n$ \texttt{= One( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} )} if such an integer exists. If the order is infinite, \texttt{Order} may return the value \texttt{infinity} (\ref{infinity}), but it also might run into an infinite loop trying to test the order. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Comparison Operations for Elements}}\label{Comparison Operations for Elements}
\logpage{[ 31, 11, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7B3BC7BA7BB2646D}{}
{
  Binary comparison operations have been introduced already in \ref{Comparisons}. The underlying operations for which methods can be installed are the
following. 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{\texttt{\symbol{92}}= and \texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}}}\logpage{[ 31, 11, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7EF67D047F03CA6F}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=({\mdseries\slshape left\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr, right\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=}}
\label{bSlash=}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}({\mdseries\slshape left\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr, right\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}}}
\label{bSlash<}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \index{equality!operation} \index{comparison!operation} Note that the comparisons via \texttt{{\textless}{\textgreater}}, \texttt{{\textless}=}, \texttt{{\textgreater}}, and \texttt{{\textgreater}=} are delegated to the operations \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=} and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}}. 

 In general, objects in \emph{different} families cannot be compared with \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}}. For the reason and for exceptions from this rule, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Comparisons}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CanEasilyCompareElements}}
\logpage{[ 31, 11, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EFE013B8634D214}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CanEasilyCompareElements({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{CanEasilyCompareElements@\texttt{CanEasilyCompareElements}}
\label{CanEasilyCompareElements}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CanEasilyCompareElementsFamily({\mdseries\slshape fam})\index{CanEasilyCompareElementsFamily@\texttt{CanEasilyCompareElementsFamily}}
\label{CanEasilyCompareElementsFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CanEasilySortElements({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{CanEasilySortElements@\texttt{CanEasilySortElements}}
\label{CanEasilySortElements}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CanEasilySortElementsFamily({\mdseries\slshape fam})\index{CanEasilySortElementsFamily@\texttt{CanEasilySortElementsFamily}}
\label{CanEasilySortElementsFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For some objects a ``normal form'' is hard to compute and thus equality of elements of a domain might be
expensive to test. Therefore \textsf{GAP} provides a (slightly technical) property with which an algorithm can test
whether an efficient equality test is available for elements of a certain
kind. 

 \texttt{CanEasilyCompareElements} indicates whether the elements in the family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} can be easily compared with \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=} (\ref{bSlash=}). 

 The default method for this property is to ask the family of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, the default method for the family is to return \texttt{false}. 

 The ability to compare elements may depend on the successful computation of
certain information. (For example for finitely presented groups it might
depend on the knowledge of a faithful permutation representation.) This
information might change over time and thus it might not be a good idea to
store a value \texttt{false} too early in a family. Instead the function \texttt{CanEasilyCompareElementsFamily} should be called for the family of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} which returns \texttt{false} if the value of \texttt{CanEasilyCompareElements} is not known for the family without computing it. (This is in fact what the
above mentioned family dispatch does.) 

 If a family knows ab initio that it can compare elements this property should
be set as implied filter \emph{and} filter for the family (the 3rd and 4th argument of \texttt{NewFamily} (\ref{NewFamily}) respectively). This guarantees that code which directly asks the family gets a
right answer. 

 The property \texttt{CanEasilySortElements} and the function \texttt{CanEasilySortElementsFamily} behave exactly in the same way, except that they indicate that objects can be
compared via \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}} (\ref{bSlash<}). This property implies \texttt{CanEasilyCompareElements}, as the ordering must be total. }

 }

\logpage{[ 31, 12, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7A2914307963E370}{}
{
  \emph{Binary} arithmetic operations have been introduced already in \ref{Arithmetic Operators}. The underlying operations for which methods can be installed are the
following. 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{\texttt{\symbol{92}}+, \texttt{\symbol{92}}*, \texttt{\symbol{92}}/,
\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}, \texttt{\symbol{92}}mod}}\logpage{[ 31, 12, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8481C9B97B214C23}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}+({\mdseries\slshape left\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr, right\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}+@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}+}}
\label{bSlash+}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*({\mdseries\slshape left\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr, right\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*}}
\label{bSlash*}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/({\mdseries\slshape left\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr, right\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/}}
\label{bSlash/}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}({\mdseries\slshape left\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr, right\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}}}
\label{bSlash^}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod({\mdseries\slshape left\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr, right\texttt{\symbol{45}}expr})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod}}
\label{bSlashmod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \index{addition!operation} \index{multiplication!operation} \index{division!operation} \index{exponentiation!operation} \index{remainder!operation} For details about special methods for \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}} and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod}, consult the appropriate index entries for them.  }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LeftQuotient}}
\logpage{[ 31, 12, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A37082878DB3930}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LeftQuotient({\mdseries\slshape elm1, elm2})\index{LeftQuotient@\texttt{LeftQuotient}}
\label{LeftQuotient}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the product \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm1}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}(\texttt{\symbol{45}}1) * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm2}}}. For some types of objects (for example permutations) this product can be
evaluated more efficiently than by first inverting \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm1}} and then forming the product with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm2}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Comm}}
\logpage{[ 31, 12, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80761843831B468E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Comm({\mdseries\slshape elm1, elm2})\index{Comm@\texttt{Comm}}
\label{Comm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the \emph{commutator} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm1}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm2}}. The commutator is defined as the product $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm1}}^{{-1}} * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm2}}^{{-1}} * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm1}} * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm2}}$. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:= (1,3)(4,6);; b:= (1,6,5,4,3,2);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Comm( a, b );|
  (1,5,3)(2,6,4)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeftQuotient( a, b );|
  (1,2)(3,6)(4,5)
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LieBracket}}
\logpage{[ 31, 12, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86A62A937A42B82E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LieBracket({\mdseries\slshape elm1, elm2})\index{LieBracket@\texttt{LieBracket}}
\label{LieBracket}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the element \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm1}} * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm2}} \texttt{\symbol{45}} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm2}} * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm1}}}. 

 The addition \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}+} (\ref{bSlash+}) is assumed to be associative but \emph{not} assumed to be commutative (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsAdditivelyCommutative} (\ref{IsAdditivelyCommutative})). The multiplication \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*} (\ref{bSlash*}) is \emph{not} assumed to be commutative or associative (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsCommutative} (\ref{IsCommutative}), \texttt{IsAssociative} (\ref{IsAssociative})). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Sqrt}}
\logpage{[ 31, 12, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E8F1FB87C229BB0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Sqrt({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{Sqrt@\texttt{Sqrt}}
\label{Sqrt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{Sqrt} returns a square root of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, that is, an object $x$ with the property that $x \cdot x = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}$ holds. If such an $x$ is not unique then the choice of $x$ depends on the type of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. For example, \texttt{ER} (\ref{ER}) is the \texttt{Sqrt} method for rationals (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsRat} (\ref{IsRat})). }

  }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Relations Between Domains}}\label{Relations Between Domains}
\logpage{[ 31, 13, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X80A2D8A7874B268B}{}
{
  Domains are often constructed relative to other domains. The probably most
usual case is to form a \emph{subset} of a domain, for example the intersection (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Intersection} (\ref{Intersection:for a list})) of two domains, or a Sylow subgroup of a given group (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{SylowSubgroup} (\ref{SylowSubgroup})). 

 In such a situation, the new domain can gain knowledge by exploiting that
several attributes are maintained under taking subsets. For example, the
intersection of an arbitrary domain with a finite domain is clearly finite, a
Sylow subgroup of an abelian group is abelian, too, and so on. 

 Since usually the new domain has access to the knowledge of the old domain(s)
only when it is created (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Constructing Subdomains} for the exception), this is the right moment to take advantage of the subset
relation, using \texttt{UseSubsetRelation} (\ref{UseSubsetRelation}). 

 Analogous relations occur when a \emph{factor structure} is created from a domain and a subset (see \texttt{UseFactorRelation} (\ref{UseFactorRelation})), and when a domain \emph{isomorphic} to a given one is created (see \texttt{UseIsomorphismRelation} (\ref{UseIsomorphismRelation})). 

 The functions \texttt{InstallSubsetMaintenance} (\ref{InstallSubsetMaintenance}), \texttt{InstallIsomorphismMaintenance} (\ref{InstallIsomorphismMaintenance}), and \texttt{InstallFactorMaintenance} (\ref{InstallFactorMaintenance}) are used to tell \textsf{GAP} under what conditions an attribute is maintained under taking subsets, or
forming factor structures or isomorphic domains. This is used only when a new
attribute or property is created, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{NewAttribute} (\ref{NewAttribute}) and \texttt{NewProperty} (\ref{NewProperty}). For the attributes already available, such as \texttt{IsFinite} (\ref{IsFinite}) and \texttt{IsCommutative} (\ref{IsCommutative}), the maintenances are already notified. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UseSubsetRelation}}
\logpage{[ 31, 13, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C03098C838ADE40}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UseSubsetRelation({\mdseries\slshape super, sub})\index{UseSubsetRelation@\texttt{UseSubsetRelation}}
\label{UseSubsetRelation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Methods for this operation transfer possibly useful information from the
domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}} to its subset \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sub}}, and vice versa. 

 \texttt{UseSubsetRelation} is designed to be called automatically whenever substructures of domains are
constructed. So the methods must be \emph{cheap}, and the requirements should be as sharp as possible! 

 To achieve that \emph{all} applicable methods are executed, all methods for this operation except the
default method must end with \texttt{TryNextMethod()}. This default method deals with the information that is available by the
calls of \texttt{InstallSubsetMaintenance} (\ref{InstallSubsetMaintenance}) in the \textsf{GAP} library. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Group( (1,2), (3,4), (5,6) );; h:= Group( (1,2), (3,4) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsAbelian( g );  HasIsAbelian( h );|
  true
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UseSubsetRelation( g, h );;  HasIsAbelian( h );  IsAbelian( h );|
  true
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UseFactorRelation}}
\logpage{[ 31, 13, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78039B628262BFA8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UseFactorRelation({\mdseries\slshape numer, denom, factor})\index{UseFactorRelation@\texttt{UseFactorRelation}}
\label{UseFactorRelation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Methods for this operation transfer possibly useful information from the
domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape numer}} or its subset \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape denom}} to the domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape factor}} that is isomorphic to the factor of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape numer}} by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape denom}}, and vice versa. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape denom}} may be \texttt{fail}, for example if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape factor}} is just known to be a factor of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape numer}} but \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape denom}} is not available as a \textsf{GAP} object; in this case those factor relations are used that are installed
without special requirements for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape denom}}. 

 \texttt{UseFactorRelation} is designed to be called automatically whenever factor structures of domains
are constructed. So the methods must be \emph{cheap}, and the requirements should be as sharp as possible! 

 To achieve that \emph{all} applicable methods are executed, all methods for this operation except the
default method must end with a call to \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}). This default method deals with the information that is available by the
calls of \texttt{InstallFactorMaintenance} (\ref{InstallFactorMaintenance}) in the \textsf{GAP} library. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Group( (1,2,3,4), (1,2) );; h:= Group( (1,2,3), (1,2) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsSolvableGroup( g );  HasIsSolvableGroup( h );|
  true
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UseFactorRelation(g, Subgroup( g, [ (1,2)(3,4), (1,3)(2,4) ] ), h);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HasIsSolvableGroup( h );  IsSolvableGroup( h );|
  true
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UseIsomorphismRelation}}
\logpage{[ 31, 13, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X839BE6467E8474D9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UseIsomorphismRelation({\mdseries\slshape old, new})\index{UseIsomorphismRelation@\texttt{UseIsomorphismRelation}}
\label{UseIsomorphismRelation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Methods for this operation transfer possibly useful information from the
domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape old}} to the isomorphic domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape new}}. 

 \texttt{UseIsomorphismRelation} is designed to be called automatically whenever isomorphic structures of
domains are constructed. So the methods must be \emph{cheap}, and the requirements should be as sharp as possible! 

 To achieve that \emph{all} applicable methods are executed, all methods for this operation except the
default method must end with a call to \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}). This default method deals with the information that is available by the
calls of \texttt{InstallIsomorphismMaintenance} (\ref{InstallIsomorphismMaintenance}) in the \textsf{GAP} library. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Group( (1,2) );;  h:= Group( [ [ -1 ] ] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( g );  HasSize( h );|
  2
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UseIsomorphismRelation( g, h );;  HasSize( h );  Size( h );|
  true
  2
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InstallSubsetMaintenance}}
\logpage{[ 31, 13, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X863C35007C7AA914}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallSubsetMaintenance({\mdseries\slshape opr, super{\textunderscore}req, sub{\textunderscore}req})\index{InstallSubsetMaintenance@\texttt{InstallSubsetMaintenance}}
\label{InstallSubsetMaintenance}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} must be a property or an attribute. The call of \texttt{InstallSubsetMaintenance} has the effect that for a domain $D$ in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super{\textunderscore}req}}, and a domain $S$ in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sub{\textunderscore}req}}, the call \texttt{UseSubsetRelation}$( D, S )$ (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{UseSubsetRelation} (\ref{UseSubsetRelation})) sets a known value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} for $D$ as value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} also for $S$. A typical example for which \texttt{InstallSubsetMaintenance} is applied is given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} \texttt{= IsFinite}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super{\textunderscore}req}} \texttt{= IsCollection and IsFinite}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sub{\textunderscore}req}} \texttt{= IsCollection}. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} is a property and the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super{\textunderscore}req}} lies in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} then we can use also the following inverse implication. If $D$ is in the filter whose intersection with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} is \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super{\textunderscore}req}} and if $S$ is in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sub{\textunderscore}req}}, $S$ is a subset of $D$, and the value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} for $S$ is \texttt{false} then the value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} for $D$ is also \texttt{false}.  }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InstallFactorMaintenance}}
\logpage{[ 31, 13, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BB7EE5078EF6F47}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallFactorMaintenance({\mdseries\slshape opr, numer{\textunderscore}req, denom{\textunderscore}req, factor{\textunderscore}req})\index{InstallFactorMaintenance@\texttt{InstallFactorMaintenance}}
\label{InstallFactorMaintenance}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} must be a property or an attribute. The call of \texttt{InstallFactorMaintenance} has the effect that for collections $N$, $D$, $F$ in the filters \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape numer{\textunderscore}req}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape denom{\textunderscore}req}}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape factor{\textunderscore}req}}, respectively, the call \texttt{UseFactorRelation}$( N, D, F )$ (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{UseFactorRelation} (\ref{UseFactorRelation})) sets a known value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} for $N$ as value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} also for $F$. A typical example for which \texttt{InstallFactorMaintenance} is applied is given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} \texttt{= IsFinite}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape numer{\textunderscore}req}} \texttt{= IsCollection and IsFinite}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape denom{\textunderscore}req}} \texttt{= IsCollection}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape factor{\textunderscore}req}} \texttt{= IsCollection}. 

 For the other direction, if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape numer{\textunderscore}req}} involves the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} then a known \texttt{false} value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} for $F$ implies a \texttt{false} value for $D$ provided that $D$ lies in the filter obtained from \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape numer{\textunderscore}req}} by removing \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}. 

 Note that an implication of a factor relation holds in particular for the case
of isomorphisms. So one need \emph{not} install an isomorphism maintained method when a factor maintained method is
already installed. For example, \texttt{UseIsomorphismRelation} (\ref{UseIsomorphismRelation}) will transfer a known \texttt{IsFinite} (\ref{IsFinite}) value because of the installed factor maintained method. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InstallIsomorphismMaintenance}}
\logpage{[ 31, 13, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79F97F0F78D89186}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallIsomorphismMaintenance({\mdseries\slshape opr, old{\textunderscore}req, new{\textunderscore}req})\index{InstallIsomorphismMaintenance@\texttt{InstallIsomorphismMaintenance}}
\label{InstallIsomorphismMaintenance}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} must be a property or an attribute. The call of \texttt{InstallIsomorphismMaintenance} has the effect that for a domain $D$ in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape old{\textunderscore}req}}, and a domain $E$ in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape new{\textunderscore}req}}, the call \texttt{UseIsomorphismRelation}$( D, E )$ (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{UseIsomorphismRelation} (\ref{UseIsomorphismRelation})) sets a known value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} for $D$ as value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} also for $E$. A typical example for which \texttt{InstallIsomorphismMaintenance} is applied is given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} \texttt{= Size}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape old{\textunderscore}req}} \texttt{= IsCollection}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape new{\textunderscore}req}} \texttt{= IsCollection}.    }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Useful Categories of Elements}}\label{Useful Categories of Elements}
\logpage{[ 31, 14, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7B97A0307EA161E5}{}
{
  This section and the following one are rather technical, and may be
interesting only for those \textsf{GAP} users who want to implement new kinds of elements. 

 It deals with certain categories of elements that are useful mainly for the
design of elements, from the viewpoint that one wants to form certain domains
of these elements. For example, a domain closed under multiplication \texttt{*} (a so\texttt{\symbol{45}}called magma, see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Magmas}) makes sense only if its elements can be multiplied, and the latter is
indicated by the category \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElement} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElement}) for each element. Again note that the underlying idea is that a domain is
regarded as \emph{generated} by given elements, and that these elements carry information about the desired
domain. For general information on categories and their hierarchies,
see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Categories}. 

 More special categories of this kind are described in the contexts where they
arise, they are \texttt{IsRowVector} (\ref{IsRowVector}), \texttt{IsMatrix} (\ref{IsMatrix}), \texttt{IsOrdinaryMatrix} (\ref{IsOrdinaryMatrix}), and \texttt{IsLieMatrix} (\ref{IsLieMatrix}).

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsMultiplicativeElementWithZero}}
\logpage{[ 31, 14, 12 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8703BFC2841BBD63}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsMultiplicativeElementWithZero({\mdseries\slshape elt})\index{IsMultiplicativeElementWithZero@\texttt{IsMultiplicativeElementWithZero}}
\label{IsMultiplicativeElementWithZero}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\textbf{\indent Returns:\ }
\texttt{true} or \texttt{false}.



 This is the category of elements in a family which can be the operands of \texttt{*} (multiplication) and the operation \texttt{MultiplicativeZeroOp} (\ref{MultiplicativeZeroOp}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@S:=Semigroup(Transformation( [ 1, 1, 1 ] ));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@M:=MagmaWithZeroAdjoined(S);|
  <<commutative transformation semigroup of degree 3 with 1 generator>
    with 0 adjoined>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:=Representative(M);|
  <semigroup with 0 adjoined elt: Transformation( [ 1, 1, 1 ] )>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsMultiplicativeElementWithZero(x);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MultiplicativeZeroOp(x);|
  <semigroup with 0 adjoined elt: 0>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 A \emph{multiplicative element\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}inverse} is an object that can be multiplied via \texttt{*} with elements in its family (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Families}), and that is an admissible argument for the operations \texttt{One} (\ref{One}) and \texttt{Inverse} (\ref{Inverse}). (Note the word ``admissible'': an object in this category does not necessarily have an inverse, \texttt{Inverse} (\ref{Inverse}) may return \texttt{fail}.) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsVector}}
\logpage{[ 31, 14, 14 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X802F34F280B29DF4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsVector({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsVector@\texttt{IsVector}}
\label{IsVector}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 A \emph{vector} is an
additive\texttt{\symbol{45}}element\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}inverse
that can be multiplied from the left and right with other objects (not
necessarily of the same type). Examples are cyclotomics, finite field
elements, and of course row vectors (see below). 

 Note that not all lists of ring elements are regarded as vectors, for example
lists of matrices are not vectors. This is because although the category \texttt{IsAdditiveElementWithInverse} (\ref{IsAdditiveElementWithInverse}) is implied by the meet of its collections category and \texttt{IsList} (\ref{IsList}), the family of a list entry may not imply \texttt{IsAdditiveElementWithInverse} (\ref{IsAdditiveElementWithInverse}) for all its elements. }
