\label{OrderOfRewritingSystem}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{OrderingOfRewritingSystem({\mdseries\slshape rws})\index{OrderingOfRewritingSystem@\texttt{OrderingOfRewritingSystem}}
\label{OrderingOfRewritingSystem}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 return the ordering of the rewriting system \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rws}}.  }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ReducedForm}}
\logpage{[ 38, 1, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8340EB2280DE6CCC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ReducedForm({\mdseries\slshape rws, u})\index{ReducedForm@\texttt{ReducedForm}}
\label{ReducedForm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Given an element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape u}} in the free (or term) algebra $T$ over which \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rws}} is defined, rewrite \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape u}} by successive applications of the rules of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rws}} until no further rewriting is possible, and return the resulting element of $T$. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsConfluent}}\logpage{[ 38, 1, 5 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8006790B86328CE8}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsConfluent({\mdseries\slshape rws})\index{IsConfluent@\texttt{IsConfluent}!for a rewriting system}
\label{IsConfluent:for a rewriting system}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsConfluent({\mdseries\slshape A})\index{IsConfluent@\texttt{IsConfluent}!for an algebra with canonical rewriting system}
\label{IsConfluent:for an algebra with canonical rewriting system}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 For a rewriting system \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rws}}, \texttt{IsConfluent} returns \texttt{true} if and only if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rws}} is confluent. A rewriting system is \emph{confluent} if, for every two words $u$ and $v$ in the free algebra $T$ which represent the same element of the algebra $A$ defined by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rws}}, \texttt{ReducedForm( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rws}}, }$u$ \texttt{) = ReducedForm( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rws}}, }$v$\texttt{)} as words in the free algebra $T$. This element is the \emph{unique normal form} of the element represented by $u$. 

 For an algebra \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape A}} with a canonical rewriting system associated with it, \texttt{IsConfluent} checks whether that rewriting system is confluent. 

 Also see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsConfluent} (\ref{IsConfluent:for pc groups}). }

}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ReducedPower({\mdseries\slshape rws, obj, pow})\index{ReducedPower@\texttt{ReducedPower}}
\label{ReducedPower}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ReducedQuotient({\mdseries\slshape rws, left, right})\index{ReducedQuotient@\texttt{ReducedQuotient}}
\label{ReducedQuotient}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ReducedScalarProduct({\mdseries\slshape rws, left, right})\index{ReducedScalarProduct@\texttt{ReducedScalarProduct}}
\label{ReducedScalarProduct}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ReducedZero({\mdseries\slshape rws})\index{ReducedZero@\texttt{ReducedZero}}
\label{ReducedZero}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 The result of \texttt{ReducedProduct} is $w$ where $[w]$ equals [\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape u}}][\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape v}}] in $A$ and $w$ is in reduced form. 

 The remaining operations are defined similarly when they are defined (as
determined by the signature of the term algebra). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Properties of rewriting systems}}\label{Properties of rewriting systems}
\logpage{[ 38, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8318649681DF783B}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsBuiltFromAdditiveMagmaWithInverses}}
\logpage{[ 38, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B647DB77D138A49}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsBuiltFromAdditiveMagmaWithInverses({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsBuiltFromAdditiveMagmaWithInverses@\texttt{IsBuilt}\-\texttt{From}\-\texttt{Additive}\-\texttt{Magma}\-\texttt{With}\-\texttt{Inverses}}
\label{IsBuiltFromAdditiveMagmaWithInverses}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsBuiltFromMagma({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsBuiltFromMagma@\texttt{IsBuiltFromMagma}}

}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\

}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsBuiltFromMagmaWithInverses({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsBuiltFromMagmaWithInverses@\texttt{IsBuiltFromMagmaWithInverses}}

 These properties may be used to identify the type of term algebra over which

\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Rewriting in Groups and Monoids}}\label{Rewriting in Groups and Monoids}
\logpage{[ 38, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7F8B7848851784DF}{}
{
  One application of rewriting is to reduce words in finitely presented groups
and monoids. The rewriting system still has to be built for a finitely
presented monoid (using \texttt{IsomorphismFpMonoid} for conversion). Rewriting then can take place for words in the underlying
free monoid. (These can be obtained from monoid elements with the command \texttt{UnderlyingElement}.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:=FreeGroup(3);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rels:=[f.1*f.2^2/f.3,f.2*f.3^2/f.1,f.3*f.1^2/f.2];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=f/rels;|
  <fp group on the generators [ f1, f2, f3 ]>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mhom:=IsomorphismFpMonoid(g);|
  MappingByFunction( <fp group on the generators
  [ f1, f2, f3 ]>, <fp monoid on the generators
  [ f1, f1^-1, f2, f2^-1, f3, f3^-1
   ]>, function( x ) ... end, function( x ) ... end )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mon:=Image(mhom);|
  <fp monoid on the generators [ f1, f1^-1, f2, f2^-1, f3, f3^-1 ]>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@k:=KnuthBendixRewritingSystem(mon);|
  Knuth Bendix Rewriting System for Monoid(
  [ f1, f1^-1, f2, f2^-1, f3, f3^-1 ] ) with rules
  [ [ f1*f1^-1, <identity ...> ], [ f1^-1*f1, <identity ...> ],
    [ f2*f2^-1, <identity ...> ], [ f2^-1*f2, <identity ...> ],
    [ f3*f3^-1, <identity ...> ], [ f3^-1*f3, <identity ...> ],
    [ f1*f2^2*f3^-1, <identity ...> ], [ f2*f3^2*f1^-1, <identity ...> ]
      , [ f3*f1^2*f2^-1, <identity ...> ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MakeConfluent(k);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:=Product(GeneratorsOfMonoid(mon));|
  f1*f1^-1*f2*f2^-1*f3*f3^-1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ReducedForm(k,UnderlyingElement(a));|
  <identity ...>
\end{Verbatim}
 

 To rewrite a word in the finitely presented group, one has to convert it to a
word in the monoid first, rewrite in the underlying free monoid and convert
back (by forming first again an element of the fp monoid) to the finitely
presented group. 

   
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r:=PseudoRandom(g);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Length(r);|
  3704
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@melm:=Image(mhom,r);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@red:=ReducedForm(k,UnderlyingElement(melm));|
  f1^-1^3*f2^-1*f1^2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@melm:=ElementOfFpMonoid(FamilyObj(One(mon)),red);|
  f1^-1^3*f2^-1*f1^2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@gpelm:=PreImagesRepresentative(mhom,melm);|
  f1^-3*f2^-1*f1^2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r=gpelm;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CategoriesOfObject(red);|
  [ "IsExtLElement", "IsExtRElement", "IsMultiplicativeElement",
    "IsMultiplicativeElementWithOne", "IsAssociativeElement", "IsWord" ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CategoriesOfObject(melm);|
  [ "IsExtLElement", "IsExtRElement", "IsMultiplicativeElement",
    "IsMultiplicativeElementWithOne", "IsAssociativeElement",
    "IsElementOfFpMonoid" ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CategoriesOfObject(gpelm);|
  [ "IsExtLElement", "IsExtRElement", "IsMultiplicativeElement",
    "IsMultiplicativeElementWithOne", "IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse",
    "IsAssociativeElement", "IsElementOfFpGroup" ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note, that the elements \texttt{red} (free monoid) \texttt{melm} (fp monoid) and \texttt{gpelm} (group) differ, though they are displayed identically. 

 Under Unix, it is possible to use the \textsf{kbmag} package to replace the built\texttt{\symbol{45}}in rewriting by this packages
efficient C implementation. You can do this (after loading the \textsf{kbmag} package) by assigning the variable \texttt{KB{\textunderscore}REW} (\ref{KBuScoreREW}) to \texttt{KBMAG{\textunderscore}REW}. Assignment to \texttt{GAPKB{\textunderscore}REW} reverts to the built\texttt{\symbol{45}}in implementation. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LoadPackage("kbmag");|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@KB_REW:=KBMAG_REW;;|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Developing rewriting systems}}\label{Developing rewriting systems}
\logpage{[ 38, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8751F8FA7DC989A2}{}
{
  The key point to note about rewriting systems is that they have properties
such as \texttt{IsConfluent} (\ref{IsConfluent:for a rewriting system}) and attributes such as \texttt{Rules} (\ref{Rules}), however they are rarely stored, but rather computed afresh each time they
are asked for, from data stored in the private members of the rewriting system
object. This is because a rewriting system often evolves through a session,
starting with some rules which define the algebra \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape A}} as relations, and then adding more rules to make the system confluent. For
example, in the case of Knuth\texttt{\symbol{45}}Bendix rewriting systems (see
Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Finitely Presented Semigroups and Monoids}), the function \texttt{CreateKnuthBendixRewritingSystem} creating the rewriting system (in the file \texttt{lib/kbsemi.gi}) uses 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  kbrws := Objectify(NewType(rwsfam,
    IsMutable and IsKnuthBendixRewritingSystem and
    IsKnuthBendixRewritingSystemRep),
    rec(family:= fam,
    reduced:=false,
    tzrules:=List(relwco,i->
     [LetterRepAssocWord(i[1]),LetterRepAssocWord(i[2])]),
    pairs2check:=CantorList(Length(r)),
    ordering:=wordord,
    freefam:=freefam));
\end{Verbatim}
 

 In particular, since we don't use the filter \texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep} in the \texttt{Objectify} (\ref{Objectify}), whenever \texttt{IsConfluent} (\ref{IsConfluent:for a rewriting system}) is called, the appropriate method to determine confluence is called. }

 }

            
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Groups}}\label{Groups}
\logpage{[ 39, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8716635F7951801B}{}
{
  This chapter explains how to create groups and defines operations for groups,
that is operations whose definition does not depend on the representation
used. However methods for these operations in most cases will make use of the
representation. 

 If not otherwise specified, in all examples in this chapter the group \texttt{g} will be the symmetric group $S_4$ acting on the letters $\{ 1, \ldots, 4 \}$.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Group Elements}}\label{Group Elements}
\logpage{[ 39, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X822370B47DEA37B1}{}
{
  Groups in \textsf{GAP} are written multiplicatively. The elements from which a group can be generated
must permit multiplication and multiplicative inversion (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Useful Categories of Elements}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:=(1,2,3);;b:=(2,3,4);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@One(a);|
  ()
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Inverse(b);|
  (2,4,3)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a*b;|
  (1,3)(2,4)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Order(a*b);|
  2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Order( [ [ 1, 1 ], [ 0, 1 ] ] );|
  infinity
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The next example may run into an infinite loop because the given matrix in
fact has infinite order. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Order( [ [ 1, 1 ], [ 0, 1 ] ] * Indeterminate( Rationals ) );|
  #I  Order: warning, order of <mat> might be infinite
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \index{order!of a group} Since groups are domains, the recommended command to compute the order of a
group is \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}). For convenience, group orders can also be computed with \texttt{Order} (\ref{Order}). 

 The operation \texttt{Comm} (\ref{Comm}) can be used to compute the commutator of two elements, the operation \texttt{LeftQuotient} (\ref{LeftQuotient}) computes the product $x^{{-1}} y$. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Creating Groups}}\label{Creating Groups}
\logpage{[ 39, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86A022F9800121F8}{}
{
  When groups are created from generators, this means that the generators must
be elements that can be multiplied and inverted (see also{\nobreakspace}\ref{Constructing Domains}). For creating a free group on a set of symbols, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{FreeGroup} (\ref{FreeGroup:for given rank}). 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Group}}\logpage{[ 39, 2, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D7B075385435151}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Group({\mdseries\slshape gen, ...})\index{Group@\texttt{Group}!for several generators}
\label{Group:for several generators}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Group({\mdseries\slshape gens[, id]})\index{Group@\texttt{Group}!for a list of generators (and an identity element)}
\label{Group:for a list of generators (and an identity element)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{Group( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gen}}, ... )} is the group generated by the arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gen}}, ... 

 If the only argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} is a list that is not a matrix then \texttt{Group( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} )} is the group generated by the elements of that list. 

 If there are two arguments, a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} and an element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape id}}, then \texttt{Group( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape id}} )} is the group generated by the elements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}, with identity \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape id}}. 

 Note that the value of the attribute \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup} (\ref{GeneratorsOfGroup}) need not be equal to the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} of generators entered as argument. Use \texttt{GroupWithGenerators} (\ref{GroupWithGenerators}) if you want to be sure that the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} is stored as value of \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup} (\ref{GeneratorsOfGroup}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2,3,4),(1,2));|
  Group([ (1,2,3,4), (1,2) ])
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GroupByGenerators}}
\logpage{[ 39, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F81960287F3E32A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GroupByGenerators({\mdseries\slshape gens})\index{GroupByGenerators@\texttt{GroupByGenerators}}
\label{GroupByGenerators}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GroupByGenerators({\mdseries\slshape gens, id})\index{GroupByGenerators@\texttt{GroupByGenerators}!with explicitly specified identity element}
\label{GroupByGenerators:with explicitly specified identity element}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{GroupByGenerators} returns the group $G$ generated by the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. If a second argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape id}} is present then this is stored as the identity element of the group. 

 The value of the attribute \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup} (\ref{GeneratorsOfGroup}) of $G$ need not be equal to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. \texttt{GroupByGenerators} is the underlying operation called by \texttt{Group} (\ref{Group:for several generators}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GroupWithGenerators}}
\logpage{[ 39, 2, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8589EF9C7B658B94}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GroupWithGenerators({\mdseries\slshape gens[, id]})\index{GroupWithGenerators@\texttt{GroupWithGenerators}}
\label{GroupWithGenerators}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{GroupWithGenerators} returns the group $G$ generated by the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. If a second argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape id}} is present then this is stored as the identity element of the group. The value
of the attribute \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup} (\ref{GeneratorsOfGroup}) of $G$ is equal to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GeneratorsOfGroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 2, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79C44528864044C5}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{GeneratorsOfGroup@\texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup}}
\label{GeneratorsOfGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns a list of generators of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} has been created by the command \texttt{GroupWithGenerators} (\ref{GroupWithGenerators}) with argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}, then the list returned by \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup} will be equal to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. For such a group, each generator can also be accessed using the \texttt{.} operator (see \texttt{GeneratorsOfDomain} (\ref{GeneratorsOfDomain})): for a positive integer $i$, \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}.i} returns the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th element of the list returned by \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup}. Moreover, if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is a free group, and \texttt{name} is the name of a generator of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} then \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}.name} also returns this generator. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=GroupWithGenerators([(1,2,3,4),(1,2)]);|
  Group([ (1,2,3,4), (1,2) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsOfGroup(g);|
  [ (1,2,3,4), (1,2) ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 While in this example \textsf{GAP} displays the group via the generating set stored in the attribute \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup}, the methods installed for \texttt{View} (\ref{View}) will in general display only some information about the group which may even
be just the fact that it is a group. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AsGroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 2, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A0747F17B50D967}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AsGroup({\mdseries\slshape D})\index{AsGroup@\texttt{AsGroup}}
\label{AsGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 if the elements of the collection \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} form a group the command returns this group, otherwise it returns \texttt{fail}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AsGroup([(1,2)]);|
  fail
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AsGroup([(),(1,2)]);|
  Group([ (1,2) ])
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ConjugateGroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 2, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E4143A08040BB47}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ConjugateGroup({\mdseries\slshape G, obj})\index{ConjugateGroup@\texttt{ConjugateGroup}}
\label{ConjugateGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the conjugate group of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, obtained by applying the conjugating element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. 

 To form a conjugate (group) by any object acting via \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}, one can also use the infix operator \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ConjugateGroup(g,(1,5));|
  Group([ (2,3,4,5), (2,5) ])
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsGroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 2, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7939B3177BBD61E4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsGroup({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsGroup@\texttt{IsGroup}}
\label{IsGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 A group is a magma\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}inverses
(see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsMagmaWithInverses} (\ref{IsMagmaWithInverses})) and associative (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsAssociative} (\ref{IsAssociative})) multiplication. 

 \texttt{IsGroup} tests whether the object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} fulfills these conditions, it does \emph{not} test whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is a set of elements that forms a group under multiplication; use \texttt{AsGroup} (\ref{AsGroup}) if you want to perform such a test. (See{\nobreakspace}\ref{Categories} for details about categories.) 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsGroup(g);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoGroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 2, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X845874BA82E1A11F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoGroup\index{InfoGroup@\texttt{InfoGroup}}
\label{InfoGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (info class)}}\\


 is the info class for the generic group theoretic functions
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Info Functions}). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Subgroups}}\label{Subgroups}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7BA181CA81D785BB}{}
{
  For the general concept of parents and subdomains, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Parents} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Constructing Subdomains}. More functions that construct certain subgroups can be found in the
sections{\nobreakspace}\ref{Normal Structure}, \ref{Specific and Parametrized Subgroups}, \ref{Sylow Subgroups and Hall Subgroups}, and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Subgroups characterized by prime powers}. 

 If a group $U$ is created as a subgroup of another group $G$, $G$ becomes the parent of $U$. There is no ``universal'' parent group, parent\texttt{\symbol{45}}child chains can be arbitrary long. \textsf{GAP} stores the result of some operations (such as \texttt{Normalizer} (\ref{Normalizer:for two groups})) with the parent as an attribute. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Subgroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C82AA387A42DCA0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Subgroup({\mdseries\slshape G, gens})\index{Subgroup@\texttt{Subgroup}}
\label{Subgroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SubgroupNC({\mdseries\slshape G, gens})\index{SubgroupNC@\texttt{SubgroupNC}}
\label{SubgroupNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Subgroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{Subgroup@\texttt{Subgroup}!for a group}
\label{Subgroup:for a group}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 creates the subgroup \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} generated by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. The \texttt{Parent} (\ref{Parent}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} will be \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The \texttt{NC} version does not check, whether the elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} actually lie in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 

 The unary version of \texttt{Subgroup} creates a (shell) subgroup that does not even know generators but can be used
to collect information about a particular subgroup over time. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@u:=Subgroup(g,[(1,2,3),(1,2)]);|
  Group([ (1,2,3), (1,2) ])
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Index (\textsf{GAP} operation)}}\logpage{[ 39, 3, 2 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X842AD37E79CE953E}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Index({\mdseries\slshape G, U})\index{Index@\texttt{Index}!for a group and its subgroup}
\label{Index:for a group and its subgroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndexNC({\mdseries\slshape G, U})\index{IndexNC@\texttt{IndexNC}!for a group and its subgroup}
\label{IndexNC:for a group and its subgroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 For a subgroup \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \texttt{Index} returns the index $[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}:\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}}] = |\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}| / |\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}}|$ of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The \texttt{NC} version does not test whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} is contained in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Index(g,u);|
  4
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IndexInWholeGroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8014135884DCC53E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndexInWholeGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{IndexInWholeGroup@\texttt{IndexInWholeGroup}}
\label{IndexInWholeGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 If the family of elements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} itself forms a group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}, this attribute returns the index of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}. It is used primarily for free groups or finitely presented groups. }

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@freegp:=FreeGroup(1);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@freesub:=Subgroup(freegp,[freegp.1^5]);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IndexInWholeGroup(freesub);|
  5
\end{Verbatim}
 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AsSubgroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7904AC9D7E9A3BB7}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AsSubgroup({\mdseries\slshape G, U})\index{AsSubgroup@\texttt{AsSubgroup}}
\label{AsSubgroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 creates a subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} which contains the same elements as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@v:=AsSubgroup(g,Group((1,2,3),(1,4)));|
  Group([ (1,2,3), (1,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Parent(v);|
  Group([ (1,2,3,4), (1,2) ])
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsSubgroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7839D8927E778334}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsSubgroup({\mdseries\slshape G, U})\index{IsSubgroup@\texttt{IsSubgroup}}
\label{IsSubgroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{IsSubgroup} returns \texttt{true} if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} is a group that is a subset of the domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. This is actually checked by calling \texttt{IsGroup( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} )} and \texttt{IsSubset( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} )}; note that special methods for \texttt{IsSubset} (\ref{IsSubset}) are available that test only generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is closed under the group operations. So in most cases, for example whenever
one knows already that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} is a group, it is better to call only \texttt{IsSubset} (\ref{IsSubset}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsSubgroup(g,u);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@v:=Group((1,2,3),(1,2));|
  Group([ (1,2,3), (1,2) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@u=v;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsSubgroup(g,v);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsNormal}}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X838186F9836F678C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsNormal({\mdseries\slshape G, U})\index{IsNormal@\texttt{IsNormal}}
\label{IsNormal}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns \texttt{true} if the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} normalizes the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} and \texttt{false} otherwise. 

 A group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} \emph{normalizes} a group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} if and only if for every $g \in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}$ and $u \in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}}$ the element $u^g$ is a member of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}}. Note that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} need not be a subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsNormal(g,u);|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsCharacteristicSubgroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8390B5117A10CC52}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsCharacteristicSubgroup({\mdseries\slshape G, N})\index{IsCharacteristicSubgroup@\texttt{IsCharacteristicSubgroup}}
\label{IsCharacteristicSubgroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 tests whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape N}} is invariant under all automorphisms of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsCharacteristicSubgroup(g,u);|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ConjugateSubgroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84F5464983655590}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ConjugateSubgroup({\mdseries\slshape G, g})\index{ConjugateSubgroup@\texttt{ConjugateSubgroup}}
\label{ConjugateSubgroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 For a group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} which has a parent group \texttt{P} (see \texttt{Parent} (\ref{Parent})), returns the subgroup of \texttt{P}, obtained by conjugating \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} using the conjugating element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} has no parent group, it just delegates to the call to \texttt{ConjugateGroup} (\ref{ConjugateGroup}) with the same arguments. 

 To form a conjugate (subgroup) by any object acting via \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}, one can also use the infix operator \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ConjugateSubgroups}}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D9990EB837075A4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ConjugateSubgroups({\mdseries\slshape G, U})\index{ConjugateSubgroups@\texttt{ConjugateSubgroups}}
\label{ConjugateSubgroups}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a list of all images of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} under conjugation action by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsSubnormal}}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82ABF80780CC27AF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsSubnormal({\mdseries\slshape G, U})\index{IsSubnormal@\texttt{IsSubnormal}}
\label{IsSubnormal}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 A subgroup \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is subnormal if it is contained in a subnormal series of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsSubnormal(g,Group((1,2,3)));|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsSubnormal(g,Group((1,2)(3,4)));|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SubgroupByProperty}}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 11 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X829766158665FB54}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SubgroupByProperty({\mdseries\slshape G, prop})\index{SubgroupByProperty@\texttt{SubgroupByProperty}}
\label{SubgroupByProperty}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 creates a subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} consisting of those elements fulfilling \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}} (which is a tester function). No test is done whether the property actually
defines a subgroup. 

 Note that currently very little functionality beyond an element test exists
for groups created this way. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SubgroupShell}}
\logpage{[ 39, 3, 12 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E95101F80583E77}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SubgroupShell({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{SubgroupShell@\texttt{SubgroupShell}}
\label{SubgroupShell}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 creates a subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} which at this point is not yet specified further (but will be later, for
example by assigning a generating set). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@u:=SubgroupByProperty(g,i->3^i=3);|
  <subgrp of Group([ (1,2,3,4), (1,2) ]) by property>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@(1,3) in u; (1,4) in u; (1,5) in u;|
  false
  true
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsOfGroup(u);|
  [ (1,2), (1,4,2) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@u:=SubgroupShell(g);|
  <group>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Closures of (Sub)groups}}\label{Closures of (Sub)groups}
\logpage{[ 39, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7B855B0485C3C6C5}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ClosureGroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D13FC1F8576FFD8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ClosureGroup({\mdseries\slshape G, obj})\index{ClosureGroup@\texttt{ClosureGroup}}
\label{ClosureGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 creates the group generated by the elements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} can be either an element or a collection of elements, in particular another
group. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=SmallGroup(24,12);;u:=Subgroup(g,[g.3,g.4]);|
  Group([ f3, f4 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ClosureGroup(u,g.2);|
  Group([ f2, f3, f4 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ClosureGroup(u,[g.1,g.2]);|
  Group([ f1, f2, f3, f4 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ClosureGroup(u,Group(g.2*g.1));|
  Group([ f1*f2^2, f3, f4 ])
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ClosureGroupAddElm}}
\logpage{[ 39, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81A20A397C308483}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ClosureGroupAddElm({\mdseries\slshape G, elm})\index{ClosureGroupAddElm@\texttt{ClosureGroupAddElm}}
\label{ClosureGroupAddElm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ClosureGroupCompare({\mdseries\slshape G, elm})\index{ClosureGroupCompare@\texttt{ClosureGroupCompare}}
\label{ClosureGroupCompare}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ClosureGroupIntest({\mdseries\slshape G, elm})\index{ClosureGroupIntest@\texttt{ClosureGroupIntest}}
\label{ClosureGroupIntest}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 These three functions together with \texttt{ClosureGroupDefault} (\ref{ClosureGroupDefault}) implement the main methods for \texttt{ClosureGroup} (\ref{ClosureGroup}). In the ordering given, they just add \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} to the generators, remove duplicates and identity elements, and test whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} is already contained in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ClosureGroupDefault}}
\logpage{[ 39, 4, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82F59F6680D1B0D5}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ClosureGroupDefault({\mdseries\slshape G, elm})\index{ClosureGroupDefault@\texttt{ClosureGroupDefault}}
\label{ClosureGroupDefault}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This functions returns the closure of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} with the element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} has the attribute \texttt{AsSSortedList} (\ref{AsSSortedList}) then also the result has this attribute. This is used to implement the default
method for \texttt{Enumerator} (\ref{Enumerator}) and \texttt{EnumeratorSorted} (\ref{EnumeratorSorted}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ClosureSubgroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 4, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A7AF14A8052F055}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ClosureSubgroup({\mdseries\slshape G, obj})\index{ClosureSubgroup@\texttt{ClosureSubgroup}}
\label{ClosureSubgroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ClosureSubgroupNC({\mdseries\slshape G, obj})\index{ClosureSubgroupNC@\texttt{ClosureSubgroupNC}}
\label{ClosureSubgroupNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For a group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} that stores a parent group (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Parents}), \texttt{ClosureSubgroup} calls \texttt{ClosureGroup} (\ref{ClosureGroup}) with the same arguments; if the result is a subgroup of the parent of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} then the parent of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is set as parent of the result, otherwise an error is raised. The check
whether the result is contained in the parent of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is omitted by the \texttt{NC} version. As a wrong parent might imply wrong properties this version should be
used with care. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Expressing Group Elements as Words in Generators}}\label{Expressing Group Elements as Words in Generators}
\logpage{[ 39, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7E19F92284F6684E}{}
{
  \index{factorization} \index{words!in generators} Using homomorphisms (see chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Group Homomorphisms}) it is possible to express group elements as words in given generators:
Create a free group (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{FreeGroup} (\ref{FreeGroup:for given rank})) on the correct number of generators and create a homomorphism from this free
group onto the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} in whose generators you want to factorize. Then the preimage of an element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is a word in the free generators, that will map on this element again. 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{EpimorphismFromFreeGroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7FE8A3B08458A1BF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{EpimorphismFromFreeGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{EpimorphismFromFreeGroup@\texttt{EpimorphismFromFreeGroup}}
\label{EpimorphismFromFreeGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For a group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} with a known generating set, this attribute returns a homomorphism from a free
group that maps the free generators to the generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 

 The option \texttt{names} can be used to prescribe a (print) name for the free generators. 

 The following example shows how to decompose elements of $S_4$ in the generators \texttt{(1,2,3,4)} and \texttt{(1,2)}: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2,3,4),(1,2));|
  Group([ (1,2,3,4), (1,2) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@hom:=EpimorphismFromFreeGroup(g:names:=["x","y"]);|
  [ x, y ] -> [ (1,2,3,4), (1,2) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PreImagesRepresentative(hom,(1,4));|
  y^-1*x^-1*(x^-1*y^-1)^2*x
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The following example stems from a real request to the \textsf{GAP} Forum. In September 2000 a \textsf{GAP} user working with puzzles wanted to express the permutation \texttt{(1,2)} as a word as short as possible in particular generators of the symmetric group $S_{16}$. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@perms := [ (1,2,3,7,11,10,9,5), (2,3,4,8,12,11,10,6),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  (5,6,7,11,15,14,13,9), (6,7,8,12,16,15,14,10) ];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@puzzle := Group( perms );;Size( puzzle );|
  20922789888000
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@hom:=EpimorphismFromFreeGroup(puzzle:names:=["a", "b", "c", "d"]);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@word := PreImagesRepresentative( hom, (1,2) );|
  a^-1*c*b*c^-1*a*b^-1*a^-2*c^-1*a*b^-1*c*b
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Length( word );|
  13
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Factorization}}
\logpage{[ 39, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8357294D7B164106}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Factorization({\mdseries\slshape G, elm})\index{Factorization@\texttt{Factorization}}
\label{Factorization}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a factorization of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} as word in the generators of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} given in the attribute \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup} (\ref{GeneratorsOfGroup}). The attribute \texttt{EpimorphismFromFreeGroup} (\ref{EpimorphismFromFreeGroup}) of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} will contain a map from the free group in which the word is expressed to the
group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The attribute \texttt{MappingGeneratorsImages} (\ref{MappingGeneratorsImages}) of this map gives a list of generators and corresponding letters. 

 The algorithm used forms all elements of the group to ensure a short word is
found. Therefore this function should \emph{not} be used when the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} has more than a few million elements. Because of this, one should not call
this function within algorithms, but use homomorphisms instead. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G:=SymmetricGroup( 6 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r:=(3,4);; s:=(1,2,3,4,5,6);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# create subgroup to force the system to use the generators r and s:|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@H:= Subgroup(G, [ r, s ] );|
  Group([ (3,4), (1,2,3,4,5,6) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Factorization( H, (1,2,3) );|
  (x2*x1)^2*x2^-2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@s*r*s*r*s^-2;|
  (1,2,3)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MappingGeneratorsImages(EpimorphismFromFreeGroup(H));|
  [ [ x1, x2 ], [ (3,4), (1,2,3,4,5,6) ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GrowthFunctionOfGroup}}
\logpage{[ 39, 5, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X871508DD808EB487}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GrowthFunctionOfGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{GrowthFunctionOfGroup@\texttt{GrowthFunctionOfGroup}}
\label{GrowthFunctionOfGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GrowthFunctionOfGroup({\mdseries\slshape G, radius})\index{GrowthFunctionOfGroup@\texttt{GrowthFunctionOfGroup}!with word length limit}
\label{GrowthFunctionOfGroup:with word length limit}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 For a group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} with a generating set given in \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup} (\ref{GeneratorsOfGroup}), this function calculates the number of elements whose shortest expression as
words in the generating set is of a particular length. It returns a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape L}}, whose $i+1$ entry counts the number of elements whose shortest word expression has length $i$. If a maximal length \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape radius}} is given, only words up to length \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape radius}} are counted. Otherwise the group must be finite and all elements are
enumerated. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GrowthFunctionOfGroup(MathieuGroup(12));|
  [ 1, 5, 19, 70, 255, 903, 3134, 9870, 25511, 38532, 16358, 382 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GrowthFunctionOfGroup(MathieuGroup(12),2);|
  [ 1, 5, 19 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GrowthFunctionOfGroup(MathieuGroup(12),99);|
  [ 1, 5, 19, 70, 255, 903, 3134, 9870, 25511, 38532, 16358, 382 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@free:=FreeGroup("a","b");|
  <free group on the generators [ a, b ]>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@product:=free/ParseRelators(free,"a2,b3");|
  <fp group on the generators [ a, b ]>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetIsFinite(product,false);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GrowthFunctionOfGroup(product,10);|
  [ 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Structure Descriptions}}\label{Structure Descriptions}
\logpage{[ 39, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X87BF1B887C91CA2E}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StructureDescription}}
\logpage{[ 39, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8199B74B84446971}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StructureDescription({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{StructureDescription@\texttt{StructureDescription}}
\label{StructureDescription}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 The method for \texttt{StructureDescription} exhibits a structure of the given group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} to some extent, using the strategy outlined below. The idea is to return a
possibly short string which gives some insight in the structure of the
considered group. It is intended primarily for small groups (order less than
100) or groups with few normal subgroups, in other cases, in particular large $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}groups, it can be very costly. Furthermore, the string
returned is \texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}} as the action on chief
factors is not described \texttt{\symbol{45}}\texttt{\symbol{45}} often not
the most useful way to describe a group.

 The string returned by \texttt{StructureDescription} is \textsc{not} an isomorphism invariant: non\texttt{\symbol{45}}isomorphic groups can have
the same string value, and two isomorphic groups in different representations
can produce different strings. The value returned by \texttt{StructureDescription} is a string of the following form: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@I,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=]
    StructureDescription(<G>) ::=
        1                                 ; trivial group
      | C<size>                           ; finite cyclic group
      | Z                                 ; infinite cyclic group
      | A<degree>                         ; alternating group
      | S<degree>                         ; symmetric group
      | D<size>                           ; dihedral group
      | Q<size>                           ; quaternion group
      | QD<size>                          ; quasidihedral group
      | PSL(<n>,<q>)                      ; projective special linear group
      | SL(<n>,<q>)                       ; special linear group
      | GL(<n>,<q>)                       ; general linear group
      | PSU(<n>,<q>)                      ; proj. special unitary group
      | O(2<n>+1,<q>)                     ; orthogonal group, type B
      | O+(2<n>,<q>)                      ; orthogonal group, type D
      | O-(2<n>,<q>)                      ; orthogonal group, type 2D
      | PSp(2<n>,<q>)                     ; proj. special symplectic group
      | Sz(<q>)                           ; Suzuki group
      | Ree(<q>)                          ; Ree group (type 2F or 2G)
      | E(6,<q>) | E(7,<q>) | E(8,<q>)    ; Lie group of exceptional type
      | 2E(6,<q>) | F(4,<q>) | G(2,<q>)
      | 3D(4,<q>)                         ; Steinberg triality group
      | M11 | M12 | M22 | M23 | M24
      | J1 | J2 | J3 | J4 | Co1 | Co2
      | Co3 | Fi22 | Fi23 | Fi24' | Suz
      | HS | McL | He | HN | Th | B
      | M | ON | Ly | Ru                  ; sporadic simple group
      | 2F(4,2)'                          ; Tits group
      | PerfectGroup(<size>,<id>)         ; the indicated group from the
                                          ; library of perfect groups
      | A x B                             ; direct product
      | N : H                             ; semidirect product
      | C(G) . G/C(G) = G' . G/G'         ; non-split extension
                                          ; (equal alternatives and
                                          ; trivial extensions omitted)
      | Phi(G) . G/Phi(G)                 ; non-split extension:
                                          ; Frattini subgroup and
                                          ; Frattini factor group
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that the \texttt{StructureDescription} is only \emph{one} possible way of building up the given group from smaller pieces. 

 The option ``short'' is recognized \texttt{\symbol{45}} if this option is set, an abbreviated
output format is used (e.g. \texttt{"6x3"} instead of \texttt{"C6 x C3"}). 

 If the \texttt{Name} (\ref{Name}) attribute is not bound, but \texttt{StructureDescription} is, \texttt{View} (\ref{View}) prints the value of the attribute \texttt{StructureDescription}. The \texttt{Print} (\ref{Print})ed representation of a group is not affected by computing a \texttt{StructureDescription}. 

 The strategy used to compute a \texttt{StructureDescription} is as follows: 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{1.}]  Lookup in a precomputed list, if the order of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is not larger than 100 and not equal to 64 or 96. 
\item[{2.}]  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is abelian, then decompose it into cyclic factors in ``elementary divisors style''. For example, \texttt{"C2 x C3 x C3"} is \texttt{"C6 x C3"}. For infinite abelian groups, \texttt{"Z"} denotes the group of integers. 
\item[{3.}]  Recognize alternating groups, symmetric groups, dihedral groups, quasidihedral
groups, quaternion groups, PSL's, SL's, GL's and simple groups not listed so
far as basic building blocks. 
\item[{4.}]  Decompose \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} into a direct product of irreducible factors. 
\item[{5.}]  Recognize semidirect products \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}=$N$:$H$, where $N$ is normal. Select a pair $N$, $H$ with the following preferences: 
\begin{description}
\item[{1.}]  if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is defined as a semidirect product of $N$, $H$ then select $N$, $H$, 
\item[{2.}]  if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is solvable, then select a solvable normal Hall subgroup $N$, if exists, and consider the semidirect decomposition of $N$ and $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}/N$, 
\item[{3.}]  find any nontrivial normal subgroup $N$ which has a complement $H$. 
\end{description}
 The option ``nice'' is recognized. If this option is set, then all semidirect products are
computed in order to find a possibly nicer presentation. Note, that this may
take a very long time if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} has many normal subgroups, e.g. if $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}/\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}'$ has many cyclic factors. If the option ``nice'' is set, then GAP would select a pair $N$, $H$ with the following preferences: 
\begin{description}
\item[{1.}]  $H$ is abelian 
\item[{2.}]  $N$ is abelian 
\item[{2a.}]  $N$ has many abelian invariants 
\item[{3.}]  $N$ is a direct product 
\item[{3a.}]  $N$ has many direct factors 
\item[{4.}]  $\phi: H \rightarrow$ Aut($N$), $h \mapsto (n \mapsto n^h)$ is injective. 
\end{description}
 
\item[{6.}]  Fall back to non\texttt{\symbol{45}}splitting extensions: If the centre or the
commutator factor group is non\texttt{\symbol{45}}trivial, write \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} as $Z(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}})$.$\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}/Z(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}})$ or $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}'$.$\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}/\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}'$, respectively. Otherwise if the Frattini subgroup is
non\texttt{\symbol{45}}trivial, write \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} as $\Phi$(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}).\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}/$\Phi$(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}). 
\item[{7.}]  If no decomposition is found (maybe this is not the case for any finite
group), try to identify \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} in the perfect groups library. If this fails also, then return a string
describing this situation. 
\end{description}
 Note that \texttt{StructureDescription} is \emph{not} intended to be a research tool, but rather an educational tool. The reasons
for this are as follows: 
\begin{description}
\item[{1.}]  ``Most'' groups do not have ``nice'' decompositions. This is in some contrast to what is often taught in elementary
courses on group theory, where it is sometimes suggested that basically every
group can be written as iterated direct or semidirect product of cyclic groups
and nonabelian simple groups. 
\item[{2.}]  In particular many $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}groups have very ``similar'' structure, and \texttt{StructureDescription} can only exhibit a little of it. Changing this would likely make the output
not essentially easier to read than a pc presentation. 
\end{description}
 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l := AllSmallGroups(12);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List(l,StructureDescription);; l;|
  [ C3 : C4, C12, A4, D12, C6 x C2 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List(AllSmallGroups(40),G->StructureDescription(G:short));|
  [ "5:8", "40", "5:8", "5:Q8", "4xD10", "D40", "2x(5:4)", "(10x2):2",
    "20x2", "5xD8", "5xQ8", "2x(5:4)", "2^2xD10", "10x2^2" ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List(AllTransitiveGroups(DegreeAction,6),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@        G->StructureDescription(G:short));|
  [ "6", "S3", "D12", "A4", "3xS3", "2xA4", "S4", "S4", "S3xS3",
    "(3^2):4", "2xS4", "A5", "(S3xS3):2", "S5", "A6", "S6" ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StructureDescription(SmallGroup(504,7));|
  "C7 : (C9 x Q8)"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StructureDescription(SmallGroup(504,7):nice);|
  "(C7 : Q8) : C9"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StructureDescription(AbelianGroup([0,2,3]));|
  "Z x C6"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StructureDescription(AbelianGroup([0,0,0,2,3,6]):short);|
  "Z^3x6^2"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StructureDescription(PSL(4,2));|
  "A8"
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Cosets}}\label{Cosets}
\logpage{[ 39, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81002AA87DDBC02F}{}
{
  \index{right cosets} \index{coset} 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RightCoset}}
\logpage{[ 39, 7, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8412ABD57986B9FC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RightCoset({\mdseries\slshape U, g})\index{RightCoset@\texttt{RightCoset}}
\label{RightCoset}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the right coset of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} with representative \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}, which is the set of all elements of the form $ug$ for all $u \in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}}$. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} must be an element of a larger group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} which contains \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}}. For element operations such as \texttt{in} a right coset behaves like a set of group elements. 

 Right cosets are external orbits for the action of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} which acts via \texttt{OnLeftInverse} (\ref{OnLeftInverse}). Of course the action of a larger group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} on right cosets is via \texttt{OnRight} (\ref{OnRight}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@u:=Group((1,2,3), (1,2));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@c:=RightCoset(u,(2,3,4));|
  RightCoset(Group( [ (1,2,3), (1,2) ] ),(2,3,4))
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ActingDomain(c);|
  Group([ (1,2,3), (1,2) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Representative(c);|
  (2,3,4)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(c);|
  6
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AsList(c);|
  [ (2,3,4), (1,4,2), (1,3,4,2), (1,3)(2,4), (2,4), (1,4,2,3) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBiCoset(c);|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RightCosets}}
\logpage{[ 39, 7, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X835F48248571364F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RightCosets({\mdseries\slshape G, U})\index{RightCosets@\texttt{RightCosets}}
\label{RightCosets}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RightCosetsNC({\mdseries\slshape G, U})\index{RightCosetsNC@\texttt{RightCosetsNC}}
\label{RightCosetsNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 computes a duplicate free list of right cosets \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} $g$ for $g \in$ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. A set of representatives for the elements in this list forms a right
transversal of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. (By inverting the representatives one obtains a list of representatives of
the left cosets of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}}.) The \texttt{NC} version does not check whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} is a subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RightCosets(g,u);|
  [ RightCoset(Group( [ (1,2,3), (1,2) ] ),()),
    RightCoset(Group( [ (1,2,3), (1,2) ] ),(1,3)(2,4)),
    RightCoset(Group( [ (1,2,3), (1,2) ] ),(1,4)(2,3)),
    RightCoset(Group( [ (1,2,3), (1,2) ] ),(1,2)(3,4)) ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CanonicalRightCosetElement}}
\logpage{[ 39, 7, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85884F177B5D98AE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CanonicalRightCosetElement({\mdseries\slshape U, g})\index{CanonicalRightCosetElement@\texttt{CanonicalRightCosetElement}}
\label{CanonicalRightCosetElement}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a ``canonical'' representative of the right coset \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} which is independent of the given representative \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}. This can be used to compare cosets by comparing their canonical
representatives. 

 The representative chosen to be the ``canonical'' one is representation dependent and only guaranteed to remain the same within
one \textsf{GAP} session. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CanonicalRightCosetElement(u,(2,4,3));|
  (3,4)
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsRightCoset}}
\logpage{[ 39, 7, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D7625A1861D9DAB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsRightCoset({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsRightCoset@\texttt{IsRightCoset}}
\label{IsRightCoset}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 The category of right cosets. 

 \index{left cosets} \textsf{GAP} does not provide left cosets as a separate data type, but as the left coset $gU$ consists of exactly the inverses of the elements of the right coset $Ug^{{-1}}$ calculations with left cosets can be emulated using right cosets by inverting
the representatives. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsBiCoset}}
\logpage{[ 39, 7, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78F4F0D8838F5ABF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsBiCoset({\mdseries\slshape C})\index{IsBiCoset@\texttt{IsBiCoset}}
\label{IsBiCoset}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 \index{bicoset} A (right) coset $Ug$ is considered a \emph{bicoset} if its set of elements simultaneously forms a left coset for the same
subgroup. This is the case if and only if the coset representative $g$ normalizes the subgroup $U$. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CosetDecomposition}}
\logpage{[ 39, 7, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82F6ABE378B928D1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CosetDecomposition({\mdseries\slshape G, S})\index{CosetDecomposition@\texttt{CosetDecomposition}}
\label{CosetDecomposition}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For a finite group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} and a subgroup $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} \leq \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}$ this function returns a partition of the elements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} according to the (right) cosets of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. The result is a list of lists, each sublist corresponding to one coset. The
first sublist is the elements list of the subgroup, the other lists are
arranged accordingly. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CosetDecomposition(SymmetricGroup(4),SymmetricGroup(3));|
  [ [ (), (2,3), (1,2), (1,2,3), (1,3,2), (1,3) ],
    [ (1,4), (1,4)(2,3), (1,2,4), (1,2,3,4), (1,3,2,4), (1,3,4) ],
    [ (1,4,2), (1,4,2,3), (2,4), (2,3,4), (1,3)(2,4), (1,3,4,2) ],
    [ (1,4,3), (1,4,3,2), (1,2,4,3), (1,2)(3,4), (2,4,3), (3,4) ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Transversals}}\label{Transversals}
\logpage{[ 39, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83C723878230D616}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RightTransversal}}
\logpage{[ 39, 8, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85C65D06822E716F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RightTransversal({\mdseries\slshape G, U})\index{RightTransversal@\texttt{RightTransversal}}
\label{RightTransversal}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 A right transversal $t$ is a list of representatives for the set $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} \setminus \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}$ of right cosets (consisting of cosets $Ug$) of $U$ in $G$. 

 The object returned by \texttt{RightTransversal} is not a plain list, but an object that behaves like an immutable list of
length $[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}:\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}}]$, except if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} is the trivial subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} in which case \texttt{RightTransversal} may return the sorted plain list of coset representatives. 

 The operation \texttt{PositionCanonical} (\ref{PositionCanonical}), called for a transversal $t$ and an element $g$ of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, will return the position of the representative in $t$ that lies in the same coset of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} as the element $g$ does. (In comparison, \texttt{Position} (\ref{Position}) will return \texttt{fail} if the element is not equal to the representative.) Functions that implement
group actions such as \texttt{Action} (\ref{Action:for a group, an action domain, etc.}) or \texttt{Permutation} (\ref{Permutation:for a group, an action domain, etc.}) (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Group Actions}) use \texttt{PositionCanonical} (\ref{PositionCanonical}), therefore it is possible to ``act'' on a right transversal to implement the action on the cosets. This is often
much more efficient than acting on cosets. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2,3,4),(1,2));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@u:=Subgroup(g,[(1,2,3),(1,2)]);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rt:=RightTransversal(g,u);|
  RightTransversal(Group([ (1,2,3,4), (1,2) ]),Group([ (1,2,3), (1,2) ]))
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Length(rt);|
  4
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Position(rt,(1,2,3));|
  fail
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that the elements of a right transversal are not necessarily ``canonical'' in the sense of \texttt{CanonicalRightCosetElement} (\ref{CanonicalRightCosetElement}), but we may compute a list of canonical coset representatives by calling that
function. (See also \texttt{PositionCanonical} (\ref{PositionCanonical}).) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List(RightTransversal(g,u),i->CanonicalRightCosetElement(u,i));|
  [ (), (2,3,4), (1,2,3,4), (3,4) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PositionCanonical(rt,(1,2,3));|
  1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rt[1];|
  ()
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Double Cosets}}\label{Double Cosets}
\logpage{[ 39, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X78B98B257E981046}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DoubleCoset}}
\logpage{[ 39, 9, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E51ED757D17254B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DoubleCoset({\mdseries\slshape U, g, V})\index{DoubleCoset@\texttt{DoubleCoset}}
\label{DoubleCoset}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 The groups \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} must be subgroups of a common supergroup \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} of which \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} is an element. This command constructs the double coset \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} which is the set of all elements of the form $ugv$ for any $u \in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}}$, $v \in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}$. For element operations such as \texttt{in}, a double coset behaves like a set of group elements. The double coset stores \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} in the attribute \texttt{LeftActingGroup}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} as \texttt{Representative} (\ref{Representative}), and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} as \texttt{RightActingGroup}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RepresentativesContainedRightCosets}}
\logpage{[ 39, 9, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F53DABD79BA4F72}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RepresentativesContainedRightCosets({\mdseries\slshape D})\index{RepresentativesContainedRightCosets@\texttt{RepresentativesContainedRightCosets}}
\label{RepresentativesContainedRightCosets}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 A double coset $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} = U g V$ can be considered as a union of right cosets $U h_i$. (It is the union of the orbit of $U g$ under right multiplication by $V$.) For a double coset \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} this function returns a set of representatives $h_i$ such that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} $= \bigcup_{{h_i}} U h_i$. The representatives returned are canonical for $U$ (see \texttt{CanonicalRightCosetElement} (\ref{CanonicalRightCosetElement})) and form a set. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@u:=Subgroup(g,[(1,2,3),(1,2)]);;v:=Subgroup(g,[(3,4)]);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@c:=DoubleCoset(u,(2,4),v);|
  DoubleCoset(Group( [ (1,2,3), (1,2) ] ),(2,4),Group( [ (3,4) ] ))
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@(1,2,3) in c;|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@(2,3,4) in c;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeftActingGroup(c);|
  Group([ (1,2,3), (1,2) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RightActingGroup(c);|
  Group([ (3,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RepresentativesContainedRightCosets(c);|
  [ (2,3,4) ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DoubleCosets}}
\logpage{[ 39, 9, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A5EFABB86E6D4D5}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DoubleCosets({\mdseries\slshape G, U, V})\index{DoubleCosets@\texttt{DoubleCosets}}
\label{DoubleCosets}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DoubleCosetsNC({\mdseries\slshape G, U, V})\index{DoubleCosetsNC@\texttt{DoubleCosetsNC}}
\label{DoubleCosetsNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 computes a duplicate free list of all double cosets \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} $g$ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} for $g \in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}$. The groups \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} must be subgroups of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The \texttt{NC} version does not check whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} are subgroups of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@dc:=DoubleCosets(g,u,v);|
  [ DoubleCoset(Group( [ (1,2,3), (1,2) ] ),(),Group( [ (3,4) ] )),
    DoubleCoset(Group( [ (1,2,3), (1,2) ] ),(1,3)(2,4),Group(
      [ (3,4) ] )), DoubleCoset(Group( [ (1,2,3), (1,2) ] ),(1,4)
      (2,3),Group( [ (3,4) ] )) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List(dc,Representative);|
  [ (), (1,3)(2,4), (1,4)(2,3) ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsDoubleCoset (operation)}}
\logpage{[ 39, 9, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85ED464F878EF24C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsDoubleCoset({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsDoubleCoset@\texttt{IsDoubleCoset}!operation}
\label{IsDoubleCoset:operation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 The category of double cosets. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DoubleCosetRepsAndSizes}}
\logpage{[ 39, 9, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A25B1C886CF8C6A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DoubleCosetRepsAndSizes({\mdseries\slshape G, U, V})\index{DoubleCosetRepsAndSizes@\texttt{DoubleCosetRepsAndSizes}}
\label{DoubleCosetRepsAndSizes}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a list of double coset representatives and their sizes, the entries
are lists of the form $[ r, n ]$ where $r$ and $n$ are an element of the double coset and the size of the coset, respectively.
This operation is faster than \texttt{DoubleCosetsNC} (\ref{DoubleCosetsNC}) because no double coset objects have to be created. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@dc:=DoubleCosetRepsAndSizes(g,u,v);|
  [ [ (), 12 ], [ (1,3)(2,4), 6 ], [ (1,4)(2,3), 6 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoCoset}}
\logpage{[ 39, 9, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84AE7EE77E5FB30E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoCoset\index{InfoCoset@\texttt{InfoCoset}}
\label{InfoCoset}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (info class)}}\\


 The information function for coset and double coset operations is \texttt{InfoCoset}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Conjugacy Classes}}\label{Conjugacy Classes}
\logpage{[ 39, 10, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D474F8F87E4E5D9}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ConjugacyClass}}
\logpage{[ 39, 10, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B2F207F7F85F5B8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ConjugacyClass({\mdseries\slshape G, g})\index{ConjugacyClass@\texttt{ConjugacyClass}}
\label{ConjugacyClass}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 creates the conjugacy class in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} with representative \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}. This class is an external set, so functions such as \texttt{Representative} (\ref{Representative}) (which returns \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}), \texttt{ActingDomain} (\ref{ActingDomain}) (which returns \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}), \texttt{StabilizerOfExternalSet} (\ref{StabilizerOfExternalSet}) (which returns the centralizer of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}) and \texttt{AsList} (\ref{AsList}) work for it. 

 A conjugacy class is an external orbit (see \texttt{ExternalOrbit} (\ref{ExternalOrbit})) of group elements with the group acting by conjugation on it. Thus element
tests or operation representatives can be computed. The attribute \texttt{Centralizer} (\ref{Centralizer:for a class of objects in a magma}) gives the centralizer of the representative (which is the same result as \texttt{StabilizerOfExternalSet} (\ref{StabilizerOfExternalSet})). (This is a slight abuse of notation: This is \emph{not} the centralizer of the class as a \emph{set} which would be the standard behaviour of \texttt{Centralizer} (\ref{Centralizer:for a class of objects in a magma}).) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ConjugacyClasses (attribute)}}
\logpage{[ 39, 10, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X871B570284BBA685}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ConjugacyClasses({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{ConjugacyClasses@\texttt{ConjugacyClasses}!attribute}
\label{ConjugacyClasses:attribute}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the conjugacy classes of elements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} as a list of class objects of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{ConjugacyClass} (\ref{ConjugacyClass}) for details). It is guaranteed that the class of the identity is in the first
position, the further arrangement depends on the method chosen (and might be
different for equal but not identical groups). 

 For very small groups (of size up to 500) the classes will be computed by the
conjugation action of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} on itself (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{ConjugacyClassesByOrbits} (\ref{ConjugacyClassesByOrbits})). This can be deliberately switched off using the ``\texttt{noaction}'' option shown below. 

 For solvable groups, the default method to compute the classes is by
homomorphic lift (see section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Conjugacy Classes in Solvable Groups}). 

 For other groups the method of \cite{HulpkeClasses} is employed. 

 \texttt{ConjugacyClasses} supports the following options that can be used to modify this strategy: 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{random}}]  The classes are computed by random search. See \texttt{ConjugacyClassesByRandomSearch} (\ref{ConjugacyClassesByRandomSearch}) below. 
\item[{\texttt{action}}]  The classes are computed by action of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} on itself. See \texttt{ConjugacyClassesByOrbits} (\ref{ConjugacyClassesByOrbits}) below. 
\item[{\texttt{noaction}}]  Even for small groups \texttt{ConjugacyClassesByOrbits} (\ref{ConjugacyClassesByOrbits}) is not used as a default. This can be useful if the elements of the group use
a lot of memory. 
\end{description}
 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=SymmetricGroup(4);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@cl:=ConjugacyClasses(g);|
  [ ()^G, (1,2)^G, (1,2)(3,4)^G, (1,2,3)^G, (1,2,3,4)^G ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Representative(cl[3]);Centralizer(cl[3]);|
  (1,2)(3,4)
  Group([ (1,2), (1,3)(2,4), (3,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(Centralizer(cl[5]));|
  4
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(cl[2]);|
  6
\end{Verbatim}
 

 In general, you will not need to have to influence the method, but simply call \texttt{ConjugacyClasses} {\textendash}\textsf{GAP} will try to select a suitable method on its own. The method specifications are
provided here mainly for expert use. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ConjugacyClassesByRandomSearch}}
\logpage{[ 39, 10, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D6ED84C86C2979B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ConjugacyClassesByRandomSearch({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{ConjugacyClassesByRandomSearch@\texttt{ConjugacyClassesByRandomSearch}}
\label{ConjugacyClassesByRandomSearch}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 computes the classes of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} by random search. This works very efficiently for almost simple groups. 

 This function is also accessible via the option \texttt{random} to the function \texttt{ConjugacyClass} (\ref{ConjugacyClass}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ConjugacyClassesByOrbits}}
\logpage{[ 39, 10, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X852B3634789D770E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ConjugacyClassesByOrbits({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{ConjugacyClassesByOrbits@\texttt{ConjugacyClassesByOrbits}}
\label{ConjugacyClassesByOrbits}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 computes the classes of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} as orbits of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} on its elements. This can be quick but unsurprisingly may also take a lot of
memory if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} becomes larger. All the classes will store their element list and thus a
membership test will be quick as well. 

 This function is also accessible via the option \texttt{action} to the function \texttt{ConjugacyClass} (\ref{ConjugacyClass}). 

 Typically, for small groups (roughly of order up to $10^3$) the computation of classes as orbits under the action is fastest; memory
restrictions (and the increasing cost of eliminating duplicates) make this
less efficient for larger groups. 

 Calculation by random search has the smallest memory requirement, but in
generally performs worse, the more classes are there. 

 The following example shows the effect of this for a small group with many
classes: 

  
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:=Group((4,5)(6,7,8),(1,2,3)(5,6,9));;ConjugacyClasses(h:noaction);;time;|
  110
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:=Group((4,5)(6,7,8),(1,2,3)(5,6,9));;ConjugacyClasses(h:random);;time;|
  300
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:=Group((4,5)(6,7,8),(1,2,3)(5,6,9));;ConjugacyClasses(h:action);;time;|
  30
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NrConjugacyClasses}}
\logpage{[ 39, 10, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8733F87B7E4C9903}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NrConjugacyClasses({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{NrConjugacyClasses@\texttt{NrConjugacyClasses}}
\label{NrConjugacyClasses}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the number of conjugacy classes of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2,3,4),(1,2));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NrConjugacyClasses(g);|
  5
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RationalClass}}
\logpage{[ 39, 10, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BD2A4427B7FE248}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RationalClass({\mdseries\slshape G, g})\index{RationalClass@\texttt{RationalClass}}
\label{RationalClass}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 creates the rational class in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} with representative \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}. A rational class consists of all elements that are conjugate to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} or to an $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} where $i$ is coprime to the order of $g$. Thus a rational class can be interpreted as a conjugacy class of cyclic
subgroups. A rational class is an external set (\texttt{IsExternalSet} (\ref{IsExternalSet})) of group elements with the group acting by conjugation on it, but not an
external orbit. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RationalClasses}}
\logpage{[ 39, 10, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81E9EF0A811072E8}{}
