\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Primitive Groups}}\label{Primitive Groups}
\logpage{[ 43, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83F8D3B578A7BEEB}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ONanScottType}}
\logpage{[ 43, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E50211A7B92455F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ONanScottType({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{ONanScottType@\texttt{ONanScottType}}
\label{ONanScottType}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the type of a primitive permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, according to the O'Nan\texttt{\symbol{45}}Scott classification. The
labelling of the different types is not consistent in the literature, we use
the following identifications. The two\texttt{\symbol{45}}letter code given is
the name of the type as used by Praeger. 
\begin{description}
\item[{1}]  Affine. (HA) 
\item[{2}]  Almost simple. (AS) 
\item[{3a}]  Diagonal, Socle consists of two normal subgroups. (HS) 
\item[{3b}]  Diagonal, Socle is minimal normal. (SD) 
\item[{4a}]  Product action with the first factor primitive of type 3a. (HC) 
\item[{4b}]  Product action with the first factor primitive of type 3b. (CD) 
\item[{4c}]  Product action with the first factor primitive of type 2. (PA) 
\item[{5}]  Twisted wreath product (TW) 
\end{description}
 See \cite{EickHulpke01} for correspondence to other labellings used in the literature. As it can
contain letters, the type is returned as a string. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is not a permutation group or does not act primitively on the points moved by
it, the result is undefined. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SocleTypePrimitiveGroup}}
\logpage{[ 43, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E89A46A86A3F4A2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SocleTypePrimitiveGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{SocleTypePrimitiveGroup@\texttt{SocleTypePrimitiveGroup}}
\label{SocleTypePrimitiveGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the socle type of the primitive permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The socle of a primitive group is the direct product of isomorphic simple
groups, therefore the type is indicated by a record with components \texttt{series}, \texttt{parameter} (both as described under \texttt{IsomorphismTypeInfoFiniteSimpleGroup} (\ref{IsomorphismTypeInfoFiniteSimpleGroup:for a group})), and \texttt{width} for the number of direct factors. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} does not act primitively on its moved points, an error is returned. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=AlternatingGroup(5);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:=DirectProduct(g,g);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p:=List([1,2],i->Projection(h,i));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ac:=Action(h,AsList(g),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@function(g,h) return Image(p[1],h)^-1*g*Image(p[2],h);end);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(ac);NrMovedPoints(ac);IsPrimitive(ac,[1..60]);|
  3600
  60
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ONanScottType(ac);|
  "3a"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SocleTypePrimitiveGroup(ac);|
  rec(
    name := "A(5) ~ A(1,4) = L(2,4) ~ B(1,4) = O(3,4) ~ C(1,4) = S(2,4) \
  ~ 2A(1,4) = U(2,4) ~ A(1,5) = L(2,5) ~ B(1,5) = O(3,5) ~ C(1,5) = S(2,\
  5) ~ 2A(1,5) = U(2,5)", parameter := 5, series := "A", width := 2 )
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Stabilizer Chains}}\label{Stabilizer Chains}
\logpage{[ 43, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7FA58C3A8283F3BD}{}
{
  Many of the algorithms for permutation groups use a \emph{stabilizer chain} of the group. The concepts of stabilizer chains, \emph{bases}, and \emph{strong generating sets} were introduced by Charles Sims in{\nobreakspace}\cite{Sim70}. An extensive account of basic algorithms together with asymptotic runtime
analysis can be found in reference{\nobreakspace}\cite[Chapter 4]{Seress2003}. A further discussion of base change is given in section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Generalized Conjugation Technique}. 

 Let $B = [ b_1, \ldots, b_n ]$ be a list of points, $G^{(1)} = G$ and $G^{{(i+1)}} = Stab_{{G^{(i)}}}(b_i)$, such that $G^{(n+1)} = \{ () \}$. Then the list $[ b_1, \ldots, b_n ]$ is called a \emph{base} of $G$, the points $b_i$ are called \emph{base points}. A set $S$ of generators for $G$ satisfying the condition $\langle S \cap G^{(i)} \rangle = G^{(i)}$ for each $1 \leq i \leq n$, is called a \emph{strong generating set} (SGS) of $G$. (More precisely we ought to say that it is a SGS of $G$ \emph{relative} to $B$). The chain of subgroups $G^{(i)}$ of $G$ itself is called the \emph{stabilizer chain} of $G$ relative to $B$. 

 Since $[ b_1, \ldots, b_n ]$, where $n$ is the degree of $G$ and $b_i$ are the moved points of $G$, certainly is a base for $G$ there exists a base for each permutation group. The number of points in a base
is called the \emph{length} of the base. A base $B$ is called \emph{reduced} if there exists no $i$ such that $G^{(i)} = G^{(i+1)}$. (This however does not imply that no subset of $B$ could also serve as a base.) Note that different reduced bases for one
permutation group $G$ may have different lengths. For example, the irreducible degree $416$ permutation representation of the Chevalley Group $G_2(4)$ possesses reduced bases of lengths $5$ and $7$. 

 Let $R^{(i)}$ be a right transversal of $G^{(i+1)}$ in $G^{(i)}$, i.e. a set of right coset representatives of the cosets of $G^{(i+1)}$ in $G^{(i)}$. Then each element $g$ of $G$ has a unique representation as a product of the form $g = r_n \ldots r_1$ with $r_i \in R^{(i)}$. The cosets of $G^{(i+1)}$ in $G^{(i)}$ are in bijective correspondence with the points in $O^{(i)} := b_i^{{G^{(i)}}}$. So we could represent a transversal as a list $T$ such that $T[p]$ is a representative of the coset corresponding to the point $p \in O^{(i)}$, i.e., an element of $G^{(i)}$ that takes $b_i$ to $p$. (Note that such a list has holes in all positions corresponding to points
not contained in $O^{(i)}$.) 

 This approach however will store many different permutations as coset
representatives which can be a problem if the degree $n$ gets bigger. Our goal therefore is to store as few different permutations as
possible such that we can still reconstruct each representative in $R^{(i)}$, and from them the elements in $G$. A \emph{factorized inverse transversal} $T$ is a list where $T[p]$ is a generator of $G^{(i)}$ such that $p^{{T[p]}}$ is a point that lies earlier in $O^{(i)}$ than $p$ (note that we consider $O^{(i)}$ as a list, not as a set). If we assume inductively that we know an element $r \in G^{(i)}$ that takes $b_i$ to $p^{{T[p]}}$, then $r T[p]^{{-1}}$ is an element in $G^{(i)}$ that takes $b_i$ to $p$. \textsf{GAP} uses such factorized inverse transversals. 

 Another name for a factorized inverse transversal is a \emph{Schreier tree}. The vertices of the tree are the points in $O^{(i)}$, and the root of the tree is $b_i$. The edges are defined as the ordered pairs $(p, p^{{T[p]}})$, for $p \in O^{(i)} \setminus \{ b_i \}$. The edge $(p, p^{{T[p]}})$ is labelled with the generator $T[p]$, and the product of edge labels along the unique path from $p$ to $b_i$ is the inverse of the transversal element carrying $b_i$ to $p$. 

 Before we describe the construction of stabilizer chains in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Construction of Stabilizer Chains}, we explain in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Randomized Methods for Permutation Groups} the idea of using non\texttt{\symbol{45}}deterministic algorithms; this is
necessary for understanding the options available for the construction of
stabilizer chains. After that, in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Stabilizer Chain Records} it is explained how a stabilizer chain is stored in \textsf{GAP}, \ref{Operations for Stabilizer Chains} lists operations for stabilizer chains, and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Low Level Routines to Modify and Create Stabilizer Chains} lists low level routines for manipulating stabilizer chains. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Randomized Methods for Permutation Groups}}\label{Randomized Methods for Permutation Groups}
\logpage{[ 43, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7C2406B97E057196}{}
{
  \index{Schreier\texttt{\symbol{45}}Sims!random} For most computations with permutation groups, it is crucial to construct
stabilizer chains efficiently. Sims's original construction in \cite{Sim70} is deterministic, and is called the Schreier\texttt{\symbol{45}}Sims
algorithm, because it is based on Schreier's Lemma (\cite[p. 96]{Hall}): given $K = \langle S \rangle$ and a transversal $T$ for $K$ mod $L$, one can obtain $|S||T|$ generators for $L$. This lemma is applied recursively, with consecutive point stabilizers $G^{(i)}$ and $G^{(i+1)}$ playing the role of $K$ and $L$. 

 In permutation groups of large degree, the number of Schreier generators to be
processed becomes too large, and the deterministic
Schreier\texttt{\symbol{45}}Sims algorithm becomes impractical. Therefore, \textsf{GAP} uses randomized algorithms. The method selection process, which is quite
different from Version 3, works the following way. 

 If a group acts on not more than a hundred points, Sims's original
deterministic algorithm is applied. In groups of degree greater than hundred,
a heuristic algorithm based on ideas in \cite{BCFS91} constructs a stabilizer chain. This construction is complemented by a
verify\texttt{\symbol{45}}routine that either proves the correctness of the
stabilizer chain or causes the extension of the chain to a correct one. The
user can influence the verification process by setting the value of the record
component \texttt{random} (cf.{\nobreakspace}\ref{Construction of Stabilizer Chains}). 

 If the \texttt{random} value equals $1000$ then a slight extension of an unpublished method of Sims is used. The outcome
of this verification process is always correct. The user also can prescribe
any integer $x$, $1 \leq x \leq 999$ as the value of \texttt{random}. In this case, a randomized verification process from \cite{BCFS91} is applied, and the result of the stabilizer chain construction is guaranteed
to be correct with probability at least $x/1000$. The practical performance of the algorithm is much better than the
theoretical guarantee. 

 If the stabilizer chain is not correct then the elements in the product of
transversals $R^{(m)} R^{(m-1)} \cdots R^{(1)}$ constitute a proper subset of the group $G$ in question. This means that a membership test with this stabilizer chain
returns \texttt{false} for all elements that are not in $G$, but it may also return \texttt{false} for some elements of $G$; in other words, the result \texttt{true} of a membership test is always correct, whereas the result \texttt{false} may be incorrect. 

 The construction and verification phases are separated because there are
situations where the verification step can be omitted; if one happens to know
the order of the group in advance then the randomized construction of the
stabilizer chain stops as soon as the product of the lengths of the basic
orbits of the chain equals the group order, and the chain will be correct (see
the \texttt{size} option of the \texttt{StabChain} (\ref{StabChain:for a group (and a record)}) command). 

 Although the worst case running time is roughly quadratic for Sims's
verification and roughly linear for the randomized one, in most examples the
running time of the stabilizer chain construction with \texttt{random} value $1000$ (i.e., guaranteed correct output) is about the same as the running time of
randomized verification with guarantee of at least $90$ percent correctness. Therefore, we suggest to use the default value \texttt{random} $= 1000$. Possible uses of \texttt{random} values less than $1000$ are when one has to run through a large collection of subgroups, and a low
value of random is used to choose quickly a candidate for more thorough
examination; another use is when the user suspects that the quadratic
bottleneck of the guaranteed correct verification is hit. 

 We will give two examples to illustrate these ideas. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:= SL(4,7);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@o:= Orbit( h, [1,0,0,0]*Z(7)^0, OnLines );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@op:= Action( h, o, OnLines );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NrMovedPoints( op );|
  400
\end{Verbatim}
 

 We created a permutation group on $400$ points. First we compute a guaranteed correct stabilizer chain
(see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{StabChain} (\ref{StabChain:for a group (and a record)})). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:= Group( GeneratorsOfGroup( op ) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StabChain( h );;  time;|
  1120
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( h );|
  2317591180800
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Now randomized verification will be used. We require that the result is
guaranteed correct with probability $90$ percent. This means that if we would do this calculation many times over, \textsf{GAP} would \emph{guarantee} that in least $90$ percent of all calculations the result is correct. In fact the results are
much better than the guarantee, but we cannot promise that this will really
happen. (For the meaning of the \texttt{random} component in the second argument of \texttt{StabChain} (\ref{StabChain:for a group (and a record)}).) 

 First the group is created anew. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:= Group( GeneratorsOfGroup( op ) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StabChain( h, rec( random:= 900 ) );;  time;|
  1410
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( h );|
  2317591180800
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The result is still correct, and the running time is actually somewhat slower.
If you give the algorithm the order of the group, then it can check its
result, and so things become faster and the result is guaranteed to be
correct. This can be done with the \texttt{size} option (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{StabChain} (\ref{StabChain:for a group (and a record)})), or by setting the size of the group beforehand with \texttt{SetSize}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:=Group( GeneratorsOfGroup( op ) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetSize( h, 2317591180800 );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StabChain( h );;  time;|
  170
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The second example gives a typical group when the verification with \texttt{random} value $1000$ is slow. The problem is that the group has a stabilizer subgroup $G^{(i)}$ such that the fundamental orbit $O^{(i)}$ is split into a lot of orbits when we stabilize $b_i$ and one additional point of $O^{(i)}$. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p1:=PermList(Concatenation([401],[1..400]));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p2:=PermList(List([1..400],i->(i*20 mod 401)));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@d:=DirectProduct(Group(p1,p2),SymmetricGroup(5));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:=Group(GeneratorsOfGroup(d));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StabChain(h);;time;Size(h);|
  1030
  192480
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:=Group(GeneratorsOfGroup(d));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StabChain(h,rec(random:=900));;time;Size(h);|
  570
  192480
\end{Verbatim}
 

 When stabilizer chains of a group $G$ are created with \texttt{random} value less than $1000$, this is noted in the group $G$, by setting of the record component \texttt{random} in the value of the attribute \texttt{StabChainOptions} (\ref{StabChainOptions}) for $G$. As errors induced by the random methods might propagate, any group or
homomorphism created from $G$ inherits a \texttt{random} component in its \texttt{StabChainOptions} (\ref{StabChainOptions}) value from the corresponding component for $G$. 

 A lot of algorithms dealing with permutation groups use randomized methods;
however, if the initial stabilizer chain construction for a group is correct,
these further methods will provide guaranteed correct output. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Construction of Stabilizer Chains}}\label{Construction of Stabilizer Chains}
\logpage{[ 43, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7C7EA55C80E457FA}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StabChain (for a group (and a record))}}
\logpage{[ 43, 8, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80B5CF78829495C2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StabChain({\mdseries\slshape G[, options]})\index{StabChain@\texttt{StabChain}!for a group (and a record)}
\label{StabChain:for a group (and a record)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StabChain({\mdseries\slshape G, base})\index{StabChain@\texttt{StabChain}!for a group and a base}
\label{StabChain:for a group and a base}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StabChainOp({\mdseries\slshape G, options})\index{StabChainOp@\texttt{StabChainOp}}
\label{StabChainOp}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StabChainMutable({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{StabChainMutable@\texttt{StabChainMutable}!for a group}
\label{StabChainMutable:for a group}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StabChainMutable({\mdseries\slshape permhomom})\index{StabChainMutable@\texttt{StabChainMutable}!for a homomorphism}
\label{StabChainMutable:for a homomorphism}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StabChainImmutable({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{StabChainImmutable@\texttt{StabChainImmutable}}
\label{StabChainImmutable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 These commands compute a stabilizer chain for the permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}; additionally, \texttt{StabChainMutable} is also an attribute for the group homomorphism \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape permhomom}} whose source is a permutation group. 

 (The mathematical background of stabilizer chains is sketched
in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Stabilizer Chains}, more information about the objects representing stabilizer chains in \textsf{GAP} can be found in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Stabilizer Chain Records}.) 

 \texttt{StabChainOp} is an operation with two arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape options}}, the latter being a record which controls some aspects of the computation of
a stabilizer chain (see below); \texttt{StabChainOp} returns a \emph{mutable} stabilizer chain. \texttt{StabChainMutable} is a \emph{mutable} attribute for groups or homomorphisms, its default method for groups is to
call \texttt{StabChainOp} with empty options record. \texttt{StabChainImmutable} is an attribute with \emph{immutable} values; its default method dispatches to \texttt{StabChainMutable}. 

 \texttt{StabChain} is a function with first argument a permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, and optionally a record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape options}} as second argument. If the value of \texttt{StabChainImmutable} for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is already known and if this stabilizer chain matches the requirements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape options}}, \texttt{StabChain} simply returns this stored stabilizer chain. Otherwise \texttt{StabChain} calls \texttt{StabChainOp} and returns an immutable copy of the result; additionally, this chain is
stored as \texttt{StabChainImmutable} value for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. If no \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape options}} argument is given, its components default to the global variable \texttt{DefaultStabChainOptions} (\ref{DefaultStabChainOptions}). If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}} is a list of positive integers, the version \texttt{StabChain( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}} )} defaults to \texttt{StabChain( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, rec( base:= \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}} ) )}. 

 If given, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape options}} is a record whose components specify properties of the desired stabilizer
chain or which may help the algorithm. Default values for all of them can be
given in the global variable \texttt{DefaultStabChainOptions} (\ref{DefaultStabChainOptions}). The following options are supported. 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{base} (default an empty list)}]  A list of points, through which the resulting stabilizer chain shall run. For
the base $B$ of the resulting stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} this means the following. If the \texttt{reduced} component of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape options}} is \texttt{true} then those points of \texttt{base} with nontrivial basic orbits form the initial segment of $B$, if the \texttt{reduced} component is \texttt{false} then \texttt{base} itself is the initial segment of $B$. Repeated occurrences of points in \texttt{base} are ignored. If a stabilizer chain for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is already known then the stabilizer chain is computed via a base change. 
\item[{\texttt{knownBase} (no default value)}]  A list of points which is known to be a base for the group. Such a known base
makes it easier to test whether a permutation given as a word in terms of a
set of generators is the identity, since it suffices to map the known base
with each factor consecutively, rather than multiplying the whole permutations
(which would mean to map every point). This speeds up the
Schreier\texttt{\symbol{45}}Sims algorithm which is used when a new stabilizer
chain is constructed; it will not affect a base change, however. The component \texttt{knownBase} bears no relation to the \texttt{base} component, you may specify a known base \texttt{knownBase} and a desired base \texttt{base} independently. 
\item[{\texttt{reduced} (default \texttt{true})}]  If this is \texttt{true} the resulting stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is reduced, i.e., the case $G^{(i)} = G^{(i+1)}$ does not occur. Setting \texttt{reduced} to \texttt{false} makes sense only if the component \texttt{base} (see above) is also set; in this case all points of \texttt{base} will occur in the base $B$ of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}, even if they have trivial basic orbits. Note that if \texttt{base} is just an initial segment of $B$, the basic orbits of the points in $B \setminus $\texttt{base} are always nontrivial. 
\item[{\texttt{tryPcgs} (default \texttt{true})}]  If this is \texttt{true} and either the degree is at most $100$ or the group is known to be solvable, \textsf{GAP} will first try to construct a pcgs (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Polycyclic Groups}) for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} which will succeed and implicitly construct a stabilizer chain if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is solvable. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} turns out non\texttt{\symbol{45}}solvable, one of the other methods will be
used. This solvability check is comparatively fast, even if it fails, and it
can save a lot of time if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is solvable. 
\item[{\texttt{random} (default \texttt{1000})}]  If the value is less than{\nobreakspace}$1000$, the resulting chain is correct with probability at least{\nobreakspace}\texttt{random}$ / 1000$. The \texttt{random} option is explained in more detail in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Randomized Methods for Permutation Groups}. 
\item[{\texttt{size} (default \texttt{Size(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}})} if this is known, i.e., if \texttt{HasSize(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}})} is \texttt{true})}]  If this component is present, its value is assumed to be the order of the
group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. This information can be used to prove that a
non\texttt{\symbol{45}}deterministically constructed stabilizer chain is
correct. In this case, \textsf{GAP} does a non\texttt{\symbol{45}}deterministic construction until the size is
correct. 
\item[{\texttt{limit} (default \texttt{Size(Parent(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}))} or \texttt{StabChainOptions(Parent(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}})).limit} if it is present)}]  If this component is present, it must be greater than or equal to the order of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The stabilizer chain construction stops if size \texttt{limit} is reached. 
\end{description}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StabChainOptions}}
\logpage{[ 43, 8, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X790C27B8783EDE68}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StabChainOptions({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{StabChainOptions@\texttt{StabChainOptions}}
\label{StabChainOptions}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 is a record that stores the options with which the stabilizer chain stored in \texttt{StabChainImmutable} (\ref{StabChainImmutable}) has been computed (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{StabChain} (\ref{StabChain:for a group (and a record)}) for the options that are supported). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DefaultStabChainOptions}}
\logpage{[ 43, 8, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87E1292E85A5D31C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DefaultStabChainOptions\index{DefaultStabChainOptions@\texttt{DefaultStabChainOptions}}
\label{DefaultStabChainOptions}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 are the options for \texttt{StabChain} (\ref{StabChain:for a group (and a record)}) which are set as default. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StabChainBaseStrongGenerators}}
\logpage{[ 43, 8, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86D64D2B81D58431}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StabChainBaseStrongGenerators({\mdseries\slshape base, sgs[, one]})\index{StabChainBaseStrongGenerators@\texttt{StabChainBaseStrongGenerators}}
\label{StabChainBaseStrongGenerators}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}} be a base for a permutation group $G$, and let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sgs}} be a strong generating set for $G$ with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}}; \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape one}} must be the appropriate identity element of $G$ (see \texttt{One} (\ref{One}), in most cases this will be \texttt{()}). This function constructs a stabilizer chain corresponding to the given base
and strong generating set without the need to find Schreier generators; so
this is much faster than the other algorithms. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sgs}} is nonempty, then the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape one}} is optional; if not given, then the \texttt{One} (\ref{One}) of \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sgs}}[1]} is taken as the identity element. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@sc := StabChainBaseStrongGenerators([1,2], [(1,3,4), (2,3,4)], ());|
  <stabilizer chain record, Base [ 1, 2 ], Orbit length 4, Size: 12>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GroupStabChain(sc) = AlternatingGroup(4);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StabChainBaseStrongGenerators([1,3], [(1,2),(3,4)]);|
  <stabilizer chain record, Base [ 1, 3 ], Orbit length 2, Size: 4>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

\logpage{[ 43, 8, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BEC5F5A7851CAAB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MinimalStabChain({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{MinimalStabChain@\texttt{MinimalStabChain}}
\label{MinimalStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the reduced stabilizer chain corresponding to the base $[ 1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots ]$. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Stabilizer Chain Records}}\label{Stabilizer Chain Records}
\logpage{[ 43, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81D7FCE47AC7F942}{}
{
  If a permutation group has a stabilizer chain, this is stored as a recursive
structure. This structure is itself a record{\nobreakspace}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} and it has 
\begin{description}
\item[{(1)}]  components that provide information about one level{\nobreakspace}$G^{(i)}$ of the stabilizer chain (which we call the ``current stabilizer'') and 
\item[{(2)}]  a component \texttt{stabilizer} that holds another such record, namely the stabilizer chain of the next
stabilizer{\nobreakspace}$G^{(i+1)}$. 
\end{description}
 

 This gives a recursive structure where the ``outermost'' record representing the ``topmost'' stabilizer is bound to the group record component \texttt{stabChain} and has the components explained below. Note: Since the structure is
recursive, \emph{never print a stabilizer chain!} (Unless you want to exercise the scrolling capabilities of your terminal.) 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{identity} }]  the identity element of the current stabilizer. 
\item[{\texttt{labels} }]  a list of permutations which contains labels for the Schreier tree of the
current stabilizer, i.e., it contains elements for the factorized inverse
transversal. The first entry in this list is always the \texttt{identity}. Note that \textsf{GAP} tries to arrange things so that the \texttt{labels} components are identical (i.e., the same \textsf{GAP} object) in every stabilizer of the chain; thus the \texttt{labels} of a stabilizer do not necessarily all lie in the this stabilizer (but see \texttt{genlabels} below). 
\item[{\texttt{genlabels} }]  a list of integers indexing some of the permutations in the \texttt{labels} component. The \texttt{labels} addressed in this way form a generating set for the current stabilizer. If the \texttt{genlabels} component is empty, the rest of the stabilizer chain represents the trivial
subgroup, and can be ignored, e.g., when calculating the size. 
\item[{\texttt{generators} }]  a list of generators for the current stabilizer. Usually, it is \texttt{labels\texttt{\symbol{123}} genlabels \texttt{\symbol{125}}}. 
\item[{\texttt{orbit} }]  the vertices of the Schreier tree, which form the basic orbit $b_i^{{G^{(i)}}}$, ordered in such a way that the base point $b_i$ is in the first position in the orbit. 
\item[{\texttt{transversal}}]  The factorized inverse transversal found during the orbit algorithm. The
element $g$ stored at \texttt{transversal}$[i]$ will map $i$ to another point $j$ that in the Schreier tree is closer to the base point. By iterated application
(\texttt{transversal}$[j]$ and so on) eventually the base point is reached and an element that maps $i$ to the base point found as product. 
\item[{\texttt{translabels}}]  An index list such that \texttt{transversal}$[j] =$ \texttt{labels}$[$ \texttt{translabels}$[j] ]$. This list takes up comparatively little memory and is used to speed up base
changes. 
\item[{\texttt{stabilizer} }]  If the current stabilizer is not yet the trivial group, the stabilizer chain
continues with the stabilizer of the current base point, which is again
represented as a record with components \texttt{labels}, \texttt{identity}, \texttt{genlabels}, \texttt{generators}, \texttt{orbit}, \texttt{translabels}, \texttt{transversal} (and perhaps \texttt{stabilizer}). This record is bound to the \texttt{stabilizer} component of the current stabilizer. The last member of a stabilizer chain is
recognized by the fact that it has no \texttt{stabilizer} component bound. 
\end{description}
 It is possible that different stabilizer chains share the same record as one
of their iterated \texttt{stabilizer} components. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2,3,4),(1,2));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StabChain(g);|
  <stabilizer chain record, Base [ 1, 2, 3 ], Orbit length 4, Size: 24>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@BaseOfGroup(g);|
  [ 1, 2, 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StabChainOptions(g);|
  rec( random := 1000 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DefaultStabChainOptions;|
  rec( random := 1000, reduced := true, tryPcgs := true )
\end{Verbatim}
 }

\logpage{[ 43, 10, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7ECF8A4586346FD4}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{BaseStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 10, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7FBE6EB57EBE8B7D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{BaseStabChain({\mdseries\slshape S})\index{BaseStabChain@\texttt{BaseStabChain}}
\label{BaseStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the base belonging to the stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{BaseOfGroup}}
\logpage{[ 43, 10, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D2A190D8308ED39}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{BaseOfGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{BaseOfGroup@\texttt{BaseOfGroup}}
\label{BaseOfGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns a base of the permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. There is \emph{no} guarantee that a stabilizer chain stored in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} corresponds to this base! }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SizeStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 10, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EF36DC78465026A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SizeStabChain({\mdseries\slshape S})\index{SizeStabChain@\texttt{SizeStabChain}}
\label{SizeStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the product of the orbit lengths in the stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}, that is, the order of the group described by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StrongGeneratorsStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 10, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8384170881B9B531}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StrongGeneratorsStabChain({\mdseries\slshape S})\index{StrongGeneratorsStabChain@\texttt{StrongGeneratorsStabChain}}

 returns a strong generating set corresponding to the stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GroupStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 10, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87F473777EFDE867}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GroupStabChain({\mdseries\slshape [G, ]S})\index{GroupStabChain@\texttt{GroupStabChain}}
\label{GroupStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 constructs a permutation group with stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}, i.e., a group with generators \texttt{Generators( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} )} to which \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is assigned as component \texttt{stabChain}. If the optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is given, the result will have the parent \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{OrbitStabChain}}

}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\

\hyperdef{L}{X780875477CD2A57D}{}

\label{IteratorStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns an iterator for the elements of the group described by the stabilizer
chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. The elements of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} are produced by iterating through all base images in turn, and in the ordering
induced by the base. For more details see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Stabilizer Chains} }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InverseRepresentative}}
\logpage{[ 43, 10, 11 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X861062AE87ACF340}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InverseRepresentative({\mdseries\slshape S, pnt})\index{InverseRepresentative@\texttt{InverseRepresentative}}
\label{InverseRepresentative}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 calculates the transversal element which maps \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} back to the base point of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. It just runs back through the Schreier tree from \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} to the root and multiplies the labels along the way. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SiftedPermutation}}
\logpage{[ 43, 10, 12 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79D2248C8787EAF2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SiftedPermutation({\mdseries\slshape S, g})\index{SiftedPermutation@\texttt{SiftedPermutation}}
\label{SiftedPermutation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 sifts the permutation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} through the stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} and returns the result after the last step. 

 The element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} is sifted as follows: \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} is replaced by \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} * InverseRepresentative( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}.orbit[1]\texttt{\symbol{94}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} )}, then \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is replaced by \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}.stabilizer} and this process is repeated until \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is trivial or \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}.orbit[1]\texttt{\symbol{94}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}} is not in the basic orbit \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}.orbit}. The remainder \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} is returned, it is the identity permutation if and only if the original \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} is in the group $G$ described by the original{\nobreakspace}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MinimalElementCosetStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 10, 13 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B870C217D0B9997}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MinimalElementCosetStabChain({\mdseries\slshape S, g})\index{MinimalElementCosetStabChain@\texttt{MinimalElementCosetStabChain}}
\label{MinimalElementCosetStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let $G$ be the group described by the stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. This function returns a permutation $h$ such that $G \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} = G h$ (that is, $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} / h \in G$) and with the additional property that the list of images under $h$ of the base belonging to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is minimal w.r.t.{\nobreakspace}lexicographical ordering. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LargestElementStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 10, 14 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87435B7884D9B353}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LargestElementStabChain({\mdseries\slshape S, id})\index{LargestElementStabChain@\texttt{LargestElementStabChain}}
\label{LargestElementStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let $G$ be the group described by the stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. This function returns the element $h \in G$ with the property that the list of images under $h$ of the base belonging to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is maximal w.r.t.{\nobreakspace}lexicographical ordering. The second argument
must be an identity element (used to start the recursion). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ApproximateSuborbitsStabilizerPermGroup}}
\logpage{[ 43, 10, 15 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X809B2C3B7C5F77AB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ApproximateSuborbitsStabilizerPermGroup({\mdseries\slshape G, pnt})\index{ApproximateSuborbitsStabilizerPermGroup@\texttt{Approximate}\-\texttt{Suborbits}\-\texttt{Stabilizer}\-\texttt{Perm}\-\texttt{Group}}
\label{ApproximateSuborbitsStabilizerPermGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns an approximation of the orbits of \texttt{Stabilizer( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} )} on all points of the orbit \texttt{Orbit( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} )}, without computing the full point stabilizer; As not all Schreier generators
are used, the result may represent the orbits of only a subgroup of the point
stabilizer. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Low Level Routines to Modify and Create Stabilizer Chains}}\label{Low Level Routines to Modify and Create Stabilizer Chains}
\logpage{[ 43, 11, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8188051F79E72A95}{}
{
  These operations modify a stabilizer chain or obtain new chains with specific
properties. They are rather technical and should only be used if such
low\texttt{\symbol{45}}level routines are deliberately required. (For all
functions in this section the parameter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is a stabilizer chain.) 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CopyStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 11, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86B31E6A81AE5FCB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CopyStabChain({\mdseries\slshape S})\index{CopyStabChain@\texttt{CopyStabChain}}
\label{CopyStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function returns a mutable copy of the stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} that has no mutable object (list or record) in common with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. The \texttt{labels} components of the result are possibly shared by several levels, but
superfluous labels are removed. (An entry in \texttt{labels} is superfluous if it does not occur among the \texttt{genlabels} or \texttt{translabels} on any of the levels which share that \texttt{labels} component.) 

 This is useful for stabiliser sub\texttt{\symbol{45}}chains that have been
obtained as the (iterated) \texttt{stabilizer} component of a bigger chain. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CopyOptionsDefaults}}
\logpage{[ 43, 11, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E167E557B567C6A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CopyOptionsDefaults({\mdseries\slshape G, options})\index{CopyOptionsDefaults@\texttt{CopyOptionsDefaults}}
\label{CopyOptionsDefaults}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 sets components in a stabilizer chain options record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape options}} according to what is known about the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. This can be used to obtain a new stabilizer chain for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} quickly. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ChangeStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 11, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87FF64AB87BFC779}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ChangeStabChain({\mdseries\slshape S, base[, reduced]})\index{ChangeStabChain@\texttt{ChangeStabChain}}
\label{ChangeStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 changes or reduces a stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} to be adapted to the base \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}}. The optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape reduced}} is interpreted as follows. 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{reduced = }\texttt{false} : }]  change the stabilizer chain, do not reduce it, 
\item[{\texttt{reduced = }\texttt{true} : }]  change the stabilizer chain, reduce it. 
\end{description}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ExtendStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 11, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8778B4657D3FD97B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExtendStabChain({\mdseries\slshape S, base})\index{ExtendStabChain@\texttt{ExtendStabChain}}
\label{ExtendStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 extends the stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} so that it corresponds to base \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}}. The original base of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} must be a subset of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape base}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ReduceStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 11, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E5E9F727D0B19D9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ReduceStabChain({\mdseries\slshape S})\index{ReduceStabChain@\texttt{ReduceStabChain}}
\label{ReduceStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 changes the stabilizer chain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} to a reduced stabilizer chain by eliminating trivial steps. }

  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RemoveStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 11, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85BF290D848C4091}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RemoveStabChain({\mdseries\slshape S})\index{RemoveStabChain@\texttt{RemoveStabChain}}
\label{RemoveStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} must be a stabilizer record in a stabilizer chain. This chain then is cut off
at \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} by changing the entries in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. This can be used to remove trailing trivial steps. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{EmptyStabChain}}
\logpage{[ 43, 11, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84E4906B86E5C089}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{EmptyStabChain({\mdseries\slshape labels, id[, pnt]})\index{EmptyStabChain@\texttt{EmptyStabChain}}
\label{EmptyStabChain}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 constructs a stabilizer chain for the trivial group with \texttt{identity} value equal to\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape id}} and \texttt{labels = }$\{ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape id}} \} \cup$ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape labels}} (but of course with \texttt{genlabels} and \texttt{generators} values an empty list). If the optional third argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} is present, the only stabilizer of the chain is initialized with the
one\texttt{\symbol{45}}point basic orbit \texttt{[ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} ]} and with \texttt{translabels} and \texttt{transversal} components. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InsertTrivialStabilizer}}
\logpage{[ 43, 11, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80C7D2E87E6EE357}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InsertTrivialStabilizer({\mdseries\slshape S, pnt})\index{InsertTrivialStabilizer@\texttt{InsertTrivialStabilizer}}
\label{InsertTrivialStabilizer}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{InsertTrivialStabilizer} initializes the current stabilizer with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} as \texttt{EmptyStabChain} (\ref{EmptyStabChain}) did, but assigns the original \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} to the new \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}.stabilizer} component, such that a new level with trivial basic orbit (but identical \texttt{labels} and \texttt{ShallowCopy}ed \texttt{genlabels} and \texttt{generators}) is inserted. This function should be used only if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} really is fixed by the generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}, because then new generators can be added and the orbit and transversal at
the same time extended with \texttt{AddGeneratorsExtendSchreierTree} (\ref{AddGeneratorsExtendSchreierTree}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsFixedStabilizer}}
\logpage{[ 43, 11, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B47B379824F6150}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsFixedStabilizer({\mdseries\slshape S, pnt})\index{IsFixedStabilizer@\texttt{IsFixedStabilizer}}
\label{IsFixedStabilizer}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns \texttt{true} if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} is fixed by all generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} and \texttt{false} otherwise. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AddGeneratorsExtendSchreierTree}}
\logpage{[ 43, 11, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8373007880EBF736}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AddGeneratorsExtendSchreierTree({\mdseries\slshape S, new})\index{AddGeneratorsExtendSchreierTree@\texttt{AddGeneratorsExtendSchreierTree}}
\label{AddGeneratorsExtendSchreierTree}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 adds the elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape new}} to the list of generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} and at the same time extends the orbit and transversal. This is the only legal
way to extend a Schreier tree (because this involves careful handling of the
tree components). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Backtrack}}\label{Backtrack}
\logpage{[ 43, 12, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86C78160854C7F30}{}
{
  A main use for stabilizer chains is in backtrack algorithms for permutation
groups. \textsf{GAP} implements a partition\texttt{\symbol{45}}backtrack algorithm as described in \cite{Leon91} and refined in \cite{Theissen97}. 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SubgroupProperty}}
\logpage{[ 43, 12, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BE3F03C80BF8B08}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SubgroupProperty({\mdseries\slshape G, Pr[, L]})\index{SubgroupProperty@\texttt{SubgroupProperty}}
\label{SubgroupProperty}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Pr}} must be a one\texttt{\symbol{45}}argument function that returns \texttt{true} or \texttt{false} for elements of the permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, and the subset of elements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} that fulfill \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Pr}} must be a subgroup. (\emph{If the latter is not true the result of this operation is unpredictable!}) This command computes this subgroup. The optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape L}} must be a subgroup of the set of all elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} fulfilling \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Pr}} and can be given if known in order to speed up the calculation. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ElementProperty}}
\logpage{[ 43, 12, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EE7DDCC87C4BC31}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ElementProperty({\mdseries\slshape G, Pr[, L[, R]]})\index{ElementProperty@\texttt{ElementProperty}}
\label{ElementProperty}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{ElementProperty} returns an element $\pi$ of the permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} such that the one\texttt{\symbol{45}}argument function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Pr}} returns \texttt{true} for $\pi$. It returns \texttt{fail} if no such element exists in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The optional arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape L}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}} are subgroups of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} such that the property \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Pr}} has the same value for all elements in the cosets \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape L}} $g$ and $g$ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}}, respectively, with $g \in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}$. 

 A typical example of using the optional subgroups \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape L}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}} is the conjugacy test for elements $a$ and $b$ for which one can set \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape L}}$:= C_{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}}(a)$ and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}}$:= C_{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}}(b)$. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@propfun:= el -> (1,2,3)^el in [ (1,2,3), (1,3,2) ];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SubgroupProperty( g, propfun, Subgroup( g, [ (1,2,3) ] ) );|
  Group([ (1,2,3), (2,3) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ElementProperty( g, el -> Order( el ) = 2 );|
  (2,4)
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Permutations} describes special operations to construct permutations in the symmetric group
without using backtrack constructions. 

 Backtrack routines are also called by the methods for permutation groups that
compute centralizers, normalizers, intersections, conjugating elements as well
as stabilizers for the operations of a permutation group via \texttt{OnPoints} (\ref{OnPoints}), \texttt{OnSets} (\ref{OnSets}), \texttt{OnTuples} (\ref{OnTuples}) and \texttt{OnSetsSets} (\ref{OnSetsSets}). Some of these methods use more specific refinements than \texttt{SubgroupProperty} (\ref{SubgroupProperty}) or \texttt{ElementProperty}. For the definition of refinements, and how one can define refinements, see
Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{The General Backtrack Algorithm with Ordered Partitions}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TwoClosure}}
\logpage{[ 43, 12, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A2D046B83DD5F5F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TwoClosure({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{TwoClosure@\texttt{TwoClosure}}
\label{TwoClosure}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 The \emph{2\texttt{\symbol{45}}closure} of a transitive permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} on $n$ points is the largest subgroup of the symmetric group $S_n$ which has the same orbits on sets of ordered pairs of points as the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} has. It also can be interpreted as the stabilizer of the orbital graphs of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@TwoClosure(Group((1,2,3),(2,3,4)));|
  Sym( [ 1 .. 4 ] )
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoBckt}}
\logpage{[ 43, 12, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X861461AB7964DC64}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoBckt\index{InfoBckt@\texttt{InfoBckt}}
\label{InfoBckt}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (info class)}}\\


 is the info class for the partition backtrack routines. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Working with large degree permutation groups}}\label{Working with large degree permutation groups}
\logpage{[ 43, 13, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X78A68F5A80ADD1B6}{}
{
  Permutation groups of large degree (usually at least a few $10000$) can pose a challenge to the heuristics used in the algorithms for
permutation groups. This section lists a few useful tricks that may speed up
calculations with such large groups enormously. 

 The first aspect concerns solvable groups: A lot of calculations (including an
initial stabilizer chain computation thanks to the algorithm from \cite{Sims90b}) are faster if a permutation group is known to be solvable. On the other
hand, proving nonsolvability can be expensive for higher degrees. Therefore \textsf{GAP} will automatically test a permutation group for solvability, only if the
degree is not exceeding $100$. (See also the \texttt{tryPcgs} component of \texttt{StabChainOptions} (\ref{StabChainOptions}).) It is therefore beneficial to tell a group of larger degree, which is known
to be solvable, that it is, using \texttt{SetIsSolvableGroup(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}},true)}. 

 The second aspect concerns memory usage. A permutation on more than $65536$ points requires $4$ bytes per point for storing. So permutations on $256000$ points require roughly 1MB of storage per permutation. Just storing the
permutations required for a stabilizer chain might already go beyond the
available memory, in particular if the base is not very short. In such a
situation it can be useful, to replace the permutations by straight line
program elements (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Straight Line Program Elements}). 

 The following code gives an example of usage: We create a group of degree $231000$. Using straight line program elements, one can compute a stabilizer chain in
about $200$ MB of memory. 

    
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Read("largeperms"); # read generators from file|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@gens:=StraightLineProgGens(permutationlist);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group(gens);|
  <permutation group with 5 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# use random algorithm (faster, but result is monte carlo)|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StabChainOptions(g).random:=1;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(g); # enforce computation of a stabilizer chain|
  3529698298145066075557232833758234188056080273649172207877011796336000
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Without straight line program elements, the same calculation runs into memory
problems after a while even with 512MB of workspace: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:=Group(permutationlist);|
  <permutation group with 5 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StabChainOptions(h).random:=1;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(h);|
  exceeded the permitted memory (`-o' command line option)
  ...
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The advantage in memory usage however is paid for in runtime: Comparisons of
elements become much more expensive. One can avoid some of the related
problems by registering a known base with the straight line program elements
(see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{StraightLineProgGens} (\ref{StraightLineProgGens})). In this case element comparison will only compare the images of the given
base points. If we are planning to do extensive calculations with the group,
it can even be worth to recreate it with straight line program elements
knowing a previously computed base: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# get the base we computed already|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@bas:=BaseStabChain(StabChainMutable(g));|
  [ 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22, 25, 28, 31, 34, 37, 40, 43, 46, 49, 52, 55,
  ...
    2530, 2533, 2554, 2563, 2569 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@gens:=StraightLineProgGens(permutationlist,bas);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group(gens);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetSize(g,|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@3529698298145066075557232833758234188056080273649172207877011796336000);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Random(g);; # enforce computation of a stabilizer chain|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 As we know already base and size, this second stabilizer chain calculation is
much faster than the first one and takes less memory. }

 }

            
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Matrix Groups}}\label{Matrix Groups}
\logpage{[ 44, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7CF51CB48610A07D}{}
{
  Matrix groups are groups generated by invertible square matrices. 

 In the following example we temporarily increase the line length limit from
its default value 80 to 83 in order to get a nicer output format. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@m1 := [ [ Z(3)^0, Z(3)^0,   Z(3) ],|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@           [   Z(3), 0*Z(3),   Z(3) ],|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@           [ 0*Z(3),   Z(3), 0*Z(3) ] ];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@m2 := [ [   Z(3),   Z(3), Z(3)^0 ],|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@           [   Z(3), 0*Z(3),   Z(3) ],|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@           [ Z(3)^0, 0*Z(3),   Z(3) ] ];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@m := Group( m1, m2 );|
  Group(
  [
    [ [ Z(3)^0, Z(3)^0, Z(3) ], [ Z(3), 0*Z(3), Z(3) ],
        [ 0*Z(3), Z(3), 0*Z(3) ] ],
    [ [ Z(3), Z(3), Z(3)^0 ], [ Z(3), 0*Z(3), Z(3) ],
        [ Z(3)^0, 0*Z(3), Z(3) ] ] ])
\end{Verbatim}
  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsMatrixGroup (Filter)}}\label{sect:IsMatrixGroup}
\logpage{[ 44, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86CEA60E7C04744C}{}
{
  For most operations, \textsf{GAP} only provides methods for finite matrix groups. Many calculations in finite
matrix groups are done via so\texttt{\symbol{45}}called ``nice monomorphisms'' (see Section \ref{Nice Monomorphisms}) that represent a faithful action on vectors. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsMatrixGroup}}
\logpage{[ 44, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E6093FF85F1C3A1}{}

\label{IsMatrixGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 The category of matrix groups. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Attributes and Properties for Matrix Groups}}\label{Attributes and Properties for Matrix Groups}
\logpage{[ 44, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7FD808E386FAF9B0}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DimensionOfMatrixGroup}}
\logpage{[ 44, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E55258C783C50CA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DimensionOfMatrixGroup({\mdseries\slshape mat\texttt{\symbol{45}}grp})\index{DimensionOfMatrixGroup@\texttt{DimensionOfMatrixGroup}}
\label{DimensionOfMatrixGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 The dimension of the matrix group. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DefaultFieldOfMatrixGroup}}
\logpage{[ 44, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D540083793CD496}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DefaultFieldOfMatrixGroup({\mdseries\slshape mat\texttt{\symbol{45}}grp})\index{DefaultFieldOfMatrixGroup@\texttt{DefaultFieldOfMatrixGroup}}
\label{DefaultFieldOfMatrixGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Is a field containing all the matrix entries. It is not guaranteed to be the
smallest field with this property. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FieldOfMatrixGroup}}
\logpage{[ 44, 2, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78A9F0E580DA613A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FieldOfMatrixGroup({\mdseries\slshape matgrp})\index{FieldOfMatrixGroup@\texttt{FieldOfMatrixGroup}}
\label{FieldOfMatrixGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 The smallest field containing all the matrix entries of all elements of the
matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. As the calculation of this can be hard, this should only be used if one \emph{really} needs the smallest field, use \texttt{DefaultFieldOfMatrixGroup} (\ref{DefaultFieldOfMatrixGroup}) to get (for example) the characteristic. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DimensionOfMatrixGroup(m);|
  3
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DefaultFieldOfMatrixGroup(m);|
  GF(3)
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TransposedMatrixGroup}}
\logpage{[ 44, 2, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X832D18C77ED608DE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TransposedMatrixGroup({\mdseries\slshape matgrp})\index{TransposedMatrixGroup@\texttt{TransposedMatrixGroup}}
\label{TransposedMatrixGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the transpose of the matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. The transpose of the transpose of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} is identical to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group( [[0,-1],[1,0]] );|
  Group([ [ [ 0, -1 ], [ 1, 0 ] ] ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@T := TransposedMatrixGroup( G );|
  Group([ [ [ 0, 1 ], [ -1, 0 ] ] ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsIdenticalObj( G, TransposedMatrixGroup( T ) );|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Actions of Matrix Groups}}\label{Actions of Matrix Groups}
\logpage{[ 44, 3, 0 ]}

{
  The basic operations for groups are described in Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Group Actions}, special actions for \emph{matrix} groups mentioned there are \texttt{OnLines} (\ref{OnLines}), \texttt{OnRight} (\ref{OnRight}), and \texttt{OnSubspacesByCanonicalBasis} (\ref{OnSubspacesByCanonicalBasis}).  

 For subtleties concerning multiplication from the left or from the right,

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ProjectiveActionOnFullSpace}}
\logpage{[ 44, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BD4F38E8624735D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ProjectiveActionOnFullSpace({\mdseries\slshape G, F, n})\index{ProjectiveActionOnFullSpace@\texttt{ProjectiveActionOnFullSpace}}
\label{ProjectiveActionOnFullSpace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} be a group of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} matrices over a field contained in the finite field \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}.   \texttt{ProjectiveActionOnFullSpace} returns the image of the projective action of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} on the full row space $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}^{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}}$. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ProjectiveActionHomomorphismMatrixGroup}}
\logpage{[ 44, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F8EA8D583C1E9B2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ProjectiveActionHomomorphismMatrixGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{ProjectiveActionHomomorphismMatrixGroup@\texttt{Projective}\-\texttt{Action}\-\texttt{Homomorphism}\-\texttt{Matrix}\-\texttt{Group}}
\label{ProjectiveActionHomomorphismMatrixGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns an action homomorphism for a faithful projective action of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} on the underlying vector space. (Note: The action is not necessarily on the
full space, if a smaller subset can be found on which the action is faithful.) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{BlowUpIsomorphism}}
\logpage{[ 44, 3, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X849C451A80B4A210}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{BlowUpIsomorphism({\mdseries\slshape matgrp, B})\index{BlowUpIsomorphism@\texttt{BlowUpIsomorphism}}
\label{BlowUpIsomorphism}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For a matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} and a basis \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape B}} of a field extension $L / K$ such that the entries of all matrices in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} lie in $L$, \texttt{BlowUpIsomorphism} returns the isomorphism with source \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} that is defined by mapping the matrix $A$ to \texttt{BlownUpMat}$( A, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape B}} )$, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{BlownUpMat} (\ref{BlownUpMat}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= GL(2,4);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@B:= CanonicalBasis( GF(4) );;  BasisVectors( B );|
  [ Z(2)^0, Z(2^2) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@iso:= BlowUpIsomorphism( g, B );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Display( Image( iso, [ [ Z(4), Z(2) ], [ 0*Z(2), Z(4)^2 ] ] ) );|
   . 1 1 .
   1 1 . 1
   . . 1 1
   . . 1 .
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@img:= Image( iso, g );|
  <matrix group with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Index( GL(4,2), img );|
  112
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsGeneralLinearGroup}}

\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Invariant Forms}}\label{Invariant Forms}
\logpage{[ 44, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7CA4097C79F5BD90}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InvariantBilinearForm}}
\logpage{[ 44, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C08385A81AB05E1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InvariantBilinearForm({\mdseries\slshape matgrp})\index{InvariantBilinearForm@\texttt{InvariantBilinearForm}}
\label{InvariantBilinearForm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For a matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}, \texttt{InvariantBilinearForm} returns a record containing at least the components \texttt{matrix}, whose value is a matrix $M$, and \texttt{baseDomain}, whose value is a field. 

 This record describes a bilinear form that is invariant under \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. For every generator $g$ of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}, the equation $g \cdot M \cdot g^{tr} = M$ holds. 

 The attribute value is set for example in groups constructed with \texttt{SymplecticGroup} (\ref{SymplecticGroup:for dimension and field size}). Together with \texttt{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingBilinearForm} (\ref{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingBilinearForm}), it can be used for efficient membership tests in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingBilinearForm}}
\logpage{[ 44, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8652FBF781940AC3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingBilinearForm({\mdseries\slshape matgrp})\index{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingBilinearForm@\texttt{IsFull}\-\texttt{Subgroup}\-\texttt{G}\-\texttt{Lor}\-\texttt{S}\-\texttt{L}\-\texttt{Respecting}\-\texttt{Bilinear}\-\texttt{Form}}
\label{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingBilinearForm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 If this property is set then the matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} is the full subgroup of \texttt{GL}$(d, q)$ or \texttt{SL}$(d, q)$ respecting the form stored as the value of \texttt{InvariantBilinearForm} (\ref{InvariantBilinearForm}) for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. 

 The value $d$ is the \texttt{DimensionOfMatrixGroup} (\ref{DimensionOfMatrixGroup}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}, and $q$ is the size of the \texttt{baseDomain} component of the record stored as \texttt{InvariantBilinearForm} (\ref{InvariantBilinearForm}). 

 The property \texttt{IsSubgroupSL} (\ref{IsSubgroupSL}) of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} determines whether \texttt{GL} or \texttt{SL} is meant for \texttt{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingBilinearForm}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InvariantBilinearFormUpToScalars}}
\logpage{[ 44, 5, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78B2705B87ED5384}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InvariantBilinearFormUpToScalars({\mdseries\slshape matgrp})\index{InvariantBilinearFormUpToScalars@\texttt{InvariantBilinearFormUpToScalars}}
\label{InvariantBilinearFormUpToScalars}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 This attribute describes a bilinear form that is invariant up to scalars under
the matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. The form is given by a record with the component \texttt{matrix} which is a matrix $J$ such that for every generator $g$ of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} the equation $g \cdot J \cdot g^{tr} = \lambda(g) J$ holds, for $\lambda(g)$ in the \texttt{FieldOfMatrixGroup} (\ref{FieldOfMatrixGroup}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsFullSubgroupGLRespectingBilinearFormUpToScalars}}
\logpage{[ 44, 5, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8461A2D87E4208EF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsFullSubgroupGLRespectingBilinearFormUpToScalars({\mdseries\slshape matgrp})\index{IsFullSubgroupGLRespectingBilinearFormUpToScalars@\texttt{IsFull}\-\texttt{Subgroup}\-\texttt{G}\-\texttt{L}\-\texttt{Respecting}\-\texttt{Bilinear}\-\texttt{Form}\-\texttt{Up}\-\texttt{To}\-\texttt{Scalars}}
\label{IsFullSubgroupGLRespectingBilinearFormUpToScalars}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 This property tests whether the matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} is the full subgroup of GL respecting, up to scalars, the form stored as the
value of \texttt{InvariantBilinearFormUpToScalars} (\ref{InvariantBilinearFormUpToScalars}) for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InvariantSesquilinearForm}}
\logpage{[ 44, 5, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82F22079852130C9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InvariantSesquilinearForm({\mdseries\slshape matgrp})\index{InvariantSesquilinearForm@\texttt{InvariantSesquilinearForm}}
\label{InvariantSesquilinearForm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For a matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}, \texttt{InvariantSesquilinearForm} returns a record containing at least the components \texttt{matrix}, whose value is a matrix $M$, and \texttt{baseDomain}, whose value is a field $F$. 

 This record describes a sesquilinear form that is invariant under \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. For every generator $g$ of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}, the equation $g \cdot M \cdot (g^{tr})^f = M$ holds, where $f$ is an automorphism of $F$. If $F$ has $q^2$ elements then $f$ raises each element of $F$ to its $q$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power. ($f$ can be obtained as a power of the \texttt{FrobeniusAutomorphism} (\ref{FrobeniusAutomorphism}) value of $F$.) 

 The attribute value is set for example in groups constructed with \texttt{GeneralUnitaryGroup} (\ref{GeneralUnitaryGroup}). Together with \texttt{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingSesquilinearForm} (\ref{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingSesquilinearForm}), it can be used for efficient membership tests in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingSesquilinearForm}}
\logpage{[ 44, 5, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B35A8AF7D8F0313}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingSesquilinearForm({\mdseries\slshape matgrp})\index{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingSesquilinearForm@\texttt{IsFull}\-\texttt{Subgroup}\-\texttt{G}\-\texttt{Lor}\-\texttt{S}\-\texttt{L}\-\texttt{Respecting}\-\texttt{Sesquilinear}\-\texttt{Form}}
\label{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingSesquilinearForm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 If this property is set then the matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} is the full subgroup of \texttt{GL}$(d, q)$ or \texttt{SL}$(d, q)$ respecting the form stored as the value of \texttt{InvariantSesquilinearForm} (\ref{InvariantSesquilinearForm}) for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. 

 The value $d$ is the \texttt{DimensionOfMatrixGroup} (\ref{DimensionOfMatrixGroup}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}, and $q$ is the size of the \texttt{baseDomain} component of the record stored as \texttt{InvariantSesquilinearForm} (\ref{InvariantSesquilinearForm}). 

 The property \texttt{IsSubgroupSL} (\ref{IsSubgroupSL}) of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} determines whether \texttt{GL} or \texttt{SL} is meant for \texttt{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingSesquilinearForm}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InvariantQuadraticForm}}
\logpage{[ 44, 5, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BCACC007EB9B613}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InvariantQuadraticForm({\mdseries\slshape matgrp})\index{InvariantQuadraticForm@\texttt{InvariantQuadraticForm}}
\label{InvariantQuadraticForm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For a matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}, \texttt{InvariantQuadraticForm} returns a record containing at least the components \texttt{matrix}, whose value is a matrix $Q$, and \texttt{baseDomain}, whose value is a field $F$. 

 The quadratic form $q$ on the natural $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}vector space $V$ on which \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} acts is given by $q(v) = v Q v^{tr}$, and the invariance under \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} is given by the equation $q(v) = q(v M)$ for all $v \in V$ and $M$ in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. (Note that the invariance of $q$ does \emph{not} imply that the matrix $Q$ is invariant under \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}.) 

 The function $q$ is defined relative to an invariant symmetric bilinear form $b$ (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{InvariantBilinearForm} (\ref{InvariantBilinearForm})), via the equation $q(\lambda x + \mu y) = \lambda^2 q(x) + \lambda \mu b(x,y) + \mu^2 q(y)$, see \cite[Chapter 3.4]{CCN85}. If $b$ is represented by the matrix $B$ then this implies $B = Q + Q^{tr}$. In characteristic different from $2$, we have $q(x) = b(x,x)/2$, so $Q$ can be chosen as the strictly upper triangular part of $B$ plus half of the diagonal part of $B$. In characteristic $2$, $B$ does not determine $Q$ but still $Q$ can be chosen as an upper (or lower) triangular matrix. 

 Whenever the \texttt{InvariantQuadraticForm} value is set in a matrix group then also the \texttt{InvariantBilinearForm} (\ref{InvariantBilinearForm}) value can be accessed, and the two values are compatible in the above sense. 

 The attribute value is set for example in groups constructed with \texttt{GeneralOrthogonalGroup} (\ref{GeneralOrthogonalGroup}). Together with \texttt{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingQuadraticForm} (\ref{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingQuadraticForm}), it can be used for efficient membership tests in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingQuadraticForm}}
\logpage{[ 44, 5, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84AB04A67DFC0274}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingQuadraticForm({\mdseries\slshape matgrp})\index{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingQuadraticForm@\texttt{IsFull}\-\texttt{Subgroup}\-\texttt{G}\-\texttt{Lor}\-\texttt{S}\-\texttt{L}\-\texttt{Respecting}\-\texttt{Quadratic}\-\texttt{Form}}
\label{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingQuadraticForm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 If this property is set then the matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} is the full subgroup of \texttt{GL}$(d, q)$ or \texttt{SL}$(d, q)$ respecting the form stored as the value of \texttt{InvariantQuadraticForm} (\ref{InvariantQuadraticForm}) for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}. 

 The value $d$ is the \texttt{DimensionOfMatrixGroup} (\ref{DimensionOfMatrixGroup}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}}, and $q$ is the size of the \texttt{baseDomain} component of the record stored as \texttt{InvariantQuadraticForm} (\ref{InvariantQuadraticForm}). 

 The property \texttt{IsSubgroupSL} (\ref{IsSubgroupSL}) of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape matgrp}} determines whether \texttt{GL} or \texttt{SL} is meant for \texttt{IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingQuadraticForm}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Sp( 2, 3 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@m:= InvariantBilinearForm( g ).matrix;|
  [ [ 0*Z(3), Z(3)^0 ], [ Z(3), 0*Z(3) ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@[ 0, 1 ] * m * [ 1, -1 ];       # evaluate the bilinear form|
  Z(3)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingBilinearForm( g );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= SU( 2, 4 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@m:= InvariantSesquilinearForm( g ).matrix;|
  [ [ 0*Z(2), Z(2)^0 ], [ Z(2)^0, 0*Z(2) ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@[ 0, 1 ] * m * [ 1, 1 ];        # evaluate the sesquilinear form|
  Z(2)^0
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingSesquilinearForm( g );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsSubgroupSL( g );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= GO( 1, 2, 3 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@m:= InvariantBilinearForm( g ).matrix;|
  [ [ 0*Z(3), Z(3)^0 ], [ Z(3)^0, 0*Z(3) ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@[ 0, 1 ] * m * [ 1, 1 ];        # evaluate the bilinear form|
  Z(3)^0
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@q:= InvariantQuadraticForm( g ).matrix;|
  [ [ 0*Z(3), Z(3)^0 ], [ 0*Z(3), 0*Z(3) ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@[ 0, 1 ] * q * [ 0, 1 ];        # evaluate the quadratic form|
  0*Z(3)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsFullSubgroupGLorSLRespectingQuadraticForm( g );|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

 tests whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is $SL_n({\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}})$ in its natural representation by $n \times n$ integer matrices. (The dimension $n$ will be read off the generating matrices.)

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InvariantLattice}}

{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InvariantLattice({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{InvariantLattice@\texttt{InvariantLattice}}
\label{InvariantLattice}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns a matrix $B$, whose rows form a basis of a ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$\texttt{\symbol{45}}lattice that is invariant under the rational matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} acting from the right. It returns \texttt{fail} if the group is not unimodular. The columns of the inverse of $B$ span a ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$\texttt{\symbol{45}}lattice invariant under \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} acting from the left. }

 is an attribute used to store the normalizer of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} in $GL_n({\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}})$, where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is an integer matrix group of dimension \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. \subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CentralizerInGLnZ}}
