\label{CentralizerInGLnZ}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 is an attribute used to store the centralizer of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} in $GL_n({\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}})$, where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is an integer matrix group of dimension \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. This attribute is used by \texttt{Centralizer( GL( n, Integers ), G )}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ZClassRepsQClass}}
\logpage{[ 44, 6, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8217762A863F1382}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZClassRepsQClass({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{ZClassRepsQClass@\texttt{ZClassRepsQClass}}
\label{ZClassRepsQClass}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 The conjugacy class in $GL_n({\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}})$ of the finite integer matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} splits into finitely many conjugacy classes in $GL_n({\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}})$. \texttt{ZClassRepsQClass( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} )} returns representative groups for these. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsBravaisGroup}}
\logpage{[ 44, 6, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84FD9FC97FB90795}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsBravaisGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{IsBravaisGroup@\texttt{IsBravaisGroup}}
\label{IsBravaisGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 test whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} coincides with its Bravais group (see \texttt{BravaisGroup} (\ref{BravaisGroup})). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{BravaisGroup}}
\logpage{[ 44, 6, 11 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7AAE301C83116451}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{BravaisGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{BravaisGroup@\texttt{BravaisGroup}}
\label{BravaisGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the Bravais group of a finite integer matrix group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. If $C$ is the cone of positive definite quadratic forms $Q$ invariant under $g \mapsto g Q g^{tr}$ for all $g \in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}$, then the Bravais group of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is the maximal subgroup of $GL_n({\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}})$ leaving the forms in that same cone invariant. Alternatively, the Bravais
group of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} can also be defined with respect to the action $g \mapsto g^{tr} Q g$ on positive definite quadratic forms $Q$. This latter definition is appropriate for groups \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} acting from the right on row vectors, whereas the former definition is
appropriate for groups acting from the left on column vectors. Both
definitions yield the same Bravais group. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{BravaisSubgroups}}

\hyperdef{L}{X788C7D9C7C2301C5}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{BravaisSubgroups({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{BravaisSubgroups@\texttt{BravaisSubgroups}}
\label{BravaisSubgroups}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the subgroups of the Bravais group of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, which are themselves Bravais groups. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{BravaisSupergroups}}
\logpage{[ 44, 6, 13 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F5FF1A481E08AD5}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{BravaisSupergroups({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{BravaisSupergroups@\texttt{BravaisSupergroups}}
\label{BravaisSupergroups}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the subgroups of $GL_n({\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}})$ that contain the Bravais group of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} and are Bravais groups themselves. }

\label{NormalizerInGLnZBravaisGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the normalizer of the Bravais group of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} in the appropriate $GL_n({\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}})$. }

\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Acting OnRight and OnLeft}}\label{Acting OnRight and OnLeft}
\logpage{[ 44, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X868288377CFA8D1B}{}
{
  In \textsf{GAP}, matrices by convention act on row vectors from the right, whereas in
crystallography the convention is to act on column vectors from the left. The
definition of certain algebraic objects important in crystallography
implicitly depends on which action is assumed. This holds true in particular
for quadratic forms invariant under a matrix group. In a similar way, the
representation of affine crystallographic groups, as they are provided by the \textsf{GAP} package \textsf{CrystGap}, depends on which action is assumed. Crystallographers are used to the action
from the left, whereas the action from the right is the natural one for \textsf{GAP}. For this reason, a number of functions which are important in
crystallography, and whose result depends on which action is assumed, are
provided in two versions, one for the usual action from the right, and one for
the crystallographic action from the left. 

 For every such function, this fact is explicitly mentioned. The naming scheme
is as follows: If \texttt{SomeThing} is such a function, there will be functions \texttt{SomeThingOnRight} and \texttt{SomeThingOnLeft}, assuming action from the right and from the left, respectively. In addition,
there is a generic function \texttt{SomeThing}, which returns either the result of \texttt{SomeThingOnRight} or \texttt{SomeThingOnLeft}, depending on the global variable \texttt{CrystGroupDefaultAction} (\ref{CrystGroupDefaultAction}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CrystGroupDefaultAction}}
\logpage{[ 44, 7, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D1318A6780CD88B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CrystGroupDefaultAction\index{CrystGroupDefaultAction@\texttt{CrystGroupDefaultAction}}
\label{CrystGroupDefaultAction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 can have either of the two values \texttt{RightAction} and \texttt{LeftAction}. The initial value is \texttt{RightAction}. For functions which have variants OnRight and OnLeft, this variable
determines which variant is returned by the generic form. The value of \texttt{CrystGroupDefaultAction} can be changed with the function \texttt{SetCrystGroupDefaultAction} (\ref{SetCrystGroupDefaultAction}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetCrystGroupDefaultAction}}
\logpage{[ 44, 7, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X792D237385977BE6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetCrystGroupDefaultAction({\mdseries\slshape action})\index{SetCrystGroupDefaultAction@\texttt{SetCrystGroupDefaultAction}}
\label{SetCrystGroupDefaultAction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 allows one to set the value of the global variable \texttt{CrystGroupDefaultAction} (\ref{CrystGroupDefaultAction}). Only the arguments \texttt{RightAction} and \texttt{LeftAction} are allowed. Initially, the value of \texttt{CrystGroupDefaultAction} (\ref{CrystGroupDefaultAction}) is \texttt{RightAction}. }

 }

 }

             
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Polycyclic Groups}}\label{Polycyclic Groups}
\logpage{[ 45, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86007B0083F60470}{}
{
  A group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is \emph{polycyclic} if there exists a subnormal series $G = C_1 > C_2 > \ldots > C_n > C_{{n+1}} = \{ 1 \}$ with cyclic factors. Such a series is called \emph{pc series} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 

 Every polycyclic group is solvable and every finite solvable group is
polycyclic. However, there are infinite solvable groups which are not
polycyclic. 

 In \textsf{GAP} there exists a large number of methods for polycyclic groups which are based
upon the polycyclic structure of these groups. These methods are usually very
efficient, especially for groups which are given by a
pc\texttt{\symbol{45}}presentation (see chapter \ref{Pc Groups}), and can be applied to many types of groups. Hence \textsf{GAP} tries to use them whenever possible, for example, for permutation groups and
matrix groups over finite fields that are known to be polycyclic (the only
exception is the representation as finitely presented group for which the
polycyclic methods cannot be used in general). 

 At the current state of implementations the \textsf{GAP} library contains methods to compute with finite polycyclic groups, while the \textsf{GAP} package \textsf{Polycyclic} by Bettina Eick and Werner Nickel allows also computations with infinite
polycyclic groups which are given by a pc\texttt{\symbol{45}}presentation. 

     
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Polycyclic Generating Systems}}\label{Polycyclic Generating Systems}
\logpage{[ 45, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7F18A01785DBAC4E}{}
{
  Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} be a polycyclic group with a pc series as above. A \emph{polycyclic generating sequence} (\emph{pcgs} for short) of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is a sequence $P := (g_1, \ldots, g_n)$ of elements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} such that $C_i = \langle C_{{i+1}}, g_i \rangle$ for $1 \leq i \leq n$. Note that each polycyclic group has a pcgs, but except for very small
groups, a pcgs is not unique. 

 For each index $i$ the subsequence of elements $(g_i, \ldots, g_n)$ forms a pcgs of the subgroup $C_i$. In particular, these \emph{tails} generate the subgroups of the pc series and hence we say that the pc series is \emph{determined} by $P$. 

 Let $r_i$ be the index of $C_{{i+1}}$ in $C_i$ which is either a finite positive number or infinity. Then $r_i$ is the order of $g_i C_{{i+1}}$ and we call the resulting list of indices the \emph{relative orders} of the pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}. 

 Moreover, with respect to a given pcgs $(g_1, \ldots, g_n)$ each element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} can be represented in a unique way as a product $g = g_1^{{e_1}} \cdot g_2^{{e_2}} \cdots g_n^{{e_n}}$ with exponents $e_i \in \{0, \ldots, r_i-1\}$, if $r_i$ is finite, and $e_i \in {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ otherwise. Words of this form are called \emph{normal words} or \emph{words in normal form}. Then the integer vector $[ e_1, \ldots, e_n ]$ is called the \emph{exponent vector} of the element $g$. Furthermore, the smallest index $k$ such that $e_k \neq 0$ is called the \emph{depth} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} and $e_k$ is the \emph{leading exponent} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}. 

 For many applications we have to assume that each of the relative orders $r_i$ is either a prime or infinity. This is equivalent to saying that there are no
trivial factors in the pc series and the finite factors of the pc series are
maximal refined. Then we obtain that $r_i$ is the order of $g C_{{i+1}}$ for all elements $g$ in $C_i \setminus C_{{i+1}}$ and we call $r_i$ the \emph{relative order} of the element $g$. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Computing a Pcgs}}\label{Computing a Pcgs}
\logpage{[ 45, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X87F7E31879AFA06C}{}
{
  Suppose a group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is given; for example, let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} be a permutation or matrix group. Then we can ask \textsf{GAP} to compute a pcgs of this group. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is not polycyclic, the result will be \texttt{fail}. 

 Note that these methods can only be applied if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is not given as finitely presented group. For finitely presented groups one
can try to compute a pcgs via the polycyclic quotient methods, see \ref{Quotient Methods}. 

 Note also that a pcgs behaves like a list. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Pcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84C3750C7A4EEC34}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Pcgs({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{Pcgs@\texttt{Pcgs}}
\label{Pcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns a pcgs for the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape grp}} is not polycyclic it returns \texttt{fail} \emph{and this result is not stored as attribute value}, in particular in this case the filter \texttt{HasPcgs} is \emph{not} set for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}! }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8635E61A7DB73BA6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPcgs({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsPcgs@\texttt{IsPcgs}}
\label{IsPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 The category of pcgs. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group((1,2,3,4),(1,2));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p := Pcgs(G);|
  Pcgs([ (3,4), (2,4,3), (1,4)(2,3), (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPcgs( p );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p[1];|
  (3,4)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group((1,2,3,4,5),(1,2));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Pcgs(G);|
  fail
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CanEasilyComputePcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 2, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B561B1685CEC2AB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CanEasilyComputePcgs({\mdseries\slshape grp})\index{CanEasilyComputePcgs@\texttt{CanEasilyComputePcgs}}
\label{CanEasilyComputePcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (filter)}}\\


 This filter indicates whether it is possible to compute a pcgs for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape grp}} cheaply. Clearly, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape grp}} must be polycyclic in this case. However, not for every polycyclic group there
is a method to compute a pcgs at low costs. This filter is used in the method
selection mainly. Note that this filter may change its value from \texttt{false} to \texttt{true}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group( (1,2,3,4),(1,2) );|
  Group([ (1,2,3,4), (1,2) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CanEasilyComputePcgs(G);|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Pcgs(G);|
  Pcgs([ (3,4), (2,4,3), (1,4)(2,3), (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CanEasilyComputePcgs(G);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Defining a Pcgs Yourself}}\label{Defining a Pcgs Yourself}
\logpage{[ 45, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7CAAD6D2838354D9}{}
{
  In a number of situations it might be useful to supply a pcgs to a group. 

 Note that the elementary operations for such a pcgs might be rather
inefficient, since \textsf{GAP} has to use generic methods in this case. It might be helpful to supply the
relative orders of the self\texttt{\symbol{45}}defined pcgs as well by \texttt{SetRelativeOrder}. See also{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsPrimeOrdersPcgs} (\ref{IsPrimeOrdersPcgs}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PcgsByPcSequence}}
\logpage{[ 45, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E139C3D80847D76}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PcgsByPcSequence({\mdseries\slshape fam, pcs})\index{PcgsByPcSequence@\texttt{PcgsByPcSequence}}
\label{PcgsByPcSequence}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PcgsByPcSequenceNC({\mdseries\slshape fam, pcs})\index{PcgsByPcSequenceNC@\texttt{PcgsByPcSequenceNC}}
\label{PcgsByPcSequenceNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 constructs a pcgs for the elements family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}} from the elements in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcs}}. The elements must lie in the family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}}. \texttt{PcgsByPcSequence} and its \texttt{NC} variant will always create a new pcgs which is not induced by any other pcgs
(cf. \texttt{InducedPcgsByPcSequence} (\ref{InducedPcgsByPcSequence})). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@fam := FamilyObj( (1,2) );; # the family of permutations|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p := PcgsByPcSequence( fam, [(1,2),(1,2,3)] );|
  Pcgs([ (1,2), (1,2,3) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RelativeOrders(p);|
  [ 2, 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ExponentsOfPcElement( p, (1,3,2) );|
  [ 0, 2 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PcElementByExponentsNC({\mdseries\slshape pcgs[, basisind], list})\index{PcElementByExponentsNC@\texttt{PcElementByExponentsNC}}
\label{PcElementByExponentsNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the element corresponding to the exponent vector \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. The exponents in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} must be in the range of permissible exponents for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. \emph{It is not guaranteed that \texttt{PcElementByExponents} will reduce the exponents modulo the relative orders}. (You should use the operation \texttt{LinearCombinationPcgs} (\ref{LinearCombinationPcgs}) for this purpose.) The \texttt{NC} version does not check that the lengths of the lists fit together and does not
check the exponent range. 

 The three argument version gives exponents only w.r.t. the generators in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} indexed by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape basisind}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LinearCombinationPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 5, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F8BD7A87DB3933A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LinearCombinationPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, list[, one]})\index{LinearCombinationPcgs@\texttt{LinearCombinationPcgs}}
\label{LinearCombinationPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the product $\prod_i \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}[i]^{{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}[i]}}$. In contrast to \texttt{PcElementByExponents} (\ref{PcElementByExponents}) this permits negative exponents. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} might be a list of group elements. In this case, an appropriate identity
element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape one}} must be given. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} can be empty. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group( (1,2,3,4),(1,2) );; P := Pcgs(G);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g := PcElementByExponents(P, [0,1,1,1]);|
  (1,2,3)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ExponentsOfPcElement(P, g);|
  [ 0, 1, 1, 1 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SiftedPcElement}}
\logpage{[ 45, 5, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8066B66D8069BAB4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SiftedPcElement({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, elm})\index{SiftedPcElement@\texttt{SiftedPcElement}}
\label{SiftedPcElement}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 sifts \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} through \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}, reducing it if the depth is the same as the depth of one of the generators
in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. Thus the identity is returned if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} lies in the group generated by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} must be an induced pcgs (see section \ref{Subgroups of Polycyclic Groups - Induced Pcgs}) and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} must lie in the span of the parent of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CanonicalPcElement}}
\logpage{[ 45, 5, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B52ADE7878A749A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CanonicalPcElement({\mdseries\slshape ipcgs, elm})\index{CanonicalPcElement@\texttt{CanonicalPcElement}}
\label{CanonicalPcElement}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 reduces \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} at the induces pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ipcgs}} such that the exponents of the reduced result \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} are zero at the depths for which there are generators in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ipcgs}}. Elements, whose quotient lies in the group generated by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ipcgs}} yield the same canonical element. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ReducedPcElement}}
\logpage{[ 45, 5, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A94AA357DB2F86C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ReducedPcElement({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, x, y})\index{ReducedPcElement@\texttt{ReducedPcElement}}
\label{ReducedPcElement}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 reduces the element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape x}} by dividing off (from the left) a power of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape y}} such that the leading coefficient of the result with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} becomes zero. The elements \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape x}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape y}} therefore have to have the same depth. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CleanedTailPcElement}}
\logpage{[ 45, 5, 11 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8702D76D8284CF3E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CleanedTailPcElement({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, elm, dep})\index{CleanedTailPcElement@\texttt{CleanedTailPcElement}}
\label{CleanedTailPcElement}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns an element in the span of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} whose exponents for indices $1$ to $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dep}}-1$ with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} are the same as those of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}, the remaining exponents are undefined. This can be used to obtain more ``simple'' elements if only representatives in a factor are required, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Factor Groups of Polycyclic Groups - Modulo Pcgs}. 

 The difference to \texttt{HeadPcElementByNumber} (\ref{HeadPcElementByNumber}) is that this function is guaranteed to zero out trailing coefficients while \texttt{CleanedTailPcElement} will only do this if it can be done cheaply. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{HeadPcElementByNumber}}
\logpage{[ 45, 5, 12 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X830A0D037DBEAA97}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{HeadPcElementByNumber({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, elm, dep})\index{HeadPcElementByNumber@\texttt{HeadPcElementByNumber}}
\label{HeadPcElementByNumber}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns an element in the span of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} whose exponents for indices $1$ to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dep}}$-1$ with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} are the same as those of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}, the remaining exponents are zero. This can be used to obtain more ``simple'' elements if only representatives in a factor are required. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Exponents of Special Products}}\label{Exponents of Special Products}
\logpage{[ 45, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7EF61EA4822870E7}{}
{
  There are certain products of elements whose exponents are used often within
algorithms, and which might be obtained more easily than by computing the
product first and to obtain its exponents afterwards. The operations in this
section provide a way to obtain such exponent vectors directly. 

 (The circumstances under which these operations give a speedup depend very
much on the pcgs and the representation of elements that is used. So the
following operations are not guaranteed to give a speedup in every case,
however the default methods are not slower than to compute the exponents of a
product and thus these operations should \emph{always} be used if applicable.) 

 The second class are exponents of products of the generators which make up the
pcgs. If the pcgs used is a family pcgs (see \texttt{FamilyPcgs} (\ref{FamilyPcgs})) then these exponents can be looked up and do not need to be computed. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ExponentsConjugateLayer}}
\logpage{[ 45, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X868D6DB07D349460}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExponentsConjugateLayer({\mdseries\slshape mpcgs, elm, e})\index{ExponentsConjugateLayer@\texttt{ExponentsConjugateLayer}}
\label{ExponentsConjugateLayer}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Computes the exponents of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape e}} with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mpcgs}}; \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} must be in the span of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mpcgs}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape e}} a pc element in the span of the parent pcgs of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mpcgs}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mpcgs}} must be the modulo pcgs for an abelian layer. (This is the usual case when
acting on a chief factor). In this case if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mpcgs}} is induced by the family pcgs (see section \ref{Subgroups of Polycyclic Groups - Induced Pcgs}), the exponents can be computed directly by looking up exponents without
having to compute in the group and having to collect a potential tail. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ExponentsOfRelativePower}}
\logpage{[ 45, 6, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X874F70697FE7B6DF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExponentsOfRelativePower({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, i})\index{ExponentsOfRelativePower@\texttt{ExponentsOfRelativePower}}
\label{ExponentsOfRelativePower}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 For $p = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}}]$ this function returns the exponent vector with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} of the element $p^e$ where $e$ is the relative order of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. For the family pcgs or pcgs induced by it (see section \ref{Subgroups of Polycyclic Groups - Induced Pcgs}), this might be faster than computing the element and computing its exponent
vector. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ExponentsOfConjugate}}
\logpage{[ 45, 6, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78CAF32F864EF656}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExponentsOfConjugate({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, i, j})\index{ExponentsOfConjugate@\texttt{ExponentsOfConjugate}}
\label{ExponentsOfConjugate}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the exponents of \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}}]\texttt{\symbol{94}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape j}}]} with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. For the family pcgs or pcgs induced by it (see section \ref{Subgroups of Polycyclic Groups - Induced Pcgs}), this might be faster than computing the element and computing its exponent
vector. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ExponentsOfCommutator}}
\logpage{[ 45, 6, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X875689897DD0CAFC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExponentsOfCommutator({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, i, j})\index{ExponentsOfCommutator@\texttt{ExponentsOfCommutator}}
\label{ExponentsOfCommutator}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the exponents of the commutator \texttt{Comm( }$\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}}], \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape j}}]$\texttt{ )} with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. For the family pcgs or pcgs induced by it, (see section \ref{Subgroups of Polycyclic Groups - Induced Pcgs}), this might be faster than computing the element and computing its exponent
vector. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Subgroups of Polycyclic Groups {\textendash} Induced Pcgs}}\label{Subgroups of Polycyclic Groups - Induced Pcgs}
\logpage{[ 45, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8676397383093D1E}{}
{
  Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} be a subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} and let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} be a pcgs of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} as above such that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} determines the subnormal series $G = C_1 > \ldots > C_{{n+1}} = \{ 1 \}$. Then the series of subgroups $U \cap C_i$ is a subnormal series of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} with cyclic or trivial factors. Hence, if we choose an element $u_{{i_j}} \in (U \cap C_{{i_j}}) \setminus (U \cap C_{{i_j+1}})$ whenever this factor is non\texttt{\symbol{45}}trivial, then we obtain a pcgs $Q = (u_{{i_1}}, \ldots, u_{{i_m}})$ of $U$. We say that $Q$ is an \emph{induced pcgs} with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}. The pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} is the \emph{parent pcgs} to the induced pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Q}}. 

 Note that the pcgs $Q$ is induced with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} if and only if the matrix of exponent vectors of the elements $u_{{i_j}}$ with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} is in upper triangular form. Thus $Q$ is not unique in general. 

 In particular, the elements of an induced pcgs do \emph{not necessarily} have leading coefficient 1 relative to the inducing pcgs. The attribute \texttt{LeadCoeffsIGS} (\ref{LeadCoeffsIGS}) holds the leading coefficients in case they have to be renormed in an
algorithm. 

 Each induced pcgs is a pcgs and hence allows all elementary operations for
pcgs. On the other hand each pcgs could be transformed into an induced pcgs
for the group defined by the pcgs, but note that an arbitrary pcgs is in
general not an induced pcgs for technical reasons. 

 An induced pcgs is ``compatible'' with its parent, see \texttt{ParentPcgs} (\ref{ParentPcgs}). 

 In \cite{SOGOS} a ``non\texttt{\symbol{45}}commutative Gauss'' algorithm is described to compute an induced pcgs of a subgroup \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} from a generating set of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}}. For calling this in \textsf{GAP}, see \ref{InducedPcgs} to \ref{ExtendedPcgs}. 

 To create a subgroup generated by an induced pcgs such that the induced pcgs
gets stored automatically, use \texttt{SubgroupByPcgs} (\ref{SubgroupByPcgs}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsInducedPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 7, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81FA878C854D63F8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsInducedPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IsInducedPcgs@\texttt{IsInducedPcgs}}
\label{IsInducedPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 The category of induced pcgs. This a subcategory of pcgs. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InducedPcgsByPcSequence}}
\logpage{[ 45, 7, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83F6759184937F1B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InducedPcgsByPcSequence({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, pcs})\index{InducedPcgsByPcSequence@\texttt{InducedPcgsByPcSequence}}
\label{InducedPcgsByPcSequence}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InducedPcgsByPcSequenceNC({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, pcs[, depths]})\index{InducedPcgsByPcSequenceNC@\texttt{InducedPcgsByPcSequenceNC}}
\label{InducedPcgsByPcSequenceNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcs}} is a list of elements that form an induced pcgs with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} this operation returns an induced pcgs with these elements. 

 In the third version, the depths of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcs}} with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} can be given (they are computed anew otherwise). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ParentPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 7, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86308E80843BF9E5}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ParentPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{ParentPcgs@\texttt{ParentPcgs}}
\label{ParentPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the pcgs by which \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} was induced. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} was not induced, it simply returns \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group( (1,2,3,4),(1,2) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@P := Pcgs(G);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@K := InducedPcgsByPcSequence( P, [(1,2,3,4),(1,3)(2,4)] );|
  Pcgs([ (1,2,3,4), (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ParentPcgs( K );|
  Pcgs([ (3,4), (2,4,3), (1,4)(2,3), (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsInducedPcgs( K );|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InducedPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 7, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F0EB20080590B23}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InducedPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, grp})\index{InducedPcgs@\texttt{InducedPcgs}}
\label{InducedPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 computes a pcgs for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape grp}} which is induced by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} has a parent pcgs, then the result is induced with respect to this parent
pcgs. 

 \texttt{InducedPcgs} is a wrapper function only. Therefore, methods for computing an induced pcgs
should be installed for the operation \texttt{InducedPcgsOp}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InducedPcgsByGenerators}}
\logpage{[ 45, 7, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8332F1197DF6FEDE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InducedPcgsByGenerators({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, gens})\index{InducedPcgsByGenerators@\texttt{InducedPcgsByGenerators}}
\label{InducedPcgsByGenerators}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InducedPcgsByGeneratorsNC({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, gens})\index{InducedPcgsByGeneratorsNC@\texttt{InducedPcgsByGeneratorsNC}}
\label{InducedPcgsByGeneratorsNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns an induced pcgs with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} for the subgroup generated by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InducedPcgsByPcSequenceAndGenerators}}
\logpage{[ 45, 7, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7AF82BD079D811E5}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InducedPcgsByPcSequenceAndGenerators({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, ind, gens})\index{InducedPcgsByPcSequenceAndGenerators@\texttt{Induced}\-\texttt{Pcgs}\-\texttt{By}\-\texttt{Pc}\-\texttt{Sequence}\-\texttt{And}\-\texttt{Generators}}
\label{InducedPcgsByPcSequenceAndGenerators}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns an induced pcgs with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} of the subgroup generated by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. Here \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}} must be an induced pcgs with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} (or a list of group elements that form such an igs) and it will be used as
initial sequence for the computation. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group( (1,2,3,4),(1,2) );;  P := Pcgs(G);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@I := InducedPcgsByGenerators( P, [(1,2,3,4)] );|
  Pcgs([ (1,2,3,4), (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@J := InducedPcgsByPcSequenceAndGenerators( P, I, [(1,2)] );|
  Pcgs([ (1,2,3,4), (2,4,3), (1,4)(2,3), (1,3)(2,4) ])
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LeadCoeffsIGS}}
\logpage{[ 45, 7, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X845FF8CA783D6CB3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LeadCoeffsIGS({\mdseries\slshape igs})\index{LeadCoeffsIGS@\texttt{LeadCoeffsIGS}}
\label{LeadCoeffsIGS}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 This attribute is used to store leading coefficients with respect to the
parent pcgs. the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th entry {\textendash}if bound{\textendash} is the leading
exponent of the element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape igs}} that has depth \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} in the parent. (It cannot be assigned to a component in the object created by \texttt{InducedPcgsByPcSequenceNC} (\ref{InducedPcgsByPcSequenceNC}) as the permutation group methods call it from within the postprocessing,
before this postprocessing however no coefficients may be computed.) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ExtendedPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 7, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X800287C680C5DEC3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExtendedPcgs({\mdseries\slshape N, gens})\index{ExtendedPcgs@\texttt{ExtendedPcgs}}
\label{ExtendedPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 extends the pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape N}} (induced w.r.t. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape home}}) to a new induced pcgs by prepending \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. No checks are performed that this really yields an induced pcgs. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SubgroupByPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 7, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X817E16D67B31389B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SubgroupByPcgs({\mdseries\slshape G, pcgs})\index{SubgroupByPcgs@\texttt{SubgroupByPcgs}}
\label{SubgroupByPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} generated by the elements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Subgroups of Polycyclic Groups {\textendash} Canonical Pcgs}}\label{Subgroups of Polycyclic Groups - Canonical Pcgs}
\logpage{[ 45, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X84068D2478C134C1}{}
{
  The induced pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Q}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} is called \emph{canonical} if the matrix of exponent vectors contains normed vectors only and above each
leading entry in the matrix there are 0's only. The canonical pcgs of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} is unique and hence such pcgs can be used to compare subgroups. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsCanonicalPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 8, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80D122B986B42F80}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsCanonicalPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IsCanonicalPcgs@\texttt{IsCanonicalPcgs}}
\label{IsCanonicalPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 An induced pcgs is canonical if the matrix of the exponent vectors of the
elements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} with respect to the \texttt{ParentPcgs} (\ref{ParentPcgs}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} is in Hermite normal form (see \cite{SOGOS}). While a subgroup can have various induced pcgs with respect to a parent
pcgs a canonical pcgs is unique. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CanonicalPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 8, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X816F6B4187032A10}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CanonicalPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{CanonicalPcgs@\texttt{CanonicalPcgs}}
\label{CanonicalPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the canonical pcgs corresponding to the induced pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group((1,2,3,4),(5,6,7));|
  Group([ (1,2,3,4), (5,6,7) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@P := Pcgs(G);|
  Pcgs([ (5,6,7), (1,2,3,4), (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@I := InducedPcgsByPcSequence(P, [(5,6,7)*(1,3)(2,4),(1,3)(2,4)] );|
  Pcgs([ (1,3)(2,4)(5,6,7), (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CanonicalPcgs(I);|
  Pcgs([ (5,6,7), (1,3)(2,4) ])
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Factor Groups of Polycyclic Groups {\textendash} Modulo Pcgs}}\label{Factor Groups of Polycyclic Groups - Modulo Pcgs}
\logpage{[ 45, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8294F5EF81B7ABA0}{}
{
  Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape N}} be a normal subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} such that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G/N}} is polycyclic with pcgs $(h_1 N, \ldots, h_r N)$. Then we call the sequence of preimages $(h_1, \ldots h_r)$ a \emph{modulo pcgs} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G/N}}. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is called the \emph{numerator} of the modulo pcgs and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape N}} is the \emph{denominator} of the modulo pcgs. 

 Modulo pcgs are often used to facilitate efficient computations with factor
groups, since they allow computations with factor groups without formally
defining the factor group at all. 

 All elementary operations of pcgs, see Sections \ref{Elementary Operations for a Pcgs} and \ref{Elementary Operations for a Pcgs and an Element}, apply to modulo pcgs as well. However, it is in general not possible to
compute induced pcgs with respect to a modulo pcgs. 

 Two more elementary operations for modulo pcgs are \texttt{NumeratorOfModuloPcgs} (\ref{NumeratorOfModuloPcgs}) and \texttt{DenominatorOfModuloPcgs} (\ref{DenominatorOfModuloPcgs}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ModuloPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 9, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7FE689A37E559F66}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ModuloPcgs({\mdseries\slshape G, N})\index{ModuloPcgs@\texttt{ModuloPcgs}}
\label{ModuloPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a modulo pcgs for the factor $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}/\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape N}}$ which must be solvable, while \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape N}} may be non\texttt{\symbol{45}}solvable. \texttt{ModuloPcgs} will return \emph{a} pcgs for the factor, there is no guarantee that it will be ``compatible'' with any other pcgs. If this is required, the \texttt{mod} operator must be used on induced pcgs, see \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod} (\ref{bSlashmod:for two pcgs}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsModuloPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 9, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X868207D77D09D915}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsModuloPcgs({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsModuloPcgs@\texttt{IsModuloPcgs}}
\label{IsModuloPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 The category of modulo pcgs. Note that each pcgs is a modulo pcgs for the
trivial subgroup. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NumeratorOfModuloPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 9, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8027CC9878031D74}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NumeratorOfModuloPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{NumeratorOfModuloPcgs@\texttt{NumeratorOfModuloPcgs}}
\label{NumeratorOfModuloPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns a generating set for the numerator of the modulo pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DenominatorOfModuloPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 9, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87DBE2797D51B2F1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DenominatorOfModuloPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{DenominatorOfModuloPcgs@\texttt{DenominatorOfModuloPcgs}}
\label{DenominatorOfModuloPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns a generating set for the denominator of the modulo pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group( (1,2,3,4,5),(1,2) );|
  Group([ (1,2,3,4,5), (1,2) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@P := ModuloPcgs(G, DerivedSubgroup(G) );|
  Pcgs([ (4,5) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NumeratorOfModuloPcgs(P);|
  [ (1,2,3,4,5), (1,2) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DenominatorOfModuloPcgs(P);|
  [ (1,3,2), (1,4,3), (2,5,4) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RelativeOrders(P);|
  [ 2 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ExponentsOfPcElement( P, (1,2,3,4,5) );|
  [ 0 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ExponentsOfPcElement( P, (4,5) );|
  [ 1 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod (for two pcgs)}}
\logpage{[ 45, 9, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E923519832F2D08}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod({\mdseries\slshape P, I})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod}!for two pcgs}
\label{bSlashmod:for two pcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\


 Modulo Pcgs can also be built from compatible induced pcgs. Let $G$ be a group with pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} and let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape I}} be an induced pcgs of a normal subgroup $N$ of $G$. (Respectively: \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape I}} are both induced with respect to the \emph{same} Pcgs.) Then we can compute a modulo pcgs of $G$ mod $N$ by 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} \texttt{mod} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape I}} 

 Note that in this case we obtain the advantage that the values of \texttt{NumeratorOfModuloPcgs} (\ref{NumeratorOfModuloPcgs}) and \texttt{DenominatorOfModuloPcgs} (\ref{DenominatorOfModuloPcgs}) are just \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape I}}, respectively, and hence are unique. 

 The resulting modulo pcgs will consist of a subset of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} and will be ``compatible'' with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} (or its parent). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group((1,2,3,4));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@P := Pcgs(G);|
  Pcgs([ (1,2,3,4), (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@I := InducedPcgsByGenerators(P, [(1,3)(2,4)]);|
  Pcgs([ (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@M := P mod I;|
  [ (1,2,3,4) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NumeratorOfModuloPcgs(M);|
  Pcgs([ (1,2,3,4), (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DenominatorOfModuloPcgs(M);|
  Pcgs([ (1,3)(2,4) ])
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CorrespondingGeneratorsByModuloPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 9, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X876A41F97FBA7754}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CorrespondingGeneratorsByModuloPcgs({\mdseries\slshape mpcgs, imgs})\index{CorrespondingGeneratorsByModuloPcgs@\texttt{CorrespondingGeneratorsByModuloPcgs}}
\label{CorrespondingGeneratorsByModuloPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mpcgs}} be a modulo pcgs for a factor of a group $G$ and let $U$ be a subgroup of $G$ generated by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape imgs}} such that $U$ covers the factor for the modulo pcgs. Then this function computes elements in $U$ corresponding to the generators of the modulo pcgs. 

 Note that the computation of induced generating sets is not possible for some
modulo pcgs. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CanonicalPcgsByGeneratorsWithImages}}
\logpage{[ 45, 9, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8480852A7D49BC3F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CanonicalPcgsByGeneratorsWithImages({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, gens, imgs})\index{CanonicalPcgsByGeneratorsWithImages@\texttt{CanonicalPcgsByGeneratorsWithImages}}
\label{CanonicalPcgsByGeneratorsWithImages}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 computes a canonical, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}induced pcgs for the span of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} and simultaneously does the same transformations on \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape imgs}}, preserving thus a correspondence between \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape imgs}}. This operation is used to represent homomorphisms from a pc group. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Factor Groups of Polycyclic Groups in their Own Representation}}\label{Factor Groups of Polycyclic Groups in their Own Representation}
\logpage{[ 45, 10, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8254C0F485F945BD}{}
{
  If substantial calculations are done in a factor it might be worth still to
construct the factor group in its own representation (for example by calling \texttt{PcGroupWithPcgs} (\ref{PcGroupWithPcgs}) on a modulo pcgs. 

 The following functions are intended for working with factor groups obtained
by factoring out the tail of a pcgs. They provide a way to map elements or
induced pcgs quickly in the factor (respectively to take preimages) without
the need to construct a homomorphism. 

 The setup is always a pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} and a pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fpcgs}} of a factor group $H = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}/\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape N}}$ which corresponds to a head of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. 

 No tests for validity of the input are performed. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ProjectedPcElement}}
\logpage{[ 45, 10, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X806C2D827E04ACF3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ProjectedPcElement({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, fpcgs, elm})\index{ProjectedPcElement@\texttt{ProjectedPcElement}}
\label{ProjectedPcElement}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the image in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape H}} of an element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ProjectedInducedPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 10, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82F39CCE7C928D3A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ProjectedInducedPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, fpcgs, ipcgs})\index{ProjectedInducedPcgs@\texttt{ProjectedInducedPcgs}}
\label{ProjectedInducedPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ipcgs}} must be an induced pcgs with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. This operation returns an induced pcgs with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fpcgs}} consisting of the nontrivial images of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ipcgs}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LiftedPcElement}}
\logpage{[ 45, 10, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X816813A078B93A6B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LiftedPcElement({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, fpcgs, elm})\index{LiftedPcElement@\texttt{LiftedPcElement}}
\label{LiftedPcElement}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a preimage in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} of an element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape H}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LiftedInducedPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 10, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83C60F1587577D65}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LiftedInducedPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, fpcgs, ipcgs, ker})\index{LiftedInducedPcgs@\texttt{LiftedInducedPcgs}}
\label{LiftedInducedPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ipcgs}} must be an induced pcgs with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fpcgs}}. This operation returns an induced pcgs with respect to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} consisting of the preimages of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ipcgs}}, appended by the elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ker}} (assuming there is a bijection of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} mod \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ker}} to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fpcgs}}). \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ker}} might be a simple element list. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Pcgs and Normal Series}}\label{Pcgs and Normal Series}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83FE235E7B208EC0}{}
{
  By definition, a pcgs determines a pc series of its underlying group. However,
in many applications it will be necessary that this pc series refines a normal
series with certain properties; for example, a normal series with abelian
factors. 

 There are functions in \textsf{GAP} to compute a pcgs through a normal series with elementary abelian factors, a
central series or the lower p\texttt{\symbol{45}}central series. See also
Section \ref{Special Pcgs} for a more explicit possibility. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPcgsElementaryAbelianSeries}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E7E89C278DDE20D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPcgsElementaryAbelianSeries({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IsPcgsElementaryAbelianSeries@\texttt{IsPcgsElementaryAbelianSeries}}
\label{IsPcgsElementaryAbelianSeries}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 returns \texttt{true} if the pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} refines an elementary abelian series. \texttt{IndicesEANormalSteps} (\ref{IndicesEANormalSteps}) then gives the indices in the Pcgs, at which the subgroups of this series
start. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries (for a group)}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X863A20B57EA37BAC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries@\texttt{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries}!for a group}
\label{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries:for a group}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries({\mdseries\slshape list})\index{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries@\texttt{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries}!for a list of normal subgroups}
\label{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries:for a list of normal subgroups}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 computes a pcgs for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} that refines an elementary abelian series. \texttt{IndicesEANormalSteps} (\ref{IndicesEANormalSteps}) gives the indices in the pcgs, at which the normal subgroups of this series
start. The second variant returns a pcgs that runs through the normal
subgroups in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IndicesEANormalSteps}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BCC1E2A80544CC7}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndicesEANormalSteps({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IndicesEANormalSteps@\texttt{IndicesEANormalSteps}}
\label{IndicesEANormalSteps}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndicesEANormalStepsBounded({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, bound})\index{IndicesEANormalStepsBounded@\texttt{IndicesEANormalStepsBounded}}
\label{IndicesEANormalStepsBounded}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} be a pcgs obtained as corresponding to a series of normal subgroups with
elementary abelian factors (for example from calling \texttt{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries} (\ref{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries:for a group})) Then \texttt{IndicesEANormalSteps} returns a sorted list of integers, indicating the tails of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} which generate these normal subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. If $i$ is an element of this list, $(g_i, \ldots, g_n)$ is a normal subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The list always starts with $1$ and ends with $n+1$. (These indices form \emph{one} series with elementary abelian subfactors, not necessarily the most refined
one.) 

 The attribute \texttt{EANormalSeriesByPcgs} (\ref{EANormalSeriesByPcgs}) returns the actual series of subgroups. 

 For arbitrary pcgs not obtained as belonging to a special series such a set of
indices not necessarily exists, and \texttt{IndicesEANormalSteps} is not guaranteed to work in this situation. 

 Typically, \texttt{IndicesEANormalSteps} is set by \texttt{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries} (\ref{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries:for a group}). 

 The variant \texttt{IndicesEANormalStepsBounded} will aim to ensure that no factor will be larger than the given bound. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{EANormalSeriesByPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7FCE308887F621FC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{EANormalSeriesByPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{EANormalSeriesByPcgs@\texttt{EANormalSeriesByPcgs}}
\label{EANormalSeriesByPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} be a pcgs obtained as corresponding to a series of normal subgroups with
elementary abelian factors (for example from calling \texttt{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries} (\ref{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries:for a group})). This attribute returns the actual series of normal subgroups, corresponding
to \texttt{IndicesEANormalSteps} (\ref{IndicesEANormalSteps}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPcgsCentralSeries}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79675266796D7254}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPcgsCentralSeries({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IsPcgsCentralSeries@\texttt{IsPcgsCentralSeries}}
\label{IsPcgsCentralSeries}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 returns \texttt{true} if the pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} refines an central elementary abelian series. \texttt{IndicesCentralNormalSteps} (\ref{IndicesCentralNormalSteps}) then gives the indices in the pcgs, at which the subgroups of this series
start. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PcgsCentralSeries}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8187FCF483659E69}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PcgsCentralSeries({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{PcgsCentralSeries@\texttt{PcgsCentralSeries}}
\label{PcgsCentralSeries}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 computes a pcgs for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} that refines a central elementary abelian series. \texttt{IndicesCentralNormalSteps} (\ref{IndicesCentralNormalSteps}) gives the indices in the pcgs, at which the normal subgroups of this series
start. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IndicesCentralNormalSteps}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7FB73FEB7BED5BFA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndicesCentralNormalSteps({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IndicesCentralNormalSteps@\texttt{IndicesCentralNormalSteps}}
\label{IndicesCentralNormalSteps}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} be a pcgs obtained as corresponding to a series of normal subgroups with
central elementary abelian factors (for example from calling \texttt{PcgsCentralSeries} (\ref{PcgsCentralSeries})). Then \texttt{IndicesCentralNormalSteps} returns a sorted list of integers, indicating the tails of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} which generate these normal subgroups of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. If $i$ is an element of this list, $(g_i, \ldots, g_n)$ is a normal subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The list always starts with $1$ and ends with $n+1$. (These indices form \emph{one} series with central elementary abelian subfactors, not necessarily the most
refined one.) 

 The attribute \texttt{CentralNormalSeriesByPcgs} (\ref{CentralNormalSeriesByPcgs}) returns the actual series of subgroups. 

 For arbitrary pcgs not obtained as belonging to a special series such a set of
indices not necessarily exists, and \texttt{IndicesCentralNormalSteps} is not guaranteed to work in this situation. 

 Typically, \texttt{IndicesCentralNormalSteps} is set by \texttt{PcgsCentralSeries} (\ref{PcgsCentralSeries}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CentralNormalSeriesByPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82266ADA86B2A689}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CentralNormalSeriesByPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{CentralNormalSeriesByPcgs@\texttt{CentralNormalSeriesByPcgs}}
\label{CentralNormalSeriesByPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} be a pcgs obtained as corresponding to a series of normal subgroups with
central elementary abelian factors (for example from calling \texttt{PcgsCentralSeries} (\ref{PcgsCentralSeries})). This attribute returns the actual series of normal subgroups, corresponding
to \texttt{IndicesCentralNormalSteps} (\ref{IndicesCentralNormalSteps}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X786E60AF7B61BF9E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IsPcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup@\texttt{IsPcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup}}
\label{IsPcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 returns \texttt{true} if the pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} refines a $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}central elementary abelian series for a $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}group. \texttt{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup} (\ref{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup}) then gives the indices in the pcgs, at which the subgroups of this series
start. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86F19DBD7D346E7F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup@\texttt{PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup}}
\label{PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 computes a pcgs for the $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} that refines a $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}central elementary abelian series. \texttt{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup} (\ref{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup}) gives the indices in the pcgs, at which the normal subgroups of this series
start. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 11 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X863968F08509E7D4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup@\texttt{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup}}
\label{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} be a pcgs obtained as corresponding to a series of normal subgroups with $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}central elementary abelian factors (for example from
calling \texttt{PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup} (\ref{PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup})). Then \texttt{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup} returns a sorted list of integers, indicating the tails of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} which generate these normal subgroups of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. If $i$ is an element of this list, $(g_i, \ldots, g_n)$ is a normal subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The list always starts with $1$ and ends with $n+1$. (These indices form \emph{one} series with central elementary abelian subfactors, not necessarily the most
refined one.) 

 The attribute \texttt{PCentralNormalSeriesByPcgsPGroup} (\ref{PCentralNormalSeriesByPcgsPGroup}) returns the actual series of subgroups. 

 For arbitrary pcgs not obtained as belonging to a special series such a set of
indices not necessarily exists, and \texttt{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup} is not guaranteed to work in this situation. 

 Typically, \texttt{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup} is set by \texttt{PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup} (\ref{PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PCentralNormalSeriesByPcgsPGroup}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 12 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A92C9EA7BAF60CA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PCentralNormalSeriesByPcgsPGroup({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{PCentralNormalSeriesByPcgsPGroup@\texttt{PCentralNormalSeriesByPcgsPGroup}}
\label{PCentralNormalSeriesByPcgsPGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} be a pcgs obtained as corresponding to a series of normal subgroups with $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}central elementary abelian factors (for example from
calling \texttt{PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup} (\ref{PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup})). This attribute returns the actual series of normal subgroups, corresponding
to \texttt{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup} (\ref{IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup}). }

\logpage{[ 45, 11, 13 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EA5BC3B7FE9D98D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPcgsChiefSeries({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IsPcgsChiefSeries@\texttt{IsPcgsChiefSeries}}
\label{IsPcgsChiefSeries}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 returns \texttt{true} if the pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} refines a chief series. \texttt{IndicesChiefNormalSteps} (\ref{IndicesChiefNormalSteps}) then gives the indices in the pcgs, at which the subgroups of this series
start. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PcgsChiefSeries}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 14 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E7326947EAE4BC9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PcgsChiefSeries({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{PcgsChiefSeries@\texttt{PcgsChiefSeries}}
\label{PcgsChiefSeries}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 computes a pcgs for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} that refines a chief series. \texttt{IndicesChiefNormalSteps} (\ref{IndicesChiefNormalSteps}) gives the indices in the pcgs, at which the normal subgroups of this series
start. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IndicesChiefNormalSteps}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 15 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C05E84A78CA405E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndicesChiefNormalSteps({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IndicesChiefNormalSteps@\texttt{IndicesChiefNormalSteps}}
\label{IndicesChiefNormalSteps}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} be a pcgs obtained as corresponding to a chief series for example from calling \texttt{PcgsChiefSeries} (\ref{PcgsChiefSeries})). Then \texttt{IndicesChiefNormalSteps} returns a sorted list of integers, indicating the tails of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} which generate these normal subgroups of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. If $i$ is an element of this list, $(g_i, \ldots, g_n)$ is a normal subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The list always starts with $1$ and ends with $n+1$. (These indices form \emph{one} series with elementary abelian subfactors, not necessarily the most refined
one.) 

 The attribute \texttt{ChiefNormalSeriesByPcgs} (\ref{ChiefNormalSeriesByPcgs}) returns the actual series of subgroups. 

 For arbitrary pcgs not obtained as belonging to a special series such a set of
indices not necessarily exists, and \texttt{IndicesChiefNormalSteps} is not guaranteed to work in this situation. 

 Typically, \texttt{IndicesChiefNormalSteps} is set by \texttt{PcgsChiefSeries} (\ref{PcgsChiefSeries}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ChiefNormalSeriesByPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 11, 16 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83C5ABC587074B14}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ChiefNormalSeriesByPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{ChiefNormalSeriesByPcgs@\texttt{ChiefNormalSeriesByPcgs}}
\label{ChiefNormalSeriesByPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} be a pcgs obtained as corresponding to a chief series (for example from
calling \texttt{PcgsChiefSeries} (\ref{PcgsChiefSeries})). This attribute returns the actual series of normal subgroups, corresponding
to \texttt{IndicesChiefNormalSteps} (\ref{IndicesChiefNormalSteps}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2,3,4),(1,2));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p:=PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries(g);|
  Pcgs([ (3,4), (2,4,3), (1,4)(2,3), (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IndicesEANormalSteps(p);|
  [ 1, 2, 3, 5 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2,3,4),(1,5)(2,6)(3,7)(4,8));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p:=PcgsCentralSeries(g);|
  Pcgs([ (1,5)(2,6)(3,7)(4,8), (5,6,7,8), (5,7)(6,8),
    (1,4,3,2)(5,6,7,8), (1,3)(2,4)(5,7)(6,8) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IndicesCentralNormalSteps(p);|
  [ 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@q:=PcgsPCentralSeriesPGroup(g);|
  Pcgs([ (1,5)(2,6)(3,7)(4,8), (5,6,7,8), (5,7)(6,8),
    (1,4,3,2)(5,6,7,8), (1,3)(2,4)(5,7)(6,8) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IndicesPCentralNormalStepsPGroup(q);|
  [ 1, 3, 5, 6 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Sum and Intersection of Pcgs}}\label{Sum and Intersection of Pcgs}
\logpage{[ 45, 12, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7E624B4E8224DE2D}{}
{
     

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SumFactorizationFunctionPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 12, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7833DAAA7C07CFD7}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SumFactorizationFunctionPcgs({\mdseries\slshape parentpcgs, n, u, kerpcgs})\index{SumFactorizationFunctionPcgs@\texttt{SumFactorizationFunctionPcgs}}
\label{SumFactorizationFunctionPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 computes the sum and intersection of the lists \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape u}} whose elements form modulo pcgs induced by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape parentpcgs}} for two subgroups modulo a kernel given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape kerpcgs}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape kerpcgs}} is a tail if the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape parent\texttt{\symbol{45}}pcgs}} it is sufficient to give the starting depth, this can be more efficient than
to construct an explicit pcgs. The factor group modulo \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape kerpcgs}} generated by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} must be elementary abelian and normal under \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape u}}. 

 The function returns a record with components 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{sum}}]  elements that form a modulo pcgs for the span of both subgroups. 
\item[{\texttt{intersection}}]  elements that form a modulo pcgs for the intersection of both subgroups. 
\item[{\texttt{factorization}}]  a function that returns for an element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape x}} in the span of \texttt{sum} a record with components \texttt{u} and \texttt{n} that give its decomposition. 
\end{description}
 

 The record components \texttt{sum} and \texttt{intersection} are \emph{not} pcgs but only lists of pc elements (to avoid unnecessary creation of induced
pcgs). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Special Pcgs}}\label{Special Pcgs}
\logpage{[ 45, 13, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83039CF97D27D819}{}
{
  In short, a special pcgs is a pcgs which has particularly nice properties, for
example it always refines an elementary abelian series, for $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}groups it even refines a central series. These nice
properties permit particularly efficient algorithms. 

 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} be a finite polycyclic group. A \emph{special pcgs} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is a pcgs which is closely related to a Hall system and the maximal subgroups
of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. These pcgs have been introduced by C. R. Leedham\texttt{\symbol{45}}Green
who also gave an algorithm to compute them. Improvements to this algorithm  are due to Bettina Eick. For a more detailed account of their definition the
reader is referred to \cite{Eick97} 

 To introduce the definition of special pcgs we first need to define the \emph{LG\texttt{\symbol{45}}series} and \emph{head complements} of a finite polycyclic group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. Let $G = G_1 > G_2 > \ldots G_m > G_{{m+1}} = \{ 1 \}$ be the lower nilpotent series of $G$; that is, $G_i$ is the smallest normal subgroup of $G_{{i-1}}$ with nilpotent factor. To obtain the LG\texttt{\symbol{45}}series of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} we need to refine this series. Thus consider a factor $F_i := G_i / G_{{i+1}}$. Since $F_i$ is finite nilpotent, it is a direct product of its Sylow subgroups $F_i = P_{{i,1}} \cdots P_{{i,r_i}}$. For each Sylow $p_j$\texttt{\symbol{45}}subgroup $P_{{i,j}}$ we can consider its lower $p_j$\texttt{\symbol{45}}central series. To obtain a characteristic central series
with elementary abelian factors of $F_i$ we loop over its Sylow subgroups. Each time we consider $P_{{i,j}}$ in this process we take the next step of its lower $p_j$\texttt{\symbol{45}}central series into the series of $F_i$. If there is no next step, then we just skip the consideration of $P_{{i,j}}$. Note that the second term of the lower $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}central series of a $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}group is in fact its Frattini subgroup. Thus the Frattini
subgroup of $F_i$ is contained in the computed series of this group. We denote the Frattini
subgroup of $F_i = G_i / G_{{i+1}}$ by $G_i^* / G_{{i+1}}$. 

 The factors $G_i / G_i^*$ are called the heads of $G$, while the (possibly trivial) factors $G_i^* / G_{{i+1}}$ are the tails of $G$. A head complement of $G$ is a subgroup $U$ of $G$ such that $U / G_i^*$ is a complement to the head $G_i / G_i^*$ in $G / G_i^*$ for some $i$. 

 Now we are able to define a special pcgs of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. It is a pcgs of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} with three additional properties. First, the pc series determined by the pcgs
refines the LG\texttt{\symbol{45}}series of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. Second, a special pcgs \emph{exhibits} a Hall system of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}; that is, for each set of primes $\pi$ the elements of the pcgs with relative order in $\pi$ form a pcgs of a Hall $\pi$\texttt{\symbol{45}}subgroup in a Hall system of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. Third, a special pcgs exhibits a head complement for each head of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 

 To record information about the LG\texttt{\symbol{45}}series with the special
pcgs we define the \emph{LGWeights} of the special pcgs. These weights are a list which contains a weight $w$ for each elements $g$ of the special pcgs. Such a weight $w$ represents the smallest subgroup of the LG\texttt{\symbol{45}}series
containing $g$. 

 Since the LG\texttt{\symbol{45}}series is defined in terms of the lower
nilpotent series, Sylow subgroups of the factors and lower $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}central series of the Sylow subgroup, the weight $w$ is a triple. More precisely, $g$ is contained in the $w[1]$th term $U$ of the lower nilpotent series of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, but not in the next smaller one $V$. Then $w[3]$ is a prime such that $g V$ is contained in the Sylow $w[3]$\texttt{\symbol{45}}subgroup $P/V$ of $U/V$. Moreover, $gV$ is contained in the $w[2]$th term of the lower $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}central series of $P/V$. 

 There are two more attributes of a special pcgs containing information about
the LG\texttt{\symbol{45}}series: the list \emph{LGLayers} and the list \emph{LGFirst}. The list of layers corresponds to the elements of the special pcgs and
denotes the layer of the LG\texttt{\symbol{45}}series in which an element
lies. The list LGFirst corresponds to the LG\texttt{\symbol{45}}series and
gives the number of the first element in the special pcgs of the corresponding
subgroup. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsSpecialPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 13, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C8A82FA786AC021}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsSpecialPcgs({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsSpecialPcgs@\texttt{IsSpecialPcgs}}
\label{IsSpecialPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\

{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SpecialPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{SpecialPcgs@\texttt{SpecialPcgs}!for a pcgs}

}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SpecialPcgs({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{SpecialPcgs@\texttt{SpecialPcgs}!for a group}
\label{SpecialPcgs:for a group}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\

\hyperdef{L}{X82DC7CE682140588}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LGWeights({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{LGWeights@\texttt{LGWeights}}

\hyperdef{L}{X824645C97E347EEE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LGLayers({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{LGLayers@\texttt{LGLayers}}

\hyperdef{L}{X7A655F4C7D9AE130}{}

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LGLength}}
\logpage{[ 45, 13, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C3912F77B12C8B6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LGLength({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{LGLength@\texttt{LGLength}}
\label{LGLength}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the length of the LG\texttt{\symbol{45}}series of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is solvable, and \texttt{fail} otherwise. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := SmallGroup( 96, 220 );|
  <pc group of size 96 with 6 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@spec := SpecialPcgs( G );|
  Pcgs([ f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LGWeights(spec);|
  [ [ 1, 1, 2 ], [ 1, 1, 2 ], [ 1, 1, 2 ], [ 1, 1, 2 ], [ 1, 1, 3 ],
    [ 1, 2, 2 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LGLayers(spec);|
  [ 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LGFirst(spec);|
  [ 1, 5, 6, 7 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LGLength( G );|
  3
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p := SpecialPcgs( Pcgs( SmallGroup( 96, 120 ) ) );|
  Pcgs([ f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LGWeights(p);|
  [ [ 1, 1, 2 ], [ 1, 1, 2 ], [ 1, 1, 2 ], [ 1, 2, 2 ], [ 1, 3, 2 ],
    [ 2, 1, 3 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Thus the first group, \texttt{SmallGroup(96, 220)}, has a lower nilpotent series of length $1$; that is, the group is nilpotent. It is a direct product of its Sylow
subgroups. Moreover the Sylow $2$\texttt{\symbol{45}}subgroup is generated by the elements \texttt{f1, f2, f3, f4, f6}, and the Sylow $3$\texttt{\symbol{45}}subgroup is generated by \texttt{f5}. The lower $2$\texttt{\symbol{45}}central series of the Sylow $2$\texttt{\symbol{45}}subgroup has length $2$ and the second subgroup in this series is generated by \texttt{f6}. 

 The second group, \texttt{SmallGroup(96, 120)}, has a lower nilpotent series of length $2$ and hence is not nilpotent. The second subgroup in this series is just the
Sylow $3$\texttt{\symbol{45}}subgroup and it is generated by \texttt{f6}. The subgroup generated by \texttt{f1}, $\ldots$, \texttt{f5} is a Sylow $2$\texttt{\symbol{45}}subgroup of the group and also a head complement to the
second head of the group. Its lower $2$\texttt{\symbol{45}}central series has length $2$. 

 In this example the \texttt{FamilyPcgs} (\ref{FamilyPcgs}) value of the groups used was a special pcgs, but this is not necessarily the
case. For performance reasons it can be worth to enforce this,
see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsomorphismSpecialPcGroup} (\ref{IsomorphismSpecialPcGroup}). }

induced pcgs compatible with a \emph{given} special pcgs use \texttt{InducedPcgs} (\ref{InducedPcgs}) for this special pcgs. }
