\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Action on Subfactors Defined by a Pcgs}}\label{Action on Subfactors Defined by a Pcgs}
\logpage{[ 45, 14, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7E86EB517DC08809}{}
{
  When working with a polycyclic group, one often needs to compute matrix
operations of the group on a factor of the group. For this purpose there are
the functions described in \ref{VectorSpaceByPcgsOfElementaryAbelianGroup} to \ref{LinearActionLayer}. 

 In certain situations, for example within the computation of conjugacy classes
of finite soluble groups as described in \cite{MeckyNeubueser89}, affine actions of groups are required. For this purpose we introduce the
functions \texttt{AffineAction} (\ref{AffineAction}) and \texttt{AffineActionLayer} (\ref{AffineActionLayer}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{VectorSpaceByPcgsOfElementaryAbelianGroup}}
\logpage{[ 45, 14, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A9BB9D0817CA949}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{VectorSpaceByPcgsOfElementaryAbelianGroup({\mdseries\slshape mpcgs, fld})\index{VectorSpaceByPcgsOfElementaryAbelianGroup@\texttt{Vector}\-\texttt{Space}\-\texttt{By}\-\texttt{Pcgs}\-\texttt{Of}\-\texttt{Elementary}\-\texttt{Abelian}\-\texttt{Group}}
\label{VectorSpaceByPcgsOfElementaryAbelianGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the vector space over \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fld}} corresponding to the modulo pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mpcgs}}. Note that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mpcgs}} has to define an elementary abelian $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}group where $p$ is the characteristic of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fld}}. }

}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\

\label{LinearOperation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a list of matrices, one for each element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}, which corresponds to the matrix action of the elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} on the basis \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape basisvectors}} via \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape linear}}. }

}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\

\label{LinearOperationLayer}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a list of matrices, one for each element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}, which corresponds to the matrix action of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} on the vector space corresponding to the modulo pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. }

\logpage{[ 45, 14, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79C2D6BF7DD69ED6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AffineAction({\mdseries\slshape gens, basisvectors, linear, transl})\index{AffineAction@\texttt{AffineAction}}
\label{AffineAction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 return a list of matrices, one for each element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}, which corresponds to the affine action of the elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} on the basis \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape basisvectors}} via \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape linear}} with translation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape transl}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AffineActionLayer}}
\logpage{[ 45, 14, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E4CB1358524497B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AffineActionLayer({\mdseries\slshape G, gens, pcgs, transl})\index{AffineActionLayer@\texttt{AffineActionLayer}}
\label{AffineActionLayer}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a list of matrices, one for each element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}, which corresponds to the affine action of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} on the vector space corresponding to the modulo pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} with translation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape transl}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := SmallGroup( 96, 51 );|
  <pc group of size 96 with 6 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@spec := SpecialPcgs( G );|
  Pcgs([ f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LGWeights( spec );|
  [ [ 1, 1, 2 ], [ 1, 1, 2 ], [ 1, 1, 3 ], [ 1, 2, 2 ], [ 1, 2, 2 ],
    [ 1, 3, 2 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mpcgs := InducedPcgsByPcSequence( spec, spec{[4,5,6]} );|
  Pcgs([ f4, f5, f6 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@npcgs := InducedPcgsByPcSequence( spec, spec{[6]} );|
  Pcgs([ f6 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@modu := mpcgs mod npcgs;|
  [ f4, f5 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mat:=LinearActionLayer( G, spec{[1,2,3]}, modu );|
  [ <an immutable 2x2 matrix over GF2>,
    <an immutable 2x2 matrix over GF2>,
    <an immutable 2x2 matrix over GF2> ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Print( mat, "\n" );|
  [ [ [ Z(2)^0, 0*Z(2) ], [ 0*Z(2), Z(2)^0 ] ],
    [ [ Z(2)^0, 0*Z(2) ], [ 0*Z(2), Z(2)^0 ] ],
    [ [ Z(2)^0, 0*Z(2) ], [ 0*Z(2), Z(2)^0 ] ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Orbit Stabilizer Methods for Polycyclic Groups}}\label{Orbit Stabilizer Methods for Polycyclic Groups}
\logpage{[ 45, 15, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7EEA8D638492F432}{}
{
  If a pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} is known for a group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, then orbits and stabilizers can be computed by a special method which is
particularly efficient. Note that within this function only the elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} and the relative orders of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} are needed. Hence this function works effectively even if the elementary
operations for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} are slow. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StabilizerPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 45, 15, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CFCCF607A30B5EE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StabilizerPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, pnt[, acts][, act]})\index{StabilizerPcgs@\texttt{StabilizerPcgs}}
\label{StabilizerPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 computes the stabilizer in the group generated by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} of the point \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}}. If given, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape acts}} are elements by which \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} acts, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape act}} is the acting function. This function returns a pcgs for the stabilizer which
is induced by the \texttt{ParentPcgs} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}, that is it is compatible with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Pcgs{\textunderscore}OrbitStabilizer}}
\logpage{[ 45, 15, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A87E72F86813132}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Pcgs{\textunderscore}OrbitStabilizer({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, domain, pnt, oprs, opr})\index{Pcgs{\textunderscore}OrbitStabilizer@\texttt{Pcgs{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{Orbit}\-\texttt{Stabilizer}}
\label{PcgsuScoreOrbitStabilizer}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 runs a solvable group orbit\texttt{\symbol{45}}stabilizer algorithm on \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} acting via the images \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oprs}} and the operation function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}. The domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape domain}} can be used to speed up search, if it is not known, \texttt{false} can be given instead. The function returns a record with components \texttt{orbit}, \texttt{stabpcgs} and \texttt{lengths}, the latter indicating the lengths of the orbit whenever it got extended.
This can be used to recompute transversal elements. This function should be
used only inside algorithms when speed is essential. }

 }

\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Conjugacy Classes in Solvable Groups}}\label{Conjugacy Classes in Solvable Groups}
\logpage{[ 45, 17, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79DCCF6D80351859}{}
{
  There are a variety of algorithms to compute conjugacy classes and
centralizers in solvable groups via epimorphic images (\cite{FelschNeubueser79}, \cite{MeckyNeubueser89}, \cite{Theissen93}). Usually these are only invoked as methods, but it is possible to access the
algorithm directly. 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ClassesSolvableGroup}}
\logpage{[ 45, 17, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79593F667A68A21D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ClassesSolvableGroup({\mdseries\slshape G, mode[, opt]})\index{ClassesSolvableGroup@\texttt{ClassesSolvableGroup}}
\label{ClassesSolvableGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 computes conjugacy classes and centralizers in solvable groups. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is the acting group. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mode}} indicates the type of the calculation: 

 0 Conjugacy classes 

 4 Conjugacy test for the two elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opt}}\texttt{.candidates} 

 In mode 0 the function returns a list of records containing components \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape representative}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape centralizer}}. In mode 4 it returns a conjugating element. 

 The optional record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opt}} may contain the following components that will affect the algorithm's
behaviour: 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{pcgs}}]  is a pcgs that will be used for the calculation. The attribute \texttt{EANormalSeriesByPcgs} (\ref{EANormalSeriesByPcgs}) must return an appropriate series of normal subgroups with elementary abelian
factors among them. The algorithm will step down this series. In the case of
the calculation of rational classes, it must be a pcgs refining a central
series. 
\item[{\texttt{candidates}}]  is a list of elements for which canonical representatives are to be computed
or for which a conjugacy test is performed. Both elements must lie in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, but this is not tested. In mode 4 these elements must be given. In mode 0 a
list of classes corresponding to \texttt{candidates} is returned (which may contain duplicates). The \texttt{representative}s chosen are canonical with respect to \texttt{pcgs}. The records returned also contain components \texttt{operator} such that \texttt{candidate \texttt{\symbol{94}} operator = representative}. 
\item[{\texttt{consider}}]  is a function \texttt{consider( fhome, rep, cenp, K, L )}. Here \texttt{fhome} is a home pcgs for the factor group $F$ in which the calculation currently takes place, \texttt{rep} is an element of the factor and \texttt{cenp} is a pcgs for the centralizer of \texttt{rep} modulo \texttt{K}. In mode 0, when lifting from $F$/\texttt{K} to $F$/\texttt{L} (note: for efficiency reasons, $F$ can be different from \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} or \texttt{L} might be not trivial) this function is called before performing the actual
lifting and only those representatives for which it returns \texttt{true} are passed to the next level. This permits for example the calculation of only
those classes with small centralizers or classes of restricted orders. 
\end{description}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CentralizerSizeLimitConsiderFunction}}
\logpage{[ 45, 17, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B358D3B7E236973}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CentralizerSizeLimitConsiderFunction({\mdseries\slshape sz})\index{CentralizerSizeLimitConsiderFunction@\texttt{Centralizer}\-\texttt{Size}\-\texttt{Limit}\-\texttt{Consider}\-\texttt{Function}}
\label{CentralizerSizeLimitConsiderFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a function (with arguments \texttt{fhome}, \texttt{rep}, \texttt{cen}, \texttt{K}, \texttt{L}) that can be used in \texttt{ClassesSolvableGroup} (\ref{ClassesSolvableGroup}) as the \texttt{consider} component of the options record. It will restrict the lifting to those
classes, for which the size of the centralizer (in the factor) is at most \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sz}}. 

 See also \texttt{SubgroupsSolvableGroup} (\ref{SubgroupsSolvableGroup}). }

 }

 }

          
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Pc Groups}}\label{Pc Groups}
\logpage{[ 46, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7EAD57C97EBF7E67}{}
{
     Pc groups are polycyclic groups that use the polycyclic presentation for
element arithmetic. This presentation gives them a ``natural'' pcgs, the \texttt{FamilyPcgs} (\ref{FamilyPcgs}) with respect to which pcgs operations as described in chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Polycyclic Groups} are particularly efficient. 

 Let $G$ be a polycyclic group with pcgs $P = (g_1, \ldots, g_n)$ and corresponding relative orders $(r_1, \ldots, r_n)$. Recall that the $r_i$ are positive integers or infinity and let $I$ be the set of indices $i$ with $r_i$ a positive integer. Then $G$ has a finite presentation on the generators $g_1, \ldots, g_n$ with relations of the following form. \begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcl}$g_i^{{r_i}}$&
=&
$g_{{i+1}}^{a(i,i,i+1)} \cdots g_n^{a(i,i,n)}$\\
&
&
for $1 \leq i \leq n$ and $i \in I$\\
$g_i^{{-1}} g_j g_i$&
=&
$g_{{i+1}}^{a(i,j,i+1)} \cdots g_n^{a(i,j,n)}$\\
&
&
for $1 \leq i < j \leq n$\\
\end{tabular}\\[2mm]
\end{center}

 For infinite groups we need additionally \begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcl}$g_i^{{-1}} g_j^{{-1}} g_i$&
=&
$g_{{i+1}}^{b(i,j,i+1)} \cdots g_n^{b(i,j,n)}$\\
&
&
for $1 \leq i < j \leq n$ and $j \not \in I$\\
$g_i g_j g_i^{{-1}}$&
=&
$g_{{i+1}}^{c(i,j,i+1)} \cdots g_n^{c(i,j,n)}$\\
&
&
for $1 \leq i < j \leq n$ and $i \not \in I$\\
$g_i g_j^{{-1}} g_i^{{-1}}$&
=&
$g_{{i+1}}^{d(i,j,i+1)} \cdots g_n^{d(i,j,n)}$\\
&
&
for $1 \leq i < j \leq n$ and $i, j, \not \in I$\\
\end{tabular}\\[2mm]
\end{center}

 Here the right hand sides are assumed to be words in normal form; that is, for $k \in I$ we have for all exponents $0 \leq a(i,j,k), b(i,j,k), c(i,j,k), d(i,j,k) < r_k$. 

 A finite presentation of this type is called a \emph{power\texttt{\symbol{45}}conjugate presentation} and a \emph{pc group} is a polycyclic group defined by a power\texttt{\symbol{45}}conjugate
presentation. Instead of conjugates we could just as well work with
commutators and then the presentation would be called a \emph{power\texttt{\symbol{45}}commutator} presentation. Both types of presentation are abbreviated as \emph{pc presentation}. Note that a pc presentation is a rewriting system. 

 Clearly, whenever a group $G$ with pcgs $P$ is given, then we can write down the corresponding pc presentation. On the
other hand, one may just write down a presentation on $n$ abstract generators $g_1, \ldots, g_n$ with relations of the above form and define a group $H$ by this. Then the subgroups $C_i = \langle g_i, \ldots, g_n \rangle$ of $H$ form a subnormal series whose factors are cyclic or trivial. In the case that
all factors are non\texttt{\symbol{45}}trivial, we say that the pc
presentation of $H$ is \emph{confluent}. Note that \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4 can only work correctly with pc groups defined by a confluent
pc presentation. 

 At the current state of implementations the \textsf{GAP} library contains methods to compute with finite polycyclic groups, while the \textsf{GAP} package \textsf{Polycyclic} by Bettina Eick and Werner Nickel allows also computations with infinite
polycyclic groups which are given by a pc\texttt{\symbol{45}}presentation. 

     Algorithms for pc groups use the methods for polycyclic groups described in
chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Polycyclic Groups}.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{The Family Pcgs}}\label{The Family Pcgs}
\logpage{[ 46, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X78E9E4D778A57A96}{}
{
  Clearly, the generators of a power\texttt{\symbol{45}}conjugate presentation
of a pc group $G$ form a pcgs of the pc group. This pcgs is called the \emph{family pcgs}. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FamilyPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 46, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79EDB35E82C99304}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FamilyPcgs({\mdseries\slshape grp})\index{FamilyPcgs@\texttt{FamilyPcgs}}
\label{FamilyPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns, for a pc group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape grp}}, a ``natural'' pcgs of some group $G$ which contains \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape grp}} and is maximal with this property. 

 The pcgs operations described in Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Polycyclic Groups} are particularly efficient with respect to this pcgs. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsFamilyPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 46, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80893D2A7FFC791B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsFamilyPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IsFamilyPcgs@\texttt{IsFamilyPcgs}}
\label{IsFamilyPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 specifies whether the pcgs is a \texttt{FamilyPcgs} (\ref{FamilyPcgs}) of a pc group. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InducedPcgsWrtFamilyPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 46, 1, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85C1596A867BE93D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InducedPcgsWrtFamilyPcgs({\mdseries\slshape grp})\index{InducedPcgsWrtFamilyPcgs@\texttt{InducedPcgsWrtFamilyPcgs}}
\label{InducedPcgsWrtFamilyPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the pcgs which induced with respect to a family pcgs (see \texttt{IsParentPcgsFamilyPcgs} (\ref{IsParentPcgsFamilyPcgs}) for further details). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsParentPcgsFamilyPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 46, 1, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8333ACCB7F530406}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsParentPcgsFamilyPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{IsParentPcgsFamilyPcgs@\texttt{IsParentPcgsFamilyPcgs}}
\label{IsParentPcgsFamilyPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 This property indicates that the pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}} is induced with respect to a family pcgs. 

 This property is needed to distinguish between different independent
polycyclic generating sequences which a pc group may have, since the
elementary operations for a non\texttt{\symbol{45}}family pcgs may not be as
efficient as the elementary operations for the family pcgs. 

 This can have a significant influence on the performance of algorithms for
polycyclic groups. Many algorithms require a pcgs that corresponds to an
elementary abelian series (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries} (\ref{PcgsElementaryAbelianSeries:for a group})) or even a special pcgs (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Special Pcgs}). If the family pcgs has the required properties, it will be used for these
purposes, if not \textsf{GAP} has to work with respect to a new pcgs which is \emph{not} the family pcgs and thus takes longer for elementary calculations like \texttt{ExponentsOfPcElement} (\ref{ExponentsOfPcElement}). 

 Therefore, if the family pcgs chosen for arithmetic is not of importance it
might be worth to \emph{change} to another, nicer, pcgs to speed up calculations. This can be achieved, for
example, by using the \texttt{Range} (\ref{Range:of a general mapping}) value of the isomorphism obtained by \texttt{IsomorphismSpecialPcGroup} (\ref{IsomorphismSpecialPcGroup}). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Elements of Pc Groups}}\label{Elements of Pc Groups}
\logpage{[ 46, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X842526BE7FEFE8BD}{}
{
  
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Comparison of elements of pc groups}}\logpage{[ 46, 2, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X869DCE7D86E32337}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=({\mdseries\slshape pcword1, pcword2})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=}!for pcwords}
\label{bSlash=:for pcwords}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}({\mdseries\slshape pcword1, pcword2})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}}!for pcwords}
\label{bSlash<:for pcwords}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\


 \index{equality!for pcwords} \index{smaller!for pcwords} The elements of a pc group $G$ are always represented as words in normal form with respect to the family pcgs
of $G$. Thus it is straightforward to compare elements of a pc group, since this
boils down to a mere comparison of exponent vectors with respect to the family
pcgs. In particular, the word problem is efficiently solvable in pc groups. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Arithmetic operations for elements of pc groups}}\logpage{[ 46, 2, 2 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D1B700882FC6C78}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*({\mdseries\slshape pcword1, pcword2})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*}!for pcwords}
\label{bSlash*:for pcwords}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Inverse({\mdseries\slshape pcword})\index{Inverse@\texttt{Inverse}!for a pcword}
\label{Inverse:for a pcword}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 However, multiplication and inversion of elements in pc groups is not as
straightforward as in arbitrary finitely presented groups where a simple
concatenation or reversion of the corresponding words is sufficient (but one
cannot solve the word problem). 

 To multiply two elements in a pc group, we first concatenate the corresponding
words and then use an algorithm called \emph{collection} to transform the new word into a word in normal form. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g := FamilyPcgs( SmallGroup( 24, 12 ) );|
  Pcgs([ f1, f2, f3, f4 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g[4] * g[1];|
  f1*f3
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@(g[2] * g[3])^-1;|
  f2^2*f3*f4
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Pc Groups versus Fp Groups}}\label{Pc Groups versus Fp Groups}
\logpage{[ 46, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X87B866C386B386E4}{}
{
  In theory pc groups are finitely presented groups. In practice the arithmetic
in pc groups is different from the arithmetic in fp groups. Thus for technical
reasons the pc groups in \textsf{GAP} do not form a subcategory of the fp groups and hence the methods for fp groups
cannot be applied to pc groups in general. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPcGroup}}
\logpage{[ 46, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D1F506D7830B1D9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPcGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{IsPcGroup@\texttt{IsPcGroup}}
\label{IsPcGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 tests whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is a pc group. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := SmallGroup( 24, 12 );|
  <pc group of size 24 with 4 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPcGroup( G );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsFpGroup( G );|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsomorphismFpGroupByPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 46, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D2735A18111FE39}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsomorphismFpGroupByPcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs, str})\index{IsomorphismFpGroupByPcgs@\texttt{IsomorphismFpGroupByPcgs}}
\label{IsomorphismFpGroupByPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 It is possible to convert a pc group to a fp group in \textsf{GAP}. The function \texttt{IsomorphismFpGroupByPcgs} computes the power\texttt{\symbol{45}}commutator presentation defined by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. The string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape str}} can be used to give a name to the generators of the fp group. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p := FamilyPcgs( SmallGroup( 24, 12 ) );|
  Pcgs([ f1, f2, f3, f4 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@iso := IsomorphismFpGroupByPcgs( p, "g" );|
  [ f1, f2, f3, f4 ] -> [ g1, g2, g3, g4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@F := Image( iso );|
  <fp group of size 24 on the generators [ g1, g2, g3, g4 ]>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RelatorsOfFpGroup( F );|
  [ g1^2, g2^-1*g1^-1*g2*g1*g2^-1, g3^-1*g1^-1*g3*g1*g4^-1*g3^-1,
    g4^-1*g1^-1*g4*g1*g4^-1*g3^-1, g2^3, g3^-1*g2^-1*g3*g2*g4^-1*g3^-1,
    g4^-1*g2^-1*g4*g2*g3^-1, g3^2, g4^-1*g3^-1*g4*g3, g4^2 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Constructing Pc Groups}}\label{Constructing Pc Groups}
\logpage{[ 46, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8581887880556E0C}{}
{
  If necessary, you can supply \textsf{GAP} with a pc presentation by hand. (Although this is the most tedious way to
input a pc group.) Note that the pc presentation has to be confluent in order
to work with the pc group in \textsf{GAP}. 

 (If you have already a suitable pcgs in another representation, use \texttt{PcGroupWithPcgs} (\ref{PcGroupWithPcgs}), see below.) 

 One way is to define a finitely presented group with a pc presentation in \textsf{GAP} and then convert this presentation into a pc group, see \texttt{PcGroupFpGroup} (\ref{PcGroupFpGroup}). Note that this does not work for arbitrary presentations of polycyclic
groups, see Chapter \ref{Quotient Methods} for further information. 

 Another way is to create and manipulate a collector of a pc group by hand and
to use it to define a pc group. This is the most technical way and has little
error checking and thus is intended mostly for experts who want to create a pc
presentation in a particular way. \textsf{GAP} provides different collectors for different collecting strategies; at the
moment, there are two collectors to choose from: the single collector for
finite pc groups (see \texttt{SingleCollector} (\ref{SingleCollector})) and the combinatorial collector for finite $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}groups. See \cite{Sims94} for further information on collecting strategies. 

 A collector is initialized with an underlying free group and the relative
orders of the pc series. Then one adds the right hand sides of the power and
the commutator or conjugate relations one by one. Note that omitted relators
are assumed to be trivial. 

 For performance reasons it is beneficial to enforce a ``syllable'' representation in the free group (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Representations for Associative Words}). 

 Note that in the end, the collector has to be converted to a group, see \texttt{GroupByRws} (\ref{GroupByRws}). 

 With these methods a pc group with arbitrary defining pcgs can be constructed.
However, for almost all applications within \textsf{GAP} we need to have a pc group whose defining pcgs is a prime order pcgs, see \texttt{IsomorphismRefinedPcGroup} (\ref{IsomorphismRefinedPcGroup}) and \texttt{RefinedPcGroup} (\ref{RefinedPcGroup}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PcGroupFpGroup}}
\logpage{[ 46, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84C10D1F7CB5274F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PcGroupFpGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{PcGroupFpGroup@\texttt{PcGroupFpGroup}}
\label{PcGroupFpGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 creates a pc group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} from an fp group (see Chapter \ref{Finitely Presented Groups}) \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} whose presentation is polycyclic. The resulting group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} has generators corresponding to the generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. They are printed in the same way as generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, but they lie in a different family. If the pc presentation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is not confluent, an error message occurs. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@F := FreeGroup(IsSyllableWordsFamily,"a","b","c","d");;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a := F.1;; b := F.2;; c := F.3;; d := F.4;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rels := [a^2, b^3, c^2, d^2, Comm(b,a)/b, Comm(c,a)/d, Comm(d,a),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@            Comm(c,b)/(c*d), Comm(d,b)/c, Comm(d,c)];|
  [ a^2, b^3, c^2, d^2, b^-1*a^-1*b*a*b^-1, c^-1*a^-1*c*a*d^-1,
    d^-1*a^-1*d*a, c^-1*b^-1*c*b*d^-1*c^-1, d^-1*b^-1*d*b*c^-1,
    d^-1*c^-1*d*c ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := F / rels;|
  <fp group on the generators [ a, b, c, d ]>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@H := PcGroupFpGroup( G );|
  <pc group of size 24 with 4 generators>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SingleCollector}}
\logpage{[ 46, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E958DB281E070FD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SingleCollector({\mdseries\slshape fgrp, relorders})\index{SingleCollector@\texttt{SingleCollector}}
\label{SingleCollector}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CombinatorialCollector({\mdseries\slshape fgrp, relorders})\index{CombinatorialCollector@\texttt{CombinatorialCollector}}
\label{CombinatorialCollector}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 initializes a single collector or a combinatorial collector, where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fgrp}} must be a free group and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape relorders}} must be a list of the relative orders of the pc series. 

 A combinatorial collector can only be set up for a finite $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}group. Here, the relative orders \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape relorders}} must all be equal and a prime. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetConjugate}}
\logpage{[ 46, 4, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86A08D887E049347}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetConjugate({\mdseries\slshape coll, j, i, w})\index{SetConjugate@\texttt{SetConjugate}}
\label{SetConjugate}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Let $f_1, \ldots, f_n$ be the generators of the underlying free group of the collector \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coll}}. 

 For \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} $<$ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape j}}, \texttt{SetConjugate} sets the conjugate $f_j^{{f_i}}$ to equal \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape w}}, which is assumed to be a canonical word in $f_{{i+1}}, \ldots, f_n$. No check of the arguments is performed. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetCommutator}}
\logpage{[ 46, 4, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B25997C7DF92B6D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetCommutator({\mdseries\slshape coll, j, i, w})\index{SetCommutator@\texttt{SetCommutator}}
\label{SetCommutator}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Let $f_1, \ldots, f_n$ be the generators of the underlying free group of the collector \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coll}}. 

 For \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} $<$ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape j}}, \texttt{SetCommutator} sets the commutator of $f_j$ and $f_i$ to equal \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape w}}, which is assumed to be a canonical word in $f_{{i+1}}, \ldots, f_n$. No check of the arguments is performed. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetPower}}
\logpage{[ 46, 4, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BC319BA8698420C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetPower({\mdseries\slshape coll, i, w})\index{SetPower@\texttt{SetPower}}
\label{SetPower}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Let $f_1, \ldots, f_n$ be the generators of the underlying free group of the collector \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coll}}, and let $r_i$ be the corresponding relative orders. 

 \texttt{SetPower} sets the power $f_i^{{r_i}}$ to equal \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape w}}, which is assumed to be a canonical word in $f_{{i+1}}, \ldots, f_n$. No check of the arguments is performed. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GroupByRws}}
\logpage{[ 46, 4, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84F0521486672C3C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GroupByRws({\mdseries\slshape coll})\index{GroupByRws@\texttt{GroupByRws}}
\label{GroupByRws}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GroupByRwsNC({\mdseries\slshape coll})\index{GroupByRwsNC@\texttt{GroupByRwsNC}}
\label{GroupByRwsNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 creates a group from a rewriting system. In the first version it is checked
whether the rewriting system is confluent, in the second version this is
assumed to be true. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsConfluent (for pc groups)}}
\logpage{[ 46, 4, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7DF4835F79667099}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsConfluent({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{IsConfluent@\texttt{IsConfluent}!for pc groups}
\label{IsConfluent:for pc groups}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 checks whether the pc group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} has been built from a collector with a confluent
power\texttt{\symbol{45}}commutator presentation. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@F := FreeGroup(IsSyllableWordsFamily, 2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@coll1 := SingleCollector( F, [2,3] );|
  <<single collector, 8 Bits>>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetConjugate( coll1, 2, 1, F.2 );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetPower( coll1, 1, F.2 );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G1 := GroupByRws( coll1 );|
  <pc group of size 6 with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsConfluent(G1);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsAbelian(G1);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@coll2 := SingleCollector( F, [2,3] );|
  <<single collector, 8 Bits>>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetConjugate( coll2, 2, 1, F.2^2 );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G2 := GroupByRws( coll2 );|
  <pc group of size 6 with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsAbelian(G2);|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsomorphismRefinedPcGroup}}
\logpage{[ 46, 4, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E6226597DFE5F8F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsomorphismRefinedPcGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{IsomorphismRefinedPcGroup@\texttt{IsomorphismRefinedPcGroup}}
\label{IsomorphismRefinedPcGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 \index{isomorphic!pc group} returns an isomorphism from a pc group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} onto an isomorphic pc group whose family pcgs is a prime order pcgs. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RefinedPcGroup}}
\logpage{[ 46, 4, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X821560A387762DD1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RefinedPcGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{RefinedPcGroup@\texttt{RefinedPcGroup}}
\label{RefinedPcGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the range of the \texttt{IsomorphismRefinedPcGroup} (\ref{IsomorphismRefinedPcGroup}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Computing Pc Groups}}\label{Computing Pc Groups}
\logpage{[ 46, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83F69FE27B024E24}{}
{
  Another possibility to get a pc group in \textsf{GAP} is to convert a polycyclic group given by some other representation to a pc
group. For finitely presented groups there are various quotient methods
available. For all other types of groups one can use the following functions. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PcGroupWithPcgs}}
\logpage{[ 46, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81C55D4F825C36D4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PcGroupWithPcgs({\mdseries\slshape mpcgs})\index{PcGroupWithPcgs@\texttt{PcGroupWithPcgs}}
\label{PcGroupWithPcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 creates a new pc group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} whose family pcgs is isomorphic to the (modulo) pcgs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mpcgs}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group( (1,2,3), (3,4,1) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PcGroupWithPcgs( Pcgs(G) );|
  <pc group of size 12 with 3 generators>
\end{Verbatim}
 

 If a pcgs is only given by a list of pc elements, \texttt{PcgsByPcSequence} (\ref{PcgsByPcSequence}) can be used: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G:=Group((1,2,3,4),(1,2));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p:=PcgsByPcSequence(FamilyObj(One(G)),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@[ (3,4), (2,4,3), (1,4)(2,3), (1,3)(2,4) ]);|
  Pcgs([ (3,4), (2,4,3), (1,4)(2,3), (1,3)(2,4) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PcGroupWithPcgs(p);|
  <pc group of size 24 with 4 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := SymmetricGroup( 5 );|
  Sym( [ 1 .. 5 ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@H := Subgroup( G, [(1,2,3,4,5), (3,4,5)] );|
  Group([ (1,2,3,4,5), (3,4,5) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@modu := ModuloPcgs( G, H );|
  Pcgs([ (4,5) ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PcGroupWithPcgs(modu);|
  <pc group of size 2 with 1 generator>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsomorphismPcGroup}}
\logpage{[ 46, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X873CEB137BA1CD6E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsomorphismPcGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{IsomorphismPcGroup@\texttt{IsomorphismPcGroup}}
\label{IsomorphismPcGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 \index{isomorphic!pc group} returns an isomorphism from \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} onto an isomorphic pc group. The series chosen for this pc representation
depends on the method chosen. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} must be a finite polycyclic group of any kind, for example a solvable
permutation group. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is finite but not solvable, \texttt{fail} is returned. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Group( (1,2,3), (3,4,1) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@iso := IsomorphismPcGroup( G );|
  Pcgs([ (2,4,3), (1,2)(3,4), (1,3)(2,4) ]) -> [ f1, f2, f3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@H := Image( iso );|
  Group([ f1, f2, f3 ])
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsomorphismSpecialPcGroup}}
\logpage{[ 46, 5, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82BE14A986FA6882}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsomorphismSpecialPcGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{IsomorphismSpecialPcGroup@\texttt{IsomorphismSpecialPcGroup}}
\label{IsomorphismSpecialPcGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns an isomorphism from \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} onto an isomorphic pc group whose family pcgs is a special pcgs. (This can be
beneficial to the runtime of calculations.) \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} must be a finite polycyclic group of any kind, for example a solvable
permutation group. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is finite but not solvable, \texttt{fail} is returned. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Saving a Pc Group}}\label{Saving a Pc Group}
\logpage{[ 46, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X85696AB9791DF047}{}
{
  As printing a polycyclic group does not display the presentation, one cannot
simply print a pc group to a file to save it. For this purpose we need the
following function. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GapInputPcGroup}}
\logpage{[ 46, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8593253380D84508}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GapInputPcGroup({\mdseries\slshape grp, string})\index{GapInputPcGroup@\texttt{GapInputPcGroup}}
\label{GapInputPcGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := SmallGroup( 24, 12 );|
  <pc group of size 24 with 4 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrintTo( "save", GapInputPcGroup( G, "H" ) );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Read( "save" );|
  #I A group of order 24 has been defined.
  #I It is called H
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@H = G;|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IdSmallGroup( H ) = IdSmallGroup( G );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RemoveFile( "save" );;|
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Operations for Pc Groups}}\label{Operations for Pc Groups}
\logpage{[ 46, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8391EE8D782D0C9E}{}
{
  All the operations described in Chapters \ref{Groups} and \ref{Polycyclic Groups} apply to a pc group. Nearly all methods for pc groups are methods for groups
with pcgs as described in Chapter \ref{Polycyclic Groups}. The only method with is special for pc groups is a method to compute
intersections of subgroups, since here a pcgs of a parent group is needed and
this can only by guaranteed within pc groups. Section \ref{2-Cohomology} describes operations and methods for arbitrary finite groups. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{$2$\texttt{\symbol{45}}Cohomology and Extensions}}\label{2-Cohomology and Extensions}
\logpage{[ 46, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X877AAB887D4507E3}{}
{
  One of the most interesting applications of pc groups is the possibility to
compute with extensions of these groups by elementary abelian groups; that is, $H$ is an extension of $G$ by $M$, if there exists a normal subgroup $N$ in $H$ which is isomorphic to $M$ such that $H/N$ is isomorphic to $G$. 

 Pc groups are particularly suited for such applications, since the $2$\texttt{\symbol{45}}cohomology can be computed efficiently for such groups
and, moreover, extensions of pc groups by elementary abelian groups can be
represented as pc groups again. 

 To define the elementary abelian group $M$ together with an action of $G$ on $M$ we consider $M$ as a MeatAxe module for $G$ over a finite field (section{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IrreducibleModules} (\ref{IrreducibleModules}) describes functions that can be used to obtain certain modules). For further
information on meataxe modules see Chapter \ref{The MeatAxe}. Note that the matrices defining the module must correspond to the pcgs of
the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 

 There exists an action of the subgroup of \emph{compatible pairs} in $Aut(G) \times Aut(M)$ which acts on the second cohomology group, see \texttt{CompatiblePairs} (\ref{CompatiblePairs}). $2$\texttt{\symbol{45}}cocycles which lie in the same orbit under this action
define isomorphic extensions of $G$. However, there may be isomorphic extensions of $G$ corresponding to cocycles in different orbits. 

 See also the \textsf{GAP} package \textsf{GrpConst} by Hans Ulrich Besche and Bettina Eick that contains methods to construct up
to isomorphism the groups of a given order. 

 Finally we note that for the computation of split extensions it is not
necessary that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} must correspond to an elementary abelian group. Here it is possible to
construct split extensions of arbitrary pc groups, see \texttt{SplitExtension} (\ref{SplitExtension}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TwoCoboundaries}}
\logpage{[ 46, 8, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78E6E11E8285E288}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TwoCoboundaries({\mdseries\slshape G, M})\index{TwoCoboundaries@\texttt{TwoCoboundaries}}
\label{TwoCoboundaries}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the group of $2$\texttt{\symbol{45}}coboundaries of a pc group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} by the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}module \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}. The generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} must correspond to the \texttt{Pcgs} (\ref{Pcgs}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The group of coboundaries is given as vector space over the field underlying \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TwoCocycles}}
\logpage{[ 46, 8, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X784FCA207B8694A6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TwoCocycles({\mdseries\slshape G, M})\index{TwoCocycles@\texttt{TwoCocycles}}
\label{TwoCocycles}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the $2$\texttt{\symbol{45}}cocycles of a pc group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} by the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}module \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}. The generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} must correspond to the \texttt{Pcgs} (\ref{Pcgs}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. The operation returns a list of vectors over the field underlying \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} and the additive group generated by these vectors is the group of $2$\texttt{\symbol{45}}cocyles. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TwoCohomology}}
\logpage{[ 46, 8, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X838065F97F60468F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TwoCohomology({\mdseries\slshape G, M})\index{TwoCohomology@\texttt{TwoCohomology}}
\label{TwoCohomology}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 This operation computes the second cohomology group for the special case of a
Pc Group. It returns a record defining the second cohomology group as factor
space of the space of cocycles by the space of coboundaries. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} must be a pc group and the generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} must correspond to the pcgs of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := SmallGroup( 4, 2 );|
  <pc group of size 4 with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mats := List( Pcgs( G ), x -> IdentityMat( 1, GF(2) ) );|
  [ [ <a GF2 vector of length 1> ], [ <a GF2 vector of length 1> ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@M := GModuleByMats( mats, GF(2) );|
  rec( IsOverFiniteField := true, dimension := 1, field := GF(2),
    generators := [ <an immutable 1x1 matrix over GF2>,
        <an immutable 1x1 matrix over GF2> ], isMTXModule := true )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@TwoCoboundaries( G, M );|
  [  ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@TwoCocycles( G, M );|
  [ [ Z(2)^0, 0*Z(2), 0*Z(2) ], [ 0*Z(2), Z(2)^0, 0*Z(2) ],
    [ 0*Z(2), 0*Z(2), Z(2)^0 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@cc := TwoCohomology( G, M );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@cc.cohom;|
  <linear mapping by matrix, <vector space of dimension 3 over GF(
  2)> -> ( GF(2)^3 )>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Extensions}}
\logpage{[ 46, 8, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8236AD927A5A0E5A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Extensions({\mdseries\slshape G, M})\index{Extensions@\texttt{Extensions}}
\label{Extensions}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns all extensions of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} by the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}module \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} up to equivalence as pc groups. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Extension}}
\logpage{[ 46, 8, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B3BE908867CE4F9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Extension({\mdseries\slshape G, M, c})\index{Extension@\texttt{Extension}}
\label{Extension}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExtensionNC({\mdseries\slshape G, M, c})\index{ExtensionNC@\texttt{ExtensionNC}}
\label{ExtensionNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the extension of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} by the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}module \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} via the cocycle \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape c}} as pc groups. The \texttt{NC} version does not check the resulting group for consistence. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SplitExtension}}
\logpage{[ 46, 8, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83DCB5AB7B6EE785}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SplitExtension({\mdseries\slshape G, M})\index{SplitExtension@\texttt{SplitExtension}}
\label{SplitExtension}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the split extension of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} by the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}module \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}. See also \texttt{SplitExtension} (\ref{SplitExtension:with specified homomorphism}) for its 3\texttt{\symbol{45}}argument version. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ModuleOfExtension}}
\logpage{[ 46, 8, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EAC6B8B7ABEEB86}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ModuleOfExtension({\mdseries\slshape E})\index{ModuleOfExtension@\texttt{ModuleOfExtension}}
\label{ModuleOfExtension}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the module of an extension \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape E}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}. This is the normal subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape E}} which corresponds to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := SmallGroup( 4, 2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mats := List( Pcgs( G ), x -> IdentityMat( 1, GF(2) ) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@M := GModuleByMats( mats, GF(2) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@co := TwoCocycles( G, M );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Extension( G, M, co[2] );|
  <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SplitExtension( G, M );|
  <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Extensions( G, M );|
  [ <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators> ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List(last, IdSmallGroup);|
  [ [ 8, 5 ], [ 8, 2 ], [ 8, 3 ], [ 8, 3 ], [ 8, 2 ], [ 8, 2 ],
    [ 8, 3 ], [ 8, 4 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that the extensions returned by \texttt{Extensions} (\ref{Extensions}) are computed up to equivalence, but not up to isomorphism. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CompatiblePairs}}
\logpage{[ 46, 8, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X824F2B2E7C11ABAF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CompatiblePairs({\mdseries\slshape [A, ]G, M[, D]})\index{CompatiblePairs@\texttt{CompatiblePairs}}
\label{CompatiblePairs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the group of compatible pairs of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} with the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}module \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} as subgroup of the direct product Aut(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}) $\times$ Aut(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}). Here Aut(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}) is considered as subgroup of a general linear group. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is solvable, then the generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} must correspond to the \texttt{Pcgs} (\ref{Pcgs}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, otherwise the generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} must correspond to the \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup} (\ref{GeneratorsOfGroup}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 

 The optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} should be a subgroup of Aut(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}) $\times$ Aut(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}). If it is given, then only the compatible pairs in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} are computed. If a group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape A}} of automorphisms of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is given as optional first argument, it is used in place of the full
automorphism group of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, avoiding the need to compute this automorphism group. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ExtensionRepresentatives}}
\logpage{[ 46, 8, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X854FFEF187C4AAB9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExtensionRepresentatives({\mdseries\slshape G, M, P})\index{ExtensionRepresentatives@\texttt{ExtensionRepresentatives}}
\label{ExtensionRepresentatives}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns all extensions of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} by the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}module \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} up to equivalence under action of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} has to be a subgroup of the group of compatible pairs of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := SmallGroup( 4, 2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mats := List( Pcgs( G ), x -> IdentityMat( 1, GF(2) ) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@M := GModuleByMats( mats, GF(2) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@A := AutomorphismGroup( G );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@B := GL( 1, 2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@D := DirectProduct( A, B );; Size(D);|
  6
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@P := CompatiblePairs( G, M, D );|
  <group of size 6 with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ExtensionRepresentatives( G, M, P );|
  [ <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators> ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Extensions( G, M );|
  [ <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>,
    <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators> ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SplitExtension (with specified homomorphism)}}
\logpage{[ 46, 8, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84E2DA897FAAF6D8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SplitExtension({\mdseries\slshape G, aut, N})\index{SplitExtension@\texttt{SplitExtension}!with specified homomorphism}
\label{SplitExtension:with specified homomorphism}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the split extensions of the pc group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} by the pc group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape N}}. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape aut}} should be a homomorphism from \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} into Aut(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape N}}). 

 In the following example we construct the holomorph of $Q_8$ as split extension of $Q_8$ by $S_4$. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@N := SmallGroup( 8, 4 );|
  <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsAbelian( N );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@A := AutomorphismGroup( N );|
  <group of size 24 with 4 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@iso := IsomorphismPcGroup( A );|
  CompositionMapping( Pcgs([ (2,6,5,3), (1,3,5)(2,4,6), (2,5)(3,6),
    (1,4)(3,6) ]) -> [ f1, f2, f3, f4 ], <action isomorphism> )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@H := Image( iso );|
  Group([ f1, f2, f3, f4 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := Subgroup( H, Pcgs(H){[1,2]} );|
  Group([ f1, f2 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@inv := InverseGeneralMapping( iso );|
  [ f1*f2, f2^2*f3, f4, f3 ] ->
  [ Pcgs([ f1, f2, f3 ]) -> [ f1*f2, f2, f3 ],
    Pcgs([ f1, f2, f3 ]) -> [ f2, f1*f2, f3 ],
    Pcgs([ f1, f2, f3 ]) -> [ f1*f3, f2, f3 ],
    Pcgs([ f1, f2, f3 ]) -> [ f1, f2*f3, f3 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@K := SplitExtension( G, inv, N );|
  <pc group of size 192 with 7 generators>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Coding a Pc Presentation}}\label{Coding a Pc Presentation}
\logpage{[ 46, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X874E4B107BD78F5A}{}
{
  If one wants to store a large number of pc groups, then it can be useful to
store them in a compressed format, since pc presentations can be space
consuming. Here we introduce a method to code and decode pc presentations by
integers. To decode a given code the size of the underlying pc group is needed
as well. For the full definition and the coding and decoding procedures see \cite{BescheEick98}. This method is used with the small groups library (see  (\textbf{smallgrp: The Small Groups Library}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CodePcgs}}
\logpage{[ 46, 9, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79948F1D7D4FF8D9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CodePcgs({\mdseries\slshape pcgs})\index{CodePcgs@\texttt{CodePcgs}}
\label{CodePcgs}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the code corresponding to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pcgs}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := CyclicGroup(512);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p := Pcgs( G );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CodePcgs( p );|
  162895587718739690298008513020159
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CodePcGroup}}
\logpage{[ 46, 9, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8041C2D88721EEA9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CodePcGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{CodePcGroup@\texttt{CodePcGroup}}
\label{CodePcGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the code for a pcgs of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := DihedralGroup(512);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CodePcGroup( G );|
  2940208627577393070560341803949986912431725641726
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PcGroupCode}}
\logpage{[ 46, 9, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X826BFDA07A707C54}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PcGroupCode({\mdseries\slshape code, size})\index{PcGroupCode@\texttt{PcGroupCode}}
\label{PcGroupCode}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a pc group of size \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape size}} corresponding to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape code}}. The argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape code}} must be a valid code for a pcgs, otherwise anything may happen. Valid codes
are usually obtained by one of the functions \texttt{CodePcgs} (\ref{CodePcgs}) or \texttt{CodePcGroup} (\ref{CodePcGroup}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@G := SmallGroup( 24, 12 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p := Pcgs( G );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@code := CodePcgs( p );|
  5790338948
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@H := PcGroupCode( code, 24 );|
  <pc group of size 24 with 4 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@map := GroupHomomorphismByImages( G, H, p, FamilyPcgs(H) );|
  Pcgs([ f1, f2, f3, f4 ]) -> Pcgs([ f1, f2, f3, f4 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBijective(map);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Random Isomorphism Testing}}\label{Random Isomorphism Testing}
\logpage{[ 46, 10, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81D211D8838B875C}{}
{
  The generic isomorphism test for groups may be applied to pc groups as well.
However, this test is often quite time consuming. Here we describe another
method to test isomorphism by a probabilistic approach. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RandomIsomorphismTest}}
\logpage{[ 46, 10, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84F6F9787CB2CF16}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RandomIsomorphismTest({\mdseries\slshape coderecs, n})\index{RandomIsomorphismTest@\texttt{RandomIsomorphismTest}}
\label{RandomIsomorphismTest}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 The first argument is a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coderecs}} containing records describing groups, and the second argument is a
non\texttt{\symbol{45}}negative integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. 

 The test returns a sublist of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coderecs}} where isomorphic copies detected by the probabilistic test have been removed. 

 The list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coderecs}} should contain records with two components, \texttt{code} and \texttt{order}, describing a group via \texttt{PcGroupCode( code, order )} (see \texttt{PcGroupCode} (\ref{PcGroupCode})). 

 The integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} gives a certain amount of control over the probability to detect all
isomorphisms. If it is $0$, then nothing will be done at all. The larger \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is, the larger is the probability of finding all isomorphisms. However, due to
the underlying method we cannot guarantee that the algorithm finds all
isomorphisms, no matter how large \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is. }

 }

 }

          
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Finitely Presented Groups}}\label{Finitely Presented Groups}
\logpage{[ 47, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7AA982637E90B35A}{}
{
  A \emph{finitely presented group} (in short: FpGroup) is a group generated by a finite set of \emph{abstract generators} subject to a finite set of \emph{relations} that these generators satisfy. Every finite group can be represented as a
finitely presented group, though in almost all cases it is computationally
much more efficient to work in another representation (even the regular
permutation representation). 

 Finitely presented groups are obtained by factoring a free group by a set of
relators. Their elements know about this presentation and compare accordingly. 

 So to create a finitely presented group you first have to generate a free
group (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{FreeGroup} (\ref{FreeGroup:for given rank}) for details). There are two ways to specify a quotient of the free group:
either by giving a list of relators or by giving a list of equations. Relators
are just words in the generators of the free group. Equations are represented
as pairs of words in the generators of the free group. In either case the
generators of the quotient are \emph{the images} of the free generators under the canonical homomorphism from the free group
onto the quotient. So for example to create the group 
\[ \langle a, b \mid a^2, b^3, (a b)^5 \rangle \]
 you can use the following commands: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f := FreeGroup( "a", "b" );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g := f / [ f.1^2, f.2^3, (f.1*f.2)^5 ];|
  <fp group on the generators [ a, b ]>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h := f / [ [f.1^2, f.1^0], [f.2^3, f.1^0], [(f.1*f.2)^4, f.2^-1*f.1^-1] ];|
  <fp group on the generators [ a, b ]>
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that you cannot call the generators by their names. These names are not
variables, but just display figures. So, if you want to access the generators
by their names, you first have to introduce the respective variables and to
assign the generators to them. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Unbind(a);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsOfGroup( g );|
  [ a, b ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a;|
  Error, Variable: 'a' must have a value
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a := g.1;; b := g.2;; # assign variables|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsOfGroup( g );|
  [ a, b ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a in f;|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a in g;|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 

 To relieve you of the tedium of typing the above assignments, \emph{when working interactively}, there is the function \texttt{AssignGeneratorVariables} (\ref{AssignGeneratorVariables}). 

 Note that the generators of the free group are different from the generators
of the FpGroup (even though they are displayed by the same names). That means
that words in the generators of the free group are not elements of the
finitely presented group. Vice versa elements of the FpGroup are not words. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a*b = b*a;|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@(b^2*a*b)^2 = a^0;|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Such calculations comparing elements of an FpGroup may run into problems:
There exist finitely presented groups for which no algorithm exists (it is
known that no such algorithm can exist) that will tell for two arbitrary words
in the generators whether the corresponding elements in the FpGroup are equal. 

 Therefore the methods used by \textsf{GAP} to compute in finitely presented groups may run into warning errors, run out
of memory or run forever. If the FpGroup is (by theory) known to be finite the
algorithms are guaranteed to terminate (if there is sufficient memory
available), but the time needed for the calculation cannot be bounded a
priori. See \ref{Coset Tables and Coset Enumeration} and \ref{Testing Finiteness of Finitely Presented Groups}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@(b^2*a*b)^2;|
  (b^2*a*b)^2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a^0;|
  <identity ...>
\end{Verbatim}
 

 A consequence of our convention is that elements of finitely presented groups
are not printed in a unique way. See also \texttt{SetReducedMultiplication} (\ref{SetReducedMultiplication}). For many ``higher level'' computations for a finite group, such as conjugacy classes or character table,
it is advisable not to use an FpGroup but an isomorphic group in a better
internal representation, such as a pc group (see \texttt{IsomorphismPcGroup} (\ref{IsomorphismPcGroup})) or a permutation group (see \texttt{IsomorphismPermGroup} (\ref{IsomorphismPermGroup})). In fact, calling a function such as \texttt{ConjugacyClasses} (\ref{ConjugacyClasses:attribute}) with an FpGroup for which \texttt{HasIsFinite} returns \texttt{false} may result in an error message, because the developers of the FpGroup code do
not want an \emph{automatic} \texttt{IsFinite} (\ref{IsFinite}) test (which may not terminate) in the function. (Once the \texttt{IsFinite} (\ref{IsFinite}) value is known, the computation in question can be done with the FpGroup, but
still it is advisable to use a better internal representation.)  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsSubgroupFpGroup and IsFpGroup}}\label{sect:IsSubgroupFpGroup}
\logpage{[ 47, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7824C8167B3CFAB1}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsSubgroupFpGroup}}
\logpage{[ 47, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7AF7E2B48199452C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsSubgroupFpGroup({\mdseries\slshape H})\index{IsSubgroupFpGroup@\texttt{IsSubgroupFpGroup}}
\label{IsSubgroupFpGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 is the category for finitely presented groups or subgroups of a finitely
presented group. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsFpGroup}}
\logpage{[ 47, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X850B9DF17D90C3A2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsFpGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{IsFpGroup@\texttt{IsFpGroup}}
\label{IsFpGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (filter)}}\\


 is a synonym for \texttt{IsSubgroupFpGroup(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}) and IsGroupOfFamily(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}})}. 

 Free groups are a special case of finitely presented groups, namely finitely
presented groups with no relators. 

 Note that \texttt{FreeGroup(infinity)} (which exists e.g. for purposes of rewriting presentations with further
generators) satisfies this filter, though of course it is not finitely
generated (and thus not finitely presented). \texttt{IsFpGroup} thus is not a proper property test and slightly misnamed for the sake of its
most prominent uses. 

 Another special case are groups given by polycyclic presentations. \textsf{GAP} uses a special representation for these groups which is created in a different
way. See chapter \ref{Pc Groups} for details. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=FreeGroup(2);|
  <free group on the generators [ f1, f2 ]>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsFpGroup(g);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:=CyclicGroup(2);|
  <pc group of size 2 with 1 generator>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsFpGroup(h);|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoFpGroup}}
\logpage{[ 47, 1, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8370BF3B78D0B14D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoFpGroup\index{InfoFpGroup@\texttt{InfoFpGroup}}
\label{InfoFpGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (info class)}}\\


 The info class for functions dealing with finitely presented groups is \texttt{InfoFpGroup}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Creating Finitely Presented Groups}}\label{Creating Finitely Presented Groups}
\logpage{[ 47, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D55E56E790F85FD}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/ (for a free group and a list of elements)}}
\logpage{[ 47, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EF4179E78BC7313}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/({\mdseries\slshape F, rels})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/}!for a free group and a list of elements}
\label{bSlash/:for a free group and a list of elements}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/({\mdseries\slshape F, eqns})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/}!for a free group and a list of pairs of elements}
\label{bSlash/:for a free group and a list of pairs of elements}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\


 \index{quotient!for finitely presented groups} creates a finitely presented group given by the presentation $\langle gens \mid \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rels}} \rangle$ or $\langle gens \mid \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape eqns}} \rangle$, respectively where $gens$ are the free generators of the free group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}. Relations can be entered either as words or as pairs of words in the
generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}. In the former case we refer to the words given as \emph{relators}, in the latter we refer to the pairs of words as \emph{equations}. The two methods can currently not be mixed. 

 The same result is obtained with the infix operator \texttt{/}, i.e., as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} \texttt{/} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rels}}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f := FreeGroup( 3 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f / [ f.1^4, f.2^3, f.3^5, f.1*f.2*f.3 ];|
  <fp group on the generators [ f1, f2, f3 ]>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f / [ [ f.1^4, f.1^0 ], [ f.2^3, f.1^0 ], [ f.1, f.2^-1*f.3^-1 ] ];|
  <fp group on the generators [ f1, f2, f3 ]>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FactorGroupFpGroupByRels}}
\logpage{[ 47, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CE0FA5F8695241E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FactorGroupFpGroupByRels({\mdseries\slshape G, elts})\index{FactorGroupFpGroupByRels@\texttt{FactorGroupFpGroupByRels}}
\label{FactorGroupFpGroupByRels}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the factor group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}/$N$ of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} by the normal closure $N$ of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elts}} where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elts}} is expected to be a list of elements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ParseRelators}}
\logpage{[ 47, 2, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B3D290B87B6EFE4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ParseRelators({\mdseries\slshape gens, rels})\index{ParseRelators@\texttt{ParseRelators}}
\label{ParseRelators}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Will translate a list of relations as given in print, e.g. $x y^2 = (x y^3 x)^2 xy = yzx$ into relators. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} must be a list of generators of a free group, each being displayed by a single
letter. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rels}} is a string that lists a sequence of equalities. These must be written in the
letters which are the names of the generators in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. Change of upper/lower case is interpreted to indicate inverses. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:=FreeGroup("x","y","z");;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AssignGeneratorVariables(f);|
  #I  Assigned the global variables [ x, y, z ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r:=ParseRelators([x,y,z],|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@"x^2 = y^5 = z^3 = (xyxyxy^4)^2 = (xz)^2 = (y^2z)^2 = 1");|
  [ x^2, y^5, z^3, (x*z)^2, (y^2*z)^2, ((x*y)^3*y^3)^2 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=f/r;|
  <fp group on the generators [ x, y, z ]>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StringFactorizationWord}}
\logpage{[ 47, 2, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85EAA789848B528E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StringFactorizationWord({\mdseries\slshape w})\index{StringFactorizationWord@\texttt{StringFactorizationWord}}
\label{StringFactorizationWord}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a string that expresses a given word \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape w}} in compact form written as a string. Inverses are expressed by changing the
upper/lower case of the generators, recurring expressions are written as
products. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StringFactorizationWord(z^-1*x*y*y*y*x*x*y*y*y*x*y^-1*x);|
  "Z(xy3x)2Yx"
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Comparison of Elements of Finitely Presented Groups}}\label{Comparison of Elements of Finitely Presented Groups}
\logpage{[ 47, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X84D693EC872DAA55}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{\texttt{\symbol{92}}= (for two elements in a f.p. group)}}
\logpage{[ 47, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X797D29628203CBD6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=({\mdseries\slshape a, b})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=}!for two elements in a f.p. group}
\label{bSlash=:for two elements in a f.p. group}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\


 \index{equality!elements of finitely presented groups} Two elements of a finitely presented group are equal if they are equal in this
group. Nevertheless they may be represented as different words in the
generators. Because of the fundamental problems mentioned in the introduction
to this chapter such a test may take very long and cannot be guaranteed to
finish. 

 The method employed by \textsf{GAP} for such an equality test use the underlying finitely presented group. First
(unless this group is known to be infinite) \textsf{GAP} tries to find a faithful permutation representation by a bounded
Todd\texttt{\symbol{45}}Coxeter. If this fails, a
Knuth\texttt{\symbol{45}}Bendix (see \ref{Rewriting Systems and the Knuth-Bendix Procedure}) is attempted and the words are compared via their normal form. 

 If only elements in a subgroup are to be tested for equality it thus can be
useful to translate the problem in a new finitely presented group by rewriting
(see \texttt{IsomorphismFpGroup} (\ref{IsomorphismFpGroup})); 

 The equality test of elements underlies many ``basic'' calculations, such as the order of an element, and the same type of problems
can arise there. In some cases, working with rewriting systems can still help
to solve the problem. The \textsf{kbmag} package provides such functionality, see the package manual for further
details. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless} (for two elements in a f.p. group)}}
\logpage{[ 47, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B350C718573B8DF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}({\mdseries\slshape a, b})\index{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}@\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}}!for two elements in a f.p. group}
\label{bSlash<:for two elements in a f.p. group}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\


 \index{smaller!elements of finitely presented groups} Compared with equality testing, problems get even worse when trying to compute
a total ordering on the elements of a finitely presented group. As any
ordering that is guaranteed to be reproducible in different runs of \textsf{GAP} or even with different groups given by syntactically equal presentations would
be prohibitively expensive to implement, the ordering of elements is depending
on a method chosen by \textsf{GAP} and not guaranteed to stay the same when repeating the construction of an
FpGroup. The only guarantee given for the \texttt{{\textless}} ordering for such elements is that it will stay the same for one family during
its lifetime. The attribute \texttt{FpElmComparisonMethod} (\ref{FpElmComparisonMethod}) is used to obtain a comparison function for a family of FpGroup elements. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FpElmComparisonMethod}}
\logpage{[ 47, 3, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87512CF485CC4128}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FpElmComparisonMethod({\mdseries\slshape fam})\index{FpElmComparisonMethod@\texttt{FpElmComparisonMethod}}
\label{FpElmComparisonMethod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}} is the elements family of a finitely presented group this attribute returns a
function \texttt{smaller(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape left}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape right}})} that will be used to compare elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetReducedMultiplication}}
\logpage{[ 47, 3, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82CB9EC982CDAEAC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetReducedMultiplication({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{SetReducedMultiplication@\texttt{SetReducedMultiplication}}
\label{SetReducedMultiplication}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For an FpGroup \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, an element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} of it or the family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} of its elements, this function will force immediate reduction when
multiplying, keeping words short at extra cost per multiplication. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Preimages in the Free Group}}\label{Preimages in the Free Group}
\logpage{[ 47, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7B0B2781796800AD}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FreeGroupOfFpGroup}}
\logpage{[ 47, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85CF3931849FB441}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FreeGroupOfFpGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{FreeGroupOfFpGroup@\texttt{FreeGroupOfFpGroup}}
\label{FreeGroupOfFpGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the underlying free group for the finitely presented group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. This is the group generated by the free generators provided by the \texttt{FreeGeneratorsOfFpGroup} (\ref{FreeGeneratorsOfFpGroup}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FreeGeneratorsOfFpGroup}}
\logpage{[ 47, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79C77C5184CA02B6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FreeGeneratorsOfFpGroup({\mdseries\slshape G})\index{FreeGeneratorsOfFpGroup@\texttt{FreeGeneratorsOfFpGroup}}
\label{FreeGeneratorsOfFpGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FreeGeneratorsOfWholeGroup({\mdseries\slshape U})\index{FreeGeneratorsOfWholeGroup@\texttt{FreeGeneratorsOfWholeGroup}}
\label{FreeGeneratorsOfWholeGroup}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{FreeGeneratorsOfFpGroup} returns the underlying free generators corresponding to the generators of the
finitely presented group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} which must be a full FpGroup. 

 \texttt{FreeGeneratorsOfWholeGroup} also works for subgroups of an FpGroup and returns the free generators of the
full group that defines the family. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RelatorsOfFpGroup}}
