That is, \texttt{IntFFESymm} returns the integer $i$ of smallest absolute value such that $i$\texttt{ * One( }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z}}\texttt{ ) = }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z}} holds. 

 For a vector \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vec}} of FFEs, the operation returns the result of applying \texttt{IntFFESymm} to every entry of the vector. 

 The correspondence between elements from a finite prime field of
characteristic $p$ (for $p < 2^{16}$) and the integers between $-p/2$ and $p/2$ is defined by choosing \texttt{Z(}$p$\texttt{)} the element corresponding to the smallest positive primitive root mod $p$ (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{PrimitiveRootMod} (\ref{PrimitiveRootMod})) and reducing results to the $-p/2 .. p/2$ range. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IntFFE(Z(13)^2);IntFFE(Z(13)^3);|
  4
  8
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IntFFESymm(Z(13)^2);IntFFESymm(Z(13)^3);|
  4
  -5
\end{Verbatim}
 See also \texttt{IntFFE} (\ref{IntFFE}) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IntVecFFE}}
\logpage{[ 59, 2, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8009968782F18888}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IntVecFFE({\mdseries\slshape vecffe})\index{IntVecFFE@\texttt{IntVecFFE}}
\label{IntVecFFE}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 is the list of integers corresponding to the vector \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vecffe}} of finite field elements in a prime field (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IntFFE} (\ref{IntFFE})). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AsInternalFFE}}
\logpage{[ 59, 2, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X807959EE82CED148}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AsInternalFFE({\mdseries\slshape ffe})\index{AsInternalFFE@\texttt{AsInternalFFE}}
\label{AsInternalFFE}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 return an internal FFE equal to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ffe}} if one exists, otherwise \texttt{fail} }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RootFFE}}
\logpage{[ 59, 2, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X794AEB148410825B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RootFFE({\mdseries\slshape F, z, k})\index{RootFFE@\texttt{RootFFE}}
\label{RootFFE}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{RootFFE} returns a finite field element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}} from \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} whose \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power is \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z}}. If no such element exists then \texttt{fail} is returned. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Creating Finite Fields}}\label{Creating Finite Fields}
\logpage{[ 59, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81B54A8378734C33}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DefaultField (for finite field elements)}}
\logpage{[ 59, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7979F51D7C43AB05}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DefaultField({\mdseries\slshape list})\index{DefaultField@\texttt{DefaultField}!for finite field elements}
\label{DefaultField:for finite field elements}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DefaultRing({\mdseries\slshape list})\index{DefaultRing@\texttt{DefaultRing}!for finite field elements}
\label{DefaultRing:for finite field elements}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{DefaultField} and \texttt{DefaultRing} for finite field elements are defined to return the \emph{smallest} field containing the given elements. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DefaultField( [ Z(4), Z(4)^2 ] );  DefaultField( [ Z(4), Z(8) ] );|
  GF(2^2)
  GF(2^6)
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GaloisField (for field size)}}
\logpage{[ 59, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8592DBB086A8A9BE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GaloisField({\mdseries\slshape p\texttt{\symbol{94}}d})\index{GaloisField@\texttt{GaloisField}!for field size}
\label{GaloisField:for field size}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GF({\mdseries\slshape p\texttt{\symbol{94}}d})\index{GF@\texttt{GF}!for field size}
\label{GF:for field size}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GaloisField({\mdseries\slshape p, d})\index{GaloisField@\texttt{GaloisField}!for characteristic and degree}
\label{GaloisField:for characteristic and degree}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GF({\mdseries\slshape p, d})\index{GF@\texttt{GF}!for characteristic and degree}
\label{GF:for characteristic and degree}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GaloisField({\mdseries\slshape subfield, d})\index{GaloisField@\texttt{GaloisField}!for subfield and degree}
\label{GaloisField:for subfield and degree}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GF({\mdseries\slshape subfield, d})\index{GF@\texttt{GF}!for subfield and degree}
\label{GF:for subfield and degree}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GaloisField({\mdseries\slshape p, pol})\index{GaloisField@\texttt{GaloisField}!for characteristic and polynomial}
\label{GaloisField:for characteristic and polynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GF({\mdseries\slshape p, pol})\index{GF@\texttt{GF}!for characteristic and polynomial}
\label{GF:for characteristic and polynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GaloisField({\mdseries\slshape subfield, pol})\index{GaloisField@\texttt{GaloisField}!for subfield and polynomial}
\label{GaloisField:for subfield and polynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GF({\mdseries\slshape subfield, pol})\index{GF@\texttt{GF}!for subfield and polynomial}
\label{GF:for subfield and polynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{GaloisField} returns a finite field. It takes two arguments. The form \texttt{GaloisField( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape d}} )}, where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape d}} are integers, can also be given as \texttt{GaloisField( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape d}} )}. \texttt{GF} is an abbreviation for \texttt{GaloisField}. 

 The first argument specifies the subfield $S$ over which the new field is to be taken. It can be a prime integer or a finite
field. If it is a prime \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}, the subfield is the prime field of this characteristic. 

 The second argument specifies the extension. It can be an integer or an
irreducible polynomial over the field $S$. If it is an integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape d}}, the new field is constructed as the polynomial extension w.r.t. the Conway
polynomial (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{ConwayPolynomial} (\ref{ConwayPolynomial})) of degree \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape d}} over $S$. If it is an irreducible polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} over $S$, the new field is constructed as polynomial extension of $S$ with this polynomial; in this case, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} is accessible as the value of \texttt{DefiningPolynomial} (\ref{DefiningPolynomial}) for the new field, and a root of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} in the new field is accessible as the value of \texttt{RootOfDefiningPolynomial} (\ref{RootOfDefiningPolynomial}). 

 Note that the subfield over which a field was constructed determines over
which field the Galois group, conjugates, norm, trace, minimal polynomial, and
trace polynomial are computed (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{GaloisGroup} (\ref{GaloisGroup:of field}), \texttt{Conjugates} (\ref{Conjugates}), \texttt{Norm} (\ref{Norm}), \texttt{Trace} (\ref{Trace:for a field element}), \texttt{MinimalPolynomial} (\ref{MinimalPolynomial:over a field}), \texttt{TracePolynomial} (\ref{TracePolynomial})). 

 The field is regarded as a vector space (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Vector Spaces}) over the given subfield, so this determines the dimension and the canonical
basis of the field. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f1:= GF( 2^4 );|
  GF(2^4)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( GaloisGroup ( f1 ) );|
  4
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@BasisVectors( Basis( f1 ) );|
  [ Z(2)^0, Z(2^4), Z(2^4)^2, Z(2^4)^3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f2:= GF( GF(4), 2 );|
  AsField( GF(2^2), GF(2^4) )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( GaloisGroup( f2 ) );|
  2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@BasisVectors( Basis( f2 ) );|
  [ Z(2)^0, Z(2^4) ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PrimitiveRoot}}
\logpage{[ 59, 3, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X788B1ECD83C70516}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrimitiveRoot({\mdseries\slshape F})\index{PrimitiveRoot@\texttt{PrimitiveRoot}}
\label{PrimitiveRoot}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 A \emph{primitive root} of a finite field is a generator of its multiplicative group. A primitive root
is always a primitive element (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{PrimitiveElement} (\ref{PrimitiveElement})), the converse is in general not true.   
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= GF( 3^5 );|
  GF(3^5)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PrimitiveRoot( f );|
  Z(3^5)
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Frobenius Automorphisms}}\label{Frobenius Automorphisms}
\logpage{[ 59, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7A5F075185CE5B06}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FrobeniusAutomorphism}}
\logpage{[ 59, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8758E4AB7D0A1955}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FrobeniusAutomorphism({\mdseries\slshape F})\index{FrobeniusAutomorphism@\texttt{FrobeniusAutomorphism}}
\label{FrobeniusAutomorphism}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 \index{homomorphisms!Frobenius, field} \index{field homomorphisms!Frobenius} \index{CompositionMapping@\texttt{CompositionMapping}!for Frobenius automorphisms} returns the Frobenius automorphism of the finite field \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} as a field homomorphism (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Ring Homomorphisms}). 

 \index{Frobenius automorphism} The \emph{Frobenius automorphism} $f$ of a finite field $F$ of characteristic $p$ is the function that takes each element $z$ of $F$ to its $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power. Each field automorphism of $F$ is a power of $f$. Thus $f$ is a generator for the Galois group of $F$ relative to the prime field of $F$, and an appropriate power of $f$ is a generator of the Galois group of $F$ over a subfield (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{GaloisGroup} (\ref{GaloisGroup:of field})). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f := GF(16);|
  GF(2^4)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x := FrobeniusAutomorphism( f );|
  FrobeniusAutomorphism( GF(2^4) )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Z(16) ^ x;|
  Z(2^4)^2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x^2;|
  FrobeniusAutomorphism( GF(2^4) )^2
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \index{Image@\texttt{Image}!for Frobenius automorphisms} The image of an element $z$ under the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power of $f$ is computed as the $p^i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power of $z$. The product of the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power and the $j$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power of $f$ is the $k$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power of $f$, where $k$ is $i j \bmod $ \texttt{Size(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}})}$-1$. The zeroth power of $f$ is \texttt{IdentityMapping( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} )}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Conway Polynomials}}\label{Conway Polynomials}
\logpage{[ 59, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X869919BB7EBE5741}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ConwayPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 59, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C2425A786F09054}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ConwayPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape p, n})\index{ConwayPolynomial@\texttt{ConwayPolynomial}}
\label{ConwayPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 is the Conway polynomial of the finite field $GF(p^n)$ as polynomial over the prime field in characteristic \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}. 

 The \emph{Conway polynomial} $\Phi_{{n,p}}$ of $GF(p^n)$ is defined by the following properties. 

 First define an ordering of polynomials of degree $n$ over $GF(p)$, as follows. $f = \sum_{{i = 0}}^n (-1)^i f_i x^i$ is smaller than $g = \sum_{{i = 0}}^n (-1)^i g_i x^i$ if and only if there is an index $m \leq n$ such that $f_i = g_i$ for all $i > m$, and $\tilde{{f_m}} < \tilde{{g_m}}$, where $\tilde{{c}}$ denotes the integer value in $\{ 0, 1, \ldots, p-1 \}$ that is mapped to $c \in GF(p)$ under the canonical epimorphism that maps the integers onto $GF(p)$. 

 $\Phi_{{n,p}}$ is \emph{primitive} over $GF(p)$ (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsPrimitivePolynomial} (\ref{IsPrimitivePolynomial})). That is, $\Phi_{{n,p}}$ is irreducible, monic, and is the minimal polynomial of a primitive root of $GF(p^n)$. 

 For all divisors $d$ of $n$ the compatibility condition $\Phi_{{d,p}}( x^{{\frac{{p^n-1}}{{p^m-1}}}} ) \equiv 0
\pmod{{\Phi_{{n,p}}(x)}}$ holds. (That is, the appropriate power of a zero of $\Phi_{{n,p}}$ is a zero of the Conway polynomial $\Phi_{{d,p}}$.) 

 With respect to the ordering defined above, $\Phi_{{n,p}}$ shall be minimal. 

 The computation of Conway polynomials can be time consuming. Therefore, \textsf{GAP} comes with a list of precomputed polynomials. If a requested polynomial is not
stored then \textsf{GAP} prints a warning and computes it by checking all polynomials in the order
defined above for the defining conditions. If $n$ is not a prime this is probably a very long computation. (Some previously
known polynomials with prime $n$ are not stored in \textsf{GAP} because they are quickly recomputed.) Use the function \texttt{IsCheapConwayPolynomial} (\ref{IsCheapConwayPolynomial}) to check in advance if \texttt{ConwayPolynomial} will give a result after a short time. 

 Note that primitivity of a polynomial can only be checked if \textsf{GAP} can factorize $p^n-1$. A sufficiently new version of the \textsf{FactInt} package contains many precomputed factors of such numbers from various
factorization projects. 

 See{\nobreakspace}\cite{L03} for further information on known Conway polynomials. 

 An interactive overview of the Conway polynomials known to \textsf{GAP} is provided by the function \texttt{BrowseConwayPolynomials} from the \textsf{GAP} package \textsf{Browse}, see \texttt{BrowseGapData} (\textbf{Browse: BrowseGapData}). 

 \index{InfoText@\texttt{InfoText}!(for Conway polynomials)} If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} is a result returned by \texttt{ConwayPolynomial} the command \texttt{Print( InfoText( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} ) );} will print some info on the origin of that particular polynomial. 

 For some purposes it may be enough to have any primitive polynomial for an
extension of a finite field instead of the Conway polynomial,
see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{RandomPrimitivePolynomial} (\ref{RandomPrimitivePolynomial}) below. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ConwayPolynomial( 2, 5 );  ConwayPolynomial( 3, 7 );|
  x_1^5+x_1^2+Z(2)^0
  x_1^7-x_1^2+Z(3)^0
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsCheapConwayPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 59, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78A7C1247E129AD9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsCheapConwayPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape p, n})\index{IsCheapConwayPolynomial@\texttt{IsCheapConwayPolynomial}}
\label{IsCheapConwayPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Returns \texttt{true} if \texttt{ConwayPolynomial( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} )} will give a result in \emph{reasonable} time. This is either the case when this polynomial is
pre\texttt{\symbol{45}}computed, or if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is a not too big prime. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RandomPrimitivePolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 59, 5, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7ECC593583E68A6C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RandomPrimitivePolynomial({\mdseries\slshape F, n[, i]})\index{RandomPrimitivePolynomial@\texttt{RandomPrimitivePolynomial}}
\label{RandomPrimitivePolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For a finite field \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} and a positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} this function returns a primitive polynomial of degree \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} over \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}, that is a zero of this polynomial has maximal multiplicative order $|\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}|^n-1$. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} is given then the polynomial is written in variable number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} over \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Indeterminate} (\ref{Indeterminate:for a ring (and a number)})), the default for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} is 1. 

 Alternatively, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} can be a prime power q, then \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} = GF(q) is assumed. And \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} can be a univariate polynomial over \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}, then the result is a polynomial in the same variable. 

 This function can work for much larger fields than those for which Conway
polynomials are available, of course \textsf{GAP} must be able to factorize $|\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}|^n-1$. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Printing, Viewing and Displaying Finite Field Elements}}\label{Printing, Viewing and Displaying Finite Field Elements}
\logpage{[ 59, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X78EE3656879C3B88}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ViewObj (for a ffe)}}
\logpage{[ 59, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80DAAA5E7C79C94C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ViewObj({\mdseries\slshape z})\index{ViewObj@\texttt{ViewObj}!for a ffe}
\label{ViewObj:for a ffe}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrintObj({\mdseries\slshape z})\index{PrintObj@\texttt{PrintObj}!for a ffe}
\label{PrintObj:for a ffe}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Display({\mdseries\slshape z})\index{Display@\texttt{Display}!for a ffe}
\label{Display:for a ffe}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\


 Internal finite field elements are viewed, printed and displayed (see section \ref{View and Print} for the distinctions between these operations) as powers of the primitive root
(except for the zero element, which is displayed as 0 times the primitive
root). Thus: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Z(2);|
  Z(2)^0
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Z(5)+Z(5);|
  Z(5)^2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Z(256);|
  Z(2^8)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Zero(Z(125));|
  0*Z(5)
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note also that each element is displayed as an element of the field it
generates, and that the size of the field is printed as a power of the
characteristic. 

 Elements of larger fields are printed as \textsf{GAP} expressions which represent them as sums of low powers of the primitive root: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Print( Z(3,20)^100, "\n" );|
  2*Z(3,20)^2+Z(3,20)^4+Z(3,20)^6+Z(3,20)^7+2*Z(3,20)^9+2*Z(3,20)^10+2*Z\
  (3,20)^12+2*Z(3,20)^15+2*Z(3,20)^17+Z(3,20)^18+Z(3,20)^19
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Print( Z(3,20)^((3^20-1)/(3^10-1)), "\n" );|
  Z(3,20)^3+2*Z(3,20)^4+2*Z(3,20)^7+Z(3,20)^8+2*Z(3,20)^10+Z(3,20)^11+2*\
  Z(3,20)^12+Z(3,20)^13+Z(3,20)^14+Z(3,20)^15+Z(3,20)^17+Z(3,20)^18+2*Z(\
  3,20)^19
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Z(3,20)^((3^20-1)/(3^10-1)) = Z(3,10);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note from the second example above, that these elements are not always written
over the smallest possible field before being output. 

 The \texttt{ViewObj} and \texttt{Display} methods for these large finite field elements use a slightly more compact, but
mathematically equivalent representation. The primitive root is represented by \texttt{z}; its $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power by \texttt{z}$i$ and $k$ times this power by $k$\texttt{z}$i$. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Z(5,20)^100;|
  z2+z4+4z5+2z6+z8+3z9+4z10+3z12+z13+2z14+4z16+3z17+2z18+2z19
\end{Verbatim}
 

 This output format is always used for \texttt{Display}. For \texttt{ViewObj} it is used only if its length would not exceed the number of lines specified
in the user preference \texttt{ViewLength} (see \texttt{SetUserPreference} (\ref{SetUserPreference}). Longer output is replaced by \texttt{{\textless}{\textless}an element of GF(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape d}}){\textgreater}{\textgreater}}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Z(2,409)^100000;|
  <<an element of GF(2, 409)>>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Display(Z(2,409)^100000);|
  z2+z3+z4+z5+z6+z7+z8+z10+z11+z13+z17+z19+z20+z29+z32+z34+z35+z37+z40+z\
  45+z46+z48+z50+z52+z54+z55+z58+z59+z60+z66+z67+z68+z70+z74+z79+z80+z81\
  +z82+z83+z86+z91+z93+z94+z95+z96+z98+z99+z100+z101+z102+z104+z106+z109\
  +z110+z112+z114+z115+z118+z119+z123+z126+z127+z135+z138+z140+z142+z143\
  +z146+z147+z154+z159+z161+z162+z168+z170+z171+z173+z174+z181+z182+z183\
  +z186+z188+z189+z192+z193+z194+z195+z196+z199+z202+z204+z205+z207+z208\
  +z209+z211+z212+z213+z214+z215+z216+z218+z219+z220+z222+z223+z229+z232\
  +z235+z236+z237+z238+z240+z243+z244+z248+z250+z251+z256+z258+z262+z263\
  +z268+z270+z271+z272+z274+z276+z282+z286+z288+z289+z294+z295+z299+z300\
  +z301+z302+z303+z304+z305+z306+z307+z308+z309+z310+z312+z314+z315+z316\
  +z320+z321+z322+z324+z325+z326+z327+z330+z332+z335+z337+z338+z341+z344\
  +z348+z350+z352+z353+z356+z357+z358+z360+z362+z364+z366+z368+z372+z373\
  +z374+z375+z378+z379+z380+z381+z383+z384+z386+z387+z390+z395+z401+z402\
  +z406+z408
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Finally note that elements of large prime fields are stored and displayed as
residue class objects. So 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Z(65537);|
  ZmodpZObj( 3, 65537 )
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

 }

            
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Abelian Number Fields}}\label{Abelian Number Fields}
\logpage{[ 60, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X80510B5880521FDC}{}
{
  An \emph{abelian number field} is a field in characteristic zero that is a finite dimensional normal
extension of its prime field such that the Galois group is abelian. In \textsf{GAP}, one implementation of abelian number fields is given by fields of cyclotomic
numbers (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Cyclotomic Numbers}). Note that abelian number fields can also be constructed with the more
general \texttt{AlgebraicExtension} (\ref{AlgebraicExtension}), a discussion of advantages and disadvantages can be found in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Internally Represented Cyclotomics}. The functions described in this chapter have been developed for fields whose
elements are in the filter \texttt{IsCyclotomic} (\ref{IsCyclotomic}), they may or may not work well for abelian number fields consisting of other
kinds of elements. 

 Throughout this chapter, ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$ will denote the cyclotomic field generated by the field ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}$ of rationals together with $n$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th roots of unity. 

 In{\nobreakspace}\ref{Construction of Abelian Number Fields}, constructors for abelian number fields are described, \ref{Operations for Abelian Number Fields} introduces operations for abelian number fields, \ref{Integral Bases of Abelian Number Fields} deals with the vector space structure of abelian number fields, and \ref{Galois Groups of Abelian Number Fields} describes field automorphisms of abelian number fields,   
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Construction of Abelian Number Fields}}\label{Construction of Abelian Number Fields}
\logpage{[ 60, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D4E43E5799753B5}{}
{
  Besides the usual construction using \texttt{Field} (\ref{Field:for several generators}) or \texttt{DefaultField} (\ref{DefaultField:for cyclotomics}) (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{DefaultField} (\ref{DefaultField:for cyclotomics})), abelian number fields consisting of cyclotomics can be created with \texttt{CyclotomicField} (\ref{CyclotomicField:for (subfield and) conductor}) and \texttt{AbelianNumberField} (\ref{AbelianNumberField}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CyclotomicField (for (subfield and) conductor)}}
\logpage{[ 60, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80D21D80850EFA4B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CyclotomicField({\mdseries\slshape [subfield, ]n})\index{CyclotomicField@\texttt{CyclotomicField}!for (subfield and) conductor}
\label{CyclotomicField:for (subfield and) conductor}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CyclotomicField({\mdseries\slshape [subfield, ]gens})\index{CyclotomicField@\texttt{CyclotomicField}!for (subfield and) generators}
\label{CyclotomicField:for (subfield and) generators}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CF({\mdseries\slshape [subfield, ]n})\index{CF@\texttt{CF}!for (subfield and) conductor}
\label{CF:for (subfield and) conductor}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CF({\mdseries\slshape [subfield, ]gens})\index{CF@\texttt{CF}!for (subfield and) generators}
\label{CF:for (subfield and) generators}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 The first version creates the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th cyclotomic field ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$. The second version creates the smallest cyclotomic field containing the
elements in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. In both cases the field can be generated as an extension of a designated
subfield \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape subfield}} (cf.{\nobreakspace}\ref{Integral Bases of Abelian Number Fields}). 

 \texttt{CyclotomicField} can be abbreviated to \texttt{CF}, this form is used also when \textsf{GAP} prints cyclotomic fields. 

 Fields constructed with the one argument version of \texttt{CF} are stored in the global list \texttt{CYCLOTOMIC{\textunderscore}FIELDS}, so repeated calls of \texttt{CF} just fetch these field objects after they have been created once.  

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CyclotomicField( 5 );  CyclotomicField( [ Sqrt(3) ] );|
  CF(5)
  CF(12)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CF( CF(3), 12 );  CF( CF(4), [ Sqrt(7) ] );|
  AsField( CF(3), CF(12) )
  AsField( GaussianRationals, CF(28) )
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AbelianNumberField}}
\logpage{[ 60, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80E5AD028143E11E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AbelianNumberField({\mdseries\slshape n, stab})\index{AbelianNumberField@\texttt{AbelianNumberField}}
\label{AbelianNumberField}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NF({\mdseries\slshape n, stab})\index{NF@\texttt{NF}}
\label{NF}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For a positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stab}} of prime residues modulo \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, \texttt{AbelianNumberField} returns the fixed field of the group described by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stab}} (cf.{\nobreakspace}\texttt{GaloisStabilizer} (\ref{GaloisStabilizer})), in the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th cyclotomic field. \texttt{AbelianNumberField} is mainly thought for internal use and for printing fields in a standard way; \texttt{Field} (\ref{Field:for several generators}) (cf.{\nobreakspace}also{\nobreakspace}\ref{Operations for Abelian Number Fields}) is probably more suitable if one knows generators of the field in question. 

 \texttt{AbelianNumberField} can be abbreviated to \texttt{NF}, this form is used also when \textsf{GAP} prints abelian number fields. 

 Fields constructed with \texttt{NF} are stored in the global list \texttt{ABELIAN{\textunderscore}NUMBER{\textunderscore}FIELDS}, so repeated calls of \texttt{NF} just fetch these field objects after they have been created once.  

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NF( 7, [ 1 ] );|
  CF(7)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= NF( 7, [ 1, 2 ] );  Sqrt(-7); Sqrt(-7) in f;|
  NF(7,[ 1, 2, 4 ])
  E(7)+E(7)^2-E(7)^3+E(7)^4-E(7)^5-E(7)^6
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GaussianRationals}}
\logpage{[ 60, 1, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X82F53C65802FF551}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GaussianRationals\index{GaussianRationals@\texttt{GaussianRationals}}
\label{GaussianRationals}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsGaussianRationals({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsGaussianRationals@\texttt{IsGaussianRationals}}
\label{IsGaussianRationals}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 \texttt{GaussianRationals} is the field ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_4 = {\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}(\sqrt{{-1}})$ of Gaussian rationals, as a set of cyclotomic numbers, see
Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Cyclotomic Numbers} for basic operations. This field can also be obtained as \texttt{CF(4)} (see \texttt{CyclotomicField} (\ref{CyclotomicField:for (subfield and) conductor})). 

 The filter \texttt{IsGaussianRationals} returns \texttt{true} for the \textsf{GAP} object \texttt{GaussianRationals}, and \texttt{false} for all other \textsf{GAP} objects. 

 (For details about the field of rationals, see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Rationals} (\ref{Rationals}).) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CF(4) = GaussianRationals;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Sqrt(-1) in GaussianRationals;|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Operations for Abelian Number Fields}}\label{Operations for Abelian Number Fields}
\logpage{[ 60, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81B5FE06781DB824}{}
{
  For operations for elements of abelian number fields, e.g., \texttt{Conductor} (\ref{Conductor:for a cyclotomic}) or \texttt{ComplexConjugate} (\ref{ComplexConjugate}), see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Cyclotomic Numbers}. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Factors (for polynomials over abelian number fields)}}
\logpage{[ 60, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B0AB0FB7A4136C4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Factors({\mdseries\slshape F})\index{Factors@\texttt{Factors}!for polynomials over abelian number fields}
\label{Factors:for polynomials over abelian number fields}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\


 Factoring of polynomials over abelian number fields consisting of cyclotomics
works in principle but is not very efficient if the degree of the field
extension is large. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:= Indeterminate( CF(5) );|
  x_1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Factors( PolynomialRing( Rationals ), x^5-1 );|
  [ x_1-1, x_1^4+x_1^3+x_1^2+x_1+1 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Factors( PolynomialRing( CF(5) ), x^5-1 );|
  [ x_1-1, x_1+(-E(5)), x_1+(-E(5)^2), x_1+(-E(5)^3), x_1+(-E(5)^4) ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsNumberField}}
\logpage{[ 60, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87D78F5E875F2E8A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsNumberField({\mdseries\slshape F})\index{IsNumberField@\texttt{IsNumberField}}
\label{IsNumberField}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 \index{number field} returns \texttt{true} if the field \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} is a finite dimensional extension of a prime field in characteristic zero, and \texttt{false} otherwise. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsAbelianNumberField}}
\logpage{[ 60, 2, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D202D707D5708FA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsAbelianNumberField({\mdseries\slshape F})\index{IsAbelianNumberField@\texttt{IsAbelianNumberField}}
\label{IsAbelianNumberField}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 \index{abelian number field} returns \texttt{true} if the field \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} is a number field (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsNumberField} (\ref{IsNumberField})) that is a Galois extension of the prime field, with abelian Galois group
(see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{GaloisGroup} (\ref{GaloisGroup:of field})). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsCyclotomicField}}
\logpage{[ 60, 2, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84CAE4627F0CD639}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsCyclotomicField({\mdseries\slshape F})\index{IsCyclotomicField@\texttt{IsCyclotomicField}}
\label{IsCyclotomicField}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 returns \texttt{true} if the field \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} is a \emph{cyclotomic field}, i.e., an abelian number field (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsAbelianNumberField} (\ref{IsAbelianNumberField})) that can be generated by roots of unity. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsNumberField( CF(9) ); IsAbelianNumberField( Field( [ ER(3) ] ) );|
  true
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsNumberField( GF(2) );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsCyclotomicField( CF(9) );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsCyclotomicField( Field( [ Sqrt(-3) ] ) );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsCyclotomicField( Field( [ Sqrt(3) ] ) );|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GaloisStabilizer}}
\logpage{[ 60, 2, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87E7313D8070B9CC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GaloisStabilizer({\mdseries\slshape F})\index{GaloisStabilizer@\texttt{GaloisStabilizer}}
\label{GaloisStabilizer}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} be an abelian number field (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsAbelianNumberField} (\ref{IsAbelianNumberField})) with conductor $n$, say. (This means that the $n$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th cyclotomic field is the smallest cyclotomic field
containing \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Conductor} (\ref{Conductor:for a cyclotomic}).) \texttt{GaloisStabilizer} returns the set of all those integers $k$ in the range $[ 1 .. n ]$ such that the field automorphism induced by raising $n$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th roots of unity to the $k$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power acts trivially on \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r5:= Sqrt(5);|
  E(5)-E(5)^2-E(5)^3+E(5)^4
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GaloisCyc( r5, 4 ) = r5;  GaloisCyc( r5, 2 ) = r5;|
  true
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GaloisStabilizer( Field( [ r5 ] ) );|
  [ 1, 4 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Integral Bases of Abelian Number Fields}}\label{Integral Bases of Abelian Number Fields}
\logpage{[ 60, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D2421AC8491D2BE}{}
{
  Each abelian number field is naturally a vector space over ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}$. Moreover, if the abelian number field $F$ contains the $n$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th cyclotomic field ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$ then $F$ is a vector space over ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$. In \textsf{GAP}, each field object represents a vector space object over a certain subfield $S$, which depends on the way $F$ was constructed. The subfield $S$ can be accessed as the value of the attribute \texttt{LeftActingDomain} (\ref{LeftActingDomain}). 

 The return values of \texttt{NF} (\ref{NF}) and of the one argument versions of \texttt{CF} (\ref{CF:for (subfield and) conductor}) represent vector spaces over ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}$, and the return values of the two argument version of \texttt{CF} (\ref{CF:for (subfield and) conductor}) represent vector spaces over the field that is given as the first argument.
For an abelian number field \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} and a subfield \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}, a \textsf{GAP} object representing \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} as a vector space over \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} can be constructed using \texttt{AsField} (\ref{AsField}). 

 \index{cyclotomic fields!CanonicalBasis} Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} be the cyclotomic field ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$, represented as a vector space over the subfield \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is the cyclotomic field ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_m$, with $m$ a divisor of $n$, then \texttt{CanonicalBasis( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} )} returns the Zumbroich basis of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} relative to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}, which consists of the roots of unity \texttt{E(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}})}\texttt{\symbol{94}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} is an element of the list \texttt{ZumbroichBase( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} )} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{ZumbroichBase} (\ref{ZumbroichBase})). If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is an abelian number field that is not a cyclotomic field then \texttt{CanonicalBasis( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} )} returns a normal \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}basis of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}, i.e., a basis that is closed under the field automorphisms of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}. 

 \index{abelian number fields!CanonicalBasis} Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} be the abelian number field \texttt{NF( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stab}} )}, with conductor \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, that is itself not a cyclotomic field, represented as a vector space over
the subfield \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is the cyclotomic field ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_m$, with $m$ a divisor of $n$, then \texttt{CanonicalBasis( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} )} returns the Lenstra basis of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} relative to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} that consists of the sums of roots of unity described by \texttt{LenstraBase( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stab}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stab}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} )} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{LenstraBase} (\ref{LenstraBase})). If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}} is an abelian number field that is not a cyclotomic field then \texttt{CanonicalBasis( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} )} returns a normal \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape S}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}basis of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= CF(8);;   # a cycl. field over the rationals|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@b:= CanonicalBasis( f );;  BasisVectors( b );|
  [ 1, E(8), E(4), E(8)^3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Coefficients( b, Sqrt(-2) );|
  [ 0, 1, 0, 1 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= AsField( CF(4), CF(8) );;  # a cycl. field over a cycl. field|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@b:= CanonicalBasis( f );;  BasisVectors( b );|
  [ 1, E(8) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Coefficients( b, Sqrt(-2) );|
  [ 0, 1+E(4) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= AsField( Field( [ Sqrt(-2) ] ), CF(8) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# a cycl. field over a non-cycl. field|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@b:= CanonicalBasis( f );;  BasisVectors( b );|
  [ 1/2+1/2*E(8)-1/2*E(8)^2-1/2*E(8)^3,
    1/2-1/2*E(8)+1/2*E(8)^2+1/2*E(8)^3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Coefficients( b, Sqrt(-2) );|
  [ E(8)+E(8)^3, E(8)+E(8)^3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= Field( [ Sqrt(-2) ] );   # a non-cycl. field over the rationals|
  NF(8,[ 1, 3 ])
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@b:= CanonicalBasis( f );;  BasisVectors( b );|
  [ 1, E(8)+E(8)^3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Coefficients( b, Sqrt(-2) );|
  [ 0, 1 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ZumbroichBase}}
\logpage{[ 60, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F52BEA0862E06F2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZumbroichBase({\mdseries\slshape n, m})\index{ZumbroichBase@\texttt{ZumbroichBase}}
\label{ZumbroichBase}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} be positive integers, such that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} divides \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. \texttt{ZumbroichBase} returns the set of exponents $i$ for which \texttt{E(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}})\texttt{\symbol{94}}}$i$ belongs to the (generalized) Zumbroich basis of the cyclotomic field ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$, viewed as a vector space over ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_m$. 

 This basis is defined as follows. Let $P$ denote the set of prime divisors of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} = \prod_{{p \in P}} p^{{\nu_p}}$, and $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} = \prod_{{p \in P}} p^{{\mu_p}}$ with $\mu_p \leq \nu_p$. Let $e_l =$ \texttt{E}$(l)$ for any positive integer $l$, and $\{ e_{{n_1}}^j \}_{{j \in J}} \otimes \{ e_{{n_2}}^k \}_{{k \in K}} = \{
e_{{n_1}}^j \cdot e_{{n_2}}^k \}_{{j \in J, k \in K}}$. 

 Then the basis is 
\[ B_{{n,m}} = \bigotimes_{{p \in P}} \bigotimes_{{k = \mu_p}}^{{\nu_p-1}} \{
e_{{p^{{k+1}}}}^j \}_{{j \in J_{{k,p}}}} \]
 where $J_{{k,p}} =$ \begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcl}$\{ 0 \}$&
;&
$k = 0, p = 2$\\
$\{ 0, 1 \}$&
;&
$k > 0, p = 2$\\
$\{ 1, \ldots, p-1 \}$&
;&
$k = 0, p \neq 2$\\
$\{ -(p-1)/2, \ldots, (p-1)/2 \}$&
;&
$k > 0, p \neq 2$\\
\end{tabular}\\[2mm]
\end{center}

 

 $B_{{n,1}}$ is equal to the basis of ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$ over the rationals which is introduced in{\nobreakspace}\cite{Zum89}. Also the conversion of arbitrary sums of roots of unity into its basis
representation, and the reduction to the minimal cyclotomic field are
described in this thesis. (Note that the notation here is slightly different
from that there.) 

 $B_{{n,m}}$ consists of roots of unity, it is an integral basis (that is, exactly the
integral elements in ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$ have integral coefficients w.r.t.{\nobreakspace}$B_{{n,m}}$, cf.{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsIntegralCyclotomic} (\ref{IsIntegralCyclotomic})), it is a normal basis for squarefree $n$ and closed under complex conjugation for odd $n$. 

 \emph{Note:} For $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, we have \texttt{ZumbroichBase(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, 1) = 2 * ZumbroichBase(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}/2, 1)} and \texttt{List( ZumbroichBase(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, 1), x \texttt{\symbol{45}}{\textgreater} E(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}})\texttt{\symbol{94}}x ) = List( ZumbroichBase(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}/2, 1), x \texttt{\symbol{45}}{\textgreater} E(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}/2)\texttt{\symbol{94}}x )}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ZumbroichBase( 15, 1 ); ZumbroichBase( 12, 3 );|
  [ 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14 ]
  [ 0, 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ZumbroichBase( 10, 2 ); ZumbroichBase( 32, 4 );|
  [ 2, 4, 6, 8 ]
  [ 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LenstraBase}}
\logpage{[ 60, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87DB9C2C858B722A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LenstraBase({\mdseries\slshape n, stabilizer, super, m})\index{LenstraBase@\texttt{LenstraBase}}
\label{LenstraBase}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} be positive integers such that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} divides \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stabilizer}} be a list of prime residues modulo \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, which describes a subfield of the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th cyclotomic field (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{GaloisStabilizer} (\ref{GaloisStabilizer})), and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}} be a list representing a supergroup of the group given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stabilizer}}. 

 \texttt{LenstraBase} returns a list $[ b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_k ]$ of lists, each $b_i$ consisting of integers such that the elements $\sum_{{j \in b_i}} $\texttt{E(n)}$^j$ form a basis of the abelian number field \texttt{NF( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stabilizer}} )}, as a vector space over the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th cyclotomic field (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{AbelianNumberField} (\ref{AbelianNumberField})). 

 This basis is an integral basis, that is, exactly the integral elements in \texttt{NF( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stabilizer}} )} have integral coefficients. (For details about this basis, see{\nobreakspace}\cite{Bre97}.) 

 If possible then the result is chosen such that the group described by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}} acts on it, consistently with the action of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stabilizer}}, i.e., each orbit of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}} is a union of orbits of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stabilizer}}. (A usual case is \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}}\texttt{ = }\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stabilizer}}, so there is no additional condition. 

 \emph{Note:} The $b_i$ are in general not sets, since for \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stabilizer}} = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}}}, the first entry is always an element of \texttt{ZumbroichBase( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}} )}; this property is used by \texttt{NF} (\ref{NF}) and \texttt{Coefficients} (\ref{Coefficients}) (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Integral Bases of Abelian Number Fields}). 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stabilizer}} must not contain the stabilizer of a proper cyclotomic subfield of the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th cyclotomic field, i.e., the result must describe a
basis for a field with conductor \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LenstraBase( 24, [ 1, 19 ], [ 1, 19 ], 1 );|
  [ [ 1, 19 ], [ 8 ], [ 11, 17 ], [ 16 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LenstraBase( 24, [ 1, 19 ], [ 1, 5, 19, 23 ], 1 );|
  [ [ 1, 19 ], [ 5, 23 ], [ 8 ], [ 16 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LenstraBase( 15, [ 1, 4 ], PrimeResidues( 15 ), 1 );|
  [ [ 1, 4 ], [ 2, 8 ], [ 7, 13 ], [ 11, 14 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The first two results describe two bases of the field ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_3(\sqrt{{6}})$, the third result describes a normal basis of ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_3(\sqrt{{5}})$. }

   }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Galois Groups of Abelian Number Fields}}\label{Galois Groups of Abelian Number Fields}
\logpage{[ 60, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7E4AB4B17C7BA10C}{}
{
  \index{abelian number fields!Galois group} \index{number fields!Galois group} \index{automorphism group!of number fields} The field automorphisms of the cyclotomic field ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$ (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Cyclotomic Numbers}) are given by the linear maps $*k$ on ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$ that are defined by \texttt{E}$(n)^{{*k}} = $\texttt{E}$(n)^k$, where $1 \leq k < n$ and \texttt{Gcd}$( n, k ) = 1$ hold (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{GaloisCyc} (\ref{GaloisCyc:for a cyclotomic})). Note that this action is \emph{not} equal to exponentiation of cyclotomics, i.e., for general cyclotomics $z$, $z^{{*k}}$ is different from $z^k$. 

 (In \textsf{GAP}, the image of a cyclotomic $z$ under $*k$ can be computed as \texttt{GaloisCyc( }$z, k$\texttt{ )}.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@( E(5) + E(5)^4 )^2; GaloisCyc( E(5) + E(5)^4, 2 );|
  -2*E(5)-E(5)^2-E(5)^3-2*E(5)^4
  E(5)^2+E(5)^3
\end{Verbatim}
 

 For \texttt{Gcd}$( n, k ) \neq 1$, the map \texttt{E}$(n) \mapsto$ \texttt{E}$(n)^k$ does \emph{not} define a field automorphism of ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$ but only a ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}$\texttt{\symbol{45}}linear map. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GaloisCyc( E(5)+E(5)^4, 5 ); GaloisCyc( ( E(5)+E(5)^4 )^2, 5 );|
  2
  -6
\end{Verbatim}
 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GaloisGroup (for abelian number fields)}}
\logpage{[ 60, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B55A90582E818F3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GaloisGroup({\mdseries\slshape F})\index{GaloisGroup@\texttt{GaloisGroup}!for abelian number fields}
\label{GaloisGroup:for abelian number fields}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\


 The Galois group $Gal( {\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n, {\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}} )$ of the field extension ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n / {\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}$ is isomorphic to the group $({\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}})^{*}$ of prime residues modulo $n$, via the isomorphism $({\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}})^{*} \rightarrow Gal(
{\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n, {\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}} )$ that is defined by $k + n {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} \mapsto ( z \mapsto z^{*k} )$. 

 The Galois group of the field extension ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n / L$ with any abelian number field $L \subseteq {\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n$ is simply the factor group of $Gal( {\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}}_n, {\ensuremath{\mathbb Q}} )$ modulo the stabilizer of $L$, and the Galois group of $L / L'$, with $L'$ an abelian number field contained in $L$, is the subgroup in this group that stabilizes $L'$. These groups are easily described in terms of $({\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}})^{*}$. Generators of $({\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}})^{*}$ can be computed using \texttt{GeneratorsPrimeResidues} (\ref{GeneratorsPrimeResidues}). 

 In \textsf{GAP}, a field extension $L / L'$ is given by the field object $L$ with \texttt{LeftActingDomain} (\ref{LeftActingDomain}) value $L'$ (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Integral Bases of Abelian Number Fields}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= CF(15);|
  CF(15)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= GaloisGroup( f );|
  <group with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( g ); IsCyclic( g ); IsAbelian( g );|
  8
  false
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Action( g, NormalBase( f ), OnPoints );|
  Group([ (1,6)(2,4)(3,8)(5,7), (1,4,3,7)(2,8,5,6) ])
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The following example shows Galois groups of a cyclotomic field and of a
proper subfield that is not a cyclotomic field. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@gens1:= GeneratorsOfGroup( GaloisGroup( CF(5) ) );|
  [ ANFAutomorphism( CF(5), 2 ) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@gens2:= GeneratorsOfGroup( GaloisGroup( Field( Sqrt(5) ) ) );|
  [ ANFAutomorphism( NF(5,[ 1, 4 ]), 2 ) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Order( gens1[1] );  Order( gens2[1] );|
  4
  2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Sqrt(5)^gens1[1] = Sqrt(5)^gens2[1];|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The following example shows the Galois group of a cyclotomic field over a
non\texttt{\symbol{45}}cyclotomic field. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= GaloisGroup( AsField( Field( [ Sqrt(5) ] ), CF(5) ) );|
  <group of size 2 with 1 generator>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@gens:= GeneratorsOfGroup( g );|
  [ ANFAutomorphism( AsField( NF(5,[ 1, 4 ]), CF(5) ), 4 ) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:= last[1];;  x^2;|
  IdentityMapping( AsField( NF(5,[ 1, 4 ]), CF(5) ) )
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ANFAutomorphism}}
\logpage{[ 60, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8643D4B47A827D9D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ANFAutomorphism({\mdseries\slshape F, k})\index{ANFAutomorphism@\texttt{ANFAutomorphism}}
\label{ANFAutomorphism}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} be an abelian number field and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}} be an integer that is coprime to the conductor (see \texttt{Conductor} (\ref{Conductor:for a collection of cyclotomics})) of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}. Then \texttt{ANFAutomorphism} returns the automorphism of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} that is defined as the linear extension of the map that raises each root of
unity in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} to its \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th power. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= CF(25);|
  CF(25)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@alpha:= ANFAutomorphism( f, 2 );|
  ANFAutomorphism( CF(25), 2 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@alpha^2;|
  ANFAutomorphism( CF(25), 4 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Order( alpha );|
  20
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@E(5)^alpha;|
  E(5)^2
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GaussianIntegers\index{GaussianIntegers@\texttt{GaussianIntegers}}
\label{GaussianIntegers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 \texttt{GaussianIntegers} is the ring ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}[\sqrt{{-1}}]$ of Gaussian integers. This is a subring of the cyclotomic field \texttt{GaussianRationals} (\ref{GaussianRationals}). }

\hyperdef{L}{X7BFD33D27BFB7C5A}{}

\label{IsGaussianIntegers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 is the defining category for the domain \texttt{GaussianIntegers} (\ref{GaussianIntegers}). }

  }

\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Vector Spaces}}\label{Vector Spaces}
\logpage{[ 61, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7DAD6700787EC845}{}
{
   
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsLeftVectorSpace (Filter)}}\label{sect:IsLeftVectorSpace}
\logpage{[ 61, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8754F7207CFDA38B}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsLeftVectorSpace}}
\logpage{[ 61, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80290A908241706B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsLeftVectorSpace({\mdseries\slshape V})\index{IsLeftVectorSpace@\texttt{IsLeftVectorSpace}}
\label{IsLeftVectorSpace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsVectorSpace({\mdseries\slshape V})\index{IsVectorSpace@\texttt{IsVectorSpace}}
\label{IsVectorSpace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 A \emph{vector space} in \textsf{GAP} is a free left module (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsFreeLeftModule} (\ref{IsFreeLeftModule})) over a division ring (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Fields and Division Rings}). 

 Whenever we talk about an $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}vector space \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} then \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} is an additive group (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsAdditiveGroup} (\ref{IsAdditiveGroup})) on which the division ring $F$ acts via multiplication from the left such that this action and the addition
in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} are left and right distributive. The division ring $F$ can be accessed as value of the attribute \texttt{LeftActingDomain} (\ref{LeftActingDomain}). 

 Vector spaces in \textsf{GAP} are always \emph{left} vector spaces, \texttt{IsLeftVectorSpace} and \texttt{IsVectorSpace} are synonyms. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Constructing Vector Spaces}}\label{Constructing Vector Spaces}
\logpage{[ 61, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X87AD06FE873619EA}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{VectorSpace}}
\logpage{[ 61, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X805413157CE9BECF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{VectorSpace({\mdseries\slshape F, gens[, zero][, "basis"]})\index{VectorSpace@\texttt{VectorSpace}}
\label{VectorSpace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For a field \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} and a collection \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} of vectors, \texttt{VectorSpace} returns the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}vector space spanned by the elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. 

 The optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape zero}} can be used to specify the zero element of the space; \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape zero}} \emph{must} be given if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} is empty. The optional string \texttt{"basis"} indicates that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} is known to be linearly independent over \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}, in particular the dimension of the vector space is immediately set; note
that \texttt{Basis} (\ref{Basis}) need \emph{not} return the basis formed by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} if the string \texttt{"basis"} is given as an argument.  
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@V:= VectorSpace( Rationals, [ [ 1, 2, 3 ], [ 1, 1, 1 ] ] );|
  <vector space over Rationals, with 2 generators>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Subspace}}
\logpage{[ 61, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78C9826780BC9AE6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Subspace({\mdseries\slshape V, gens[, "basis"]})\index{Subspace@\texttt{Subspace}}
\label{Subspace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SubspaceNC({\mdseries\slshape V, gens[, "basis"]})\index{SubspaceNC@\texttt{SubspaceNC}}
\label{SubspaceNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For an $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}vector space \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} and a list or collection \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} that is a subset of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}, \texttt{Subspace} returns the $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}vector space spanned by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}; if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} is empty then the trivial subspace (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{TrivialSubspace} (\ref{TrivialSubspace})) of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} is returned. The parent (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Parents}) of the returned vector space is set to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}. 

 \texttt{SubspaceNC} does the same as \texttt{Subspace}, except that it omits the check whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} is a subset of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}. 

 The optional string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape "basis"}} indicates that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} is known to be linearly independent over $F$. In this case the dimension of the subspace is immediately set, and both \texttt{Subspace} and \texttt{SubspaceNC} do \emph{not} check whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} really is linearly independent and whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} is a subset of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}.  
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@V:= VectorSpace( Rationals, [ [ 1, 2, 3 ], [ 1, 1, 1 ] ] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@W:= Subspace( V, [ [ 0, 1, 2 ] ] );|
  <vector space over Rationals, with 1 generator>
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AsVectorSpace}}
\logpage{[ 61, 2, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B001BAF7D5FD5D0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AsVectorSpace({\mdseries\slshape F, D})\index{AsVectorSpace@\texttt{AsVectorSpace}}
\label{AsVectorSpace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} be a division ring and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} a domain. If the elements in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} form an \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}vector space then \texttt{AsVectorSpace} returns this \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}vector space, otherwise \texttt{fail} is returned. 

 \texttt{AsVectorSpace} can be used for example to view a given vector space as a vector space over a
smaller or larger division ring. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@V:= FullRowSpace( GF( 27 ), 3 );|
  ( GF(3^3)^3 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Dimension( V );  LeftActingDomain( V );|
  3
  GF(3^3)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@W:= AsVectorSpace( GF( 3 ), V );|
  <vector space over GF(3), with 9 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Dimension( W );  LeftActingDomain( W );|
  9
  GF(3)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AsVectorSpace( GF( 9 ), V );|
  fail
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AsSubspace}}
\logpage{[ 61, 2, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D4F84C27EDAC89B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AsSubspace({\mdseries\slshape V, U})\index{AsSubspace@\texttt{AsSubspace}}
\label{AsSubspace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} be an $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}vector space, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} a collection. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} is a subset of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} such that the elements of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} form an $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}vector space then \texttt{AsSubspace} returns this vector space, with parent set to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{AsVectorSpace} (\ref{AsVectorSpace})). Otherwise \texttt{fail} is returned. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@V:= VectorSpace( Rationals, [ [ 1, 2, 3 ], [ 1, 1, 1 ] ] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@W:= VectorSpace( Rationals, [ [ 1/2, 1/2, 1/2 ] ] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@U:= AsSubspace( V, W );|
  <vector space over Rationals, with 1 generator>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Parent( U ) = V;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AsSubspace( V, [ [ 1, 1, 1 ] ] );|
  fail
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Operations and Attributes for Vector Spaces}}\label{Operations and Attributes for Vector Spaces}
\logpage{[ 61, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X789FB2D883E53662}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GeneratorsOfLeftVectorSpace}}
\logpage{[ 61, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X849651C6830C94A1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GeneratorsOfLeftVectorSpace({\mdseries\slshape V})\index{GeneratorsOfLeftVectorSpace@\texttt{GeneratorsOfLeftVectorSpace}}
\label{GeneratorsOfLeftVectorSpace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GeneratorsOfVectorSpace({\mdseries\slshape V})\index{GeneratorsOfVectorSpace@\texttt{GeneratorsOfVectorSpace}}
\label{GeneratorsOfVectorSpace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For an $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}vector space \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}, \texttt{GeneratorsOfLeftVectorSpace} returns a list of vectors in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} that generate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} as an $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}vector space. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GeneratorsOfVectorSpace( FullRowSpace( Rationals, 3 ) );|
  [ [ 1, 0, 0 ], [ 0, 1, 0 ], [ 0, 0, 1 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TrivialSubspace}}
\logpage{[ 61, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86DC71A9835430FD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TrivialSubspace({\mdseries\slshape V})\index{TrivialSubspace@\texttt{TrivialSubspace}}
\label{TrivialSubspace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For a vector space \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}, \texttt{TrivialSubspace} returns the subspace of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} that consists of the zero vector in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@V:= GF(3)^3;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@triv:= TrivialSubspace( V );|
  <vector space of dimension 0 over GF(3)>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AsSet( triv );|
  [ [ 0*Z(3), 0*Z(3), 0*Z(3) ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Domains of Subspaces of Vector Spaces}}\label{Domains of Subspaces of Vector Spaces}
\logpage{[ 61, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8125675583357131}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Subspaces}}
\logpage{[ 61, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7975E41A7B29C3FD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Subspaces({\mdseries\slshape V[, k]})\index{Subspaces@\texttt{Subspaces}}
\label{Subspaces}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Called with a finite vector space \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}, \texttt{Subspaces} returns the domain of all subspaces of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}. 

 Called with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} and a nonnegative integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}, \texttt{Subspaces} returns the domain of all \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}dimensional subspaces of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}. 

 Special \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}) and \texttt{Iterator} (\ref{Iterator}) methods are provided for these domains.  }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsSubspacesVectorSpace}}
\logpage{[ 61, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A8F5C367FAE3D1B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsSubspacesVectorSpace({\mdseries\slshape D})\index{IsSubspacesVectorSpace@\texttt{IsSubspacesVectorSpace}}
\label{IsSubspacesVectorSpace}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 The domain of all subspaces of a (finite) vector space or of all subspaces of
fixed dimension, as returned by \texttt{Subspaces} (\ref{Subspaces}) (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Subspaces} (\ref{Subspaces})) lies in the category \texttt{IsSubspacesVectorSpace}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@D:= Subspaces( GF(3)^3 );|
  Subspaces( ( GF(3)^3 ) )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( D );|
  28
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@iter:= Iterator( D );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NextIterator( iter );|
  <vector space of dimension 0 over GF(3)>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NextIterator( iter );|
  <vector space of dimension 1 over GF(3)>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsSubspacesVectorSpace( D );|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

    }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Bases of Vector Spaces}}\label{Bases of Vector Spaces}
\logpage{[ 61, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X828AA09B87F14FAD}{}
{
  In \textsf{GAP}, a \emph{basis} of a free left $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}module $V$ is a list of vectors $B = [ v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n ]$ in $V$ such that $V$ is generated as a left $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}module by these vectors and such that $B$ is linearly independent over $F$. The integer $n$ is the dimension of $V$ (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Dimension} (\ref{Dimension})). In particular, as each basis is a list (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Lists}), it has a length (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Length} (\ref{Length})), and the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th vector of $B$ can be accessed as $B[i]$. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@V:= Rationals^3;|
  ( Rationals^3 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@B:= Basis( V );|
  CanonicalBasis( ( Rationals^3 ) )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Length( B );|
  3
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@B[1];|
  [ 1, 0, 0 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The operations described below make sense only for bases of \emph{finite} dimensional vector spaces. (In practice this means that the vector spaces must
be \emph{low} dimensional, that is, the dimension should not exceed a few hundred.) 

 Besides the basic operations for lists (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Basic Operations for Lists}), the \emph{basic operations for bases} are \texttt{BasisVectors} (\ref{BasisVectors}), \texttt{Coefficients} (\ref{Coefficients}), \texttt{LinearCombination} (\ref{LinearCombination}), and \texttt{UnderlyingLeftModule} (\ref{UnderlyingLeftModule}). These and other operations for arbitrary bases are described
in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Operations for Vector Space Bases}. 

 For special kinds of bases, further operations are defined (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Operations for Special Kinds of Bases}). 

 \textsf{GAP} supports the following three kinds of bases. 

 \emph{Relative bases} delegate the work to other bases of the same free left module, via basechange
matrices (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{RelativeBasis} (\ref{RelativeBasis})). 

 \emph{Bases handled by nice bases} delegate the work to bases of isomorphic left modules over the same left
acting domain (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Vector Spaces Handled By Nice Bases}). 

 Finally, of course there must be bases in \textsf{GAP} that really do the work. 

 For example, in the case of a Gaussian row or matrix space \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Row and Matrix Spaces}), \texttt{Basis( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} )} is a semi\texttt{\symbol{45}}echelonized basis (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsSemiEchelonized} (\ref{IsSemiEchelonized})) that uses Gaussian elimination; such a basis is of the third kind. \texttt{Basis( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vectors}} )} is either semi\texttt{\symbol{45}}echelonized or a relative basis. Other
examples of bases of the third kind are canonical bases of finite fields and
of abelian number fields. 

 Bases handled by nice bases are described in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Vector Spaces Handled By Nice Bases}. Examples are non\texttt{\symbol{45}}Gaussian row and matrix spaces, and
subspaces of finite fields and abelian number fields that are themselves not
fields. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsBasis}}
\logpage{[ 61, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8739510881F5D862}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsBasis({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsBasis@\texttt{IsBasis}}
\label{IsBasis}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 In \textsf{GAP}, a \emph{basis} of a free left module is an object that knows how to compute coefficients
w.r.t.{\nobreakspace}its basis vectors (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Coefficients} (\ref{Coefficients})). Bases are constructed by \texttt{Basis} (\ref{Basis}). Each basis is an immutable list, the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th entry being the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th basis vector. 

 (See{\nobreakspace}\ref{Mutable Bases} for mutable bases.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@V:= GF(2)^2;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@B:= Basis( V );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBasis( B );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBasis( [ [ 1, 0 ], [ 0, 1 ] ] );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBasis( Basis( Rationals^2, [ [ 1, 0 ], [ 0, 1 ] ] ) );|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Basis}}
\logpage{[ 61, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X837BE54C80DE368E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Basis({\mdseries\slshape V[, vectors]})\index{Basis@\texttt{Basis}}
\label{Basis}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{BasisNC({\mdseries\slshape V, vectors})\index{BasisNC@\texttt{BasisNC}}
\label{BasisNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Called with a free left $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}module \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} as the only argument, \texttt{Basis} returns an $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}basis of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} whose vectors are not further specified. 

 If additionally a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vectors}} of vectors in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} is given that forms an $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}basis of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} then \texttt{Basis} returns this basis; if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vectors}} is not linearly independent over $F$ or does not generate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} as a free left $F$\texttt{\symbol{45}}module then \texttt{fail} is returned. 

 \texttt{BasisNC} does the same as the two argument version of \texttt{Basis}, except that it does not check whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vectors}} form a basis. 

 If no basis vectors are prescribed then \texttt{Basis} need not compute basis vectors; in this case, the vectors are computed in the
first call to \texttt{BasisVectors} (\ref{BasisVectors}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@V:= VectorSpace( Rationals, [ [ 1, 2, 7 ], [ 1/2, 1/3, 5 ] ] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@B:= Basis( V );|
  SemiEchelonBasis( <vector space over Rationals, with
  2 generators>, ... )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@BasisVectors( B );|
  [ [ 1, 2, 7 ], [ 0, 1, -9/4 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@B:= Basis( V, [ [ 1, 2, 7 ], [ 3, 2, 30 ] ] );|
  Basis( <vector space over Rationals, with 2 generators>,
  [ [ 1, 2, 7 ], [ 3, 2, 30 ] ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Basis( V, [ [ 1, 2, 3 ] ] );|
  fail
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CanonicalBasis}}
\logpage{[ 61, 5, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C8EBFF5805F8C51}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CanonicalBasis({\mdseries\slshape V})\index{CanonicalBasis@\texttt{CanonicalBasis}}
\label{CanonicalBasis}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 If the vector space \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} supports a \emph{canonical basis} then \texttt{CanonicalBasis} returns this basis, otherwise \texttt{fail} is returned. 

 The defining property of a canonical basis is that its vectors are uniquely
determined by the vector space. If canonical bases exist for two vector spaces
over the same left acting domain (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{LeftActingDomain} (\ref{LeftActingDomain})) then the equality of these vector spaces can be decided by comparing the
canonical bases. 

 The exact meaning of a canonical basis depends on the type of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}. Canonical bases are defined for example for Gaussian row and matrix spaces
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Row and Matrix Spaces}). 

 If one designs a new kind of vector spaces (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{How to Implement New Kinds of Vector Spaces}) and defines a canonical basis for these spaces then the \texttt{CanonicalBasis} method one installs (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod})) must \emph{not} call \texttt{Basis} (\ref{Basis}). On the other hand, one probably should install a \texttt{Basis} (\ref{Basis}) method that simply calls \texttt{CanonicalBasis}, the value of the method (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Method Installation} and \ref{Applicable Methods and Method Selection}) being \texttt{CANONICAL{\textunderscore}BASIS{\textunderscore}FLAGS}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@vecs:= [ [ 1, 2, 3 ], [ 1, 1, 1 ], [ 1, 1, 1 ] ];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@V:= VectorSpace( Rationals, vecs );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@B:= CanonicalBasis( V );|
  CanonicalBasis( <vector space over Rationals, with 3 generators> )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@BasisVectors( B );|
  [ [ 1, 0, -1 ], [ 0, 1, 2 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RelativeBasis}}
\logpage{[ 61, 5, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8786D40B84120F38}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RelativeBasis({\mdseries\slshape B, vectors})\index{RelativeBasis@\texttt{RelativeBasis}}
\label{RelativeBasis}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RelativeBasisNC({\mdseries\slshape B, vectors})\index{RelativeBasisNC@\texttt{RelativeBasisNC}}
\label{RelativeBasisNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 A relative basis is a basis of the free left module \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} that delegates the computation of coefficients etc. to another basis of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}} via a basechange matrix. 

 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape B}} be a basis of the free left module \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vectors}} a list of vectors in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}. 

 \texttt{RelativeBasis} checks whether \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vectors}} form a basis of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape V}}, and in this case a basis is returned in which \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vectors}} are the basis vectors; otherwise \texttt{fail} is returned. 

 \texttt{RelativeBasisNC} does the same, except that it omits the check. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Operations for Vector Space Bases}}\label{Operations for Vector Space Bases}
\logpage{[ 61, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X839B9C4880EBFB5F}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{BasisVectors}}
\logpage{[ 61, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B1F17AE8027A590}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{BasisVectors({\mdseries\slshape B})\index{BasisVectors@\texttt{BasisVectors}}
\label{BasisVectors}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For a vector space basis \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape B}}, \texttt{BasisVectors} returns the list of basis vectors of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape B}}. The lists \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape B}} and \texttt{BasisVectors( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape B}} )} are equal; the main purpose of \texttt{BasisVectors} is to provide access to a list of vectors that does \emph{not} know about an underlying vector space. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@V:= VectorSpace( Rationals, [ [ 1, 2, 7 ], [ 1/2, 1/3, 5 ] ] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@B:= Basis( V, [ [ 1, 2, 7 ], [ 0, 1, -9/4 ] ] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@BasisVectors( B );|
  [ [ 1, 2, 7 ], [ 0, 1, -9/4 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UnderlyingLeftModule}}
\logpage{[ 61, 6, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81E8AE88843B70FF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UnderlyingLeftModule({\mdseries\slshape B})\index{UnderlyingLeftModule@\texttt{UnderlyingLeftModule}}
\label{UnderlyingLeftModule}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For a basis \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape B}} of a free left module $V$, \texttt{UnderlyingLeftModule} returns $V$.
