\logpage{[ 65, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86D2CA90847C091B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GroupRing({\mdseries\slshape R, G})\index{GroupRing@\texttt{GroupRing}}
\label{GroupRing}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 is the group ring of the group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, over the ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsFreeMagmaRing}}
\logpage{[ 65, 1, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A24B95C8210BD09}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsFreeMagmaRing({\mdseries\slshape D})\index{IsFreeMagmaRing@\texttt{IsFreeMagmaRing}}
\label{IsFreeMagmaRing}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 A domain lies in the category \texttt{IsFreeMagmaRing} if it has been constructed as a free magma ring. In particular, if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} lies in this category then the operations \texttt{LeftActingDomain} (\ref{LeftActingDomain}) and \texttt{UnderlyingMagma} (\ref{UnderlyingMagma}) are applicable to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, and yield the ring $R$ and the magma $M$ such that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} is the magma ring $RM$. 

 So being a magma ring in \textsf{GAP} includes the knowledge of the ring and the magma. Note that a magma ring $RM$ may abstractly be generated as a magma ring by a magma different from the
underlying magma $M$. For example, the group ring of the dihedral group of order $8$ over the field with $3$ elements is also spanned by a quaternion group of order $8$ over the same field. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@d8:= DihedralGroup( 8 );|
  <pc group of size 8 with 3 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@rm:= FreeMagmaRing( GF(3), d8 );|
  <algebra-with-one over GF(3), with 3 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@emb:= Embedding( d8, rm );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@gens:= List( GeneratorsOfGroup( d8 ), x -> x^emb );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x1:= gens[1] + gens[2];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x2:= ( gens[1] - gens[2] ) * gens[3];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x3:= gens[1] * gens[2] * ( One( rm ) - gens[3] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g1:= x1 - x2 + x3;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g2:= x1 + x2;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@q8:= Group( g1, g2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( q8 );|
  8
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ForAny( [ d8, q8 ], IsAbelian );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List( [ d8, q8 ], g -> Number( AsList( g ), x -> Order( x ) = 2 ) );|
  [ 5, 1 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Dimension( Subspace( rm, q8 ) );|
  8
\end{Verbatim}
 }

\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Elements of Free Magma Rings}}\label{Elements of Free Magma Rings}
\logpage{[ 65, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8402D3897F2C5955}{}
{
  In order to treat elements of free magma rings uniformly, also without an
external representation, the attributes \texttt{CoefficientsAndMagmaElements} (\ref{CoefficientsAndMagmaElements}) and \texttt{ZeroCoefficient} (\ref{ZeroCoefficient}) were introduced that allow one to ``take an element of an arbitrary magma ring into pieces''. 

 Conversely, for constructing magma ring elements from coefficients and magma
elements, \texttt{ElementOfMagmaRing} (\ref{ElementOfMagmaRing}) can be used. (Of course one can also embed each magma element into the magma
ring, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Natural Embeddings related to Magma Rings}, and then form the linear combination, but many unnecessary intermediate
elements are created this way.) 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsMagmaRingObjDefaultRep}}
\logpage{[ 65, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X827B2D7D7E41780C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsMagmaRingObjDefaultRep({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsMagmaRingObjDefaultRep@\texttt{IsMagmaRingObjDefaultRep}}
\label{IsMagmaRingObjDefaultRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Representation)}}\\


 The default representation of a magma ring element is a list of length 2, at
first position the zero coefficient, at second position a list with the
coefficients at the even positions, and the magma elements at the odd
positions, with the ordering as defined for the magma elements. 

 It is assumed that arithmetic operations on magma rings produce only
normalized elements. }

\logpage{[ 65, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D9C684A81E66310}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRing({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRing@\texttt{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRing}}
\label{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRing}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRingCollection({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRingCollection@\texttt{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRingCollection}}
\label{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRingCollection}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 The category of elements of a free magma ring (See \texttt{IsFreeMagmaRing} (\ref{IsFreeMagmaRing})). }

\logpage{[ 65, 2, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X869768AF7B444BF8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRingFamily({\mdseries\slshape Fam})\index{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRingFamily@\texttt{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRingFamily}}
\label{IsElementOfFreeMagmaRingFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 Elements of families in this category have trivial normalisation, i.e.,
efficient methods for \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=} and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CoefficientsAndMagmaElements}}
\logpage{[ 65, 2, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X843D1D8578C33513}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CoefficientsAndMagmaElements({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{CoefficientsAndMagmaElements@\texttt{CoefficientsAndMagmaElements}}
\label{CoefficientsAndMagmaElements}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\

even positions their coefficients in the element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ZeroCoefficient}}
\logpage{[ 65, 2, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78C3DB417E353390}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZeroCoefficient({\mdseries\slshape elm})\index{ZeroCoefficient@\texttt{ZeroCoefficient}}
\label{ZeroCoefficient}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For an element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} of a magma ring (modulo relations) $RM$, \texttt{ZeroCoefficient} returns the zero element of the coefficient ring $R$. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ElementOfMagmaRing}}
\logpage{[ 65, 2, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8671DE0A81BEEFB0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ElementOfMagmaRing({\mdseries\slshape Fam, zerocoeff, coeffs, mgmelms})\index{ElementOfMagmaRing@\texttt{ElementOfMagmaRing}}
\label{ElementOfMagmaRing}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{ElementOfMagmaRing} returns the element $\sum_{{i = 1}}^n c_i m_i'$, where $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coeffs}} = [ c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n ]$ is a list of coefficients, $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mgmelms}} = [ m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_n ]$ is a list of magma elements, and $m_i'$ is the image of $m_i$ under an embedding of a magma containing $m_i$ into a magma ring whose elements lie in the family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Fam}}. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape zerocoeff}} must be the zero of the coefficient ring containing the $c_i$. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Natural Embeddings related to Magma Rings}}\label{Natural Embeddings related to Magma Rings}
\logpage{[ 65, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X80366F1480ACD8DF}{}
{
  \index{Embedding@\texttt{Embedding}!for magma rings} Neither the coefficient ring $R$ nor the magma $M$ are regarded as subsets of the magma ring $RM$, so one has to use \emph{embeddings} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Embedding} (\ref{Embedding:for two domains})) explicitly whenever one needs for example the magma ring element
corresponding to a given magma element. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= Rationals;;  g:= SymmetricGroup( 3 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@fg:= FreeMagmaRing( f, g );|
  <algebra-with-one over Rationals, with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Dimension( fg );|
  6
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@gens:= GeneratorsOfAlgebraWithOne( fg );|
  [ (1)*(1,2,3), (1)*(1,2) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@( 3*gens[1] - 2*gens[2] ) * ( gens[1] + gens[2] );|
  (-2)*()+(3)*(2,3)+(3)*(1,3,2)+(-2)*(1,3)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@One( fg );|
  (1)*()
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@emb:= Embedding( g, fg );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@elm:= (1,2,3)^emb;  elm in fg;|
  (1)*(1,2,3)
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@new:= elm + One( fg );|
  (1)*()+(1)*(1,2,3)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@new^2;|
  (1)*()+(2)*(1,2,3)+(1)*(1,3,2)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@emb2:= Embedding( f, fg );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@elm:= One( f )^emb2;  elm in fg;|
  (1)*()
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Magma Rings modulo Relations}}\label{Magma Rings modulo Relations}
\logpage{[ 65, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81B002EE799B5E77}{}
{
  A more general construction than that of free magma rings allows one to create
rings that are not free $R$\texttt{\symbol{45}}modules on a given magma $M$ but arise from the magma ring $RM$ by factoring out certain identities. Examples for such structures are finitely
presented (associative) algebras and free Lie algebras (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{FreeLieAlgebra} (\ref{FreeLieAlgebra:for ring, rank (and name)})).  

 In \textsf{GAP}, the use of magma rings modulo relations is limited to situations where a
normal form of the elements is known and where one wants to guarantee that all
elements actually constructed are in normal form. (In particular, the
computation of the normal form must be cheap.) This is because the methods for
comparing elements in magma rings modulo relations via \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=} and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}} just compare the involved coefficients and magma elements, and also the vector
space functions regard those monomials as linearly independent over the
coefficients ring that actually occur in the representation of an element of a
magma ring modulo relations. 

 Thus only very special finitely presented algebras will be represented as
magma rings modulo relations, in general finitely presented algebras are dealt
with via the mechanism described in Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Finitely Presented Algebras}. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations}}
\logpage{[ 65, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X869D54847E881848}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations@\texttt{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations}}
\label{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelationsCollection({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelationsCollection@\texttt{IsElement}\-\texttt{Of}\-\texttt{Magma}\-\texttt{Ring}\-\texttt{Modulo}\-\texttt{Relations}\-\texttt{Collection}}
\label{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelationsCollection}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 This category is used, e.{\nobreakspace}g., for elements of free Lie algebras. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelationsFamily}}
\logpage{[ 65, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X875BEB1A840FFAA4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelationsFamily({\mdseries\slshape Fam})\index{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelationsFamily@\texttt{IsElement}\-\texttt{Of}\-\texttt{Magma}\-\texttt{Ring}\-\texttt{Modulo}\-\texttt{Relations}\-\texttt{Family}}
\label{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelationsFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 The family category for the category \texttt{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations} (\ref{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NormalizedElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations}}
\logpage{[ 65, 4, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85956ED27FA6AC68}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NormalizedElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations({\mdseries\slshape F, descr})\index{NormalizedElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations@\texttt{Normalized}\-\texttt{Element}\-\texttt{Of}\-\texttt{Magma}\-\texttt{Ring}\-\texttt{Modulo}\-\texttt{Relations}}
\label{NormalizedElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} be a family of magma ring elements modulo relations, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape descr}} the description of an element in a magma ring modulo relations. \texttt{NormalizedElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations} returns a description of the same element, but normalized
w.r.t.{\nobreakspace}the relations. So two elements are equal if and only if
the result of \texttt{NormalizedElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations} is equal for their internal data, that is, \texttt{CoefficientsAndMagmaElements} (\ref{CoefficientsAndMagmaElements}) will return the same for the corresponding two elements. 

 \texttt{NormalizedElementOfMagmaRingModuloRelations} is allowed to return \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape descr}} itself, it need not make a copy. This is the case for example in the case of
free magma rings. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsMagmaRingModuloRelations}}
\logpage{[ 65, 4, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X804B5AAB813E184D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsMagmaRingModuloRelations({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsMagmaRingModuloRelations@\texttt{IsMagmaRingModuloRelations}}
\label{IsMagmaRingModuloRelations}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 A \textsf{GAP} object lies in the category \texttt{IsMagmaRingModuloRelations} if it has been constructed as a magma ring modulo relations. Each element of
such a ring has a unique normal form, so \texttt{CoefficientsAndMagmaElements} (\ref{CoefficientsAndMagmaElements}) is well\texttt{\symbol{45}}defined for it. 

 This category is not inherited to factor structures, which are in general best
described as finitely presented algebras, see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Finitely Presented Algebras}. }

 }

\logpage{[ 65, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D859DBF81DFA751}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloSpanOfZeroFamily}}
\logpage{[ 65, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B3D45A6802B695C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloSpanOfZeroFamily({\mdseries\slshape Fam})\index{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloSpanOfZeroFamily@\texttt{IsElement}\-\texttt{Of}\-\texttt{Magma}\-\texttt{Ring}\-\texttt{Modulo}\-\texttt{Span}\-\texttt{Of}\-\texttt{Zero}\-\texttt{Family}}
\label{IsElementOfMagmaRingModuloSpanOfZeroFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 We need this for the normalization method, which takes a family as first
argument. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsMagmaRingModuloSpanOfZero}}
\logpage{[ 65, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X872713EE84DA9B72}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsMagmaRingModuloSpanOfZero({\mdseries\slshape RM})\index{IsMagmaRingModuloSpanOfZero@\texttt{IsMagmaRingModuloSpanOfZero}}
\label{IsMagmaRingModuloSpanOfZero}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 The category of magma rings modulo the span of a zero element. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MagmaRingModuloSpanOfZero}}
\logpage{[ 65, 5, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A7F880D7D7D3722}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MagmaRingModuloSpanOfZero({\mdseries\slshape R, M, z})\index{MagmaRingModuloSpanOfZero@\texttt{MagmaRingModuloSpanOfZero}}
\label{MagmaRingModuloSpanOfZero}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}} be a ring, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} a magma, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z}} an element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}} with the property that $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z}} * m = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z}}$ holds for all $m \in M$. The element \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z}} could be called a ``zero element'' of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}, but note that in general \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z}} cannot be obtained as \texttt{Zero( }$m$\texttt{ )} for each $m \in M$, so this situation does not match the definition of \texttt{Zero} (\ref{Zero}). 

 \texttt{MagmaRingModuloSpanOfZero} returns the magma ring $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape M}}$ modulo the relation given by the identification of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z}} with zero. This is an example of a magma ring modulo relations,
see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Magma Rings modulo Relations}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Technical Details about the Implementation of Magma Rings}}\label{Technical Details about the Implementation of Magma Rings}
\logpage{[ 65, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79889F017F2EB7ED}{}
{
  The \emph{family} containing elements in the magma ring $RM$ in fact contains all elements with coefficients in the family of elements of $R$ and magma elements in the family of elements of $M$. So arithmetic operations with coefficients outside $R$ or with magma elements outside $M$ might create elements outside $RM$. 

 It should be mentioned that each call of \texttt{FreeMagmaRing} (\ref{FreeMagmaRing}) creates a new family of elements, so for example the elements of two group
rings of permutation groups over the same ring lie in different families and
therefore are regarded as different. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= SymmetricGroup( 3 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:= AlternatingGroup( 3 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsSubset( g, h );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= GF(2);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@fg:= GroupRing( f, g );|
  <algebra-with-one over GF(2), with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@fh:= GroupRing( f, h );|
  <algebra-with-one over GF(2), with 1 generator>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsSubset( fg, fh );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@o1:= One( fh );  o2:= One( fg );  o1 = o2;|
  (Z(2)^0)*()
  (Z(2)^0)*()
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@emb:= Embedding( g, fg );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@im:= Image( emb, h );|
  <group of size 3 with 1 generator>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsSubset( fg, im );|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 

 There is \emph{no} generic \emph{external representation} for elements in an arbitrary free magma ring. For example, polynomials are
elements of a free magma ring, and they have an external representation
relying on the special form of the underlying monomials. On the other hand,
elements in a group ring of a permutation group do not admit such an external
representation. 

 For convenience, magma rings constructed with \texttt{FreeAlgebra} (\ref{FreeAlgebra:for ring, rank (and name)}), \texttt{FreeAssociativeAlgebra} (\ref{FreeAssociativeAlgebra:for ring, rank (and name)}), \texttt{FreeAlgebraWithOne} (\ref{FreeAlgebraWithOne:for ring, rank (and name)}), and \texttt{FreeAssociativeAlgebraWithOne} (\ref{FreeAssociativeAlgebraWithOne:for ring, rank (and name)}) support an external representation of their elements, which is defined as a
list of length 2, the first entry being the zero coefficient, the second being
a list with the external representations of the magma elements at the odd
positions and the corresponding coefficients at the even positions. 

 As the above examples show, there are several possible representations of
magma ring elements, the representations used for polynomials (see Chapter
{\nobreakspace}\ref{Polynomials and Rational Functions}) as well as the default representation \texttt{IsMagmaRingObjDefaultRep} (\ref{IsMagmaRingObjDefaultRep}) of magma ring elements. The latter simply stores the zero coefficient and a
list containing the coefficients of the element at the even positions and the
corresponding magma elements at the odd positions, where the succession is
compatible with the ordering of magma elements via \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}}. }

 }

             
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Polynomials and Rational Functions}}\label{Polynomials and Rational Functions}
\logpage{[ 66, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7A14A6588268810A}{}
{
  Let $R$ be a commutative ring\texttt{\symbol{45}}with\texttt{\symbol{45}}one. We call
a free associative algebra $A$ over $R$ a \emph{polynomial ring} over $R$. The free generators of $A$ are called \emph{indeterminates} (to avoid naming conflicts with the word \emph{variables} which will be used to denote \textsf{GAP} variables only) , they are usually denoted by $x_1, x_2, \ldots$. The number of indeterminates is called the \emph{rank} of $A$. The elements of $A$ are called \emph{polynomials}. Products of indeterminates are called \emph{monomials}, every polynomial can be expressed as a finite sum of products of monomials
with ring elements in a form like $r_{{1,0}} x_1 + r_{{1,1}} x_1 x_2 + r_{{0,1}} x_2 + \cdots$ with $r_{{i,j}} \in R$. 

 A polynomial ring of rank 1 is called an \emph{univariate} polynomial ring, its elements are \emph{univariate polynomials}. 

 Polynomial rings of smaller rank naturally embed in rings of higher rank; if $S$ is a subring of $R$ then a polynomial ring over $S$ naturally embeds in a polynomial ring over $R$ of the same rank. Note however that \textsf{GAP} does not consider $R$ as a subset of a polynomial ring over $R$; for example the zero of $R$ ($0$) and the zero of the polynomial ring ($0x^0$) are different objects. 

 Internally, indeterminates are represented by positive integers, but it is
possible to give names to them to have them printed in a nicer way. Beware,
however that there is not necessarily any relation between the way an
indeterminate is called and the way it is printed. See section \ref{Indeterminates} for details. 

 If $R$ is an integral domain, the polynomial ring $A$ over $R$ is an integral domain as well and one can therefore form its quotient field $Q$. This field is called a \emph{field of rational functions}. Again $A$ embeds naturally into $Q$ and \textsf{GAP} will perform this embedding implicitly. (In fact it implements the ring of
rational functions over $R$.) To avoid problems with leading coefficients, however, $R$ must be a unique factorization domain.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Indeterminates}}\label{Indeterminates}
\logpage{[ 66, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7A8FADCD875826DA}{}
{
  Internally, indeterminates are created for a \emph{family} of objects (for example all elements of finite fields in characteristic $3$ are in one family). Thus a variable ``x'' over the rationals is also an ``x'' over the integers, while an ``x'' over \texttt{GF(3)} is different. 

 Within one family, every indeterminate has a number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} and as long as no other names have been assigned, this indeterminate will be
displayed as ``\texttt{x{\textunderscore}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}}}''. Indeterminate numbers can be arbitrary nonnegative integers. 

 It is possible to assign names to indeterminates; these names are strings and
only provide a means for printing the indeterminates in a nice way.
Indeterminates that have not been assigned a name will be printed as ``\texttt{x{\textunderscore}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}}}''. 

 (Because of this printing convention, the name \texttt{x{\textunderscore}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}}} is interpreted specially to always denote the variable with internal number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}}.) 

 The indeterminate names have not necessarily any relations to variable names:
this means that an indeterminate whose name is ``\texttt{x}'' cannot be accessed using the variable \texttt{x}, unless \texttt{x} was defined to be that indeterminate. 

 When asking for indeterminates with certain names, \textsf{GAP} usually will take the first (with respect to the internal numbering)
indeterminates that are not yet named, name these accordingly and return them.
Thus when asking for named indeterminates, no relation between names and
indeterminate numbers can be guaranteed. The attribute \texttt{IndeterminateNumberOfLaurentPolynomial(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape indet}})} will return the number of the indeterminate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape indet}}. 

 When asked to create an indeterminate with a name that exists already for the
family, \textsf{GAP} will by default return this existing indeterminate. If you explicitly want a \emph{new} indeterminate, distinct from the already existing one with the \emph{same} name, you can add the \texttt{new} option to the function call. (This is in most cases not a good idea.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@R:=PolynomialRing(GF(3),["x","y","z"]);|
  GF(3)[x,y,z]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List(IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing(R),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  IndeterminateNumberOfLaurentPolynomial);|
  [ 1, 2, 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@R:=PolynomialRing(GF(3),["z"]);|
  GF(3)[z]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List(IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing(R),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  IndeterminateNumberOfLaurentPolynomial);|
  [ 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@R:=PolynomialRing(GF(3),["x","y","z"]:new);|
  GF(3)[x,y,z]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List(IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing(R),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  IndeterminateNumberOfLaurentPolynomial);|
  [ 4, 5, 6 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@R:=PolynomialRing(GF(3),["z"]);|
  GF(3)[z]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List(IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing(R),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  IndeterminateNumberOfLaurentPolynomial);|
  [ 3 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Indeterminate}}\logpage{[ 66, 1, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79D0380D7FA39F7D}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Indeterminate({\mdseries\slshape R[, nr]})\index{Indeterminate@\texttt{Indeterminate}!for a ring (and a number)}
\label{Indeterminate:for a ring (and a number)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Indeterminate({\mdseries\slshape R[, name][, avoid]})\index{Indeterminate@\texttt{Indeterminate}!for a ring (and a name, and an exclusion list)}
\label{Indeterminate:for a ring (and a name, and an exclusion list)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Indeterminate({\mdseries\slshape fam, nr})\index{Indeterminate@\texttt{Indeterminate}!for a family and a number}
\label{Indeterminate:for a family and a number}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{X({\mdseries\slshape R[, nr]})\index{X@\texttt{X}!for a ring (and a number)}
\label{X:for a ring (and a number)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{X({\mdseries\slshape R[, name][, avoid]})\index{X@\texttt{X}!for a ring (and a name, and an exclusion list)}
\label{X:for a ring (and a name, and an exclusion list)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{X({\mdseries\slshape fam, nr})\index{X@\texttt{X}!for a family and a number}
\label{X:for a family and a number}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the indeterminate number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} over the ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} is not given it defaults to 1. If the number is not specified a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape avoid}} of indeterminates may be given. The function will return an indeterminate that
is guaranteed to be different from all the indeterminates in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape avoid}}. The third usage returns an indeterminate called \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} (also avoiding the indeterminates in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape avoid}} if given). 

 \texttt{X} is simply a synonym for \texttt{Indeterminate}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:=Indeterminate(GF(3),"x");|
  x
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@y:=X(GF(3),"y");z:=X(GF(3),"X");|
  y
  X
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@X(GF(3),2);|
  y
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@X(GF(3),"x_3");|
  X
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@X(GF(3),[y,z]);|
  x
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X816C8D797C804380}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction({\mdseries\slshape rfun})\index{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction@\texttt{Indeterminate}\-\texttt{Number}\-\texttt{Of}\-\texttt{Univariate}\-\texttt{Rational}\-\texttt{Function}}
\label{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the number of the indeterminate in which the univariate rational
function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rfun}} is expressed. (This also provides a way to obtain the number of a given
indeterminate.) 

 A constant rational function might not possess an indeterminate number. In
this case \texttt{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction} will default to a value of 1. Therefore two univariate polynomials may be
considered to be in the same univariate polynomial ring if their
indeterminates have the same number or one if of them is constant. (see
also{\nobreakspace}\texttt{CIUnivPols} (\ref{CIUnivPols}) and{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsLaurentPolynomialDefaultRep} (\ref{IsLaurentPolynomialDefaultRep})). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IndeterminateOfUnivariateRationalFunction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 1, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A2FA46885EF403D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndeterminateOfUnivariateRationalFunction({\mdseries\slshape rfun})\index{IndeterminateOfUnivariateRationalFunction@\texttt{Indeterminate}\-\texttt{Of}\-\texttt{Univariate}\-\texttt{Rational}\-\texttt{Function}}
\label{IndeterminateOfUnivariateRationalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the indeterminate in which the univariate rational function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rfun}} is expressed. (cf. \texttt{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction} (\ref{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction}).) 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction(z);|
  3
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IndeterminateOfUnivariateRationalFunction(z^5+z);|
  X
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IndeterminateName}}
\logpage{[ 66, 1, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7FD4AC807A1C8E27}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndeterminateName({\mdseries\slshape fam, nr})\index{IndeterminateName@\texttt{IndeterminateName}}
\label{IndeterminateName}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{HasIndeterminateName({\mdseries\slshape fam, nr})\index{HasIndeterminateName@\texttt{HasIndeterminateName}}
\label{HasIndeterminateName}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetIndeterminateName({\mdseries\slshape fam, nr, name})\index{SetIndeterminateName@\texttt{SetIndeterminateName}}
\label{SetIndeterminateName}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{SetIndeterminateName} assigns the name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} to indeterminate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} in the rational functions family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}}. It issues an error if the indeterminate was already named. 

 \texttt{IndeterminateName} returns the name of the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th indeterminate (and returns \texttt{fail} if no name has been assigned). 

 \texttt{HasIndeterminateName} tests whether indeterminate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} has already been assigned a name. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IndeterminateName(FamilyObj(x),2);|
  "y"
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HasIndeterminateName(FamilyObj(x),4);|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetIndeterminateName(FamilyObj(x),10,"bla");|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Indeterminate(GF(3),10);|
  bla
\end{Verbatim}
 

 As a convenience there is a special method installed for \texttt{SetName} that will assign a name to an indeterminate. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:=Indeterminate(GF(3),5);|
  x_5
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetName(a,"ah");|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a^5+a;|
  ah^5+ah
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CIUnivPols}}
\logpage{[ 66, 1, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X791A06E67F784328}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CIUnivPols({\mdseries\slshape upol1, upol2})\index{CIUnivPols@\texttt{CIUnivPols}}
\label{CIUnivPols}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function (whose name stands for ``common indeterminate of univariate polynomials'') takes two univariate polynomials as arguments. If both polynomials are given
in the same indeterminate number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape indnum}} (in this case they are ``compatible'' as univariate polynomials) it returns \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape indnum}}. In all other cases it returns \texttt{fail}. \texttt{CIUnivPols} also accepts if either polynomial is constant but formally expressed in
another indeterminate, in this situation the indeterminate of the other
polynomial is selected. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Operations for Rational Functions}}\label{Operations for Rational Functions}
\logpage{[ 66, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86A68FD582F4F757}{}
{
  The rational functions form a field, therefore all arithmetic operations are
applicable to rational functions. 

 \index{addition!rational functions} \index{subtraction!rational functions} \index{product!rational functions} \index{quotient!rational functions} \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} + \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}} 

 \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} \texttt{\symbol{45}} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}} 

 \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}} 

 \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} / \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}} 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:=Indeterminate(Rationals,1);;y:=Indeterminate(Rationals,2);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:=3+x*y+x^5;;g:=5+x^2*y+x*y^2;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:=g/f;|
  (x_1^2*x_2+x_1*x_2^2+5)/(x_1^5+x_1*x_2+3)
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that the quotient \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}/\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}} of two polynomials might be represented as a rational function again. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} is known to divide \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} the call \texttt{Quotient(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}})} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Quotient} (\ref{Quotient})) should be used instead. 

 \index{mod!Laurent polynomials} \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} mod \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}}  

 For two Laurent polynomials \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}, \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} mod \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}} is the Euclidean remainder (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{EuclideanRemainder} (\ref{EuclideanRemainder})) of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} modulo \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}.        

 As calculating a multivariate Gcd can be expensive, it is not guaranteed that
rational functions will always be represented as a quotient of coprime
polynomials. In certain unfortunate situations this might lead to a degree
explosion. To ensure cancellation you can use \texttt{Gcd} (\ref{Gcd:for (a ring and) several elements}) on the \texttt{NumeratorOfRationalFunction} (\ref{NumeratorOfRationalFunction}) and \texttt{DenominatorOfRationalFunction} (\ref{DenominatorOfRationalFunction}) values of a given rational function. 

 All polynomials as well as all the univariate polynomials in the same
indeterminate form subrings of this field. If two rational functions are known
to be in the same subring, the result will be expressed as element in this
subring. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Comparison of Rational Functions}}\label{Comparison of Rational Functions}
\logpage{[ 66, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X824B6D328643CE04}{}
{
  \index{comparison!rational functions} \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} = \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}} 

 Two rational functions \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} are equal if the product \texttt{Numerator(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}) * Denominator(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}})} equals \texttt{Numerator(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}) * Denominator(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}})}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:=Indeterminate(Rationals,"x");;y:=Indeterminate(Rationals,"y");;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:=3+x*y+x^5;;g:=5+x^2*y+x*y^2;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:=g/f;|
  (x^2*y+x*y^2+5)/(x^5+x*y+3)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@b:=(g*f)/(f^2);|
  (x^7*y+x^6*y^2+5*x^5+x^3*y^2+x^2*y^3+3*x^2*y+3*x*y^2+5*x*y+15)/(x^10+2\
  *x^6*y+6*x^5+x^2*y^2+6*x*y+9)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a=b;|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \index{smaller!rational functions} \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} {\textless} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}} 

 The ordering of rational functions is defined in several steps. Monomials
(products of indeterminates) are sorted first by degree, then
lexicographically (with $x_1>x_2$) (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{MonomialGrlexOrdering} (\ref{MonomialGrlexOrdering})). Products of monomials with ring elements (``terms'') are compared first by their monomials and then by their coefficients. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x>y;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x^2*y<x*y^2;|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x*y<x^2*y;|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x^2*y < 5* y*x^2;|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 Polynomials are compared by comparing the largest terms in turn until they
differ. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x+y<y;|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x<x+1;|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 Rational functions are compared by comparing the polynomial \texttt{Numerator(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}) * Denominator(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}})} with the polynomial \texttt{Numerator(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}}) * Denominator(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}})}. (As the ordering of monomials used by \textsf{GAP} is invariant under multiplication this is independent of common factors in
numerator and denominator.) 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f/g<g/f;|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f/g<(g*g)/(f*g);|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 

 For univariate polynomials this reduces to an ordering first by total degree
and then lexicographically on the coefficients. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Properties and Attributes of Rational Functions}}\label{Properties and Attributes of Rational Functions}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D871EA180E9486C}{}
{
  All these tests are applicable to \emph{every} rational function. Depending on the internal representation of the rational
function, however some of these tests (in particular, univariateness) might be
expensive in some cases. 

 For reasons of performance within algorithms it can be useful to use other
attributes, which give a slightly more technical representation. See
section{\nobreakspace}\ref{The Representations of Rational Functions} for details. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPolynomialFunction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86C92F677DA9347F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPolynomialFunction({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsPolynomialFunction@\texttt{IsPolynomialFunction}}
\label{IsPolynomialFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsRationalFunction({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsRationalFunction@\texttt{IsRationalFunction}}
\label{IsRationalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 A rational function is an element of the quotient field of a polynomial ring
over an UFD. It is represented as a quotient of two polynomials, its numerator
(see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{NumeratorOfRationalFunction} (\ref{NumeratorOfRationalFunction})) and its denominator (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{DenominatorOfRationalFunction} (\ref{DenominatorOfRationalFunction})) 

 A polynomial function is an element of a polynomial ring (not necessarily an
UFD), or a rational function. 

 \textsf{GAP} considers \texttt{IsRationalFunction} as a subcategory of \texttt{IsPolynomialFunction}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NumeratorOfRationalFunction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D7D2667803D8D8A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NumeratorOfRationalFunction({\mdseries\slshape ratfun})\index{NumeratorOfRationalFunction@\texttt{NumeratorOfRationalFunction}}
\label{NumeratorOfRationalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the numerator of the rational function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ratfun}}. 

 As no proper multivariate gcd has been implemented yet, numerators and
denominators are not guaranteed to be reduced! }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DenominatorOfRationalFunction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78DC1B5B866ADB6C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DenominatorOfRationalFunction({\mdseries\slshape ratfun})\index{DenominatorOfRationalFunction@\texttt{DenominatorOfRationalFunction}}
\label{DenominatorOfRationalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the denominator of the rational function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ratfun}}. 

 As no proper multivariate gcd has been implemented yet, numerators and
denominators are not guaranteed to be reduced! 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:=Indeterminate(Rationals,1);;y:=Indeterminate(Rationals,2);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DenominatorOfRationalFunction((x*y+x^2)/y);|
  y
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NumeratorOfRationalFunction((x*y+x^2)/y);|
  x^2+x*y
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7974B0707C8DAB6C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape ratfun})\index{IsPolynomial@\texttt{IsPolynomial}}
\label{IsPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 A polynomial is a rational function whose denominator is one. (If the
coefficients family forms a field this is equivalent to the denominator being
constant.) 

 If the base family is not a field, it may be impossible to represent the
quotient of a polynomial by a ring element as a polynomial again, but it will
have to be represented as a rational function. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPolynomial((x*y+x^2*y^3)/y);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPolynomial((x*y+x^2)/y);|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{AsPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7914771F7C6013EF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{AsPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape poly})\index{AsPolynomial@\texttt{AsPolynomial}}
\label{AsPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape poly}} is a rational function that is a polynomial this attribute returns an equal
rational function $p$ such that $p$ is equal to its numerator and the denominator of $p$ is one. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@AsPolynomial((x*y+x^2*y^3)/y);|
  x^2*y^2+x
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsUnivariateRationalFunction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8738F73583273FCA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsUnivariateRationalFunction({\mdseries\slshape ratfun})\index{IsUnivariateRationalFunction@\texttt{IsUnivariateRationalFunction}}
\label{IsUnivariateRationalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 A rational function is univariate if its numerator and its denominator are
both polynomials in the same one indeterminate. The attribute \texttt{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction} (\ref{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction}) can be used to obtain the number of this common indeterminate. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CoefficientsOfUnivariateRationalFunction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F1F67527A35A9CE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CoefficientsOfUnivariateRationalFunction({\mdseries\slshape rfun})\index{CoefficientsOfUnivariateRationalFunction@\texttt{Coefficients}\-\texttt{Of}\-\texttt{Univariate}\-\texttt{Rational}\-\texttt{Function}}
\label{CoefficientsOfUnivariateRationalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rfun}} is a univariate rational function, this attribute returns a list \texttt{[ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ncof}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dcof}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} ]} where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ncof}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dcof}} are coefficient lists of univariate polynomials \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape d}} and a valuation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} such that $\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rfun}} = x^{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}}} \cdot \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} / \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape d}}$ where $x$ is the variable with the number given by \texttt{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction} (\ref{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction}). Numerator and denominator are guaranteed to be cancelled. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsUnivariatePolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86A2546685D0016B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsUnivariatePolynomial({\mdseries\slshape ratfun})\index{IsUnivariatePolynomial@\texttt{IsUnivariatePolynomial}}
\label{IsUnivariatePolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 A univariate polynomial is a polynomial in only one indeterminate. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CoefficientsOfUnivariatePolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78C9524D7F2708C2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CoefficientsOfUnivariatePolynomial({\mdseries\slshape pol})\index{CoefficientsOfUnivariatePolynomial@\texttt{CoefficientsOfUnivariatePolynomial}}
\label{CoefficientsOfUnivariatePolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 \texttt{CoefficientsOfUnivariatePolynomial} returns the coefficient list of the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}}, sorted in ascending order. (It returns the empty list if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} is 0.) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsLaurentPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79138FF28213B6EC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsLaurentPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape ratfun})\index{IsLaurentPolynomial@\texttt{IsLaurentPolynomial}}
\label{IsLaurentPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 A Laurent polynomial is a univariate rational function whose denominator is a
monomial. Therefore every univariate polynomial is a Laurent polynomial. 

 The attribute \texttt{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial} (\ref{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial}) gives a compact representation as Laurent polynomial. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsConstantRationalFunction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 11 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F2A49208341C2A8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsConstantRationalFunction({\mdseries\slshape ratfun})\index{IsConstantRationalFunction@\texttt{IsConstantRationalFunction}}
\label{IsConstantRationalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (property)}}\\


 A constant rational function is a function whose numerator and denominator are
polynomials of degree 0. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPrimitivePolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 12 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X834B54947FAADEA4}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPrimitivePolynomial({\mdseries\slshape F, pol})\index{IsPrimitivePolynomial@\texttt{IsPrimitivePolynomial}}
\label{IsPrimitivePolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 For a univariate polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} of degree $d$ in the indeterminate $X$, with coefficients in a finite field \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}} with $q$ elements, \texttt{IsPrimitivePolynomial} returns \texttt{true} if 
\begin{enumerate}
\item  \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} divides $X^{{q^d-1}} - 1$, and 
\item  for each prime divisor $p$ of $q^d - 1$, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} does not divide $X^{{(q^d-1)/p}} - 1$, 
\end{enumerate}
 and \texttt{false} otherwise. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SplittingField}}
\logpage{[ 66, 4, 13 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87531E03849391C1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SplittingField({\mdseries\slshape f})\index{SplittingField@\texttt{SplittingField}}
\label{SplittingField}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the smallest field which contains the coefficients of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} and the roots of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Univariate Polynomials}}\label{Univariate Polynomials}
\logpage{[ 66, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X82E2F1707FC2E553}{}
{
  Some of the operations are actually defined on the larger domain of Laurent
polynomials (see \ref{Laurent Polynomials}). For this section you can simply ignore the word ``Laurent'' if it occurs in a description. 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UnivariatePolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8379F8CB7D0076BA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UnivariatePolynomial({\mdseries\slshape ring, cofs[, ind]})\index{UnivariatePolynomial@\texttt{UnivariatePolynomial}}
\label{UnivariatePolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 constructs an univariate polynomial over the ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ring}} in the indeterminate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}} with the coefficients given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cofs}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UnivariatePolynomialByCoefficients}}
\logpage{[ 66, 5, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85178A3E7B4F11E0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UnivariatePolynomialByCoefficients({\mdseries\slshape fam, cofs, ind})\index{UnivariatePolynomialByCoefficients@\texttt{UnivariatePolynomialByCoefficients}}
\label{UnivariatePolynomialByCoefficients}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 constructs an univariate polynomial over the coefficients family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}} and in the indeterminate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}} with the coefficients given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cofs}}. This function should be used in algorithms to create polynomials as it
avoids overhead associated with \texttt{UnivariatePolynomial} (\ref{UnivariatePolynomial}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DegreeOfLaurentPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 5, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78AF77C383245254}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DegreeOfLaurentPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape pol})\index{DegreeOfLaurentPolynomial@\texttt{DegreeOfLaurentPolynomial}}
\label{DegreeOfLaurentPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 The degree of a univariate (Laurent) polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} is the largest exponent $n$ of a monomial $x^n$ of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}}. The degree of a zero polynomial is defined to be \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}infinity}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p:=UnivariatePolynomial(Rationals,[1,2,3,4],1);|
  4*x^3+3*x^2+2*x+1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UnivariatePolynomialByCoefficients(FamilyObj(1),[9,2,3,4],73);|
  4*x_73^3+3*x_73^2+2*x_73+9
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CoefficientsOfUnivariatePolynomial(p);|
  [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DegreeOfLaurentPolynomial(p);|
  3
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DegreeOfLaurentPolynomial(Zero(p));|
  -infinity
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IndeterminateNumberOfLaurentPolynomial(p);|
  1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IndeterminateOfLaurentPolynomial(p);|
  x
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RootsOfPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 5, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CBB760C87B04F75}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RootsOfPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape [R, ]p})\index{RootsOfPolynomial@\texttt{RootsOfPolynomial}}
\label{RootsOfPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For a univariate polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}, this function returns all roots of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} over the ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}}. If the ring is not specified, it defaults to the ring specified by the
coefficients of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} via \texttt{DefaultRing} (\ref{DefaultRing:for ring elements})). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:=X(Rationals,"x");;p:=x^4-1;|
  x^4-1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootsOfPolynomial(p);|
  [ 1, -1 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootsOfPolynomial(CF(4),p);|
  [ 1, -1, E(4), -E(4) ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RootsOfUPol}}
\logpage{[ 66, 5, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80CEB10D7879767F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RootsOfUPol({\mdseries\slshape [field, ]upol})\index{RootsOfUPol@\texttt{RootsOfUPol}}
\label{RootsOfUPol}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function returns a list of all roots of the univariate polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape upol}} in its default domain. If the optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape field}} is a field then the roots in this field are computed. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape field}} is the string \texttt{"split"} then the splitting field of the polynomial is taken. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@RootsOfUPol(50-45*x-6*x^2+x^3);|
  [ 10, 1, -5 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{QuotRemLaurpols}}
\logpage{[ 66, 5, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7887FBC78149BB0C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{QuotRemLaurpols({\mdseries\slshape left, right, mode})\index{QuotRemLaurpols@\texttt{QuotRemLaurpols}}
\label{QuotRemLaurpols}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This internal function for euclidean division of polynomials takes two
polynomials \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape left}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape right}} and computes their quotient. No test is performed whether the arguments indeed
are polynomials. Depending on the integer variable \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mode}}, which may take values in a range from 1 to 4, it returns respectively: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item  the quotient (there might be some remainder), 
\item  the remainder, 
\item  a list \texttt{[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape q}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape r}}]} of quotient and remainder, 
\item  the quotient if there is no remainder and \texttt{fail} otherwise. 
\end{enumerate}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UnivariatenessTestRationalFunction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 5, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7DDADF157879EFBF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UnivariatenessTestRationalFunction({\mdseries\slshape f})\index{UnivariatenessTestRationalFunction@\texttt{UnivariatenessTestRationalFunction}}
\label{UnivariatenessTestRationalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 takes a rational function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} and tests whether it is univariate rational function (or even a Laurent
polynomial). It returns a list \texttt{[isunivariate, indet, islaurent, cofs]}. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} is a univariate rational function then \texttt{isunivariate} is \texttt{true} and \texttt{indet} is the number of the appropriate indeterminate. 

 Furthermore, if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} is a Laurent polynomial, then \texttt{islaurent} is also \texttt{true}. In this case the fourth entry, \texttt{cofs}, is the value of the attribute \texttt{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial} (\ref{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial}) for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}. 

 If \texttt{isunivariate} is \texttt{true} but \texttt{islaurent} is \texttt{false}, then \texttt{cofs} is the value of the attribute \texttt{CoefficientsOfUnivariateRationalFunction} (\ref{CoefficientsOfUnivariateRationalFunction}) for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}. 

 Otherwise, each entry of the returned list is equal to \texttt{fail}. As there is no proper multivariate gcd, this may also happen for the
rational function which may be reduced to univariate (see example). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UnivariatenessTestRationalFunction( 50-45*x-6*x^2+x^3 );|
  [ true, 1, true, [ [ 50, -45, -6, 1 ], 0 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UnivariatenessTestRationalFunction( (-6*y^2+y^3) / (y+1) );|
  [ true, 2, false, [ [ -6, 1 ], [ 1, 1 ], 2 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UnivariatenessTestRationalFunction( (-6*y^2+y^3) / (x+1));|
  [ false, fail, false, fail ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UnivariatenessTestRationalFunction( ((y+2)*(x+1)) / ((y-1)*(x+1)) );|
  [ fail, fail, fail, fail ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoPoly}}
\logpage{[ 66, 5, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A3BC96B7A50DE98}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoPoly\index{InfoPoly@\texttt{InfoPoly}}
\label{InfoPoly}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (info class)}}\\


 is the info class for univariate polynomials. }

 We remark that some functions for multivariate polynomials (which will be
defined in the following sections) permit a different syntax for univariate
polynomials which drops the requirement to specify the indeterminate. Examples
are \texttt{Value} (\ref{Value:for rat. function, a list of indeterminates, a value (and a one)}), \texttt{Discriminant} (\ref{Discriminant}), \texttt{Derivative} (\ref{Derivative}), \texttt{LeadingCoefficient} (\ref{LeadingCoefficient}) and \texttt{LeadingMonomial} (\ref{LeadingMonomial}): 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p:=UnivariatePolynomial(Rationals,[1,2,3,4],1);|
  4*x^3+3*x^2+2*x+1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Value(p,Z(5));|
  Z(5)^2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeadingCoefficient(p);|
  4
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Derivative(p);|
  12*x^2+6*x+2
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Polynomials as Univariate Polynomials in one Indeterminate}}\label{Polynomials as Univariate Polynomials in one Indeterminate}
\logpage{[ 66, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81499B5A823E6EA3}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DegreeIndeterminate}}
\logpage{[ 66, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X826B99B17ABD11BE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DegreeIndeterminate({\mdseries\slshape pol, ind})\index{DegreeIndeterminate@\texttt{DegreeIndeterminate}}
\label{DegreeIndeterminate}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the degree of the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} in the indeterminate (or indeterminate number) \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:=x^5+3*x*y+9*y^7+4*y^5*x+3*y+2;|
  9*y^7+4*x*y^5+x^5+3*x*y+3*y+2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DegreeIndeterminate(f,1);|
  5
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DegreeIndeterminate(f,y);|
  7
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PolynomialCoefficientsOfPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 6, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85646FD07F9C60F5}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PolynomialCoefficientsOfPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape pol, ind})\index{PolynomialCoefficientsOfPolynomial@\texttt{PolynomialCoefficientsOfPolynomial}}
\label{PolynomialCoefficientsOfPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{PolynomialCoefficientsOfPolynomial} returns the coefficient list (whose entries are polynomials not involving the
indeterminate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}}) describing the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} viewed as a polynomial in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}}. Instead of the indeterminate, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}} can also be an indeterminate number. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PolynomialCoefficientsOfPolynomial(f,2);|
  [ x^5+2, 3*x+3, 0, 0, 0, 4*x, 0, 9 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LeadingCoefficient}}
\logpage{[ 66, 6, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80710E9B7D8340BD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LeadingCoefficient({\mdseries\slshape pol})\index{LeadingCoefficient@\texttt{LeadingCoefficient}}
\label{LeadingCoefficient}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the leading coefficient (that is the coefficient of the leading
monomial, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{LeadingMonomial} (\ref{LeadingMonomial})) of the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LeadingMonomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 6, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B3EAE41795598A5}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LeadingMonomial({\mdseries\slshape pol})\index{LeadingMonomial@\texttt{LeadingMonomial}}
\label{LeadingMonomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the leading monomial (with respect to the ordering given by \texttt{MonomialExtGrlexLess} (\ref{MonomialExtGrlexLess})) of the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} as a list containing indeterminate numbers and exponents. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeadingCoefficient(f,1);|
  1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeadingCoefficient(f,2);|
  9
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeadingMonomial(f);|
  [ 2, 7 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeadingCoefficient(f);|
  9
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Derivative}}
\logpage{[ 66, 6, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B57CEE2780D0E0B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Derivative({\mdseries\slshape ratfun[, ind]})\index{Derivative@\texttt{Derivative}}
\label{Derivative}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ratfun}} is a univariate rational function then \texttt{Derivative} returns the \emph{derivative} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ufun}} by its indeterminate. For a rational function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ratfun}}, the derivative by the indeterminate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}} is returned, regarding \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ratfun}} as univariate in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}}. Instead of the desired indeterminate, also the number of this indeterminate
can be given as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Derivative(f,2);|
  63*y^6+20*x*y^4+3*x+3
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Discriminant}}
\logpage{[ 66, 6, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C7D790A7D6E11AD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Discriminant({\mdseries\slshape pol[, ind]})\index{Discriminant@\texttt{Discriminant}}
\label{Discriminant}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} is a univariate polynomial then \texttt{Discriminant} returns the \emph{discriminant} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} by its indeterminate. The two\texttt{\symbol{45}}argument form returns the
discriminant of a polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} by the indeterminate number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}}, regarding \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} as univariate in this indeterminate. Instead of the indeterminate number, the
indeterminate itself can also be given as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Discriminant(f,1);|
  20503125*y^28+262144*y^25+27337500*y^22+19208040*y^21+1474560*y^17+136\
  68750*y^16+18225000*y^15+6075000*y^14+1105920*y^13+3037500*y^10+648972\
  0*y^9+4050000*y^8+900000*y^7+62208*y^5+253125*y^4+675000*y^3+675000*y^\
  2+300000*y+50000
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Discriminant(f,1) = Discriminant(f,x);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Resultant}}
\logpage{[ 66, 6, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X857AD5587EF49029}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Resultant({\mdseries\slshape pol1, pol2, ind})\index{Resultant@\texttt{Resultant}}
\label{Resultant}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 computes the resultant of the polynomials \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol1}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol2}} with respect to the indeterminate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}}, or indeterminate number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}}. The resultant considers \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol1}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol2}} as univariate in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}} and returns an element of the corresponding base ring (which might be a
polynomial ring). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Resultant(x^4+y,y^4+x,1);|
  y^16+y
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Resultant(x^4+y,y^4+x,2);|
  x^16+x
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Multivariate Polynomials}}\label{Multivariate Polynomials}
\logpage{[ 66, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X85ABC4687DF05777}{}
{
  
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Value}}\logpage{[ 66, 7, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7A70769C7F52CD2D}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Value({\mdseries\slshape ratfun, indets, vals[, one]})\index{Value@\texttt{Value}!for rat. function, a list of indeterminates, a value (and a one)}
\label{Value:for rat. function, a list of indeterminates, a value (and a one)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Value({\mdseries\slshape upol, value[, one]})\index{Value@\texttt{Value}!for a univariate rat. function, a value (and a one)}
\label{Value:for a univariate rat. function, a value (and a one)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 The first variant takes a rational function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ratfun}} and specializes the indeterminates given in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape indets}} to the values given in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vals}}, replacing the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th entry in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape indets}} by the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th entry in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vals}}. If this specialization results in a constant polynomial, an element of the
coefficient ring is returned. If the specialization would specialize the
denominator of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ratfun}} to zero, an error is raised. 

 A variation is the evaluation at elements of another ring $R$, for which a multiplication with elements of the coefficient ring of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ratfun}} are defined. In this situation the identity element of $R$ may be given by a further argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape one}} which will be used for $x^0$ for any specialized indeterminate $x$. 

 The second version takes an univariate rational function and specializes the
value of its indeterminate to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}}. Again, an optional argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape one}} may be given. \texttt{Value( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape upol}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} )} can also be expressed as \texttt{upol( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} )}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Value(x*y+y+x^7,[x,y],[5,7]);|
  78167
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that the default values for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape one}} can lead to different results than one would expect: For example for a matrix $M$, the values $M+M^0$ and $M+1$ are \emph{different}. As \texttt{Value} defaults to the one of the coefficient ring, when evaluating matrices in
polynomials always the correct \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape one}} should be given! }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Minimal Polynomials}}\label{Minimal Polynomials}
\logpage{[ 66, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7ED3E7D17C7AC732}{}
{
  \index{MinimalPolynomial@\texttt{MinimalPolynomial}!over a ring} 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MinimalPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 8, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8643915A8424DAF8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MinimalPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape R, elm[, ind]})\index{MinimalPolynomial@\texttt{MinimalPolynomial}}
\label{MinimalPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the \emph{minimal polynomial} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}} over the ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}}, expressed in the indeterminate number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}} is not given, it defaults to 1. 

 The minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of smallest degree with
coefficients in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}} that has value zero at \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elm}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MinimalPolynomial(Rationals,[[2,0],[0,2]]);|
  x-2
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }
