\hyperdef{L}{X837B8E55832CDFEB}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CyclotomicPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 9, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X827FC7FE81EE4C02}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CyclotomicPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape F, n})\index{CyclotomicPolynomial@\texttt{CyclotomicPolynomial}}
\label{CyclotomicPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 is the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}th cyclotomic polynomial over the ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape F}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CyclotomicPolynomial(Rationals,5);|
  x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Polynomial Factorization}}\label{Polynomial Factorization}
\logpage{[ 66, 10, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8551EF5187509D69}{}
{
  At the moment \textsf{GAP} provides only methods to factorize polynomials over finite fields (see
Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Finite Fields}), over subfields of cyclotomic fields (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Abelian Number Fields}), and over algebraic extensions of these (see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Algebraic extensions of fields}). 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Factors (of polynomial)}}
\logpage{[ 66, 10, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83511D517B544F36}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Factors({\mdseries\slshape [R, ]poly[, opt]})\index{Factors@\texttt{Factors}!of polynomial}
\label{Factors:of polynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (method)}}\\


 returns a list of the irreducible factors of the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape poly}} in the polynomial ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}}. (That is factors over the \texttt{CoefficientsRing} (\ref{CoefficientsRing}) value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}}.) 

 For univariate factorizations, it is possible to pass a record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opt}} as a third argument. This record can contain the following components: 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{onlydegs}}]  is a set of positive integers. The factorization assumes that all irreducible
factors have a degree in this set. 
\item[{\texttt{stopdegs}}]  is a set of positive integers. The factorization will stop once a factor of
degree in \texttt{stopdegs} has been found and will return the factorization found so far. 
\end{description}
 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= CyclotomicPolynomial( GF(2), 7 );|
  x_1^6+x_1^5+x_1^4+x_1^3+x_1^2+x_1+Z(2)^0
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Factors( f );|
  [ x_1^3+x_1+Z(2)^0, x_1^3+x_1^2+Z(2)^0 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Factors( PolynomialRing( GF(8) ), f );|
  [ x_1+Z(2^3), x_1+Z(2^3)^2, x_1+Z(2^3)^3, x_1+Z(2^3)^4, x_1+Z(2^3)^5,
    x_1+Z(2^3)^6 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:= MinimalPolynomial( Rationals, E(4) );|
  x^2+1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Factors( f );|
  [ x^2+1 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Factors( PolynomialRing( Rationals ), f );|
  [ x^2+1 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Factors( PolynomialRing( CF(4) ), f );|
  [ x+(-E(4)), x+E(4) ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FactorsSquarefree}}
\logpage{[ 66, 10, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7F5A4ACB7AF9E329}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FactorsSquarefree({\mdseries\slshape pring, upol, opt})\index{FactorsSquarefree@\texttt{FactorsSquarefree}}
\label{FactorsSquarefree}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a factorization of the squarefree, monic, univariate polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape upol}} in the polynomial ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pring}}; \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opt}} must be a (possibly empty) record of options. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape upol}} must not have zero as a root. This function is used by the factoring
algorithms. 

 The current method for multivariate factorization reduces to univariate
factorization by use of a reduction homomorphism of the form $f(x_1,x_2,x_3) \mapsto f(x,x^p,x^{{p^2}})$. It can be very time intensive for larger degrees. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Factors(x^10-y^10);|
  [ x-y, x+y, x^4-x^3*y+x^2*y^2-x*y^3+y^4, x^4+x^3*y+x^2*y^2+x*y^3+y^4 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Polynomials over the Rationals}}\label{Polynomials over the Rationals}
\logpage{[ 66, 11, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7F45E9E47EA2C18B}{}
{
  The following functions are only available to polynomials with rational
coefficients: 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PrimitivePolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 11, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E66494B7B05A055}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PrimitivePolynomial({\mdseries\slshape f})\index{PrimitivePolynomial@\texttt{PrimitivePolynomial}}
\label{PrimitivePolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 takes a polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} with rational coefficients and computes a new polynomial with integral
coefficients, obtained by multiplying with the Lcm of the denominators of the
coefficients and casting out the content (the Gcd of the coefficients). The
operation returns a list [\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape newpol}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coeff}}] with rational \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coeff}} such that \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coeff}}*\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape newpol}}=\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PolynomialModP}}
\logpage{[ 66, 11, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A73A3877EB73566}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PolynomialModP({\mdseries\slshape pol, p})\index{PolynomialModP@\texttt{PolynomialModP}}
\label{PolynomialModP}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 for a rational polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} this function returns a polynomial over the field with \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} elements, obtained by reducing the coefficients modulo \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GaloisType}}
\logpage{[ 66, 11, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7AB9A6257ED694EC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GaloisType({\mdseries\slshape f})\index{GaloisType@\texttt{GaloisType}}
\label{GaloisType}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} be an irreducible polynomial with rational coefficients. This function returns
the type of Gal(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}) (considered as a transitive permutation group of the roots of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}). It returns a number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} if Gal(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}) is permutation isomorphic to \texttt{TransitiveGroup(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}})} where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} is the degree of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}. 

 Identification is performed by factoring appropriate Galois resolvents as
proposed in \cite{MS85}. This function is provided for rational polynomials of degree up to 15.
However, in some cases the required calculations become unfeasibly large. 

 For a few polynomials of degree 14, a complete discrimination is not yet
possible, as it would require computations, that are not feasible with current
factoring methods. 

 This function requires the transitive groups library to be installed (see  (\textbf{transgrp: Transitive Permutation Groups})). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ProbabilityShapes}}
\logpage{[ 66, 11, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EB610D37D156DC6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ProbabilityShapes({\mdseries\slshape f})\index{ProbabilityShapes@\texttt{ProbabilityShapes}}
\label{ProbabilityShapes}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} be an irreducible polynomial with rational coefficients. This function returns
a list of the most likely type(s) of Gal(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}) (see \texttt{GaloisType} (\ref{GaloisType})), based on factorization modulo a set of primes. It is very fast, but the
result is only probabilistic. 

 This function requires the transitive groups library to be installed (see  (\textbf{transgrp: Transitive Permutation Groups})). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:=x^9-9*x^7+27*x^5-39*x^3+36*x-8;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GaloisType(f);|
  25
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@TransitiveGroup(9,25);|
  [1/2.S(3)^3]3
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ProbabilityShapes(f);|
  [ 25 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Factorization of Polynomials over the Rationals}}\label{Factorization of Polynomials over the Rationals}
\logpage{[ 66, 12, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7C178AB9866FDDE5}{}
{
  The following operations are used by \textsf{GAP} inside the factorization algorithm but might be of interest also in other
contexts. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{BombieriNorm}}
\logpage{[ 66, 12, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8723075C81D2CCA6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{BombieriNorm({\mdseries\slshape pol})\index{BombieriNorm@\texttt{BombieriNorm}}
\label{BombieriNorm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 computes weighted Norm [\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}}]$_2$ of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}} which is a good measure for factor coefficients (see \cite{BTW93}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MinimizedBombieriNorm}}
\logpage{[ 66, 12, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X856D769D878AF7AE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MinimizedBombieriNorm({\mdseries\slshape f})\index{MinimizedBombieriNorm@\texttt{MinimizedBombieriNorm}}
\label{MinimizedBombieriNorm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 This function applies linear Tschirnhaus transformations ($x \mapsto x + i$) to the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}}, trying to get the Bombieri norm of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape f}} small. It returns a list \texttt{[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape new{\textunderscore}polynomial}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i{\textunderscore}of{\textunderscore}transformation}}]}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{HenselBound}}
\logpage{[ 66, 12, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8139BB0F87399F2C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{HenselBound({\mdseries\slshape pol[, minpol, den]})\index{HenselBound@\texttt{HenselBound}}
\label{HenselBound}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the Hensel bound of the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}}. If the computation takes place over an algebraic extension, then the minimal
polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape minpol}} and denominator \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape den}} must be given. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{OneFactorBound}}
\logpage{[ 66, 12, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79CC9C8D7C9F6B6A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{OneFactorBound({\mdseries\slshape pol})\index{OneFactorBound@\texttt{OneFactorBound}}
\label{OneFactorBound}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns the coefficient bound for a single factor of the rational polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Laurent Polynomials}}\label{Laurent Polynomials}
\logpage{[ 66, 13, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X844B3C6C87A0E7E0}{}
{
  A univariate polynomial can be written in the form $r_0 + r_1 x + \cdots + r_n x^n$, with $r_i \in R$. Formally, there is no reason to start with 0, if $m$ is an integer, we can consider objects of the form $r_m x^m + r_{{m+1}} x^{{m+1}} + \cdots + r_n x^n$. We call these \emph{Laurent polynomials}. Laurent polynomials also can be considered as quotients of a univariate
polynomial by a power of the indeterminate. The addition and multiplication of
univariate polynomials extends to Laurent polynomials (though it might be
impossible to interpret a Laurent polynomial as a function) and many functions
for univariate polynomials extend to Laurent polynomials (or extended versions
for Laurent polynomials exist). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LaurentPolynomialByCoefficients}}
\logpage{[ 66, 13, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8467263B7EFA013E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LaurentPolynomialByCoefficients({\mdseries\slshape fam, cofs, val[, ind]})\index{LaurentPolynomialByCoefficients@\texttt{LaurentPolynomialByCoefficients}}
\label{LaurentPolynomialByCoefficients}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 constructs a Laurent polynomial over the coefficients family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}} and in the indeterminate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}} (defaulting to 1) with the coefficients given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cofs}} and valuation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 13, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86D58AB67F86469F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape laurent})\index{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial@\texttt{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial}}
\label{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For a Laurent polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape laurent}}, this function returns a pair \texttt{[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cof}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}}]}, consisting of the coefficient list (in ascending order) \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cof}} and the valuation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape laurent}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p:=LaurentPolynomialByCoefficients(FamilyObj(1),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@[1,2,3,4,5],-2);|
  5*x^2+4*x+3+2*x^-1+x^-2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@NumeratorOfRationalFunction(p);DenominatorOfRationalFunction(p);|
  5*x^4+4*x^3+3*x^2+2*x+1
  x^2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial(p*p);|
  [ [ 1, 4, 10, 20, 35, 44, 46, 40, 25 ], -4 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IndeterminateNumberOfLaurentPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 13, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8381E1B582F38C85}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndeterminateNumberOfLaurentPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape pol})\index{IndeterminateNumberOfLaurentPolynomial@\texttt{Indeterminate}\-\texttt{Number}\-\texttt{Of}\-\texttt{Laurent}\-\texttt{Polynomial}}
\label{IndeterminateNumberOfLaurentPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Is a synonym for \texttt{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction} (\ref{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction}). }

 }

\logpage{[ 66, 14, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7C1708D27F97B05F}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UnivariateRationalFunctionByCoefficients}}
\logpage{[ 66, 14, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X83DD411179888783}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UnivariateRationalFunctionByCoefficients({\mdseries\slshape fam, ncof, dcof, val[, ind]})\index{UnivariateRationalFunctionByCoefficients@\texttt{Univariate}\-\texttt{Rational}\-\texttt{Function}\-\texttt{By}\-\texttt{Coefficients}}
\label{UnivariateRationalFunctionByCoefficients}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 constructs a univariate rational function over the coefficients family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}} and in the indeterminate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ind}} (defaulting to 1) with numerator and denominator coefficients given by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ncof}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dcof}} and valuation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TaylorSeriesRationalFunction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 14, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B1EE4E07A9631C6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TaylorSeriesRationalFunction({\mdseries\slshape ratfun, at, deg]})\index{TaylorSeriesRationalFunction@\texttt{TaylorSeriesRationalFunction}}
\label{TaylorSeriesRationalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 Computes the taylor series up to degree \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape deg}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ratfun}} at \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape at}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@TaylorSeriesRationalFunction((x^5+3*x+7)/(x^5+x+1),0,11);|
  -50*x^11+36*x^10-26*x^9+22*x^8-18*x^7+14*x^6-10*x^5+4*x^4-4*x^3+4*x^2-4*x+7
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Polynomial Rings and Function Fields}}\label{Polynomial Rings and Function Fields}
\logpage{[ 66, 15, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7C59471783C3FEDC}{}
{
  While polynomials depend only on the family of the coefficients, polynomial
rings $A$ are defined over a base ring $R$. A polynomial is an element of $A$ if and only if all its coefficients are contained in $R$. Besides providing domains and an easy way to create polynomials, polynomial
rings can affect the behavior of operations like factorization into
irreducibles. 

 If you need to work with a polynomial ring and its indeterminates the
following two approaches will produce a ring that contains given variables
(see section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Indeterminates} for details about the internal numbering): Either, first create the ring and
then get the indeterminates with \texttt{IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing} (\ref{IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r := PolynomialRing(Rationals,["a","b"]);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@indets := IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing(r);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a := indets[1]; a := indets[2];|
  a
  b
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Alternatively, first create the indeterminates and then create the ring
including these indeterminates. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:=Indeterminate(Rationals,"a":old);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@b:=Indeterminate(Rationals,"b":old);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PolynomialRing(Rationals,[a,b]);;|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 As a convenient shortcut, intended mainly for interactive working, the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th indeterminate of a polynomial ring $R$ can be accessed as $R.i$, which corresponds exactly to \texttt{IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing}$( R )[i]$ or, if it has the name \texttt{nam}, as $R$\texttt{.nam}. \emph{Note} that the number $i$ is in general \emph{not} the indeterminate number, but simply an index into the indeterminates list of $R$. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r := PolynomialRing(Rationals, ["a", "b"]:old );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r.1; r.2; r.a; r.b;|
  a
  b
  a
  b
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IndeterminateNumberOfLaurentPolynomial(r.1);|
  3
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Polynomials as \textsf{GAP} objects can exist without a polynomial ring being defined and polynomials
cannot be associated to a particular polynomial ring. (For example dividing a
polynomial which is in a polynomial ring over the integers by another integer
will result in a polynomial over the rationals, not in a rational function
over the integers.) 

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PolynomialRing}}\logpage{[ 66, 15, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D2F16E480060330}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PolynomialRing({\mdseries\slshape R, rank[, avoid]})\index{PolynomialRing@\texttt{PolynomialRing}!for a ring and a rank (and an exclusion list)}
\label{PolynomialRing:for a ring and a rank (and an exclusion list)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PolynomialRing({\mdseries\slshape R, names[, avoid]})\index{PolynomialRing@\texttt{PolynomialRing}!for a ring and a list of names (and an exclusion list)}
\label{PolynomialRing:for a ring and a list of names (and an exclusion list)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PolynomialRing({\mdseries\slshape R, indets})\index{PolynomialRing@\texttt{PolynomialRing}!for a ring and a list of indeterminates}
\label{PolynomialRing:for a ring and a list of indeterminates}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PolynomialRing({\mdseries\slshape R, indetnums})\index{PolynomialRing@\texttt{PolynomialRing}!for a ring and a list of indeterminate numbers}
\label{PolynomialRing:for a ring and a list of indeterminate numbers}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 creates a polynomial ring over the ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}}. If a positive integer \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rank}} is given, this creates the polynomial ring in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rank}} indeterminates. These indeterminates will have the internal index numbers 1 to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rank}}. The second usage takes a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape names}} of strings and returns a polynomial ring in indeterminates labelled by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape names}}. These indeterminates have ``new'' internal index numbers as if they had been created by calls to \texttt{Indeterminate} (\ref{Indeterminate:for a ring (and a number)}). (If the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape avoid}} is given it contains indeterminates that should be avoided, in this case
internal index numbers are incremented to skip these variables.) In the third
version, a list of indeterminates \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape indets}} is given. This creates the polynomial ring in the indeterminates \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape indets}}. Finally, the fourth version specifies indeterminates by their index numbers. 

 To get the indeterminates of a polynomial ring use \texttt{IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing} (\ref{IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing}). (Indeterminates created independently with \texttt{Indeterminate} (\ref{Indeterminate:for a ring (and a number)}) will usually differ, though they might be given the same name and display
identically, see Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Indeterminates}.) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing}}
\logpage{[ 66, 15, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80D585E1793D4552}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing({\mdseries\slshape pring})\index{IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing@\texttt{IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing}}
\label{IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IndeterminatesOfFunctionField({\mdseries\slshape ffield})\index{IndeterminatesOfFunctionField@\texttt{IndeterminatesOfFunctionField}}
\label{IndeterminatesOfFunctionField}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns a list of the indeterminates of the polynomial ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pring}}, respectively the function field \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ffield}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CoefficientsRing}}
\logpage{[ 66, 15, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8235D10781BE8003}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CoefficientsRing({\mdseries\slshape pring})\index{CoefficientsRing@\texttt{CoefficientsRing}}
\label{CoefficientsRing}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the ring of coefficients of the polynomial ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pring}}, that is the ring over which \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pring}} was defined. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r:=PolynomialRing(GF(7));|
  GF(7)[x_1]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r:=PolynomialRing(GF(7),3);|
  GF(7)[x_1,x_2,x_3]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing(r);|
  [ x_1, x_2, x_3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r2:=PolynomialRing(GF(7),[5,7,12]);|
  GF(7)[x_5,x_7,x_12]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CoefficientsRing(r);|
  GF(7)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r:=PolynomialRing(GF(7),3);|
  GF(7)[x_1,x_2,x_3]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r2:=PolynomialRing(GF(7),3,IndeterminatesOfPolynomialRing(r));|
  GF(7)[x_4,x_5,x_6]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r:=PolynomialRing(GF(7),["x","y","z","z2"]);|
  GF(7)[x,y,z,z2]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 is the category of polynomial rings over the rationals (see

\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Univariate Polynomial Rings}}\label{Univariate Polynomial Rings}
\logpage{[ 66, 16, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X85CA757B844F12AE}{}
{
  
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{UnivariatePolynomialRing}}\logpage{[ 66, 16, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X84DC2A59797A26DE}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UnivariatePolynomialRing({\mdseries\slshape R[, nr]})\index{UnivariatePolynomialRing@\texttt{UnivariatePolynomialRing}!for a ring (and an indeterminate number)}
\label{UnivariatePolynomialRing:for a ring (and an indeterminate number)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UnivariatePolynomialRing({\mdseries\slshape R[, name][, avoid]})\index{UnivariatePolynomialRing@\texttt{UnivariatePolynomialRing}!for a ring (and a name and an exclusion list)}
\label{UnivariatePolynomialRing:for a ring (and a name and an exclusion list)}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns a univariate polynomial ring in the indeterminate \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} over the base ring \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape R}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape nr}} is not given it defaults to 1. 

 If the number is not specified a list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape avoid}} of indeterminates may be given. Then the function will return a ring in an
indeterminate that is guaranteed to be different from all the indeterminates
in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape avoid}}. 

 Also a string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} can be prescribed as the name of the indeterminate chosen (also avoiding the
indeterminates in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape avoid}} if given). }

\logpage{[ 66, 16, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A43D74B812401CA}{}

\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]

  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r2:=PolynomialRing(Rationals,["q"]);|
  Rationals[q]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsUnivariatePolynomialRing(r);|

  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsUnivariatePolynomialRing(r2);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Monomial Orderings}}\label{Monomial Orderings}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86E2ADEA784AD163}{}
{
  It is often desirable to consider the monomials within a polynomial to be
arranged with respect to a certain ordering. Such an ordering is called a \emph{monomial ordering} if it is total, invariant under multiplication with other monomials and admits
no infinite descending chains. For details on monomial orderings see \cite{coxlittleoshea}. 

 In \textsf{GAP}, monomial orderings are represented by objects that provide a way to compare
monomials (as polynomials as well as {\textendash}for efficiency purposes
within algorithms{\textendash} in the internal representation as lists). 

 Normally the ordering chosen should be \emph{admissible}, i.e. it must be compatible with products: If $a < b$ then $ca < cb$ for all monomials $a, b$ and $c$. 

 Each monomial ordering provides the two functions \texttt{MonomialComparisonFunction} (\ref{MonomialComparisonFunction}) and \texttt{MonomialExtrepComparisonFun} (\ref{MonomialExtrepComparisonFun}) to compare monomials. These functions work as ``is less than'', i.e. they return \texttt{true} if and only if the left argument is smaller. 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsMonomialOrdering}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79D4CBBF820EA204}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsMonomialOrdering({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsMonomialOrdering@\texttt{IsMonomialOrdering}}
\label{IsMonomialOrdering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 A monomial ordering is an object representing a monomial ordering. Its
attributes \texttt{MonomialComparisonFunction} (\ref{MonomialComparisonFunction}) and \texttt{MonomialExtrepComparisonFun} (\ref{MonomialExtrepComparisonFun}) are actual comparison functions. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LeadingMonomialOfPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D052A017A73E91E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LeadingMonomialOfPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape pol, ord})\index{LeadingMonomialOfPolynomial@\texttt{LeadingMonomialOfPolynomial}}
\label{LeadingMonomialOfPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the leading monomial (with respect to the ordering \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ord}}) of the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:=Indeterminate(Rationals,"x");;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@y:=Indeterminate(Rationals,"y");;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@z:=Indeterminate(Rationals,"z");;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@lexord:=MonomialLexOrdering();grlexord:=MonomialGrlexOrdering();|
  MonomialLexOrdering()
  MonomialGrlexOrdering()
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@f:=2*x+3*y+4*z+5*x^2-6*z^2+7*y^3;|
  7*y^3+5*x^2-6*z^2+2*x+3*y+4*z
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeadingMonomialOfPolynomial(f,lexord);|
  x^2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeadingMonomialOfPolynomial(f,grlexord);|
  y^3
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LeadingTermOfPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B6231137BA8B95F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LeadingTermOfPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape pol, ord})\index{LeadingTermOfPolynomial@\texttt{LeadingTermOfPolynomial}}
\label{LeadingTermOfPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the leading term (with respect to the ordering \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ord}}) of the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}}, i.e. the product of leading coefficient and leading monomial. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LeadingCoefficientOfPolynomial}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X798E707D86141087}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LeadingCoefficientOfPolynomial({\mdseries\slshape pol, ord})\index{LeadingCoefficientOfPolynomial@\texttt{LeadingCoefficientOfPolynomial}}
\label{LeadingCoefficientOfPolynomial}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the leading coefficient (that is the coefficient of the leading
monomial, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{LeadingMonomialOfPolynomial} (\ref{LeadingMonomialOfPolynomial})) of the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pol}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeadingTermOfPolynomial(f,lexord);|
  5*x^2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeadingTermOfPolynomial(f,grlexord);|
  7*y^3
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@LeadingCoefficientOfPolynomial(f,lexord);|
  5
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MonomialComparisonFunction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EDE941781BA7F8B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MonomialComparisonFunction({\mdseries\slshape O})\index{MonomialComparisonFunction@\texttt{MonomialComparisonFunction}}
\label{MonomialComparisonFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape O}} is an object representing a monomial ordering, this attribute returns a \emph{function} that can be used to compare or sort monomials (and polynomials which will be
compared by their monomials in decreasing order) in this order. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MonomialComparisonFunction(lexord);|
  function( a, b ) ... end
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l:=[f,Derivative(f,x),Derivative(f,y),Derivative(f,z)];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Sort(l,MonomialComparisonFunction(lexord));l;|
  [ -12*z+4, 21*y^2+3, 10*x+2, 7*y^3+5*x^2-6*z^2+2*x+3*y+4*z ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MonomialExtrepComparisonFun}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EDC3A457E7B591E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MonomialExtrepComparisonFun({\mdseries\slshape O})\index{MonomialExtrepComparisonFun@\texttt{MonomialExtrepComparisonFun}}
\label{MonomialExtrepComparisonFun}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape O}} is an object representing a monomial ordering, this attribute returns a \emph{function} that can be used to compare or sort monomials \emph{in their external representation} (as lists). This comparison variant is used inside algorithms that manipulate
the external representation. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MonomialLexOrdering}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X852D7BB37ECE98E1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MonomialLexOrdering({\mdseries\slshape [vari]})\index{MonomialLexOrdering@\texttt{MonomialLexOrdering}}
\label{MonomialLexOrdering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function creates a lexicographic ordering for monomials. Monomials are
compared first by the exponents of the largest variable, then the exponents of
the second largest variable and so on. 

 The variables are ordered according to their (internal) index, i.e., $x_1$ is larger than $x_2$ and so on. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vari}} is given, and is a list of variables or variable indices, instead this
arrangement of variables (in descending order; i.e. the first variable is
larger than the second) is used as the underlying order of variables. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l:=List(Tuples([1..3],3),i->x^(i[1]-1)*y^(i[2]-1)*z^(i[3]-1));|
  [ 1, z, z^2, y, y*z, y*z^2, y^2, y^2*z, y^2*z^2, x, x*z, x*z^2, x*y,
    x*y*z, x*y*z^2, x*y^2, x*y^2*z, x*y^2*z^2, x^2, x^2*z, x^2*z^2,
    x^2*y, x^2*y*z, x^2*y*z^2, x^2*y^2, x^2*y^2*z, x^2*y^2*z^2 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Sort(l,MonomialComparisonFunction(MonomialLexOrdering()));l;|
  [ 1, z, z^2, y, y*z, y*z^2, y^2, y^2*z, y^2*z^2, x, x*z, x*z^2, x*y,
    x*y*z, x*y*z^2, x*y^2, x*y^2*z, x*y^2*z^2, x^2, x^2*z, x^2*z^2,
    x^2*y, x^2*y*z, x^2*y*z^2, x^2*y^2, x^2*y^2*z, x^2*y^2*z^2 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Sort(l,MonomialComparisonFunction(MonomialLexOrdering([y,z,x])));l;|
  [ 1, x, x^2, z, x*z, x^2*z, z^2, x*z^2, x^2*z^2, y, x*y, x^2*y, y*z,
    x*y*z, x^2*y*z, y*z^2, x*y*z^2, x^2*y*z^2, y^2, x*y^2, x^2*y^2,
    y^2*z, x*y^2*z, x^2*y^2*z, y^2*z^2, x*y^2*z^2, x^2*y^2*z^2 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Sort(l,MonomialComparisonFunction(MonomialLexOrdering([z,x,y])));l;|
  [ 1, y, y^2, x, x*y, x*y^2, x^2, x^2*y, x^2*y^2, z, y*z, y^2*z, x*z,
    x*y*z, x*y^2*z, x^2*z, x^2*y*z, x^2*y^2*z, z^2, y*z^2, y^2*z^2,
    x*z^2, x*y*z^2, x*y^2*z^2, x^2*z^2, x^2*y*z^2, x^2*y^2*z^2 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MonomialGrlexOrdering}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 8 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X786C866C824D2688}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MonomialGrlexOrdering({\mdseries\slshape [vari]})\index{MonomialGrlexOrdering@\texttt{MonomialGrlexOrdering}}
\label{MonomialGrlexOrdering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function creates a degree/lexicographic ordering. In this ordering
monomials are compared first by their total degree, then lexicographically
(see \texttt{MonomialLexOrdering} (\ref{MonomialLexOrdering})). 

 The variables are ordered according to their (internal) index, i.e., $x_1$ is larger than $x_2$ and so on. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vari}} is given, and is a list of variables or variable indices, instead this
arrangement of variables (in descending order; i.e. the first variable is
larger than the second) is used as the underlying order of variables. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MonomialGrevlexOrdering}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 9 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8094C733808D1799}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MonomialGrevlexOrdering({\mdseries\slshape [vari]})\index{MonomialGrevlexOrdering@\texttt{MonomialGrevlexOrdering}}
\label{MonomialGrevlexOrdering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function creates a ``grevlex'' ordering. In this ordering monomials are compared first by total degree and
then backwards lexicographically. (This is different than ``grlex'' ordering with variables reversed.) 

 The variables are ordered according to their (internal) index, i.e., $x_1$ is larger than $x_2$ and so on. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape vari}} is given, and is a list of variables or variable indices, instead this
arrangement of variables (in descending order; i.e. the first variable is
larger than the second) is used as the underlying order of variables. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Sort(l,MonomialComparisonFunction(MonomialGrlexOrdering()));l;|
  [ 1, z, y, x, z^2, y*z, y^2, x*z, x*y, x^2, y*z^2, y^2*z, x*z^2,
    x*y*z, x*y^2, x^2*z, x^2*y, y^2*z^2, x*y*z^2, x*y^2*z, x^2*z^2,
    x^2*y*z, x^2*y^2, x*y^2*z^2, x^2*y*z^2, x^2*y^2*z, x^2*y^2*z^2 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Sort(l,MonomialComparisonFunction(MonomialGrevlexOrdering()));l;|
  [ 1, z, y, x, z^2, y*z, x*z, y^2, x*y, x^2, y*z^2, x*z^2, y^2*z,
    x*y*z, x^2*z, x*y^2, x^2*y, y^2*z^2, x*y*z^2, x^2*z^2, x*y^2*z,
    x^2*y*z, x^2*y^2, x*y^2*z^2, x^2*y*z^2, x^2*y^2*z, x^2*y^2*z^2 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Sort(l,MonomialComparisonFunction(MonomialGrlexOrdering([z,y,x])));l;|
  [ 1, x, y, z, x^2, x*y, y^2, x*z, y*z, z^2, x^2*y, x*y^2, x^2*z,
    x*y*z, y^2*z, x*z^2, y*z^2, x^2*y^2, x^2*y*z, x*y^2*z, x^2*z^2,
    x*y*z^2, y^2*z^2, x^2*y^2*z, x^2*y*z^2, x*y^2*z^2, x^2*y^2*z^2 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{EliminationOrdering}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 10 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84AC871283A74EC0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{EliminationOrdering({\mdseries\slshape elim[, rest]})\index{EliminationOrdering@\texttt{EliminationOrdering}}
\label{EliminationOrdering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function creates an elimination ordering for eliminating the variables in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elim}}. Two monomials are compared first by the exponent vectors for the variables
listed in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elim}} (a lexicographic comparison with respect to the ordering indicated in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elim}}). If these submonomial are equal, the submonomials given by the other
variables are compared by a graded lexicographic ordering (with respect to the
variable order given in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rest}}, if called with two parameters). 

 Both \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape elim}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rest}} may be a list of variables or a list of variable indices. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PolynomialReduction}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 11 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C99593584D478D7}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PolynomialReduction({\mdseries\slshape poly, gens, order})\index{PolynomialReduction@\texttt{PolynomialReduction}}
\label{PolynomialReduction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 reduces the polynomial \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape poly}} by the ideal generated by the polynomials in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}, using the order \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape order}} of monomials. Unless \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} is a Gr{\"o}bner basis the result is not guaranteed to be unique. 

 The operation returns a list of length two, the first entry is the remainder
after the reduction. The second entry is a list of quotients corresponding to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. 

 Note that the strategy used by \texttt{PolynomialReduction} differs from the standard textbook reduction algorithm, which is provided by \texttt{PolynomialDivisionAlgorithm} (\ref{PolynomialDivisionAlgorithm}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PolynomialReducedRemainder}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 12 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7DE7D4467EBAD916}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PolynomialReducedRemainder({\mdseries\slshape poly, gens, order})\index{PolynomialReducedRemainder@\texttt{PolynomialReducedRemainder}}
\label{PolynomialReducedRemainder}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 this operation does the same way as \texttt{PolynomialReduction} (\ref{PolynomialReduction}) but does not keep track of the actual quotients and returns only the remainder
(it is therefore slightly faster). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PolynomialDivisionAlgorithm}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 13 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C8239057FD4EC03}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PolynomialDivisionAlgorithm({\mdseries\slshape poly, gens, order})\index{PolynomialDivisionAlgorithm@\texttt{PolynomialDivisionAlgorithm}}
\label{PolynomialDivisionAlgorithm}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function implements the division algorithm for multivariate polynomials
as given in \cite[Theorem 3 in Chapter 2]{coxlittleoshea}. (It might be slower than \texttt{PolynomialReduction} (\ref{PolynomialReduction}) but the remainders are guaranteed to agree with the textbook.) 

 The operation returns a list of length two, the first entry is the remainder
after the reduction. The second entry is a list of quotients corresponding to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@bas:=[x^3*y*z,x*y^2*z,z*y*z^3+x];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@pol:=x^7*z*bas[1]+y^5*bas[3]+x*z;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PolynomialReduction(pol,bas,MonomialLexOrdering());|
  [ -y*z^5, [ x^7*z, 0, y^5+z ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PolynomialReducedRemainder(pol,bas,MonomialLexOrdering());|
  -y*z^5
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PolynomialDivisionAlgorithm(pol,bas,MonomialLexOrdering());|
  [ -y*z^5, [ x^7*z, 0, y^5+z ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{MonomialExtGrlexLess}}
\logpage{[ 66, 17, 14 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A30E10B820311D1}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{MonomialExtGrlexLess({\mdseries\slshape a, b})\index{MonomialExtGrlexLess@\texttt{MonomialExtGrlexLess}}
\label{MonomialExtGrlexLess}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 implements comparison of monomial in their external representation by a ``grlex'' order with $x_1>x_2$ (This is exactly the same as the ordering by \texttt{MonomialGrlexOrdering} (\ref{MonomialGrlexOrdering}), see{\nobreakspace} \ref{Monomial Orderings}). The function takes two monomials \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape a}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape b}} in expanded form and returns whether the first is smaller than the second.
(This ordering is also used by \textsf{GAP} internally for representing polynomials as a linear combination of monomials.) 

 See section{\nobreakspace}\ref{The Defining Attributes of Rational Functions} for details on the expanded form of monomials. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Groebner Bases}}\label{Groebner Bases}
\logpage{[ 66, 18, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79BAB2937E6085D6}{}
{
  A \emph{Groebner Basis} of an ideal $I$i, in a polynomial ring $R$, with respect to a monomial ordering, is a set of ideal generators \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} such that the ideal generated by the leading monomials of all polynomials in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is equal to the ideal generated by the leading monomials of all polynomials in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape I}}. 

 For more details on Groebner bases see \cite{coxlittleoshea}. 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{GroebnerBasis}}\logpage{[ 66, 18, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7A43611E876B7560}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GroebnerBasis({\mdseries\slshape L, O})\index{GroebnerBasis@\texttt{GroebnerBasis}!for a list and a monomial ordering}
\label{GroebnerBasis:for a list and a monomial ordering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GroebnerBasis({\mdseries\slshape I, O})\index{GroebnerBasis@\texttt{GroebnerBasis}!for an ideal and a monomial ordering}
\label{GroebnerBasis:for an ideal and a monomial ordering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{GroebnerBasisNC({\mdseries\slshape L, O})\index{GroebnerBasisNC@\texttt{GroebnerBasisNC}}
\label{GroebnerBasisNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape O}} be a monomial ordering and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape L}} be a list of polynomials that generate an ideal \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape I}}. This operation returns a Groebner basis of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape I}} with respect to the ordering \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape O}}. 

 \texttt{GroebnerBasisNC} works like \texttt{GroebnerBasis} with the only distinction that the first argument has to be a list of
polynomials and that no test is performed to check whether the ordering is
defined for all occurring variables. 

 Note that \textsf{GAP} at the moment only includes a na{\"\i}ve implementation of Buchberger's
algorithm (which is mainly intended as a teaching tool). It might not be
sufficient for serious problems. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l:=[x^2+y^2+z^2-1,x^2+z^2-y,x-y];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GroebnerBasis(l,MonomialLexOrdering());|
  [ x^2+y^2+z^2-1, x^2+z^2-y, x-y, -y^2-y+1, -z^2+2*y-1,
    1/2*z^4+2*z^2-1/2 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GroebnerBasis(l,MonomialLexOrdering([z,x,y]));|
  [ x^2+y^2+z^2-1, x^2+z^2-y, x-y, -y^2-y+1 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GroebnerBasis(l,MonomialGrlexOrdering());|
  [ x^2+y^2+z^2-1, x^2+z^2-y, x-y, -y^2-y+1, -z^2+2*y-1 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ReducedGroebnerBasis}}\logpage{[ 66, 18, 2 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7DEF286384967C9E}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ReducedGroebnerBasis({\mdseries\slshape L, O})\index{ReducedGroebnerBasis@\texttt{ReducedGroebnerBasis}!for a list and a monomial ordering}
\label{ReducedGroebnerBasis:for a list and a monomial ordering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ReducedGroebnerBasis({\mdseries\slshape I, O})\index{ReducedGroebnerBasis@\texttt{ReducedGroebnerBasis}!for an ideal and a monomial ordering}
\label{ReducedGroebnerBasis:for an ideal and a monomial ordering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 a Groebner basis $B$ (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{GroebnerBasis} (\ref{GroebnerBasis:for a list and a monomial ordering})) is \emph{reduced} if no monomial in a polynomial in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape B}} is divisible by the leading monomial of another polynomial in $B$. This operation computes a Groebner basis with respect to the monomial
ordering \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape O}} and then reduces it. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ReducedGroebnerBasis(l,MonomialGrlexOrdering());|
  [ x-y, z^2-2*y+1, y^2+y-1 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ReducedGroebnerBasis(l,MonomialLexOrdering());|
  [ z^4+4*z^2-1, -1/2*z^2+y-1/2, -1/2*z^2+x-1/2 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ReducedGroebnerBasis(l,MonomialLexOrdering([y,z,x]));|
  [ x^2+x-1, z^2-2*x+1, -x+y ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 For performance reasons it can be advantageous to define monomial orderings
once and then to reuse them: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ord:=MonomialGrlexOrdering();;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@GroebnerBasis(l,ord);|
  [ x^2+y^2+z^2-1, x^2+z^2-y, x-y, -y^2-y+1, -z^2+2*y-1 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ReducedGroebnerBasis(l,ord);|
  [ x-y, z^2-2*y+1, y^2+y-1 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{StoredGroebnerBasis}}
\logpage{[ 66, 18, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7FC1EFE78498C17C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{StoredGroebnerBasis({\mdseries\slshape I})\index{StoredGroebnerBasis@\texttt{StoredGroebnerBasis}}
\label{StoredGroebnerBasis}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 For an ideal \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape I}} in a polynomial ring, this attribute holds a list $[ B, O ]$ where $B$ is a Groebner basis for the monomial ordering $O$. this can be used to test membership or canonical coset representatives. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoGroebner}}
\logpage{[ 66, 18, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C55702786D284A7}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoGroebner\index{InfoGroebner@\texttt{InfoGroebner}}
\label{InfoGroebner}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (info class)}}\\


 This info class gives information about Groebner basis calculations. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Rational Function Families}}\label{Rational Function Families}
\logpage{[ 66, 19, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8113DD9B781CA6C1}{}
{
  All rational functions defined over a ring lie in the same family, the
rational functions family over this ring. 

 In \textsf{GAP} therefore the family of a polynomial depends only on the family of the
coefficients, all polynomials whose coefficients lie in the same family are ``compatible''. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RationalFunctionsFamily}}
\logpage{[ 66, 19, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X855DD73C78A90BC3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RationalFunctionsFamily({\mdseries\slshape fam})\index{RationalFunctionsFamily@\texttt{RationalFunctionsFamily}}
\label{RationalFunctionsFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 creates a family containing rational functions with coefficients in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}}. All elements of the \texttt{RationalFunctionsFamily} are rational functions (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsRationalFunction} (\ref{IsRationalFunction})). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPolynomialFunctionsFamily}}
\logpage{[ 66, 19, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X86E097307D188D3B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPolynomialFunctionsFamily({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsPolynomialFunctionsFamily@\texttt{IsPolynomialFunctionsFamily}}
\label{IsPolynomialFunctionsFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsRationalFunctionsFamily({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsRationalFunctionsFamily@\texttt{IsRationalFunctionsFamily}}
\label{IsRationalFunctionsFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 \texttt{IsPolynomialFunctionsFamily} is the category of a family of polynomials. For families over an UFD, the
category becomes \texttt{IsRationalFunctionsFamily} (as rational functions and quotients are only provided for families over an
UFD.)  

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@fam:=RationalFunctionsFamily(FamilyObj(1));|
  NewFamily( "RationalFunctionsFamily(...)", [ 618, 620 ],
  [ 82, 85, 89, 93, 97, 100, 103, 107, 111, 618, 620 ] )
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{CoefficientsFamily}}
\logpage{[ 66, 19, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7AADCA45826866FB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{CoefficientsFamily({\mdseries\slshape rffam})\index{CoefficientsFamily@\texttt{CoefficientsFamily}}
\label{CoefficientsFamily}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rffam}} has been created as \texttt{RationalFunctionsFamily(\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cfam}})} this attribute holds the coefficients family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cfam}}. 

 \textsf{GAP} does \emph{not} embed the base ring in the polynomial ring. While multiplication and addition
of base ring elements to rational functions return the expected results,
polynomials and rational functions are not equal. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@1=Indeterminate(Rationals)^0;|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{The Representations of Rational Functions}}\label{The Representations of Rational Functions}
\logpage{[ 66, 20, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7E360788785DE530}{}
{
  \textsf{GAP} uses four representations of rational functions: Rational functions given by
numerator and denominator, polynomials, univariate rational functions (given
by coefficient lists for numerator and denominator and valuation) and Laurent
polynomials (given by coefficient list and valuation). 

 These representations do not necessarily reflect mathematical properties:
While an object in the Laurent polynomials representation must be a Laurent
polynomial it might turn out that a rational function given by numerator and
denominator is actually a Laurent polynomial and the property tests in
section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Properties and Attributes of Rational Functions} will find this out. 

 Each representation is associated one or several ``defining attributes'' that give an ``external'' representation (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{The Defining Attributes of Rational Functions}) of the representation in the form of lists and are the defining information
that tells a rational function what it is. 

 \textsf{GAP} also implements methods to compute these attributes for rational functions in \emph{other} representations, provided it would be possible to express an \emph{mathematically equal} rational function in the representation associated with the attribute. (That
is one can always get a numerator/denominator representation of a polynomial
while an arbitrary function of course can compute a polynomial representation
only if it is a polynomial.) 

 Therefore these attributes can be thought of as ``conceptual'' representations that allow us {\textendash}as far as possible{\textendash} to
consider an object as a rational function, a polynomial or a Laurent
polynomial, regardless of the way it is represented in the computer. 

 Functions thus usually do not need to care about the representation of a
rational function. Depending on its (known in the context or determined)
properties, they can access the attribute representing the rational function
in the desired way. 

 Consequently, methods for rational functions are installed for properties and
not for representations. 

 When \emph{creating} new rational functions however they must be created in one of the three
representations. In most cases this will be the representation for which the ``conceptual'' representation in which the calculation was done is the defining attribute. 

 Iterated operations (like forming the product over a list) therefore will tend
to stay in the most suitable representation and the calculation of another
conceptual representation (which may be comparatively expensive in certain
circumstances) is not necessary. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{The Defining Attributes of Rational Functions}}\label{The Defining Attributes of Rational Functions}
\logpage{[ 66, 21, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7F44CF87801DB965}{}
{
  In general, rational functions are given in terms of monomials. They are
represented by lists, using numbers (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Indeterminates}) for the indeterminates. 

 \index{Expanded form of monomials} A monomial is a product of powers of indeterminates. A monomial is stored as a
list (we call this the \emph{expanded form} of the monomial) of the form \texttt{[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape inum}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape exp}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape inum}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape exp}},...]} where each \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape inum}} is the number of an indeterminate and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape exp}} the corresponding exponent. The list must be sorted according to the numbers
of the indeterminates. Thus for example, if $x$, $y$ and $z$ are the first three indeterminates, the expanded form of the monomial $x^5 z^8 = z^8 x^5$ is \texttt{[ 1, 5, 3, 8 ]}. \index{External representation of polynomials} The representation of a polynomials is a list of the form \texttt{[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mon}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coeff}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mon}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coeff}},...]} where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape mon}} is a monomial in expanded form (that is given as list) and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coeff}} its coefficient. The monomials must be sorted according to the total
degree/lexicographic order (This is the same as given by the ``grlex'' monomial ordering, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{MonomialGrlexOrdering} (\ref{MonomialGrlexOrdering})). We call this the \emph{external representation} of a polynomial. (The reason for ordering is that addition of polynomials
becomes linear in the number of monomials instead of quadratic; the reason for
the particular ordering chose is that it is compatible with multiplication and
thus gives acceptable performance for quotient calculations.) 

 The attributes that give a representation of a rational function as a Laurent
polynomial are \texttt{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial} (\ref{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial}) and \texttt{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction} (\ref{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction}). 

 Algorithms should use only the attributes \texttt{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun} (\ref{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun}), \texttt{ExtRepDenominatorRatFun} (\ref{ExtRepDenominatorRatFun}), \texttt{ExtRepPolynomialRatFun} (\ref{ExtRepPolynomialRatFun}), \texttt{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial} (\ref{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial}) and {\textendash}if the univariate function is not constant{\textendash} \texttt{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction} (\ref{IndeterminateNumberOfUnivariateRationalFunction}) as the low\texttt{\symbol{45}}level interface to work with a polynomial. They
should not refer to the actual representation used. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsRationalFunctionDefaultRep}}
\logpage{[ 66, 21, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X791E16C67A352263}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsRationalFunctionDefaultRep({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsRationalFunctionDefaultRep@\texttt{IsRationalFunctionDefaultRep}}
\label{IsRationalFunctionDefaultRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Representation)}}\\


 is the default representation of rational functions. A rational function in
this representation is defined by the attributes \texttt{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun} (\ref{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun}) and \texttt{ExtRepDenominatorRatFun} (\ref{ExtRepDenominatorRatFun}), the values of which are external representations of polynomials. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun}}
\logpage{[ 66, 21, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7DF955C87CBFC12B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun({\mdseries\slshape ratfun})\index{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun@\texttt{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun}}
\label{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the external representation of the numerator polynomial of the
rational function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ratfun}}. Numerator and denominator are not guaranteed to be cancelled against each
other. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ExtRepDenominatorRatFun}}
\logpage{[ 66, 21, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8059E74D7DCABDBC}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExtRepDenominatorRatFun({\mdseries\slshape ratfun})\index{ExtRepDenominatorRatFun@\texttt{ExtRepDenominatorRatFun}}
\label{ExtRepDenominatorRatFun}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the external representation of the denominator polynomial of the
rational function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ratfun}}. Numerator and denominator are not guaranteed to be cancelled against each
other. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ZeroCoefficientRatFun}}
\logpage{[ 66, 21, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84F546F87B5ECFE0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZeroCoefficientRatFun({\mdseries\slshape ratfun})\index{ZeroCoefficientRatFun@\texttt{ZeroCoefficientRatFun}}
\label{ZeroCoefficientRatFun}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 returns the zero of the coefficient ring. This might be needed to represent
the zero polynomial for which the external representation of the numerator is
the empty list. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsPolynomialDefaultRep}}
\logpage{[ 66, 21, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X833CE16579AB26E0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsPolynomialDefaultRep({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsPolynomialDefaultRep@\texttt{IsPolynomialDefaultRep}}
\label{IsPolynomialDefaultRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Representation)}}\\


 is the default representation of polynomials. A polynomial in this
representation is defined by the components and \texttt{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun} (\ref{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun}) where \texttt{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun} (\ref{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun}) is the external representation of the polynomial. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ExtRepPolynomialRatFun}}
\logpage{[ 66, 21, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8406EE2E8775FBAB}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExtRepPolynomialRatFun({\mdseries\slshape polynomial})\index{ExtRepPolynomialRatFun@\texttt{ExtRepPolynomialRatFun}}
\label{ExtRepPolynomialRatFun}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (attribute)}}\\


 returns the external representation of a polynomial. The difference to \texttt{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun} (\ref{ExtRepNumeratorRatFun}) is that rational functions might know to be a polynomial but can still have a
non\texttt{\symbol{45}}vanishing denominator. In this case \texttt{ExtRepPolynomialRatFun} has to call a quotient routine. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsLaurentPolynomialDefaultRep}}
\logpage{[ 66, 21, 7 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E1B98CC7BADAF56}{}

 This representation is used for Laurent polynomials and univariate

\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Creation of Rational Functions}}\label{Creation of Rational Functions}
\logpage{[ 66, 22, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X791FADD278A2F32F}{}
{
  The operations \texttt{LaurentPolynomialByCoefficients} (\ref{LaurentPolynomialByCoefficients}), \texttt{PolynomialByExtRep} (\ref{PolynomialByExtRep}) and \texttt{RationalFunctionByExtRep} (\ref{RationalFunctionByExtRep}) are used to construct objects in the three basic representations for rational
functions. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RationalFunctionByExtRep}}
\logpage{[ 66, 22, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X81297E4587A9F2A6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RationalFunctionByExtRep({\mdseries\slshape rfam, num, den})\index{RationalFunctionByExtRep@\texttt{RationalFunctionByExtRep}}
\label{RationalFunctionByExtRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RationalFunctionByExtRepNC({\mdseries\slshape rfam, num, den})\index{RationalFunctionByExtRepNC@\texttt{RationalFunctionByExtRepNC}}
\label{RationalFunctionByExtRepNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 constructs a rational function (in the representation \texttt{IsRationalFunctionDefaultRep} (\ref{IsRationalFunctionDefaultRep})) in the rational function family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rfam}}, the rational function itself is given by the external representations \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape num}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape den}} for numerator and denominator. No cancellation takes place. 

 The variant \texttt{RationalFunctionByExtRepNC} does not perform any test of the arguments and thus potentially can create
illegal objects. It only should be used if speed is required and the arguments
are known to be in correct form. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{PolynomialByExtRep}}
\logpage{[ 66, 22, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X79E445AF7849F48A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PolynomialByExtRep({\mdseries\slshape rfam, extrep})\index{PolynomialByExtRep@\texttt{PolynomialByExtRep}}
\label{PolynomialByExtRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{PolynomialByExtRepNC({\mdseries\slshape rfam, extrep})\index{PolynomialByExtRepNC@\texttt{PolynomialByExtRepNC}}
\label{PolynomialByExtRepNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 constructs a polynomial (in the representation \texttt{IsPolynomialDefaultRep} (\ref{IsPolynomialDefaultRep})) in the rational function family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rfam}}, the polynomial itself is given by the external representation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape extrep}}. 

 The variant \texttt{PolynomialByExtRepNC} does not perform any test of the arguments and thus potentially can create
invalid objects. It only should be used if speed is required and the arguments
are known to be in correct form. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@fam:=RationalFunctionsFamily(FamilyObj(1));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@p:=PolynomialByExtRep(fam,[[1,2],1,[2,1,15,7],3]);|
  3*y*x_15^7+x^2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@q:=p/(p+1);|
  (3*y*x_15^7+x^2)/(3*y*x_15^7+x^2+1)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ExtRepNumeratorRatFun(q);|
  [ [ 1, 2 ], 1, [ 2, 1, 15, 7 ], 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ExtRepDenominatorRatFun(q);|
  [ [  ], 1, [ 1, 2 ], 1, [ 2, 1, 15, 7 ], 3 ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LaurentPolynomialByExtRep}}
\logpage{[ 66, 22, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7E2A46D68472F492}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LaurentPolynomialByExtRep({\mdseries\slshape fam, cofs, val, ind})\index{LaurentPolynomialByExtRep@\texttt{LaurentPolynomialByExtRep}}
\label{LaurentPolynomialByExtRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LaurentPolynomialByExtRepNC({\mdseries\slshape fam, cofs, val, ind})\index{LaurentPolynomialByExtRepNC@\texttt{LaurentPolynomialByExtRepNC}}
\label{LaurentPolynomialByExtRepNC}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 creates a Laurent polynomial in the family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}} with [\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cofs}},\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}}] as value of \texttt{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial} (\ref{CoefficientsOfLaurentPolynomial}). No coefficient shifting is performed. This is the lowest level function to
create a Laurent polynomial but will rely on the coefficients being shifted
properly and will not perform any tests. Unless this is guaranteed for the
parameters, \texttt{LaurentPolynomialByCoefficients} (\ref{LaurentPolynomialByCoefficients}) should be used. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Arithmetic for External Representations of Polynomials}}\label{Arithmetic for External Representations of Polynomials}
\logpage{[ 66, 23, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X809028CD7C0EA7CE}{}
{
  The following operations are used internally to perform the arithmetic for
polynomials in their ``external'' representation (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{The Defining Attributes of Rational Functions}) as lists. 

 Functions to perform arithmetic with the coefficient lists of Laurent
polynomials are described in Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Coefficient List Arithmetic}. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ZippedSum}}
\logpage{[ 66, 23, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X855094857A78ABF9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZippedSum({\mdseries\slshape z1, z2, czero, funcs})\index{ZippedSum@\texttt{ZippedSum}}
\label{ZippedSum}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 computes the sum of two external representations of polynomials \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z1}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z2}}. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape czero}} is the appropriate coefficient zero and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape funcs}} a list [ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape monomial{\textunderscore}less}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coefficient{\textunderscore}sum}} ] containing a monomial comparison and a coefficient addition function. This
list can be found in the component \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}}\texttt{!.zippedSum} of the rational functions family. 

 Note that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coefficient{\textunderscore}sum}} must be a proper ``summation'' function, not a function computing differences. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ZippedProduct}}
\logpage{[ 66, 23, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B911136782F0F6D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ZippedProduct({\mdseries\slshape z1, z2, czero, funcs})\index{ZippedProduct@\texttt{ZippedProduct}}
\label{ZippedProduct}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 computes the product of two external representations of polynomials \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z1}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape z2}}. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape czero}} is the appropriate coefficient zero and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape funcs}} a list [ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape monomial{\textunderscore}prod}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape monomial{\textunderscore}less}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coefficient{\textunderscore}sum}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape coefficient{\textunderscore}prod}}] containing functions to multiply and compare monomials, to add and to
multiply coefficients. This list can be found in the component \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}}!.zippedProduct} of the rational functions family. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{QuotientPolynomialsExtRep}}
\logpage{[ 66, 23, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87E5EB8985AF04CD}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{QuotientPolynomialsExtRep({\mdseries\slshape fam, a, b})\index{QuotientPolynomialsExtRep@\texttt{QuotientPolynomialsExtRep}}
\label{QuotientPolynomialsExtRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape a}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape b}} the external representations of two polynomials in the rational functions
family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}}. This function computes the external representation of the quotient of both
polynomials, it returns \texttt{fail} if the polynomial described by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape b}} does not divide the polynomial described by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape a}}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Cancellation Tests for Rational Functions}}\label{Cancellation Tests for Rational Functions}
\logpage{[ 66, 24, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X811B7D8E79E4BD46}{}
{
  The operation \texttt{Gcd} (\ref{Gcd:for (a ring and) several elements}) can be used to test for common factors of two polynomials. This however would
be too expensive to be done in the arithmetic, thus uses the following
operations internally to try to keep the denominators as small as possible 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RationalFunctionByExtRepWithCancellation}}
\logpage{[ 66, 24, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X878A1AC87B492E3D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RationalFunctionByExtRepWithCancellation({\mdseries\slshape rfam, num, den})\index{RationalFunctionByExtRepWithCancellation@\texttt{Rational}\-\texttt{Function}\-\texttt{By}\-\texttt{Ext}\-\texttt{Rep}\-\texttt{With}\-\texttt{Cancellation}}
\label{RationalFunctionByExtRepWithCancellation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 constructs a rational function as \texttt{RationalFunctionByExtRep} (\ref{RationalFunctionByExtRep}) does but tries to cancel out common factors of numerator and denominator,
calling \texttt{TryGcdCancelExtRepPolynomials} (\ref{TryGcdCancelExtRepPolynomials}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TryGcdCancelExtRepPolynomials}}
\logpage{[ 66, 24, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BFB55887A153003}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TryGcdCancelExtRepPolynomials({\mdseries\slshape fam, a, b})\index{TryGcdCancelExtRepPolynomials@\texttt{TryGcdCancelExtRepPolynomials}}
\label{TryGcdCancelExtRepPolynomials}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Let \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape a}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape b}} be the external representations of two polynomials. This function tries to
