\item  starting \textsf{GAP} with no packages (except needed for \textsf{GAP}) using \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r \texttt{\symbol{45}}A} options and calling \texttt{LoadPackage("packagename");} 
\item  starting \textsf{GAP} with no packages (except needed for \textsf{GAP}) using \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r \texttt{\symbol{45}}A} options and calling \texttt{LoadPackage("packagename" : OnlyNeeded );} 
\item  starting \textsf{GAP} in the default configuration (with no options) and calling \texttt{LoadPackage("packagename");} 
\item  starting \textsf{GAP} in the default configuration (with no options) and calling \texttt{LoadPackage("packagename" : OnlyNeeded );} 
\item  finally, together with all other packages using \texttt{LoadAllPackages} (\ref{LoadAllPackages}) (see below) in four possible combinations of starting \textsf{GAP} with/without \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r \texttt{\symbol{45}}A} options and calling \texttt{LoadAllPackages} (\ref{LoadAllPackages}) with/without \texttt{reversed} option. 
\end{itemize}
 The test of loading all packages is the most subtle one. Quite often it
reveals problems which do not occur in the default configuration but may cause
difficulties to the users of specialised packages. 

 Additionally, we recommend using \texttt{ShowPackageVariables} (\ref{ShowPackageVariables}) to see information about variables created by your package to check if any
have either short names (no more than three characters) or names breaking a
recommended naming convention that the \textsf{GAP} core system. \textsf{GAP} packages also should not use global variables starting in the lowercase (see
Section \ref{Functions and Variables and Choices of Their Names}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{LoadAllPackages}}
\logpage{[ 76, 20, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80A0D21D78CF8494}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LoadAllPackages({\mdseries\slshape : reversed})\index{LoadAllPackages@\texttt{LoadAllPackages}}
\label{LoadAllPackages}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 loads all \textsf{GAP} packages from their list sorted in alphabetical order (needed and suggested
packages will be loaded when required). This is a technical function to check
packages compatibility, so it should NOT be used to run anything except tests;
it is known that \textsf{GAP} performance is slower if all packages are loaded. To introduce some variations
of the order in which packages will be loaded for testing purposes, \texttt{LoadAllPackages} accepts option \texttt{reversed} to load packages from their list sorted in the reverse alphabetical order. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Testing a \textsf{GAP} package with the \textsf{GAP} standard test suite}}\label{Testing a GAP package with the GAP standard test suite}
\logpage{[ 76, 20, 4 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7C90C8B87BF6EF0B}{}
{
  The \texttt{tst} directory of the \textsf{GAP} installation contains a selection of test files and scripts such as \texttt{testinstall.g} and \texttt{teststandard.g} which are a part of the \textsf{GAP} standard test suite. 

 It is important to check that your package does not break \textsf{GAP} standard tests. To perform a clean test and avoid interfering with other
packages, first you must start a new \textsf{GAP} session and then read either \texttt{testinstall.g} or \texttt{teststandard.g} as demonstrated below. 

 The quicker test, \texttt{testinstall.g}, should run in about a minute depending on your hardware speed. It may be
started with the command 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Read( Filename( DirectoriesLibrary( "tst" ), "testinstall.g" ) );|
\end{Verbatim}
 You will get a large number of lines with output about the progress of the
tests, for example: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  You should start GAP4 using `gap -A -x 80 -r'.
  
  Architecture: SOMETHING-SOMETHING-gcc-default64
  
  testing: ..../gap-4.X.Y/tst/testinstall/alghom.tst
        84 ms (55 ms GC) and 2.90MB allocated for alghom.tst
  testing: ..../gap-4.X.Y/tst/testinstall/algmat.tst
       839 ms (114 ms GC) and 219MB allocated for algmat.tst
  [ further lines deleted ]
  testing: ..../gap-4.X.Y/tst/testinstall/zmodnze.tst
       127 ms (119 ms GC) and 1.29MB allocated for zmodnze.tst
  -----------------------------------
  total     62829 ms (24136 ms GC) and 8.61GB allocated
                0 failures in 252 files
  
  #I  No errors detected while testing
\end{Verbatim}
 

 (optionally, you may start \textsf{GAP} with the command line options which you will see in the test output, to run it
in a more conservative settings). 

 The more thorough test is \texttt{teststandard.g} which exercises more of \textsf{GAP}'s capabilities, also including all test files from \texttt{teststandard.g}. It runs quite a bit longer, maybe 10\texttt{\symbol{45}}20 minutes, and
produces an output similar to the testinstall.g test. To run it, also start a
new \textsf{GAP} session and then call 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Read( Filename( DirectoriesLibrary( "tst" ), "teststandard.g" ) );|
\end{Verbatim}
 You may repeat the same check loading your package with \texttt{OnlyNeeded} option. Remember to perform each subsequent test in a new \textsf{GAP} session. 

 Also you may perform individual tests from the \texttt{tst} directory of the \textsf{GAP} installation loading them with \texttt{Test} (\ref{Test}). 

 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Access to the \textsf{GAP} Development Version}}\label{Access to the GAP Development Version}
\logpage{[ 76, 21, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81B52B657CA75BDA}{}
{
  We are aiming at providing a stable platform for package development and
testing with official \textsf{GAP} releases. We also invite everyone to contribute by submitting patches, pull
requests, and bug reports. We would like to make the contributing process as
easy as possible. 

 The main GAP development repository is hosted on GitHub at \href{https://github.com/gap-system/gap} {\texttt{https://github.com/gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system/gap}}. Many \textsf{GAP} packages also have public repositories and issue trackers, and we are keeping
a list of such packages at \href{https://gap-packages.github.io/} {\texttt{https://gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}packages.github.io/}}. 

 For further information about contributing to the GAP development, please see \href{https://github.com/gap-system/gap/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md} {\texttt{https://github.com/gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system/gap/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md}}. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Version control and continuous integration for \textsf{GAP} packages}}\label{Version control and continuous integration for GAP packages}
\logpage{[ 76, 22, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X836CDF8F7A846A1C}{}
{
  As we have mentioned above, many \textsf{GAP} packages have public repositories and issue trackers on GitHub, and we are
keeping a list of such packages at \href{https://gap-packages.github.io/} {\texttt{https://gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}packages.github.io/}}. We welcome establishing public repositories for new packages and migrating
existing package repositories there as well. Such repositories may be hosted
under their authors' accounts or under the gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}packages
organisation (\href{https://github.com/gap-packages/} {\texttt{https://github.com/gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}packages/}}). The latter has the benefit that while the authors will preserve their
deciding role on all aspects of the package development, the package will
become more visible for potential collaborators and \textsf{GAP} developers may help to set up \emph{continuous integration} for your package so that every commit to the repository will trigger automated
running of package tests and reporting any failures to package maintainers. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Selecting a license for a \textsf{GAP} Package}}\label{Selecting a license for a GAP Package}
\logpage{[ 76, 23, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X82EBCBC5829B6001}{}
{
  As it was mentioned in the description of the \texttt{LICENSE} file in Section \ref{Structure of a GAP Package}, it is advised to make clear in the documentation of the package the basis on
which it is being distributed to users. \textsf{GAP} itself is distributed under the GNU Public License version 2 (version 2 or
later). We would encourage you to consider the GPL license for your packages,
but you might wish to be more restrictive (for instance forbidding
redistribution for profit) or less restrictive (allowing your software to be
incorporated into commercial software). See ``Choosing a License for the Distribution of Your Package'' from \href{https://www.gap-system.org/Packages/Authors/authors.html} {\texttt{https://www.gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system.org/Packages/Authors/authors.html}} and also \href{https://choosealicense.com/} {\texttt{https://choosealicense.com/}} for further details. 

 In the past many \textsf{GAP} packages used the text ``We adopt the copyright regulations of \textsf{GAP} as detailed in the copyright notice in the \textsf{GAP} manual'' or a similar statement. We now advise to be more explicit by making the exact
reference to the GPL license, for example: 

 \emph{ \textsf{packagename} is free software; you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms of
the \href{https://www.fsf.org/licenses/gpl.html} {GNU General Public License} as published by the Free Software Foundation; either version 2 of the License,
or (at your option) any later version. } and also including a copy of the full text of the license. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Releasing a GAP Package}}\label{Releasing a GAP Package}
\logpage{[ 76, 24, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8074AAAE79911BE5}{}
{
  The \textsf{GAP} distribution provides archives in several different formats. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{.tar.gz}}]  a standard UNIX \texttt{tar} archive, compressed with \texttt{gzip} 
\item[{\texttt{.tar.bz2}}]  a standard UNIX \texttt{tar} archive, compressed with \texttt{bzip2} 
\item[{\texttt{.zip}}]  an archive in \texttt{zip} format, where text files should have UNIX style line breaks 
\end{description}
 

 For convenience of possible users it is sensible that you provide an archive
of your package in at least one of these formats. 

 For example, if you wish to supply a \texttt{.tar.gz} archive, you may create it with the command 

 {\nobreakspace}\texttt{tar \texttt{\symbol{45}}cvzf packagename\texttt{\symbol{45}}version.tar.gz
packagename} 

 \noindent Because the release of the \textsf{GAP} package is independent of the version of \textsf{GAP}, a \textsf{GAP} package should be wrapped up in separate file that can be installed onto any
version of \textsf{GAP}. In this way, a package can be upgraded any time without the need to wait for
new \textsf{GAP} releases. To ensure this, the package should be archived from the \textsf{GAP} \texttt{pkg} directory, that is all files are archived with the path starting at the
package's name. 

 \index{GAPDocManualLab@\texttt{GAPDocManualLab}} The archive of a \textsf{GAP} package should contain all files necessary for the package to work. In
particular there should be a compiled documentation, which includes the \texttt{manual.six}, \texttt{manual.toc} and \texttt{manual.lab} file in the documentation subdirectory which are created by \textsf{GAPDoc} while {\TeX}ing the documentation. (The first two files are needed by the \textsf{GAP} help system, and the \texttt{manual.lab} file is needed if the main manuals or another package is referring to your
package. Use the command \texttt{GAPDocManualLab( packagename );} to create this file for your help books if you use \textsf{GAPDoc}.) 

 Note that wrapping the \textsf{GAP} distribution as a single archive containing the core system and all currently
redistributed packages, will change file timestamps, so one should not rely on
them anywhere in the package. 

 For packages hosted on GitHub publishing package release and establishing its
website can be very efficiently automated using two tools: ReleaseTools (\href{https://github.com/gap-system/ReleaseTools} {\texttt{https://github.com/gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system/ReleaseTools}}) and GitHubPagesForGAP (\href{https://github.com/gap-system/GitHubPagesForGAP} {\texttt{https://github.com/gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system/GitHubPagesForGAP}}). }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{The homepage of a Package}}\label{The homepage of a Package}
\logpage{[ 76, 25, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8232CC1385C4B1DD}{}
{
  If you want to distribute your package you should create its homepage
containing some basic information, archives for download, the \texttt{README} file with installation instructions, and a copy of the package's \texttt{PackageInfo.g} file. 

 The responsibility to maintain this homepage is with the package
authors/maintainers. 

 If you tell the \textsf{GAP} Group about your package (say, by mail to \href{mailto://support@gap-system.org} {\texttt{support@gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system.org}}) we may consider either 
\begin{itemize}
\item  adding a link to your package homepage from the \textsf{GAP} website (thus, the package will be an \emph{undeposited contribution}); 
\item  or redistributing the current version of your package as a part of the \textsf{GAP} distribution (this, the package will be \emph{deposited}), also ; 
\end{itemize}
 Please also consider submitting your package to the \textsf{GAP} package refereeing process (see \href{https://www.gap-system.org/Contacts/submit.html} {\texttt{https://www.gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system.org/Contacts/submit.html}} for further information). 

 For packages hosted on GitHub publishing package release and establishing its
website can be very efficiently automated using two tools: GitHubPagesForGAP (\href{https://github.com/gap-system/GitHubPagesForGAP} {\texttt{https://github.com/gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system/GitHubPagesForGAP}}) and ReleaseTools (\href{https://github.com/gap-system/ReleaseTools} {\texttt{https://github.com/gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system/ReleaseTools}}). }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Some things to keep in mind}}\label{Some things to keep in mind}
\logpage{[ 76, 26, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X796D7F7583E845BE}{}
{
  
\begin{itemize}
\item  Some packages still use for their manuals the old ``gapmacro'' format, support for which may be discontinued in the future. We encourage
authors of those packages to eventually convert their documentation \textsf{GAPDoc}. New packages are recommended to use \textsf{GAPDoc}, which, for example, is capable of creating HTML documentation with MathJax
support, allows easy extraction of examples from documentation for testing,
etc. One could also use the \textsf{AutoDoc} which simplifies writing documentation by generating most of the \textsf{GAPDoc} code automatically. 
\item  The concept of an autoloaded package, which existed before \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4.5, has been integrated with the \emph{needed} and \emph{suggested} mechanism that exists between packages. \textsf{GAP} itself now ``needs'' certain packages (for instance \textsf{GAPDoc}) and ``suggests'' others (typically the packages that were autoloaded). The decisions which
packages \textsf{GAP} should need or suggest are made by developers based on technical criteria.
They can be easily overridden by a user using the new \texttt{gap.ini} (see \ref{sect:gap.ini}). The default file ensures that all formerly autoloaded packages are still
loaded if present. 
\item  Optional \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{126}}/.gap} directory for user's customisations which may contain e.g. locally installed
packages (see \ref{GAP Root Directories}). If package installation instructions explain how to install the package in
a non\texttt{\symbol{45}}standard location, they should mention this. 
\item  Packages loading mechanism allows to make loading packages more informative,
while avoiding confusing the user with warning and error messages for packages
they didn't know they were loading. For example, many messages are stored but
not displayed using the function \texttt{LogPackageLoadingMessage} (\ref{LogPackageLoadingMessage}) and there is a function \texttt{DisplayPackageLoadingLog} (\ref{DisplayPackageLoadingLog}) to show log messages that occur during package loading. Packages are
encouraged to use these mechanisms to report problems in loading (e.g.
binaries not compiled), rather than printing messages directly. 
\end{itemize}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Package release checklists}}\label{Package release checklists}
\logpage{[ 76, 27, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X82CE0A518440CCBB}{}
{
  The following checklists should be useful to package authors and maintainers,
as well as to everyone involved in the depositing and refereeing of \textsf{GAP} packages. 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Checklist for releasing a new package}}\label{Checklist for releasing a new package}
\logpage{[ 76, 27, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X80E3926A7CF8B6DC}{}
{
  
\begin{itemize}
\item  Test that the package: 
\begin{itemize}
\item  does not break \texttt{testinstall.g} and \texttt{teststandard.g}, and does not slow them down noticeably (see \ref{Testing a GAP package with the GAP standard test suite}); 
\item  may be loaded in various configurations (see \ref{Testing GAP package loading}); 
\item  follows the guidelines of Section \ref{Functions and Variables and Choices of Their Names} about names of functions and variables; 
\end{itemize}
 
\item  \texttt{PackageInfo.g} file: 
\begin{itemize}
\item  correctly specifies package version, release date, and package authors; 
\item  passes validation using \texttt{ValidatePackageInfo} (\ref{ValidatePackageInfo}); 
\item  besides mandatory components, which are required to pass validation, also has
relevant optional components (such as, for example, URLs of public source code
repository and issue tracker; hints to distinguish binary and text files in
case of non\texttt{\symbol{45}}standard file names and extensions, etc.); 
\end{itemize}
 
\item  Package documentation: 
\begin{itemize}
\item  is built and included in the package archive together with its source files; 
\item  states the same version, release date and package authors as specified in the \texttt{PackageInfo.g} file; 
\item  has the same version, release date and package authors details as stated in
the \texttt{PackageInfo.g} file; 
\item  is searchable using the \textsf{GAP} help system in all formats (text, HTML and PDF); 
\item  is clear about the license under which the package is distributed, and refers
to the \texttt{LICENSE} file which should be included in the package; 
\end{itemize}
 
\item  Package archive(s): 
\begin{itemize}
\item  have correct permissions for all files and directories after their unpacking
(755 for directories and executables, if any; 644 for other files); 
\item  contain files with correct line breaks for the given format (see Section \ref{Releasing a GAP Package}); 
\item  contain no hidden system files and directories that are not supposed to be
included in the package, e.g. \texttt{.gitignore}, \texttt{.git} etc.; 
\end{itemize}
 
\item  Package availability: 
\begin{itemize}
\item  not only the package archive(s), but also the \texttt{PackageInfo.g} and \texttt{README} files are available online; 
\end{itemize}
 
\end{itemize}
 }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Checklist for upgrading the package for the next major release of \textsf{GAP}}}\label{Checklist for upgrading the package for the next major release of GAP}
\logpage{[ 76, 27, 2 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X820D4B207A41AEA6}{}
{
  \textsf{GAP} ecosystem is not static: both the core \textsf{GAP} system and packages redistributed with \textsf{GAP} are in constant development. \textsf{GAP} has a policy that changes that may have a disruptive effect on packages
redistributed with \textsf{GAP} should only be introduced in major \textsf{GAP} releases. When the next \textsf{GAP} major release is prepared, a beta version for package authors will be made
available in order to give them an opportunity to check and update, if
necessary, their packages for the public release of the next major version of \textsf{GAP}. 

 The following checklist will help you to check how well your package is ready
to work with the next major release of \textsf{GAP} 

 
\begin{itemize}
\item  Check that the package functionality works as expected, package tests run with
no discrepancies, and manual examples correspond to new version of \textsf{GAP}. This is a convenient opportunity to polish existing and add new tests, and
improve manual examples. 
\item  Revise package dependencies: check that the \texttt{PackageInfo.g} file has correct list of needed and suggested packages (see Section \ref{Package dependencies}). 
\item  Revise licensing information: check that the package states clearly under
which conditions it is distributed and includes a \texttt{LICENSING} file with the text of a license (see Section \ref{Selecting a license for a GAP Package}). 
\item  Rebuild the package documentation to update
cross\texttt{\symbol{45}}references to main \textsf{GAP} manuals and, if relevant, to the documentation of other \textsf{GAP} packages. This will ensure that cross\texttt{\symbol{45}}references from the
package manual to the main \textsf{GAP} manuals are correct and that the \textsf{GAP} help system will be able to navigate to the more precise location in the
package manual. This will also improve the layout of the package documentation
by picking up the changes in documenting tools. 
\item  Check if the package still relies on some obsolete variables (see Chapter \ref{Replaced and Removed Command Names}) and replace their usage by the new commands. To perform such check, start \textsf{GAP} with `\texttt{\symbol{45}}O` command line option to disable loading obsoletes,
and then load your package. 
\item  Check for any specific advice in release notes for the beta release for
package authors. 
\end{itemize}
 }

 }

 }

       
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Replaced and Removed Command Names}}\label{Replaced and Removed Command Names}
\logpage{[ 77, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X78C85ED17F00DCC1}{}
{
  \index{obsolete} \index{deprecated} \index{legacy} In general we try to keep \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4 compatible with former releases as much as possible.
Nevertheless, from time to time it seems appropriate to remove some commands
or to change the names of some commands or variables. There are various
reasons for that: Some functionality was improved and got another (hopefully
better) interface, names turned out to be too special or too general for the
underlying functionality, or names are found to be unintuitive or inconsistent
with other names. 

 In this chapter we collect such old names while pointing to the sections which
explain how to substitute them. Usually, old names will be available for
several releases; they may be removed when they don't seem to be used any
more. 

 Information about obsolete names is printed by \texttt{Info} (\ref{Info}) using the \texttt{InfoObsolete} (\ref{InfoObsolete}) Info class. By default \texttt{InfoObsolete} (\ref{InfoObsolete}) is set to 1. Newly obsoleted identifiers should at first be outputted at info
level 2. Once they have been removed from all packages, they should then be
moved to info level 1, so they are visible to normal users, for at least one
major release before being removed. 

 The functions \texttt{DeclareObsoleteSynonym} and \texttt{DeclareObsoleteSynonymAttr} take an optional final parameter, specifying the info level at which the given
obsolete symbol should be reported. It defaults to 2 and 1, respectively. 

 The obsolete \textsf{GAP} code is collected in two library files, \texttt{lib/obsolete.gd} and \texttt{lib/obsolete.gi}. By default, these files are read when \textsf{GAP} is started. It may be useful to omit reading these files, for example in order
to make sure that one's own \textsf{GAP} code does not rely on the obsolete variables. For that, one can use the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}O} command line option (see \ref{Command Line Options}) or set the user preference \texttt{ReadObsolete} in the file \texttt{gap.ini} to \texttt{false} (see \ref{sect:gap.ini}). Note that the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}O} command line option overrides \texttt{ReadObsolete}. 

 (Note that the condition whether the library files with the obsolete \textsf{GAP} code shall be read has changed. In \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4.3 and 4.4, the global variables \texttt{GAP{\textunderscore}OBSOLESCENT} and \texttt{GAPInfo.ReadObsolete} {\textendash}to be set in the user's \texttt{.gaprc} file{\textendash} were used to control this behaviour.)  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Group Actions {\textendash} Name Changes}}\label{Group Actions - Name Changes}
\logpage{[ 77, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7AA51AC9870D2360}{}
{
  \index{group operations} The concept of a group action is sometimes referred to as a ``group operation''. In \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}3 as well as in older versions of \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4 the term \texttt{Operation} was used instead of \texttt{Action}. We decided to change the names to avoid confusion with the term ``operation'' as in \texttt{DeclareOperation} (\ref{DeclareOperation}) and ``operations for Xyz''. 

 Here are some examples of such name changes. 

 \begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{l|l}\emph{OLD}&
\emph{NOW USE}\\
\hline
\texttt{Operation}\index{Operation@\texttt{Operation}}&
\texttt{Action} (\ref{Action:for a group, an action domain, etc.})\\
\texttt{RepresentativeOperation}\index{RepresentativeOperation@\texttt{RepresentativeOperation}}&
\texttt{RepresentativeAction} (\ref{RepresentativeAction})\\
\texttt{OperationHomomorphism}\index{OperationHomomorphism@\texttt{OperationHomomorphism}}&
\texttt{ActionHomomorphism} (\ref{ActionHomomorphism:for a group, an action domain, etc.})\\
\texttt{FunctionOperation}\index{FunctionOperation@\texttt{FunctionOperation}}&
\texttt{FunctionAction} (\ref{FunctionAction})\\
\texttt{IsLexicographicallyLess}\index{IsLexicographicallyLess@\texttt{IsLexicographicallyLess}}&
\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}} (\ref{bSlash<})\\
\end{tabular}\\[2mm]

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Package Interface {\textendash} Obsolete Functions and Name Changes}}\label{Package Interface - Obsolete Functions and Name Changes}
\logpage{[ 77, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X831734077B00CB3B}{}
{
  With \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4.4 the package interface was changed. Thereby some functions
became obsolete and the names of some others were made more consistent. 

 \index{DeclarePackage@\texttt{DeclarePackage}} \index{DeclareAutoPackage@\texttt{DeclareAutoPackage}} \index{DeclarePackageDocumentation@\texttt{DeclarePackageDocumentation}} \index{DeclarePackageAutoDocumentation@\texttt{DeclarePackageAutoDocumentation}} The following functions are no longer needed: \texttt{DeclarePackage}, \texttt{DeclareAutoPackage}, \texttt{DeclarePackageDocumentation} and \texttt{DeclarePackageAutoDocumentation}. They are substituted by entries in the packages' \texttt{PackageInfo.g} files, see \ref{The PackageInfo.g File}. 

 Furthermore, the global variable \texttt{PACKAGES{\textunderscore}VERSIONS} is no longer needed, since this information is now contained in the \texttt{GAPInfo.PackagesInfo} record (see \ref{GAPInfo}). The global variable \texttt{Revisions} is also no longer needed, since the function \texttt{DisplayRevision} was made obsolete in \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4.5 and removed in \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4.7. 

 The following function names were changed. 

 \index{RequirePackage@\texttt{RequirePackage}} \index{ReadPkg@\texttt{ReadPkg}} \index{RereadPkg@\texttt{RereadPkg}} \begin{center}

\emph{NOW USE}\\
\hline
\texttt{RequirePackage}&
\texttt{LoadPackage} (\ref{LoadPackage})\\
\texttt{ReadPkg}&
\texttt{ReadPackage} (\ref{ReadPackage})\\
\texttt{RereadPkg}&
\texttt{RereadPackage} (\ref{RereadPackage})\\
\end{tabular}\\[2mm]
\end{center}

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Normal Forms of Integer Matrices {\textendash} Name Changes}}\label{Normal Forms of Integer Matrices - Name Changes}
\logpage{[ 77, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79676CD27EF0F096}{}
{
  \index{Smith normal form} \index{Hermite normal form} Former versions of \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4 documented several functions for computing the Smith or
Hermite normal form of integer matrices. Some of them were never implemented
and it was unclear which commands to use. The functionality of all of these

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InfoObsolete}}
\logpage{[ 77, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87348614848EAD64}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InfoObsolete\index{InfoObsolete@\texttt{InfoObsolete}}
\label{InfoObsolete}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (info class)}}\\


 is an info class to display warnings when an obsolete variable is used. By
default, the info level for this class is set to 1, which will only show
variables which will be removed in the next major version of GAP. Setting it
to 2 will trigger further warnings, for variables which have alternative
names, or may be removed in future. This class can be set to 0 to disable all
obsolete warnings. 

 To check that the \textsf{GAP} code does not use any obsolete variables at parsing time, and not at a
runtime, use the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}O} command line option, see \ref{Command Line Options}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{The former .gaprc file}}\label{obsolete-gaprc}
\logpage{[ 77, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7F2FF72A7AD60E0C}{}
{
  Up to \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4.4, a file \texttt{.gaprc} in the user's home directory (if available, and \textsf{GAP} was started without \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r} option) was read automatically during startup, early enough for influencing
the autoloading of packages and late enough for being allowed to execute any \textsf{GAP} code. On Windows machines this file was called \texttt{gap.rc}. 

 In \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4.5 the startup mechanism has changed, see \ref{sect:gap.ini} for details. These new configuration files are now contained in a directory \texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot}. 

 For the sake of partial backwards compatibility, also the former file \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{126}}/.gaprc} is still supported for such initializations, but this file is read only if the
directory \texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot} does not exist. In that case the \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{126}}/.gaprc} is read at the same time as \texttt{gaprc} would be read, i.{\nobreakspace}e., too late for influencing the startup of \textsf{GAP}. 

 As before, the command line option \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}r} disables reading \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{126}}/.gaprc}, see \ref{Command Line Options}. 

 To migrate from the old setup to the new one introduced with \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}4.5, first have a look at the function \texttt{WriteGapIniFile} (\ref{WriteGapIniFile}). Many users will find that all or most of what was set in the old \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{126}}/.gaprc} file can now be done via the user preferences in a \texttt{gap.ini} file. If you had code for new functions or abbreviations in your old \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{126}}/.gaprc} file or you were reading additional files, then move this into the file \texttt{gaprc} (without the leading dot, same name for all operating systems) in the
directory \texttt{GAPInfo.UserGapRoot}. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Semigroup properties}}\label{obsolete-semigroups-properties}
\logpage{[ 77, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7C89E03285799F40}{}
{
  Until Version 4.8 of \textsf{GAP} there was inconsistent use of the following properties of semigroups: \texttt{IsGroupAsSemigroup}, \texttt{IsMonoidAsSemigroup}, and \texttt{IsSemilatticeAsSemigroup}. \texttt{IsGroupAsSemigroup} was true for semigroups that mathematically defined a group, and for
semigroups in the category \texttt{IsGroup} (\ref{IsGroup}); \texttt{IsMonoidAsSemigroup} was true for semigroups that mathematically defined monoids, but did not
belong to the category \texttt{IsMonoid} (\ref{IsMonoid}); and \texttt{IsSemilatticeAsSemigroup} was simply a property of semigroups, there is no category \texttt{IsSemilattice}. 

 From Version 4.8 onwards, \texttt{IsMonoidAsSemigroup} returns \texttt{true} for semigroups in the category \texttt{IsMonoid} (\ref{IsMonoid}), and \texttt{IsSemilatticeAsSemigroup} has been moved to the \textsf{Semigroups} under the new name \texttt{IsSemilattice} (\textbf{Semigroups: IsSemilattice}). }

 }

        
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Method Selection}}\label{Method Selection}
\logpage{[ 78, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8058CC8187162644}{}
{
  \index{operation}\index{method} This chapter explains how \textsf{GAP} decides which function to call for which types of objects. It assumes that you
have read the chapters about objects (Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Objects and Elements}) and types (Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Types of Objects}). 

 An \emph{operation} is a special \textsf{GAP} function that bundles a set of functions, its \emph{methods}. 

 All methods of an operation compute the same result. But each method is
installed for specific types of arguments. 

 If an operation is called with a tuple of arguments, one of the applicable
methods is selected and called. 

 Special cases of methods are partial methods, immediate methods, and logical
implications.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Operations and Methods}}\label{Operations and Methods}
\logpage{[ 78, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7AEED9AB824CD4DA}{}
{
  

 Operations are functions in the category \texttt{IsOperation} (\ref{IsOperation}). 

 So on the one hand, \emph{operations} are \textsf{GAP} functions, that is, they can be applied to arguments and return a result or
cause a side\texttt{\symbol{45}}effect. 

 On the other hand, operations are more. Namely, an operation corresponds to a
set of \textsf{GAP} functions, called the \emph{methods} of the operation. 

 Each call of an operation causes a suitable method to be selected and then
called. The choice of which method to select is made according to the types of
the arguments, the underlying mechanism is described in the following
sections. 

 Examples of operations are the binary infix operators \texttt{=}, \texttt{+} etc., and \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}) is the operation that is called for each argument of \texttt{Print} (\ref{Print}). 

 Also all attributes and properties are operations. Each attribute has a
special method which is called if the attribute value is already stored; this
method of course simply returns this value. 

 The setter of an attribute is called automatically if an attribute value has
been computed. Attribute setters are operations, too. They have a default
method that ignores the request to store the value. Depending on the type of
the object, there may be another method to store the value in a suitable way,
and then set the attribute tester for the object to \texttt{true}. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsOperation}}
\logpage{[ 78, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X874C7C6D8650D648}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsOperation({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsOperation@\texttt{IsOperation}}
\label{IsOperation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (Category)}}\\


 is the category of operations. Every operation is a function, but not vice
versa. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MinimalPolynomial;|
  <Operation "MinimalPolynomial">
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsOperation(MinimalPolynomial);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsFunction(MinimalPolynomial);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Factorial;|
  function( n ) ... end
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsOperation(Factorial);|
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TypeOfOperation}}
\logpage{[ 78, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X813BE52887A3E0FA}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TypeOfOperation({\mdseries\slshape object})\index{TypeOfOperation@\texttt{TypeOfOperation}}
\label{TypeOfOperation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 returns a string from the list \texttt{[ "Attribute", "Operation", "Property", "Category", "Representation",
"Filter", "Setter"]} reflecting which type of operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape op}} is. 

 (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Categories}, \ref{Representation}, \ref{Attributes}, \ref{Setter and Tester for Attributes}, \ref{Properties}, \ref{Other Filters}) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ShowDeclarationsOfOperation}}
\logpage{[ 78, 1, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X838E29D485D2BAB9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ShowDeclarationsOfOperation({\mdseries\slshape oper})\index{ShowDeclarationsOfOperation@\texttt{ShowDeclarationsOfOperation}}
\label{ShowDeclarationsOfOperation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Displays information about all declarations of the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oper}}, including the location of each declaration and the argument filters. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ShowDeclarationsOfOperation(IsFinite);|
  Available declarations for operation <Property "IsFinite">:
    1: GAPROOT/lib/coll.gd:1451 with 1 argument, and filters [ IsListOrCollection ]
    2: GAPROOT/lib/float.gd:212 with 1 argument, and filters [ IsFloat ]
    3: GAPROOT/lib/ctbl.gd:1195 with 1 argument, and filters [ IsNearlyCharacterTable ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NewOperation}}
\logpage{[ 78, 1, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85A9E019795B79D6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewOperation({\mdseries\slshape name, args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts})\index{NewOperation@\texttt{NewOperation}}
\label{NewOperation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NewOperation} returns an operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}} describes requirements about the arguments of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}, namely the number of arguments must be equal to the length of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}, and the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th argument must lie in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}$[i]$. 

 Each method that is installed for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} via \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) must require that the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th argument lies in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}$[i]$. 

 One can install methods for other argument tuples via \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod}), this way it is also possible to install methods for a different number of
arguments than the length of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareOperation}}
\logpage{[ 78, 1, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X843F48137B899BC3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareOperation({\mdseries\slshape name, filters})\index{DeclareOperation@\texttt{DeclareOperation}}
\label{DeclareOperation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 does the same as \texttt{NewOperation} (\ref{NewOperation}) and then binds the new operation to the global variable \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The variable must previously be writable, and is made
read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only by this function. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Tag Based Operations}}\logpage{[ 78, 1, 6 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X799081B4854DC003}{}
{
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewTagBasedOperation({\mdseries\slshape name, requirements})\index{NewTagBasedOperation@\texttt{NewTagBasedOperation}}
\label{NewTagBasedOperation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareTagBasedOperation({\mdseries\slshape name, requirements})\index{DeclareTagBasedOperation@\texttt{DeclareTagBasedOperation}}
\label{DeclareTagBasedOperation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallTagBasedMethod({\mdseries\slshape oper[, tag], meth})\index{InstallTagBasedMethod@\texttt{InstallTagBasedMethod}}
\label{InstallTagBasedMethod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NewTagBasedOperation} returns an operation with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} that is declared as \emph{tag based} w.r.t. the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape requirements}} of filters for its arguments. If an operation with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} exists already before the call then this operation is returned, otherwise a
new operation gets created. 

 \texttt{DeclareTagBasedOperation} does the same and additionally binds the returned operation to the global
variable \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} if the operation is new. 

 Declaring the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oper}} as tag based w.r.t. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape requirements}} means that \texttt{InstallTagBasedMethod} can be used to install the method \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape meth}} for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oper}}, a function whose arguments satisfy \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape requirements}}, with the following meaning. 

 
\begin{itemize}
\item  The method \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape meth}} is applicable if the first argument of the call to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oper}} is identical (in the sense of \texttt{IsIdenticalObj} (\ref{IsIdenticalObj})) with the tag \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape tag}} that has been specified in the \texttt{InstallTagBasedMethod} call. 
\item  If none of the tag based methods for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oper}} has a \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape tag}} that is identical with the first argument of the call to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oper}} and if there is a tag based method for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oper}} for which no \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape tag}} was specified then this method is applicable. 
\end{itemize}
 

 Thus at most \emph{one} tag based method for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oper}} is applicable, and if a method without \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape tag}} has been installed then it serves as the default method. This is in contrast
to the situation with constructors (see \ref{Constructors}) where the first argument is a filter that is used as a tag, but several
methods can be applicable in a call to a constructor and one cannot define a
default method for it. 

 Typical use cases for tag based operations are operations that shall create
objects in particular internal representations; the filters that define these
representations are then used as the first argument, and one wants that either
the unique method that belongs to this filter or a default method is called. 

 Currently it is possible to declare an operation as tag based only for \emph{one} list of requirements. 

 Installing methods with \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) for a tag based operation is possible. However, installing such methods with
the same requirements as the ones for the tag based methods will have no
effect because the handling of tag based methods gets installed with \texttt{InstallEarlyMethod} (\ref{InstallEarlyMethod}) and thus has higher priority. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Constructors}}\label{Constructors}
\logpage{[ 78, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86EC0F0A78ECBC10}{}
{
  Constructors are a special type of operation used to make new objects. The key
difference compared to regular operations is that method selection works
slightly differently for them: The first argument in a call to a constructor
must always be a filter \ref{Filters}. The result of a method is expected to lie in that filter. Moreover, while
normally method selection matches on the type of each argument, for a
constructor the first argument is treated differently: instead of matching its
type, the argument itself (which is a filter) must be a subset of the filter
specified by the method which is being tested for match. In other words, the
argument filter must imply the method filter. 

 Also, method ranking works differently: instead of the sum of the ranks of the
types of all arguments, only the rank of the filter given as first argument is
considered; and for it, the normal ranking order is reversed. This ensures
that if multiple constructor methods match, the ``most general'' method is selected. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DeclareConstructor("XCons",[IsMagma,IsInt]);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InstallMethod(XCons, [IsGroup, IsInt], function(t,x) return CyclicGroup(x); end);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InstallMethod(XCons, [IsPermGroup, IsInt], function(t,x) return SymmetricGroup(x); end);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InstallMethod(XCons, [IsSemigroup, IsInt], function(t,x) return FullTransformationMonoid(x); end);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@XCons(IsGroup,3);|
  <pc group of size 3 with 1 generator>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@XCons(IsPermGroup,3);|
  Sym( [ 1 .. 3 ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@XCons(IsSemigroup,4);|
  <full transformation monoid of degree 4>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# if multiple methods match, the most general is selected:|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@XCons(IsMagma,3);|
  <full transformation monoid of degree 3>
\end{Verbatim}
 The example above shows some basic examples (usually a constructor will
produce isomorphic objects in different representations, not different objects
as in this case). 

 If no method has been installed which guarantees to produce a suitable
objecty, a "No Method Found" error will be returned. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|XCons(IsFullTransformationMonoid,4);A
  Error, no method found! For debugging hints type ?Recovery from NoMethodFound
  Error, no 1st choice method found for `XCons' on 2 arguments
  called from read-eval loop at *stdin*:8
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop
  @gapbrkprompt|brk>A @gapinput|quit;A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|XCons(IsNilpotentGroup,4);A
  Error, no method found! For debugging hints type ?Recovery from NoMethodFound
  Error, no 1st choice method found for `XCons' on 2 arguments
  called from read-eval loop at *stdin*:8
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop
  @gapbrkprompt|brk>A @gapinput|A
\end{Verbatim}
 Note that in both these cases there are methods that actually produce results
of the required types, but they have not been installed with this information,
so are not selected. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NewConstructor}}
\logpage{[ 78, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X783FA45E7858A8CF}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NewConstructor({\mdseries\slshape name, args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts})\index{NewConstructor@\texttt{NewConstructor}}
\label{NewConstructor}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{NewConstructor} returns a constructor \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cons}} with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}} describes requirements about the arguments of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cons}}. Namely the number of arguments must be equal to the length of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}, and the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th argument must lie in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}$[i]$ for $i \neq 1$. A constructor expects the first argument to be a \emph{filter} instead of an object and it must be a subset of the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}$[1]$. 

 Each method that is installed for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cons}} via \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) must require that the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th argument lies in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}$[i]$ for $i \neq 1$. Its first argument is a filter and must be a subset of the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}$[1]$. 

 One can install methods for other argument tuples via \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod}), this way it is also possible to install methods for a different number of
arguments than the length of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}. 

 Note that the method selection for constructors works slightly differently
than for usual operations. As stated above, applicabilty to the first argument
in an argument tuple is tested by determining whether the
argument\texttt{\symbol{45}}filter is a \emph{subset} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}$[1]$. 

 The rank of a method installed for a constructor is determined solely by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}$[1]$ of the method. Instead of taking the sum of the ranks of filters involved in
its \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}$[1]$, the sum of $-1$ times these values is taken. The result is added to the number \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} used in the call of \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}). 

 This has the following effects on the method selection for constructors. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cons}} is called with an argument tuple whose first argument is the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}}, any method whose first argument is \emph{more} specific than \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} is applicable (if its other \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}} also match). Then the method with the ``most general'' filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}$[1]$ is chosen, since the rank is computed by taking $-1$ times the ranks of the involved filters. Thus, a constructor is chosen which
returns an object in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} using as few extra filters as possible, which presumably is both more flexible
to use and easier to construct. 

 The following example showcases this behaviour. Note that the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}} is only used for method dispatch. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareFilter( "IsMyObj" );
  DeclareFilter( "IsMyFilter" );
  DeclareFilter( "IsMyOtherFilter" );
  BindGlobal( "MyFamily", NewFamily( "MyFamily" ) );
  
  DeclareConstructor( "NewMyObj", [ IsMyObj ] );
  
  InstallMethod( NewMyObj,
  [ IsMyObj ],
  function( filter )
      local type;
      Print("General constructor\n");
      type := NewType( MyFamily, IsMyObj );
      return Objectify( type, [] );
  end );
  InstallMethod( NewMyObj,
  [ IsMyObj and IsMyFilter and IsMyOtherFilter ],
  function( filter )
      local type;
      Print("Special constructor\n");
      type := NewType( MyFamily, IsMyObj and IsMyFilter and IsMyOtherFilter );
      return Objectify( type, [] );
  end );
\end{Verbatim}
 If only IsMyObj is given, both methods are applicable and the general
constructor is called. If also IsMyFilter is given, only the special
constructor is applicable. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a := NewMyObj( IsMyObj );;|
  General constructor
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsMyOtherFilter(a);|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@b := NewMyObj( IsMyObj and IsMyFilter );;|
  Special constructor
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsMyOtherFilter(b);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@c := NewMyObj( IsMyObj and IsMyFilter and IsMyOtherFilter );;|
  Special constructor
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsMyOtherFilter(c);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareConstructor}}
\logpage{[ 78, 2, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EB6830886F62CC0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareConstructor({\mdseries\slshape name, filters})\index{DeclareConstructor@\texttt{DeclareConstructor}}
\label{DeclareConstructor}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 does the same as \texttt{NewConstructor} (\ref{NewConstructor}) and then binds the result to the global variable \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The variable must previously be writable, and is made
read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only by this function. 

 Note that for operations which are constructors special rules with respect to
applicability and rank of the corresponding methods apply (see section \texttt{NewConstructor} (\ref{NewConstructor})). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Method Installation}}\label{Method Installation}
\logpage{[ 78, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X795EE8257848B438}{}
{
  In order to describe what it means to select a method of an operation, we must
describe how the methods are connected to their operations. 

 For attributes and properties there is \texttt{InstallImmediateMethod} (\ref{InstallImmediateMethod}). 

 For declaring that a filter is implied by other filters there is \texttt{InstallTrueMethod} (\ref{InstallTrueMethod}). 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InstallMethod}}
\logpage{[ 78, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X837EFDAB7BEF290B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallMethod({\mdseries\slshape opr[, info][, famp], args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts[, val], method})\index{InstallMethod@\texttt{InstallMethod}}
\label{InstallMethod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 installs a function method \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape method}} for the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}; \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}} should be a list of requirements for the arguments, each entry being a filter;
if supplied \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} should be a short but informative string that describes for what situation the
method is installed, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famp}} should be a function to be applied to the families of the arguments. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} should be an integer that measures the priority of the method, or a function
of no arguments which should return such an integer and will be called each
time method order is being recalculated (see \texttt{InstallTrueMethod} (\ref{InstallTrueMethod})). 

 The default values for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famp}}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} are the empty string, the function \texttt{ReturnTrue} (\ref{ReturnTrue}), and the integer zero, respectively. 

 The exact meaning of the arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famp}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} is explained in Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Applicable Methods and Method Selection}. 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} expects its methods to require certain filters for their arguments. For
example, the argument of a method for the operation \texttt{Zero} (\ref{Zero}) must be in the category \texttt{IsAdditiveElementWithZero} (\ref{IsAdditiveElementWithZero}). It is not possible to use \texttt{InstallMethod} to install a method for which the entries of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}} do not imply the respective requirements of the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}. If one wants to override this restriction, one has to use \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod}) instead. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InstallOtherMethod}}
\logpage{[ 78, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D2C12DB841CE539}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallOtherMethod({\mdseries\slshape opr[, info][, famp], args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts[, val], method})\index{InstallOtherMethod@\texttt{InstallOtherMethod}}
\label{InstallOtherMethod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 installs a function method \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape method}} for the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}, in the same way as for \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}), but without the restriction that the number of arguments must match a
declaration of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} and without the restriction that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}} imply the respective requirements of the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InstallEarlyMethod}}
\logpage{[ 78, 3, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D54FB8A80C0AC3C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallEarlyMethod({\mdseries\slshape opr, method})\index{InstallEarlyMethod@\texttt{InstallEarlyMethod}}
\label{InstallEarlyMethod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 installs a special "early" function method \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape method}} for the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}. An early method is special in that it bypasses method dispatch, and is
always the first method to be called when invoking the operation. 

 This can be used to avoid method selection overhead for certain special cases,
i.e., as an optimization. Overall, we recommend to use this feature very
sparingly, as it is tool with sharp edges: for example, any inputs that are
handled by an early method can not be intercepted by a regular method, no
matter how high its rank is; this can preclude other kinds of optimizations. 

 Also, unlike regular methods, no checks are performed on the arguments. Not
even the required filters for the operation are tested, so early methods must
be careful in validating their inputs. This also means that any operation can
have at most one such early method for each arity (i.e., one early method
taking 1 argument, one early method taking 2 arguments, etc.). 

 If an early method determines that it is not applicable, it can resume regular
method dispatch by invoking \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}). 

 For an example application of early methods, they are used by \texttt{First} (\ref{First}) to deal with internal lists, for which computing the exact type (needed for
method selection) can be very expensive. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InstallMethodWithRandomSource}}
\logpage{[ 78, 3, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X78CA646678B0539F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallMethodWithRandomSource({\mdseries\slshape opr, info[, famp], args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts[, val], method})\index{InstallMethodWithRandomSource@\texttt{InstallMethodWithRandomSource}}
\label{InstallMethodWithRandomSource}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallOtherMethodWithRandomSource({\mdseries\slshape opr, info[, famp], args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts[, val], method})\index{InstallOtherMethodWithRandomSource@\texttt{InstallOtherMethodWithRandomSource}}
\label{InstallOtherMethodWithRandomSource}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 These functions are designed to simplify adding new methods for \texttt{Random} (\ref{Random:for a list or collection}), \texttt{PseudoRandom} (\ref{PseudoRandom}), and \texttt{Randomize} (\ref{Randomize:for a vector object}) to \textsf{GAP} which can be called both with, and without, a random source. 

 They accept the same arguments as \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) and \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod}), with the extra requirement that the first member of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}} must be \texttt{IsRandomSource} (\ref{IsRandomSource}), and the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} argument is compulsory and must begin 'for a random source and'. 

 This function then installs two methods: first it calls \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) (or \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod})) with unchanged arguments. Then it calls \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) (or \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod})) a second time to install another method which lacks the initial random
source argument; this additional method simply invokes the original method,
with \texttt{GlobalMersenneTwister} (\ref{GlobalMersenneTwister}) added as first argument. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Applicable Methods and Method Selection}}\label{Applicable Methods and Method Selection}
\logpage{[ 78, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X851FC6387CA2B241}{}
{
  A method installed as above is \emph{applicable} for an arguments tuple if the following conditions are satisfied. 

 The number of arguments equals the length of the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}, the $i$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th argument lies in the filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filts}}$[i]$, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famp}} returns \texttt{true} when applied to the families of the arguments. The maximal number of arguments
supported for methods is six, one gets an error message if one tries to
install a method with at least seven arguments. 

 So \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filt}} describes conditions for each argument, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famp}} describes a relation between the arguments. 

 For unary operations such as attributes and properties, there is no such
relation to postulate, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famp}} is \texttt{ReturnTrue} (\ref{ReturnTrue}) for these operations, a function that always returns \texttt{true}. For binary operations, the usual value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famp}} is \texttt{IsIdenticalObj} (\ref{IsIdenticalObj}), which means that both arguments must lie in the same family. 

 Note that any properties which occur among the filters in the filter list will \emph{not} be tested by the method selection if they are not yet known. (More exact: if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}} is a property then the filter implicitly uses not \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}} but \texttt{Has\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape prop}}}.) If this is desired you must explicitly enforce a test (see
section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Redispatching}) below. 

 If no method is applicable, the error message ``no method found'' is signaled. 

 Otherwise, the applicable method with highest \emph{rank} is selected and then called. This rank is usually given by the sum of the
ranks of the filters in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filt}}, \emph{including involved filters}. This value can be modified by the optional \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} argument used in the call of \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}), as follows. 

 
\begin{itemize}
\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} is an integer then add this value to the rank computed from the filters. 
\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} is a function with zero arguments then add the value returned by this function
to the rank computed from the filters. 
\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} is a list of the form \texttt{[ filters ]} or \texttt{[ filters, abs ]}, where \texttt{filters} is a list of filters and \texttt{abs}, if given, is an integer, then ignore the filters in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filt}} for the rank computation, and instead take the sum of the filters in \texttt{filters} (including involved filters) plus \texttt{abs}. 
\end{itemize}
 

 So the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} can be used to raise or lower the priority of a method relative to other
methods for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}. The variant where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} is a function can be useful if one wants to shift the rank of the method by
the rank of certain filters; note that such ranks need not be constant during
a \textsf{GAP} session, they can grow due to implications, see \texttt{InstallTrueMethod} (\ref{InstallTrueMethod}). The variant where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} is a list can be useful for example if one wants that certain filters that are
involved in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape args\texttt{\symbol{45}}filt}} are required but shall not count for the rank of the method. 

 Note that for operations which are constructors special rules with respect to
applicability and rank of the corresponding methods apply (see \texttt{NewConstructor} (\ref{NewConstructor})). 

 Note that from the applicable methods an efficient one shall be selected. This
is a method that needs only little time and storage for the computations. 

 It seems to be impossible for \textsf{GAP} to select an optimal method in all cases. The present ranking of methods is
based on the assumption that a method installed for a special situation shall
be preferred to a method installed for a more general situation. 

 For example, a method for computing a Sylow subgroup of a nilpotent group is
expected to be more efficient than a method for arbitrary groups. So the more
specific method will be selected if \textsf{GAP} knows that the group given as argument is nilpotent. 

 Of course there is no obvious way to decide between the efficiency of
incommensurable methods. For example, take an operation with one method for
permutation groups, another method for nilpotent groups, but no method for
nilpotent permutation groups, and call this operation with a permutation group
known to be nilpotent. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Partial Methods}}\label{Partial Methods}
\logpage{[ 78, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X846865A681D4A623}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{TryNextMethod}}
\logpage{[ 78, 5, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7EED949B83046A7F}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{TryNextMethod({\mdseries\slshape })\index{TryNextMethod@\texttt{TryNextMethod}}
\label{TryNextMethod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 After a method has been selected and called, the method may recognize that it
cannot compute the desired result, and give up by calling \texttt{TryNextMethod()}. 

 In effect, the execution of the method is terminated, and the method selection
calls the next method that is applicable w.r.t. the original arguments. In
other words, the applicable method is called that is subsequent to the one
that called \texttt{TryNextMethod}, according to decreasing rank of the methods. 

 For example, since every finite group of odd order is solvable, one may
install a method for the property \texttt{IsSolvableGroup} (\ref{IsSolvableGroup}) that checks whether the size of the argument is an odd integer, returns \texttt{true} if so, and gives up otherwise. 

 Care is needed if a partial method might modify the type of one of its
arguments, for example by computing an attribute or property. If this happens,
and the type has really changed, then the method should not exit using \texttt{TryNextMethod()} but should call the operation again, as the new information in the type may
cause some methods previously judged inapplicable to be applicable. For
example, if the above method for \texttt{IsSolvableGroup} (\ref{IsSolvableGroup}) actually computes the size, (rather than just examining a stored size), then
it must take care to check whether the type of the group has changed. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Redispatching}}\label{Redispatching}
\logpage{[ 78, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7B85DD797A907106}{}
{
  As mentioned above the method selection will not test unknown properties. In
situations, in which algorithms are only known (or implemented) under certain
conditions, however such a test might be actually desired. 

 One way to achieve this would be to install the method under weaker conditions
and explicitly test the properties first, exiting via \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}) if some of them are not fulfilled. A problem of this approach however is that
such methods then automatically are ranked lower and that the code does not
look nice. 

 A much better way is to use redispatching: Before deciding that no method has
been found one tests these properties and if they turn out to be true the
method selection is started anew (and will then find a method). 

 This can be achieved via the following function: 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{RedispatchOnCondition}}
\logpage{[ 78, 6, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7D4A46CE7BCFCCF5}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{RedispatchOnCondition({\mdseries\slshape oper[, info], fampred, reqs, cond, val})\index{RedispatchOnCondition@\texttt{RedispatchOnCondition}}
\label{RedispatchOnCondition}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This function installs a method for the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oper}} under the conditions \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fampred}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape reqs}} which has absolute value \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}}; that is, the value of the filters \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape reqs}} is disregarded. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cond}} is a list of filters. If not all the values of properties involved in these
filters are already known for actual arguments of the method, they are
explicitly tested and if they are fulfilled \emph{and} stored after this test, the operation is dispatched again. Otherwise the
method exits with \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}). If supplied, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} should be a short but informative string that describes these conditions. This
can be used to enforce tests like \texttt{IsFinite} (\ref{IsFinite}) in situations when all existing methods require this property. The list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cond}} may have unbound entries in which case the corresponding argument is ignored
for further tests. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Immediate Methods}}\label{Immediate Methods}
\logpage{[ 78, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X87D38D2584D0A8AF}{}
{
  Usually a method is called only if its operation has been called and if this
method has been selected, see \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}). 

 For attributes and properties, one can install also \emph{immediate methods}. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InstallImmediateMethod}}
\logpage{[ 78, 7, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87B47AC0849611F8}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallImmediateMethod({\mdseries\slshape opr[, info], filter, rank, method})\index{InstallImmediateMethod@\texttt{InstallImmediateMethod}}
\label{InstallImmediateMethod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{InstallImmediateMethod} installs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape method}} as an immediate method for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}, which must be an attribute or a property, with requirement \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}} and rank \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rank}} (the rank can be omitted, in which case 0 is used as rank). The rank must be
an integer value that measures the priority of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape method}} among the immediate methods for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}. If supplied, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} should be a short but informative string that describes the situation in which
the method is called. 

 An immediate method is called automatically as soon as the object lies in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}}, provided that the value is not yet known. Afterwards the attribute setter is
called in order to store the value, unless the method exits via \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}). 

 Note the difference to \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) that no family predicate occurs because \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} expects only one argument, and that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}} is not a list of requirements but the argument requirement itself. 

 Immediate methods are thought of as a possibility for objects to gain useful
knowledge. They must not be used to force the storing of ``defining information'' in an object. In other words, \textsf{GAP} should work even if all immediate methods are completely disabled. Therefore,
the call to \texttt{InstallImmediateMethod} installs \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape method}} also as an ordinary method for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} with requirement \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filter}}. 

 Note that in such a case \textsf{GAP} executes a computation for which it was not explicitly asked by the user. So
one should install only those methods as immediate methods that are \emph{extremely cheap}. To emphasize this, immediate methods are also called \emph{zero cost methods}. The time for their execution should really be approximately zero. 

 For example, the size of a permutation group can be computed very cheaply if a
stabilizer chain of the group is known. So it is reasonable to install an
immediate method for \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}) with requirement \texttt{IsGroup and Tester( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stab}} )}, where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stab}} is the attribute corresponding to the stabilizer chain. 

 Another example would be the implementation of the conclusion that every
finite group of prime power order is nilpotent. This could be done by
installing an immediate method for the attribute \texttt{IsNilpotentGroup} (\ref{IsNilpotentGroup}) with requirement \texttt{IsGroup and Tester( Size )}. This method would then check whether the size is a finite prime power,
return \texttt{true} in this case and otherwise call \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}). But this requires factoring of an integer, which cannot be guaranteed to be
very cheap, so one should not install this method as an immediate method. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{IsNoImmediateMethodsObject}}
\logpage{[ 78, 7, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X80C3A19E7B99BB41}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsNoImmediateMethodsObject({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{IsNoImmediateMethodsObject@\texttt{IsNoImmediateMethodsObject}}
\label{IsNoImmediateMethodsObject}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (filter)}}\\


 If this filter is set immediate methods will be ignored for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. This can be crucial for performance for objects like pcgs (see Section \ref{Polycyclic Generating Systems}), of which many are created, which are collections, but for which all those
immediate methods for \texttt{IsTrivial} (\ref{IsTrivial}) et cetera do not really make sense. Other examples of objects in \texttt{IsNoImmediateMethodsObject} are compressed vectors and matrices over small finite fields, see the sections \ref{Row Vectors over Finite Fields} and \ref{Matrices over Finite Fields}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Logical Implications}}\label{Logical Implications}
\logpage{[ 78, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7FB5016E83DB4349}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InstallTrueMethod}}
\logpage{[ 78, 8, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X860B8B707995CFE3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallTrueMethod({\mdseries\slshape newfil, filt})\index{InstallTrueMethod@\texttt{InstallTrueMethod}}
\label{InstallTrueMethod}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 It may happen that a filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape newfil}} shall be implied by another filter \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}}, which is usually a meet of other properties, or the meet of some properties
and some categories. Such a logical implication can be installed as an ``immediate method'' for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape newfil}} that requires \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}} and that always returns \texttt{true}. (This should not be mixed up with the methods installed via \texttt{InstallImmediateMethod} (\ref{InstallImmediateMethod}), which have to be called at runtime for the actual objects.) 

 \texttt{InstallTrueMethod} has the effect that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape newfil}} becomes an implied filter of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filt}}, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters}. 

 For example, each cyclic group is abelian, each finite vector space is finite
dimensional, and each division ring is integral. The first of these
implications is installed as follows. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallTrueMethod( IsCommutative, IsGroup and IsCyclic );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Contrary to the immediate methods installed with \texttt{InstallImmediateMethod} (\ref{InstallImmediateMethod}), logical implications cannot be switched off. This means that after the above
implication has been installed, one can rely on the fact that every object in
the filter \texttt{IsGroup and IsCyclic} whose type gets created after the installation of the implication will also be
in the filter \texttt{IsCommutative} (\ref{IsCommutative}). In particular, it may happen that an object which existed already before the
installation of the implication lies in \texttt{IsGroup and IsCyclic} but not in \texttt{IsCommutative} (\ref{IsCommutative}). Thus it is advisable to install all implications between filters before one
starts creating (types of) objects lying in these filters. 

 Adding logical implications can change the rank of filters (see \texttt{RankFilter} (\ref{RankFilter})) and consequently the rank, and so choice of methods for operations (see \ref{Applicable Methods and Method Selection}). By default \texttt{InstallTrueMethod} adjusts the method selection data structures to take care of this, but this
process can be time\texttt{\symbol{45}}consuming, so functions \texttt{SuspendMethodReordering} (\ref{SuspendMethodReordering}) and \texttt{ResumeMethodReordering} (\ref{ResumeMethodReordering}) are provided to allow control of this process. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SuspendMethodReordering}}
\logpage{[ 78, 8, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B26BDF68754DF7A}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SuspendMethodReordering({\mdseries\slshape })\index{SuspendMethodReordering@\texttt{SuspendMethodReordering}}
\label{SuspendMethodReordering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ResumeMethodReordering({\mdseries\slshape })\index{ResumeMethodReordering@\texttt{ResumeMethodReordering}}
\label{ResumeMethodReordering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ResetMethodReordering({\mdseries\slshape })\index{ResetMethodReordering@\texttt{ResetMethodReordering}}
\label{ResetMethodReordering}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 These functions control whether the method reordering process described in \texttt{InstallTrueMethod} (\ref{InstallTrueMethod}) is invoked or not. Since this process can be comparatively
time\texttt{\symbol{45}}consuming, it is usually suspended when a lot of
implications are due to be installed, for instance when loading the library,
or a package. This is done by calling \texttt{SuspendMethodReordering} once the installations are done, \texttt{ResumeMethodReordering} should be called. These pairs of calls can be nested. When the outermost pair
is complete, method reordering takes place and is enabled in \texttt{InstallTrueMethod} (\ref{InstallTrueMethod}) thereafter. \texttt{ResetMethodReordering} effectively exits all nested suspensions, resuming reordering immediately.
This function is mainly provided for error recovery and similar purposes and
is called on quitting from a break loop. }

 }
