\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Operations and Mathematical Terms}}\label{Operations and Mathematical Terms}
\logpage{[ 78, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X855FE25783FB0D4E}{}
{
  \index{overload} Usually an operation stands for a mathematical concept, and the name of the
operation describes this uniquely. Examples are the property \texttt{IsFinite} (\ref{IsFinite}) and the attribute \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}). But there are cases where the same mathematical term is used to denote
different concepts, for example \texttt{Degree} is defined for polynomials, group characters, and permutation actions, and \texttt{Rank} is defined for matrices, free modules, $p$\texttt{\symbol{45}}groups, and transitive permutation actions. 

 It is in principle possible to install methods for the operation \texttt{Rank} that are applicable to the different types of arguments, corresponding to the
different contexts. But this is not the approach taken in the \textsf{GAP} library. Instead there are operations such as \texttt{RankMat} (\ref{RankMat}) for matrices and \texttt{DegreeOfCharacter} (\ref{DegreeOfCharacter}) (in fact these are attributes) which are installed as methods of the ``ambiguous'' operations \texttt{Rank} and \texttt{Degree}. 

 The idea is to distinguish between on the one hand different ways to compute
the same thing (e.g.{\nobreakspace}different methods for \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=} (\ref{bSlash=}), \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}), etc.), and on the other hand genuinely different things (such as the degree
of a polynomial and a permutation action). 

 The former is the basic purpose of operations and attributes. The latter is
provided as a user convenience where mathematical usage forces it on us \emph{and} where no conflicts arise. In programming the library, we use the underlying
mathematically precise operations or attributes, such as \texttt{RankMat} (\ref{RankMat}) and \texttt{RankAction} (\ref{RankAction:for a group, an action domain, etc.}). These should be attributes if appropriate, and the only role of the
operation \texttt{Rank} is to decide which attribute the user meant. That way, stored information is
stored with ``full mathematical precision'' and is less likely to be retrieved for a wrong purpose later. 

 One word about possible conflicts. A typical example is the mathematical term ``centre'', which is defined as $\{ x \in M | a * x = x * a \forall a \in M \}$ for a magma $M$, and as $\{ x \in L | l * x = 0 \forall l \in L \}$ for a Lie algebra $L$. Here it is \emph{not} possible to introduce an operation \texttt{Centre} (\ref{Centre}) that delegates to attributes \texttt{CentreOfMagma} and \texttt{CentreOfLieAlgebra}, depending on the type of the argument. This is because any Lie algebra in \textsf{GAP} is also a magma, so both \texttt{CentreOfMagma} and \texttt{CentreOfLieAlgebra} would be defined for a Lie algebra, with different meaning if the
characteristic is two. So we cannot achieve that one operation in \textsf{GAP} corresponds to the mathematical term ``centre''. 

 ``Ambiguous'' operations such as \texttt{Rank} are declared in the library file \texttt{lib/overload.g}. }

 }

           
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Creating New Objects}}\label{Creating New Objects}
\logpage{[ 79, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83548994805AD1C9}{}
{
  This chapter is divided into three parts. 

 In the first part, it is explained how to create objects with given type
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Creating Objects}). 

 In the second part, first a few small examples are given, for dealing with the
usual cases of component objects (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects}) and positional objects (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Positional Objects}), and for the implementation of new kinds of lists (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Implementing New List Objects} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Arithmetic Issues in the Implementation of New Kinds of Lists}). Finally, the external representation of objects is introduced
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{External Representation}), as a tool for representation independent access to an object. 

 The third part deals with some rules concerning the organization of the \textsf{GAP} library; namely, some commands for creating global variables are explained
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Global Variables in the Library}) that correspond to the ones discussed in the first part of the chapter, and
the idea of distinguishing declaration and implementation part of \textsf{GAP} packages is outlined (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Declaration and Implementation Part}). 

 See also Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{An Example -- Residue Class Rings} for examples how the functions from the first part are used, and why it is
useful to have a declaration part and an implementation part.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Creating Objects}}\label{Creating Objects}
\logpage{[ 79, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X82E86CF37B123FD4}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Objectify}}
\logpage{[ 79, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CB5C12E813F512B}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{Objectify({\mdseries\slshape type, data})\index{Objectify@\texttt{Objectify}}
\label{Objectify}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 New objects are created by \texttt{Objectify}. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}} must be a plain list or a plain record, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape type}} is the type that the desired object shall have. \texttt{Objectify} turns \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}} into an object with type \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape type}}. That is, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}} is changed, and afterwards it will not be a list or a record unless \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape type}} is of type list resp. record. 

 If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}} is a list then \texttt{Objectify} turns it into a positional object, if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}} is a record then \texttt{Objectify} turns it into a component object (for examples, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Positional Objects}). 

 \texttt{Objectify} does also return the object that it made out of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}}. 

 For examples where \texttt{Objectify} is used, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects}, \ref{Positional Objects}, and the example in Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{An Example -- Residue Class Rings}. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ObjectifyWithAttributes}}
\logpage{[ 79, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X85377AC07E775066}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ObjectifyWithAttributes({\mdseries\slshape obj, type, attr1, val1, attr2, val2, ...})\index{ObjectifyWithAttributes@\texttt{ObjectifyWithAttributes}}
\label{ObjectifyWithAttributes}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 Attribute assignments will change the type of an object. If you create many
objects, code of the form 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  o:=Objectify(type,rec());
  SetMyAttribute(o,value);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 will take a lot of time for type changes. You can avoid this by setting the
attributes immediately while the object is created, as follows. \texttt{ObjectifyWithAttributes} takes a plain list or record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} and turns it an object just like \texttt{Objectify} (\ref{Objectify}) and sets attribute \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr1}} to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val1}}, sets attribute \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr2}} to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val2}} and so forth. 

 If the filter list of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape type}} includes that these attributes are set (and the properties also include values
of the properties) and if no special setter methods are installed for any of
the involved attributes then they are set simultaneously without type changes.
This can produce a substantial speedup. 

 If the conditions of the last sentence are not fulfilled, an ordinary \texttt{Objectify} (\ref{Objectify}) with subsequent setter calls for the attributes is performed instead. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Component Objects}}\label{Component Objects}
\logpage{[ 79, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X866E223484649E5A}{}
{
  \index{"!.@\texttt{"!.}} A \emph{component object} is an object in the representation \texttt{IsComponentObjectRep} (\ref{IsComponentObjectRep}) or a subrepresentation of it. Such an object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cobj}} is built from subobjects that can be accessed via \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cobj}}!.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}}, similar to components of a record. Also analogously to records, values can
be assigned to components of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cobj}} via \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cobj}}!.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}:= \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}}}. For the creation of component objects, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Creating Objects}. One must be \emph{very careful} when using the \texttt{!.} operator, in order to interpret the component in the right way, and even more
careful when using the assignment to components using \texttt{!.}, in order to keep the information stored in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cobj}} consistent. 

 First of all, in the access or assignment to a component as shown above, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} must be among the admissible component names for the representation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cobj}}, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{NewRepresentation} (\ref{NewRepresentation}). Second, preferably only few low level functions should use \texttt{!.}, whereas this operator should not occur in ``user interactions''. 

 Note that even if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cobj}} claims that it is immutable, i.e., if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape cobj}} is not in the category \texttt{IsMutable} (\ref{IsMutable}), access and assignment via \texttt{!.} and \texttt{!.:=} work. This is necessary for being able to store newly discovered information
in immutable objects. 

 The following example shows the implementation of an iterator
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Iterators}) for the domain of integers, which is represented as component object.
See{\nobreakspace}\ref{Positional Objects} for an implementation using positional objects. (In practice, such an iterator
can be implemented more elegantly using \texttt{IteratorByFunctions} (\ref{IteratorByFunctions}), see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Example -- Constructing Iterators}.) 

 The used succession of integers is $0, 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3, \ldots$, that is, $a_n = n/2$ if $n$ is even, and $a_n = (1-n)/2$ otherwise. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareRepresentation( "IsIntegersIteratorCompRep",
      IsComponentObjectRep, [ "counter" ] );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The above command creates a new representation (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{NewRepresentation} (\ref{NewRepresentation})) \texttt{IsIntegersIteratorCompRep}, as a subrepresentation of \texttt{IsComponentObjectRep} (\ref{IsComponentObjectRep}), and with one admissible component \texttt{counter}. So no other components than \texttt{counter} will be needed. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( Iterator,
      "method for `Integers'",
      [ IsIntegers ],
      function( Integers )
      return Objectify( NewType( IteratorsFamily,
                                     IsIterator
                                 and IsIntegersIteratorCompRep ),
                        rec( counter := 0 ) );
      end );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 After the above method installation, one can already ask for \texttt{Iterator( Integers )}. Note that exactly the domain of integers is described by the filter \texttt{IsIntegers} (\ref{IsIntegers}). 

 By the call to \texttt{NewType} (\ref{NewType}), the returned object lies in the family containing all iterators, which is \texttt{IteratorsFamily}, it lies in the category \texttt{IsIterator} (\ref{IsIterator}) and in the representation \texttt{IsIntegersIteratorCompRep}; furthermore, it has the component \texttt{counter} with value \texttt{0}. 

 What is missing now are methods for the two basic operations of iterators,
namely \texttt{IsDoneIterator} (\ref{IsDoneIterator}) and \texttt{NextIterator} (\ref{NextIterator}). The former must always return \texttt{false}, since there are infinitely many integers. The latter must return the next
integer in the iteration, and update the information stored in the iterator,
that is, increase the value of the component \texttt{counter}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( IsDoneIterator,
      "method for iterator of `Integers'",
      [ IsIterator and IsIntegersIteratorCompRep ],
      ReturnFalse );
  
  InstallMethod( NextIterator,
      "method for iterator of `Integers'",
      [ IsIntegersIteratorCompRep ],
      function( iter )
      iter!.counter:= iter!.counter + 1;
      if iter!.counter mod 2 = 0 then
        return iter!.counter / 2;
      else
        return ( 1 - iter!.counter ) / 2;
      fi;
      end );
\end{Verbatim}
 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{NamesOfComponents}}
\logpage{[ 79, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X823965BF7DFDACC9}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{NamesOfComponents({\mdseries\slshape comobj})\index{NamesOfComponents@\texttt{NamesOfComponents}}
\label{NamesOfComponents}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For a component object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape comobj}}, \texttt{NamesOfComponents} returns a list of strings, which are the names of components currently bound
in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape comobj}}. 

 For a record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape comobj}} in internal representation, \texttt{NamesOfComponents} returns the result of \texttt{RecNames} (\ref{RecNames}). }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Positional Objects}}\label{Positional Objects}
\logpage{[ 79, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X834893D07FAA6FD2}{}
{
  \index{"![]@\texttt{"![]}} A \emph{positional object} is an object in the representation \texttt{IsPositionalObjectRep} (\ref{IsPositionalObjectRep}) or a subrepresentation of it. Such an object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pobj}} is built from subobjects that can be accessed via \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pobj}}![\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}}]}, similar to positions in a list. Also analogously to lists, values can be
assigned to positions of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pobj}} via \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pobj}}![\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}}]:= \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}}}. For the creation of positional objects, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Creating Objects}. 

 One must be \emph{very careful} when using the \texttt{![]} operator, in order to interpret the position in the right way, and even more
careful when using the assignment to positions using \texttt{![]}, in order to keep the information stored in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pobj}} consistent. 

 First of all, in the access or assignment to a position as shown above, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}} must be among the admissible positions for the representation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pobj}}, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{NewRepresentation} (\ref{NewRepresentation}). Second, preferably only few low level functions should use \texttt{![]}, whereas this operator should not occur in ``user interactions''. 

 Note that even if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pobj}} claims that it is immutable, i.e., if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pobj}} is not in the category \texttt{IsMutable} (\ref{IsMutable}), access and assignment via \texttt{![]} work. This is necessary for being able to store newly discovered information
in immutable objects. 

 The following example shows the implementation of an iterator
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Iterators}) for the domain of integers, which is represented as positional object.
See{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects} for an implementation using component objects, and more details. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareRepresentation( "IsIntegersIteratorPosRep",
      IsPositionalObjectRep, [ 1 ] );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The above command creates a new representation (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{NewRepresentation} (\ref{NewRepresentation})) \texttt{IsIntegersIteratorPosRep}, as a subrepresentation of \texttt{IsPositionalObjectRep} (\ref{IsPositionalObjectRep}), and with only the first position being admissible for storing data. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( Iterator,
      "method for `Integers'",
      [ IsIntegers ],
      function( Integers )
      return Objectify( NewType( IteratorsFamily,
                                     IsIterator
                                 and IsIntegersIteratorPosRep ),
                        [ 0 ] );
      end );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 After the above method installation, one can already ask for \texttt{Iterator( Integers )}. Note that exactly the domain of integers is described by the filter \texttt{IsIntegers} (\ref{IsIntegers}). 

 By the call to \texttt{NewType} (\ref{NewType}), the returned object lies in the family containing all iterators, which is \texttt{IteratorsFamily}, it lies in the category \texttt{IsIterator} (\ref{IsIterator}) and in the representation \texttt{IsIntegersIteratorPosRep}; furthermore, the first position has value \texttt{0}. 

 What is missing now are methods for the two basic operations of iterators,
namely \texttt{IsDoneIterator} (\ref{IsDoneIterator}) and \texttt{NextIterator} (\ref{NextIterator}). The former must always return \texttt{false}, since there are infinitely many integers. The latter must return the next
integer in the iteration, and update the information stored in the iterator,
that is, increase the value stored in the first position. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( IsDoneIterator,
      "method for iterator of `Integers'",
      [ IsIterator and IsIntegersIteratorPosRep ],
      ReturnFalse );
  
  InstallMethod( NextIterator,
      "method for iterator of `Integers'",
      [ IsIntegersIteratorPosRep ],
      function( iter )
      iter![1]:= iter![1] + 1;
      if iter![1] mod 2 = 0 then
        return iter![1] / 2;
      else
        return ( 1 - iter![1] ) / 2;
      fi;
      end );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 It should be noted that one can of course install both the methods shown in
Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects} and \ref{Positional Objects}. The call \texttt{Iterator( Integers )} will cause one of the methods to be selected, and for the returned iterator,
which will have one of the representations we constructed, the right \texttt{NextIterator} (\ref{NextIterator}) method will be chosen. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Implementing New List Objects}}\label{Implementing New List Objects}
\logpage{[ 79, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X82309B3F81DD2237}{}
{
  This section gives some hints for the quite usual situation that one wants to
implement new objects that are lists. More precisely, one either wants to deal
with lists that have additional features, or one wants that some objects also
behave as lists. An example can be found in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Example -- Constructing Enumerators}. 

 A \emph{list} in \textsf{GAP} is an object in the category \texttt{IsList} (\ref{IsList}). Basic operations for lists are \texttt{Length} (\ref{Length}), \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{bSlash[bSlash]}), and \texttt{IsBound\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{IsBoundbSlash[bSlash]}) (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Basic Operations for Lists}). 

 Note that the access to the position \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}} in the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} via \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}}]} is handled by the call \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}} )} to the operation \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{bSlash[bSlash]}). To explain the somewhat strange name \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} of this operation, note that non\texttt{\symbol{45}}alphanumeric characters
like \texttt{[} and \texttt{]} may occur in \textsf{GAP} variable names only if they are escaped by a \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}} character. 

 Analogously, the check \texttt{IsBound( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}}] )} whether the position \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}} of the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}} is bound is handled by the call \texttt{IsBound\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}} )} to the operation \texttt{IsBound\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{IsBoundbSlash[bSlash]}). 

 For mutable lists, also assignment to positions and unbinding of positions via
the operations \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]\texttt{\symbol{92}}:\texttt{\symbol{92}}=} (\ref{bSlash[bSlash]bSlash:bSlash=}) and \texttt{Unbind\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{UnbindbSlash[bSlash]}) are basic operations. The assignment \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}}]:= \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}}} is handled by the call \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]\texttt{\symbol{92}}:\texttt{\symbol{92}}=( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape val}} )}, and \texttt{Unbind( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}}] )} is handled by the call \texttt{Unbind\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}} )}. 

 All other operations for lists, e.g., \texttt{Add} (\ref{Add}), \texttt{Append} (\ref{Append}), \texttt{Sum} (\ref{Sum}), are based on these operations. This means that it is sufficient to install
methods for the new list objects only for the basic operations. 

 So if one wants to implement new list objects then one creates them as objects
in the category \texttt{IsList} (\ref{IsList}), and installs methods for \texttt{Length} (\ref{Length}), \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{bSlash[bSlash]}), and \texttt{IsBound\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{IsBoundbSlash[bSlash]}). If the new lists shall be mutable, one needs to install also methods for \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]\texttt{\symbol{92}}:\texttt{\symbol{92}}=} (\ref{bSlash[bSlash]bSlash:bSlash=}) and \texttt{Unbind\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{UnbindbSlash[bSlash]}). 

 One application for this is the implementation of \emph{enumerators} for domains. An enumerator for the domain $D$ is a dense list whose entries are in bijection with the elements of $D$. If $D$ is large then it is not useful to write down all elements. Instead one can
implement such a bijection implicitly. This works also for infinite domains. 

 In this situation, one implements a new representation of the lists that are
already available in \textsf{GAP}, in particular the family of such a list is the same as the family of the
domain $D$. 

 But it is also possible to implement new kinds of lists that lie in new
families, and thus are not equal to lists that were available in \textsf{GAP} before. An example for this is the implementation of matrices whose
multiplication via ``\texttt{*}'' is the Lie product of matrices. 

 In this situation, it makes no sense to put the new matrices into the same
family as the original matrices. Note that the product of two Lie matrices
shall be defined but not the product of an ordinary matrix and a Lie matrix.
So it is possible to have two lists that have the same entries but that are
not equal w.r.t. ``\texttt{=}'' because they lie in different families. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Example {\textendash} Constructing Enumerators}}\label{Example -- Constructing Enumerators}
\logpage{[ 79, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X849D8BC278649EA5}{}
{
  When dealing with countable sets, a usual task is to define enumerations,
i.e., bijections to the positive integers. In \textsf{GAP}, this can be implemented via \emph{enumerators} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Enumerators}). These are lists containing the elements in a specified ordering, and the
operations \texttt{Position} (\ref{Position}) and list access via \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{bSlash[bSlash]}) define the desired bijection. For implementing such an enumerator, one mainly
needs to install the appropriate functions for these operations. 

 A general setup for creating such lists is given by \texttt{EnumeratorByFunctions} (\ref{EnumeratorByFunctions:for a domain and a record}). 

 If the set in question is a domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} for which a \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}) method is available then all one has to do is to write down the functions for
computing the $n$\texttt{\symbol{45}}th element of the list and for computing the position of a
given \textsf{GAP} object in the list, to put them into the components \texttt{ElementNumber} and \texttt{NumberElement} of a record, and to call \texttt{EnumeratorByFunctions} (\ref{EnumeratorByFunctions:for a domain and a record}) with the domain \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} and this record as arguments. For example, the following lines of code install
an \texttt{Enumerator} (\ref{Enumerator}) method for the case that \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} is the domain of rational integers. (Note that \texttt{IsIntegers} (\ref{IsIntegers}) is a filter that describes exactly the domain of rational integers.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( Enumerator,
      "for integers",
      [ IsIntegers ],
      Integers -> EnumeratorByFunctions( Integers, rec(
                      ElementNumber := function( e, n ) ... end,
                      NumberElement := function( e, x ) ... end ) ) );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The bodies of the functions have been omitted above; here is the code that is
actually used in \textsf{GAP}. (The ordering coincides with that for the iterators for the domain of
rational integers that have been discussed in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Positional Objects}.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|enum:= Enumerator( Integers );A
  <enumerator of Integers>
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|Print( enum!.NumberElement, "\n" );A
  function ( e, x )
      local  pos;
      if not IsInt( x )  then
          return fail;
      elif 0 < x  then
          pos := 2 * x;
      else
          pos := -2 * x + 1;
      fi;
      return pos;
  end
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|Print( enum!.ElementNumber, "\n" );A
  function ( e, n )
      if n mod 2 = 0  then
          return n / 2;
      else
          return (1 - n) / 2;
      fi;
      return;
  end
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The situation becomes slightly more complicated if the set $S$ in question is not a domain. This is because one must provide also at least a
method for computing the length of the list, and because one has to determine
the family in which it lies (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Creating Objects}). The latter should usually not be a problem since either $S$ is nonempty and all its elements lie in the same family {\textendash}in this
case one takes the collections family of any element in $S${\textendash} or the family of the enumerator must be \texttt{ListsFamily}. 

 An example in the \textsf{GAP} library is an enumerator for the set of $k$\texttt{\symbol{45}}tuples over a finite set; the function is called \texttt{EnumeratorOfTuples} (\ref{EnumeratorOfTuples}).   

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|Print( EnumeratorOfTuples, "\n" );A
  function ( set, k )
      local  enum;
      if k = 0  then
          return Immutable( [ [  ] ] );
      elif IsEmpty( set )  then
          return Immutable( [  ] );
      fi;
      enum
       := EnumeratorByFunctions( CollectionsFamily( FamilyObj( set ) ),
         rec(
            ElementNumber := function ( enum, n )
                  local  nn, t, i;
                  nn := n - 1;
                  t := [  ];
                  for i  in [ 1 .. enum!.k ]  do
                      t[i] := RemInt( nn, Length( enum!.set ) ) + 1;
                      nn := QuoInt( nn, Length( enum!.set ) );
                  od;
                  if nn <> 0  then
                      Error( "<enum>[", n,
                       "] must have an assigned value" );
                  fi;
                  nn := enum!.set{Reversed( t )};
                  MakeImmutable( nn );
                  return nn;
              end,
            NumberElement := function ( enum, elm )
                  local  n, i;
                  if not IsList( elm )  then
                      return fail;
                  fi;
                  elm := List( elm, function ( x )
                          return Position( enum!.set, x );
                      end );
                  if fail in elm or Length( elm ) <> enum!.k  then
                      return fail;
                  fi;
                  n := 0;
                  for i  in [ 1 .. enum!.k ]  do
                      n := Length( enum!.set ) * n + elm[i] - 1;
                  od;
                  return n + 1;
              end,
            Length := function ( enum )
                  return Length( enum!.set ) ^ enum!.k;
              end,
            PrintObj := function ( enum )
                  Print( "EnumeratorOfTuples( ", enum!.set, ", ",
                   enum!.k, " )" );
                  return;
              end,
            set := Set( set ),
            k := k ) );
      SetIsSSortedList( enum, true );
      return enum;
  end
\end{Verbatim}
 

 We see that the enumerator is a homogeneous list that stores individual
functions \texttt{ElementNumber}, \texttt{NumberElement}, \texttt{Length}, and \texttt{PrintObj}; besides that, the data components $S$ and $k$ are contained. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Example {\textendash} Constructing Iterators}}\label{Example -- Constructing Iterators}
\logpage{[ 79, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7F6BF6CE7AD04EFC}{}
{
  Iterators are a kind of objects that is implemented for several collections in
the \textsf{GAP} library and which might be interesting also in other cases, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Iterators}. A general setup for implementing new iterators is provided by \texttt{IteratorByFunctions} (\ref{IteratorByFunctions}). 

 All one has to do is to write down the functions for \texttt{NextIterator} (\ref{NextIterator}), \texttt{IsDoneIterator} (\ref{IsDoneIterator}), and \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}), and to call \texttt{IteratorByFunctions} (\ref{IteratorByFunctions}) with this record as argument. For example, the following lines of code install
an \texttt{Iterator} (\ref{Iterator}) method for the case that the argument is the domain of rational integers. 

 (Note that \texttt{IsIntegers} (\ref{IsIntegers}) is a filter that describes exactly the domain of rational integers.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( Iterator,
      "for integers",
      [ IsIntegers ],
      Integers -> IteratorByFunctions( rec(
                      NextIterator:= function( iter ) ... end,
                      IsDoneIterator := ReturnFalse,
                      ShallowCopy := function( iter ) ... end ) ) );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The bodies of two of the functions have been omitted above; here is the code
that is actually used in \textsf{GAP}. (The ordering coincides with that for the iterators for the domain of
rational integers that have been discussed in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Positional Objects}.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|iter:= Iterator( Integers );A
  <iterator of Integers at 0>
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|Print( iter!.NextIterator, "\n" );A
  function ( iter )
      iter!.counter := iter!.counter + 1;
      if iter!.counter mod 2 = 0  then
          return iter!.counter / 2;
      else
          return (1 - iter!.counter) / 2;
      fi;
      return;
  end
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|Print( iter!.ShallowCopy, "\n" );A
  function ( iter )
      return rec(
          counter := iter!.counter );
  end
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that the \texttt{ShallowCopy} component of the record must be a function that does not return an iterator
but a record that can be used as the argument of \texttt{IteratorByFunctions} (\ref{IteratorByFunctions}) in order to create the desired shallow copy. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Arithmetic Issues in the Implementation of New Kinds of Lists}}\label{Arithmetic Issues in the Implementation of New Kinds of Lists}
\logpage{[ 79, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X829629E87E30090C}{}
{
  When designing a new kind of list objects in \textsf{GAP}, defining the arithmetic behaviour of these objects is an issue. 

 There are situations where arithmetic operations of list objects are
unimportant in the sense that adding two such lists need not be represented in
a special way. In such cases it might be useful either to support no
arithmetics at all for the new lists, or to enable the default arithmetic
methods. The former can be achieved by not setting the filters \texttt{IsGeneralizedRowVector} (\ref{IsGeneralizedRowVector}) and \texttt{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector}) in the types of the lists, the latter can be achieved by setting the filter \texttt{IsListDefault} (\ref{IsListDefault}). (for details, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Filters Controlling the Arithmetic Behaviour of Lists}). An example for ``wrapped lists'' with default behaviour are vector space bases; they are lists with additional
properties concerning the computation of coefficients, but arithmetic
properties are not important. So it is no loss to enable the default methods
for these lists. 

 However, often the arithmetic behaviour of new list objects is important, and
one wants to keep these lists away from default methods for addition,
multiplication etc. For example, the sum and the product of (compatible) block
matrices shall be represented as a block matrix, so the default methods for
sum and product of matrices shall not be applicable, although the results will
be equal to those of the default methods in the sense that their entries at
corresponding positions are equal. 

 So one does not set the filter \texttt{IsListDefault} (\ref{IsListDefault}) in such cases, and thus one can implement one's own methods for arithmetic
operations.  (Of course ``can'' means on the other hand that one \emph{must} implement such methods if one is interested in arithmetics of the new lists.) 

 The specific binary arithmetic methods for the new lists will usually cover
the case that both arguments are of the new kind, and perhaps also the
interaction between a list of the new kind and certain other kinds of lists
may be handled if this appears to be useful. 

 For the last situation, interaction between a new kind of lists and other
kinds of lists, \textsf{GAP} provides already a setup. Namely, there are the categories \texttt{IsGeneralizedRowVector} (\ref{IsGeneralizedRowVector}) and \texttt{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector}), which are concerned with the additive and the multiplicative behaviour,
respectively, of lists. For lists in these filters, the structure of the
results of arithmetic operations is prescribed (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Additive Arithmetic for Lists} and \ref{Multiplicative Arithmetic for Lists}). 

 For example, if one implements block matrices in \texttt{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector}) then automatically the product of such a block matrix and a (plain) list of
such block matrices will be defined as the obvious list of matrix products,
and a default method for plain lists will handle this multiplication. (Note
that this method will rely on a method for computing the product of the block
matrices, and of course no default method is available for that.) Conversely,
if the block matrices are not in \texttt{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector}) then the product of a block matrix and a (plain) list of block matrices is not
defined. (There is no default method for it, and one can define the result and
provide a method for computing it.) 

 Thus if one decides to set the filters \texttt{IsGeneralizedRowVector} (\ref{IsGeneralizedRowVector}) and \texttt{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector}) for the new lists, on the one hand one loses freedom in defining arithmetic
behaviour, but on the other hand one gains several default methods for a more
or less natural behaviour. 

 If a list in the filter \texttt{IsGeneralizedRowVector} (\ref{IsGeneralizedRowVector}) (\texttt{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeGeneralizedRowVector})) lies in \texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep} (\ref{IsAttributeStoringRep}), the values of additive (multiplicative) nesting depth is stored in the list
and need not be calculated for each arithmetic operation. One can then store
the value(s) already upon creation of the lists, with the effect that the
default arithmetic operations will access elements of these lists only if this
is unavoidable. For example, the sum of two plain lists of ``wrapped matrices'' with stored nesting depths are computed via the method for adding two such
wrapped lists, and without accessing any of their rows (which might be
expensive). In this sense, the wrapped lists are treated as black boxes. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{External Representation}}\label{External Representation}
\logpage{[ 79, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7EBB961E7FE1B0EB}{}
{
  An operation is defined for elements rather than for objects in the sense that
if the arguments are replaced by objects that are equal to the old arguments
w.r.t. the equivalence relation ``\texttt{=}'' then the result must be equal to the old result w.r.t.{\nobreakspace}``\texttt{=}''. 

 But the implementation of many methods is representation dependent in the
sense that certain representation dependent subobjects are accessed. 

 For example, a method that implements the addition of univariate polynomials
may access coefficients lists of its arguments only if they are really stored,
while in the case of sparsely represented polynomials a different approach is
needed. 

 In spite of this, for many operations one does not want to write an own method
for each possible representations of each argument, for example because none
of the methods could in fact take advantage of the actually given
representations of the objects. Another reason could be that one wants to
install first a representation independent method, and then add specific
methods as they are needed to gain more efficiency, by really exploiting the
fact that the arguments have certain representations. 

 For the purpose of admitting representation independent code, one can define
an \emph{external representation} of objects in a given family, install methods to compute this external
representation for each representation of the objects, and then use this
external representation of the objects whenever they occur. 

 We cannot provide conversion functions that allow us to first convert any
object in question to one particular ``standard representation'', and then access the data in the way defined for this representation, simply
because it may be impossible to choose such a ``standard representation'' uniformly for all objects in the given family. 

 So the aim of an external representation of an object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is a different one, namely to describe the data from which \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is composed. In particular, the external representation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is \emph{not} one possible (``standard'') representation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, in fact the external representation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is in general different from \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} w.r.t.{\nobreakspace}``\texttt{=}'', first of all because the external representation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} does in general not lie in the same family as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. 

 For example the external representation of a rational function is a list of
length two or three, the first entry being the zero coefficient, the second
being a list describing the coefficients and monomials of the numerator, and
the third, if bound, being a list describing the coefficients and monomials of
the denominator. In particular, the external representation of a polynomial is
a list and not a polynomial. 

 The other way round, the external representation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} encodes \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} in such a way that from this data and the family of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, one can create an object that is equal to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}. Usually the external representation of an object is a list or a record. 

 Although the external representation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is by definition independent of the actually available representations for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, it is usual that a representation of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} exists for which the computation of the external representation is obtained by
just ``unpacking'' \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, in the sense that the desired data is stored in a component or a position of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}, if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is a component object (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects}) or a positional object (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Positional Objects}). 

 To implement an external representation means to install methods for the
following two operations. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ExtRepOfObj}}
\logpage{[ 79, 8, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8542B32A8206118C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ExtRepOfObj({\mdseries\slshape obj})\index{ExtRepOfObj@\texttt{ExtRepOfObj}}
\label{ExtRepOfObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ObjByExtRep({\mdseries\slshape fam, data})\index{ObjByExtRep@\texttt{ObjByExtRep}}
\label{ObjByExtRep}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{ExtRepOfObj} returns the external representation of its argument, and \texttt{ObjByExtRep} returns an object in the family \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape fam}} that has external representation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape data}}. 

 Of course, \texttt{ObjByExtRep( FamilyObj( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} ), ExtRepOfObj( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} ) )} must be equal to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} w.r.t. the operation \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}=} (\ref{bSlash=}). But it is \emph{not} required that equal objects have equal external representations. 

 Note that if one defines a new representation of objects for which an external
representation does already exist then one \emph{must} install a method to compute this external representation for the objects in
the new representation. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Mutability and Copying}}\label{Mutability and Copying}
\logpage{[ 79, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8090219A7C76AF55}{}
{
  Any \textsf{GAP} object is either mutable or immutable. This can be tested with the function \texttt{IsMutable} (\ref{IsMutable}). The intended meaning of (im)mutability is a mathematical one: an immutable
object should never change in such a way that it represents a different
Element. Objects \emph{may} change in other ways, for instance to store more information, or represent an
element in a different way. 

 Immutability is enforced in different ways for built\texttt{\symbol{45}}in
objects (like records, or lists) and for external objects (made using \texttt{Objectify} (\ref{Objectify})). 

 For built\texttt{\symbol{45}}in objects which are immutable, the kernel will
prevent you from changing them. Thus 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l := [1,2,4];|
  [ 1, 2, 4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MakeImmutable(l);|
  [ 1, 2, 4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l[3] := 5;|
  Error, List Assignment: <list> must be a mutable list
\end{Verbatim}
 

 For external objects, the situation is different. An external object which
claims to be immutable (i.e. its type does not contain \texttt{IsMutable} (\ref{IsMutable})) should not admit any methods which change the element it represents. The
kernel does \emph{not} prevent the use of \texttt{!.} and \texttt{![} to change the underlying data structure. This is used for instance by the code
that stores attribute values for reuse. In general, these \texttt{!} operations should only be used in methods which depend on the representation
of the object. Furthermore, we would \emph{not} recommend users to install methods which depend on the representations of
objects created by the library or by \textsf{GAP} packages, as there is certainly no guarantee of the representations being the
same in future versions of \textsf{GAP}. 

 Here we see an immutable object (the group $S_4$), in which we improperly install a new component. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|g := SymmetricGroup(IsPermGroup,4);A
  Sym( [ 1 .. 4 ] )
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|IsMutable(g);A
  false
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|NamesOfComponents(g);A
  [ "Size", "NrMovedPoints", "MovedPoints",
    "GeneratorsOfMagmaWithInverses" ]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|g!.silly := "rubbish";A
  "rubbish"
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|NamesOfComponents(g);A
  [ "Size", "NrMovedPoints", "MovedPoints",
    "GeneratorsOfMagmaWithInverses", "silly" ]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|g!.silly;A
  "rubbish"
\end{Verbatim}
 

 On the other hand, if we form an immutable externally represented list, we
find that \textsf{GAP} will not let us change the object. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@e := Enumerator(g);|
  <enumerator of perm group>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsMutable(e);|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsList(e);|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@e[3];|
  (1,2,4)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@e[3] := false;|
  Error, The list you are trying to assign to is immutable
\end{Verbatim}
 

 When we consider copying objects, another filter \texttt{IsCopyable} (\ref{IsCopyable}), enters the game and we find that \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}) and \texttt{StructuralCopy} (\ref{StructuralCopy}) behave quite differently. Objects can be divided for this purpose into three:
mutable objects, immutable but copyable objects, and
non\texttt{\symbol{45}}copyable objects (called constants). 

 A mutable or copyable object should have a method for the operation \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}), which should make a new mutable object, sharing its
top\texttt{\symbol{45}}level subobjects with the original. The exact
definition of top\texttt{\symbol{45}}level subobject may be defined by the
implementor for new kinds of object. 

 \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}) applied to a constant simply returns the constant. 

 \texttt{StructuralCopy} (\ref{StructuralCopy}) is expected to be much less used than \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}). Applied to a mutable object, it returns a new mutable object which shares no
mutable sub\texttt{\symbol{45}}objects with the input. Applied to an immutable
object (even a copyable one), it just returns the object. It is not an
operation (indeed, it's a rather special kernel function). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@e1 := StructuralCopy(e);|
  <enumerator of perm group>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsMutable(e1);|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@e2 := ShallowCopy(e);|
  [ (), (1,4), (1,2,4), (1,3,4), (2,4), (1,4,2), (1,2), (1,3,4,2),
    (2,3,4), (1,4,2,3), (1,2,3), (1,3)(2,4), (3,4), (1,4,3), (1,2,4,3),
    (1,3), (2,4,3), (1,4,3,2), (1,2)(3,4), (1,3,2), (2,3), (1,4)(2,3),
    (1,2,3,4), (1,3,2,4) ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 There are two other related functions: \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}), which makes a new immutable object which shares no mutable subobjects with
its input and \texttt{MakeImmutable} (\ref{MakeImmutable}) which changes an object and its mutable subobjects \emph{in place} to be immutable. It should only be used on ``new'' objects that you have just created, and which cannot share mutable subobjects
with anything else. 

 Both \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}) and \texttt{MakeImmutable} (\ref{MakeImmutable}) work on external objects by just resetting the \texttt{IsMutable} (\ref{IsMutable}) filter in the object's type. This should make ineligible any methods that
might change the object. As a consequence, you must allow for the possibility
of immutable versions of any objects you create. 

 So, if you are implementing your own external objects. The rules amount to the
following: 

 
\begin{enumerate}
\item  You decide if your objects should be mutable or copyable or constants, by
fixing whether their type includes \texttt{IsMutable} (\ref{IsMutable}) or \texttt{IsCopyable} (\ref{IsCopyable}). 
\item  You install methods for your objects respecting that decision: 
\begin{description}
\item[{for constants:}]  no methods change the underlying elements; 
\item[{for copyables:}]  you provide a method for \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}); 
\item[{for mutables:}]  you may have methods that change the underlying elements and these should
explicitly require \texttt{IsMutable} (\ref{IsMutable}). 
\end{description}
 
\end{enumerate}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Global Variables in the Library}}\label{Global Variables in the Library}
\logpage{[ 79, 10, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X87E29BA57C8208A4}{}
{
  Global variables in the \textsf{GAP} library are usually read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only in order to prevent them from
being overwritten accidentally. See also Section \ref{More About Global Variables}. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareGlobalName}}
\logpage{[ 79, 10, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X828E14ED7EE39522}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareGlobalName({\mdseries\slshape name})\index{DeclareGlobalName@\texttt{DeclareGlobalName}}
\label{DeclareGlobalName}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For global variables, sometimes code needs to reference them before a value
can sensibly be assigned to them. For example, consider the following
definition of a recursive function: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  BindGlobal( "fun", function(n)
    if n > 0 then
      return 2*fun(n-1);
    fi;
    return 1;
  end );
\end{Verbatim}
 The problem with that code is that it triggers a syntax warning about access
to an unbound global variable, as \texttt{fun} only gets assigned after the complete statement has been parsed, yet that
statement references \texttt{fun}. 

 To resolve this, one can declare the variable with \texttt{DeclareGlobalName} before assigning it via \texttt{BindGlobal} (\ref{BindGlobal}). This informs \textsf{GAP} that a global variable with the specified name will eventually be defined, and
that thus no syntax warnings pertaining to its use should be printed. 

 We recommend using \texttt{DeclareGlobalName} instead of \texttt{DeclareGlobalVariable} (\ref{DeclareGlobalVariable}) or \texttt{DeclareGlobalFunction} (\ref{DeclareGlobalFunction}) whenever possible. 

 \texttt{DeclareGlobalName} shall be used in the declaration part of the respective package
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Declaration and Implementation Part}), values can then be assigned to the new variable as usual, preferably via \texttt{BindGlobal} (\ref{BindGlobal}), in the implementation part (again, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Declaration and Implementation Part}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareGlobalVariable}}
\logpage{[ 79, 10, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8324B5DE8300E0F2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareGlobalVariable({\mdseries\slshape name[, description]})\index{DeclareGlobalVariable@\texttt{DeclareGlobalVariable}}
\label{DeclareGlobalVariable}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 For global variables that are \emph{not} functions, instead of using \texttt{BindGlobal} (\ref{BindGlobal}) one can also declare the variable with \texttt{DeclareGlobalVariable} which creates a new global variable named by the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. 

 In the past the main application of this was to allow access to variables
before they were assigned. Starting with \textsf{GAP} 4.12 we recommend to instead use \texttt{DeclareGlobalName} (\ref{DeclareGlobalName}) for this kind of problem. The main remaining application for \texttt{DeclareGlobalVariable} is when one needs flushable values. 

 If used at all, then \texttt{DeclareGlobalVariable} shall be used in the declaration part of the respective package
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Declaration and Implementation Part}), values can then be assigned to the new variable with \texttt{InstallValue} (\ref{InstallValue}), \texttt{InstallFlushableValue} (\ref{InstallFlushableValue}) or \texttt{InstallFlushableValueFromFunction} (\ref{InstallFlushableValueFromFunction}), in the implementation part (again, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Declaration and Implementation Part}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InstallValue}}
\logpage{[ 79, 10, 3 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7A23F09886E936D2}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallValue({\mdseries\slshape gvar, value})\index{InstallValue@\texttt{InstallValue}}
\label{InstallValue}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallFlushableValue({\mdseries\slshape gvar, value})\index{InstallFlushableValue@\texttt{InstallFlushableValue}}
\label{InstallFlushableValue}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallFlushableValueFromFunction({\mdseries\slshape gvar, func})\index{InstallFlushableValueFromFunction@\texttt{InstallFlushableValueFromFunction}}
\label{InstallFlushableValueFromFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{InstallValue} assigns the value \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape value}} to the global variable \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gvar}} if it was previously declared via \texttt{DeclareGlobalVariable} (\ref{DeclareGlobalVariable}). \texttt{InstallFlushableValue} does the same but additionally provides that each call of \texttt{FlushCaches} (\ref{FlushCaches}) will assign a structural copy of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape value}} to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gvar}}. \texttt{InstallFlushableValueFromFunction} instead assigns the result of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape func}} to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gvar}} (\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape func}} is re\texttt{\symbol{45}}evaluated for each invocation of \texttt{FlushCaches} (\ref{FlushCaches}) 

 \texttt{InstallValue} does \emph{not} work if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape value}} is an ``immediate object'', i.e., an internally represented small integer or finite field element. It
also fails for booleans. In addition, the use of any other type of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape value}} except for a list or record is deprecated. Furthermore, \texttt{InstallFlushableValue} works only if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape value}} is a list or a record. (Note that \texttt{InstallFlushableValue} makes sense only for \emph{mutable} global variables.) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{FlushCaches}}
\logpage{[ 79, 10, 4 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87A4316C818B3DE3}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{FlushCaches({\mdseries\slshape })\index{FlushCaches@\texttt{FlushCaches}}
\label{FlushCaches}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (operation)}}\\


 \texttt{FlushCaches} resets the value of each global variable that has been declared with \texttt{DeclareGlobalVariable} (\ref{DeclareGlobalVariable}) and for which the initial value has been set with \texttt{InstallFlushableValue} (\ref{InstallFlushableValue}) or \texttt{InstallFlushableValueFromFunction} (\ref{InstallFlushableValueFromFunction}) to this initial value. 

 \texttt{FlushCaches} should be used only for debugging purposes, since the involved global
variables include for example lists that store finite fields and cyclotomic
fields used in the current \textsf{GAP} session, in order to avoid that these fields are constructed anew in each call
to \texttt{GF} (\ref{GF:for field size}) and \texttt{CF} (\ref{CF:for (subfield and) conductor}). }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareGlobalFunction}}
\logpage{[ 79, 10, 5 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X834A8CC587A609BE}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareGlobalFunction({\mdseries\slshape name})\index{DeclareGlobalFunction@\texttt{DeclareGlobalFunction}}
\label{DeclareGlobalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InstallGlobalFunction({\mdseries\slshape oper, func})\index{InstallGlobalFunction@\texttt{InstallGlobalFunction}}
\label{InstallGlobalFunction}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \textsf{GAP} functions that are not operations and that are intended to be called by users
should be notified to \textsf{GAP} via \texttt{DeclareGlobalFunction}. \texttt{DeclareGlobalFunction} returns a function that serves as a placeholder for the function that will be
installed later. The placeholder will print an error message if it is called.
See also{\nobreakspace}\texttt{DeclareSynonym} (\ref{DeclareSynonym}). 

 In the past the main application of this was to allow access to variables
before they were assigned. Starting with \textsf{GAP} 4.12 we recommend to use \texttt{DeclareGlobalName} (\ref{DeclareGlobalName})/\texttt{BindGlobal} (\ref{BindGlobal}) instead of \texttt{DeclareGlobalVariable} (\ref{DeclareGlobalVariable})/\texttt{InstallGlobalFunction} whenever possible. 

 If used at all, then \texttt{DeclareGlobalVariable} (\ref{DeclareGlobalVariable}) shall be used in the declaration part of the respective package
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Declaration and Implementation Part}). 

 A global function declared with \texttt{DeclareGlobalFunction} can be given its value \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape func}} via \texttt{InstallGlobalFunction}; \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gvar}} is the global variable (or a string denoting its name) named with the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} argument of the call to \texttt{DeclareGlobalFunction}. For example, a declaration like 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareGlobalFunction( "SumOfTwoCubes" );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 in the ``declaration part'' (see Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Declaration and Implementation Part}) might have a corresponding ``implementation part'' of: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallGlobalFunction( SumOfTwoCubes, function(x, y) return x^3 + y^3; end);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{DeclareSynonym}}
\logpage{[ 79, 10, 6 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X851654DA87616207}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareSynonym({\mdseries\slshape name, value})\index{DeclareSynonym@\texttt{DeclareSynonym}}
\label{DeclareSynonym}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{DeclareSynonymAttr({\mdseries\slshape name, value})\index{DeclareSynonymAttr@\texttt{DeclareSynonymAttr}}
\label{DeclareSynonymAttr}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{DeclareSynonym} assigns the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} to a global variable as a synonym for \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape value}}. Two typical intended usages are to declare an ``and\texttt{\symbol{45}}filter'', e.g. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareSynonym( "IsGroup", IsMagmaWithInverses and IsAssociative );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 and to provide a previously declared global function with an alternative name,
e.g. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareGlobalFunction( "SizeOfSomething" );
  DeclareSynonym( "OrderOfSomething", SizeOfSomething );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 \emph{Note:} Before using \texttt{DeclareSynonym} in the way of this second example, one should determine whether the synonym is
really needed. Perhaps an extra index entry in the documentation would be
sufficient. 

 When \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape value}} is actually an attribute then \texttt{DeclareSynonymAttr} should be used; this binds also globals variables \texttt{Set}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} and \texttt{Has}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} for its setter and tester, respectively. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareSynonymAttr( "IsField", IsDivisionRing and IsCommutative );
  DeclareAttribute( "GeneratorsOfDivisionRing", IsDivisionRing );
  DeclareSynonymAttr( "GeneratorsOfField", GeneratorsOfDivisionRing );
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Declaration and Implementation Part}}\label{Declaration and Implementation Part}
\logpage{[ 79, 11, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7837CA9A83D93B38}{}
{
  Each package of \textsf{GAP} code consists of two parts, the \emph{declaration part} that defines the new categories and operations for the objects the package
deals with, and the \emph{implementation part} where the corresponding methods are installed. The declaration part should be
representation independent, representation dependent information should be
dealt with in the implementation part. 

 \textsf{GAP} functions that are not operations and that are intended to be called by users
should be notified to \textsf{GAP} in the declaration part via \texttt{DeclareGlobalFunction} (\ref{DeclareGlobalFunction}). Values for these functions can be installed in the implementation part via \texttt{InstallGlobalFunction} (\ref{InstallGlobalFunction}). 

 Calls to the following functions belong to the declaration part. 
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{DeclareAttribute} (\ref{DeclareAttribute}),
\item \texttt{DeclareCategory} (\ref{DeclareCategory}),
\item \texttt{DeclareFilter} (\ref{DeclareFilter}),
\item \texttt{DeclareOperation} (\ref{DeclareOperation}),
\item \texttt{DeclareGlobalFunction} (\ref{DeclareGlobalFunction}),
\item \texttt{DeclareGlobalName} (\ref{DeclareGlobalName}),
\item \texttt{DeclareGlobalVariable} (\ref{DeclareGlobalVariable}),
\item \texttt{DeclareSynonym} (\ref{DeclareSynonym}),
\item \texttt{DeclareSynonymAttr} (\ref{DeclareSynonymAttr}),
\item \texttt{DeclareProperty} (\ref{DeclareProperty}),
\item \texttt{InstallTrueMethod} (\ref{InstallTrueMethod}).
\end{itemize}
 Calls to the following functions belong to the implementation part. 
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{DeclareRepresentation} (\ref{DeclareRepresentation}),
\item \texttt{InstallGlobalFunction} (\ref{InstallGlobalFunction}),
\item \texttt{InstallValue} (\ref{InstallValue}),
\item \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}),
\item \texttt{InstallImmediateMethod} (\ref{InstallImmediateMethod}),
\item \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod}),
\item \texttt{NewFamily} (\ref{NewFamily}),
\item \texttt{NewType} (\ref{NewType}),
\item \texttt{Objectify} (\ref{Objectify}).
\end{itemize}
 \index{DeclareRepresentation@\texttt{DeclareRepresentation}!belongs to implementation part} Whenever both a \texttt{New}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Something}} and a \texttt{Declare}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Something}} variant of a function exist (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Global Variables in the Library}), the use of \texttt{Declare}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Something}} is recommended because this protects the variables in question from being
overwritten. Note that there are \emph{no} functions \texttt{DeclareFamily} and \texttt{DeclareType} since families and types are created dynamically, hence usually no global
variables are associated to them. Further note that \texttt{DeclareRepresentation} (\ref{DeclareRepresentation}) is regarded as belonging to the implementation part, because usually
representations of objects are accessed only in very few places, and all code
that involves a particular representation is contained in one file;
additionally, representations of objects are often not interesting for the
user, so there is no need to provide a user interface or documentation about
representations. 

 It should be emphasized that ``declaration'' means only an explicit notification of mathematical or technical terms or of
concepts to \textsf{GAP}. For example, declaring a category or property with name \texttt{IsInteresting} does of course not tell \textsf{GAP} what this shall mean, and it is necessary to implement possibilities to create
objects that know already that they lie in \texttt{IsInteresting} in the case that it is a category, or to install implications or methods in
order to compute for a given object whether \texttt{IsInteresting} is \texttt{true} or \texttt{false} for it in the case that \texttt{IsInteresting} is a property. }

 }

           
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Examples of Extending the System}}\label{Examples of Extending the System}
\logpage{[ 80, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8186831682A00097}{}
{
  This chapter gives a few examples of how one can extend the functionality of \textsf{GAP}. 

 They are arranged in ascending difficulty. We show how to install new methods,
add new operations and attributes and how to implement new features using
categories and representations. (As we do not introduce completely new kinds
of objects in these example it will not be necessary to declare any families.)
Finally we show a simple way how to create new objects with an own arithmetic. 

 The examples given are all very rudimentary {\textendash} no particular error
checks are performed and the user interface sometimes is quite clumsy. These
examples may be constructed for presentation purposes only and they do not
necessarily constitute parts of the \textsf{GAP} library. 

 Even more complex examples that create whole classes of objects anew will be
given in the following two chapters \ref{An Example -- Residue Class Rings} and \ref{An Example -- Designing Arithmetic Operations}.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Addition of a Method}}\label{Addition of a Method}
\logpage{[ 80, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7B42DF6E7CCF507D}{}
{
  The easiest case is the addition of a new algorithm as a method for an
existing operation for the existing structures. 

 For example, assume we wanted to implement a better method for computing the
exponent of a nilpotent group (it is the product of the exponents of the Sylow
subgroups). 

 The first task is to find which operation is used by \textsf{GAP} (it is \texttt{Exponent} (\ref{Exponent})) and how it is declared. We can find this in the Reference Manual (in our
particular case in section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Numerical Group Attributes}) and the declaration in the library file \texttt{lib/grp.gd}. The easiest way to find the place of the declaration is usually to \texttt{grep} over all \texttt{.gd} and \texttt{.g} files, see section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Library Files}. 

 In our example the declaration in the library is: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareAttribute("Exponent",IsGroup);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Similarly we find that the filter \texttt{IsNilpotentGroup} (\ref{IsNilpotentGroup}) represents the concept of being nilpotent. 

 We then write a function that implements the new algorithm which takes the
right set of arguments and install it as a method. In our example this
installation would be: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod(Exponent,"for nilpotent groups",
    [IsGroup and IsNilpotent],
  function(G)
    [function body omitted]
  end);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 We have left out the optional rank argument of \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}), which normally is a wise choice {\textendash}\textsf{GAP} automatically uses an internal ranking based on the filters that is only
offset by the given rank. So our method will certainly be regarded as ``better'' than a method that has been installed for mere groups or for solvable groups
but will be ranked lower than the library method for abelian groups. 

 That's all. Using \ref{ApplicableMethod} we can check for a nilpotent group that indeed our new method will be used. 

 When testing, remember that the method selection will not check for properties
that are not known. (This is done internally by checking the property tester
first.) Therefore the method would not be applicable for the group \texttt{g} in the following definition but only for the {\textendash}mathematically
identical but endowed with more knowledge by \textsf{GAP}{\textendash} group \texttt{h}. (Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Enforcing Property Tests} shows a way around this.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:=Group((1,2),(1,3)(2,4));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@h:=Group((1,2),(1,3)(2,4));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsNilpotentGroup(h); # enforce test|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HasIsNilpotentGroup(g);|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HasIsNilpotentGroup(h);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Let's now look at a slightly more complicated example: We want to implement a
better method for computing normalizers in a nilpotent permutation group.
(Such an algorithm can be found for example in \cite{luksrakocziwright97}.) 

 We already know \texttt{IsNilpotentGroup} (\ref{IsNilpotentGroup}), the filter \texttt{IsPermGroup} (\ref{IsPermGroup}) represents the concept of being a group of permutations. 

 \textsf{GAP} uses \texttt{Normalizer} (\ref{Normalizer:for two groups}) to compute normalizers, however the declaration is a bit more complicated. In
the library we find 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InParentFOA( "Normalizer", IsGroup, IsObject, NewAttribute );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The full mechanism of \texttt{InParentFOA} (\ref{InParentFOA}) is described in chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Function-Operation-Attribute Triples}, however for our purposes it is sufficient to know that for such a function
the actual work is done by an operation \texttt{NormalizerOp}, an underlying operation for \texttt{Normalizer} (\ref{Normalizer:for two groups}) (and all the complications are just there to be able to remember certain
results) and that the declaration of this operation is given by the first
arguments, it would be: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareOperation( "NormalizerOp", [IsGroup, IsObject] );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 This time we decide to enter a non\texttt{\symbol{45}}default family predicate
in the call to \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}). We could just leave it out as in the previous call; this would yield the
default value, the function \texttt{ReturnTrue} (\ref{ReturnTrue}) of arbitrary many arguments which always returns \texttt{true}. However, then the method might be called in some cases of inconsistent input
(for example matrix groups in different characteristics) that ought to fall
through the method selection to raise an error. 

 In our situation, we want the second group to be a subgroup of the first, so
necessarily both must have the same family and we can use \texttt{IsIdenticalObj} (\ref{IsIdenticalObj}) as family predicate. 

 Now we can install the method. Again this manual is lazy and does not show you
the actual code: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod(NormalizerOp,"for nilpotent permutation groups",IsIdenticalObj,
    [IsPermGroup and IsNilpotentGroup,
     IsPermGroup and IsNilpotentGroup],
  function(G,U)
    [ function body omitted ]
  end);
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Extending the Range of Definition of an Existing Operation}}\label{Extending the Range of Definition of an Existing Operation}
\logpage{[ 80, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X837CF3267EF0CFB3}{}
{
  It might be that the operation has been defined so far only for a set of
objects that is too restrictive for our purposes (or we want to install a
method that takes another number of arguments). If this is the case, the call
to \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) causes an error message. We can avoid this by using \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod}) instead. It is also possible to re\texttt{\symbol{45}}declare an operation
with another number of arguments and/or different filters for its arguments. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Enforcing Property Tests}}\label{Enforcing Property Tests}
\logpage{[ 80, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7D880DB779EBA8D5}{}
{
  As mentioned in Section \ref{Applicable Methods and Method Selection}, \textsf{GAP} does not check unknown properties to test whether a method might be
applicable. In some cases one wants to enforce this, however, because the gain
from knowing the property outweighs the cost of its determination. 

 In this situation one has to install a method \emph{without} the additional property (so it can be tried even if the property is not yet
known) and at high rank (so it will be used before other methods). The first
thing to do in the actual function then is to test the property and to bail
out with \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod}) if it turns out to be \texttt{false}. 

 The above \texttt{Exponent} (\ref{Exponent}) example thus would become:  
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod(Exponent,"test abelianity", [IsGroup],
    50,# enforced high rank
  function(G)
    if not IsAbelian(G) then
      TryNextMethod();
    fi;
    [remaining function body omitted]
  end);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The value ``50'' used in this example is quite arbitrary. A better way is to use values that
are given by the system inherently: We want this method still to be ranked as
high, \emph{as if it had} the \texttt{IsAbelian} (\ref{IsAbelian}) requirement. So we have \textsf{GAP} compute the extra rank of this: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod(Exponent,"test abelianity", [IsGroup],
    # enforced absolute rank of `IsGroup and IsAbelian' installation: Subtract
    # the rank of `IsGroup' and add the rank of `IsGroup and IsAbelian':
    RankFilter(IsGroup and IsAbelian)
    -RankFilter(IsGroup),
  function(G)
\end{Verbatim}
 the slightly complicated construction of addition and subtraction is necessary
because \texttt{IsGroup} (\ref{IsGroup}) and \texttt{IsAbelian} (\ref{IsAbelian}) might imply the \emph{same} elementary filters which we otherwise would count twice. 

 A somehow similar situation occurs with matrix groups. Most methods for matrix
groups are only applicable if the group is known to be finite. 

 However we should not enforce a finiteness test early (someone else later
might install good methods for infinite groups while the finiteness test would
be too expensive) but just before \textsf{GAP} would give a ``no method found'' error. This is done by redispatching, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Redispatching}. For example to enforce such a final finiteness test for normalizer
calculations could be done by: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  RedispatchOnCondition(NormalizerOp,IsIdenticalObj,
    [IsMatrixGroup,IsMatrixGroup],[IsFinite,IsFinite],0);
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Adding a new Operation}}\label{Adding a new Operation}
\logpage{[ 80, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X797545848520A44B}{}
{
  Next, we will consider how to add own operations. As an example we take the
Sylow normalizer in a group of a given prime. This operation gets two
arguments, the first has to be a group, the second a prime number. 

 There is a function \texttt{IsPrimeInt} (\ref{IsPrimeInt}), but no property for being prime (which would be pointless as integers cannot
store property values anyhow). So the second argument gets specified only as
positive integer: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  SylowNormalizer:=NewOperation("SylowNormalizer",[IsGroup,IsPosInt]);
\end{Verbatim}
 (Note that we are using \texttt{NewOperation} (\ref{NewOperation}) instead of \texttt{DeclareOperation} (\ref{DeclareOperation}) as used in the library. The only difference other than that \texttt{DeclareOperation} (\ref{DeclareOperation}) saves some typing, is that it also protects the variables against overwriting.
When testing code (when one probably wants to change things) this might be
restricting. If this does not bother you, you can use 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareOperation("SylowNormalizer",[IsGroup,IsPosInt]);
\end{Verbatim}
 as well.) 

 The filters \texttt{IsGroup} (\ref{IsGroup}) and \texttt{IsPosInt} (\ref{IsPosInt}) given are \emph{only} used to test that \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) installs methods with suitable arguments and will be completely ignored when
using \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod}). Technically one could therefore simply use \texttt{IsObject} (\ref{IsObject}) for all arguments in the declaration. The main point of using more specific
filters here is to help documenting with which arguments the function is to be
used (so for example a call \texttt{SylowNormalizer(5,G)} would be invalid). 

 Of course initially there are no useful methods for newly declared operations;
you will have to write and install them yourself. 

 If the operation only takes one argument and has reproducible results without
side effects, it might be worth declaring it as an attribute instead; see
Section \ref{Adding a new Attribute}. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Adding a new Attribute}}\label{Adding a new Attribute}
\logpage{[ 80, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X874AF11D864AEC1B}{}
{
  \index{NewAttribute@\texttt{NewAttribute}!example} \index{DeclareAttribute@\texttt{DeclareAttribute}!example} Now we look at an example of how to add a new attribute. As example we
consider the set of all primes that divide the size of a group. 

 First we have to declare the attribute: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  PrimesDividingSize:=NewAttribute("PrimesDividingSize",IsGroup);
\end{Verbatim}
