 (See{\nobreakspace}\texttt{NewAttribute} (\ref{NewAttribute})). This implicitly declares attribute tester and setter, it is convenient
however to assign these to variables as well: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  HasPrimesDividingSize:=Tester(PrimesDividingSize);
  SetPrimesDividingSize:=Setter(PrimesDividingSize);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Alternatively, there is a declaration command \texttt{DeclareAttribute} (\ref{DeclareAttribute}) that executes all three assignments simultaneously and protects the variables
against overwriting: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareAttribute("PrimesDividingSize",IsGroup);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Next we have to install method(s) for the attribute that compute its value.
(This is not strictly necessary. We could use the attribute also without
methods only for storing and retrieving information, but calling it for
objects for which the value is not known would produce a ``no method found'' error.) For this purpose we can imagine the attribute simply as an
one\texttt{\symbol{45}}argument operation: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod(PrimesDividingSize,"for finite groups",
    [IsGroup and IsFinite],
  function(G)
    return PrimeDivisors(Size(G));
  end);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The function installed \emph{must} always return a value (or call \texttt{TryNextMethod} (\ref{TryNextMethod})). If the object is in the representation \texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep} (\ref{IsAttributeStoringRep}) this return value once computed will be automatically stored and retrieved if
the attribute is called a second time. We don't have to call setter or tester
ourselves. (This storage happens by \textsf{GAP} internally calling the attribute setter with the return value of the function.
Retrieval is by a high\texttt{\symbol{45}}ranking method which is installed
under the condition \texttt{HasPrimesDividingSize}. This method was installed automatically when the attribute was declared.) }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Adding a new Representation}}\label{Adding a new Representation}
\logpage{[ 80, 6, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8111D831783C9ED6}{}
{
  \index{NewRepresentation@\texttt{NewRepresentation}!example} \index{DeclareRepresentation@\texttt{DeclareRepresentation}!example} Next, we look at the implementation of a new representation of existing
objects. In most cases we want to implement this representation only for
efficiency reasons while keeping all the existing functionality. 

 For example, assume we wanted (following \cite{wielandt69}) to implement permutation groups defined by relations. 

 Next, we have to decide a few basics about the representation. All existing
permutation groups in the library are attribute storing and we probably want
to keep this for our new objects. Thus the representation must be a
subrepresentation of \texttt{IsComponentObjectRep} (\ref{IsComponentObjectRep}) and \texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep} (\ref{IsAttributeStoringRep}). Furthermore we want each object to be a permutation group and we can imply
this directly in the representation. 

 We also decide that we store the degree (the largest point that might be
moved) in a component \texttt{degree} and the defining relations in a component \texttt{relations} (we do not specify the format of relations here. In an actual implementation
one would have to design this as well, but it does not affect the declarations
this chapter is about). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareRepresentation(
    "IsPermutationGroupByRelations",
    IsComponentObjectRep and IsAttributeStoringRep and IsPermGroup,
    ["degree","relations"]);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 (If we wanted to implement sparse matrices we might for example rather settle
for a positional object in which we store a list of the nonzero entries.) 

 We can make the new representation a subrepresentation of an existing one. In
such a case of course we have to provide all structure of this ``parent'' representation as well. 

 Next we need to check in which family our new objects will be. This will be
the same family as of every other permutation group, namely the \texttt{CollectionsFamily(PermutationsFamily)} (where the family \texttt{PermutationsFamily = FamilyObj((1,2,3))} has been defined already in the library). 

 Now we can write a function to create our new objects. Usually it is helpful
to look at functions from the library that are used in similar situations (for
example \texttt{GroupByGenerators} (\ref{GroupByGenerators}) in our case) to make sure we have not forgotten any further requirements in
the declaration we might have to add here. However in most cases the function
is straightforward: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  PermutationGroupByRelations:=function(degree,relations)
  local g
    g:=Objectify(NewType(CollectionsFamily(PermutationsFamily),
                 IsPermutationGroupByRelations),
                 rec(degree:=degree,relations:=relations));
    return g;
  end;
\end{Verbatim}
 

 It also is a good idea to install a \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}) and possibly also a \texttt{ViewObj} (\ref{ViewObj}) method {\textendash}otherwise testing becomes quite hard: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod(PrintObj,"for perm grps. given by relations",
    [IsPermutationGroupByRelations],
  function(G)
    Print("PermutationGroupByRelations(", G!.degree,",",G!.relations,")");
  end);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Next we have to write enough methods for the new representation so that the
existing algorithms can be used. In particular we will have to implement
methods for all operations for which library or kernel provides methods for
the existing (alternative) representations. In our particular case there are
no such methods. (If we would have implemented sparse matrices we would have
had to implement methods for the list access and assignment functions, see \ref{Basic Operations for Lists}.) However the existing way permutation groups are represented is by
generators. To be able to use the existing machinery we want to be able to
obtain a generating set also for groups in our new representation. This can be
done (albeit not very effectively) by a stabilizer calculation in the
symmetric group given by the \texttt{degree} component. The operation function to use is probably a bit complicated and
will depend on the format of the \texttt{relations} (we have not specified in this example). In the following method we use \texttt{operationfunction} as a placeholder; 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod(GeneratorsOfGroup,"for perm grps. given by relations",
    [IsPermutationGroupByRelations],
  function(G)
  local S,U;
    S:=SymmetricGroup(G!.degree);
    U:=Stabilizer(S,G!.relations,  operationfunction );
    return GeneratorsOfGroup(U);
  end);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 This is all we \emph{must} do. Of course for performance reasons one might want to install methods for
further operations as well. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Components versus Attributes}}\label{Components versus Attributes}
\logpage{[ 80, 7, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86AA65D4815CAE95}{}
{
  In the last section we introduced two new components, \texttt{G!.degree} and \texttt{G!.relations}. Technically, we could have used attributes instead. There is no clear
distinction which variant is to be preferred: An attribute expresses part of
the functionality available to certain objects (and thus could be computed
later and probably even for a wider class of objects), a component is just
part of the internal definition of an object. 

 So if the data is ``of general interest'', if we want the user to have access to it, attributes are preferable.
Moreover, attributes can be used by the method selection (by specifying the
filter \texttt{HasAttr} for an attribute \texttt{Attr}). They provide a clean interface and their immutability makes it safe to hand
the data to a user who potentially could corrupt a components entries. 

 On the other hand more ``technical'' data (say the encoding of a sparse matrix) is better hidden from the user in a
component, as declaring it as an attribute would not give any advantage. 

 Resource\texttt{\symbol{45}}wise, attributes need more memory (the attribute
setter and tester are implicitly declared, and one filter bit is required),
the attribute access is one further function call in the kernel, thus
components might be an immeasurable bit faster. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Adding new Concepts}}\label{Adding new Concepts}
\logpage{[ 80, 8, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7E29DEC0813F8897}{}
{
  Now we look how to implement a new concept for existing objects and fit this
in the method selection. Three examples that will be made more explicit below
would be groups for which a ``length'' of elements (as a word in certain generators) is defined, groups that can be
decomposed as a semidirect product and M\texttt{\symbol{45}}groups. 

 In each case we have two possibilities for the declaration. We can either
declare it as a property or as a category. Both are eventually filter(s) and
in this way indistinguishable for the method selection. However, the value of
a property for a particular object can be unknown at first and later in the
session be computed (to be \texttt{true} or \texttt{false}). This is implemented by reserving two filters for each property, one
indicating whether the property value is known, and one, provided the value is
known, to indicate the actual boolean value. Contrary to this, the decision
whether or not an object lies in a category is taken at creation time and this
is implemented using a single filter. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{Property:}]  Properties also are attributes: If a property value is not known for an
object, \textsf{GAP} tries to find a method to compute the property value. If no suitable method is
found, an error is raised. 
\item[{Category:}]  An object is in a category if it has been created in it. Testing the category
for an object simply returns this value. Existing objects cannot enter a new
category later in life. This means that in most cases one has to write own
code to create objects in a new category. 

 If we want to implement a completely new concept so that new operations are
defined only for the new objects {\textendash}for example bialgebras for which
a second scalar multiplication is defined{\textendash} usually a category is
chosen. 

 Technically, the behaviour of the category \texttt{IsXYZ}, declared as subcategory of \texttt{IsABC} is therefore exactly the same as if we would declare \texttt{IsXYZ} to be a property for \texttt{IsABC} and install the following method: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod(IsXYZ,"return false if not known",[IsABC],ReturnFalse);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 (The word \texttt{category} also has a well\texttt{\symbol{45}}defined mathematical meaning, but this does
not need to concern us at this point. The set of objects which is defined to
be a (\textsf{GAP}) category does not need to be a category in the mathematical sense, vice
versa not every mathematical category is declared as a (\textsf{GAP}) category.) 
\end{description}
 Eventually the choice between category and property often becomes a matter of
taste or style. 

 Sometimes there is even a third possibility (if you have \textsf{GAP}{\nobreakspace}3 experience this might reflect most closely ``an object whose operations record is \texttt{XYOps}''): We might want to indicate this new concept simply by the fact that certain
attributes are set. In this case we could simply use the respective attribute
tester(s). 

 The examples given below each give a short argument why the respective
solution was chosen, but one could argue as well for other choices.  
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Example: M\texttt{\symbol{45}}groups}}\label{Example: M-groups}
\logpage{[ 80, 8, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7DC936877A3330D0}{}
{
    M\texttt{\symbol{45}}groups are finite groups for which all irreducible
complex representations are induced from linear representations of subgroups,
it turns out that they are all solvable and that every supersolvable group is
an M\texttt{\symbol{45}}group. See \cite{Isa76} for further details. 

 Solvability and supersolvability both are testable properties. We therefore
declare \texttt{IsMGroup} as a property for solvable groups: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  IsMGroup:=NewProperty("IsMGroup",IsSolvableGroup);
\end{Verbatim}
 The filter \texttt{IsSolvableGroup} (\ref{IsSolvableGroup}) in this declaration \emph{only} means that methods for \texttt{IsMGroup} by default can only be installed for groups that are (and know to be) solvable
(though they could be installed for more general situations using \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod})). It does not yet imply that M\texttt{\symbol{45}}groups are solvable. We
must do this deliberately via an implication and we use the same technique to
imply that every supersolvable group is an M\texttt{\symbol{45}}group. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallTrueMethod(IsSolvableGroup,IsMGroup);
  InstallTrueMethod(IsMGroup,IsSupersolvableGroup);
\end{Verbatim}
    

 Now we might install a method that tests for solvable groups whether they are
M\texttt{\symbol{45}}groups: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod(IsMGroup,"for solvable groups",[IsSolvableGroup],
  function(G)
    [... code omitted. The function must return `true' or `false' ...]
  end);
\end{Verbatim}
 Note that this example of declaring the \texttt{IsMGroup} property for solvable groups is not a part of the \textsf{GAP} library, which uses a similar but different filter \texttt{IsMonomialGroup} (\ref{IsMonomialGroup}). }

  
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Example: Groups with a word length}}\label{Example: Groups with a word length}
\logpage{[ 80, 8, 2 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7CD762FD82DED051}{}
{
  Our second example is that of groups for whose elements a \emph{word length} is defined. (We assume that the word length is only defined in the context of
the group with respect to a preselected generating set but not for single
elements alone. However we will not delve into any details of how this length
is defined and how it could be computed.) 

 Having a word length is a feature which enables other operations (for example
a ``word length'' function). This is exactly what categories are intended for and therefore we
use one. 

 First, we declare the category. All objects in this category are groups and so
we inherit the supercategory \texttt{IsGroup} (\ref{IsGroup}): 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareCategory("IsGroupWithWordLength",IsGroup);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 We also define the operation which is ``enabled'' by this category, the word length of a group element, which is defined for a
group and an element (remember that group elements are described by the
category \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse})): 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareOperation("WordLengthOfElement",[IsGroupWithWordLength,
    IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse]);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 We then would proceed by installing methods to compute the word length in
concrete cases and might for example add further operations to get shortest
words in cosets. }

  
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Example: Groups with a decomposition as semidirect product}}\label{Example: Groups with a decomposition as semidirect product}
\logpage{[ 80, 8, 3 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X782AC35979925C71}{}
{
  

 \index{DeclareAttribute"!example@\texttt{DeclareAttribute"!example}} The third example is groups which have a (nontrivial) decomposition as a
semidirect product. If this information has been found out, we want to be able
to use it in algorithms. (Thus we do not only need the fact \emph{that} there is a decomposition, but also the decomposition itself.) 

 We also want this to be applicable to every group and not only for groups
which have been explicitly constructed via \texttt{SemidirectProduct} (\ref{SemidirectProduct:for acting group, action, and a group}). 

 Instead we simply declare an attribute \texttt{SemidirectProductDecomposition} for groups. (Again, in this manual we don't go in the details of how such an
decomposition would look like). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareAttribute("SemidirectProductDecomposition",IsGroup);
\end{Verbatim}
 

 If a decomposition has been found, it can be stored in a group using \texttt{SetSemidirectProductDecomposition}. (At the moment all groups in \textsf{GAP} are attribute storing.) 

 Methods that rely on the existence of such a decomposition then get installed
for the tester filter \texttt{HasSemidirectProductDecomposition}.   }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Creating Own Arithmetic Objects}}\label{Creating Own Arithmetic Objects}
\logpage{[ 80, 9, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7BD325C5791C6A06}{}
{
  Finally let's look at a way to create new objects with a
user\texttt{\symbol{45}}defined arithmetic such that one can form for example
groups, rings or vector spaces of these elements. This topic is discussed in
much more detail in chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{An Example -- Designing Arithmetic Operations}, in this section we present a simple approach that may be useful to get
started but does not permit you to exploit all potential features. 

 The basic design is that the user designs some way to represent her objects in
terms of \textsf{GAP}s built\texttt{\symbol{45}}in types, for example as a list or a record. We
call this the ``defining data'' of the new objects. Also provided are functions that perform arithmetic on
this ``defining data'', that is they take objects of this form and return objects that represent the
result of the operation. The function \texttt{ArithmeticElementCreator} (\ref{ArithmeticElementCreator}) then is called to provide a wrapping such that proper new \textsf{GAP}\texttt{\symbol{45}}objects are created which can be multiplied etc. with the
default infix operations such as \texttt{*}. 

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{ArithmeticElementCreator}}
\logpage{[ 80, 9, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X87A88E3D7F6E2A7C}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ArithmeticElementCreator({\mdseries\slshape spec})\index{ArithmeticElementCreator@\texttt{ArithmeticElementCreator}}
\label{ArithmeticElementCreator}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 offers a simple interface to create new arithmetic elements by providing
functions that perform addition, multiplication and so forth, conforming to
the specification \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape spec}}. \texttt{ArithmeticElementCreator} creates a new category, representation and family for the new arithmetic
elements being defined, and returns a function which takes the ``defining data'' of an element and returns the corresponding new arithmetic element. 

 \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape spec}} is a record with one or more of the following components: 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{ElementName}}]  string used to identify the new type of object. A global identifier \texttt{Is\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ElementName}}} will be defined to indicate a category for these now objects. (Therefore it is
not clever to have blanks in the name). Also a collections category is
defined. (You will get an error message if the identifier \texttt{Is\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape ElementName}}} is already defined.) 
\item[{\texttt{Equality}, \texttt{LessThan}, \texttt{One}, \texttt{Zero}, \texttt{Multiplication}, \texttt{Inverse}, \texttt{Addition}, \texttt{AdditiveInverse}}]  functions defining the arithmetic operations. The functions interface on the
level of ``defining data'', the actual methods installed will perform the unwrapping and wrapping as
objects. Components are optional, but of course if no multiplication is
defined elements cannot be multiplied and so forth. 

 There are default methods for \texttt{Equality} and \texttt{LessThan} which simply calculate on the defining data. If one is defined, it must be
ensured that the other is compatible (so that $a < b$ implies not $(a = b)$) 
\item[{\texttt{Print}}]  a function which prints the object. By default, just the defining data is
printed. 
\item[{\texttt{MathInfo}}]  filters determining the mathematical properties of the elements created. A
typical value is for example \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse} for group elements. 
\item[{\texttt{RepInfo}}]  filters determining the representational properties of the elements created.
The objects created are always component objects, so in most cases the only
reasonable option is \texttt{IsAttributeStoringRep} to permit the storing of attributes. 
\end{description}
 

 All components are optional and will be filled in with default values (though
of course an empty record will not result in useful objects). 

 Note that the resulting objects are \emph{not equal} to their defining data (even though by default they print as only the defining
data). The operation \texttt{UnderlyingElement} can be used to obtain the defining data of such an element. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Example: ArithmeticElementCreator}}\label{expl:ArithmeticElementCreator}
\logpage{[ 80, 9, 2 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79E535CC7B82BA47}{}
{
  As the first example we look at subsets of $\{ 1, \ldots, 4 \}$ and define an ``addition'' as union and ``multiplication'' as intersection. These operations are both commutative and we want the
resulting elements to know this. 

 We therefore use the following specification: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# the whole set|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@w := [1,2,3,4];|
  [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@PosetElementSpec :=rec(|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  # name of the new elements|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  ElementName := "PosetOn4",|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  # arithmetic operations|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  One := a -> w,|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  Zero := a -> [],|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  Multiplication := function(a, b) return Intersection(a, b); end,|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  Addition := function(a, b) return Union(a, b); end,|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  # Mathematical properties of the elements|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@  MathInfo := IsCommutativeElement and|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@              IsAssociativeElement and|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@              IsAdditivelyCommutativeElement|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@);;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mkposet := ArithmeticElementCreator(PosetElementSpec);|
  function( x ) ... end
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Now we can create new elements, perform arithmetic on them and form domains: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a := mkposet([1,2,3]);|
  [ 1, 2, 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CategoriesOfObject(a);|
  [ "IsExtAElement", "IsNearAdditiveElement",
    "IsNearAdditiveElementWithZero", "IsAdditiveElement",
    "IsExtLElement", "IsExtRElement", "IsMultiplicativeElement",
    "IsMultiplicativeElementWithOne", "IsAssociativeElement",
    "IsAdditivelyCommutativeElement", "IsCommutativeElement",
    "IsPosetOn4" ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a=[1,2,3];|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UnderlyingElement(a)=[1,2,3];|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@b:=mkposet([2,3,4]);|
  [ 2, 3, 4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a+b;|
  [ 1 .. 4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a*b;|
  [ 2, 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@s:=Semigroup(a,b);|
  <commutative semigroup with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size(s);|
  3
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The categories \texttt{IsPosetOn4} and \texttt{IsPosetOn4Collection} can be used to install methods specific to the new objects. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsPosetOn4Collection(s);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

 }

          
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{An Example {\textendash} Residue Class Rings}}\label{An Example -- Residue Class Rings}
\logpage{[ 81, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8125CC6A87409887}{}
{
  In this chapter, we give an example how \textsf{GAP} can be extended by new data structures and new functionality. In order to
focus on the issues of the implementation, the mathematics in the example
chosen is trivial. Namely, we will discuss computations with elements of
residue class rings ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$. 

 The first attempt is straightforward (see Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{A First Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings}), it deals with the implementation of the necessary arithmetic operations.
Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Why Proceed in a Different Way?} deals with the question why it might be useful to use an approach that
involves creating a new data structure and integrating the algorithms dealing
with these new \textsf{GAP} objects into the system. Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{A Second Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings} shows how this can be done in our example, and Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Compatibility of Residue Class Rings with Prime Fields}, the question of further compatibility of the new objects with known \textsf{GAP} objects is discussed. Finally, Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Further Improvements in Implementing Residue Class Rings} gives some hints how to improve the implementation presented before.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{A First Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings}}\label{A First Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings}
\logpage{[ 81, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81008A74838A792E}{}
{
  Suppose we want to do computations with elements of a ring ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$, where $n$ is a positive integer. 

 First we have to decide how to represent the element $k + n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ in \textsf{GAP}. If the modulus $n$ is fixed then we can use the integer $k$. More precisely, we can use any integer $k'$ such that $k - k'$ is a multiple of $n$. If different moduli are likely to occur then using a list of the form $[ k, n ]$, or a record of the form \texttt{rec( residue := \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}, modulus := \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} )} is more appropriate. In the following, let us assume the list representation $[ k, n ]$ is chosen. Moreover, we decide that the residue $k$ in all such lists satisfies $0 \leq k < n$, i.e., the result of adding two residue classes represented by $[ k_1, n ]$ and $[ k_2, n ]$ (of course with same modulus $n$) will be $[ k, n ]$ with $k_1 + k_2$ congruent to $k$ modulo $n$ and $0 \leq k < n$. 

 Now we can implement the arithmetic operations for residue classes. Note that
the result of the \texttt{mod} operator is normalized as required. The division by a noninvertible residue
class results in \texttt{fail}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@resclass_sum := function( c1, c2 )|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   if c1[2] <> c2[2] then Error( "different moduli" ); fi;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   return [ ( c1[1] + c2[1] ) mod c1[2], c1[2] ];|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@end;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@resclass_diff := function( c1, c2 )|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   if c1[2] <> c2[2] then Error( "different moduli" ); fi;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   return [ ( c1[1] - c2[1] ) mod c1[2], c1[2] ];|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@end;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@resclass_prod := function( c1, c2 )|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   if c1[2] <> c2[2] then Error( "different moduli" ); fi;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   return [ ( c1[1] * c2[1] ) mod c1[2], c1[2] ];|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@end;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@resclass_quo := function( c1, c2 )|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   local quo;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   if c1[2] <> c2[2] then Error( "different moduli" ); fi;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   quo:= QuotientMod( c1[1], c2[1], c1[2] );|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   if quo <> fail then|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@     quo:= [ quo, c1[2] ];|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   fi;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   return quo;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@end;;|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 With these functions, we can in principle compute with residue classes. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@list:= List( [ 0 .. 3 ], k -> [ k, 4 ] );|
  [ [ 0, 4 ], [ 1, 4 ], [ 2, 4 ], [ 3, 4 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@resclass_sum( list[2], list[4] );|
  [ 0, 4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@resclass_diff( list[1], list[2] );|
  [ 3, 4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@resclass_prod( list[2], list[4] );|
  [ 3, 4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@resclass_prod( list[3], list[4] );|
  [ 2, 4 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List( list, x -> resclass_quo( list[2], x ) );|
  [ fail, [ 1, 4 ], fail, [ 3, 4 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Why Proceed in a Different Way?}}\label{Why Proceed in a Different Way?}
\logpage{[ 81, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X78B6425787FDB0E5}{}
{
  It depends on the computations we intended to do with residue classes whether
or not the implementation described in the previous section is satisfactory
for us. 

 Probably we are mainly interested in more complex data structures than the
residue classes themselves, for example in matrix algebras or matrix groups
over a ring such as ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / 4{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$. For this, we need functions to add, multiply, invert
etc.{\nobreakspace}matrices of residue classes. Of course this is not a
difficult task, but it requires to write additional \textsf{GAP} code. 

 And when we have implemented the arithmetic operations for matrices of residue
classes, we might be interested in domain operations such as computing the
order of a matrix group over ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / 4{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$, a Sylow $2$ subgroup, and so on. The problem is that a residue class represented as a pair $[ k, n ]$ is not regarded as a group element by \textsf{GAP}. We have not yet discussed how a matrix of residue classes shall be
represented, but if we choose the obvious representation of a list of lists of
our residue classes then also this is not a valid group element in \textsf{GAP}. Hence we cannot apply the function \texttt{Group} (\ref{Group:for a list of generators (and an identity element)}) to create a group of residue classes or a group of matrices of residue
classes. This is because \textsf{GAP} assumes that group elements can be multiplied via the infix operator \texttt{*} (equivalently, via the operation \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*} (\ref{bSlash*})). Note that in fact the multiplication of two lists $[ k_1, n ]$, $[ k_2, n ]$ is defined, but we have $[ k_1, n ] * [ k_2, n ] = k_1 * k_2 + n * n$, the standard scalar product of two row vectors of same length. That is, the
multiplication with \texttt{*} is not compatible with the function \texttt{resclass{\textunderscore}prod} introduced in the previous section. Similarly, ring elements are assumed to be
added via the infix operator \texttt{+}; the addition of residue classes is not compatible with the available
addition of row vectors. 

 What we have done in the previous section can be described as implementation
of a ``standalone'' arithmetic for residue classes. In order to use the machinery of the \textsf{GAP} library for creating higher level objects such as matrices, polynomials, or
domains over residue class rings, we have to ``integrate'' this implementation into the \textsf{GAP} library. The key step will be to create a new kind of \textsf{GAP} objects. This will be done in the following sections; there we assume that
residue classes and residue class rings are not yet available in \textsf{GAP}; in fact they are available, and their implementation is very close to what
is described here. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{A Second Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings}}\label{A Second Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings}
\logpage{[ 81, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X85B914DD81732492}{}
{
  Faced with the problem to implement elements of the rings ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$, we must define the \emph{types} of these elements as far as is necessary to distinguish them from other \textsf{GAP} objects. 

 As is described in Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Types of Objects}, the type of an object comprises several aspects of information about this
object; the \emph{family} determines the relation of the object to other objects, the \emph{categories} determine what operations the object admits, the \emph{representation} determines how an object is actually represented, and the \emph{attributes} describe knowledge about the object. 

 First of all, we must decide about the \emph{family} of each residue class. A natural way to do this is to put the elements of each
ring ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ into a family of their own. This means that for example elements of ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / 3{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / 9{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ lie in different families. So the only interesting relation between the
families of two residue classes is equality; binary arithmetic operations with
two residue classes will be admissible only if their families are equal. Note
that in the naive approach in Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{A First Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings}, we had to take care of different moduli by a check in each function; these
checks may disappear in the new approach because of our choice of families. 

 Note that we do not need to tell \textsf{GAP} anything about the above decision concerning the families of the objects that
we are going to implement, that is, the \emph{declaration part} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Declaration and Implementation Part}) of the little \textsf{GAP} package we are writing contains nothing about the distribution of the new
objects into families. (The actual construction of a family happens in the
function \texttt{MyZmodnZ} shown below.) 

 Second, we want to describe methods to add or multiply two elements in ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$, and these methods shall be not applicable to other \textsf{GAP} objects. The natural way to do this is to create a new \emph{category} in which all elements of all rings ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ lie. This is done as follows. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DeclareCategory( "IsMyZmodnZObj", IsScalar );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@cat:= CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObj );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@cat:= CategoryCollections( cat );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@cat:= CategoryCollections( cat );;|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 So all elements in the rings ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ will lie in the category \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj}, which is a subcategory of \texttt{IsScalar} (\ref{IsScalar}). The latter means that one can add, subtract, multiply and divide two such
elements that lie in the same family, with the obvious restriction that the
second operand of a division must be invertible. (The name \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj} is chosen because \texttt{IsZmodnZObj} (\ref{IsZmodnZObj}) is already defined in \textsf{GAP}, for an implementation of residue classes that is very similar to the one
developed in this manual chapter. Using this different name, one can simply
enter the \textsf{GAP} code of this chapter into a \textsf{GAP} session, either interactively or by reading a file with this code, and
experiment after each step whether the expected behaviour has been achieved,
and what is still missing.) 

 The next lines of \textsf{GAP} code above create the categories \texttt{CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObj )} and two higher levels of collections categories of this, which will be needed
later; it is important to create these categories before collections of the
objects in \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj} actually arise. 

 Note that the only difference between \texttt{DeclareCategory} (\ref{DeclareCategory}) and \texttt{NewCategory} (\ref{NewCategory}) is that in a call to \texttt{DeclareCategory} (\ref{DeclareCategory}), a variable corresponding to the first argument is set to the new category,
and this variable is read\texttt{\symbol{45}}only. The same holds for \texttt{DeclareRepresentation} (\ref{DeclareRepresentation}) and \texttt{NewRepresentation} (\ref{NewRepresentation}) etc. 

 There is no analogue of categories in the implementation in
Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{A First Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings}, since there it was not necessary to distinguish residue classes from other \textsf{GAP} objects. Note that the functions there assumed that their arguments were
residue classes, and the user was responsible not to call them with other
arguments. Thus an important aspect of types is to describe arguments of
functions explicitly. 

 Third, we must decide about the \emph{representation} of our objects. This is something we know already from Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{A First Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings}, where we chose a list of length two. Here we may choose between two
essentially different representations for the new \textsf{GAP} objects, namely as ``component object'' (record\texttt{\symbol{45}}like) or ``positional object'' (list\texttt{\symbol{45}}like). We decide to store the modulus of each residue
class in its family, and to encode the element $k + n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ by the unique residue in the range $[ 0 .. n-1 ]$ that is congruent to $k$ modulo $n$, and the object itself is chosen to be a positional object with this residue
at the first and only position (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Positional Objects}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DeclareRepresentation("IsMyModulusRep", IsPositionalObjectRep, [1]);|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The fourth ingredients of a type, \emph{attributes}, are usually of minor importance for element objects. In particular, we do
not need to introduce special attributes for residue classes. 

 Having defined what the new objects shall look like, we now declare a global
function (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Declaration and Implementation Part}), to create an element when family and residue are given. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DeclareGlobalFunction( "MyZmodnZObj" );|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Now we have declared what we need, and we can start to implement the missing
methods resp. functions; so the following command belongs to the \emph{implementation part} of our package (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Declaration and Implementation Part}). 

 The probably most interesting function is the one to construct a residue
class. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallGlobalFunction( MyZmodnZObj, function( Fam, residue )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return Objectify( NewType( Fam, IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep ),A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|                     [ residue mod Fam!.modulus ] );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that we normalize \texttt{residue} explicitly using \texttt{mod}; we assumed that the modulus is stored in \texttt{Fam}, so we must take care of this below. If \texttt{Fam} is a family of residue classes, and \texttt{residue} is an integer, \texttt{MyZmodnZObj} returns the corresponding object in the family \texttt{Fam}, which lies in the category \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj} and in the representation \texttt{IsMyModulusRep}. 

 \texttt{MyZmodnZObj} needs an appropriate family as first argument, so let us see how to get our
hands on this. Of course we could write a handy function to create such a
family for given modulus, but we choose another way. In fact we do not really
want to call \texttt{MyZmodnZObj} explicitly when we want to create residue classes. For example, if we want to
enter a matrix of residues then usually we start with a matrix of
corresponding integers, and it is more elegant to do the conversion via
multiplying the matrix with the identity of the required ring ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$; this is also done for the conversion of integral matrices to finite field
matrices. (Note that we will have to install a method for this.) So it is
often sufficient to access this identity, for example via \texttt{One( MyZmodnZ( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} ) )}, where \texttt{MyZmodnZ} returns a domain representing the ring ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ when called with the argument $n$. We decide that constructing this ring is a natural place where the creation
of the family can be hidden, and implement the function. (Note that the
declaration belongs to the declaration part, and the installation belongs to
the implementation part, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Declaration and Implementation Part}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|DeclareGlobalFunction( "MyZmodnZ" );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallGlobalFunction( MyZmodnZ, function( n )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   local F, R;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   if not IsPosInt( n ) thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     Error( "<n> must be a positive integer" );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   fi;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   # Construct the family of element objects of our ring.A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   F:= NewFamily( Concatenation( "MyZmod", String( n ), "Z" ),A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|                  IsMyZmodnZObj );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   # Install the data.A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   F!.modulus:= n;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   # Make the domain.A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   R:= RingWithOneByGenerators( [ MyZmodnZObj( F, 1 ) ] );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   SetIsWholeFamily( R, true );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   SetName( R, Concatenation( "(Integers mod ", String(n), ")" ) );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   # Return the ring.A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return R;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that the modulus \texttt{n} is stored in the component \texttt{modulus} of the family, as is assumed by \texttt{MyZmodnZ}. Thus it is not necessary to store the modulus in each element. When storing \texttt{n} with the \texttt{!.} operator as value of the component \texttt{modulus}, we used that all families are in fact represented as component objects
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects}). 

 We see that we can use \texttt{RingWithOneByGenerators} (\ref{RingWithOneByGenerators}) to construct a ring with one if we have the appropriate generators. The
construction via \texttt{RingWithOneByGenerators} (\ref{RingWithOneByGenerators}) makes sure that \texttt{IsRingWithOne} (\ref{IsRingWithOne}) (and \texttt{IsRing} (\ref{IsRing})) is \texttt{true} for each output of \texttt{MyZmodnZ}. So the main problem is to create the identity element of the ring, which in
our case suffices to generate the ring. In order to create this element via \texttt{MyZmodnZObj}, we have to construct its family first, at each call of \texttt{MyZmodnZ}. 

 Also note that we may enter known information about the ring. Here we store
that it contains the whole family of elements; this is useful for example when
we want to check the membership of an element in the ring, which can be
decided from the type of the element if the ring contains its whole elements
family. Giving a name to the ring causes that it will be printed via printing
the name. (By the way: This name \texttt{(Integers mod \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}})} looks like a call to \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod} (\ref{bSlashmod}) with the arguments \texttt{Integers} (\ref{Integers}) and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}; a construction of the ring via this call seems to be more natural than by
calling \texttt{MyZmodnZ}; later we shall install a \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod} (\ref{bSlashmod}) method in order to admit this construction.) 

 Now we can read the above code into \textsf{GAP}, and the following works already. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@R:= MyZmodnZ( 4 );|
  (Integers mod 4)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsRing( R );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@gens:= GeneratorsOfRingWithOne( R );|
  [ <object> ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 But of course this means just to ask for the information we have explicitly
stored in the ring. Already the questions whether the ring is finite and how
many elements it has, cannot be answered by \textsf{GAP}. Clearly we know the answers, and we could store them in the ring, by setting
the value of the property \texttt{IsFinite} (\ref{IsFinite}) to \texttt{true} and the value of the attribute \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}) to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} (the argument of the call to \texttt{MyZmodnZ}). If we do not want to do so then \textsf{GAP} could only try to find out the number of elements of the ring via forming the
closure of the generators under addition and multiplication, but up to now, \textsf{GAP} does not know how to add or multiply two elements of our ring. 

 So we must install some methods for arithmetic and other operations if the
elements are to behave as we want. 

 We start with a method for showing elements nicely on the screen. There are
different operations for this purpose. One of them is \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}), which is called for each argument in an explicit call to \texttt{Print} (\ref{Print}). Another one is \texttt{ViewObj} (\ref{ViewObj}), which is called in the read\texttt{\symbol{45}}eval\texttt{\symbol{45}}print
loop for each object. \texttt{ViewObj} (\ref{ViewObj}) shall produce short and human readable information about the object in
question, whereas \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}) shall produce information that may be longer and is (if reasonable) readable
by \textsf{GAP}. We cannot satisfy the latter requirement for a \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}) method because there is no way to make a family \textsf{GAP} readable. So we decide to display the expression \texttt{( k mod n )} for an object that is given by the residue \texttt{k} and the modulus \texttt{n}, which would be fine as a \texttt{ViewObj} (\ref{ViewObj}) method. Since the default for \texttt{ViewObj} (\ref{ViewObj}) is to call \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}), and since no other \texttt{ViewObj} (\ref{ViewObj}) method is applicable to our elements, we need only a \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}) method. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( PrintObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   Print( "( ", x![1], " mod ", FamilyObj(x)!.modulus, " )" );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 So we installed a method for the operation \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}) (first argument), and we gave it a suitable information message (second
argument), see{\nobreakspace}\ref{ApplicableMethod} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Tracing Methods} for applications of this information string. The third argument tells \textsf{GAP} that the method is applicable for objects that lie in the category \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj} and in the representation \texttt{IsMyModulusRep}. and the fourth argument is the method itself. More details about \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) can be found in{\nobreakspace}\ref{Method Installation}. 

 Note that the requirement \texttt{IsMyModulusRep} for the argument \texttt{x} allows us to access the residue as \texttt{x![1]}. Since the family of \texttt{x} has the component \texttt{modulus} bound if it is constructed by \texttt{MyZmodnZ}, we may access this component. We check whether the method installation has
some effect. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@gens;|
  [ ( 1 mod 4 ) ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Next we install methods for the comparison operations. Note that we can assume
that the residues in the representation chosen are normalized. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \=,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for two elements in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep, IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y ) return x![1] = y![1]; end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \<,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for two elements in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep, IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y ) return x![1] < y![1]; end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The third argument used in these installations specifies the required relation
between the families of the arguments (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Families}). This argument of a method installation, if present, is a function that
shall be applied to the families of the arguments. \texttt{IsIdenticalObj} (\ref{IsIdenticalObj}) means that the methods are applicable only if both arguments lie in the same
family. (In installations for unary methods, obviously no relation is
required, so this argument is left out there.) 

 Up to now, we see no advantage of the new approach over the one in
Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{A First Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings}. For a residue class represented as \texttt{[ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} ]}, the way it is printed on the screen is sufficient, and equality and
comparison of lists are good enough to define equality and comparison of
residue classes if needed. But this is not the case in other situations. For
example, if we would have decided that the residue \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}} need not be normalized then we would have needed functions in
Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{A First Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings} that compute whether two residue classes are equal, and which of two residue
classes is regarded as larger than another. Note that we are free to define
what ``larger'' means for objects that are newly introduced. 

 Next we install methods for the arithmetic operations, first for the additive
structure. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|B,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>B @gapinput|InstallMethod( \+,B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   "for two elements in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   [IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep, IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep],B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   function( x, y )B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   return MyZmodnZObj( FamilyObj( x ), x![1] + y![1] );B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   end );B
  @gapprompt|gap>B @gapinput|B
  @gapprompt|gap>B @gapinput|InstallMethod( ZeroOp,B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   "for element in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodnZObj ],B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   x -> MyZmodnZObj( FamilyObj( x ), 0 ) );B
  @gapprompt|gap>B @gapinput|B
  @gapprompt|gap>B @gapinput|InstallMethod( AdditiveInverseOp,B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   "for element in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],B
  @gapprompt|>B @gapinput|   x -> MyZmodnZObj( FamilyObj( x ), AdditiveInverse( x![1] ) ) );B
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Here the new approach starts to pay off. The method for the operation \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}+} (\ref{bSlash+}) allows us to use the infix operator \texttt{+} for residue classes. The method for \texttt{ZeroOp} (\ref{ZeroOp}) is used when we call this operation or the attribute \texttt{Zero} (\ref{Zero}) explicitly, and \texttt{ZeroOp} (\ref{ZeroOp}) it is also used when we ask for \texttt{0 * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rescl}}}, where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rescl}} is a residue class. 

 (Note that \texttt{Zero} (\ref{Zero}) and \texttt{ZeroOp} (\ref{ZeroOp}) are distinguished because \texttt{0 * \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}}} is guaranteed to return a \emph{mutable} result whenever a mutable version of this result exists in \textsf{GAP} {\textendash}for example if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape obj}} is a matrix{\textendash} whereas \texttt{Zero} (\ref{Zero}) is an attribute and therefore returns \emph{immutable} results; for our example there is no difference since the residue classes are
always immutable, nevertheless we have to install the method for \texttt{ZeroOp} (\ref{ZeroOp}). The same holds for \texttt{AdditiveInverse} (\ref{AdditiveInverse}), \texttt{One} (\ref{One}), and \texttt{Inverse} (\ref{Inverse}).) 

 Similarly, \texttt{AdditiveInverseOp} (\ref{AdditiveInverseOp}) can be either called directly or via the unary \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}} operator; so we can compute the additive inverse of the residue class \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rescl}} as \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{45}}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rescl}}}. 

 It is not necessary to install methods for subtraction, since this is handled
via addition of the additive inverse of the second argument if no other method
is installed. 

 Let us try what we can do with the methods that are available now. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:= gens[1];  y:= x + x;|
  ( 1 mod 4 )
  ( 2 mod 4 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@0 * x;  -x;|
  ( 0 mod 4 )
  ( 3 mod 4 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@y = -y;  x = y;  x < y;  -x < y;|
  true
  false
  true
  false
\end{Verbatim}
 

 We might want to admit the addition of integers and elements in rings ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$, where an integer is implicitly identified with its residue modulo $n$. To achieve this, we install methods to add an integer to an object in \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj} from the left and from the right. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \+,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/nZ (ModulusRep) and integer",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep, IsInt ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return MyZmodnZObj( FamilyObj( x ), x![1] + y );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \+,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for integer and element in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsInt, IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return MyZmodnZObj( FamilyObj( y ), x + y![1] );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Now we can do also the following. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@2 + x;  7 - x;  y - 2;|
  ( 3 mod 4 )
  ( 2 mod 4 )
  ( 0 mod 4 )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Similarly we install the methods dealing with the multiplicative structure. We
need methods to multiply two of our objects, and to compute identity and
inverse. The operation \texttt{OneOp} (\ref{OneOp}) is called when we ask for \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rescl}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}0}, and \texttt{InverseOp} (\ref{InverseOp}) is called when we ask for \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape rescl}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}1}. Note that the method for \texttt{InverseOp} (\ref{InverseOp}) returns \texttt{fail} if the argument is not invertible. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \*,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for two elements in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep, IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return MyZmodnZObj( FamilyObj( x ), x![1] * y![1] );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( OneOp,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodnZObj ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   elm -> MyZmodnZObj( FamilyObj( elm ), 1 ) );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( InverseOp,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( elm )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   local residue;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   residue:= QuotientMod( 1, elm![1], FamilyObj( elm )!.modulus );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   if residue <> fail thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     residue:= MyZmodnZObj( FamilyObj( elm ), residue );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   fi;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return residue;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 To be able to multiply our objects with integers, we need not (but we may, and
we should if we are going for efficiency) install special methods. This is
because in general, \textsf{GAP} interprets the multiplication of an integer and an additive object as
abbreviation of successive additions, and there is one generic method for such
a multiplication that uses only additions and {\textendash}in the case of a
negative integer{\textendash} taking the additive inverse. Analogously, there
is a generic method for powering by integers that uses only multiplications
and taking the multiplicative inverse. 

 Note that we could also interpret the multiplication with an integer as a
shorthand for the multiplication with the corresponding residue class. We are
lucky that this interpretation is compatible with the one that is already
available. If this would not be the case then of course we would get into
trouble by installing a concurrent multiplication that computes something
different from the multiplication that is already defined, since \textsf{GAP} does not guarantee which of the applicable methods is actually chosen
(see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Applicable Methods and Method Selection}). 

 Now we have implemented methods for the arithmetic operations for our
elements, and the following calculations work. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@y:= 2 * x;  z:= (-5) * x;|
  ( 2 mod 4 )
  ( 3 mod 4 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@y * z;  y * y;|
  ( 2 mod 4 )
  ( 0 mod 4 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@y^-1;  y^0;|
  fail
  ( 1 mod 4 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@z^-1;|
  ( 3 mod 4 )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 There are some other operations in \textsf{GAP} that we may want to accept our elements as arguments. An example is the
operation \texttt{Int} (\ref{Int}) that returns, e.g., the integral part of a rational number or the integer
corresponding to an element in a finite prime field. For our objects, we may
define that \texttt{Int} (\ref{Int}) returns the normalized residue. 

 Note that we \emph{define} this behaviour for elements but we \emph{implement} it for objects in the representation \texttt{IsMyModulusRep}. This means that if someone implements another representation of residue
classes then this person must be careful to implement \texttt{Int} (\ref{Int}) methods for objects in this new representation compatibly with our definition,
i.e., such that the result is independent of the representation. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( Int,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   z -> z![1] );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Another example of an operation for which we might want to install a method is \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod} (\ref{bSlashmod}). We make the ring print itself as \texttt{Integers} (\ref{Integers}) mod the modulus, and then it is reasonable to allow a construction this way,
which makes the \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}) output of the ring \textsf{GAP} readable. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( PrintObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for full collection Z/nZ",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObj ) and IsWholeFamily ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( R )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   Print( "(Integers mod ",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|          ElementsFamily( FamilyObj(R) )!.modulus, ")" );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \mod,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for `Integers', and a positive integer",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsIntegers, IsPosRat and IsInt ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( Integers, n ) return MyZmodnZ( n ); end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Let us try this. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Int( y );|
  2
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Integers mod 1789;|
  (Integers mod 1789)
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Probably it is not necessary to emphasize that with the approach of
Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{A First Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings}, installing methods for existing operations is usually not possible or at
least not recommended. For example, installing the function \texttt{resclass{\textunderscore}sum} defined in Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{A First Attempt to Implement Elements of Residue Class Rings} as a \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}+} (\ref{bSlash+}) method for adding two lists of length two (with integer entries) would not be
compatible with the general definition of the addition of two lists of same
length. Installing a method for the operation \texttt{Int} (\ref{Int}) that takes a list \texttt{[ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} ]} and returns \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape k}} would in principle be possible, since there is no \texttt{Int} (\ref{Int}) method for lists yet, but it is not sensible to do so because one can think of
other interpretations of such a list where different \texttt{Int} (\ref{Int}) methods could be installed with the same right. 

 As mentioned in Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{Why Proceed in a Different Way?}, one advantage of the new approach is that with the implementation we have up
to now, automatically also matrices of residue classes can be treated. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@r:= Integers mod 16;|
  (Integers mod 16)
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@x:= One( r );|
  ( 1 mod 16 )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mat:= IdentityMat( 2 ) * x;|
  [ [ ( 1 mod 16 ), ( 0 mod 16 ) ], [ ( 0 mod 16 ), ( 1 mod 16 ) ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mat[1][2]:= x;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mat;|
  [ [ ( 1 mod 16 ), ( 1 mod 16 ) ], [ ( 0 mod 16 ), ( 1 mod 16 ) ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Order( mat );|
  16
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mat + mat;|
  [ [ ( 2 mod 16 ), ( 2 mod 16 ) ], [ ( 0 mod 16 ), ( 2 mod 16 ) ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@last^4;|
  [ [ ( 0 mod 16 ), ( 0 mod 16 ) ], [ ( 0 mod 16 ), ( 0 mod 16 ) ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Such matrices, if they are invertible, are valid as group elements. One
technical problem is that the default algorithm for inverting matrices may
give up since Gaussian elimination need not be successful over rings
containing zero divisors. Therefore we install a simpleminded inversion method
that inverts an integer matrix. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( InverseOp,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for an ordinary matrix over a ring Z/nZ",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMatrix and IsOrdinaryMatrixA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     and CategoryCollections( CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObj ) ) ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( mat )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   local one, modulus;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   one:= One( mat[1][1] );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   modulus:= FamilyObj( one )!.modulus;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   mat:= InverseOp( List( mat, row -> List( row, Int ) ) );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   if mat <> fail thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     mat:= ( mat mod modulus ) * one;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   fi;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   if not IsMatrix( mat ) thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     mat:= fail;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   fi;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return mat;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Additionally we install a method for finding a domain that contains the matrix
entries; this is used by some \textsf{GAP} library functions. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InstallMethod( DefaultFieldOfMatrixGroup,|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@    "for a matrix group over a ring Z/nZ",|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@    [ IsMatrixGroup and CategoryCollections( CategoryCollections(|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@          CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObj ) ) ) ],|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@    G -> RingWithOneByGenerators([ One( Representative( G )[1][1] ) ]));|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Now we can deal with matrix groups over residue class rings. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mat2:= IdentityMat( 2 ) * x;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@mat2[2][1]:= x;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Group( mat, mat2 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( g );|
  3072
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Factors( last );|
  [ 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@syl3:= SylowSubgroup( g, 3 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@gens:= GeneratorsOfGroup( syl3 );|
  [ [ [ ( 1 mod 16 ), ( 7 mod 16 ) ], [ ( 11 mod 16 ), ( 14 mod 16 ) ]
       ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Order( gens[1] );|
  3
\end{Verbatim}
 

 It should be noted that this way more involved methods for matrix groups may
not be available. For example, many questions about a finite matrix group can
be delegated to an isomorphic permutation group via a
so\texttt{\symbol{45}}called ``nice monomorphism''; this can be controlled by the filter \texttt{IsHandledByNiceMonomorphism} (\ref{IsHandledByNiceMonomorphism}). 

 By the way, also groups of (invertible) residue classes can be formed, but
this may be of minor interest. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Group( x );;  Size( g );|
  #I  default `IsGeneratorsOfMagmaWithInverses' method returns `true' for
  [ ( 1 mod 16 ) ]
  1
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@g:= Group( 3*x );;  Size( g );|
  #I  default `IsGeneratorsOfMagmaWithInverses' method returns `true' for
  [ ( 3 mod 16 ) ]
  4
\end{Verbatim}
 

 (The messages above tell that \textsf{GAP} does not know a method for deciding whether the given elements are valid group
elements. We could add an appropriate \texttt{IsGeneratorsOfMagmaWithInverses} method if we would want.) 

 Having done enough for the elements, we may install some more methods for the
rings if we want to use them as arguments. These rings are finite, and there
are many generic methods that will work if they are able to compute the list
of elements of the ring, so we install a method for this. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InstallMethod( Enumerator,|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   "for full collection Z/nZ",|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   [ CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObj ) and IsWholeFamily ],|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   function( R )|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   local F;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   F:= ElementsFamily( FamilyObj(R) );|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   return List( [ 0 .. Size( R ) - 1 ], x -> MyZmodnZObj( F, x ) );|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   end );|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that this method is applicable only to full rings ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$, for proper subrings it would return a wrong result. Furthermore, it is not
required that the argument is a ring; in fact this method is applicable also
to the additive group formed by all elements in the family, provided that it
knows to contain the whole family. 

 Analogously, we install methods to compute the size, a random element, and the
units of full rings ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( Random,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for full collection Z/nZ",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObj ) and IsWholeFamily ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   R -> MyZmodnZObj( ElementsFamily( FamilyObj(R) ),A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|                   Random( 0, Size( R ) - 1 ) ) );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( Size,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for full ring Z/nZ",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObj ) and IsWholeFamily ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   R -> ElementsFamily( FamilyObj(R) )!.modulus );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( Units,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for full ring Z/nZ",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [     CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObj )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     and IsWholeFamily and IsRing ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( R )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   local F;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   F:= ElementsFamily( FamilyObj( R ) );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return List( PrimeResidues( Size(R) ), x -> MyZmodnZObj( F, x ) );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The \texttt{Units} (\ref{Units}) method has the disadvantage that the result is returned as a list (in fact
this list is also strictly sorted). We could improve the implementation by
returning the units as a group; if we do not want to take the full list of
elements as generators, we can use the function \texttt{GeneratorsPrimeResidues} (\ref{GeneratorsPrimeResidues}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InstallMethod( Units,|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   "for full ring Z/nZ",|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   [     CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObj )|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@     and IsWholeFamily and IsRing ],|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   function( R )|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   local G, gens;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   gens:= GeneratorsPrimeResidues( Size( R ) ).generators;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   if not IsEmpty( gens ) and gens[ 1 ] = 1 then|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@     gens:= gens{ [ 2 .. Length( gens ) ] };|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   fi;|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   gens:= Flat( gens ) * One( R );|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   return GroupByGenerators( gens, One( R ) );|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   end );|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Each ring ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ is finite, and we could install a method that returns \texttt{true} when \texttt{IsFinite} (\ref{IsFinite}) is called with ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ as argument. But we can do this more elegantly via installing a \emph{logical implication}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InstallTrueMethod( IsFinite,|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObj ) and IsDomain );|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 In effect, every domain that consists of elements in \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj} will automatically store that it is finite, even if \texttt{IsFinite} (\ref{IsFinite}) is not called for it. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Compatibility of Residue Class Rings with Prime Fields}}\label{Compatibility of Residue Class Rings with Prime Fields}
\logpage{[ 81, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X83127B258512C436}{}
{
  The above implementation of residue classes and residue class rings has at
least two disadvantages. First, if $p$ is a prime then the ring ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / p{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ is in fact a field, but the return values of \texttt{MyZmodnZ} are never regarded as fields because they are not in the category \texttt{IsMagmaWithInversesIfNonzero} (\ref{IsMagmaWithInversesIfNonzero}). Second, and this makes the example really interesting, there are already
elements of finite prime fields implemented in \textsf{GAP}, and we may want to identify them with elements in ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / p{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$. 

 To be more precise, elements of finite fields in \textsf{GAP} lie in the category \texttt{IsFFE} (\ref{IsFFE}), and there is already a representation, \texttt{IsInternalRep} (\ref{IsInternalRep}), of these elements via discrete logarithms. The aim of this section is to
make \texttt{IsMyModulusRep} an alternative representation of elements in finite prime fields. 

 Note that this is only one step towards the desired compatibility. Namely,
after having a second representation of elements in finite prime fields, we
may wish that the function \texttt{GF} (\ref{GF:for field size}) (which is the usual function to create finite fields in \textsf{GAP}) is able to return \texttt{MyZmodnZ( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} )} when \texttt{GF( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} )} is called for a prime \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}. Moreover, then we have to decide about a default representation of elements
in \texttt{GF( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} )} for primes \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} for which both representations are available. Of course we can force the new
representation by explicitly calling \texttt{MyZmodnZ} and \texttt{MyZmodnZObj} whenever we want, but it is not a priori clear in which situation which
representation is preferable. 

 The same questions will occur when we want to implement a new representation
for non\texttt{\symbol{45}}prime fields. The steps of this implementation will
be the same as described in this chapter, and we will have to achieve
compatibility with both the internal representation of elements in small
finite fields and the representation \texttt{IsMyModulusRep} of elements in arbitrary prime fields. 

 But let us now turn back to the task of this section. We first adjust the
setup of the declaration part of the previous section, and then repeat the
installations with suitable modifications. 

 (We should start a new \textsf{GAP} session for that, otherwise \textsf{GAP} will complain that the objects to be declared are already bound; additionally,
the methods installed above may be not compatible with the ones we want.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DeclareCategory( "IsMyZmodnZObj", IsScalar );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DeclareCategory( "IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime", IsMyZmodnZObj );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DeclareSynonym( "IsMyZmodpZObj", IsMyZmodnZObj and IsFFE );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DeclareRepresentation( "IsMyModulusRep", IsPositionalObjectRep, [ 1 ] );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DeclareGlobalFunction( "MyZmodnZObj" );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@DeclareGlobalFunction( "MyZmodnZ" );|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 As in the previous section, all (newly introduced) elements of rings ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ lie in the category \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj}. But now we introduce two subcategories, namely \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime} for all elements in rings ${\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} / n{\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}$ where $n$ is not a prime, and \texttt{IsMyZmodpZObj} for elements in finite prime fields. All objects in the latter are
automatically known to lie in the category \texttt{IsFFE} (\ref{IsFFE}) of finite field elements. 

 It would be reasonable if also those internally represented elements in the
category \texttt{IsFFE} (\ref{IsFFE}) that do in fact lie in a prime field would also lie in the category \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj} (and thus in fact in \texttt{IsMyZmodpZObj}). But this cannot be achieved because internally represented finite field
elements do in general not store whether they lie in a prime field. 

 As for the implementation part, again let us start with the definitions of \texttt{MyZmodnZObj} and \texttt{MyZmodnZ}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallGlobalFunction( MyZmodnZObj, function( Fam, residue )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   if IsFFEFamily( Fam ) thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     return Objectify( NewType( Fam, IsMyZmodpZObjA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|                                 and IsMyModulusRep ),A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|                   [ residue mod Characteristic( Fam ) ] );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   elseA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     return Objectify( NewType( Fam, IsMyZmodnZObjNonprimeA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|                                 and IsMyModulusRep ),A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|                   [ residue mod Fam!.modulus ] );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   fi;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|end );A
  
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallGlobalFunction( MyZmodnZ, function( n )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   local F, R;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   if not ( IsInt( n ) and IsPosRat( n ) ) thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     Error( "<n> must be a positive integer" );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   elif IsPrimeInt( n ) thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     # Construct the family of element objects of our field.A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     F:= FFEFamily( n );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     # Make the domain.A
