  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     R:= FieldOverItselfByGenerators( [ MyZmodnZObj( F, 1 ) ] );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     SetIsPrimeField( R, true );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   elseA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     # Construct the family of element objects of our ring.A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     F:= NewFamily( Concatenation( "MyZmod", String( n ), "Z" ),A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|                    IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     # Install the data.A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     F!.modulus:= n;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     # Make the domain.A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     R:= RingWithOneByGenerators( [ MyZmodnZObj( F, 1 ) ] );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     SetIsWholeFamily( R, true );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     SetName( R, Concatenation( "(Integers mod ",String(n),")" ) );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   fi;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   # Return the ring resp. field.A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return R;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that the result of \texttt{MyZmodnZ} with a prime as argument is a field that does not contain the whole family of
its elements, since all finite field elements of a fixed characteristic lie in
the same family. Further note that we cannot expect a family of finite field
elements to have a component \texttt{modulus}, so we use \texttt{Characteristic} (\ref{Characteristic}) to get the modulus. Requiring that \texttt{Fam!.modulus} works also if \texttt{Fam} is a family of finite field elements would violate the rule that an extension
of \textsf{GAP} should not force changes in existing code, in this case code dealing with
families of finite field elements. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( PrintObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   Print( "( ", x![1], " mod ", FamilyObj(x)!.modulus, " )" );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( PrintObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/pZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   Print( "( ", x![1], " mod ", Characteristic(x), " )" );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \=,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for two elements in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     IsMyZmodnZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y ) return x![1] = y![1]; end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The above method to check equality is independent of whether the arguments
have a prime or nonprime modulus, so we installed it for arguments in \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj}. Now we install also methods to compare objects in \texttt{IsMyZmodpZObj} with the ``old'' finite field elements. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \=,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/pZ (ModulusRep) and internal FFE",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep, IsFFE and IsInternalRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return DegreeFFE( y ) = 1 and x![1] = IntFFE( y );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \=,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for internal FFE and element in Z/pZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsFFE and IsInternalRep, IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return DegreeFFE( x ) = 1 and IntFFE( x ) = y![1];A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The situation with the operation \texttt{{\textless}} is more difficult. Of course we are free to define the comparison of objects
in \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime}, but for the finite field elements, the comparison must be compatible with
the predefined comparison of the ``old'' finite field elements. The definition of the \texttt{{\textless}} comparison of internally represented finite field elements can be found in
Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Finite Fields}. In situations where the documentation does not provide the required
information, one has to look it up in the \textsf{GAP} code; for example, the comparison in our case can be found in the appropriate
source code file of the \textsf{GAP} kernel. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \<,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for two elements in Z/nZ (ModulusRep, nonprime)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime and IsMyModulusRep,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y ) return x![1] < y![1]; end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \<,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for two elements in Z/pZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   local p, r;      # characteristic and primitive rootA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   if x![1] = 0 thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     return y![1] <> 0;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   elif y![1] = 0 thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     return false;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   elseA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     p:= Characteristic( x );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     r:= PrimitiveRootMod( p );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     return LogMod( x![1], r, p ) < LogMod( y![1], r, p );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   fi;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \<,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/pZ (ModulusRep) and internal FFE",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep, IsFFE and IsInternalRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return x![1] * One( y ) < y;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \<,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for internal FFE and element in Z/pZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsFFE and IsInternalRep, IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return x < y![1] * One( x );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Now we install the same methods for the arithmetic operations \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}+} (\ref{bSlash+}), \texttt{ZeroOp} (\ref{ZeroOp}), \texttt{AdditiveInverseOp} (\ref{AdditiveInverseOp}), \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*} (\ref{bSlash*}), and \texttt{OneOp} (\ref{OneOp}) as in the previous section, without listing them below. Also the same \texttt{Int} (\ref{Int}) method is installed for objects in \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj}. Note that it is compatible with the definition of \texttt{Int} (\ref{Int}) for finite field elements. And of course the same method for \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}mod} (\ref{bSlashmod}) is installed. 

 We have to be careful, however, with the methods for \texttt{InverseOp} (\ref{InverseOp}), \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/} (\ref{bSlash/}), and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}} (\ref{bSlash^}). These methods and the missing methods for arithmetic operations with one
argument in \texttt{IsMyModulusRep} and the other in \texttt{IsInternalRep} (\ref{IsInternalRep}) are given below. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \+,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/pZ (ModulusRep) and internal FFE",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep, IsFFE and IsInternalRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y ) return x![1] + y; end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \+,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for internal FFE and element in Z/pZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsFFE and IsInternalRep, IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y ) return x + y![1]; end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \*,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/pZ (ModulusRep) and internal FFE",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep, IsFFE and IsInternalRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y ) return x![1] * y; end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( \*,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for internal FFE and element in Z/pZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   IsIdenticalObj,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsFFE and IsInternalRep, IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x, y ) return x * y![1]; end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( InverseOp,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/nZ (ModulusRep, nonprime)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   local residue;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   residue:= QuotientMod( 1, x![1], FamilyObj(x)!.modulus );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   if residue <> fail thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     residue:= MyZmodnZObj( FamilyObj(x), residue );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   fi;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return residue;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( InverseOp,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for element in Z/pZ (ModulusRep)",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ IsMyZmodpZObj and IsMyModulusRep ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( x )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   local residue;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   residue:= QuotientMod( 1, x![1], Characteristic( FamilyObj(x) ) );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   if residue <> fail thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     residue:= MyZmodnZObj( FamilyObj(x), residue );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   fi;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return residue;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The operation \texttt{DegreeFFE} (\ref{DegreeFFE:for a FFE}) is defined for finite field elements, we need a method for objects in \texttt{IsMyZmodpZObj}. Note that we need not require \texttt{IsMyModulusRep} since no access to representation dependent data occurs. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@InstallMethod( DegreeFFE,|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   "for element in Z/pZ",|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   [ IsMyZmodpZObj ],|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@   z -> 1 );|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The methods for \texttt{Enumerator} (\ref{Enumerator}), \texttt{Random} (\ref{Random:for a list or collection}), \texttt{Size} (\ref{Size}), and \texttt{Units} (\ref{Units}), that we had installed in the previous section had all assumed that their
argument contains the whole family of its elements. So these methods make
sense only for the nonprime case. For the prime case, there are already
methods for these operations with argument a field. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( Enumerator,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for full ring Z/nZ",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime ) and IsWholeFamily ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( R )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   local F;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   F:= ElementsFamily( FamilyObj( R ) );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return List( [ 0 .. Size( R ) - 1 ], x -> MyZmodnZObj( F, x ) );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( Random,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for full ring Z/nZ",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime ) and IsWholeFamily ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   R -> MyZmodnZObj( ElementsFamily( FamilyObj( R ) ),A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|                   Random( 0, Size( R ) - 1 ) ) );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( Size,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for full ring Z/nZ",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [ CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime ) and IsWholeFamily ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   R -> ElementsFamily( FamilyObj( R ) )!.modulus );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallMethod( Units,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   "for full ring Z/nZ",A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   [     CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     and IsWholeFamily and IsRing ],A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   function( R )A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   local G, gens;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   gens:= GeneratorsPrimeResidues( Size( R ) ).generators;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   if not IsEmpty( gens ) and gens[ 1 ] = 1 thenA
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|     gens:= gens{ [ 2 .. Length( gens ) ] };A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   fi;A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   gens:= Flat( gens ) * One( R );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   return GroupByGenerators( gens, One( R ) );A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   end );A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|A
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|InstallTrueMethod( IsFinite,A
  @gapprompt|>A @gapinput|   CategoryCollections( IsMyZmodnZObjNonprime ) and IsDomain );A
\end{Verbatim}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Further Improvements in Implementing Residue Class Rings}}\label{Further Improvements in Implementing Residue Class Rings}
\logpage{[ 81, 5, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81CA1C7087A815DE}{}
{
  There are of course many possibilities to improve the implementation. 

 With the setup as described above, subsequent calls \texttt{MyZmodnZ( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} )} with the same \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}} yield incompatible rings in the sense that elements of one ring cannot be
added to elements of an other one. The solution for this problem is to keep a
global list of all results of \texttt{MyZmodnZ} in the current \textsf{GAP} session, and to return the stored values whenever possible. Note that this
approach would admit \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}) methods that produce \textsf{GAP} readable output. 

 One can improve the \texttt{Units} (\ref{Units}) method for the full ring in such a way that a group is returned and not only a
list of its elements; then the result of \texttt{Units} (\ref{Units}) can be used, e.{\nobreakspace}g., as input for the operation \texttt{SylowSubgroup} (\ref{SylowSubgroup}). 

 To make computations more efficient, one can install methods for \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{45}}}, \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}/} (\ref{bSlash/}), and \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}\texttt{\symbol{94}}} (\ref{bSlash^}); one reason for doing so may be that this avoids the unnecessary construction
of the additive or multiplicative inverse, or of intermediate powers. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( \-, "two elements in Z/nZ (ModulusRep)", ... );
  InstallMethod( \-, "Z/nZ-obj. (ModulusRep) and integer", ... );
  InstallMethod( \-, "integer and Z/nZ-obj. (ModulusRep)", ... );
  InstallMethod( \-, "Z/pZ-obj. (ModulusRep) and internal FFE", ... );
  InstallMethod( \-, "internal FFE and Z/pZ-obj. (ModulusRep)", ... );
  InstallMethod( \*, "Z/nZ-obj. (ModulusRep) and integer", ... );
  InstallMethod( \*, "integer and Z/nZ-obj. (ModulusRep)", ... );
  InstallMethod( \/, "two Z/nZ-objs. (ModulusRep, nonprime)", ... );
  InstallMethod( \/, "two Z/pZ-objs. (ModulusRep)", ... );
  InstallMethod( \/, "Z/nZ-obj. (ModulusRep) and integer", ... );
  InstallMethod( \/, "integer and Z/nZ-obj. (ModulusRep)", ... );
  InstallMethod( \/, "Z/pZ-obj. (ModulusRep) and internal FFE", ... );
  InstallMethod( \/, "internal FFE and Z/pZ-obj. (ModulusRep)", ... );
  InstallMethod( \^, "Z/nZ-obj. (ModulusRep, nonprime) & int.", ... );
  InstallMethod( \^, "Z/pZ-obj. (ModulusRep), and integer", ... );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The call to \texttt{NewType} (\ref{NewType}) in \texttt{MyZmodnZObj} can be avoided by storing the required type, e.g., in the family. But note
that it is \emph{not} admissible to take the type of an existing object as first argument of \texttt{Objectify} (\ref{Objectify}). For example, suppose two objects in \texttt{IsMyZmodnZObj} shall be added. Then we must not use the type of one of the arguments in a
call of \texttt{Objectify} (\ref{Objectify}), because the argument may have knowledge that is not correct for the result
of the addition. One may think of the property \texttt{IsOne} (\ref{IsOne}) that may hold for both arguments but certainly not for their sum. 

 For comparing two objects in \texttt{IsMyZmodpZObj} via ``\texttt{{\textless}}'', we had to install a quite expensive method because of the compatibility with
the comparison of finite field elements that did already exist. In fact \textsf{GAP} supports finite fields with elements represented via discrete logarithms only
up to a given size. So in principle we have the freedom to define a cheaper
comparison via ``\texttt{{\textless}}'' for objects in \texttt{IsMyZmodpZObj} if the modulus is large enough. This is possible by introducing two categories \texttt{IsMyZmodpZObjSmall} and \texttt{IsMyZmodpZObjLarge}, which are subcategories of \texttt{IsMyZmodpZObj}, and to install different \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}} (\ref{bSlash<}) methods for pairs of objects in these categories. }

 }

          
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{An Example {\textendash} Designing Arithmetic Operations}}\label{An Example -- Designing Arithmetic Operations}
\logpage{[ 82, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7E485C967A5778C9}{}
{
  In this chapter, we give a {\textendash}hopefully typical{\textendash} example
of extending \textsf{GAP} by new objects with prescribed arithmetic operations (for a simple approach
that may be useful to get started though does not permit to exploit all
potential features, see also \texttt{ArithmeticElementCreator} (\ref{ArithmeticElementCreator})).  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{New Arithmetic Operations vs. New Objects}}\label{New Arithmetic Operations vs. New Objects}
\logpage{[ 82, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7EA9422E7ACA7276}{}
{
  A usual procedure in mathematics is the definition of new operations for given
objects; here are a few typical examples. The Lie bracket defines an
interesting new multiplicative structure on a given (associative) algebra.
Forming a group ring can be viewed as defining a new addition for the elements
of the given group, and extending the multiplication to sums of group elements
in a natural way. Forming the exterior algebra of a given vector space can be
viewed as defining a new multiplication for the vectors in a natural way. 

 \textsf{GAP} does \emph{not} support such a procedure. The main reason for this is that in \textsf{GAP}, the multiplication in a group, a ring etc.{\nobreakspace}is always written
as \texttt{*}, and the addition in a vector space, a ring etc.{\nobreakspace} is always
written as \texttt{+}. Therefore it is not possible to define the Lie bracket as a ``second multiplication'' for the elements of a given algebra; in fact, the multiplication in Lie
algebras in \textsf{GAP} is denoted by \texttt{*}. Analogously, constructing the group ring as sketched above is impossible if
an addition is already defined for the elements; note the difference between
the usual addition of matrices and the addition in the group ring of a matrix
group! (See Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Magma Rings} for an example.) Similarly, there is already a multiplication defined for row
vectors (yielding the standard scalar product), hence these vectors cannot be
regarded as elements of the exterior algebra of the space. 

 In situations such as the ones mentioned above, \textsf{GAP}'s way to deal with the structures in question is the following. Instead of
defining \emph{new} operations for the \emph{given} objects, \emph{new} objects are created to which the \emph{given} arithmetic operations \texttt{*} and \texttt{+} are then made applicable. 

 With this construction, matrix Lie algebras consist of matrices that are
different from the matrices with associative multiplication; technically, the
type of a matrix determines how it is multiplied with other matrices
(see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{IsMatrix} (\ref{IsMatrix})). A matrix with the Lie bracket as its multiplication can be created with the
function \texttt{LieObject} (\ref{LieObject}) from a matrix with the usual associative multiplication. 

 Group rings (more general: magma rings, see Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Magma Rings}) can be constructed with \texttt{FreeMagmaRing} (\ref{FreeMagmaRing}) from a coefficient ring and a group. The elements of the group are not
contained in such a group ring, one has to use an embedding map for creating a
group ring element that corresponds to a given group element. 

 It should be noted that the \textsf{GAP} approach to the construction of Lie algebras from associative algebras is
generic in the sense that all objects in the filter \texttt{IsLieObject} (\ref{IsLieObject}) use the same methods for their addition, multiplication etc., by delegating to
the ``underlying'' objects of the associative algebra, no matter what these objects actually are.
Analogously, also the construction of group rings is generic. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Designing new Multiplicative Objects}}\label{Designing new Multiplicative Objects}
\logpage{[ 82, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7BE9D84482B421F9}{}
{
  The goal of this section is to implement objects with a prescribed
multiplication. Let us assume that we are given a field $F$, and that we want to define a new multiplication $*$ on $F$ that is given by $a * b = a b - a - b + 2$; here $a b$ denotes the ordinary product in $F$. 

 By the discussion in Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{New Arithmetic Operations vs. New Objects}, we know that we cannot define a new multiplication on $F$ itself but have to create new objects. 

 We want to distinguish these new objects from all other \textsf{GAP} objects, in order to describe for example the situation that two of our
objects shall be multiplied. This distinction is made via the \emph{type} of the objects. More precisely, we declare a new \emph{filter}, a function that will return \texttt{true} for our new objects, and \texttt{false} for all other \textsf{GAP} objects. This can be done by calling \texttt{DeclareFilter} (\ref{DeclareFilter}), but since our objects will know about the value already when they are
constructed, the filter can be created with \texttt{DeclareCategory} (\ref{DeclareCategory}) or \texttt{NewCategory} (\ref{NewCategory}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareCategory( "IsMyObject", IsObject );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The idea is that the new multiplication will be installed only for objects
that ``lie in the category \texttt{IsMyObject}''. 

 The next question is what internal data our new objects store, and how they
are accessed. The easiest solution is to store the ``underlying'' object from the field $F$. \textsf{GAP} provides two general possibilities how to store this, namely
record\texttt{\symbol{45}}like and list\texttt{\symbol{45}}like structures
(for examples, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Component Objects} and{\nobreakspace}\ref{Positional Objects}). We decide to store the data in a list\texttt{\symbol{45}}like structure, at
position 1. This \emph{representation} is declared as follows. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareRepresentation( "IsMyObjectListRep", IsPositionalObjectRep, [ 1 ] );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Of course we can argue that this declaration is superfluous because \emph{all} objects in the category \texttt{IsMyObject} will be represented this way; it is possible to proceed like that, but often
(in more complicated situations) it turns out to be useful that several
representations are available for ``the same element''. 

 For creating the type of our objects, we need to specify to which \emph{family} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Families}) the objects shall belong. For the moment, we need not say anything about
relations to other \textsf{GAP} objects, thus the only requirement is that all new objects lie in the \emph{same} family; therefore we create a \emph{new} family. Also we are not interested in properties that some of our objects have
and others do not have, thus we need only one type, and store it in a global
variable. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  MyType:= NewType( NewFamily( "MyFamily" ),
                    IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The next step is to write a function that creates a new object. It may look as
follows. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  MyObject:= val -> Objectify( MyType, [ Immutable( val ) ] );
\end{Verbatim}
 Note that we store an \emph{immutable copy} of the argument in the returned object; without doing so, for example if the
argument would be a mutable matrix then the corresponding new object would be
changed whenever the matrix is changed (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Mutability and Copyability} for more details about mutability). 

 Having entered the above \textsf{GAP} code, we can create some of our objects. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|a:= MyObject( 3 );  b:= MyObject( 5 );A
  <object>
  <object>
  @gapprompt|gap>A @gapinput|a![1];  b![1];A
  3
  5
\end{Verbatim}
 But clearly a lot is missing. Besides the fact that the desired multiplication
is not yet installed, we see that also the way how the objects are printed is
not satisfactory. 

 Let us improve the latter first. There are two \textsf{GAP} functions \texttt{View} (\ref{View}) and \texttt{Print} (\ref{Print}) for showing objects on the screen. \texttt{View} (\ref{View}) is thought to show a short and human readable form of the object, and \texttt{Print} (\ref{Print}) is thought to show a not necessarily short form that is \textsf{GAP} readable whenever this makes sense. We decide to show \texttt{a} as \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape 3}}} by \texttt{View} (\ref{View}), and to show the construction \texttt{MyObject( 3 )} by \texttt{Print} (\ref{Print}); the methods are installed for the underlying operations \texttt{ViewObj} (\ref{ViewObj}) and \texttt{PrintObj} (\ref{PrintObj}). 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( ViewObj,
      "for object in `IsMyObject'",
      [ IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep ],
      function( obj )
      Print( "<", obj![1], ">" );
      end );
  
  InstallMethod( PrintObj,
      "for object in `IsMyObject'",
      [ IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep ],
      function( obj )
      Print( "MyObject( ", obj![1], " )" );
      end );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 This is the result of the above installations. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a; Print( a, "\n" );|
  <3>
  MyObject( 3 )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 And now we try to install the multiplication. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( \*,
      "for two objects in `IsMyObject'",
      [ IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep,
        IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep ],
      function( a, b )
      return MyObject( a![1] * b![1] - a![1] - b![1] + 2 );
      end );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 When we enter the above code, \textsf{GAP} runs into an error. This is due to the fact that the operation \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*} (\ref{bSlash*}) is declared for two arguments that lie in the category \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElement} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElement}). One could circumvent the check whether the method matches the declaration of
the operation, by calling \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod}) instead of \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}). But it would make sense if our objects would lie in \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElement} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElement}), for example because some generic methods for objects with multiplication
would be available then, such as powering by positive integers via repeated
squaring. So we want that \texttt{IsMyObject} implies \texttt{IsMultiplicativeElement} (\ref{IsMultiplicativeElement}). The easiest way to achieve such implications is to use the implied filter as
second argument of the \texttt{DeclareCategory} (\ref{DeclareCategory}) call; but since we do not want to start anew, we can also install the
implication afterwards. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallTrueMethod( IsMultiplicativeElement, IsMyObject );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Afterwards, installing the multiplication works without problems. Note that \texttt{MyType} and therefore also \texttt{a} and \texttt{b} are \emph{not} affected by this implication, so we construct them anew. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MyType:= NewType( NewFamily( "MyFamily" ),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@                     IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:= MyObject( 3 );;  b:= MyObject( 5 );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a*b;  a^27;|
  <9>
  <134217729>
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Powering the new objects by negative integers is not possible yet, because \textsf{GAP} does not know how to compute the inverse of an element $a$, say, which is defined as the unique element $a'$ such that both $a a'$ and $a' a$ are ``the unique multiplicative neutral element that belongs to $a$''. 

 And also this neutral element, if it exists, cannot be computed by \textsf{GAP} in our current situation. It does, however, make sense to ask for the
multiplicative neutral element of a given magma, and for inverses of elements
in the magma. 

 But before we can form domains of our objects, we must define when two objects
are regarded as equal; note that this is necessary in order to decide about
the uniqueness of neutral and inverse elements. In our situation, equality is
defined in the obvious way. For being able to form sets of our objects, also
an ordering via \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}{\textless}} (\ref{bSlash<}) is defined for them. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( \=,
      "for two objects in `IsMyObject'",
      [ IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep,
        IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep ],
      function( a, b )
      return a![1] = b![1];
      end );
  
  InstallMethod( \<,
      "for two objects in `IsMyObject'",
      [ IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep,
        IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep ],
      function( a, b )
      return a![1] < b![1];
      end );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Let us look at an example. We start with finite field elements because then
the domains are finite, hence the generic methods for such domains will have a
chance to succeed. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:= MyObject( Z(7) );|
  <Z(7)>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@m:= Magma( a );|
  <magma with 1 generator>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@e:= MultiplicativeNeutralElement( m );|
  <Z(7)^2>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@elms:= AsList( m );|
  [ <Z(7)>, <Z(7)^2>, <Z(7)^5> ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ForAll( elms, x -> ForAny( elms, y -> x*y = e and y*x = e ) );|
  true
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List( elms, x -> First( elms, y -> x*y = e and y*x = e ) );|
  [ <Z(7)^5>, <Z(7)^2>, <Z(7)> ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 So a multiplicative neutral element exists, in fact all elements in the magma \texttt{m} are invertible. But what about the following. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@b:= MyObject( Z(7)^0 );  m:= Magma( a, b );|
  <Z(7)^0>
  <magma with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@elms:= AsList( m );|
  [ <Z(7)^0>, <Z(7)>, <Z(7)^2>, <Z(7)^5> ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@e:= MultiplicativeNeutralElement( m );|
  <Z(7)^2>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ForAll( elms, x -> ForAny( elms, y -> x*y = e and y*x = e ) );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@List( elms, x -> b * x );|
  [ <Z(7)^0>, <Z(7)^0>, <Z(7)^0>, <Z(7)^0> ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Here we found a multiplicative neutral element, but the element \texttt{b} does not have an inverse. If an addition would be defined for our elements
then we would say that \texttt{b} behaves like a zero element. 

 When we started to implement the new objects, we said that we wanted to define
the new multiplication for elements of a given field $F$. In principle, the current implementation would admit also something like \texttt{MyObject( 2 ) * MyObject( Z(7) )}. But if we decide that our initial assumption holds, we may define the
identity and the inverse of the object \texttt{{\textless}a{\textgreater}} as \texttt{{\textless}2*e{\textgreater}} and \texttt{{\textless}a/(a\texttt{\symbol{45}}e){\textgreater}}, respectively, where \texttt{e} is the identity element in $F$ and \texttt{/} denotes the division in $F$; note that the element \texttt{{\textless}e{\textgreater}} is not invertible, and that the above definitions are determined by the
multiplication defined for our objects. Further note that after the
installations shown below, also \texttt{One( MyObject( 1 ) )} is defined. 

 (For technical reasons, we do not install the intended methods for the
attributes \texttt{One} (\ref{One}) and \texttt{Inverse} (\ref{Inverse}) but for the operations \texttt{OneOp} (\ref{OneOp}) and \texttt{InverseOp} (\ref{InverseOp}). This is because for certain kinds of objects {\textendash}mainly
matrices{\textendash} one wants to support a method to compute a \emph{mutable} identity or inverse, and the attribute needs only a method that takes this
object, makes it immutable, and then returns this object. As stated above, we
only want to deal with immutable objects, so this distinction is not really
interesting for us.) 

 A more interesting point to note is that we should mark our objects as likely
to be invertible, since we add the possibility to invert them. Again, this
could have been part of the declaration of \texttt{IsMyObject}, but we may also formulate an implication for the existing category. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallTrueMethod( IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse, IsMyObject );
  
  InstallMethod( OneOp,
      "for an object in `IsMyObject'",
      [ IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep ],
      a -> MyObject( 2 * One( a![1] ) ) );
  
  InstallMethod( InverseOp,
      "for an object in `IsMyObject'",
      [ IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep ],
      a -> MyObject( a![1] / ( a![1] - One( a![1] ) ) ) );
\end{Verbatim}
 Now we can form groups of our (nonzero) elements. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MyType:= NewType( NewFamily( "MyFamily" ),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@                  IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep );;|
  gap>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:= MyObject( Z(7) );|
  <Z(7)>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@b:= MyObject( 0*Z(7) );  g:= Group( a, b );|
  <0*Z(7)>
  <group with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( g );|
  6
\end{Verbatim}
 

 We are completely free to define an \emph{addition} for our elements, a natural one is given by \texttt{{\textless}a{\textgreater} + {\textless}b{\textgreater} =
{\textless}a+b\texttt{\symbol{45}}1{\textgreater}}. As we did for the multiplication, we first change \texttt{IsMyObject} such that the additive structure is also known. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallTrueMethod( IsAdditiveElementWithInverse, IsMyObject );
\end{Verbatim}
 Next we install the methods for the addition, and those to compute the
additive neutral element and the additive inverse. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|B,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( \+,
      "for two objects in `IsMyObject'",
      [ IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep,
        IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep ],
      function( a, b )
      return MyObject( a![1] + b![1] - 1 );
      end );
  
  InstallMethod( ZeroOp,
      "for an object in `IsMyObject'",
      [ IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep ],
      a -> MyObject( One( a![1] ) ) );
  
  InstallMethod( AdditiveInverseOp,
      "for an object in `IsMyObject'",
      [ IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep ],
      a -> MyObject( a![1] / ( a![1] - One( a![1] ) ) ) );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Let us try whether the addition works. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MyType:= NewType( NewFamily( "MyFamily" ),|
  !gapprompt@>| !gapinput@                  IsMyObject and IsMyObjectListRep );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a:= MyObject( Z(7) );;  b:= MyObject( 0*Z(7) );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@m:= AdditiveMagma( a, b );|
  <additive magma with 2 generators>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Size( m );|
  7
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Similar as installing a multiplication automatically makes powering by
integers available, multiplication with integers becomes available with the
addition. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@2 * a;|
  <Z(7)^5>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@a+a;|
  <Z(7)^5>
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@MyObject( 2*Z(7)^0 ) * a;|
  <Z(7)>
\end{Verbatim}
 

 In particular we see that this multiplication does \emph{not} coincide with the multiplication of two of our objects, that is, an integer \emph{cannot} be used as a shorthand for one of the new objects in a multiplication. 

 (It should be possible to create a \emph{field} with the new multiplication and addition. Currently this fails, due to missing
methods for computing several kinds of generators from field generators, for
computing the characteristic in the case that the family does not know this in
advance, for checking with \texttt{AsField} (\ref{AsField}) whether a domain is in fact a field, for computing the closure as a field.) 

 It should be emphasized that the mechanism described above may be not suitable
for the situation that one wants to consider many different multiplications ``on the same set of objects'', since the installation of a new multiplication requires the declaration of
at least one new filter and the installation of several methods. But the
design of \textsf{GAP} is not suitable for such dynamic method installations. 

 Turning this argument the other way round, the implementation of the new
arithmetics defined by the above multiplication and addition is available for
any field $F$, one need not repeat it for each field one is interested in. 

 Similar to the above situation, the construction of a magma ring $RM$ from a coefficient ring $R$ and a magma $M$ is implemented only once, since the definition of the arithmetic operations
depends only on the given multiplication of $M$ and not on $M$ itself. So the addition is not implemented for the elements in $M$ or {\textendash}more precisely{\textendash} for an isomorphic copy. In some
sense, the addition is installed ``for the multiplication'', and as mentioned in Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{New Arithmetic Operations vs. New Objects}, there is only one multiplication \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}*} (\ref{bSlash*}) in \textsf{GAP}. }

 }

          
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Library Files}}\label{Library Files}
\logpage{[ 83, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X848C952A87FB36E2}{}
{
  This chapter describes some of the conventions used in the \textsf{GAP} library files. These conventions are intended as a help on how to read library
files and how to find information in them. So everybody is recommended to
follow these conventions, although they do not prescribe a compulsory
programming style {\textendash}\textsf{GAP} itself will not bother with the formatting of files. 

 Filenames have traditionally \textsf{GAP} adhered to the 8+3 convention (to make it possible to use the same filenames
even on a MS\texttt{\symbol{45}}DOS file system) and been in lower case
(systems that do not recognize lower case in file names will convert them
automatically to upper case). It is no longer so important to adhere to these
conventions, but at the very least filenames should adhere to a 16+5
convention, and be distinct even after identifying upper and lower case.
Directory names of packages, however, \emph{must} be in lower case (the \texttt{LoadPackage} (\ref{LoadPackage}) command assumes this).  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{File Types}}\label{File Types}
\logpage{[ 83, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7FF5DC397C79392C}{}
{
  The \textsf{GAP} library consists of the following types of files, distinguished by their
suffixes: 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{.g} }]  Files which contain parts of the ``inner workings'' of \textsf{GAP}. These files usually do not contain mathematical functionality, except for
providing links to kernel functions. 
\item[{\texttt{.gd} }]  Declaration files. These files contain declarations of all categories,
attributes, operations, and global functions. These files also contain the
operation definitions in comments. 
\item[{\texttt{.gi} }]  Implementation files. These files contain all installations of methods and
global functions. Usually declarations of representations are also considered
to be part of the implementation and are therefore found in the \texttt{.gi} files. 
\end{description}
 

 As a rule of thumb, all \texttt{.gd} files are read in before the \texttt{.gi} files are read. Therefore a \texttt{.gi} file usually may use any operation or global function (it has been declared
before), and no care has to be taken towards the order in which the \texttt{.gi} files are read. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Finding Implementations in the Library}}\label{Finding Implementations in the Library}
\logpage{[ 83, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X845CCBE082CDF4BB}{}
{
  For a concretely given function, you can use \texttt{FilenameFunc} (\ref{FilenameFunc}) and \texttt{StartlineFunc} (\ref{StartlineFunc}) for finding the file where this function is defined, and the line in this file
where the definition of this function starts. This does not work for arbitrary
functions, see Section \texttt{FilenameFunc} (\ref{FilenameFunc}) for the restrictions. 

 If you are interested in getting the function which implements a method for
specific arguments, you can use \ref{ApplicableMethod}. If \texttt{FilenameFunc} (\ref{FilenameFunc}) does not work for this method then setting the print level of \ref{ApplicableMethod} higher will give you the installation string for this method, which can be
used for searching in library files. 

 To find the occurrence of functions, methods, function names, and installation
strings in the library, one can use the \texttt{grep} tool under UNIX. To find a function, search for the function name in the \texttt{.gd} files; as global variables are usually declared only once, only few files will
show up. The function installation is likely to occur in the corresponding \texttt{.gi} file. 

 To find a method from the known operation name and the installation string,
search for the string ``\texttt{Method(}'' (this catches both \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) and \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod})) and the installation string or the operation name. 

 The following tools from the \textsf{GAP} package \textsf{Browse} can be used for accessing the code of functions. 

 
\begin{itemize}
\item  \texttt{BrowseGapMethods} (\textbf{Browse: BrowseGapMethods see BrowseGapData}) shows an overview of \textsf{GAP}'s operations and methods, and allows one to navigate through the files that
contain the implementations of the methods, using a pager. 
\item  \texttt{BrowseProfile} (\textbf{Browse: BrowseProfile}) shows profiling results (similar to \texttt{DisplayProfile} (\ref{DisplayProfile})) and allows one to navigate through the files that contain the
implementations of the functions that were actually used, using a pager. 
\end{itemize}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Undocumented Variables}}\label{Undocumented Variables}
\logpage{[ 83, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X801428EB86E7113C}{}
{
  For several global variables in \textsf{GAP}, no information is available via the help system (see Section{\nobreakspace} (\textbf{Tutorial: Help}), for a quick overview of the help system, or Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{The Help System}, for details). There are various reasons for ``hiding'' a variable from the user; namely, the variable may be regarded as of minor
importance (for example, it may be a function called by documented \textsf{GAP} functions that first compute many input parameters for the undocumented
function), or it belongs to a part of \textsf{GAP} that is still experimental in the sense that the meaning of the variable has
not yet been fixed or even that it is not clear whether the variable will
vanish in a more developed version. 

 As a consequence, it is dangerous to use undocumented variables because they
are not guaranteed to exist or to behave the same in future versions of \textsf{GAP}. 

 Conversely, for \emph{documented} variables, the definitions in the \textsf{GAP} manual can be relied on for future \textsf{GAP} versions (unless they turn out to be erroneous); if the \textsf{GAP} developers find that some piece of minor, but documented functionality is an
insurmountable obstacle to important developments, they may make the smallest
possible incompatible change to the functionality at the time of a major
release. However, in any such case it will be announced clearly in the \textsf{GAP} Forum what has been changed and why. 

 So on the one hand, the developers of \textsf{GAP} want to keep the freedom of changing undocumented \textsf{GAP} code. On the other hand, users may be interested in using undocumented
variables. 

 In this case, whenever you write \textsf{GAP} code involving undocumented variables, and want to make sure that this code
will work in future versions of \textsf{GAP}, you may ask at \href{mailto://support@gap-system.org} {\texttt{support@gap\texttt{\symbol{45}}system.org}} for documentation about the variables in question. The \textsf{GAP} developers then decide whether these variables shall be documented or not, and
if yes, what the definitions shall be. 

 In the former case, the new documentation is added to the \textsf{GAP} manual, this means that from then on, this definition is protected against
changes. 

 In the latter case (which may occur for example if the variables in question
are still experimental), you may add the current values of these variables to
your private code if you want to be sure that nothing will be broken later due
to changes in \textsf{GAP}. }

 }

            
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Interface to the GAP Help System}}\label{Interface to the GAP Help System}
\logpage{[ 84, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79A6CE6C86A976AE}{}
{
  In this chapter we describe which information the help system needs about a
manual book and how to tell it this information. The code which implements
this interface can be found in \texttt{lib/helpbase.gi}. 

 If you are intending to use a documentation format that is already used by
some other help book you probably don't need to know anything from this
chapter. However, if you want to create a new format and make it available to \textsf{GAP} then hopefully you will find the necessary information here. 

 The basic idea of the help system is as follows: One tells \textsf{GAP} a directory which contains a file \texttt{manual.six}, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Installing and Removing a Help Book}. When the \textsf{GAP} help is asked something about this book it reads in some basic information
from the file \texttt{manual.six}: strings like section headers, function names, and index entries to be
searched by the online help; information about the available formats of this
book like text, html, dvi, and pdf; the actual files containing the
documentation, corresponding section numbers, and page numbers: and so on.
See{\nobreakspace}\ref{The manual.six File} for a description of the format of the \texttt{manual.six} file. 

 It turns out that there is almost no restriction on the format of the \texttt{manual.six} file, except that it must provide a string, say \texttt{"myownformat"} which identifies the format of the help book. Then the basic actions on a help
book are delegated by the help system to handler functions stored in a record \texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}BOOK{\textunderscore}HANDLER.myownformat}. See{\nobreakspace}\ref{The Help Book Handler} for information which functions must be provided by the handler and what they
are supposed to do. The main work to teach \textsf{GAP} to use a new document format is to write these handler functions and to
produce an appropriate \texttt{manual.six} file.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Installing and Removing a Help Book}}\label{Installing and Removing a Help Book}
\logpage{[ 84, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7AFEAB6B84387635}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{HELP{\textunderscore}ADD{\textunderscore}BOOK}}
\logpage{[ 84, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CD0B8507A3D231D}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}ADD{\textunderscore}BOOK({\mdseries\slshape short, long, dir})\index{HELP{\textunderscore}ADD{\textunderscore}BOOK@\texttt{HEL}\-\texttt{P{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{A}\-\texttt{D}\-\texttt{D{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{BOOK}}
\label{HELPuScoreADDuScoreBOOK}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This command tells \textsf{GAP} that in directory \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dir}} (given as either a string describing the path relative to the \textsf{GAP} root directory \texttt{GAPInfo.RootPaths[1]} or as directory object) contains the basic information about a help book. The
string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape short}} is used as an identifying name for that book by the online help. The string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape long}} should be a short explanation of the content of the book. Both strings
together should easily fit on a line, since they are displayed with \texttt{?books}. 

 It is possible to reinstall a book with different strings \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape short}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape long}}; (for example, documentation of a not\texttt{\symbol{45}}loaded \textsf{GAP} package indicates this in the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape short}} and if you later load the package, \textsf{GAP} quietly changes the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape short}} as it reinstalls its documentation). 

 The only condition necessary to make the installation of a book \emph{valid} is that the directory \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dir}} must contain a file \texttt{manual.six}. The next section explains how this file must look. }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{HELP{\textunderscore}REMOVE{\textunderscore}BOOK}}
\logpage{[ 84, 1, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7BDEB25D7AFC4322}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}REMOVE{\textunderscore}BOOK({\mdseries\slshape short})\index{HELP{\textunderscore}REMOVE{\textunderscore}BOOK@\texttt{HEL}\-\texttt{P{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{R}\-\texttt{E}\-\texttt{M}\-\texttt{O}\-\texttt{V}\-\texttt{E{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{BOOK}}
\label{HELPuScoreREMOVEuScoreBOOK}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This command tells \textsf{GAP} not to use the help book with identifying name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape short}} any more. The book can be re\texttt{\symbol{45}}installed using \texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}ADD{\textunderscore}BOOK} (\ref{HELPuScoreADDuScoreBOOK}). 

 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{The manual.six File}}\label{The manual.six File}
\logpage{[ 84, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8713EEAE840CEDA3}{}
{
  The first non\texttt{\symbol{45}}empty line of \texttt{manual.six} should be of the form 

 \texttt{\#SIXFORMAT} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape myownformat}} 

 where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape myownformat}} is an identifying string for this format. The reading of the (remainder of
the) file is then delegated to the function \texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}BOOK{\textunderscore}HANDLER.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape myownformat}}.ReadSix} which must exist. Thus there are no further regulations for the format of the \texttt{manual.six} file, other that what you yourself impose. If such a line is missing then it
is assumed that the \texttt{manual.six} file complies with the \texttt{gapmacro.tex} documentation format, which internally is referred to as the \texttt{default} format for historical reasons. In that case reading the file is delegated to \texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}BOOK{\textunderscore}HANDLER.default.ReadSix}. 

 Section \ref{The Help Book Handler} explains how the return value of \texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}BOOK{\textunderscore}HANDLER.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape myownformat}}.ReadSix} should look like and which further function should be contained in \texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}BOOK{\textunderscore}HANDLER.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape myownformat}}}. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{The Help Book Handler}}\label{The Help Book Handler}
\logpage{[ 84, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7AD7541E7C30D5B3}{}
{
  \index{document formats!for help books} For each document format \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape myownformat}} there must be a record \texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}BOOK{\textunderscore}HANDLER.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape myownformat}}} of functions with the following names and functionality. 

 An implementation example of such a set of handler functions is the \texttt{default} format, which is the format name used for the \texttt{gapmacro.tex} documentation format, and this is contained in the file \texttt{lib/helpdef.gi}. 

 The package \textsf{GAPDoc} (see Chapter{\nobreakspace} (\textbf{GAPDoc: Introduction and Example})) also defines a format (as it should) which is called: \texttt{GapDocGAP} (the case \emph{is} significant). 

 As you can see by the above two examples, the name for a document format can
be anything, but it should be in some way meaningful. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{ \texttt{ReadSix( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stream}} )}}]  For an input text stream \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stream}} to a \texttt{manual.six} file, this must return a record \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} which has at least the following two components: \texttt{bookname} which is the short identifying name of the help book, and \texttt{entries}. Here \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}\texttt{.entries} must be a list with one entry per search string (which can be a section
header, function name, index entry, or whatever seems sensible to be searched
for matching a help query). A \emph{match} for the \textsf{GAP} help is a pair (\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}}) where \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} refers to an index for the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}\texttt{.entries} and this corresponds to a certain position in the document. There is one
further regulation for the format of the entries of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}\texttt{.entries}. They must be lists and the first element of such a list must be a string
which is printed by \textsf{GAP} for example when several matches are found for a query (so it should
essentially be the string which is searched for the match, except that it may
contain upper and lower case letters or some markup). There may be other
components in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} which are needed by the functions below, but their names and formats are not
prescribed. The \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape stream}} argument is typically generated using \texttt{InputTextFile} (\ref{InputTextFile}), e.g. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@dirs := DirectoriesLibrary( "doc/ref" );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@file := Filename( dirs, "manual.six" );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@stream := InputTextFile( file );;|
\end{Verbatim}
 
\item[{\texttt{ShowChapters( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} )} }]  This must return a text string or list of text lines which contains the
chapter headers of the book \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}\texttt{.bookname}. 
\item[{\texttt{ShowSection( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} )} }]  This must return a text string or list of text lines which contains the
section (and chapter) headers of the book \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}\texttt{.bookname}. 
\item[{\texttt{SearchMatches( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape topic}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape frombegin}} )} }]  This function must return a list of indices of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}\texttt{.entries} for entries which match the search string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape topic}}. If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape frombegin}} is \texttt{true} then those parts of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape topic}} which are separated by spaces should be considered as the beginnings of words
to decide the matching. It \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape frombegin}} is \texttt{false}, a substring search should be performed. The string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape topic}} can be assumed to be already normalized (transformed to lower case, and
whitespace normalized). The function must return a list with two entries \texttt{[exact, match]} where \texttt{exact} is the list of indices for exact matches and \texttt{match} a list of indices of the remaining matches. 
\item[{\texttt{MatchPrevChap( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} )} }]  This should return the match [\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \texttt{j}] which points to the beginning of the chapter containing match [\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}}], respectively to the beginning of the previous chapter if [\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}}] is already the beginning of a chapter. (Corresponds to \texttt{?{\textless}{\textless}}.) 
\item[{\texttt{MatchNextChap( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} )} }]  Like the previous function except that it should return the match for the
beginning of the next chapter. (Corresponds to \texttt{?{\textgreater}{\textgreater}}.) 
\item[{\texttt{MatchPrev( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} )} }]  This should return the previous section (or appropriate portion of the
document). (Corresponds to \texttt{?{\textless}}.) 
\item[{\texttt{MatchNext( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} )} }]  Like the previous function except that it should return the next section (or
appropriate portion of the document). (Corresponds to \texttt{?{\textgreater}}.) 
\item[{\texttt{HelpData( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape type}} )} }]  This returns for match [\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}}] some data whose format depends on the string \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape type}}, or \texttt{fail} if these data are not available. The values of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape type}} which currently must be handled and the corresponding result format are
described in the list below. 
\item[{\texttt{SubsectionNumber( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}} )} }]  This returns some \textsf{GAP} object that identifies the position in the book where the display of this
entry is started. This can be useful to detect if several help book entries
actually point to the same place. 
\end{description}
 

 The \texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}BOOK{\textunderscore}HANDLER.\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape myownformat}}.HelpData} function must recognize the following values of the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape type}} argument. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{ \texttt{"text"} }]  This must return a corresponding text string in a format which can be fed into
the \texttt{Pager}, see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{Pager} (\ref{Pager}). 
\item[{\texttt{"url"} }]  If the help book is available in HTML format this must return an URL as a
string (Probably a \texttt{file://} URL containing a label for the exact start position in that file). Otherwise
it returns \texttt{fail}. 
\item[{\texttt{"dvi"} }]  If the help book is available in dvi\texttt{\symbol{45}}format this must
return a record of form \texttt{rec( file := \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape filename}}, page := \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pagenumber}} )}. Otherwise it returns \texttt{fail}. 
\item[{\texttt{"pdf"} }]  Same as case \texttt{"dvi"}, but for the corresponding pdf\texttt{\symbol{45}}file. 
\item[{\texttt{"secnr"} }]  This must return a pair like \texttt{[[3,3,1], "3.3.1"]} which gives the section number as chapter number, section number, subsection
number triple and a corresponding string (a chapter itself is encoded like \texttt{[[4,0,0], "4."]}). Useful for cross\texttt{\symbol{45}}referencing between help books. 
\end{description}
 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Introducing new Viewer for the Online Help}}\label{Introducing new Viewer for the Online Help}
\logpage{[ 84, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X861927BF822FB162}{}
{
  To introduce a new viewer for the online help, one should extend the global
record \texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}VIEWER{\textunderscore}INFO} (\ref{HELPuScoreVIEWERuScoreINFO}), the structure of which is explained below. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{HELP{\textunderscore}VIEWER{\textunderscore}INFO}}
\logpage{[ 84, 4, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X84B011847A4D90F0}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}VIEWER{\textunderscore}INFO\index{HELP{\textunderscore}VIEWER{\textunderscore}INFO@\texttt{HEL}\-\texttt{P{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{V}\-\texttt{I}\-\texttt{E}\-\texttt{W}\-\texttt{E}\-\texttt{R{\textunderscore}}\-\texttt{INFO}}
\label{HELPuScoreVIEWERuScoreINFO}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (global variable)}}\\


 The record \texttt{HELP{\textunderscore}VIEWER{\textunderscore}INFO} contains one component for each help viewer. Each such component is a record
with two components: \texttt{.type} and \texttt{.show}. 

 The component \texttt{.type} refers to one of the \texttt{type}s recognized by the \texttt{HelpData} handler function explained in the previous section (currently one of \texttt{"text"}, \texttt{"url"}, \texttt{"dvi"}, or \texttt{"pdf"}). 

 The component \texttt{.show} is a function which gets as input the result of a corresponding \texttt{HelpData} handler call, if it was not \texttt{fail}. This function has to perform the actual display of the data. (E.g., by
calling a function like \texttt{Pager} (\ref{Pager}) or by starting up an external viewer program.) }

 }

 }

           
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Function\texttt{\symbol{45}}Operation\texttt{\symbol{45}}Attribute Triples}}\label{Function-Operation-Attribute Triples}
\logpage{[ 85, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8350247A8501969F}{}
{
  \textsf{GAP} is eager to maintain information that it has gathered about an object,
possibly by lengthy calculations. The most important mechanism for information
maintenance is the automatic storage and look\texttt{\symbol{45}}up that takes
place for \emph{attributes}; and this was already mentioned in section{\nobreakspace} (\textbf{Tutorial: Attributes}). In this chapter we will describe further mechanisms that allow storage of
results that are not values of attributes. 

 \index{FOA triples} The idea which is common to all sections is that certain operations, which are
not themselves attributes, have an attribute associated with them. To
automatically delegate tasks to the attribute, \textsf{GAP} knows, in addition to the \emph{operation} and the \emph{attributes} also a \emph{function}, which is ``wrapped around'' the other two. This ``wrapper function'' is called by the user and decides whether to call the operation or the
attribute or possibly both. The whole \emph{f}unction\texttt{\symbol{45}}\emph{o}peration\texttt{\symbol{45}}\emph{a}ttribute triple (or \emph{FOA triple}) is set up by a single \textsf{GAP} command which writes the wrapper function and already installs some methods,
e.g., for the attribute to fall back on the operation. The idea is then that
subsequent methods, which perform the actual computation, are installed only
for the operation, whereas the wrapper function remains unaltered, and in
general no additional methods for the attribute are required either.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Key Dependent Operations}}\label{Key Dependent Operations}
\logpage{[ 85, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86F03E0D7C18C6B0}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{KeyDependentOperation}}
\logpage{[ 85, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CABFDAA8596757E}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{KeyDependentOperation({\mdseries\slshape name, dom\texttt{\symbol{45}}req, key\texttt{\symbol{45}}req, key\texttt{\symbol{45}}test})\index{KeyDependentOperation@\texttt{KeyDependentOperation}}
\label{KeyDependentOperation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 There are several functions that require as first argument a domain, e.g., a
group, and as second argument something much simpler, e.g., a prime. \texttt{SylowSubgroup} (\ref{SylowSubgroup}) is an example. Since its value depends on two arguments, it cannot be an
attribute, yet one would like to store the Sylow subgroups once they have been
computed. 

 The idea is to provide an attribute of the group, called \texttt{ComputedSylowSubgroups}, and to store the groups in this list. The name implies that the value of
this attribute may change in the course of a \textsf{GAP} session, whenever a newly\texttt{\symbol{45}}computed Sylow subgroup is put
into the list. Therefore, this is a \emph{mutable attribute} (see \ref{Attributes}). The list contains primes in each bound odd position and a corresponding
Sylow subgroup in the following even position. More precisely, if \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} = ComputedSylowSubgroups( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} )[ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape even}} \texttt{\symbol{45}} 1 ]} then \texttt{ComputedSylowSubgroups( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} )[ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape even}} ]} holds the value of \texttt{SylowSubgroup( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} )}. The pairs are sorted in increasing order of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}, in particular at most one Sylow \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} subgroup of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} is stored for each prime \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}. This attribute value is maintained by the function \texttt{SylowSubgroup} (\ref{SylowSubgroup}), which calls the operation \texttt{SylowSubgroupOp( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} )} to do the real work, if the prime \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} cannot be found in the list. So methods that do the real work should be
installed for \texttt{SylowSubgroupOp} and not for \texttt{SylowSubgroup} (\ref{SylowSubgroup}). 

 The same mechanism works for other functions as well, e.g., for \texttt{PCore} (\ref{PCore}), but also for \texttt{HallSubgroup} (\ref{HallSubgroup}), where the second argument is not a prime but a set of primes. 

 \texttt{KeyDependentOperation} declares the two operations and the attribute as described above, with names \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{Op}, and \texttt{Computed}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{s}, as well as tester and setter operations \texttt{Has}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} and \texttt{Set}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}, respectively. Note, however, that the tester is not a filter. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dom\texttt{\symbol{45}}req}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape key\texttt{\symbol{45}}req}} specify the required filters for the first and second argument of the
operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{Op}, which are needed to create this operation with \texttt{DeclareOperation} (\ref{DeclareOperation}). \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape dom\texttt{\symbol{45}}req}} is also the required filter for the corresponding attribute \texttt{Computed}\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{s}. The fourth argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape key\texttt{\symbol{45}}test}} is in general a function to which the second argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} of \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}} )} will be passed. This function can perform tests on \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape info}}, and raise an error if appropriate. 

 For example, to set up the three objects \texttt{SylowSubgroup} (\ref{SylowSubgroup}), \texttt{SylowSubgroupOp}, \texttt{ComputedSylowSubgroups} together, the declaration file \texttt{lib/grp.gd} contains the following line of code. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  KeyDependentOperation( "SylowSubgroup", IsGroup, IsPosInt, "prime" );
\end{Verbatim}
 In this example, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape key\texttt{\symbol{45}}test}} has the value \texttt{"prime"}, which is silently replaced by a function that tests whether its argument is
a prime. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@s4 := Group((1,2,3,4),(1,2));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SylowSubgroup( s4, 7 );;  ComputedSylowSubgroups( s4 );|
  [ 7, Group(()) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SylowSubgroup( s4, 2 );;  ComputedSylowSubgroups( s4 );|
  [ 2, Group([ (3,4), (1,4)(2,3), (1,3)(2,4) ]), 7, Group(()) ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@HasSylowSubgroup( s4, 5 );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetSylowSubgroup( s4, 5, Group(()));; ComputedSylowSubgroups( s4 );|
  [ 2, Group([ (3,4), (1,4)(2,3), (1,3)(2,4) ]), 5, Group(()), 7, Group(()) ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!|B,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt|gap>B !gapinput|SylowSubgroup( s4, 6 );B
  Error, SylowSubgroup: <p> must be a prime
  Stack trace:
  *[1] <<compiled GAP function>>
     @ GAPROOT/lib/oper1.g:964
   [2] <<compiled GAP function "SylowSubgroup default method">>
     @ GAPROOT/lib/oper1.g:1007
  <function "SylowSubgroup default method">( <arguments> )
   called from read-eval loop at *stdin*:3
  you can enter 'quit;' to quit to outer loop, or
  you can enter 'return;' to continue
  !gapbrkprompt|brk>B !gapinput|quit;B
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Thus the prime test need not be repeated in the methods for the operation \texttt{SylowSubgroupOp} (which are installed to do the real work). Note that no methods need be
installed for \texttt{SylowSubgroup} (\ref{SylowSubgroup}) and \texttt{ComputedSylowSubgroups}. If a method is installed with \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) for a wrapper operation such as \texttt{SylowSubgroup} (\ref{SylowSubgroup}) then a warning is signalled provided the \texttt{InfoWarning} (\ref{InfoWarning}) level is at least \texttt{1}. (Use \texttt{InstallMethod} (\ref{InstallMethod}) in order to suppress the warning.) }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{In Parent Attributes}}\label{In Parent Attributes}
\logpage{[ 85, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X78D4D0FF780C8A85}{}
{
  

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{InParentFOA}}
\logpage{[ 85, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7C0E62D8813A4EE6}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{InParentFOA({\mdseries\slshape name, super, sub, AorP})\index{InParentFOA@\texttt{InParentFOA}}
\label{InParentFOA}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 This section describes how you can add new ``in parent attributes'' (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Constructing Subdomains} and \ref{Parents}). As an example, we describe how \texttt{Index} (\ref{Index:for a group and its subgroup}) and its related functions are implemented. 

 There are two operations \texttt{Index} (\ref{Index:for a group and its subgroup}) and \texttt{IndexOp}, and an attribute \texttt{IndexInParent}. They are created together as shown below, and after they have been created,
methods need be installed only for \texttt{IndexOp}. In the creation process, \texttt{IndexInParent} already gets one default method installed (in addition to the usual system
getter of each attribute, see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Attributes}), namely \texttt{D \texttt{\symbol{45}}{\textgreater} IndexOp( Parent( D ), D )}. 

 The operation \texttt{Index} (\ref{Index:for a group and its subgroup}) proceeds as follows. 
\begin{itemize}
\item  If it is called with the two arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sub}}, and if \texttt{HasParent( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sub}} )} and \texttt{IsIdenticalObj( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super}}, Parent( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sub}} ) )} are \texttt{true}, \texttt{IndexInParent} is called with argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sub}}, and the result is returned. 
\item  Otherwise, \texttt{IndexOp} is called with the same arguments that \texttt{Index} (\ref{Index:for a group and its subgroup}) was called with, and the result is returned. 
\end{itemize}
 (Note that it is in principle possible to install even \texttt{Index} (\ref{Index:for a group and its subgroup}) and \texttt{IndexOp} methods for a number of arguments different from two, with \texttt{InstallOtherMethod} (\ref{InstallOtherMethod}), see \ref{Attributes}). 

 The call of \texttt{InParentFOA} declares the operations and the attribute as described above, with names \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{Op}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{InParent}. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape super\texttt{\symbol{45}}req}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sub\texttt{\symbol{45}}req}} specify the required filters for the first and second argument of the
operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{Op}, which are needed to create this operation with \texttt{DeclareOperation} (\ref{DeclareOperation}). \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape sub\texttt{\symbol{45}}req}} is also the required filter for the corresponding attribute \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{InParent}; note that \texttt{HasParent} (\ref{HasParent}) is \emph{not} required for the argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{InParent}, because even without a parent stored, \texttt{Parent( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} )} is legal, meaning \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape U}} itself (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Parents}). The fourth argument must be \texttt{DeclareProperty} (\ref{DeclareProperty}) if \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{InParent} takes only boolean values (for example in the case \texttt{IsNormalInParent}), and \texttt{DeclareAttribute} (\ref{DeclareAttribute}) otherwise. 

 For example, to set up the three objects \texttt{Index} (\ref{Index:for a group and its subgroup}), \texttt{IndexOp}, and \texttt{IndexInParent} together, the declaration file \texttt{lib/domain.gd} contains the following line of code. 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InParentFOA( "Index", IsGroup, IsGroup, DeclareAttribute );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that no methods need be installed for \texttt{Index} (\ref{Index:for a group and its subgroup}) and \texttt{IndexInParent}. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Operation Functions}}\label{Operation Functions}
\logpage{[ 85, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7CD4A0867BD825F7}{}
{
  \index{ExternalSet@\texttt{ExternalSet}!computing orbits} \index{G-sets@$G$\texttt{\symbol{45}}sets!computing orbits} \index{Orbits@\texttt{Orbits}!as attributes for external sets} Chapter{\nobreakspace}\ref{Group Actions} and, in particular, the Section{\nobreakspace}\ref{About Group Actions}   explain that certain operations such as \ref{Orbits}), besides their usual usage with arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}, can also be applied to an external set ($G$\texttt{\symbol{45}}set), in which case they can be interpreted as attributes.
Moreover, they can also be interpreted as attributes for permutation groups,
meaning the natural action on the set of its moved points. 

 The definition of \ref{Orbits} says that a method should be a function with arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oprs}}, and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}}, as in the case of the operation \texttt{ExternalSet} (\ref{ExternalSet}) when specified via \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oprs}} (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{External Sets}). All other syntax variants allowed for \ref{Orbits} (e.g., leaving out \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oprs}}) are handled by default methods. 

 The default methods for \ref{Orbits} support the following behaviour. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item  If the only argument is an external set \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape xset}} and the attribute tester \texttt{HasOrbits( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape xset}} )} returns \texttt{true}, the stored value of that attribute is returned. 
\item  If the only argument is an external set \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape xset}} and the attribute value is not known, the default arguments are obtained from
the data of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape xset}}.
