\item  If \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oprs}} are not specified, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} is set to \texttt{Pcgs( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} )} if \texttt{CanEasilyComputePcgs( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} )} is \texttt{true}, and to \texttt{GeneratorsOfGroup( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} )} otherwise; \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oprs}} is set to \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}. 
\item  The default value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} is \texttt{OnPoints} (\ref{OnPoints}). 
\item  In the case of an operation of a permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} on \texttt{MovedPoints( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} )} via \texttt{OnPoints} (\ref{OnPoints}), if the attribute tester \texttt{HasOrbits( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} )} returns \texttt{true}, the stored attribute value is returned. 
\item  The operation is called as \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape result}}:= Orbits( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape oprs}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} )}. 
\item  In the case of an external set \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape xset}} or a permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} in its natural action, the attribute setter is called to store \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape result}}. 
\item  \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape result}} is returned. 
\end{enumerate}
 

 The declaration of operations that match the above pattern is done as follows. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{OrbitsishOperation}}
\logpage{[ 85, 3, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7CA3826A7EBDE208}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{OrbitsishOperation({\mdseries\slshape name, reqs, usetype, AorP})\index{OrbitsishOperation@\texttt{OrbitsishOperation}}
\label{OrbitsishOperation}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 declares an attribute \texttt{op}, with name \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}. The second argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape reqs}} specifies the list of required filters for the usual
(five\texttt{\symbol{45}}argument) methods that do the real work. 

 If the third argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape usetype}} is \texttt{true}, the function call \texttt{op( xset )} will {\textendash}if the value of \texttt{op} for \texttt{xset} is not yet known{\textendash} delegate to the five\texttt{\symbol{45}}argument
call of \texttt{op} with second argument \texttt{xset} rather than with \texttt{D}. This allows certain methods for \texttt{op} to make use of the type of \texttt{xset}, in which the types of the external subsets of \texttt{xset} and of the external orbits in \texttt{xset} are stored. (This is used to avoid repeated calls of \texttt{NewType} (\ref{NewType}) in functions like \texttt{ExternalOrbits( xset )}, which call \texttt{ExternalOrbit( xset, pnt )} for several values of \texttt{pnt}.) 

 For property testing functions such as \texttt{IsTransitive} (\ref{IsTransitive:for a group, an action domain, etc.}), the fourth argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape AorP}} must be \texttt{NewProperty} (\ref{NewProperty}), otherwise it must be \texttt{NewAttribute} (\ref{NewAttribute}); in the former case, a property is returned, in the latter case an attribute
that is not a property. 

 For example, to set up the operation \texttt{Orbits} (\ref{Orbits:operation}), the declaration file \texttt{lib/oprt.gd} contains the following line of code: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  OrbitsishOperation( "Orbits", OrbitsishReq, false, NewAttribute );
\end{Verbatim}
 The global variable \texttt{OrbitsishReq} contains the standard requirements 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  OrbitsishReq := [ IsGroup, IsList,
                    IsList,
                    IsList,
                    IsFunction ];
\end{Verbatim}
 which are usually entered in calls to \texttt{OrbitsishOperation}. 

 The new operation, e.g., \texttt{Orbits} (\ref{Orbits:operation}), can be called either as \texttt{Orbits( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape xset}} )} for an external set \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape xset}}, or as \texttt{Orbits( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} )} for a permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, meaning the orbits on the moved points of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} via \texttt{OnPoints} (\ref{OnPoints}), or as 

 \texttt{Orbits( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Omega}}[, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape acts}}][, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape act}}] )}, 

 with a group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, a domain or list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Omega}}, generators \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, and corresponding elements \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape acts}} that act on \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Omega}} via the function \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape act}}; the default of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape gens}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape acts}} is a list of group generators of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, the default of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape act}} is \texttt{OnPoints} (\ref{OnPoints}). 

 Only methods for the five\texttt{\symbol{45}}argument version need to be
installed for doing the real work. (And of course methods for one argument in
case one wants to define a new meaning of the attribute.) }

 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{OrbitishFO}}
\logpage{[ 85, 3, 2 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B23C48482ADB237}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{OrbitishFO({\mdseries\slshape name, reqs, famrel, usetype, realenum})\index{OrbitishFO@\texttt{OrbitishFO}}
\label{OrbitishFO}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 is used to create operations like \texttt{Orbit} (\ref{Orbit}). This function is analogous to \texttt{OrbitsishOperation} (\ref{OrbitsishOperation}), but for operations \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape orbish}} like \texttt{Orbit( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Omega}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} )}. Since the return values of these operations depend on the additional
argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}}, there is no associated attribute. 

 The call of \texttt{OrbitishFO} declares a wrapper function and its operation, with names \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{Op}. 

 The second argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape reqs}} specifies the list of required filters for the operation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}\texttt{Op}. 

 The third argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famrel}} is used to test the family relation between the second and third argument of \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} )}. For example, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famrel}} is \texttt{IsCollsElms} in the case of \texttt{Orbit} (\ref{Orbit}) because \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} must be an element of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}. Similarly, in the call \texttt{Blocks( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}} )}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}} must be a subset of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, and the family relation must be \texttt{IsIdenticalObj} (\ref{IsIdenticalObj}). 

 The fourth argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape usetype}} serves the same purpose as in the case of \texttt{OrbitsishOperation} (\ref{OrbitsishOperation}). \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape usetype}} can also be an attribute, such as \texttt{BlocksAttr} or \texttt{MaximalBlocksAttr}. In this case, if only one of the two arguments \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape Omega}} and \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}} is given, blocks with no seed are computed, they are stored as attribute
values according to the rules of \texttt{OrbitsishOperation} (\ref{OrbitsishOperation}). 

 If the 5th argument is set to \texttt{true}, the action for an external set should use the enumerator, otherwise it uses
the \texttt{HomeEnumerator} (\ref{HomeEnumerator}) value. This will make a difference for external orbits as part of a larger
domain. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Example: Orbit and OrbitOp}}\label{Example: Orbit and OrbitOp}
\logpage{[ 85, 3, 3 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X834E92F07DD0BF04}{}
{
  For example, to setup the function \texttt{Orbit} (\ref{Orbit}) and its operation \texttt{OrbitOp}, the declaration file \texttt{lib/oprt.gd} contains the following line of code: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  OrbitishFO( "Orbit", OrbitishReq, IsCollsElms, false, false );
\end{Verbatim}
 The variable \texttt{OrbitishReq} contains the standard requirements 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  OrbitishReq  := [ IsGroup, IsList, IsObject,
                    IsList,
                    IsList,
                    IsFunction ];
\end{Verbatim}
 which are usually entered in calls to \texttt{OrbitishFO} (\ref{OrbitishFO}). 

 The relation test via \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famrel}} is used to provide a uniform construction of the wrapper functions created by \texttt{OrbitishFO} (\ref{OrbitishFO}), in spite of the different syntax of the specific functions. For example, \texttt{Orbit} (\ref{Orbit}) admits the calls \texttt{Orbit( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} )} and \texttt{Orbit( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pnt}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} )}, i.e., the second argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}} may be omitted; \texttt{Blocks} (\ref{Blocks:for a group, an action domain, etc.}) admits the calls \texttt{Blocks( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} )} and \texttt{Blocks( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} )}, i.e., the third argument may be omitted. The translation to the appropriate
call of \texttt{OrbitOp} or \texttt{BlocksOp}, for either operation with five or six arguments, is handled via \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famrel}}. 

 As a consequence, there must not only be methods for \texttt{OrbitOp} with the six arguments corresponding to \texttt{OrbitishReq}, but also methods for only five arguments (i.e., without \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}). Plenty of examples are contained in the implementation file \texttt{lib/oprt.gi}. 

 In order to handle a few special cases (currently \texttt{Blocks} (\ref{Blocks:for a group, an action domain, etc.}) and \texttt{MaximalBlocks} (\ref{MaximalBlocks:for a group, an action domain, etc.})), also the following form of \texttt{OrbitishFO} (\ref{OrbitishFO}) is supported. 

 \texttt{OrbitishFO( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape name}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape reqs}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape famrel}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} )} 

 The functions in question depend upon an argument \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}}, so they cannot be regarded as attributes. However, they are most often
called without giving \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}}, meaning ``choose any minimal resp. maximal block system''. In this case, the result can be stored as the value of the attribute \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape attr}} that was entered as fourth argument of \texttt{OrbitishFO} (\ref{OrbitishFO}). This attribute is considered by a call \texttt{Blocks( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape D}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape opr}} )} (i.e., without \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape seed}}) in the same way as \texttt{Orbits} (\ref{Orbits:attribute}) considers \texttt{OrbitsAttr}. 

 To set this up, the declaration file \texttt{lib/oprt.gd} contains the following lines: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareAttribute( "BlocksAttr", IsExternalSet );
  OrbitishFO( "Blocks",
      [ IsGroup, IsList, IsList,
        IsList,
        IsList,
        IsFunction ], IsIdenticalObj, BlocksAttr, true );
\end{Verbatim}
 And this extraordinary FOA triple works as follows: 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@s4 := Group((1,2,3,4),(1,2));;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Blocks( s4, MovedPoints(s4), [1,2] );|
  [ [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Tester( BlocksAttr )( s4 );|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Blocks( s4, MovedPoints(s4) );|
  [ [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Tester( BlocksAttr )( s4 );  BlocksAttr( s4 );|
  true
  [ [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

 }

              
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{Weak Pointers}}\label{Weak Pointers}
\logpage{[ 86, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86390538806F67CF}{}
{
  This chapter describes the use of the kernel feature of \emph{weak pointers}. This feature is primarily intended for use only in \textsf{GAP} internals, and should be used extremely carefully otherwise. 

 The garbage collector (see Section \ref{Garbage Collection}) is the part of the kernel that manages memory in the user's workspace. It
will normally only reclaim the storage used by an object when the object
cannot be reached as a subobject of any \textsf{GAP} variable, or from any reference in the kernel. We say that any link to object $a$ from object $b$ ``keeps object $a$ alive'', as long as $b$ is alive. It is occasionally convenient, however, to have a link to an object
which \emph{does not keep it alive}, and this is a weak pointer. The most common use is in caches, and similar
structures, where it is only necessary to remember how to solve problem $x$ as long as some other link to $x$ exists. 

 The following section \ref{Weak Pointer Objects} describes the semantics of the objects that contain weak pointers. Following
sections describe the functions available to manipulate them.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Weak Pointer Objects}}\label{Weak Pointer Objects}
\logpage{[ 86, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86D963DC7968899B}{}
{
  A \emph{weak pointer object} is similar to a mutable plain list, except that it does not keep its
subobjects alive during a garbage collection. From the \textsf{GAP} viewpoint this means that its entries may become unbound, apparently
spontaneously, at any time. Considerable care is therefore needed in
programming with such an object. 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{WeakPointerObj}}
\logpage{[ 86, 1, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X8155EE1386F46063}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{WeakPointerObj({\mdseries\slshape list})\index{WeakPointerObj@\texttt{WeakPointerObj}}
\label{WeakPointerObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 \texttt{WeakPointerObj} returns a weak pointer object which contains the same subobjects as the list \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}, that is it returns a \emph{shallow} weak copy of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape list}}. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@w := WeakPointerObj( [ 1, , [2,3], fail, rec( a := 1) ] );|
  WeakPointerObj( [ 1, , [ 2, 3 ], fail, rec( a := 1 ) ] )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 After some computations involving garbage collections (but not necessarily in
the \emph{first} garbage collection after the above assignment), \textsf{GAP} will notice that the list and the record stored in \texttt{w} are not referenced by other objects than \texttt{w}, and that therefore these entries may disappear. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CollectGarbage( true );|
  
  ... (perhaps more computations and garbage collections) ...
  
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CollectGarbage( true );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@w;|
  WeakPointerObj( [ 1, , , fail ] )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note that \texttt{w} has failed to keep its list and record subobjects alive during the garbage
collections. Certain subobjects, such as small integers and elements of small
finite fields, are not stored in the workspace, and so are not subject to
garbage collection, while certain other objects, such as the boolean values,
are always reachable from global variables or the kernel and so are never
garbage collected. 

 Subobjects reachable without going through a weak pointer object do not
evaporate, as in: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@w := WeakPointerObj( [ 1, , , fail ] );|
  WeakPointerObj( [ 1, , , fail ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@l := [1,2,3];;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@w[1] := l;;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@w;|
  WeakPointerObj( [ [ 1, 2, 3 ], , , fail ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@CollectGarbage( true );|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@w;|
  WeakPointerObj( [ [ 1, 2, 3 ], , , fail ] )
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Note also that the global variables \texttt{last}, \texttt{last2} and \texttt{last3} will keep things alive {\textendash}this can be confusing when debugging. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Low Level Access Functions for Weak Pointer Objects}}\label{Low Level Access Functions for Weak Pointer Objects}
\logpage{[ 86, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7F4476958497F239}{}
{
  \index{ElmWPObj} 

\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{SetElmWPObj}}
\logpage{[ 86, 2, 1 ]}\nobreak
\hyperdef{L}{X7B9748ED7BAAA379}{}
{\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{SetElmWPObj({\mdseries\slshape wp, pos, val})\index{SetElmWPObj@\texttt{SetElmWPObj}}
\label{SetElmWPObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{UnbindElmWPObj({\mdseries\slshape wp, pos})\index{UnbindElmWPObj@\texttt{UnbindElmWPObj}}
\label{UnbindElmWPObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{ElmWPObj({\mdseries\slshape wp, pos})\index{ElmWPObj@\texttt{ElmWPObj}}
\label{ElmWPObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{IsBoundElmWPObj({\mdseries\slshape wp, pos})\index{IsBoundElmWPObj@\texttt{IsBoundElmWPObj}}
\label{IsBoundElmWPObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\
\noindent\textcolor{FuncColor}{$\triangleright$\enspace\texttt{LengthWPObj({\mdseries\slshape wp})\index{LengthWPObj@\texttt{LengthWPObj}}
\label{LengthWPObj}
}\hfill{\scriptsize (function)}}\\


 The functions \texttt{SetElmWPObj} and \texttt{UnbindElmWPObj} set and unbind entries in a weak pointer object. 

 The function \texttt{ElmWPObj} returns the element at position \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}} of the weak pointer object \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape wp}}, if there is one, and \texttt{fail} otherwise. A return value of \texttt{fail} can thus arise either because (a) the value \texttt{fail} is stored at position \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}}, or (b) no value is stored at position \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}}. Since \texttt{fail} cannot vanish in a garbage collection, these two cases can safely be
distinguished by a \emph{subsequent} call to \texttt{IsBoundElmWPObj}, which returns \texttt{true} if there is currently a value bound at position \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape pos}} of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape wp}} and \texttt{false} otherwise. 

 Note that it is \emph{not} safe to write: 

 \texttt{if IsBoundElmWPObj(w,i) then x:= ElmWPObj(w,i); fi;} 

 and treat \texttt{x} as reliably containing a value taken from \texttt{w}, as a badly timed garbage collection could leave \texttt{x} containing \texttt{fail}. Instead use 

 \texttt{x := ElmWPObj(w,i); if x {\textless}{\textgreater} fail or
IsBoundElmWPObj(w,i) then . . .}. 

 Here is an example. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@w := WeakPointerObj( [ 1, , [2,3], fail, rec() ] );|
  WeakPointerObj( [ 1, , [ 2, 3 ], fail, rec(  ) ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@SetElmWPObj(w,5,[]);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@w;|
  WeakPointerObj( [ 1, , [ 2, 3 ], fail, [  ] ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@UnbindElmWPObj(w,1);|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@w;|
  WeakPointerObj( [ , , [ 2, 3 ], fail, [  ] ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ElmWPObj(w,3);|
  [ 2, 3 ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ElmWPObj(w,1);|
  fail
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Now after some computations and garbage collections $\ldots$ 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@2;; 3;; 4;; CollectGarbage( true );  # clear last, last2, last3|
\end{Verbatim}
 

 $\ldots$ we get the following. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ElmWPObj(w,3);|
  fail
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@w;|
  WeakPointerObj( [ , , , fail ] )
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@ElmWPObj(w,4);|
  fail
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBoundElmWPObj(w,3);|
  false
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@IsBoundElmWPObj(w,4);|
  true
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Accessing Weak Pointer Objects as Lists}}\label{Accessing Weak Pointer Objects as Lists}
\logpage{[ 86, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8468DD647DDEFD82}{}
{
  Weak pointer objects are members of \texttt{ListsFamily} and the categories \texttt{IsList} (\ref{IsList}) and \texttt{IsMutable} (\ref{IsMutable}). Methods based on the low\texttt{\symbol{45}}level functions in the previous
section, are installed for the list access operations, enabling them to be
used as lists. However, it is \emph{not recommended} that these be used in programming. They are supplied mainly as a convenience
for interactive working, and may not be safe, since functions and methods for
lists may assume that after \texttt{IsBound(w[i])} returns \texttt{true}, access to \texttt{w[i]} is safe. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Copying Weak Pointer Objects}}\label{Copying Weak Pointer Objects}
\logpage{[ 86, 4, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X830918AC8702A189}{}
{
  A \texttt{ShallowCopy} (\ref{ShallowCopy}) method is installed, which makes a new weak pointer object containing the same
objects as the original. 

 It is possible to apply \texttt{StructuralCopy} (\ref{StructuralCopy}) to a weak pointer object, obtaining a new weak pointer object containing
copies of the objects in the original. This \emph{may not be safe} if a badly timed garbage collection occurs during copying. 

 Applying \texttt{Immutable} (\ref{Immutable}) to a weak pointer object produces an immutable plain list containing immutable
copies of the objects contained in the weak pointer object. An immutable weak
pointer object is a contradiction in terms. }

 }

           
\chapter{\textcolor{Chapter }{More about Stabilizer Chains}}\label{More about Stabilizer Chains}
\logpage{[ 87, 0, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X81F4282081027945}{}
{
  This chapter contains some rather technical complements to the material
handled in the chapters{\nobreakspace}\ref{Permutations} and \ref{Permutation Groups}.  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Generalized Conjugation Technique}}\label{Generalized Conjugation Technique}
\logpage{[ 87, 1, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X870717BA831A0365}{}
{
  The command \texttt{ConjugateGroup( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} )} (see{\nobreakspace}\texttt{ConjugateGroup} (\ref{ConjugateGroup})) for a permutation group \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} with stabilizer chain equips its result also with a stabilizer chain, namely
with the chain of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape G}} conjugate by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}. Conjugating a stabilizer chain by a permutation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} means replacing all the points which appear in the \texttt{orbit} components by their images under \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} and replacing every permutation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} which appears in a \texttt{labels} or \texttt{transversal} component by its conjugate $g^p$. The conjugate $g^p$ acts on the mapped points exactly as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape g}} did on the original points, i.e., $(pnt.p). g^p = (pnt.g).p$. Since the entries in the \texttt{translabels} components are integers pointing to positions of the \texttt{labels} list, the \texttt{translabels} lists just have to be permuted by \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} for the conjugated stabilizer. Then \texttt{generators} is reconstructed as \texttt{labels\texttt{\symbol{123}} genlabels \texttt{\symbol{125}}} and \texttt{transversal\texttt{\symbol{123}} orbit \texttt{\symbol{125}}} as \texttt{labels\texttt{\symbol{123}} translabels\texttt{\symbol{123}} orbit
\texttt{\symbol{125}} \texttt{\symbol{125}}}. 

 \index{generalized conjugation technique} This conjugation technique can be generalized. Instead of mapping points and
permutations under the same permutation \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}}, it is sometimes desirable (e.g., in the context of permutation group
homomorphisms) to map the points with an arbitrary mapping $map$ and the permutations with a homomorphism $hom$ such that the compatibility of the actions is still valid: $map(pnt).hom(g) = map(pnt.g)$. (Of course the ordinary conjugation is a special case of this, with $map(pnt) = pnt.p$ and $hom(g) = g^p$.) 

 In the generalized case, the ``conjugated'' chain need not be a stabilizer chain for the image of $hom$, since the ``preimage'' of the stabilizer of $map(b)$ (where $b$ is a base point) need not fix $b$, but only fixes the preimage $map^{{-1}}( map(b) )$ setwise. Therefore the method can be applied only to one level and the next
stabilizer must be computed explicitly. But if $map$ is injective, we have $map(b).hom(g) = map(b)$ if and only if $b.g = b$, and if this holds, then $g = w(g_1, \ldots, g_n)$ is a word in the generators $g_1, \ldots, g_n$ of the stabilizer of{\nobreakspace}$b$ and  $hom(g) =^* w( hom(g_1), \ldots, hom(g_n) )$ is in the ``conjugated'' stabilizer. If, more generally, $hom$ is a right inverse to a homomorphism $\varphi$ (i.e., $\varphi(hom(g)) = g$ for all $g$), equality $*$ holds modulo the kernel of $\varphi$; in this case the ``conjugated'' chain can be made into a real stabilizer chain by extending each level with
the generators of the kernel and appending a proper stabilizer chain of the
kernel at the end. These special cases will occur in the algorithms for
permutation group homomorphisms (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Group Homomorphisms}). 

 To ``conjugate'' the points (i.e., \texttt{orbit}) and permutations (i.e., \texttt{labels}) of the Schreier tree, a loop is set up over the \texttt{orbit} list constructed during the orbit algorithm, and for each vertex $b$ with unique edge $a(l)b$ ending at $b$, the label $l$ is mapped with $hom$ and $b$ with $map$. We assume that the \texttt{orbit} list was built w.r.t.{\nobreakspace}a certain ordering $<$ of the labels, where $l' < l$ means that every point in the orbit was mapped with $l'$ before it was mapped with $l$. This shape of the \texttt{orbit} list is guaranteed if the Schreier tree is extended only by \texttt{AddGeneratorsExtendSchreierTree} (\ref{AddGeneratorsExtendSchreierTree}), and it is then also guaranteed for the ``conjugated'' Schreier tree. (The ordering of the labels cannot be read from the Schreier
tree, however.) 

 In the generalized case, it can happen that the edge $a(l)b$ bears a label $l$ whose image is ``old'', i.e., equal to the image of an earlier label $l' < l$. Because of the compatibility of the actions we then have $map(b) = map(a).hom(l)^{{-1}} = map(a).hom(l')^{{-1}} = map(a{{l'}}^{{-1}})$, so $map(b)$ is already equal to the image of the vertex $a{{l'}}^{{-1}}$. This vertex must have been encountered before $b = al^{{-1}}$ because $l' < l$. We conclude that the image of a label can be ``old'' only if the vertex at the end of the corresponding edge has an ``old'' image, too, but then it need not be ``conjugated'' at all. A similar remark applies to labels which map under $hom$ to the identity. }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{The General Backtrack Algorithm with Ordered Partitions}}\label{The General Backtrack Algorithm with Ordered Partitions}
\logpage{[ 87, 2, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X8174E19F87C3A8AB}{}
{
  Section \ref{Backtrack} describes the basic functions for a backtrack search. The purpose of this
section is to document how the general backtrack algorithm is implemented in \textsf{GAP} and which parts you have to modify if you want to write your own backtrack
routines. 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Internal representation of ordered partitions}}\label{Internal representation of ordered partitions}
\logpage{[ 87, 2, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X82E18F38824B5856}{}
{
  \index{ordered partitions!internal representation} \textsf{GAP} represents an ordered partition as a record with the following components. 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{points}}]  a list of all points contained in the partition, such that the points of each
cell from lie consecutively, 
\item[{\texttt{cellno}}]  a list whose \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}}th entry is the number of the cell which contains the point \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape i}}, 
\item[{\texttt{firsts}}]  a list such that \texttt{points[firsts[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape j}}]]} is the first point in \texttt{points} which is in cell \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape j}}, 
\item[{\texttt{lengths}}]  a list of the cell lengths. 
\end{description}
 Some of the information is redundant, e.g., the \texttt{lengths} could also be read off the \texttt{firsts} list, but since this need not be increasing, it would require some searching.
Similar for \texttt{cellno}, which could be replaced by a systematic search of \texttt{points}, keeping track of what cell is currently being traversed. With the above
components, the \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}th cell of a partition \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} is expressed as \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.points\texttt{\symbol{123}} [ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.firsts[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}] .. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.firsts[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}] + \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.lengths[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}] \texttt{\symbol{45}} 1 ] \texttt{\symbol{125}}}. The most important operations, however, to be performed upon \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}} are the splitting of a cell and the reuniting of the two parts. Following the
strategy of J.{\nobreakspace}Leon,  this is done as follows: 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{(1)}]  The points which make up the cell that is to be split are sorted so that the
ones that remain inside occupy positions \texttt{[ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.firsts[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}] .. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape last}} ]} in the list \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.points} (for a suitable value of \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape last}}). 
\item[{(2)}]  The points at positions \texttt{[ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape last}} + 1 .. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.firsts[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}] + \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.lengths[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}] \texttt{\symbol{45}} 1 ]} will form the additional cell. For this new cell requires additional entries
are added to the lists \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.firsts} (namely, \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape last}}+1}) and \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.lengths} (namely, \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.firsts[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}] + \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.lengths[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}] \texttt{\symbol{45}} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape last}} \texttt{\symbol{45}} 1}). 
\item[{(3)}]  The entries of the sublist \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.cellno\texttt{\symbol{123}} [ \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape last}}+1 .. \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.firsts[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}] + P.lengths[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}]\texttt{\symbol{45}}1 ] \texttt{\symbol{125}}} must be set to the number of the new cell. 
\item[{(4)}]  The entry \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.lengths[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}]} must be reduced to \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape last}} \texttt{\symbol{45}} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.firsts[\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape m}}] + 1}. 
\end{description}
 

 Then reuniting the two cells requires only the reversal of
steps{\nobreakspace}2 to{\nobreakspace}4 above. The list \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape P}}.points} need not be rearranged. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Functions for setting up an R\texttt{\symbol{45}}base}}\label{Functions for setting up an R-base}
\logpage{[ 87, 2, 2 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X785508067969766B}{}
{
  This subsection explains some \textsf{GAP} functions which are local to the library file \texttt{lib/stbcbckt.gi} which contains the code for backtracking in permutation groups. They are
mentioned here because you might find them helpful when you want to implement
your own backtracking function based on the partition concept. An important
argument to most of the functions is the R\texttt{\symbol{45}}base $R$, which you should regard as a black box. We will tell you how to set it up,
how to maintain it and where to pass it as argument, but it is not necessary
for you to know its internal representation. However, if you insist to learn
the whole story: Here are the record components from which an
R\texttt{\symbol{45}}base is made up: 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{domain}}]  the set $\Omega$ on which the group $G$ operates 
\item[{\texttt{base}}]  the sequence $(a_1, \ldots, a_r)$ of base points 
\item[{\texttt{partition}}]  an ordered partition, initially $\Pi_0$, this will be refined to $\Pi_1, \ldots, \Pi_r$ during the backtrack algorithm 
\item[{\texttt{where}}]  a list such that $a_i$ lies in cell number \texttt{where}$[i]$ of $\Pi_i$ 
\item[{\texttt{rfm}}]  a list whose $i$th entry is a list of refinements which take $\Sigma_i$ to $\Sigma_{{i+1}}$; the structure of a refinement is described below 
\item[{\texttt{chain}}]  a (copy of a) stabilizer chain for $G$ (not if $G$ is a symmetric group) 
\item[{\texttt{fix}}]  only if $G$ is a symmetric group: a list whose $i$ entry contains \texttt{Fixcells( }$\Pi_i$\texttt{ )} 
\item[{\texttt{level}}]  initially equal to \texttt{chain}, this will be changed to chains for the stabilizers $G_{{a_1 \ldots a_i}}$ for $i = 1, \ldots, r$ during the backtrack algorithm; if $G$ is a symmetric group, only the number of moved points is stored for each
stabilizer 
\item[{\texttt{lev}}]  a list whose $i$th entry remembers the \texttt{level} entry for $G_{{a_1 \ldots a_{{i-1}}}}$ 
\item[{\texttt{level2}, \texttt{lev2}}]  a similar construction for a second group (used in intersection calculations), \texttt{false} otherwise. This second group $H$ activated if the R\texttt{\symbol{45}}base is constructed as \texttt{EmptyRBase( }$[ G, H ], \Omega, \Pi_0$\texttt{ )} (if $G = H$, \textsf{GAP} sets \texttt{level2 = }\texttt{true} instead). 
\item[{\texttt{nextLevel}}]  this is described below 
\end{description}
 

 As our guiding example, we present code for the function \texttt{Centralizer} (\ref{Centralizer:for a magma and a submagma}) which calculates the centralizer of an element $g$ in the group $G$. (The real code is more general and has a few more subtleties.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=]
  Pi_0 := TrivialPartition( omega );
  R := EmptyRBase( G, omega, Pi_0 );
  R.nextLevel := function( Pi, rbase )
  local  fix, p, q, where;
  NextRBasePoint( Pi, rbase );
  fix := Fixcells( Pi );
  for p  in fix  do
    q := p ^ g;
    where := IsolatePoint( Pi, q );
    if where <> false  then
      Add( fix, q );
      ProcessFixpoint( R, q );
      AddRefinement( R, "Centralizer", [ Pi.cellno[ p ], q, where ] );
      if Pi.lengths[ where ] = 1  then
        p := FixpointCellNo( Pi, where );
        ProcessFixpoint( R, p );
        AddRefinement( R, "ProcessFixpoint", [ p, where ] );
      fi;
    fi;
  od;
  end;
  
  return PartitionBacktrack(
    G,
    c -> g ^ c = g,
    false,
    R,
    [ Pi_0, g ],
    L, R );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The list numbers below refer to the line numbers of the code above. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{1.}]  \texttt{omega} is the set on which \texttt{G} acts and \texttt{Pi{\textunderscore}0} is the first member of the decreasing sequence of partitions mentioned in \ref{Backtrack}. We set \texttt{Pi{\textunderscore}0 = omega}, which is constructed as \texttt{TrivialPartition( omega )}, but we could have started with a finer partition, e.g., into unions of \texttt{g}\texttt{\symbol{45}}cycles of the same length. 
\item[{2.}]  This statement sets up the R\texttt{\symbol{45}}base in the variable \texttt{R}. 
\item[{3.\texttt{\symbol{45}}21.}]  These lines define a function \texttt{R.nextLevel} which is called whenever an additional member in the sequence \texttt{Pi{\textunderscore}0 }$\geq \Pi_1 \geq \ldots$ of partitions is needed. If $\Pi_i$ does not yet contain enough base points in one\texttt{\symbol{45}}point cells, \textsf{GAP} will call \texttt{R.nextLevel( }$\Pi_i,$\texttt{ R )}, and this function will choose a new base point $a_{{i+1}}$, refine $\Pi_i$ to $\Pi_{{i+1}}$ (thereby \emph{changing} the first argument) and store all necessary information in{\nobreakspace}\texttt{R}. 
\item[{5.}]  This statement selects a new base point $a_{{i+1}}$, which is not yet in a one\texttt{\symbol{45}}point cell of $\Pi$ and still moved by the stabilizer $G_{{a_1 \ldots a_i}}$ of the earlier base points. If certain points of \texttt{omega} should be preferred as base point (e.g., because they belong to long cycles of \texttt{g}), a list of points starting with the most wanted ones, can be given as an
optional third argument to \texttt{NextRBasePoint} (actually, this is done in the real code for \texttt{Centralizer} (\ref{Centralizer:for a magma and a submagma})). 
\item[{6.}]  \texttt{Fixcells( }$\Pi$\texttt{ )} returns the list of points in one\texttt{\symbol{45}}point cells of $\Pi$ (ordered as the cells are ordered in $\Pi$). 
\item[{7.}]  For every point $p \in fix$, if we know the image $p$\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}$g$ under $c \in C_G(e)$, we also know $( p$\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}$g )$\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}$c = ( p$\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}$c )$\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}$g$. We therefore want to isolate these extra points in $\Pi$. 
\item[{9.}]  This statement puts point $q$ in a cell of its own, returning in \texttt{where} the number of the cell of $\Pi$ from which $q$ was taken. If $q$ was already the only point in its cell, \texttt{where = }\texttt{false} instead. 
\item[{12.}]  This command does the necessary bookkeeping for the extra base point $q$: It prescribes $q$ as next base in the stabilizer chain for $G$ (needed, e.g., in line{\nobreakspace}5) and returns \texttt{false} if $q$ was already fixed the stabilizer of the earlier base points (and \texttt{true} otherwise; this is not used here). Another call to \texttt{ProcessFixpoint} like this was implicitly made by the function \texttt{NextRBasePoint} to register the chosen base point. By contrast, the point $q$ was not chosen this way, so \texttt{ProcessFixpoint} must be called explicitly for{\nobreakspace}$q$. 
\item[{13.}]  This statement registers the function which will be used during the backtrack
search to perform the corresponding refinements on the ``image partition'' $\Sigma_i$ (to yield the refined $\Sigma_{{i+1}}$). After choosing an image $b_{{i+1}}$ for the base point $a_{{i+1}}$, \textsf{GAP} will compute $\Sigma_i \wedge (\{ b_{{i+1}} \}, \Omega \setminus \{ b_{{i+1}} \})$ and store this partition in $I$\texttt{.partition}, where $I$ is a black box similar to $R$, but corresponding to the current ``image partition'' (hence it is an ``R\texttt{\symbol{45}}image'' in analogy to the R\texttt{\symbol{45}}base). Then \textsf{GAP} will call the function \texttt{Refinements.Centralizer( R, I, Pi.cellno[ p ], p, where )}, with the then current values of $R$ and $I$, but where $\Pi$\texttt{.cellno}$[ p ]$, $p$, \texttt{where} still have the values they have at the time of this \texttt{AddRefinement} command. This function call will further refine $I$\texttt{.partition} to yield $\Sigma_{{i+1}}$ as it is programmed in the function \texttt{Refinements.Centralizer}, which is described below. (The global variable \texttt{Refinements} is a record which contains all refinement functions for all backtracking
procedures.) 
\item[{14.\texttt{\symbol{45}}19.}]  If the cell from which $q$ was taken out had only two points, we now have an additional
one\texttt{\symbol{45}}point cell. This condition is checked in
line{\nobreakspace}13 and if it is true, this extra fixpoint $p$ is taken (line{\nobreakspace}15), processed like $q$ before (line{\nobreakspace}16) and is then (line{\nobreakspace}17) passed to
another refinement function \texttt{Refinements.ProcessFixpoint( R, I, p, where )}, which is also described below. 
\item[{23.\texttt{\symbol{45}}29.}]  This command starts the backtrack search. Its result will be the centralizer
as a subgroup of $G$. Its arguments are 
\item[{24.}]  the group we want to run through, 
\item[{25.}]  the property we want to test, as a \textsf{GAP} function, 
\item[{26.}]  \texttt{false} if we are looking for a subgroup, \texttt{true} in the case of a representative search (when the result would be one
representative), 
\item[{27.}]  the R\texttt{\symbol{45}}base, 
\item[{28.}]  a list of data, to be stored in $I$\texttt{.data}, which has in position{\nobreakspace}1 the first member $\Sigma_0$ of the decreasing sequence of ``image partitions'' mentioned in \ref{Backtrack}. In the centralizer example, position{\nobreakspace}2 contains the element
that is to be centralized. In the case of a representative search, i.e., a
conjugacy test $g$\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}}$c$\texttt{ ?= }$h$, we would have $h$ instead of $g$ here, and possibly a $\Sigma_0$ different from $\Pi_0$ (e.g., a partition into unions of $h$\texttt{\symbol{45}}cycles of same length). 
\item[{29.}]  two subgroups $L \leq C_G(g)$ and $R \leq C_G(h)$ known in advance (we have $L = R$ in the centralizer case). 
\end{description}
 }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Refinement functions for the backtrack search}}\label{Refinement functions for the backtrack search}
\logpage{[ 87, 2, 3 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X82427DA47D458224}{}
{
  The last subsection showed how the refinement process leading from $\Pi_i$ to $\Pi_{{i+1}}$ is coded in the function $R$\texttt{.nextLevel}, this has to be executed once the base point $a_{{i+1}}$. The analogous refinement step from $\Sigma_i$ to $\Sigma_{{i+1}}$ must be performed for each choice of an image $b_{{i+1}}$ for $a_{{i+1}}$, and it will depend on the corresponding value of $\Sigma_i \wedge (\{b_{{i+1}}\}, \Omega \setminus \{b_{{i+1}}\})$. But before we can continue our centralizer example, we must, for the
interested reader, document the record components of the other black box $I$, as we did above for the R\texttt{\symbol{45}}base black box $R$. Most of the components change as \textsf{GAP} walks up and down the levels of the search tree. 
\begin{description}
\item[{\texttt{data}}]  this will be mentioned below 
\item[{\texttt{depth}}]  the level $i$ in the search tree of the current node $\Sigma_i$ 
\item[{\texttt{bimg}}]  a list of images of the points in $R$\texttt{.base} 
\item[{\texttt{partition}}]  the partition $\Sigma_i$ of the current node 
\item[{\texttt{level}}]  the stabilizer chain $R$\texttt{.lev}$[i]$ at the current level 
\item[{\texttt{perm}}]  a permutation mapping \texttt{Fixcells}$( \Pi_i )$ to \texttt{Fixcells}$( \Sigma_i )$; this implies mapping $(a_1, \ldots, a_i)$ to $(b_1, \ldots, b_i)$ 
\item[{\texttt{level2}, \texttt{perm2}}]  a similar construction for the second stabilizer chain, \texttt{false} otherwise (and \texttt{true} if $R$\texttt{.level2 = }\texttt{true}) 
\end{description}
 

 As declared in the above code for \texttt{Centralizer} (\ref{Centralizer:for a magma and a submagma}), the refinement is performed by the function \texttt{Refinement.Centralizer}$( R, I, \Pi$\texttt{.cellno}$[p], p, where )$. The functions in the record \texttt{Refinement} always take two additional arguments before the ones specified in the \texttt{AddRefinement} call (in line{\nobreakspace}13 above), namely the R\texttt{\symbol{45}}base $R$ and the current value $I$ of the ``R\texttt{\symbol{45}}image''. In our example, $p$ is a fixpoint of $\Pi = \Pi_i \wedge (\{ a_{{i+1}} \}, \Omega \setminus \{ a_{{i+1}} \})$ such that $where = \Pi$\texttt{.cellno}$[ p^g ]$. The \texttt{Refinement} functions must return \texttt{false} if the refinement is unsuccessful (e.g., because it leads to $\Sigma_{{i+1}}$ having different cell sizes from $\Pi_{{i+1}}$) and \texttt{true} otherwise. Our particular function looks like this. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=]
  Refinements.Centralizer := function( R, I, cellno, p, where )
  local  Sigma, q;
  Sigma := I.partition;
  q := FixpointCellNo( Sigma, cellno ) ^ I.data[ 2 ];
  return IsolatePoint( Sigma, q ) = where and ProcessFixpoint( I, p, q );
  end;
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The list numbers below refer to the line numbers of the code immediately
above. 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{3.}]  The current value of $\Sigma_i \wedge (\{ b_{{i+1}} \}, \Omega \setminus \{ b_{{i+1}} \})$ is always found in $I$\texttt{.partition}. 
\item[{4.}]  The image of the only point in cell number $cellno = \Pi_i$\texttt{.cellno}$[ p ]$ in $\Sigma$ under $g = I$\texttt{.data}$[ 2 ]$ is calculated. 
\item[{5.}]  The function returns \texttt{true} only if the image $q$ has the same cell number in $\Sigma$ as $p$ had in $\Pi$ (i.e., $where$) and if $q$ can be prescribed as an image for $p$ under the coset of the stabilizer $G_{{a_1 \ldots a_{{i+1}}}}.c$ where $c \in G$ is an (already constructed) element mapping the earlier base points $a_1, \ldots, a_{{i+1}}$ to the already chosen images $b_1, \ldots, b_{{i+1}}$. This latter condition is tested by \texttt{ProcessFixpoint}$( I, p, q )$ which, if successful, also does the necessary bookkeeping in $I$. In analogy to the remark about line{\nobreakspace}12 in the program above,
the chosen image $b_{{i+1}}$ for the base point $a_{{i+1}}$ has already been processed implicitly by the function \texttt{PartitionBacktrack}, and this processing includes the construction of an element $c \in G$ which maps \texttt{Fixcells}$( \Pi_i )$ to \texttt{Fixcells}$( \Sigma_i )$ and $a_{{i+1}}$ to $b_{{i+1}}$. By contrast, the extra fixpoints $p$ and $q$ in $\Pi_{{i+1}}$ and $\Sigma_{{i+1}}$ were not chosen automatically, so they require an explicit call of \texttt{ProcessFixpoint}, which replaces the element $c$ by some $c'.c$ (with $c' \in G_{{a_1 \ldots a_{{i+1}}}}$) which in addition maps $p$ to $q$, or returns \texttt{false} if this is impossible. 
\end{description}
 

 You should now be able to guess what \texttt{Refinements.ProcessFixpoint}$( R, I, p, where )$ does: it simply returns \texttt{ProcessFixpoint}$( I, p, $\texttt{FixpointCellNo}$( I$\texttt{.partition}$, where ) )$. 

 \emph{Summary.} 

 When you write your own backtrack functions using the partition technique, you
have to supply an R\texttt{\symbol{45}}base, including a component \texttt{nextLevel}, and the functions in the \texttt{Refinements} record which you need. Then you can start the backtrack by passing the
R\texttt{\symbol{45}}base and the additional data (for the \texttt{data} component of the ``R\texttt{\symbol{45}}image'') to \texttt{PartitionBacktrack}. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Functions for meeting ordered partitions}}\label{Functions for meeting ordered partitions}
\logpage{[ 87, 2, 4 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X86CCA2B384A74856}{}
{
  A kind of refinement that occurs in particular in the normalizer calculation
involves computing the meet of $\Pi$ (cf.{\nobreakspace}lines{\nobreakspace}6ff.{\nobreakspace}above) with an
arbitrary other partition $\Lambda$, not just with one point. To do this efficiently, \textsf{GAP} uses the following two functions. 

 \texttt{StratMeetPartition( }$R$, $\Pi$, $\Lambda$ \texttt{[}, $g$ \texttt{] )} 

 \texttt{MeetPartitionStrat( }$R$, $I$\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{123}}, }$\Lambda'$\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{125}}[, \texttt{\symbol{123}}}$g'$\texttt{\texttt{\symbol{125}}]}, $strat$ \texttt{)} 

 \index{meet strategy} Such a \texttt{StratMeetPartition} command would typically appear in the function call $R$\texttt{.nextLevel}$( \Pi, R )$ (during the refinement of $\Pi_i$ to $\Pi_{{i+1}}$). This command replaces $\Pi$ by $\Pi \wedge \Lambda$ (thereby \emph{changing} the second argument) and returns a ``meet strategy'' $strat$. This is (for us) a black box which serves two purposes: First, it allows \textsf{GAP} to calculate faster the corresponding meet $\Sigma \wedge \Lambda'$, which must then appear in a \texttt{Refinements} function (during the refinement of $\Sigma_i$ to $\Sigma_{{i+1}}$). It is faster to compute $\Sigma \wedge \Lambda'$ with the ``meet strategy'' of $\Pi \wedge \Lambda$ because if the refinement of $\Sigma$ is successful at all, the intersection of a cell from the left hand side of
the $\wedge$ sign with a cell from the right hand side must have the same size in both
cases (and $strat$ records these sizes, so that only non\texttt{\symbol{45}}empty intersections
must be calculated for $\Sigma \wedge \Lambda'$). Second, if there is a discrepancy between the behaviour prescribed by $strat$ and the behaviour observed when refining $\Sigma$, the refinement can immediately be abandoned. 

 On the other hand, if you only want to meet a partition $\Pi$ with $\Lambda$ for a one\texttt{\symbol{45}}time use, without recording a strategy, you can
simply type \texttt{StratMeetPartition}$( \Pi, \Lambda )$ as in the following example, which also demonstrates some other
partition\texttt{\symbol{45}}related commands. 

                
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@P := Partition( [[1,2],[3,4,5],[6]] );;  Cells( P );|
  [ [ 1, 2 ], [ 3, 4, 5 ], [ 6 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Q := Partition( OnTuplesTuples( last, (1,3,6) ) );;  Cells( Q );|
  [ [ 3, 2 ], [ 6, 4, 5 ], [ 1 ] ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StratMeetPartition( P, Q );|
  [  ]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@# The ``meet strategy'' was not recorded, ignore this result.|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@Cells( P );|
  [ [ 1 ], [ 5, 4 ], [ 6 ], [ 2 ], [ 3 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 

 You can even say \texttt{StratMeetPartition}$( \Pi, \Delta )$ where $\Delta$ is simply a subset of $\Omega$, it will then be interpreted as the partition $(\Delta, \Omega \setminus \Delta)$. 

 \textsf{GAP} makes use of the advantages of a ``meet strategy'' if the refinement function in \texttt{Refinements} contains a \texttt{MeetPartitionStrat} command where $strat$ is the ``meet strategy'' calculated by \texttt{StratMeetPartition} before. Such a command replaces $I$\texttt{.partition} by its meet with $\Lambda'$, again changing the argument $I$. The necessary reversal of these changes when backtracking from a node (and
prescribing the next possible image for a base point) is automatically done by
the function \texttt{PartitionBacktrack}. 

 In all cases, an additional argument $g$ means that the meet is to be taken not with $\Lambda$, but instead with $\Lambda.{{g^{{-1}}}}$, where operation on ordered partitions is meant cellwise (and setwise on each
cell). (Analogously for the primed arguments.) 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@P := Partition( [[1,2],[3,4,5],[6]] );;|
  !gapprompt@gap>| !gapinput@StratMeetPartition( P, P, (1,6,3) );;  Cells( P );|
  [ [ 1 ], [ 5, 4 ], [ 6 ], [ 2 ], [ 3 ] ]
\end{Verbatim}
 Note that $P.(1,3,6) = Q$. }

 }

  
\section{\textcolor{Chapter }{Stabilizer Chains for Automorphisms Acting on Enumerators}}\label{Stabilizer Chains for Automorphisms Acting on Enumerators}
\logpage{[ 87, 3, 0 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X7CA84E967B053C2C}{}
{
  This section describes a way of representing the automorphism group of a group
as permutation group, following \cite{Sims97}. The code however is not yet included in the \textsf{GAP} library. 

 In this section we present an example in which objects we already know
(namely, automorphisms of solvable groups) are equipped with the
permutation\texttt{\symbol{45}}like operations \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{94}}} and \texttt{/} for action on positive integers. To achieve this, we must define a new type of
objects which behave like permutations but are represented as automorphisms
acting on an enumerator. Our goal is to generalize the
Schreier\texttt{\symbol{45}}Sims algorithm for construction of a stabilizer
chain to groups of such new automorphisms. 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{An operation domain for automorphisms}}\label{An operation domain for automorphisms}
\logpage{[ 87, 3, 1 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X864007907EA923FB}{}
{
  The idea we describe here is due to C.{\nobreakspace}Sims. We consider a group $A$ of automorphisms of a group $G$, given by generators, and we would like to know its order. Of course we could
follow the strategy of the Schreier\texttt{\symbol{45}}Sims algorithm
(described in \ref{Stabilizer Chains}) for $A$ acting on $G$. This would involve a call of \texttt{StabChainStrong( EmptyStabChain( [], One( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape A}} ) ), GroupGenerators( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape A}} ) )} where \texttt{StabChainStrong} is a function as the one described in the pseudo\texttt{\symbol{45}}code
below: 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=]
  StabChainStrong := function( S, newgens )
    Extend the Schreier tree of S with newgens.
    for sch  in  Schreier generators  do
      if not sch in S.stabilizer  then
        StabChainStrong( S.stabilizer, [ sch ] );
      fi;
    od;
  end;
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The membership test $sch \notin S$\texttt{.stabilizer} can be performed because the stabilizer chain of $S$\texttt{.stabilizer} is already correct at that moment. We even know a base in advance, namely any
generating set for $G$. Fix such a generating set $(g_1, \ldots, g_d)$ and observe that this base is generally very short compared to the degree $|G|$ of the operation. The problem with the Schreier\texttt{\symbol{45}}Sims
algorithm, however, is then that the length of the first basic orbit $g_1.A$ would already have the magnitude of $|G|$, and the basic orbits at deeper levels would not be much shorter. For the
advantage of a short base we pay the high price of long basic orbits, since
the product of the (few) basic orbit lengths must equal $|A|$. Such long orbits make the Schreier\texttt{\symbol{45}}Sims algorithm
infeasible, so we have to look for a longer base with shorter basic orbits. 

 Assume that $G$ is solvable and choose a characteristic series with elementary abelian
factors. For the sake of simplicity we assume that $N < G$ is an elementary abelian characteristic subgroup with elementary abelian
factor group $G/N$. Since $N$ is characteristic, $A$ also acts as a group of automorphisms on the factor group $G/N$, but of course not necessarily faithfully. To retain a faithful action, we
let $A$ act on the disjoint union $G/N$ with $G$, and choose as base $(g_1 N, \ldots, g_d N, g_1, \ldots, g_d)$. Now the first $d$ basic orbits lie inside $G/N$ and can have length at most $[G:N]$. Since the base points $g_1 N, \ldots, g_d N$ form a generating set for $G/N$, their iterated stabilizer $A^{(d+1)}$ acts trivially on the factor group $G/N$, i.e., it leaves the cosets $g_i N$ invariant. Accordingly, the next $d$ basic orbits lie inside $g_i N$ (for $i = 1, \ldots, d$) and can have length at most{\nobreakspace}$|N|$. 

 Generalizing this method to a characteristic series $G = N_0 > N_1 > \ldots > N_l = \{ 1 \}$ of length $l > 2$, we can always find a base of length $l.d$ such that each basic orbit is contained in a coset of a characteristic factor,
i.e. in a set of the form $g_i N_{{j-1}} / N_j$ (where $g_i$ is one of the generators of $G$ and $1 \leq j \leq l$). In particular, the length of the basic orbits is bounded by the size of the
corresponding characteristic factors. To implement a
Schreier\texttt{\symbol{45}}Sims algorithm for such a base, we must be able to
let automorphisms act on cosets of characteristic factors $g_i N_{{j-1}} / N_j$, for varying $i$ and $j$. We would like to translate each such action into an action on $\{ 1, \ldots, [ N_{{j-1}}:N_j] \}$, because then we need not enumerate the operation domain, which is the
disjoint union of $G / N_1$, $G / N_2 \ldots G / N_l$, as a whole. Enumerating it as a whole would result in basic orbits like \texttt{orbit}$ \subseteq \{ 1001, \ldots, 1100 \}$ with a \texttt{transversal} list whose first 1000 entries would be unbound, but still require
4{\nobreakspace}bytes of memory each (see{\nobreakspace}\ref{Stabilizer Chain Records}). 

 Identifying each coset $g_i N_{{j-1}} / N_j$ into $\{ 1, \ldots, [N_{{j-1}}:N_j] \}$ of course means that we have to change the action of the automorphisms on
every level of the stabilizer chain. Such flexibility is not possible with
permutations because their effect on positive integers is ``hardwired'' into them, but we can install new operations for automorphisms. }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Enumerators for cosets of characteristic factors}}\label{Enumerators for cosets of characteristic factors}
\logpage{[ 87, 3, 2 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X84A94914876C03F0}{}
{
  So far we have not used the fact that the characteristic factors are
elementary abelian, but we will do so from here on. Our first task is to
implement an enumerator (see \texttt{AsList} (\ref{AsList}) and \ref{Enumerators}) for a coset of a characteristic factor in a solvable group $G$. We assume that such a coset $g N/M$ is given by 

 
\begin{description}
\item[{(1)}]  a pcgs for the group $G$ (see \texttt{Pcgs} (\ref{Pcgs})), let $n = $\texttt{Length( }$pcgs$\texttt{ )}; 
\item[{(2)}]  a range $range = [ start .. stop ]$ indicating that $N = \langle pcgs\{ [ start .. n ] \} \rangle$ and $M = \langle pcgs\{ [ stop + 1 .. n ] \} \rangle$, i.e., the cosets of $pcgs\{ range \}$ form a base for the vector space $N/M$; 
\item[{(3)}]  the representative $g$. 
\end{description}
 

 We first define a new representation for such enumerators and then construct
them by simply putting these three pieces of data into a record object. The
enumerator should behave as a list of group elements (representing cosets
modulo $M$), consequently, its family will be the family of the $pcgs$ itself. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareRepresentation( "IsCosetSolvableFactorEnumeratorRep", IsEnumerator,
      [ "pcgs", "range", "representative" ] );
  
  EnumeratorCosetSolvableFactor := function( pcgs, range, g )
      return Objectify( NewType( FamilyObj( pcgs ),
                     IsCosetSolvableFactorEnumeratorRep ),
                     rec( pcgs := pcgs,
                         range := range,
                representative := g ) );
  end;
\end{Verbatim}
 

 The definition of the operations \texttt{Length} (\ref{Length}), \texttt{\texttt{\symbol{92}}[\texttt{\symbol{92}}]} (\ref{bSlash[bSlash]}) and \texttt{Position} (\ref{Position}) is now straightforward. The code has sometimes been abbreviated and is meant ``cum grano salis'', e.g., the declaration of the local variables has been left out. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( Length, [ IsCosetSolvableFactorEnumeratorRep ],
      enum -> Product( RelativeOrdersPcgs( enum!.pcgs ){ enum!.range } ) );
  
  InstallMethod( \[\], [ IsCosetSolvableFactorEnumeratorRep,
          IsPosRat and IsInt ],
      function( enum, pos )
      elm := ();
      pos := pos - 1;
      for i  in Reversed( enum!.range )  do
          p := RelativeOrderOfPcElement( enum!.pcgs, i );
          elm := enum!.pcgs[ i ] ^ ( pos mod p ) * elm;
          pos := QuoInt( pos, p );
      od;
      return enum!.representative * elm;
  end );
  
  InstallMethod( Position, [ IsCosetSolvableFactorEnumeratorRep,
          IsObject, IsZeroCyc ],
      function( enum, elm, zero )
      exp := ExponentsOfPcElement( enum!.pcgs,
                     LeftQuotient( enum!.representative, elm ) );
      pos := 0;
      for i  in enum!.range  do
          pos := pos * RelativeOrderOfPcElement( pcgs, i ) + exp[ i ];
      od;
      return pos + 1;
  end );
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 
\subsection{\textcolor{Chapter }{Making automorphisms act on such enumerators}}\label{Making automorphisms act on such enumerators}
\logpage{[ 87, 3, 3 ]}
\hyperdef{L}{X79B146E9786FE153}{}
{
  Our next task is to make automorphisms of the solvable group $pcgs$\texttt{!.group} act on $[ 1 .. $\texttt{Length}$( enum ) ]$ for such an enumerator $enum$. We achieve this by introducing a new representation of automorphisms on
enumerators and by putting the enumerator together with the automorphism into
an object which behaves like a permutation. Turning an ordinary automorphism
into such a special automorphism requires then the construction of a new
object which has the new type. We provide an operation \texttt{PermOnEnumerator( \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape model}}, \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape aut}} )} which constructs such a new object having the same type as \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape model}}, but representing the automorphism \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape aut}}. So \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape aut}} can be either an ordinary automorphism or one which already has an enumerator
in its type, but perhaps different from the one we want (i.e. from the one in \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape model}}). 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|B,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  DeclareCategory( "IsPermOnEnumerator",
      IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse and IsPerm );
  
  DeclareRepresentation( "IsPermOnEnumeratorDefaultRep",
      IsPermOnEnumerator and IsAttributeStoringRep,
      [ "perm" ] );
  
  DeclareOperation( "PermOnEnumerator",
      [ IsEnumerator, IsObject ] );
  
  InstallMethod( PermOnEnumerator,
      [ IsEnumerator, IsObject ],
      function( enum, a )
      SetFilterObj( a, IsMultiplicativeElementWithInverse );
      a := Objectify( NewKind( PermutationsOnEnumeratorsFamily,
                   IsPermOnEnumeratorDefaultRep ),
                   rec( perm := a ) );
      SetEnumerator( a, enum );
      return a;
  end );
  
  InstallMethod( PermOnEnumerator,
      [ IsEnumerator, IsPermOnEnumeratorDefaultRep ],
      function( enum, a )
      a := Objectify( TypeObj( a ), rec( perm := a!.perm ) );
      SetEnumerator( a, enum );
      return a;
  end );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 Next we have to install new methods for the operations which calculate the
product of two automorphisms, because this product must again have the right
type. We also have to write a function which uses the enumerators to apply
such an automorphism to positive integers. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=@|A,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=Example]
  InstallMethod( \*, IsIdenticalObj,
      [ IsPermOnEnumeratorDefaultRep, IsPermOnEnumeratorDefaultRep ],
      function( a, b )
      perm := a!.perm * b!.perm;
      SetIsBijective( perm, true );
      return PermOnEnumerator( Enumerator( a ), perm );
  end );
  
  InstallMethod( \^,
      [ IsPosRat and IsInt, IsPermOnEnumeratorDefaultRep ],
      function( p, a )
      return PositionCanonical( Enumerator( a ),
                     Enumerator( a )[ p ] ^ a!.perm );
  end );
\end{Verbatim}
 

 How the corresponding methods for \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape p}} / \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape aut}}} and \texttt{\mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape aut}} \texttt{\symbol{94}} \mbox{\texttt{\mdseries\slshape n}}} look like is obvious. 

 Now we can formulate the recursive procedure \texttt{StabChainStrong} which extends the stabilizer chain by adding in new generators $newgens$. We content ourselves again with pseudo\texttt{\symbol{45}}code, emphasizing
only the lines which set the \texttt{EnumeratorDomainPermutation}. We assume that initially $S$ is a stabilizer chain for the trivial subgroup with a level for each pair $(range,g)$ characterizing an enumerator (as described above). We also assume that the \texttt{identity} element at each level already has the type corresponding to that level. 

 
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=!@|,fontsize=\small,frame=single,label=]
  StabChainStrong := function( S, newgens )
    for i  in [ 1 .. Length( newgens ) ]  do
      newgens[ i ] := AutomorphismOnEnumerator( S.identity, newgens[ i ] );
    od;
    Extend the Schreier tree of S with newgens.
    for sch  in  Schreier generators  do
      if not sch in S.stabilizer  then
        StabChainStrong( S.stabilizer, [ sch ] );
      fi;
    od;
  end;
\end{Verbatim}
 }

 }

 }
